docs.text: Data Analytics ¶ Learn to turn a business question into a recommendation you can defend, using Python, clear charts and real analytical habits. Welcome! I'm Aayush, your facilitator for this training programme. We will explore and explain data from five areas of a business: retail and e-commerce, finance, operations, marketing and HR. Along the way you will also practise on sports, technology, government and other datasets. This site is still being built Right now you will find the Foundations section, the course roadmap and the first Python lessons. More lessons and cases are on their way, and the Tableau section is in draft; its steps have not yet been tried end to end. The business cases are previews. They are not ready-to-run assignments yet. Course at a glance ¶ In-person, hands-on classes. Each session has a lecture followed by a lab. Bring your laptop. Spreadsheet basics are enough. No coding experience is assumed. Session 1 starts from the very beginning. Python in your browser. You run every lesson in Google Colab: nothing to install, and every result on these pages comes from the same code you run. Synthetic and public data only. Never private workplace data. Portfolio and briefing. You finish with a practical portfolio and an executive briefing grounded in checked evidence. Tableau after Python. A separate Tableau section shows how to build the same analyses as interactive dashboards. Where to start ¶ Work through these pages in order: Foundations : why data analytics and clear presentation matter, with real examples. Learning roadmap : what each stage of the course covers. Setup and practice : getting started with Google Colab and keeping notes. Analytical workflow : the seven steps we use in every analysis. Business cases : the five business problems you will solve. Session 1 lecture : why data analytics matters, then its lab on Python and Colab basics. How we will practise ¶ Every topic follows the same rhythm: Watch a short demonstration. Run the working code yourself, step by step. Change a few lines to answer a related question on your own. Debug a deliberate mistake. Recommend an action to a stakeholder. One habit to build from day one Before you trust a chart, check three things: what each row means, how the metric is defined, and what evidence supports the number. You will never be asked to write programs from scratch. Each lesson gives you working code to read, run and then modify. Instructor solutions are shared separately after each practice round. docs.text: Business case previews ¶ Five business problems, one for each department. Each case teaches a core skill and a common mistake to catch. Previews, not assignments yet These are proposed case themes. Individual files have not been released yet. We combine selected Tableau sample datasets with synthetic (made-up) teaching data. Meridian Commerce is a proposed fictional company used only for the synthetic cases. Real datasets keep their own context, units and dates. The five core cases ¶ Retail ¶ Decision: Which customer segment deserves a closer investigation? You will practise: what a row means, distinct orders, average order value, Sales and Profit, ratios, discounts, customers, trends and the limits of a returns list. Mistake to catch: treating order lines as orders. Finance ¶ Decision: Which departments need a spending review? You will practise: budget versus actual, time periods, reconciliation and whether a cost difference is favourable. Mistake to catch: repeating a monthly budget on every transaction row. Operations ¶ Decision: Where should delivery reliability improve? You will practise: promised dates, overdue open shipments, distributions, median and mean. Mistake to catch: dropping undelivered shipments from the service measure. Marketing ¶ Decision: Which campaigns need closer evaluation before budget moves? You will practise: weighted funnel rates, cost per conversion, return on ad spend and the limits of attribution. Mistake to catch: averaging percentages that have different denominators. HR ¶ Decision: How is the workforce changing, and which comparisons are fair? You will practise: historical headcount, turnover, cohorts, tenure and recruitment timelines. All employee records are synthetic. Mistake to catch: dividing past exits by the current headcount. What every case includes ¶ Stakeholder brief : the decision and why it matters Data dictionary : what each field means Metric definitions : exact formulas and scope Worked example : a guided walk-through Exercises : guided and independent practice Debugging task : find and fix a mistake Recommendation challenge : advise the stakeholder Validation checkpoints : confirm your numbers Each case also has an optional pandas connection. Instructor answers are supplied separately. Combining evidence across departments ¶ Before combining findings, explain any differences in grain, period and units. Within the synthetic company, marketing-attributed revenue is a view of the same retail revenue. Do not count it twice. Separate catalog datasets do not describe that fictional company. A good recommendation weighs trade-offs. It does not add incompatible KPIs together. Additional practice choices ¶ You will also be able to practise on topics beyond the five departments: Topic Example dataset Sports World Cup match results Technology Mobile operating-system usage (a data-quality exercise), start-up funding Government US construction spending, US home sales Other Science, education and entertainment datasets These are transfer exercises: the same process, with source-specific definitions and checks. They fit into your existing practice time or optional extensions. The five core cases remain the foundation of your portfolio. Every dataset is reviewed first A dataset appearing in a catalog does not tell us what each row means, which calculations it supports or whether it can be shared. Each lesson will give you the exact reviewed file and dictionary, or instructions to download it from the source, before you use it.

docs.text: DATA 300: Data Driven Decision Making ¶ DATA 300 for the China classroom: a pre-class online week, seven intensive teaching days on campus, and a post-class online week, covering descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics for better business decisions. Course materials All pre-class and teaching-day pages are ready. The course starts on Tuesday 10 November 2026 . What the course covers ¶ The course moves from describing what happened, to predicting what will happen, to deciding what to do. You will use Python in Jupyter , Tableau and Excel . Theme You will learn to Descriptive analytics Explore and clean data, summarise it, and find patterns Communicating results Build clear charts and dashboards that support a decision Text mining Turn customer reviews into measurable sentiment and themes Forecasting Project a time series forward and say how sure you are Predictive modelling Build and judge a linear regression model Simulation Model uncertainty in a spreadsheet and compare decisions Business intelligence Combine everything into a managerial recommendation, with ethics in mind Course learning outcomes ¶ By the end of the course you will be able to: CLO 1: Describe the principles of descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics to solve business data challenges. CLO 2: Design and use data visualisation and modelling tools to communicate user-centred analytics for strategic decisions. CLO 3: Apply computational problem-solving to perform data and text mining, discovering relationships in structured and unstructured data. CLO 4: Develop predictive models using time series forecasting, linear regression and spreadsheet simulation to project future outcomes. CLO 5: Evaluate the impact of business intelligence tools within a comprehensive case study to generate managerial reports that consider ethical and societal contexts. How the course is organised ¶ Module When Where Pre-class The week before 10 November Online: setup, Python basics, Activity 1 In-class Module 1 Tuesday 10 – Thursday 12 November On campus In-class Module 2 Monday 16 – Thursday 19 November On campus Post-class The week after 19 November Online: capstone and remaining assignments Graded work ¶ Module Item Weight Pre-class Activity 1: Self-assessment and readiness check (JupyterLab and Tableau) 4% Module 1 · Day 1 Lab 1: Data exploration 3% Module 1 · Day 2 Lab 2: Dashboard creation 3% Module 1 · Day 3 Assignment 1: Data visualisation and descriptive analytics report 6% Module 1 · Day 3 Lab 3: Text mining application 3% Module 1 · Day 3 Midterm exam 15% Module 1 · Day 3 Lab 4: Forecasting 3% Module 2 · Day 1 Assignment 2: Predictive data mining report 6% Module 2 · Day 1 Lab 5: Predictive linear regression modelling 2% Module 2 · Day 2 Lab 6: Advanced spreadsheet simulation 2% Module 2 · Day 3 Assignment 3: Spreadsheet simulation and decision model 6% Module 2 · Day 3 Lab 7: BI case study implementation 2% Module 2 · Day 4 Final exam 20% Post-class Assignment 4: Final comprehensive assignment (capstone) 25% Total 100% See the schedule for when each item happens, and setup for what to install before the course starts. docs.text: Pre-class: Activity 1 — Readiness check ¶ A short diagnostic that checks your tools and your starting point: run a small exploratory analysis of the Palmer Penguins data in Jupyter, build two quick views of the Sample – Superstore data in Tableau, answer five questions and submit one combined PDF. Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Activity 1 (Self-Assessment and Readiness Check), for local Jupyter without internet access. Graded Yes: 4% of the course grade Outcomes CLO 1, 2, 3 and 4 Tools JupyterLab (Anaconda) and Tableau Desktop You submit One PDF, YourLastName_DATA300_Week1_Readiness.pdf , on GAP (Moodle) Deadline Monday 9 November, 23:59 China Standard Time, before the course starts (see the schedule ) What you will do ¶ Part Tool You produce A. Jupyter This notebook Summary tables, two charts, answers to questions 1–3, and a PDF of the notebook B. Tableau Tableau Desktop Two worksheets, answers to questions 4–5, and a PDF of the workbook C. Submission A word processor and a PDF tool Your answers as a PDF, then all three PDFs combined into one file You do not need to write code from scratch: the code below works as given. Your job is to run it, read the output and answer the questions. Before you start ¶ Keep this notebook in the course folder, next to the data folder. Save your own copy under the name the course uses: File → Save Notebook As… and type YourLastName_Data300_Self_Check.ipynb (with your real last name). Work in that copy. Part A: Exploratory analysis in Jupyter ¶ The Palmer Penguins data records measurements of adult penguins of three species (Adelie, Chinstrap and Gentoo) on three islands near Palmer Station, Antarctica. One row is one penguin . A1. Import the libraries ¶ Anaconda already includes these, so there is nothing to install. Run the cell. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import pandas as pd import seaborn as sns print ( "Libraries loaded: pandas" , pd . __version__ , "| seaborn" , sns . __version__ ) Libraries loaded: pandas 2.2.3 | seaborn 0.13.2 A2. Load the data ¶ The file is in the data folder, so it loads without internet. df = pd . read_csv ( "data/penguins.csv" ) print ( "Rows and columns:" , df . shape ) Rows and columns: (344, 7) A3. First rows and summary statistics ¶ head() shows the first five penguins. describe() summarises every numeric column. Read the count row: a count lower than the number of rows means some values are missing (not recorded). print ( "--- First 5 rows of the dataset ---" ) display ( df . head ()) print ( " \n --- Summary statistics ---" ) display ( df . describe ()) --- First 5 rows of the dataset --- .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } species island bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g sex 0 Adelie Torgersen 39.1 18.7 181.0 3750.0 MALE 1 Adelie Torgersen 39.5 17.4 186.0 3800.0 FEMALE 2 Adelie Torgersen 40.3 18.0 195.0 3250.0 FEMALE 3 Adelie Torgersen NaN NaN NaN NaN NaN 4 Adelie Torgersen 36.7 19.3 193.0 3450.0 FEMALE --- Summary statistics --- .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } bill_length_mm bill_depth_mm flipper_length_mm body_mass_g count 342.000000 342.000000 342.000000 342.000000 mean 43.921930 17.151170 200.915205 4201.754386 std 5.459584 1.974793 14.061714 801.954536 min 32.100000 13.100000 172.000000 2700.000000 25% 39.225000 15.600000 190.000000 3550.000000 50% 44.450000 17.300000 197.000000 4050.000000 75% 48.500000 18.700000 213.000000 4750.000000 max 59.600000 21.500000 231.000000 6300.000000 A4. Chart 1: flipper length against body mass, by species ¶ A scatter plot with one dot per penguin. Colour shows the species. species_colours = { "Adelie" : "#2a78d6" , "Chinstrap" : "#eb6834" , "Gentoo" : "#1baf7a" } plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) sns . scatterplot ( data = df , x = "flipper_length_mm" , y = "body_mass_g" , hue = "species" , palette = species_colours , ) plt . title ( "Penguin body mass vs. flipper length by species" ) plt . xlabel ( "Flipper length (mm)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Body mass (g)" ) plt . show () A5. Chart 2: body mass by island and sex ¶ A box plot shows how values are spread within each group: the box covers the middle half of the penguins, the line inside it is the median, and the whiskers and dots show the rest. sex_colours = { "MALE" : "#2a78d6" , "FEMALE" : "#eb6834" } plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) sns . boxplot ( data = df , x = "island" , y = "body_mass_g" , hue = "sex" , palette = sex_colours , ) plt . title ( "Body mass distribution by island and sex" ) plt . xlabel ( "Island" ) plt . ylabel ( "Body mass (g)" ) plt . show () A6. Answer questions 1–3 ¶ Use the outputs above to answer. Double-click the cell below, replace each Your answer with one or two sentences, then press Shift + Enter . Copy the same answers into your answers document in Part C. # Topic Question 1 Descriptive statistics In the summary statistics table, what is the mean body mass ( body_mass_g ) of the penguins, in grams? 2 Relationship between two variables In Chart 1, what happens to body mass as flipper length increases? Describe the general pattern. 3 Comparing groups In Chart 1, which species (Adelie, Chinstrap or Gentoo) forms the cluster with the highest body mass? My answers to questions 1–3 1. Mean body mass: Your answer 2. Pattern between flipper length and body mass: Your answer 3. Species with the heaviest cluster: Your answer A7. Export this notebook to PDF ¶ Choose Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells . Check that both tables, both charts and your answers are visible. Choose File → Print (or Ctrl + P / Cmd + P). In the print window, set the destination to Save as PDF . Under More settings , tick Background graphics so the chart colours are kept. Save the file as Data300_Self_Check_Results_LastName.pdf , with your last name. This is your Jupyter results PDF . If the PDF looks wrong Charts missing usually means the notebook was not run before printing: run all cells and print again. Very wide tables may be cut at the page edge; that is acceptable here. Part B: Tableau readiness ¶ Tableau is a widely used business intelligence (BI) tool. These steps are done in Tableau Desktop , not in this notebook. Tick each step as you go. B1. Get and activate Tableau ¶ Your facilitator will tell you whether Tableau is already installed on the lab PCs. On your own laptop: request a free student licence from Tableau's academic programme for students, using your university email address. You may need to confirm you are a student (for example with your student ID). The licence key arrives by email. Download Tableau Desktop , install it, and activate it with the key. No licence yet? Verification can take a few days. Tell your facilitator: you can use Tableau Public Desktop for practice, or a lab PC, and complete Part B there. B2. Open the built-in data ¶ Start Tableau Desktop. On the start page, under Saved Data Sources , click Sample – Superstore . It contains made-up sales data for a retail company. A blank worksheet, Sheet 1 , opens. B3. Worksheet 1: Sales by Category ¶ In the Data pane on the left, drag Category onto the Rows shelf. Drag Sales onto the Columns shelf. Tableau draws a horizontal bar chart: one bar per category, its length the total sales. Optional: click Sort Descending on the toolbar so the longest bar is on top. Double-click the sheet tab and rename it Sales by Category . B4. Worksheet 2: Profit map ¶ Click the New Worksheet icon at the bottom of the window (the tab with a plus sign). In the Data pane, double-click State/Province (in older versions of Tableau it is called State ). Tableau draws a map with a dot for each state. Drag Profit onto Color on the Marks card. States are now coloured by total profit: blue for a profit, orange for a loss. Rename the sheet Profit Map . B5. Answer questions 4–5 ¶ Write these in your answers document (Part C). # Question 4 From worksheet 1 (Sales by Category), which product category has the highest total sales? 5 From worksheet 2 (Profit Map), name at least one US state that is making a loss (coloured orange). B6. Save the Tableau output as PDF ¶ In Tableau, choose File → Print to PDF . Select Entire Workbook so both worksheets are included. Click OK and save the file as Tableau_Results.pdf . Using Tableau Public? Tableau Public Desktop may not offer Print to PDF . Take a screenshot of each worksheet, paste both into a document, and save that as Tableau_Results.pdf . Part C: Submission ¶ C1. Your answers as a PDF ¶ In Word (or any word processor), write your answers to all five questions , numbered 1–5. Put your name and student ID at the top. Save or export it as Answers.pdf . C2. Combine the three PDFs ¶ Combine these three files, in this order, into one PDF: Answers.pdf Your Jupyter results PDF, Data300_Self_Check_Results_LastName.pdf Tableau_Results.pdf Use any PDF tool you have: for example Preview on macOS (drag the pages of one PDF into the sidebar of another), Adobe Acrobat, or a tool your facilitator recommends. Online PDF tools may be slow or blocked; ask your facilitator if you cannot combine the files. Name the combined file YourLastName_DATA300_Week1_Readiness.pdf . C3. Upload ¶ Upload the single combined PDF to the Activity 1 submission on GAP (Moodle) . Checklist before you upload ¶ The notebook was restarted and run all before printing; both tables and both charts appear in the Jupyter PDF. Questions 1–3 are answered in the notebook and in Answers.pdf . Both Tableau worksheets appear in Tableau_Results.pdf . Questions 4–5 are answered in Answers.pdf . The three PDFs are combined in the order Answers, Jupyter, Tableau. The file is named YourLastName_DATA300_Week1_Readiness.pdf and uploaded to GAP (Moodle). How it is marked ¶ The activity is marked with the course's activity rubric: four criteria for CLOs 1–4 (20 points each), plus professional formatting (10 points) and clear academic writing (10 points). In practice this means: complete, correct answers written in clear full sentences; all required outputs present and readable; and the files named and combined as asked. Stuck? Setup problems are exactly what this activity is meant to uncover. If a cell will not run or Tableau will not install, take a screenshot and contact your facilitator through the pre-class online support, before the deadline.

docs.text: Pre-class: Python and Jupyter basics ¶ Learn just enough Jupyter, Python and pandas to run every notebook in this course: cells and outputs, variables and lists, loading a table, selecting, filtering and grouping, the kind of data each column holds, what one row means, and a first chart. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . What you will be able to do ¶ Open, run, edit, restart and export a notebook in JupyterLab. Use Python variables, numbers, text, lists and dictionaries, and call a function. Load a CSV file into a pandas DataFrame and inspect it with head , shape , dtypes and describe . Select columns, filter rows, group and count. Name the level of measurement of a column and choose a sensible summary for it. Say what one row of a table represents (its grain ). Draw a first chart with matplotlib and seaborn. How the course uses code Every notebook gives you working code with explanations. You read it, run it, then change a few lines. You will not be asked to write programs from scratch. Part Topic 1 A tour of JupyterLab 2 Python essentials 3 DataFrames with pandas 4 Data types and levels of measurement 5 What does a row mean? 6 A first chart Part 1: A tour of JupyterLab ¶ JupyterLab is the program you use to open and run notebooks. You start it from Anaconda Navigator (click Launch under JupyterLab) or by typing jupyter lab in Anaconda Prompt (Windows) or Terminal (macOS). It opens in your web browser but runs on your computer , so it works without internet. Area What it is for File browser (left) Open the course folder and double-click a notebook ( .ipynb ) Notebook (centre) A list of cells , run from top to bottom Toolbar Run, stop, restart, add cells, choose the cell type Kernel (top right) The Python process that runs your code. "Idle" means ready Two kinds of cell ¶ Cell type Contains When you run it Markdown Formatted text, like this cell It shows as formatted text Code Python Python runs it and shows the result underneath Keys worth learning first ¶ Key Action Shift + Enter Run the cell and move to the next one Enter Start editing the selected cell Esc Stop editing (the cell stays selected) A / B (not editing) Add a cell above / below M / Y (not editing) Turn the cell into Markdown / Code D, D (not editing) Delete the cell Ctrl + S (Cmd + S on macOS) Save Run the next cell with Shift + Enter . The number in brackets on its left, [1] , records the order in which cells ran. price = 120 quantity = 3 price * quantity 360 Predict, then reveal: running cells out of order The next cell uses quantity . Suppose you went back up, changed quantity = 3 to quantity = 10 and ran only that cell, then ran the next one. Which value would the next cell use? Write your guess, then try it. print ( "Quantity Python remembers right now:" , quantity ) Quantity Python remembers right now: 3 Python remembers whatever ran last , not what is written higher up on the page. That is the most common source of confusion in notebooks. The cure: Restart and run all Choose Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells . Python forgets everything and runs the notebook from the top, in order. Do this before you export or submit any notebook, so the outputs match the code. Exporting to PDF ¶ Every graded lab is submitted as a PDF: Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells , and check every output and chart is visible. File → Print (or Ctrl + P / Cmd + P). In the print window, set the destination to Save as PDF . Under More settings , tick Background graphics so chart colours print. Save with the file name the lab asks for. Check your understanding You change a number in cell 3 of a notebook but forget to rerun cells 4 to 10, then export to PDF. What could be wrong in the PDF, and how do you prevent it? Part 2: Python essentials ¶ Variables and types ¶ A variable is a name for a value. = stores the value under the name. Every value has a type . store = "Shanghai West" # text: a string, inside quotes orders = 42 # whole number: an int average_basket = 18.75 # decimal number: a float is_open = True # True or False: a bool print ( type ( store ), type ( orders ), type ( average_basket ), type ( is_open )) print ( "Revenue estimate:" , orders * average_basket ) <class 'str'> <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'bool'> Revenue estimate: 787.5 print shows several things on one line. An f-string (a string starting with f ) puts values inside text, and :.2f rounds to two decimals: print ( f " { store } had { orders } orders, about { orders * average_basket : .2f } dollars in total." ) Shanghai West had 42 orders, about 787.50 dollars in total. Lists: several values in order ¶ A list holds values in square brackets. Python counts positions from 0 . monthly_sales = [ 120 , 95 , 140 , 180 ] print ( "First month:" , monthly_sales [ 0 ]) print ( "Last month: " , monthly_sales [ - 1 ]) print ( "Total:" , sum ( monthly_sales ), "| months:" , len ( monthly_sales )) First month: 120 Last month: 180 Total: 535 | months: 4 Dictionaries: values looked up by name ¶ A dictionary pairs keys with values , inside curly brackets. A table is like a dictionary of columns. prices = { "coffee" : 3.5 , "tea" : 2.8 , "cake" : 4.2 } print ( "Price of tea:" , prices [ "tea" ]) prices [ "juice" ] = 3.9 # add a new key print ( "Items on the menu:" , list ( prices . keys ())) Price of tea: 2.8 Items on the menu: ['coffee', 'tea', 'cake', 'juice'] Calling functions and methods ¶ A function does a job when you call it with brackets: len(monthly_sales) , round(3.14159, 2) , max(...) . A method is a function that belongs to a value and is called with a dot: store.upper() . print ( round ( 3.14159 , 2 )) print ( max ( monthly_sales )) print ( store . upper ()) print ( sorted ( prices , key = prices . get )) # menu items from cheapest to dearest 3.14 180 SHANGHAI WEST ['tea', 'coffee', 'juice', 'cake'] When something goes wrong ¶ Errors are normal. Read the last line of the red message first. Error message Usual cause Fix NameError: name 'x' is not defined A cell that creates x has not run yet Run the earlier cells, or restart and run all SyntaxError A missing bracket, quote or comma Look at the line the arrow points to KeyError: 'Tip' A column or key spelled differently (capital letters count) Check the exact name, for example with df.columns FileNotFoundError The notebook is not next to the data folder Open the notebook from inside the course folder Check your understanding What does monthly_sales[1] return, and why not 120 ? What type is prices["cake"] ? Part 3: DataFrames with pandas ¶ pandas is the Python library analysts use for tables. A table in pandas is a DataFrame : rows and named columns, like a spreadsheet you control with code. Our table records restaurant bills: one row per table served, with the bill, the tip, and details about the party. It comes from a well-known teaching dataset (Bryant and Smith, 1995) in which one waiter recorded every tip over a few months. Money is in US dollars . Load and look ¶ import pandas as pd tips = pd . read_csv ( "data/tips.csv" ) tips . head () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } total_bill tip sex smoker day time size 0 16.99 1.01 Female No Sun Dinner 2 1 10.34 1.66 Male No Sun Dinner 3 2 21.01 3.50 Male No Sun Dinner 3 3 23.68 3.31 Male No Sun Dinner 2 4 24.59 3.61 Female No Sun Dinner 4 head() shows the first five rows. Next, the size of the table and the type of each column: print ( "Rows and columns:" , tips . shape ) print () print ( tips . dtypes ) Rows and columns: (244, 7) total_bill float64 tip float64 sex object smoker object day object time object size int64 dtype: object float64 means decimal numbers, int64 whole numbers, and object text. describe() summarises every numeric column: how many values, the mean, standard deviation, minimum, quartiles and maximum. tips . describe () . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } total_bill tip size count 244.00 244.00 244.00 mean 19.79 3.00 2.57 std 8.90 1.38 0.95 min 3.07 1.00 1.00 25% 13.35 2.00 2.00 50% 17.80 2.90 2.00 75% 24.13 3.56 3.00 max 50.81 10.00 6.00 For text columns, describe(include="object") counts values and shows the most common one: tips . describe ( include = "object" ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } sex smoker day time count 244 244 244 244 unique 2 2 4 2 top Male No Sat Dinner freq 157 151 87 176 Select columns ¶ tips [ "tip" ] . head () # one column, as a Series 0 1.01 1 1.66 2 3.50 3 3.31 4 3.61 Name: tip, dtype: float64 tips [[ "day" , "time" , "total_bill" , "tip" ]] . head () # several columns: a list inside the brackets .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } day time total_bill tip 0 Sun Dinner 16.99 1.01 1 Sun Dinner 10.34 1.66 2 Sun Dinner 21.01 3.50 3 Sun Dinner 23.68 3.31 4 Sun Dinner 24.59 3.61 Filter rows ¶ A condition inside the brackets keeps only the rows where it is true. Combine conditions with & (and) or | (or), each in its own brackets. dinners = tips [ tips [ "time" ] == "Dinner" ] big_weekend = tips [( tips [ "day" ] . isin ([ "Sat" , "Sun" ])) & ( tips [ "size" ] >= 4 )] print ( "Dinner bills:" , len ( dinners )) print ( "Weekend parties of four or more:" , len ( big_weekend )) Dinner bills: 176 Weekend parties of four or more: 36 Add a column ¶ New columns are calculated from existing ones, row by row. The tip as a percentage of the bill: tips [ "tip_percent" ] = 100 * tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ] tips [[ "total_bill" , "tip" , "tip_percent" ]] . head () . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } total_bill tip tip_percent 0 17.0 1.0 5.9 1 10.3 1.7 16.1 2 21.0 3.5 16.7 3 23.7 3.3 14.0 4 24.6 3.6 14.7 Group and count ¶ value_counts() counts how often each value appears. groupby splits the table into groups and summarises each one. tips [ "day" ] . value_counts () day Sat 87 Sun 76 Thur 62 Fri 19 Name: count, dtype: int64 tips . groupby ( "day" ) . agg ( bills = ( "total_bill" , "count" ), average_bill = ( "total_bill" , "mean" ), average_tip_percent = ( "tip_percent" , "mean" ), ) . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } bills average_bill average_tip_percent day Fri 19 17.15 16.99 Sat 87 20.44 15.32 Sun 76 21.41 16.69 Thur 62 17.68 16.13 Each line inside agg reads: new column name = (column to use, summary to compute) . Predict, then reveal Which is larger: the number of lunch bills or dinner bills? Guess from what you know about restaurants, then change "day" to "time" in the value_counts() cell above and run it. Check your understanding Write the code that keeps only bills from smokers ( smoker is "Yes" ) and computes their average tip_percent . Which two ideas from this part do you combine? Part 4: Data types and levels of measurement ¶ The type pandas shows ( int64 , object ) is about how a value is stored . The level of measurement is about what it means , and it decides which calculations make sense. Level What the values do Examples What makes sense Nominal Name a group; no order Sex, smoker, product ID, postcode Count, share, mode Ordinal Name a group in order ; gaps not equal Shirt size, satisfaction 1–5 + median, "higher than" Interval Ordered with equal gaps ; zero is arbitrary Temperature in °C, calendar dates + differences, mean Ratio Equal gaps and a true zero Bill, tip, party size, age + ratios: "twice as much" Nominal and ordinal variables are categorical . Interval and ratio variables are numeric (quantitative). The columns of the tips table: Column Stored as Level A sensible summary total_bill , tip float64 Ratio Mean, median, total size int64 Ratio (a count of people) Mean, median, counts per size sex , smoker , time object Nominal Counts and shares day object Nominal, or ordinal if you care about the order of days Counts; sort in real day order Predict, then reveal: numbers that are not quantities pandas sorts text alphabetically . In what order will the days appear in the next cell? Is that the order you want in a report? print ( "Alphabetical:" , sorted ( tips [ "day" ] . unique ())) day_order = [ "Thur" , "Fri" , "Sat" , "Sun" ] tips [ "day" ] = pd . Categorical ( tips [ "day" ], categories = day_order , ordered = True ) print ( "Real order: " , list ( tips [ "day" ] . cat . categories )) tips [ "day" ] . value_counts ( sort = False ) Alphabetical: ['Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun', 'Thur'] Real order: ['Thur', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun'] day Thur 62 Fri 19 Sat 87 Sun 76 Name: count, dtype: int64 An ordered categorical keeps the real order, so tables and charts list Thursday to Sunday. Remember An ID or postcode stored as a number is still nominal : its average means nothing. Always ask what a column means before you average it. Check your understanding A survey stores satisfaction as 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 in an int64 column. Which level is it? Why is "the share scoring 4 or 5" safer to report than the mean? Part 5: What does a row mean? ¶ The grain of a table is what one row represents. Here: one table's bill on one visit, served by one waiter. Grain decides what counting means: len(tips) counts bills (tables served) , not customers. The number of customers is the sum of size , because each row is a party. print ( "Bills (rows): " , len ( tips )) print ( "Customers (sum of size): " , tips [ "size" ] . sum ()) Bills (rows): 244 Customers (sum of size): 627 The table has no ID column , so nothing guarantees that each row is a different bill. Predict, then reveal Do you expect any row to appear twice, with every value identical? If one does, is it a mistake? print ( "Fully duplicated rows:" , tips . duplicated () . sum ()) tips [ tips . duplicated ( keep = False )] Fully duplicated rows: 1 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } total_bill tip sex smoker day time size tip_percent 198 13.0 2.0 Female Yes Thur Lunch 2 15.384615 202 13.0 2.0 Female Yes Thur Lunch 2 15.384615 Two different parties could really have had the same bill, tip, day and size. Without an ID (a primary key ) we cannot tell a genuine repeat from a double entry, so we keep the row and note it. Deleting data needs evidence. Grain also limits what you can conclude All these bills come from one waiter in one restaurant . They describe that waiter's tips, not tipping in general. Check your understanding A sales table has one row per product within an order . Why does len(sales) not give the number of orders? Which pandas method would? Part 6: A first chart ¶ A chart needs a title , labelled axes with units , and ends with plt.show() . A histogram shows how one numeric column is spread out: how many bills fall into each range of values. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax . hist ( tips [ "total_bill" ], bins = 20 , color = "#2a78d6" , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . set_title ( "How big are the bills? Total bill per table served" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Total bill (US dollars)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of bills" ) plt . show () seaborn builds on matplotlib and makes charts of a DataFrame in one call. A scatter plot shows two numbers for each row; hue colours the dots by a category. import seaborn as sns fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4.5 )) sns . scatterplot ( data = tips , x = "total_bill" , y = "tip" , hue = "time" , palette = { "Lunch" : "#eb6834" , "Dinner" : "#2a78d6" }, ax = ax , ) ax . set_title ( "Larger bills tend to come with larger tips" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Total bill (US dollars)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Tip (US dollars)" ) plt . show () Check your understanding The histogram title asks a question. Write a better title that states the main message of the chart in one sentence. In the scatter plot, what does one dot represent? (Hint: the grain.) Quick reference ¶ You want to… Code Load a CSV file df = pd.read_csv("data/file.csv") See the first rows / size / types df.head() / df.shape / df.dtypes Summary statistics df.describe() One column / several columns df["tip"] / df[["day", "tip"]] Filter rows df[df["time"] == "Dinner"] New column df["tip_percent"] = 100 * df["tip"] / df["total_bill"] Count values df["day"].value_counts() Summary per group df.groupby("day").agg(average_tip=("tip", "mean")) Duplicated rows df.duplicated().sum() Histogram / scatter plot plt.hist(...) / sns.scatterplot(data=df, x=..., y=...) Summary ¶ A notebook is cells run in order. Restart and run all before you export; export with File → Print → Save as PDF . Python stores values in variables; lists hold values in order, dictionaries by name; functions are called with brackets. A DataFrame is a table: inspect it with head , shape , dtypes , describe ; select, filter, group and count with one line each. Storage type is not meaning. Name the level of measurement before choosing a summary. Know the grain before you count anything. Quiz ¶ What does Shift + Enter do, and what does the number in [ ] beside a cell tell you? What is the difference between tips["tip"] and tips[["tip"]] ? Which code gives the average tip for each value of time ? Is size in the tips table nominal, ordinal, interval or ratio? Why? What does one row of the tips table represent, and how do you count customers? Next: Activity 1 ¶ Activity 1, the readiness check , uses exactly these skills on a new table, the Palmer Penguins, and then checks that Tableau is ready. Complete it before the course starts.

Write your guess, then try it. print ( "Quantity Python remembers right now:" , quantity ) Quantity Python remembers right now: 3 Python remembers whatever ran last , not what is written higher up on the page. That is the most common source of confusion in notebooks. The cure: Restart and run all Choose Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells . Python forgets everything and runs the notebook from the top, in order. Do this before you export or submit any notebook, so the outputs match the code.

docs.text: A variable is a name for a value. = stores the value under the name. Every value has a type . store = "Shanghai West" # text: a string, inside quotes orders = 42 # whole number: an int average_basket = 18.75 # decimal number: a float is_open = True # True or False: a bool print ( type ( store ), type ( orders ), type ( average_basket ), type ( is_open )) print ( "Revenue estimate:" , orders * average_basket ) <class 'str'> <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'bool'> Revenue estimate: 787.5 print shows several things on one line. An f-string (a string starting with f ) puts values inside text, and :.2f rounds to two decimals: print ( f " { store } had { orders } orders, about { orders * average_basket : .2f } dollars in total." ) Shanghai West had 42 orders, about 787.50 dollars in total.

docs.text: A list holds values in square brackets. Python counts positions from 0 . monthly_sales = [ 120 , 95 , 140 , 180 ] print ( "First month:" , monthly_sales [ 0 ]) print ( "Last month: " , monthly_sales [ - 1 ]) print ( "Total:" , sum ( monthly_sales ), "| months:" , len ( monthly_sales )) First month: 120 Last month: 180 Total: 535 | months: 4

docs.text: A dictionary pairs keys with values , inside curly brackets. A table is like a dictionary of columns. prices = { "coffee" : 3.5 , "tea" : 2.8 , "cake" : 4.2 } print ( "Price of tea:" , prices [ "tea" ]) prices [ "juice" ] = 3.9 # add a new key print ( "Items on the menu:" , list ( prices . keys ())) Price of tea: 2.8 Items on the menu: ['coffee', 'tea', 'cake', 'juice']

docs.text: A function does a job when you call it with brackets: len(monthly_sales) , round(3.14159, 2) , max(...) . docs.text: pandas is the Python library analysts use for tables. A table in pandas is a DataFrame : rows and named columns, like a spreadsheet you control with code. Our table records restaurant bills: one row per table served, with the bill, the tip, and details about the party. It comes from a well-known teaching dataset (Bryant and Smith, 1995) in which one waiter recorded every tip over a few months. Money is in US dollars .

docs.text: The type pandas shows ( int64 , object ) is about how a value is stored . The level of measurement is about what it means , and it decides which calculations make sense. Level What the values do Examples What makes sense Nominal Name a group; no order Sex, smoker, product ID, postcode Count, share, mode Ordinal Name a group in order ; gaps not equal Shirt size, satisfaction 1–5 + median, "higher than" Interval Ordered with equal gaps ; zero is arbitrary Temperature in °C, calendar dates + differences, mean Ratio Equal gaps and a true zero Bill, tip, party size, age + ratios: "twice as much" Nominal and ordinal variables are categorical . Interval and ratio variables are numeric (quantitative). The columns of the tips table: Column Stored as Level A sensible summary total_bill , tip float64 Ratio Mean, median, total size int64 Ratio (a count of people) Mean, median, counts per size sex , smoker , time object Nominal Counts and shares day object Nominal, or ordinal if you care about the order of days Counts; sort in real day order Predict, then reveal: numbers that are not quantities pandas sorts text alphabetically . In what order will the days appear in the next cell? Is that the order you want in a report? print ( "Alphabetical:" , sorted ( tips [ "day" ] . unique ())) day_order = [ "Thur" , "Fri" , "Sat" , "Sun" ] tips [ "day" ] = pd . Categorical ( tips [ "day" ], categories = day_order , ordered = True ) print ( "Real order: " , list ( tips [ "day" ] . cat . categories )) tips [ "day" ] . value_counts ( sort = False ) Alphabetical: ['Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun', 'Thur'] Real order: ['Thur', 'Fri', 'Sat', 'Sun'] day Thur 62 Fri 19 Sat 87 Sun 76 Name: count, dtype: int64 An ordered categorical keeps the real order, so tables and charts list Thursday to Sunday. Remember An ID or postcode stored as a number is still nominal : its average means nothing. Always ask what a column means before you average it. Check your understanding A survey stores satisfaction as 1, 2, 3, 4 or 5 in an int64 column. Which level is it? Why is "the share scoring 4 or 5" safer to report than the mean?
docs.title: Part 4: Data types and levels of measurement

docs.text: The grain of a table is what one row represents. Here: one table's bill on one visit, served by one waiter. Grain decides what counting means: len(tips) counts bills (tables served) , not customers. The number of customers is the sum of size , because each row is a party. print ( "Bills (rows): " , len ( tips )) print ( "Customers (sum of size): " , tips [ "size" ] . sum ()) Bills (rows): 244 Customers (sum of size): 627 The table has no ID column , so nothing guarantees that each row is a different bill. Predict, then reveal Do you expect any row to appear twice, with every value identical? If one does, is it a mistake? print ( "Fully duplicated rows:" , tips . duplicated () . sum ()) tips [ tips . duplicated ( keep = False )] Fully duplicated rows: 1 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } total_bill tip sex smoker day time size tip_percent 198 13.0 2.0 Female Yes Thur Lunch 2 15.384615 202 13.0 2.0 Female Yes Thur Lunch 2 15.384615 Two different parties could really have had the same bill, tip, day and size. Without an ID (a primary key ) we cannot tell a genuine repeat from a double entry, so we keep the row and note it. Deleting data needs evidence. Grain also limits what you can conclude All these bills come from one waiter in one restaurant . They describe that waiter's tips, not tipping in general. Check your understanding A sales table has one row per product within an order . Why does len(sales) not give the number of orders? Which pandas method would?
docs.title: Part 5: What does a row mean?

docs.text: A chart needs a title , labelled axes with units , and ends with plt.show() . A histogram shows how one numeric column is spread out: how many bills fall into each range of values. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) ax . hist ( tips [ "total_bill" ], bins = 20 , color = "#2a78d6" , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . set_title ( "How big are the bills? Total bill per table served" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Total bill (US dollars)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of bills" ) plt . show () seaborn builds on matplotlib and makes charts of a DataFrame in one call. A scatter plot shows two numbers for each row; hue colours the dots by a category. import seaborn as sns fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4.5 )) sns . scatterplot ( data = tips , x = "total_bill" , y = "tip" , hue = "time" , palette = { "Lunch" : "#eb6834" , "Dinner" : "#2a78d6" }, ax = ax , ) ax . set_title ( "Larger bills tend to come with larger tips" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Total bill (US dollars)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Tip (US dollars)" ) plt . show () Check your understanding The histogram title asks a question. Write a better title that states the main message of the chart in one sentence. In the scatter plot, what does one dot represent? (Hint: the grain.)

docs.text: A notebook is cells run in order. Restart and run all before you export; export with File → Print → Save as PDF . docs.text: Day 1 lab: Applied Lab 1 — Data exploration ¶ Explore more than 50,000 diamonds for a jewellery retailer: inspect the table and its data quality, compare average prices across cut and colour grades with a pivot table, and read a correlation heatmap, a violin plot and a hexbin plot. Then explain in your own words what drives diamond prices, and why one summary table seems to contradict common sense. Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Applied Lab 1 (Data Exploration), for local Jupyter without internet access. Graded Yes: 3% of the course grade Outcomes CLO 1, 2 and 3 Tool JupyterLab (Anaconda) You submit One PDF, YourLastName_DATA300_AppliedLab1.pdf , in the Applied Lab 1 drop-box on GAP (Moodle) Deadline End of today, 23:59 China Standard Time, unless your facilitator says otherwise (see the schedule ) The business scenario ¶ You are a data analyst at LuxeGems , an international jewellery retailer. The purchasing team wants to buy diamonds at competitive prices without giving up margin. They have sent you a table of more than 50,000 diamonds with their physical attributes and retail prices in US dollars : Column Meaning carat Weight (1 carat = 0.2 grams) cut Quality of the cut, from Fair (lowest) through Good, Very Good and Premium to Ideal (highest) color Colour grade, from D (colourless, best) to J (slightly yellow, lowest) clarity How free the stone is of flaws, from I1 (lowest) to IF (flawless) depth , table Proportions of the cut stone, in per cent x , y , z Length, width and depth in millimetres price Retail price (US dollars) Your job is to explore the raw data, judge its quality, see how the attributes relate to price, and explain one result that looks wrong at first sight. This is descriptive and diagnostic analytics: what is in the data, and why does it look the way it does? Before you start ¶ Keep this notebook in the course folder, next to the data folder. Save your own copy: File → Save Notebook As… and type YourLastName_Data300_AppliedLab1.ipynb (with your real last name). Work in that copy. The code below works as given. Run each cell in order with Shift + Enter , read the output, and answer the questions in Part 5. You may add cells of your own to check an answer. Part 1: Load the libraries and the data ¶ Everything needed is part of Anaconda, so nothing is installed. The data loads from the data folder, without internet. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd import seaborn as sns diamonds = pd . read_csv ( "data/diamonds.csv" ) cut_order = [ "Fair" , "Good" , "Very Good" , "Premium" , "Ideal" ] # lowest to highest quality color_order = [ "D" , "E" , "F" , "G" , "H" , "I" , "J" ] # best to lowest grade print ( "Rows and columns:" , diamonds . shape ) diamonds . head () Rows and columns: (53940, 10) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } carat cut color clarity depth table price x y z 0 0.23 Ideal E SI2 61.5 55.0 326 3.95 3.98 2.43 1 0.21 Premium E SI1 59.8 61.0 326 3.89 3.84 2.31 2 0.23 Good E VS1 56.9 65.0 327 4.05 4.07 2.31 3 0.29 Premium I VS2 62.4 58.0 334 4.20 4.23 2.63 4 0.31 Good J SI2 63.3 58.0 335 4.34 4.35 2.75 Part 2: Structural inspection and data quality ¶ Before any analysis, check the size of the table, the type of each column, whether values are missing, and the range of each number. print ( "--- Dataset information ---" ) diamonds . info () print ( " \n --- Missing values per column ---" ) print ( diamonds . isnull () . sum ()) print ( " \n --- Descriptive statistics (numeric columns) ---" ) diamonds . describe () . round ( 2 ) --- Dataset information --- <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> RangeIndex: 53940 entries, 0 to 53939 Data columns (total 10 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 carat 53940 non-null float64 1 cut 53940 non-null object 2 color 53940 non-null object 3 clarity 53940 non-null object 4 depth 53940 non-null float64 5 table 53940 non-null float64 6 price 53940 non-null int64 7 x 53940 non-null float64 8 y 53940 non-null float64 9 z 53940 non-null float64 dtypes: float64(6), int64(1), object(3) memory usage: 4.1+ MB --- Missing values per column --- carat 0 cut 0 color 0 clarity 0 depth 0 table 0 price 0 x 0 y 0 z 0 dtype: int64 --- Descriptive statistics (numeric columns) --- .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; In the statistics table, also read the min row for x , y and z . Is every value physically possible for a real stone? (You are not asked to fix anything; noting it is good analytical practice.) Part 3: Pivot table — average price by cut and colour ¶ A pivot table compares one measure across two categories. Here: the average price with cut in the rows and colour in the columns. .reindex(cut_order) lists the cuts from Fair to Ideal instead of alphabetically. price_pivot = pd . pivot_table ( data = diamonds , values = "price" , index = "cut" , columns = "color" , aggfunc = "mean" , ) . reindex ( cut_order ) print ( "--- Average diamond price (US dollars) by cut quality and colour grade ---" ) price_pivot . round ( 2 ) --- Average diamond price (US dollars) by cut quality and colour grade --- .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } color D E F G H I J cut Fair 4291.06 3682.31 3827.00 4239.25 5135.68 4685.45 4975.66 Good 3405.38 3423.64 3495.75 4123.48 4276.25 5078.53 4574.17 Very Good 3470.47 3214.65 3778.82 3872.75 4535.39 5255.88 5103.51 Premium 3631.29 3538.91 4324.89 4500.74 5216.71 5946.18 6294.59 Ideal 2629.09 2597.55 3374.94 3720.71 3889.33 4451.97 4918.19 Use this table for questions 3 and 4. Read the column for colour E from the Fair row to the Ideal row. Is that the order you would expect? Part 4: Visualising more than 50,000 diamonds ¶ A plain scatter plot of 50,000 points becomes an unreadable blob. Three charts handle this better: Chart Shows Correlation heatmap The straight-line relationship between every pair of numeric columns, from −1 to +1 Violin plot The full shape of the price distribution within each cut Hexbin plot Where the diamonds are concentrated when carat is plotted against price 4.1 Correlation heatmap ¶ sns . set_theme ( style = "whitegrid" ) numeric_cols = diamonds . select_dtypes ( include = [ np . number ]) corr_matrix = numeric_cols . corr () plt . figure ( figsize = ( 9 , 7 )) sns . heatmap ( corr_matrix , annot = True , fmt = ".2f" , cmap = "coolwarm" , linewidths = 0.5 , vmin =- 1 , vmax = 1 , cbar_kws = { "label" : "Correlation coefficient r" }, ) plt . title ( "Correlation heatmap of diamond attributes" , fontsize = 14 ) plt . show () 4.2 Violin plot: price by cut quality ¶ plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 5.5 )) sns . violinplot ( data = diamonds , x = "cut" , y = "price" , order = cut_order , color = "#2a78d6" , cut = 0 ) plt . title ( "Price distribution by cut quality" , fontsize = 14 ) plt . xlabel ( "Cut quality (lowest to highest)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Price (US dollars)" ) plt . show () 4.3 Hexbin density plot: carat against price ¶ plt . figure ( figsize = ( 9 , 6 )) plt . hexbin ( diamonds [ "carat" ], diamonds [ "price" ], gridsize = 40 , cmap = "Blues" , mincnt = 1 ) plt . colorbar ( label = "Number of diamonds in the hexagon" ) plt . title ( "Density of diamonds by carat weight and price" , fontsize = 14 ) plt . xlabel ( "Carat weight (carats)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Price (US dollars)" ) plt . show () Part 5: Questions ¶ Answer all six questions in complete sentences in the answer cell below. Base every answer on the outputs in this notebook, and quote the numbers you use. Section A: Data quality and structure ¶ # Question 1 How many rows (diamonds) and columns does the dataset have, according to Part 2? 2 Does any column have missing (null) values that would need cleaning before further analysis? Say how you can tell. Section B: Pivot table and diagnosis ¶ # Question 3 In the pivot table (Part 3), look at colour grade E . Which has the higher average price: Fair cut or Ideal cut? Give both values. 4 A better cut should be worth more, so why can Fair-cut diamonds show a higher average price than Ideal-cut diamonds in this table? Think about an attribute the table ignores, and name the general idea this illustrates. You may add a cell to check your explanation. Section C: Correlation and charts ¶ # Question 5 (a) In the heatmap (Part 4.1), which numeric attribute has the strongest positive correlation with price ? State its correlation coefficient r . (b) In the violin plot (Part 4.2), are prices roughly symmetric (a bell shape) or strongly right-skewed? Where are most prices concentrated? 6 In the hexbin plot (Part 4.3), what does the darkest cluster tell LuxeGems about the diamonds in this data? Give the approximate carat range and price range where the diamonds are most concentrated. Writing tips Lead with the answer, then the evidence: "Most diamonds are small and cheap: the darkest hexagons lie between … and … carats and … and … dollars." Name the chart or table you used. Keep units (US dollars, carats). My answers Name: Your name · Student ID: Your ID 1. Rows and columns: Your answer 2. Missing values: Your answer 3. Fair versus Ideal at colour E: Your answer 4. Why Fair can look more expensive: Your answer 5. (a) Strongest correlate of price and its r: Your answer 5. (b) Shape of the price distribution: Your answer 6. Densest region in the hexbin plot: Your answer Going further (not graded) ¶ If you have time, test your answer to question 4. The cell below compares cuts at colour E among diamonds of almost the same weight : three narrow windows around popular sizes. Holding weight nearly constant removes most of its effect, so any remaining gap is closer to the effect of the cut itself. The cell shows the average price in each window and, underneath, how many diamonds each average is based on. e_grade = diamonds [ diamonds [ "color" ] == "E" ] windows = { "0.30-0.34 ct" : ( 0.30 , 0.34 ), "0.70-0.74 ct" : ( 0.70 , 0.74 ), "1.00-1.04 ct" : ( 1.00 , 1.04 )} average_price = {} diamond_count = {} for label , ( low , high ) in windows . items (): same_size = e_grade [ e_grade [ "carat" ] . between ( low , high )] average_price [ label ] = same_size . groupby ( "cut" )[ "price" ] . mean () diamond_count [ label ] = same_size . groupby ( "cut" )[ "price" ] . count () print ( "Colour E: average price (US dollars) by cut, for diamonds of almost the same weight" ) print ( pd . DataFrame ( average_price ) . reindex ( cut_order ) . round ( 0 )) print () print ( "Number of diamonds behind each average" ) print ( pd . DataFrame ( diamond_count ) . reindex ( cut_order )) print () print ( "Colour E, all weights: average carat by cut" ) print ( e_grade . groupby ( "cut" )[ "carat" ] . mean () . reindex ( cut_order ) . round ( 2 )) Colour E: average price (US dollars) by cut, for diamonds of almost the same weight 0.30-0.34 ct 0.70-0.74 ct 1.00-1.04 ct cut Fair 722.0 2318.0 4475.0 Good 621.0 2572.0 5448.0 Very Good 682.0 2812.0 6096.0 Premium 781.0 2709.0 5906.0 Ideal 812.0 3023.0 6265.0 Number of diamonds behind each average 0.30-0.34 ct 0.70-0.74 ct 1.00-1.04 ct cut Fair 10 27 61 Good 96 110 178 Very Good 236 288 292 Premium 364 221 257 Ideal 997 350 217 Colour E, all weights: average carat by cut cut Fair 0.86 Good 0.75 Very Good 0.68 Premium 0.72 Ideal 0.58 Name: carat, dtype: float64 Compare Fair and Ideal within each weight window with the overall pivot table in Part 3, and look at the average carat of each cut. Does the ranking change once weight is held nearly constant? Which averages rest on so few diamonds that you would not trust them on their own? A natural next step, which you will meet on Day 4, is a regression model that adjusts for carat, colour and clarity at the same time. Part 6: Export and submit ¶ 1. Export to PDF ¶ Choose Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells . Check that every table and all three charts appear, and that your answers are in the answer cell. Choose File → Print (or Ctrl + P / Cmd + P). Set the destination to Save as PDF . Under More settings , tick Background graphics so the heatmap, violin and hexbin colours are kept. Save the file as YourLastName_DATA300_AppliedLab1.pdf , with your real last name. 2. Upload ¶ Log in to GAP (Moodle) , open the DATA 300: Applied Lab 1 drop-box, upload the PDF and click Submit . Checklist before you upload ¶ The notebook was restarted and run all ; the dataset information, missing-value counts, statistics table and pivot table all appear. The heatmap, violin plot and hexbin plot appear, in colour. All six questions are answered in complete sentences, with the numbers you used. Your name and student ID are in the answer cell. The file is named YourLastName_DATA300_AppliedLab1.pdf and uploaded to the Applied Lab 1 drop-box on GAP (Moodle). How it is marked ¶ The lab uses the course's lab rubric: CLO 1 (describing descriptive analytics for a business problem, 25 points), CLO 2 (using visualisation tools to communicate findings, 25 points), CLO 3 (computational problem-solving to find relationships in the data, 30 points), professional formatting (10 points) and clear academic writing (10 points). In practice: all outputs present, correct answers supported by evidence from the outputs, a clear explanation of question 4, and a correctly named PDF. Stuck? docs.text: Day 1 lecture: Data-driven decisions ¶ Organisations make better decisions when they combine data, analysis and judgement. This lecture maps the course, explains the four kinds of analytics, sets out how an analysis is organised, and shows live why summary numbers alone can mislead. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . What you will be able to do ¶ Find your way around the course: its outcomes, graded work and schedule. Explain why data-driven decisions tend to beat decisions made on instinct alone, and where judgement still matters. Tell descriptive , diagnostic , predictive and prescriptive analytics apart, with a business example of each. Follow the path from question to data , analysis , validation and decision , and turn a vague request into an answerable question. Show with code why summary statistics are not enough, using Anscombe's quartet and the Datasaurus Dozen. Name the most common ways numbers mislead. Reading: Gordon (2023), Business analytics , Chapter 1 (how data and analytics can improve human decisions) and Chapter 4 (analysis fundamentals). How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first: being wrong is how you learn what to check. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words, alone or with the person next to you. Part Topic 1 The course map 2 Why data-driven decisions? 3 Four kinds of analytics 4 Analysis fundamentals: from question to decision 5 Statistics are not enough: Anscombe's quartet 6 The Datasaurus Dozen 7 A preview of how numbers mislead Part 1: The course map ¶ DATA 300 Data Driven Decision Making moves from describing what happened, to predicting what will happen, to deciding what to do. You will work in Python with Jupyter , Tableau and Excel . Course learning outcomes (CLOs) ¶ Every graded item is tied to one or more of these outcomes. CLO By the end of the course you can… 1 Describe the principles of descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics to solve business data challenges 2 Design and use data visualisation and modelling tools to communicate user-centred analytics for strategic decisions 3 Apply computational problem-solving to data and text mining, finding relationships in structured and unstructured data 4 Build predictive models with time-series forecasting, linear regression and spreadsheet simulation 5 Evaluate business intelligence tools in a full case study and write managerial reports that consider ethical and societal context How the course is organised ¶ Module When Where Pre-class The week before 10 November Online: setup, Python basics, Activity 1 In-class Module 1 Tuesday 10 – Thursday 12 November On campus (today is Module 1, Day 1) In-class Module 2 Monday 16 – Thursday 19 November On campus Post-class The week after 19 November Online: capstone and remaining assignments Graded work ¶ Module Item Weight Pre-class Activity 1: Self-assessment and readiness check (JupyterLab and Tableau) 4% Module 1 · Day 1 Lab 1: Data exploration ( today ) 3% Module 1 · Day 2 Lab 2: Dashboard creation 3% Module 1 · Day 3 Assignment 1: Data visualisation and descriptive analytics report 6% Module 1 · Day 3 Lab 3: Text mining application 3% Module 1 · Day 3 Midterm exam 15% Module 1 · Day 3 Lab 4: Forecasting 3% Module 2 · Day 1 Assignment 2: Predictive data mining report 6% Module 2 · Day 1 Lab 5: Predictive linear regression modelling 2% Module 2 · Day 2 Lab 6: Advanced spreadsheet simulation 2% Module 2 · Day 3 Assignment 3: Spreadsheet simulation and decision model 6% Module 2 · Day 3 Lab 7: BI case study implementation 2% Module 2 · Day 4 Final exam 20% Post-class Assignment 4: Final comprehensive assignment (capstone) 25% Total 100% All work is submitted as a PDF on GAP (Moodle) . Part 2: Why data-driven decisions? ¶ Every organisation decides things all the time: what to stock, whom to hire, which customers to target, how much to charge. Many of those decisions are still made on gut feeling , habit or the opinion of the most senior person in the room. The idea in one line ¶ The course textbook's subtitle sums it up: good decisions combine data, analysis and judgement . Data on its own decides nothing. Analysis turns data into evidence. Judgement, from people who know the business, decides what the evidence means and what to do. Why instinct alone is risky ¶ Human judgement is valuable, but it has predictable weak spots. Psychologists have named many of them: Weak spot What happens Example at work Confirmation bias We notice evidence that agrees with us and ignore the rest A manager who believes a promotion worked only looks at the stores where sales rose Anchoring The first number we hear pulls our estimate towards it Next year's budget is "last year plus 5%" whatever has changed Availability Vivid or recent events feel more common than they are One angry customer email leads to a policy change for everyone Overconfidence We are more certain than our track record justifies Sales forecasts that are always too optimistic Data and analysis do not remove these biases, but they give everyone something to check against . A decision based on evidence can also be explained, repeated and improved, because you can see what it rested on. Where judgement still matters ¶ Analytics supports decisions; it does not make them. People still have to: choose the question worth answering; judge whether the data is trustworthy and relevant; weigh things the data does not capture: ethics, strategy, staff morale, reputation; take responsibility for the decision. Stories where data changed the outcome ¶ Story What happened The habit it teaches John Snow , London, 1854 Mapping cholera deaths showed them clustered around one water pump. Its handle was removed. A simple, well-chosen picture can overturn what "everyone knows". Florence Nightingale , 1850s Her diagrams showed most soldiers died of preventable disease in hospitals, not of wounds. Analysis only changes things when decision-makers understand it. Moneyball , baseball, 2002 A low-budget team found undervalued players by measuring on-base percentage. Measuring the right thing can matter more than having the most money. Walmart , hurricane, 2004 Sales patterns before earlier storms guided what to stock before a new one. Past patterns can guide everyday operational decisions. Google Flu Trends , 2008–2015 Estimating flu from searches worked for a while, then failed badly and was shut down. More data is not automatically better data. Every result needs validation. The full stories are in Why data analytics matters . Predict, then reveal Four of these stories are successes; one is a failure. Before reading the last row, ask yourself: what could make a model that once worked stop working? Then read the last row. Check your understanding Think of one decision at a workplace or organisation you know that was made on gut feeling. What data could have informed it, and which of the four weak spots might have affected it? Part 3: Four kinds of analytics ¶ Analytics answers four kinds of question. Each builds on the one before. Kind Question it answers Typical methods Example Descriptive What happened? Totals, averages, tables, charts, dashboards Sales fell 8% last quarter Diagnostic Why did it happen? Breakdowns by group, comparisons, correlation The fall came almost entirely from one region after a competitor opened Predictive What is likely to happen next? Forecasting, regression, classification If nothing changes, that region will keep losing sales next quarter Prescriptive What should we do? Simulation, optimisation, scenario comparison Test a local loyalty offer in that region before changing national prices Many textbooks, including ours, group the first two together and speak of descriptive, predictive and prescriptive analytics. Diagnostic work is the bridge: it explains the description before anyone predicts or prescribes. Across the business ¶ Function Descriptive Predictive Prescriptive Retail Sales by product last month Demand next month How much stock to order Finance Spending against budget Cash position next quarter Which costs to cut first Marketing Response rate of each campaign Which customers are likely to respond Whom to send the next offer to Operations Average delivery time Late deliveries during the holiday peak How many drivers to schedule HR Staff turnover by department Who is at risk of leaving Which retention programme to fund Where each kind appears in this course ¶ Kind Course topics Descriptive and diagnostic Data exploration, visualisation, dashboards, text mining (Days 1–3) Predictive Forecasting (Day 3) and regression (Day 4) Prescriptive Spreadsheet simulation and decision models (Days 5–6) A small live example ¶ The cell below loads the table of restaurant bills you met in the pre-class Python and Jupyter basics notebook. Each row is one table's bill and the tip it left (in US dollars, from a real restaurant study). We use it only to see the first three kinds of question in code. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd tips = pd . read_csv ( "data/tips.csv" ) tips [ "tip_percent" ] = 100 * tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ] # Descriptive: what happened? Average tip on each day. print ( "Descriptive: average tip (US dollars) by day" ) print ( tips . groupby ( "day" )[ "tip" ] . mean () . round ( 2 )) Descriptive: average tip (US dollars) by day day Fri 2.73 Sat 2.99 Sun 3.26 Thur 2.77 Name: tip, dtype: float64 Predict, then reveal One day has the highest average tip. Is that because people are more generous that day, or because they spend more ? Write your guess, then run the next cell, which looks at the average bill and the tip as a percentage of the bill. # Diagnostic: why? Compare the bill size and the tip as a share of the bill. print ( "Diagnostic: average bill and tip percentage by day" ) tips . groupby ( "day" ) . agg ( average_bill = ( "total_bill" , "mean" ), average_tip_percent = ( "tip_percent" , "mean" ), ) . round ( 2 ) Diagnostic: average bill and tip percentage by day .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } average_bill average_tip_percent day Fri 17.15 16.99 Sat 20.44 15.32 Sun 21.41 16.69 Thur 17.68 16.13 Compare the two columns in the output above. Where the average tip is high, look at whether the bill or the percentage is what differs. A difference in amounts can come from a difference in spending rather than in generosity: that is a diagnostic finding. Now a prediction: the straight line that best fits tip against bill lets us estimate the tip on a new bill. # Predictive: what is likely? Fit a straight line of tip against bill. slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( tips [ "total_bill" ], tips [ "tip" ], 1 ) new_bill = 40 print ( f "Best-fit line: tip = { intercept : .2f } + { slope : .3f } x bill" ) print ( f "Predicted tip on a { new_bill } -dollar bill: { intercept + slope * new_bill : .2f } dollars" ) Best-fit line: tip = 0.92 + 0.105 x bill Predicted tip on a 40-dollar bill: 5.12 dollars Prescriptive analytics would go one step further: compare options (for example, which evening to add a second server) against an objective (service quality, wages) under constraints (staff available), and recommend one. You will build that kind of model in Excel on Day 5. Check your understanding Which kind of analytics is each statement? "Deliveries in the North got slower because the new carrier skips Saturday collections." "We expect about 400 returns in December." "Move the slow carrier's routes to the faster one for one month and measure the effect." "We shipped 12,000 parcels in October." "A customer who has not ordered for 90 days is likely to leave." Part 4: Analysis fundamentals — from question to decision ¶ A useful analysis supports a decision . It follows the same path every time: Question → Data → Analysis → Validation → Decision Stage Ask Keep as evidence 1. Question Who must decide what, and by when? The decision and a one-sentence question 2. Data What does each row represent? What is missing? How must it be prepared? The grain, units, scope, and a log of every change 3. Analysis Which comparison or metric actually answers the question? The metric definition, filters and calculation 4. Validation Do totals reconcile? Can I explain odd values? Does a chart agree with the numbers? Spot checks, counts and totals, edge cases 5. Decision What action follows, and what is still uncertain? A clear chart, the action, one caveat and a follow-up measure The course site describes the same path as seven steps , splitting out preparation and visualisation. Step 1 in detail: a question you can answer ¶ A manager says: "Sales feel uneven across our customer groups." That is a feeling, not a question. A question you can answer with data names four things: Part Ask yourself Example Decision What will someone do differently? Choose one customer segment to investigate next month Population Which records count? All order lines in the sales table Period Which dates? Orders placed in the last three years Measure What will we compare? Total sales by customer segment "Which customer segment had the highest total sales over the last three years, so we can choose one segment to investigate next month?" Step 2 in detail: what does one row mean? ¶ A manager asks: "How many orders did we have?" The sales file has one row per order line , so an order with three products takes three rows. Counting rows counts lines , not orders. You must first know what one row represents (the table's grain ), then count distinct order numbers. You practised this in the pre-class Python and Jupyter basics notebook. Step 4 in detail: validation ¶ A plausible number is not a checked number Before you report a result: do the parts add up to the total? Does a count match a simple manual check? Can you explain the largest and smallest values? Have you looked at the data in a chart, not only at summary numbers? Parts 5 and 6 show why that last check matters. Check your understanding A colleague asks: "Is the new website working?" Which of the four parts (decision, population, period, measure) are missing? Suggest one value for each. Part 5: Statistics are not enough — Anscombe's quartet ¶ In 1973 the statistician Francis Anscombe made four small datasets to make one point. We build them in code, compute their summary statistics, and only then look at them. The code stores all four datasets in one table. Each row is one point: which set it belongs to ( set ) and its x and y values. # Anscombe's quartet (1973): four small datasets, eleven points each. x = [ 10 , 8 , 13 , 9 , 11 , 14 , 6 , 4 , 12 , 7 , 5 ] anscombe = pd . concat ([ pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "I" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 8.04 , 6.95 , 7.58 , 8.81 , 8.33 , 9.96 , 7.24 , 4.26 , 10.84 , 4.82 , 5.68 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "II" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 9.14 , 8.14 , 8.74 , 8.77 , 9.26 , 8.10 , 6.13 , 3.10 , 9.13 , 7.26 , 4.74 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "III" , "x" : x , "y" : [ 7.46 , 6.77 , 12.74 , 7.11 , 7.81 , 8.84 , 6.08 , 5.39 , 8.15 , 6.42 , 5.73 ]}), pd . DataFrame ({ "set" : "IV" , "x" : [ 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 8 , 19 , 8 , 8 , 8 ], "y" : [ 6.58 , 5.76 , 7.71 , 8.84 , 8.47 , 7.04 , 5.25 , 12.50 , 5.56 , 7.91 , 6.89 ]}), ], ignore_index = True ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , anscombe . shape ) anscombe . head () Rows, columns: (44, 3) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } set x y 0 I 10 8.04 1 I 8 6.95 2 I 13 7.58 3 I 9 8.81 4 I 11 8.33 Now the summary statistics for each set. groupby("set") splits the table into the four sets; agg computes several summaries for each one. The correlation measures how closely the points follow a straight line, from −1 to +1. summary = anscombe . groupby ( "set" ) . agg ( mean_x = ( "x" , "mean" ), mean_y = ( "y" , "mean" ), sd_x = ( "x" , "std" ), sd_y = ( "y" , "std" ), ) summary [ "correlation" ] = anscombe . groupby ( "set" )[[ "x" , "y" ]] . apply ( lambda d : d [ "x" ] . corr ( d [ "y" ])) summary . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mean_x mean_y sd_x sd_y correlation set I 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 II 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 III 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 IV 9.0 7.5 3.32 2.03 0.82 Finally, the straight line that best fits each set. np.polyfit(x, y, 1) returns its slope and intercept. for name , points in anscombe . groupby ( "set" ): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) print ( f "Set { name : >3 } : best-fit line y = { intercept : .2f } + { slope : .3f } x" ) Set I: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set II: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set III: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Set IV: best-fit line y = 3.00 + 0.500 x Predict, then reveal Read the outputs above. The four sets share their means, spreads, correlation and best-fit line. Sketch what you think a scatter plot of each set looks like. Will the four pictures be similar? Then run the next cell. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) line_x = np . array ([ 2 , 20 ]) for ax , ( name , points ) in zip ( axes . flat , anscombe . groupby ( "set" )): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], 1 ) ax . plot ( line_x , intercept + slope * line_x , color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 ) ax . scatter ( points [ "x" ], points [ "y" ], s = 40 , color = "#2a78d6" , zorder = 3 ) ax . set_title ( f "Set { name } " ) for ax in axes [ 1 ]: ax . set_xlabel ( "x (no units)" ) for ax in axes [:, 0 ]: ax . set_ylabel ( "y (no units)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same statistics, same trend line, four different stories" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Set What the picture shows What the statistics hide I A loose, roughly straight-line relationship Nothing: the summary describes it well II A smooth curve The relationship is not a straight line III A perfect line except for one outlier One unusual point drags the trend line IV Almost every point has the same x; one far point creates the "trend" Remove that point and there is no trend to measure Remember Summary statistics compress data, and compression throws information away. A chart shows you what was thrown away. Plot first, then summarise. Check your understanding In set IV, suppose the one point far to the right is a data-entry error and you remove it. What happens to the correlation? Why can you not even compute it? Part 6: The Datasaurus Dozen ¶ In 2017 Justin Matejka and George Fitzmaurice pushed Anscombe's idea further. Starting from a dinosaur drawn with data points (originally by Alberto Cairo), they nudged the points step by step into twelve other shapes while keeping the summary statistics almost identical. Their data is in the course folder, so it loads without internet. # The Datasaurus Dozen (Matejka and Fitzmaurice, 2017), from the open-source # datasauRus package (MIT licence), bundled in the data folder. dozen = pd . read_csv ( "data/datasaurus_dozen.csv" ) print ( "Rows, columns:" , dozen . shape ) print ( "Datasets:" , dozen [ "dataset" ] . nunique ()) dozen . head () Rows, columns: (1846, 3) Datasets: 13 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } dataset x y 0 dino 55.3846 97.1795 1 dino 51.5385 96.0256 2 dino 46.1538 94.4872 3 dino 42.8205 91.4103 4 dino 40.7692 88.3333 Predict, then reveal The table has thirteen datasets.
