docs.text: Day 2 lecture: Building dashboards in Tableau ¶ This morning you learned what makes a chart and a dashboard clear. This afternoon you build them in Tableau: connecting to data, dimensions and measures, aggregation, the Marks card, filters, calculated fields, sheets, dashboards, actions, formatting and printing to PDF. Short Python cells show the same ideas in pandas, so you can see that both tools do the same arithmetic. Open Tableau Desktop and this notebook side by side. Follow the numbered steps in Tableau; run the Python cells in JupyterLab with Shift + Enter . What you will be able to do ¶ Connect Tableau to a saved data source and to a CSV file, and check the data types. Tell dimensions from measures and discrete (blue) from continuous (green) fields. Explain how Tableau aggregates a measure for each mark, and change the aggregation. Use the Marks card (Color, Size, Label, Detail, Tooltip) and the Filters shelf. Write a calculated field , including a ratio KPI computed as a ratio of sums . Assemble sheets into a dashboard , add a filter action , and format it for a reader. Save a packaged workbook and print a dashboard to PDF for submission. Reading: Tableau Software (n.d.), What is data visualization? and Tableau for students (licence and download). Part Topic 1 The Tableau workspace 2 Connecting to data 3 Dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous 4 Aggregation and the level of detail 5 The Marks card 6 Filters 7 Calculated fields and a ratio KPI 8 From sheets to a dashboard 9 Actions: making the dashboard interactive 10 Formatting for the reader 11 Saving, printing to PDF and publishing 12 Assignment 1 briefing Field names differ between versions Tableau has changed its Sample – Superstore data several times: dates, field names ( State or State/Province ) and some values differ between versions. Use the names you see in your Data pane. When a CSV column is called total_bill , Tableau may display it as Total Bill ; it is the same field. import pandas as pd pd . set_option ( "display.float_format" , " {:,.2f} " . format ) tips = pd . read_csv ( "data/tips.csv" ) print ( "Rows (bills):" , len ( tips )) print ( "Columns:" , list ( tips . columns )) Rows (bills): 244 Columns: ['total_bill', 'tip', 'sex', 'smoker', 'day', 'time', 'size'] Part 1: The Tableau workspace ¶ When you open a worksheet, the screen has the same parts every time: Area Where What it does Data pane Left Lists the fields of the connected data, dimensions above the line, measures below Columns and Rows shelves Top Fields placed here define the chart's axes and headers Marks card Left of the view Chooses the mark type and what drives colour, size, labels, detail and tooltips Filters shelf Above the Marks card Fields placed here limit which rows are used View (canvas) Centre The chart itself Show Me Top right Suggests chart types for the fields you have selected Sheet tabs Bottom Worksheets, dashboards and stories; plus the Data Source tab The three icons next to the sheet tabs create a new worksheet , a new dashboard and a new story . How Tableau thinks You never write "draw a bar chart". You drag fields onto shelves , and Tableau decides the chart from what you placed where. A measure on Rows and a dimension on Columns gives a bar chart; a date on Columns gives a line. Show Me is a shortcut, not a different method. Part 2: Connecting to data ¶ The built-in sample ¶ Open Tableau Desktop. On the start page, under Saved Data Sources (left side), click Sample – Superstore . A blank worksheet, Sheet 1 , opens. The Data pane lists tables such as Orders , People and Returns . A CSV file ¶ On the start page, under Connect → To a File , click Text file . Go to the course folder notebooks/China_Classroom/data/ and open tips.csv . The Data Source page shows a preview of the rows. Above each column an icon shows the data type Tableau guessed: Icon Type Example in tips # Number total_bill , tip , size Abc Text (string) sex , smoker , day , time Calendar Date (none in tips) Globe Geographic (none in tips) Click a type icon to change it if the guess is wrong. Then click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom to start building. Check what one row means As in Python, look at the preview and say what one row is before you build anything. In tips.csv one row is one bill (one table served). In Superstore's Orders table one row is one order line (one product in one order), not one order. The Python version of "connect and preview" is the cell you ran above, plus head() : tips . head () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } total_bill tip sex smoker day time size 0 16.99 1.01 Female No Sun Dinner 2 1 10.34 1.66 Male No Sun Dinner 3 2 21.01 3.50 Male No Sun Dinner 3 3 23.68 3.31 Male No Sun Dinner 2 4 24.59 3.61 Female No Sun Dinner 4 Part 3: Dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous ¶ Tableau sorts every field in two ways. Meaning Examples Typical use Dimension A field you group by : categories, names, dates Category, Region, day , smoker Headers, colours, filters Measure A number you aggregate (add up, average) Sales, Profit, total_bill , tip Axes, bar lengths, sizes And separately, by colour of the pill: Pill colour Kind What it draws Blue Discrete : separate values Headers and separate panes (Jan, Feb, Mar as labels) Green Continuous : a range of values An axis (a time line from 2023 to 2026) Usually dimensions are discrete and measures continuous, but not always. A date can be either: YEAR(Order Date) as a blue pill gives one column per year; a green continuous month gives one long timeline. In Lab 2 you will change a date pill from discrete to continuous to draw a monthly trend. A number that is really a category In tips.csv , size (the number of people at the table) arrives as a measure, so Tableau would add it up . To compare party sizes, right-click size in the Data pane → Convert to Dimension , and Tableau treats each size as a group. In Python the same decision is whether you write groupby("size") or ["size"].sum() . Check your understanding For each Superstore field, say dimension or measure, and discrete or continuous in a typical chart: Region , Sales , Order Date on a monthly trend line, Quantity , Customer Name . Part 4: Aggregation and the level of detail ¶ When you drag a measure into the view, Tableau does not draw one mark per row. It draws one mark for each combination of the dimensions in the view , and aggregates the measure inside each mark. The default aggregation is SUM . In Tableau (with Sample – Superstore): Drag Region to Columns and Sales to Rows. The pill reads SUM(Sales) : one bar per region, each the total of its order lines. Right-click the SUM(Sales) pill → Measure (Sum) → Average . The pill becomes AVG(Sales) and each bar shows the average order line , a different question. Drag Segment to Color. Now there is one mark for each region and segment: the level of detail got finer, and each mark aggregates fewer rows. Button What it encodes Good use Watch out Mark type (dropdown) Bar, Line, Circle, Square, Text, Map, Pie… Leave on Automatic until you need a specific type Pie only for two or three parts Color A dimension (categories) or measure (scale) Highlight one thing, or profit (diverging) Rainbow palettes; colour alone Size A measure Secondary information Area is read inaccurately (this morning, Part 2) Label Writes values on marks Direct labels instead of an axis Too many labels clutter Detail Splits marks without encoding them Needed for maps and for tooltip fields Makes the level of detail finer Tooltip Text shown on hover Exact values, definitions Hover does not exist on a printed PDF Try it (Superstore): on a sheet with Sub-Category on Rows and SUM(Sales) on Columns, drag Profit onto Color . Click Color → Edit Colors to check where the centre sits. Part 6: Filters ¶ A filter limits which rows reach the view. Drag a dimension (for example Region ) to the Filters shelf, tick the values to keep, click OK . Right-click the pill on the Filters shelf → Show Filter to put a filter control next to the chart for the reader. To make one filter change several sheets: on the filter control's menu (small arrow) → Apply to Worksheets → All Using This Data Source (or Selected Worksheets ). Measures can be filtered too: drag Sales to Filters and choose a range of SUM(Sales) . In pandas, a filter is a boolean condition applied before grouping: dinner = tips [ tips [ "time" ] == "Dinner" ] # filter: keep dinner bills only print ( "Bills after the filter:" , len ( dinner ), "of" , len ( tips )) dinner . groupby ( "smoker" )[ "tip" ] . sum () . round ( 2 ) # then aggregate, as Tableau does Bills after the filter: 176 of 244 smoker No 331.45 Yes 214.62 Name: tip, dtype: float64 State the filter on the page A filtered chart answers a narrower question. Put the filter in the title or the scope note ("Dinner bills only"), or the reader will assume the whole dataset. Part 7: Calculated fields and a ratio KPI ¶ A calculated field is a new field defined by a formula. Create one with Analysis → Create Calculated Field , or right-click in the Data pane → Create → Calculated Field . Give it a name, type the formula, and check that the message under the box says The calculation is valid . Row-level versus aggregate calculations ¶ Formula What Tableau does Result in the view (with AVG) [Tip] / [Total Bill] Computes the ratio for every row , then you aggregate it (Tableau suggests SUM; you would choose AVG) The mean of ratios : each bill's tip % averaged SUM([Tip]) / SUM([Total Bill]) Adds up the tips and the bills for each mark, then divides The ratio of sums : the share of all spending that went to tips This morning (Part 11) you saw that these answer different questions, and that a KPI tile should normally use the ratio of sums . In Tableau, the SUM(...) / SUM(...) form is how you write it. Superstore's standard KPI is: Profit Ratio = SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) After creating it, right-click the field → Default Properties → Number Format → Percentage so it always displays as a percentage. Here are both versions in pandas, for each value of smoker : kpi = tips . groupby ( "smoker" ) . agg ( tips_sum = ( "tip" , "sum" ), bills_sum = ( "total_bill" , "sum" )) kpi [ "ratio of sums %" ] = 100 * kpi [ "tips_sum" ] / kpi [ "bills_sum" ] # SUM([Tip]) / SUM([Total Bill]) kpi [ "mean of ratios %" ] = 100 * ( tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ]) . groupby ( tips [ "smoker" ]) . mean () # AVG([Tip] / [Total Bill]) kpi .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } tips_sum bills_sum ratio of sums % mean of ratios % smoker No 451.77 2,897.43 15.59 15.93 Yes 279.81 1,930.34 14.50 16.32 The two percentage columns in the output above differ. Look closely: do they even rank smokers and non-smokers in the same order ? If a dashboard tile said "Tip rate" without saying which one, two analysts could report different numbers from the same data. Name the formula in the tile or the scope note. Other useful calculations IF SUM([Profit]) < 0 THEN "Loss" ELSE "Profit" END : a label you can put on Color. DATEDIFF('day', [Order Date], [Ship Date]) : days to ship, per row. COUNTD([Order ID]) : distinct orders, because Superstore has several rows per order. Check your understanding In Superstore, why does AVG([Profit] / [Sales]) give a different number from SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) for the whole company? Which one would you put on an executive dashboard, and why? Part 8: From sheets to a dashboard ¶ A dashboard is built from worksheets : build and title each chart on its own sheet first, then arrange them. Plan before you build ¶ Use this morning's principles. On paper, sketch: The decision and the audience (for example: a regional manager deciding which products to review). The 3–5 views , each answering one part of the question. The layout : headline and KPIs at the top left, detail below and to the right. Build ¶ Build each sheet and rename its tab (double-click the tab), for example Sales trend , Profit by state , Sales by sub-category . The tab name becomes the default title on the dashboard. Click the New Dashboard icon at the bottom. On the left, under Size , choose Automatic so the dashboard fills the screen (or a Fixed size such as A4 landscape if you will print it). Under Sheets , drag each sheet onto the canvas. Grey shaded areas show where it will land: top, bottom, left or right of what is already there. Leave objects Tiled (the default) so they line up in a grid; Floating objects sit on top and are easy to misalign. Add a Text object (under Objects ) for the headline message and a small one for the scope note (period, data source, units). Remove legends you do not need (click the legend → x ), and delete repeated titles. Check your understanding Your dashboard has six sheets and three legends and still has no headline. Using this morning's principles, name three changes. Part 9: Actions: making the dashboard interactive ¶ Actions let a click on one view change the others. The quick way: Use as Filter ¶ On the dashboard, click once on a view (for example a map) to select it. A grey border appears with small icons at its top right. Click the funnel icon ( Use as Filter ). Now clicking a mark in that view (a state) filters every other view on the dashboard. To clear the selection, click the same mark again, or click an empty part of the view, or press Esc . The full way: Dashboard → Actions ¶ Dashboard → Actions → Add Action offers: Action Effect Filter Clicking a mark keeps only the matching rows in the target views (this is what Use as Filter creates) Highlight Clicking a mark highlights matching marks elsewhere and greys the rest, without removing them Go to Sheet / URL / parameter / set Navigation and advanced uses For each action choose the source sheet , target sheets , and whether it runs on Hover , Select (click) or Menu , and what happens when the selection is cleared ( Show all values is usually what a reader expects). In Python there is no clicking, but the idea of one filter driving every view is a function with a parameter. Every number below is recomputed for the chosen group: def mini_dashboard ( data , smoker = None ): """Recompute every KPI for one selection, as a dashboard filter action does.""" view = data if smoker is None else data [ data [ "smoker" ] == smoker ] return pd . Series ({ "bills" : len ( view ), "total spend (dollars)" : view [ "total_bill" ] . sum (), "tip rate, sum/sum (%)" : 100 * view [ "tip" ] . sum () / view [ "total_bill" ] . sum (), "average party size" : view [ "size" ] . mean (), }) . round ( 2 ) pd . DataFrame ({ "All bills" : mini_dashboard ( tips ), "Click: smoker = Yes" : mini_dashboard ( tips , "Yes" ), "Click: smoker = No" : mini_dashboard ( tips , "No" ), }) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } All bills Click: smoker = Yes Click: smoker = No bills 244.00 93.00 151.00 total spend (dollars) 4,827.77 1,930.34 2,897.43 tip rate, sum/sum (%) 15.15 14.50 15.59 average party size 2.57 2.41 2.67 Actions do not print A PDF shows one state of the dashboard. Before printing, clear all selections so the reader sees the whole picture, unless the assignment asks for a filtered view; then say in a caption which state is selected. Part 10: Formatting for the reader ¶ Apply this morning's design rules inside Tableau: Goal Where in Tableau Message titles Double-click a sheet title on the dashboard and type the finding; keep units in the axis title Sort bars by value The Sort Descending button in the toolbar, or right-click the dimension → Sort Number formats (thousands separators, %) Right-click the measure pill or axis → Format → Numbers Colour-blind-safe colours Color → Edit Colors → choose the Color Blind palette for categories; keep orange–blue for profit and loss Remove clutter Format → Lines : set grid lines to None; right-click an axis → uncheck Show Header when bars are labelled Direct labels Click Label on the Marks card → Show mark labels Readable tooltips Click Tooltip on the Marks card and rewrite it as a sentence Scope note A small Text object at the bottom: data source, period, filters, units Bars still start at zero in Tableau Tableau's bar axes start at zero by default. If you right-click an axis → Edit Axis and untick Include zero , you have built this morning's misleading truncated bar chart. Part 11: Saving, printing to PDF and publishing ¶ Task How Notes Save your work File → Save As → Tableau Packaged Workbook ( .twbx ) A .twbx contains the data, so it opens on another computer. A .twb does not Print to PDF (for GAP) File → Print to PDF → Range : Active Sheet (with the dashboard tab open) → OK → choose a file name Choose landscape paper; check that nothing is cut off Export an image Dashboard → Export Image Useful for a Word report Publish to the web Server → Tableau Public → Save to Tableau Public Anyone on the internet can see it. Never publish confidential or personal data ; course submissions go to GAP as PDF Before you print, check The dashboard tab is the active sheet . No mark is selected and no filter is left on by accident. Every title is a message, every axis has units, and the scope note is visible. Open the PDF and read it as the reader will: is anything cut off or too small? Summary ¶ Tableau draws one mark per combination of dimensions in the view and aggregates each measure in that mark (SUM by default), exactly like groupby in pandas. Blue pills are discrete (headers), green pills are continuous (axes). Dates can be either. The Marks card maps fields to colour, size, label, detail and tooltip; the Filters shelf limits rows. Ratio KPIs are calculated fields written as SUM([numerator]) / SUM([denominator]) . A dashboard is a few titled sheets, laid out for one decision, connected by actions , with a headline and a scope note. Submit dashboards as a PDF from File → Print to PDF ; keep a .twbx copy of your work. Closing quiz ¶ What is the difference between a dimension and a measure? Give one example of each from Superstore. A pill is green. What does that tell you, and what will it draw? You put SUM(Sales) on Rows and Region on Columns, then add Segment to Color. What happens to the number of marks? Write the calculated field for a profit ratio KPI. Why not AVG([Profit] / [Sales]) ? What does the funnel ( Use as Filter ) icon on a dashboard view do? docs.text: This morning you learned what makes a chart and a dashboard clear. docs.text: When you open a worksheet, the screen has the same parts every time: Area Where What it does Data pane Left Lists the fields of the connected data, dimensions above the line, measures below Columns and Rows shelves Top Fields placed here define the chart's axes and headers Marks card Left of the view Chooses the mark type and what drives colour, size, labels, detail and tooltips Filters shelf Above the Marks card Fields placed here limit which rows are used View (canvas) Centre The chart itself Show Me Top right Suggests chart types for the fields you have selected Sheet tabs Bottom Worksheets, dashboards and stories; plus the Data Source tab The three icons next to the sheet tabs create a new worksheet , a new dashboard and a new story . How Tableau thinks You never write "draw a bar chart". You drag fields onto shelves , and Tableau decides the chart from what you placed where. docs.text: Tableau sorts every field in two ways. Meaning Examples Typical use Dimension A field you group by : categories, names, dates Category, Region, day , smoker Headers, colours, filters Measure A number you aggregate (add up, average) Sales, Profit, total_bill , tip Axes, bar lengths, sizes And separately, by colour of the pill: Pill colour Kind What it draws Blue Discrete : separate values Headers and separate panes (Jan, Feb, Mar as labels) Green Continuous : a range of values An axis (a time line from 2023 to 2026) Usually dimensions are discrete and measures continuous, but not always. A date can be either: YEAR(Order Date) as a blue pill gives one column per year; a green continuous month gives one long timeline. In Lab 2 you will change a date pill from discrete to continuous to draw a monthly trend. A number that is really a category In tips.csv , size (the number of people at the table) arrives as a measure, so Tableau would add it up . To compare party sizes, right-click size in the Data pane → Convert to Dimension , and Tableau treats each size as a group. In Python the same decision is whether you write groupby("size") or ["size"].sum() . docs.text: Tableau draws one mark per combination of dimensions in the view and aggregates each measure in that mark (SUM by default), exactly like groupby in pandas. Blue pills are discrete (headers), green pills are continuous (axes). Dates can be either. The Marks card maps fields to colour, size, label, detail and tooltip; the Filters shelf limits rows. Ratio KPIs are calculated fields written as SUM([numerator]) / SUM([denominator]) . A dashboard is a few titled sheets, laid out for one decision, connected by actions , with a headline and a scope note. docs.text: Day 2 lecture: Visualising and communicating results ¶ A chart is an argument made with shapes and colours. This lecture shows how the eye reads a chart, how charts mislead and how to rebuild them honestly, how to turn findings into a short story for a decision-maker, how to design a dashboard around a few good KPIs, and how marketing teams measure their funnel. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . What you will be able to do ¶ Choose a chart from the task the reader has to do, and explain why position and length beat angle, area and colour. Use pre-attentive attributes , data-ink and Gestalt principles to direct the reader's eye. Choose categorical , sequential or diverging colour, and keep charts readable for colour-blind readers. Spot a misleading chart (truncated bars, dual axes, scaled areas, crowded pies) and rebuild it honestly. Turn findings into a story: audience , big idea , situation, complication, resolution and message titles . Explain what the Challenger O-ring data show when the flights with no damage are included. Lay out a dashboard with 3–5 views and KPI tiles, and compute ratio KPIs as a ratio of sums . Read a marketing funnel and compute conversion rate, CPA and ROAS ; explain segmentation, customer lifetime value and the limits of attribution. Reading: Tableau Software (n.d.), What is data visualization? ; the course pages Designing clear visuals and Storytelling with data . Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words, alone or with the person next to you. "Has the share of online sales grown over the last three years?" "Do customers who get bigger discounts buy more items?" "Which of our 12 warehouses had the highest return rate last quarter?" Part 2: How accurately we read encodings ¶ An encoding is how a number becomes something visible: a position, a length, an angle, an area, a colour. Experiments by William Cleveland and Robert McGill (1984), repeated many times since, found that people judge some encodings much more accurately than others. Rank Encoding Example 1 (most accurate) Position on a common scale Dots or bar ends against one axis 2 Length Bars that start at the same baseline 3 Angle and slope Pie slices, line steepness 4 Area Bubbles, treemaps 5 (least accurate) Colour intensity and hue Shaded maps, heatmaps Put the most important comparison on position or length . Use colour and area for secondary information or for highlighting. Predict, then reveal Five made-up values are drawn as pie slices and as bubbles. Rank them from largest to smallest using only these two pictures, and write your ranking down. values = pd . Series ({ "A" : 20 , "B" : 23 , "C" : 17 , "D" : 21 , "E" : 19 }) # made-up values fig , ( ax_pie , ax_bubble ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.8 )) ax_pie . pie ( values , labels = values . index , startangle = 90 , counterclock = False , colors = OKABE_ITO [: 5 ]) ax_pie . set_title ( "Angle and area" ) ax_bubble . scatter ( range ( len ( values )), [ 0 ] * len ( values ), s = values * 60 , color = BLUE ) for i , label in enumerate ( values . index ): ax_bubble . text ( i , - 0.35 , label , ha = "center" ) ax_bubble . set_xlim ( - 0.7 , 4.7 ) ax_bubble . set_ylim ( - 0.6 , 0.6 ) ax_bubble . axis ( "off" ) ax_bubble . set_title ( "Area only" ) plt . show () Now the same five values as bars on a common baseline. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 6 , 3.5 )) ax . bar ( values . index , values , color = BLUE ) ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . set_title ( "Position and length: the ranking is easy" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Value (made-up units)" ) plt . show () print ( "True ranking:" , ", " . join ( values . sort_values ( ascending = False ) . index )) True ranking: B, D, A, E, C Most people get the slices and bubbles partly wrong when values are close, and nearly everyone gets the bars right. This is the main reason analysts prefer bars and dots. Check your understanding A colleague shows a map where each province's profit is shown only by its shade of green. Name one question this map answers badly, and a chart that answers it better. Part 3: Pre-attentive attributes ¶ Some differences are seen in a fraction of a second, before you consciously search: colour , size , position , orientation , shape , enclosure . They are called pre-attentive attributes. Predict, then reveal The next cell draws two panels. In each, find the odd one out. Which panel is faster, and why? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2 ) # fixed seed: the made-up dots look the same every run fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 4.2 )) xy = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , size = ( 48 , 2 )) ax1 . scatter ( xy [ 1 :, 0 ], xy [ 1 :, 1 ], s = 70 , color = GREY ) ax1 . scatter ( xy [ 0 , 0 ], xy [ 0 , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE ) ax1 . set_title ( "Find the odd one out (colour only)" ) xy2 = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , size = ( 48 , 2 )) half = len ( xy2 ) // 2 ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ 1 : half , 0 ], xy2 [ 1 : half , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE , marker = "s" ) ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ half :, 0 ], xy2 [ half :, 1 ], s = 70 , color = BLUE , marker = "o" ) ax2 . scatter ( xy2 [ 0 , 0 ], xy2 [ 0 , 1 ], s = 70 , color = ORANGE , marker = "o" ) ax2 . set_title ( "Find the orange circle (colour AND shape)" ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . set_yticks ([]) ax . grid ( False ) for spine in ax . spines . values (): spine . set_visible ( False ) plt . show () On the left the orange dot "pops out" at once. On the right you must scan, because the target differs only by a combination of colour and shape, and combinations are not pre-attentive. Lessons for charts: Use one pre-attentive attribute to mark what matters, usually one strong colour against grey. If everything is highlighted, nothing is. Five bright colours give the eye five places to look. Do not ask the reader to decode combinations ("orange squares are Saturday dinners"). Part 4: Data-ink and decluttering ¶ Edward Tufte's data-ink ratio asks: how much of the ink shows data? Everything else (heavy grids, borders, colours with no meaning, rotated labels) costs the reader attention. Here is matplotlib's default style showing the average fuel economy of each maker with at least ten models. plt.style.context("default") switches off our clean style for this one chart. big_makers = by_maker [ by_maker >= 10 ] . index avg_mpg = cars [ cars [ "maker" ] . isin ( big_makers )] . groupby ( "maker" )[ "mpg" ] . mean () with plt . style . context ( "default" ): fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4.5 )) avg_mpg . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax , color = plt . cm . tab20 . colors , edgecolor = "black" ) ax . grid ( True ) ax . set_title ( "Average MPG by Maker" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "mpg" ) plt . show () Predict, then reveal List three things on this chart that do not help the reader, and one question it makes hard to answer. Then run the next cell. sorted_mpg = avg_mpg . sort_values () best = sorted_mpg . index [ - 1 ] usa_makers = set ( cars . loc [ cars [ "origin" ] == "usa" , "maker" ]) colours = [ GREY if maker in usa_makers else BLUE for maker in sorted_mpg . index ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 5.5 )) ax . barh ( sorted_mpg . index , sorted_mpg , color = colours ) for name , value in sorted_mpg . items (): ax . text ( value + 0.3 , name , f " { value : .1f } " , va = "center" , fontsize = 8 , color = INK ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , sorted_mpg . max () * 1.12 ) ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . grid ( False ) for side in ( "left" , "bottom" ): ax . spines [ side ] . set_visible ( False ) ranked = list ( sorted_mpg . index [:: - 1 ]) # most economical first n_foreign_top = next (( i for i , m in enumerate ( ranked ) if m in usa_makers ), len ( ranked )) ax . set_title ( f "The { n_foreign_top } most economical makers are all non-US makers" if n_foreign_top >= 2 else f " { best } has the highest average fuel economy" , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , "Average miles per gallon, makers with at least 10 models, 1970-1982; blue = non-US maker, grey = US maker" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 8.5 , color = INK ) plt . show () What changed, and why: Change Principle Sorted by value The ranking is now the reading order Horizontal bars Long labels are readable without tilting your head Colour with a meaning (blue = non-US maker), grey for the rest One pre-attentive attribute, one message Values written on the bars, value axis removed Exact numbers without tracing a grid The title states the finding; the subtitle states scope and units The reader knows what to look for and what was counted Do not overdo it Decluttering stops when removing something would lose meaning: units, the period, the scope or a zero line. The aim is clarity, not minimalism. Check your understanding The "after" chart removed the value axis. Give one situation where you should keep a value axis instead of writing numbers on the bars. Part 5: Gestalt: what belongs together ¶ Gestalt principles describe how we group what we see. You can use them to decide what the reader compares. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 4 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.2 )) gx , gy = np . meshgrid ( np . arange ( 6 ), np . arange ( 4 )) gx , gy = gx . ravel (), gy . ravel () axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( gx + ( gx // 2 ) * 0.9 , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) # columns pushed into pairs axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Proximity" ) axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = [ ORANGE if row % 2 else BLUE for row in gy ]) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Similarity" ) axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) axes [ 2 ] . add_patch ( Rectangle (( 1.6 , - 0.5 ), 1.8 , 4 , color = GREY , alpha = 0.5 , zorder = 0 )) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "Enclosure" ) axes [ 3 ] . scatter ( gx , gy , s = 60 , color = BLUE ) for x0 in ( 0 , 2 , 4 ): for y0 in ( 0 , 2 ): axes [ 3 ] . plot ([ x0 , x0 + 1 ], [ y0 , y0 + 1 ], color = INK , linewidth = 1.5 , zorder = 0 ) axes [ 3 ] . set_title ( "Connection" ) for ax in axes : ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . set_yticks ([]) ax . grid ( False ) ax . set_aspect ( "equal" ) for spine in ax . spines . values (): spine . set_visible ( False ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Principle What you saw Use in charts Proximity Pairs of columns Bars placed close together are compared first Similarity Rows, although spacing is equal Same colour = same category in every panel Enclosure The boxed columns form a group Shade a period (a promotion, a holiday) Connection Joined dots read as pairs Lines join points that belong to one series Proximity decides the comparison ¶ The same numbers, grouped two ways: the tip as a percentage of the bill, for male and female bill payers on each day. The percentage is total tips divided by total bills for each group (a ratio of sums , explained in Part 11). Which question does each chart answer easily? groups = tips . groupby ([ "day" , "sex" ])[[ "tip" , "total_bill" ]] . sum () tip_pct = ( 100 * groups [ "tip" ] / groups [ "total_bill" ]) . unstack () . reindex ( DAYS ) fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 ), sharey = True ) tip_pct . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax1 , rot = 0 , color = [ ORANGE , BLUE ], width = 0.8 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Grouped by day: compare women and men on each day" , fontsize = 10 ) tip_pct . T . plot ( kind = "bar" , ax = ax2 , rot = 0 , color = OKABE_ITO [: 4 ], width = 0.8 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Grouped by sex: compare days for each group" , fontsize = 10 ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . set_xlabel ( "" ) ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , fontsize = 8 ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Tips as % o f bills" ) plt . show () Bars that sit next to each other get compared. Put next to each other the things your question compares. Part 6: Colour with a job, and accessibility ¶ Colour should do one of three jobs. Match the palette to the job. Data Palette type Example Rule Categories with no order Categorical: distinct hues Regions, channels At most about six; same category, same colour everywhere Ordered amounts from low to high Sequential: one hue, light to dark Average mpg by origin and year Darker = more Values around a meaningful middle Diverging: two hues, neutral centre Above or below the overall average; profit or loss The neutral colour sits exactly at the middle value The helper below draws a table as a heatmap and writes each value in its cell, in white on dark cells and black on light cells. def heatmap ( ax , table , cmap , norm = None , fmt = " {:.0f} " ): image = ax . imshow ( table . values , cmap = cmap , norm = norm , aspect = "auto" ) ax . set_xticks ( range ( table . shape [ 1 ]), table . columns ) ax . set_yticks ( range ( table . shape [ 0 ]), table . index ) ax . grid ( False ) for ( i , j ), value in np . ndenumerate ( table . values ): r , g , b , _ = image . cmap ( image . norm ( value )) text_colour = "white" if 0.299 * r + 0.587 * g + 0.114 * b < 0.5 else "black" ax . text ( j , i , fmt . format ( value ), ha = "center" , va = "center" , fontsize = 8 , color = text_colour ) return image mpg_year = cars . pivot_table ( index = "origin" , columns = "model_year" , values = "mpg" , aggfunc = "mean" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 10 , 2.6 )) heatmap ( ax , mpg_year , cmap = "Blues" ) ax . set_title ( "Average miles per gallon by origin and model year (19xx); darker = more economical" ) plt . show () Predict, then reveal: diverging Now the question changes: which cells are above the overall average fuel economy, and which are below ? The next cell subtracts the overall average and draws the result twice, first with a sequential palette and then with a diverging palette centred on zero. In which one can you see the answer at a glance? overall = cars [ "mpg" ] . mean () gap = mpg_year - overall limit = gap . abs () . max () . max () fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 2 , 1 , figsize = ( 10 , 5.2 )) heatmap ( ax1 , gap , cmap = "viridis" , fmt = " {:+.0f} " ) ax1 . set_title ( "Sequential palette: where is zero?" , fontsize = 10 ) heatmap ( ax2 , gap , cmap = "RdBu" , norm = TwoSlopeNorm ( vcenter = 0 , vmin =- limit , vmax = limit ), fmt = " {:+.0f} " ) ax2 . set_title ( "Diverging palette centred on 0: red = below average, blue = above" , fontsize = 10 ) fig . suptitle ( f "Average mpg minus the overall average ( { overall : .1f } mpg), by origin and model year" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () With the diverging palette, every below-average cell is red and every above-average cell blue, and the palest cells are close to average. The sequential palette hid the most important boundary in the data: zero. Colour-blind safety and accessibility About 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women have some colour-vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green. Avoid red against green as the only difference. Red–blue or orange–blue are safer. This course uses blue, orange and aqua, with grey for context. Use a tested palette such as Okabe–Ito for categories ( OKABE_ITO in the setup cell). Never rely on colour alone. Add labels, positions or text that carry the same meaning, so the chart still works printed in black and white. Keep enough contrast between text and background, and font sizes readable from the back of the room. Highlight one series, grey the rest ¶ The question decides which line gets the colour. Here: which origin's cars improved fuel economy the most between the first and last model year? Part 7: Honest axes and misleading charts ¶ A chart can be built entirely from true numbers and still leave a false impression. Each example below shows a before that misleads and an after that rebuilds it honestly. Misleading chart 1: the truncated bar axis ¶ A bar's length is the encoding. If the axis does not start at zero, the lengths lie. The tip as a percentage of the bill, by day (total tips ÷ total bills): day_totals = tips . groupby ( "day" )[[ "tip" , "total_bill" ]] . sum () . reindex ( DAYS ) day_pct = 100 * day_totals [ "tip" ] / day_totals [ "total_bill" ] fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.8 )) ax1 . bar ( day_pct . index , day_pct , color = BLUE ) ax1 . set_ylim ( day_pct . min () * 0.98 , day_pct . max () * 1.01 ) ax1 . set_title ( "Before: truncated axis" ) ax2 . bar ( day_pct . index , day_pct , color = BLUE ) for i , value in enumerate ( day_pct ): ax2 . text ( i , value , f " { value : .1f } %" , ha = "center" , va = "bottom" , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax2 . set_ylim ( 0 , day_pct . max () * 1.15 ) ax2 . set_title ( "After: axis from zero, values labelled" ) for ax in ( ax1 , ax2 ): ax . grid ( axis = "x" , visible = False ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Tips as % o f bills" ) plt . show () print ( "Highest day divided by lowest day:" , round ( day_pct . max () / day_pct . min (), 2 )) Highest day divided by lowest day: 1.09 On the left, one day looks several times more generous than another. The printed ratio shows the true difference. Lines are different. A line's message is its shape (rising, falling, seasonal), read from position, not length. A line chart may zoom in to the range of the data, as long as the axis is labelled. The rule: bars from zero; lines may zoom, with labels . Part 8: Message titles, annotation and small multiples ¶ A descriptive title ("Fuel economy against weight") tells the reader what is on the chart. A message title tells them what to see ("Heavier cars travel fewer miles per gallon"). Managers read titles first, and sometimes only titles. Two rules: The message must be true for the chart as drawn : the same period and filters. If the data change, re-check the title. Keep the scope (period, population, units) in a subtitle or note, so the message stays short. Before: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) ax . scatter ( cars [ "weight" ], cars [ "mpg" ]) ax . set_title ( "mpg vs weight" ) plt . show () After: grey points for context, a straight trend line, one annotation that turns the slope into a sentence, and a message title. The code checks the claim before writing it: it only says "heavier cars travel fewer miles" if the correlation is clearly negative. slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( cars [ "weight" ], cars [ "mpg" ], 1 ) r = cars [ "weight" ] . corr ( cars [ "mpg" ]) line_x = np . array ([ cars [ "weight" ] . min (), cars [ "weight" ] . max ()]) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.2 )) ax . scatter ( cars [ "weight" ], cars [ "mpg" ], s = 14 , color = GREY ) ax . plot ( line_x , intercept + slope * line_x , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2.5 ) ax . annotate ( f "Each extra 1,000 lb: about { - slope * 1000 : .1f } fewer mpg" , xy = ( 3500 , intercept + slope * 3500 ), xytext = ( 3300 , 40 ), fontsize = 9 , color = INK , arrowprops = { "arrowstyle" : "->" , "color" : INK }) ax . set_title ( "Heavier cars travel fewer miles per gallon" if r < - 0.5 else "Fuel economy and weight are only weakly related" , pad = 22 ) ax . text ( 0 , 1.02 , f "398 car models, 1970-1982; correlation { r : .2f } ; association, not proof of cause" , transform = ax . transAxes , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Weight (lb)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Miles per gallon" ) plt . show () Annotation is text on the chart that explains one thing at the place it happens: a peak, a policy change, a slope. Use one to three notes per chart. Small multiples ¶ When one chart has too many series, draw many small charts with the same axes , one per group. Tufte called these small multiples . Each panel below shows one origin in blue, with the other cars in grey for context. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.8 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) for ax , origin in zip ( axes , [ "usa" , "europe" , "japan" ]): ax . scatter ( cars [ "weight" ], cars [ "mpg" ], s = 8 , color = GREY ) mine = cars [ cars [ "origin" ] == origin ] ax . scatter ( mine [ "weight" ], mine [ "mpg" ], s = 12 , color = BLUE ) ax . set_title ( f " { origin } ( { len ( mine ) } models)" , fontsize = 10 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Weight (lb)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Miles per gallon" ) fig . suptitle ( "Non-US makers built mostly light cars; in every origin, lighter cars go further per gallon" , x = 0.01 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Small multiples checklist Same axes in every panel ( sharex=True, sharey=True ), unless you say clearly that they differ. Panels in a meaningful order (by size, geography or time), not alphabetical by default. One highlight colour, the same in every panel. Exploratory versus explanatory ¶ Exploratory Explanatory Purpose Find out what is in the data Tell someone what you found and what to do Audience You and your team A decision-maker Number of charts Many, quick, rough As few as possible Titles Describe what is plotted State the message Style Defaults are fine Clean, highlighted, annotated, with a scope note Most charts you make while exploring should never reach a manager. The skill is choosing the few that matter and redrawing them so the message is impossible to miss. Audience and the decision ¶ Before drawing anything, answer three questions: Who is the audience, and what do they already know? What decision do they face, and by when? What do you want them to do or believe after seeing your work? Audience What they need What to leave out Executive The recommendation, two or three numbers, the main risk Method details, every breakdown Manager of one area Their area against the rest, the trend, what to check next Other areas' detail Analyst colleague Definitions, data checks, code Nothing; they need the working The big idea ¶ Before building any chart, write your main message as one sentence that states your point of view , says what is at stake , and is written for your audience . Example: "Cars from non-US makers were far more economical through the 1970s, so a fuel-price rise would hurt the US makers' customers most; the US makers should prioritise lighter models." If you cannot write the sentence, you are not ready to present. Keep analysing. Situation, complication, resolution ¶ A short business story has three parts: Part Question it answers Example (car makers, 1970s) Situation What is true and agreed? US makers sell the most models Complication What problem does the data reveal? Their cars average far fewer miles per gallon, mostly because they are heavier Resolution What should we do? Develop lighter models first, and track average weight and mpg each model year The situation is short, because the audience usually knows it. The complication is why they are listening. The resolution is your recommendation. Message titles ¶ Descriptive title Message title Average mpg by maker The most economical makers are all non-US makers mpg by origin and year Every origin improved; European cars improved the most Tip % by day Tip percentages differ by little more than a point between days Check your understanding Write a situation, complication and resolution, one sentence each, for the small-multiples chart at the end of Part 8. Which sentence needs evidence that the chart does not contain? Part 10: The Challenger case ¶ On 28 January 1986 the space shuttle Challenger broke apart shortly after launch, killing all seven crew. The cause was the failure of rubber O-ring seals in a booster rocket, which had stiffened in the cold. The air temperature at launch was about 36°F (2°C) , far colder than any earlier flight. The evening before, engineers at the contractor Morton Thiokol warned about the cold and recommended not launching below the coldest temperature previously flown. In a teleconference their recommendation was challenged, managers reversed it, and the launch went ahead. The data on earlier flights are small enough to type in. Each row is one of the 23 flights before Challenger for which the boosters were recovered. Leaving them out removed the evidence that warm launches were safer than cold ones. In the shaded band below 65°F, read the table: what share of flights had damage, compared with warmer launches? The dashed line is far to the left of every earlier flight. Challenger launched well outside all experience, so no chart of earlier flights could show what would happen at 36°F. That itself is the warning. The lesson for analysts: the rows you leave out can change the answer. The zeros were the comparison group. Two views of the lesson Edward Tufte argued in Visual Explanations (1997) that the charts prepared before and after the accident failed to show the link between temperature and damage clearly, and that a simple scatter of all flights would have. Others, including some of the Thiokol engineers (Robison, Boisjoly, Hoeker and Young, 2002) and the sociologist Diane Vaughan ( The Challenger Launch Decision , 1996), point out that the engineers did argue that cold was the danger, under time pressure, and that the decision was shaped by schedule, organisational culture and a habit of accepting earlier damage as normal. Both lead to the same lesson: when the stakes are high, show the full comparison so the risk is impossible to miss, and know that a good chart is necessary but not enough. Part 11: Dashboards and KPIs ¶ A dashboard is a small set of views on one page that answers a recurring question for one audience. This afternoon you build one in Tableau; the principles are the same in any tool. Principle What it means in practice Start from the decision One question for one audience. A dashboard that answers everything answers nothing Layout hierarchy Readers start at the top left . Put the headline numbers and main message there; detail below and to the right 3–5 views at most Each view earns its place by answering part of the question KPI tiles A few headline numbers, each with a comparison (vs last period, vs target), so the reader knows whether it is good Consistent colours If orange means "needs attention", use it for nothing else, in every view Filters and actions One control that changes every view (in Tableau: a filter or a dashboard action) Scope and source note Period, units, filters, data source and known limits, small but always on the page Accessibility Colour-blind-safe colours, enough contrast, and never colour alone What makes a good KPI? ¶ A KPI (key performance indicator) is a metric tied to a goal. A good one is defined (everyone computes it the same way), comparable (over time or against a target), actionable (someone can change it) and hard to game . When a measure becomes a target, people can improve the number without improving the business (Goodhart's law), so pair KPIs that keep each other honest, such as sales with profit ratio. Ratio of sums versus mean of ratios ¶ Many KPIs are ratios : tips ÷ bills, profit ÷ sales, conversions ÷ visits. When you combine groups, there are two tempting ways to get the overall ratio: Ratio of sums: add up the numerators, add up the denominators, then divide. Mean of ratios: compute each group's ratio, then average them. Predict, then reveal Store A sold 10,000 with a profit of 1,000; a small kiosk B sold 100 with a profit of 50. What is the company's overall profit ratio? Closer to A's ratio, or to the simple average of the two ratios? stores = pd . DataFrame ({ "sales" : [ 10_000 , 100 ], "profit" : [ 1_000 , 50 ]}, index = [ "A" , "B" ]) stores [ "profit_ratio" ] = stores [ "profit" ] / stores [ "sales" ] print ( stores ) print () print ( "Mean of the two ratios:" , f " { stores [ 'profit_ratio' ] . mean () : .1% } " ) print ( "Ratio of the sums: " , f " { stores [ 'profit' ] . sum () / stores [ 'sales' ] . sum () : .1% } " ) sales profit profit_ratio A 10000 1000 0.10 B 100 50 0.50 Mean of the two ratios: 30.0% Ratio of the sums: 10.4% The kiosk's high ratio counts as much as the big store's in the simple mean, although it sold a hundred times less. The ratio of sums is what the company actually earned per unit of sales. It equals the average of the store ratios weighted by each store's share of sales. The same choice appears in the tips data. "The tip percentage" could mean either number below: per_bill_pct = 100 * tips [ "tip" ] / tips [ "total_bill" ] print ( f "Mean of each bill's tip %: { per_bill_pct . mean () : .2f } %" ) print ( f "Total tips / total bills (ratio of sums): { 100 * tips [ 'tip' ] . sum () / tips [ 'total_bill' ] . sum () : .2f } %" ) print ( f "Largest single-bill tip %: { per_bill_pct . max () : .1f } % on a bill of " f " { tips . loc [ per_bill_pct . idxmax (), 'total_bill' ] : .2f } dollars" ) Mean of each bill's tip %: 16.08% Total tips / total bills (ratio of sums): 15.15% Largest single-bill tip %: 71.0% on a bill of 7.25 dollars The two answers in the output above differ because small bills tend to leave a higher percentage tip, and in the mean of ratios each small bill gets the same vote as a large one. Neither number is wrong, but they answer different questions: Question Use "Of all the money customers spent, what share went to tips?" (server income, a KPI) Ratio of sums "How generous is a typical table?" Mean (or median) of each bill's ratio, labelled as such Totals first, then divide For a KPI tile, compute the ratio from totals. The stages shrink so fast that a log scale is needed to see them all on one chart (each grid step is ten times the one before). A log axis has no zero, so bars would have meaningless lengths: we use dots, read by position. COUNTS = [ "spend" , "impressions" , "clicks" , "sessions" , "orders" , "revenue" ] stages = [ "impressions" , "clicks" , "sessions" , "orders" ] company = funnel [ stages ] . sum () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.2 )) ax . scatter ( company , stages , s = 80 , color = BLUE , zorder = 3 ) # dots, not bars: a log axis has no zero ax . set_xscale ( "log" ) ax . invert_yaxis () for i , value in enumerate ( company ): ax . text ( value , i , f " { value : ,.0f } " , va = "center" , fontsize = 9 ) ax . set_xlim ( company . min () / 3 , company . max () * 30 ) ax . set_title ( "Each funnel stage is a small fraction of the one before" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Count over 12 weeks (log scale; synthetic data)" ) ax . grid ( axis = "y" , visible = False ) plt . show () Now the KPIs for each channel. groupby adds up the counts first; then we divide the sums. A zero denominator gives "not available" ( NaN ), never 0. def safe_div ( numerator , denominator ): """numerator / denominator, left blank (NaN, 'not available') wherever the denominator is 0.""" return numerator / denominator . where ( denominator != 0 ) def add_kpis ( totals ): """Add funnel KPIs to a table of SUMMED counts (ratios of sums).""" t = totals . copy () t [ "CTR %" ] = 100 * safe_div ( t [ "clicks" ], t [ "impressions" ]) t [ "conv %" ] = 100 * safe_div ( t [ "orders" ], t [ "sessions" ]) t [ "CPA" ] = safe_div ( t [ "spend" ], t [ "orders" ]) t [ "ROAS" ] = safe_div ( t [ "revenue" ], t [ "spend" ]) t [ "AOV" ] = safe_div ( t [ "revenue" ], t [ "orders" ]) return t by_channel = add_kpis ( funnel . groupby ( "channel" )[ COUNTS ] . sum ()) . sort_values ( "spend" , ascending = False ) by_channel [[ "spend" , "orders" , "revenue" , "CTR %" , "conv %" , "CPA" , "ROAS" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } spend orders revenue CTR % conv % CPA ROAS channel Search 48,727.58 5284 322,961.42 2.99 4.04 9.22 6.63 Social 37,566.34 1133 56,152.17 0.79 1.49 33.16 1.49 Display 24,305.94 170 9,260.35 0.15 0.79 142.98 0.38 Email 1,814.09 1025 64,734.18 2.52 2.95 1.77 35.68 Predict, then reveal Look at Email's ROAS in the table above. Is Email really many times better at turning money into revenue? Look at its spend and orders columns before you answer, then run the next cell. share = by_channel [[ "spend" , "orders" ]] / by_channel [[ "spend" , "orders" ]] . sum () * 100 share . columns = [ " % o f spend" , " % o f orders" ] share . join ( by_channel [[ "ROAS" ]]) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } % of spend % of orders ROAS channel Search 43.35 69.42 6.63 Social 33.42 14.88 1.49 Display 21.62 2.23 0.38 Email 1.61 13.47 35.68 Email takes a tiny share of the spend but a real share of the orders. Its "spend" covers only a small sending cost; it leaves out building the mailing list, writing the emails and any discounts offered. A ratio with a tiny denominator looks extreme. Report Email's ROAS, but do not rank it against paid media as if the costs were comparable. Two limits of ROAS ¶ ROAS is not profit. Revenue of 4 per unit of spend sounds good, but if the product's profit ratio is 20%, each unit of spend earns 0.8 of profit: a loss before any other cost. ROAS is not causal. Revenue "attributed" to a channel includes customers who would have bought anyway. Only an experiment (show the ads to a random group, hold out another) measures the extra sales the ads caused. Attribution: who gets the credit? ¶ Customers often meet several channels before they buy. An attribution rule decides which channel gets the credit. Here are five made-up customer journeys: journeys = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer" : [ "C1" , "C2" , "C3" , "C4" , "C5" ], "path" : [[ "Social" , "Search" ], [ "Display" , "Social" , "Email" ], [ "Search" ], [ "Social" , "Email" ], [ "Display" , "Search" ]], }) journeys [ "first_touch" ] = journeys [ "path" ] . str [ 0 ] journeys [ "last_touch" ] = journeys [ "path" ] . str [ - 1 ] credit = pd . DataFrame ({ "first-touch credit" : journeys [ "first_touch" ] . value_counts (), "last-touch credit" : journeys [ "last_touch" ] . value_counts (), }) . reindex ([ "Search" , "Social" , "Display" , "Email" ]) . fillna ( 0 ) . astype ( int ) print ( journeys [[ "customer" , "path" ]] . to_string ( index = False )) credit customer path C1 [Social, Search] C2 [Display, Social, Email] C3 [Search] C4 [Social, Email] C5 [Display, Search] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } first-touch credit last-touch credit Search 1 3 Social 2 0 Display 2 0 Email 0 2 The same five purchases, two rules, two different "best" channels. Last-touch favours channels that close the sale (search, email); first-touch favours channels that introduce people (social, display). Neither rule is the truth: each is a convention. When a report says "Search drove 40% of sales", ask which rule and remember that a rule is not an experiment. Segmentation ¶ Segmentation splits customers into groups that behave differently, so each group can get a different offer. A useful segment is large enough to matter, different in a way you can measure, and reachable. A first look with the tips data, segmenting bills by party size : segments = tips . assign ( party = pd . cut ( tips [ "size" ], [ 0 , 1 , 2 , 4 , 6 ], labels = [ "1" , "2" , "3-4" , "5-6" ])) seg = segments . groupby ( "party" , observed = True ) . agg ( bills = ( "total_bill" , "size" ), revenue = ( "total_bill" , "sum" ), tips = ( "tip" , "sum" ), people = ( "size" , "sum" ), ) seg [ " % o f bills" ] = 100 * seg [ "bills" ] / seg [ "bills" ] . sum () seg [ " % o f revenue" ] = 100 * seg [ "revenue" ] / seg [ "revenue" ] . sum () seg [ "spend per person" ] = seg [ "revenue" ] / seg [ "people" ] seg [ "tip % (sum/sum)" ] = 100 * seg [ "tips" ] / seg [ "revenue" ] seg [[ "bills" , " % o f bills" , " % o f revenue" , "spend per person" , "tip % (sum/sum)" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } bills % of bills % of revenue spend per person tip % (sum/sum) party 1 4 1.64 0.60 7.24 19.85 2 156 63.93 53.15 8.22 15.70 3-4 75 30.74 40.25 7.42 14.51 5-6 9 3.69 6.00 5.91 14.17 Read the output above as a marketer: which segment brings most of the revenue, and which spends most per person ? Segments differ in size and in value ; a promotion aimed at a small, high-value segment and one aimed at the largest segment are different decisions. Customer lifetime value (CLV), the intuition ¶ A customer is worth more than one order. A simple CLV estimate multiplies what a customer brings per year by how long they stay: CLV ≈ average order value × orders per year × profit ratio × expected years as a customer Compare CLV with what it costs to win a customer (the CPA for new customers). If winning a customer costs more than they are ever worth, the campaign destroys value however good its ROAS looks. A worked example with the synthetic funnel's AOV and assumed loyalty figures: aov_all = funnel [ "revenue" ] . sum () / funnel [ "orders" ] . sum () cpa_all = funnel [ "spend" ] . sum () / funnel [ "orders" ] . sum () # Assumptions (made up for teaching): a 20% profit ratio; loyal customers order more often and stay longer. PROFIT_RATIO = 0.20 clv = pd . DataFrame ({ "orders per year" : [ 1.0 , 4.0 ], "expected years" : [ 1.0 , 3.0 ], }, index = [ "one-off buyer" , "loyal customer" ]) clv [ "CLV" ] = aov_all * clv [ "orders per year" ] * PROFIT_RATIO * clv [ "expected years" ] clv [ "CLV / CPA" ] = clv [ "CLV" ] / cpa_all print ( f "Average order value (all channels): { aov_all : .2f } currency units" ) print ( f "Cost per order, used here as the cost of winning a customer: { cpa_all : .2f } currency units" ) clv Average order value (all channels): 59.53 currency units Cost per order, used here as the cost of winning a customer: 14.77 currency units .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } orders per year expected years CLV CLV / CPA one-off buyer 1.00 1.00 11.91 0.81 loyal customer 4.00 3.00 142.86 9.67 In the output above, compare each row's CLV with the cost per order: a CLV / CPA below 1 means the customer is worth less than it cost to win them. The same acquisition cost can be a loss on a one-off buyer and a good investment for a loyal customer. That is why marketers care about retention , not only acquisition. The figures are assumptions: a real CLV needs purchase histories, and should be stated with its assumptions. A small marketing dashboard ¶ Everything in this lecture comes together on one page: a headline, four KPI tiles with comparisons, three views and a scope note. Views: three charts, each answering one part of the question. Colour: grey means "for comparison"; orange appears only for the channel that needs attention. Not colour alone: channels are labelled at the line ends and on the bars. Scope note: it says the data are synthetic, gives units and formulas, and states the main limit of ROAS. Summary ¶ Idea One-line takeaway Task first Compare → bars; distribution → histogram; relationship → scatter; time → line Encodings Position and length are read best; angle, area and colour worse Pre-attentive, data-ink, Gestalt One highlight against grey; remove what carries no data; place side by side what must be compared Colour Categorical, sequential or diverging by the data; colour-blind safe; never colour alone Honest charts Bars from zero; no dual axes (index instead); scale areas, not sides; show the full window Communication Audience and decision first; one big idea; situation, complication, resolution; message titles Challenger The rows you leave out can change the answer Dashboards One decision, 3–5 views, KPI tiles with comparisons, scope note; ratio KPIs as ratio of sums Marketing Funnel rates and CPA/ROAS are ratios of sums; ROAS is not profit or causation; attribution is a convention; CLV against CPA Closing quiz ¶ Answer in your own words, alone, in two or three minutes per question. docs.title: Lecture: Visualising and communicating results

docs.text: A chart is an argument made with shapes and colours. This lecture shows how the eye reads a chart, how charts mislead and how to rebuild them honestly, how to turn findings into a short story for a decision-maker, how to design a dashboard around a few good KPIs, and how marketing teams measure their funnel. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter .

Use pre-attentive attributes , data-ink and Gestalt principles to direct the reader's eye. Choose categorical , sequential or diverging colour, and keep charts readable for colour-blind readers. Spot a misleading chart (truncated bars, dual axes, scaled areas, crowded pies) and rebuild it honestly. Turn findings into a story: audience , big idea , situation, complication, resolution and message titles . Explain what the Challenger O-ring data show when the flights with no damage are included. Lay out a dashboard with 3–5 views and KPI tiles, and compute ratio KPIs as a ratio of sums . Read a marketing funnel and compute conversion rate, CPA and ROAS ; explain segmentation, customer lifetime value and the limits of attribution. Reading: Tableau Software (n.d.), What is data visualization? ; the course pages Designing clear visuals and Storytelling with data .
