docs.text: Day 3 lab: Applied Lab 4 — Forecasting ¶ Forecast atmospheric CO₂ the way a professional would: test whether the series is stationary, hide the most recent fifth of the data, fit a seasonal ARIMA model to the rest, forecast the hidden period, and prove the model's accuracy with RMSE and MAE before anyone relies on it. Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Applied Lab 4 (Forecasting), for local Jupyter without internet access. Graded Yes: 3% of the course grade Outcomes CLO 1, 2 and 5 Tool JupyterLab (Anaconda), with statsmodels and scikit-learn You submit One PDF, YourLastName_DATA300_AppliedLab4.pdf , in the Applied Lab 4 drop-box on GAP (Moodle) Deadline Thursday 12 November, 23:59 China Standard Time, unless your facilitator says otherwise (see the schedule ) The business scenario ¶ You are a data scientist at Global Climate Analytics . You have been asked to predict future levels of carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the atmosphere from the long record measured at the Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii. Concentrations are in parts per million (ppm) . Your forecast will be presented to environmental policymakers, so you must first show that it is accurate. You cannot do that by forecasting the unknown future. Instead you hold back the most recent part of the history, let the model forecast those months without seeing them, and compare its forecasts with what was actually measured. Your tasks: Stationarity: test the series with the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test. Train/test split: divide the series in time order into a training set (the first 80%) and a test set (the last 20%). Model and evaluate: fit a Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA) model on the training set only, forecast the test period, and measure the error with RMSE and MAE. This is predictive analytics, judged by the standards a business intelligence team would apply before a forecast supports a decision. Before you start ¶ Keep this notebook in the course folder. Save your own copy: File → Save Notebook As… and type YourLastName_Data300_AppliedLab4.ipynb (with your real last name). Work in that copy. The code below works as given. Run each cell in order with Shift + Enter , read the output, and answer the questions in Part 4. You may add cells of your own to check an answer. Part 1: Load the data and test for stationarity ¶ The CO₂ data ship inside statsmodels , so they load without internet. The raw series is weekly with some missing weeks; the cell averages it to monthly values and fills any month without a measurement with the value of the month before. ARIMA models assume the series is stationary : its average and spread do not drift over time. The ADF test checks this. Its null hypothesis is that the series is not stationary: ADF p-value Conclusion p > 0.05 Not enough evidence of stationarity: the series has a trend and must be differenced p ≤ 0.05 The series can be treated as stationary # 1. Libraries import warnings import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , mean_squared_error from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller warnings . filterwarnings ( "ignore" ) # hide notices about future library changes and fitting messages # 2. Load the CO2 series that ships with statsmodels dataset = sm . datasets . co2 . load_pandas () df = dataset . data # 3. Weekly to monthly averages ("ME" = month end); fill months with no measurement df = df . resample ( "ME" ) . mean () . ffill () # 4. Plot the monthly series plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 4 )) plt . plot ( df . index , df [ "co2" ], color = "#2a78d6" ) plt . title ( "Monthly CO2 levels (Mauna Loa Observatory)" ) plt . ylabel ( "CO2 (ppm)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Date" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () # 5. Stationarity test: Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) print ( "--- Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test results ---" ) adf_result = adfuller ( df [ "co2" ]) print ( f "ADF statistic: { adf_result [ 0 ] : .4f } " ) print ( f "p-value: { adf_result [ 1 ] : .4f } " ) if adf_result [ 1 ] > 0.05 : print ( "Conclusion: the p-value is above 0.05. The series is NOT stationary (it has a trend)." ) else : print ( "Conclusion: the p-value is 0.05 or below. The series IS stationary." ) --- Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test results --- ADF statistic: 2.2848 p-value: 0.9989 Conclusion: the p-value is above 0.05. The series is NOT stationary (it has a trend). Use this output for question 1. Part 2: Train/test split in time order ¶ A time series must be split in time order , never at random: the model learns from the earlier training set (the first 80% of months) and is judged on the later test set (the last 20%), which it never sees during fitting. This is how a forecast is used in real life: the past predicts the future. # 1. Sequential split: first 80% for training, last 20% for testing train_size = int ( len ( df ) * 0.8 ) train_data , test_data = df . iloc [: train_size ], df . iloc [ train_size :] print ( f "Total observations: { len ( df ) } months" ) print ( f "Training period: { len ( train_data ) } months ( { train_data . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { train_data . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } )" ) print ( f "Test period: { len ( test_data ) } months ( { test_data . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { test_data . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } )" ) # 2. Show the split plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 4 )) plt . plot ( train_data . index , train_data [ "co2" ], label = "Training data (80%)" , color = "#2a78d6" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , test_data [ "co2" ], label = "Test data (20%), hidden from the model" , color = "#eb6834" ) plt . title ( "Sequential train / test split" ) plt . ylabel ( "CO2 (ppm)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Date" ) plt . legend ( loc = "upper left" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () Total observations: 526 months Training period: 420 months (Mar 1958 to Feb 1993) Test period: 106 months (Mar 1993 to Dec 2001) Part 3: SARIMA model and accuracy ¶ The series has a long upward trend and a strong 12-month seasonal pattern, so we fit a Seasonal ARIMA model, written SARIMA(p, d, q) × (P, D, Q)ₛ: Part Values here Meaning (p, d, q) (1, 1, 1) One autoregressive term, one difference to remove the trend, one moving-average error term (P, D, Q, s) (1, 1, 1, 12) The same three ideas at the seasonal lag of 12 months The model is fitted on the training data only . It then forecasts every month of the test period, and two measures compare the forecasts with the actual values: Measure Meaning MAE , mean absolute error The average size of the miss, in ppm RMSE , root mean squared error Like MAE, but large misses count more; always at least as large as MAE Fitting can take 10–20 seconds. # 1. Fit the SARIMA model on the TRAINING data only print ( "Fitting the SARIMA model (this may take 10-20 seconds)..." ) model = sm . tsa . statespace . SARIMAX ( train_data [ "co2" ], order = ( 1 , 1 , 1 ), seasonal_order = ( 1 , 1 , 1 , 12 ), ) sarima_result = model . fit ( disp = False ) # 2. Forecast every month of the TEST period forecast_steps = len ( test_data ) predictions = sarima_result . get_forecast ( steps = forecast_steps ) pred_mean = predictions . predicted_mean # 3. Accuracy on the hidden test period rmse = np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], pred_mean )) mae = mean_absolute_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], pred_mean ) print ( " \n --- Out-of-sample accuracy on the test period ---" ) print ( f "Root mean squared error (RMSE): { rmse : .2f } ppm" ) print ( f "Mean absolute error (MAE): { mae : .2f } ppm" ) # 4. Compare the forecast with what actually happened plt . figure ( figsize = ( 12 , 6 )) plt . plot ( train_data . index [ - 50 :], train_data [ "co2" ][ - 50 :], label = "Recent training data" , color = "#2a78d6" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , test_data [ "co2" ], label = "Actual test data" , color = "#eb6834" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , pred_mean , label = "SARIMA forecast (out of sample)" , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" ) plt . title ( "SARIMA forecast against the hidden test period" ) plt . ylabel ( "CO2 (ppm)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Date" ) plt . legend ( loc = "upper left" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () Fitting the SARIMA model (this may take 10-20 seconds)... --- Out-of-sample accuracy on the test period --- Root mean squared error (RMSE): 2.13 ppm Mean absolute error (MAE): 1.81 ppm Use the error measures and the chart above for questions 3 and 4. In the chart, the black dashed line is the model's forecast and the solid orange line is what was actually measured. Part 4: Questions ¶ Answer all four questions in complete sentences in the answer cell below. Base every answer on the outputs in this notebook, and quote the numbers you use. # Question 1 Stationarity and differencing. (a) What exact p-value did the ADF test in Part 1 give? (b) Using that p-value, explain why the model differences the series once (the non-seasonal setting d = 1) instead of fitting an ARMA model to the undifferenced series. 2 Why hold back a test period? Part 2 kept the last 20% of the history away from the model while it was fitted. In a real consulting project, why is this time-ordered train/test check much stronger evidence than fitting the model to 100% of the history? Name the risk it protects against. 3 Judging the error. (a) State the MAE you obtained in Part 3. (b) CO₂ concentrations in this data are roughly 350 ppm or more. Is this error excellent , acceptable or poor ? Justify your judgement, for example by expressing the error as a percentage of the level, or by comparing it with the size of the yearly seasonal swing visible in the charts. 4 Reading the forecast chart. In the final chart of Part 3, did the SARIMA forecast reproduce (a) the overall upward direction and (b) the repeating yearly up-and-down pattern of CO₂? Describe any systematic gap you see between the dashed and the solid line. Writing tips Lead with the answer, then the evidence: "The ADF p-value of … is well above 0.05, so …" . Keep units (ppm, months). For question 3, a policymaker should be able to understand your judgement without knowing what RMSE means. My answers Name: Your name · Student ID: Your ID 1. (a) ADF p-value: Your answer 1. (b) Why difference once (d = 1): Your answer 2. Why a time-ordered train/test check, and the risk it reduces: Your answer 3. (a) MAE: Your answer 3. (b) Excellent, acceptable or poor, and why: Your answer 4. Trend, seasonal pattern and any systematic gap: Your answer Going further (not graded) ¶ Two checks a careful analyst adds. First, a baseline : the seasonal naive forecast simply repeats the value from the same month one year earlier. A model is only worth its complexity if it beats this. Second, a 95% forecast interval : the range the model expects the actual values to fall in. The cell below computes both for the same test period. # Seasonal naive baseline: each test month gets the value from 12 months earlier # (for test months beyond the first year, that value is itself the earlier forecast) history = list ( train_data [ "co2" ]) naive = [] for _ in range ( len ( test_data )): naive . append ( history [ - 12 ]) history . append ( history [ - 12 ]) naive = pd . Series ( naive , index = test_data . index ) baseline = pd . DataFrame ({ "MAE (ppm)" : [ mean_absolute_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], pred_mean ), mean_absolute_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], naive )], "RMSE (ppm)" : [ np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], pred_mean )), np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], naive ))], }, index = [ "SARIMA" , "Seasonal naive baseline" ]) print ( baseline . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) # 95% forecast interval from the SARIMA model interval = predictions . conf_int ( alpha = 0.05 ) inside = (( test_data [ "co2" ] >= interval . iloc [:, 0 ]) & ( test_data [ "co2" ] <= interval . iloc [:, 1 ])) . mean () print ( f " \n Share of test months inside the 95% interval: { inside : .0% } " ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 12 , 5 )) plt . fill_between ( test_data . index , interval . iloc [:, 0 ], interval . iloc [:, 1 ], color = "#2a78d6" , alpha = 0.2 , label = "95 % f orecast interval" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , test_data [ "co2" ], label = "Actual test data" , color = "#eb6834" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , pred_mean , label = "SARIMA forecast" , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , naive , label = "Seasonal naive baseline" , color = "#9a9890" , linestyle = ":" ) plt . title ( "SARIMA forecast with its 95 % i nterval, against a simple baseline" ) plt . ylabel ( "CO2 (ppm)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Date" ) plt . legend ( loc = "upper left" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () MAE (ppm) RMSE (ppm) SARIMA 1.81 2.13 Seasonal naive baseline 7.93 9.13 Share of test months inside the 95% interval: 100% Does SARIMA beat the baseline, and by how much? Why does the interval widen towards the end of the test period? Do the actual values stay inside it, or drift towards one edge, and what does that suggest about the trend in the 1990s? The raw series is weekly with some missing weeks; the cell averages it to monthly values and fills any month without a measurement with the value of the month before. Its null hypothesis is that the series is not stationary: ADF p-value Conclusion p > 0.05 Not enough evidence of stationarity: the series has a trend and must be differenced p ≤ 0.05 The series can be treated as stationary # 1. Libraries import warnings import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , mean_squared_error from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller warnings . filterwarnings ( "ignore" ) # hide notices about future library changes and fitting messages # 2. Load the CO2 series that ships with statsmodels dataset = sm . datasets . co2 . load_pandas () df = dataset . data # 3. Weekly to monthly averages ("ME" = month end); fill months with no measurement df = df . resample ( "ME" ) . mean () . ffill () # 4. Plot the monthly series plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 4 )) plt . plot ( df . index , df [ "co2" ], color = "#2a78d6" ) plt . title ( "Monthly CO2 levels (Mauna Loa Observatory)" ) plt . ylabel ( "CO2 (ppm)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Date" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () # 5. Stationarity test: Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) print ( "--- Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test results ---" ) adf_result = adfuller ( df [ "co2" ]) print ( f "ADF statistic: { adf_result [ 0 ] : .4f } " ) print ( f "p-value: { adf_result [ 1 ] : .4f } " ) if adf_result [ 1 ] > 0.05 : print ( "Conclusion: the p-value is above 0.05. The series is NOT stationary (it has a trend)." ) else : print ( "Conclusion: the p-value is 0.05 or below. The series IS stationary." ) --- Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test results --- ADF statistic: 2.2848 p-value: 0.9989 Conclusion: the p-value is above 0.05. The series is NOT stationary (it has a trend). Use this output for question 1.
docs.title: Part 1: Load the data and test for stationarity

docs.text: A time series must be split in time order , never at random: the model learns from the earlier training set (the first 80% of months) and is judged on the later test set (the last 20%), which it never sees during fitting. This is how a forecast is used in real life: the past predicts the future. # 1. Sequential split: first 80% for training, last 20% for testing train_size = int ( len ( df ) * 0.8 ) train_data , test_data = df . iloc [: train_size ], df . iloc [ train_size :] print ( f "Total observations: { len ( df ) } months" ) print ( f "Training period: { len ( train_data ) } months ( { train_data . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { train_data . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } )" ) print ( f "Test period: { len ( test_data ) } months ( { test_data . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { test_data . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } )" ) # 2. Show the split plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 4 )) plt . plot ( train_data . index , train_data [ "co2" ], label = "Training data (80%)" , color = "#2a78d6" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , test_data [ "co2" ], label = "Test data (20%), hidden from the model" , color = "#eb6834" ) plt . title ( "Sequential train / test split" ) plt . ylabel ( "CO2 (ppm)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Date" ) plt . legend ( loc = "upper left" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () Total observations: 526 months Training period: 420 months (Mar 1958 to Feb 1993) Test period: 106 months (Mar 1993 to Dec 2001)
docs.title: Part 2: Train/test split in time order

docs.text: The series has a long upward trend and a strong 12-month seasonal pattern, so we fit a Seasonal ARIMA model, written SARIMA(p, d, q) × (P, D, Q)ₛ: Part Values here Meaning (p, d, q) (1, 1, 1) One autoregressive term, one difference to remove the trend, one moving-average error term (P, D, Q, s) (1, 1, 1, 12) The same three ideas at the seasonal lag of 12 months The model is fitted on the training data only . It then forecasts every month of the test period, and two measures compare the forecasts with the actual values: Measure Meaning MAE , mean absolute error The average size of the miss, in ppm RMSE , root mean squared error Like MAE, but large misses count more; always at least as large as MAE Fitting can take 10–20 seconds. # 1. Fit the SARIMA model on the TRAINING data only print ( "Fitting the SARIMA model (this may take 10-20 seconds)..." ) model = sm . tsa . statespace . SARIMAX ( train_data [ "co2" ], order = ( 1 , 1 , 1 ), seasonal_order = ( 1 , 1 , 1 , 12 ), ) sarima_result = model . fit ( disp = False ) # 2. Forecast every month of the TEST period forecast_steps = len ( test_data ) predictions = sarima_result . get_forecast ( steps = forecast_steps ) pred_mean = predictions . predicted_mean # 3. Accuracy on the hidden test period rmse = np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], pred_mean )) mae = mean_absolute_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], pred_mean ) print ( " \n --- Out-of-sample accuracy on the test period ---" ) print ( f "Root mean squared error (RMSE): { rmse : .2f } ppm" ) print ( f "Mean absolute error (MAE): { mae : .2f } ppm" ) # 4. Compare the forecast with what actually happened plt . figure ( figsize = ( 12 , 6 )) plt . plot ( train_data . index [ - 50 :], train_data [ "co2" ][ - 50 :], label = "Recent training data" , color = "#2a78d6" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , test_data [ "co2" ], label = "Actual test data" , color = "#eb6834" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , pred_mean , label = "SARIMA forecast (out of sample)" , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" ) plt . title ( "SARIMA forecast against the hidden test period" ) plt . ylabel ( "CO2 (ppm)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Date" ) plt . legend ( loc = "upper left" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () Fitting the SARIMA model (this may take 10-20 seconds)... --- Out-of-sample accuracy on the test period --- Root mean squared error (RMSE): 2.13 ppm Mean absolute error (MAE): 1.81 ppm Use the error measures and the chart above for questions 3 and 4. In the chart, the black dashed line is the model's forecast and the solid orange line is what was actually measured.

docs.text: Two checks a careful analyst adds. First, a baseline : the seasonal naive forecast simply repeats the value from the same month one year earlier. A model is only worth its complexity if it beats this. Second, a 95% forecast interval : the range the model expects the actual values to fall in. The cell below computes both for the same test period. # Seasonal naive baseline: each test month gets the value from 12 months earlier # (for test months beyond the first year, that value is itself the earlier forecast) history = list ( train_data [ "co2" ]) naive = [] for _ in range ( len ( test_data )): naive . append ( history [ - 12 ]) history . append ( history [ - 12 ]) naive = pd . Series ( naive , index = test_data . index ) baseline = pd . DataFrame ({ "MAE (ppm)" : [ mean_absolute_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], pred_mean ), mean_absolute_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], naive )], "RMSE (ppm)" : [ np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], pred_mean )), np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test_data [ "co2" ], naive ))], }, index = [ "SARIMA" , "Seasonal naive baseline" ]) print ( baseline . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) # 95% forecast interval from the SARIMA model interval = predictions . conf_int ( alpha = 0.05 ) inside = (( test_data [ "co2" ] >= interval . iloc [:, 0 ]) & ( test_data [ "co2" ] <= interval . iloc [:, 1 ])) . mean () print ( f " \n Share of test months inside the 95% interval: { inside : .0% } " ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 12 , 5 )) plt . fill_between ( test_data . index , interval . iloc [:, 0 ], interval . iloc [:, 1 ], color = "#2a78d6" , alpha = 0.2 , label = "95 % f orecast interval" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , test_data [ "co2" ], label = "Actual test data" , color = "#eb6834" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , pred_mean , label = "SARIMA forecast" , color = "black" , linestyle = "--" ) plt . plot ( test_data . index , naive , label = "Seasonal naive baseline" , color = "#9a9890" , linestyle = ":" ) plt . title ( "SARIMA forecast with its 95 % i nterval, against a simple baseline" ) plt . ylabel ( "CO2 (ppm)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Date" ) plt . legend ( loc = "upper left" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () MAE (ppm) RMSE (ppm) SARIMA 1.81 2.13 Seasonal naive baseline 7.93 9.13 Share of test months inside the 95% interval: 100% Does SARIMA beat the baseline, and by how much? Why does the interval widen towards the end of the test period? Do the actual values stay inside it, or drift towards one edge, and what does that suggest about the trend in the 1990s?

docs.text: Day 3 lecture: Forecasting ¶ Budgets, stock orders, staff rosters and climate policy all rest on a forecast. This lecture shows how to read a time series as trend, seasonality and noise, how to forecast it with moving averages, exponential smoothing and ARIMA models, how to test a forecast honestly on data the model has never seen, and how to report the uncertainty with a forecast interval. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . What you will be able to do ¶ Describe a time series by its trend , seasonality and noise , and split it with a decomposition . Smooth a series with a moving average and explain why a trailing average lags behind a trend. Split a time series into training and test periods in time order, and explain why it must not be shuffled. Compute and interpret MAE , RMSE and MAPE , and compare models with a baseline . Explain exponential smoothing (simple, Holt and Holt-Winters) as a weighted average that forgets the past. Explain the idea of ARIMA : autoregression, differencing to remove trend ( stationarity ), and moving-average errors; read an ADF test . Produce a forecast interval , explain why it widens with the horizon, and state a forecast for a decision-maker. Reading: TransImpact (n.d.), Forecasting methods: The complete guide . How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words, alone or with the person next to you. Part Topic 1 Why forecast, and the words we use 2 The data: CO₂ at Mauna Loa 3 Trend, seasonality and decomposition 4 Moving averages 5 Train and test in time order 6 Measuring forecast error, and baselines 7 Exponential smoothing 8 The ARIMA idea 9 Forecast intervals 10 Choosing a model and making the decision Part 1: Why forecast, and the words we use ¶ A forecast is an estimate of a future value, made from past data and stated with its uncertainty. It is predictive analytics: it answers what is likely to happen? The decision about what to do with it is prescriptive . Decision Series to forecast Horizon How much milk tea powder to order next month Monthly drinks sold 1 month How many call-centre staff to roster next week Calls per hour 1–2 weeks Next year's budget Monthly revenue 12 months Emission targets Atmospheric CO₂ Years Word Meaning Time series Values of one measure recorded at regular intervals, in time order Horizon How far ahead we forecast (1 month, 12 months, …) Point forecast The single most likely value Forecast interval A range expected to contain the future value with a stated probability, for example 95% Holdout or test period Recent data hidden from the model, used to measure its error The setup cell loads the libraries. Every model in this lecture comes from statsmodels , part of Anaconda. import warnings import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing , SimpleExpSmoothing from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller # Recent statsmodels versions print a notice that adfuller's output format will change # in a future release. It does not change any result, so we hide that notice. warnings . filterwarnings ( "ignore" , category = FutureWarning ) BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" # context INK = "#55534e" # notes and labels plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 10 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) Part 2: The data: CO₂ at Mauna Loa ¶ The Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii has measured carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the air since 1958. The measure is the concentration in parts per million (ppm) : how many CO₂ molecules there are in every million molecules of air. The series ships inside statsmodels , so it loads without internet. It is weekly, with some weeks missing; we average it to monthly values, and fill the few months with no measurement by carrying the previous month forward. weekly = sm . datasets . co2 . load_pandas () . data monthly_raw = weekly [ "co2" ] . resample ( "ME" ) . mean () # "ME" = month end co2 = monthly_raw . ffill () print ( "Weekly rows:" , len ( weekly ), "| weeks with no value:" , weekly [ "co2" ] . isna () . sum ()) print ( "Monthly values:" , len ( co2 ), "from" , co2 . index [ 0 ] . strftime ( "%b %Y" ), "to" , co2 . index [ - 1 ] . strftime ( "%b %Y" )) print ( "Months with no measurement, filled from the month before:" , monthly_raw . isna () . sum ()) co2 . head () Weekly rows: 2284 | weeks with no value: 59 Monthly values: 526 from Mar 1958 to Dec 2001 Months with no measurement, filled from the month before: 5 1958-03-31 316.100000 1958-04-30 317.200000 1958-05-31 317.433333 1958-06-30 317.433333 1958-07-31 315.625000 Freq: ME, Name: co2, dtype: float64 fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 13 , 4 ), gridspec_kw = { "width_ratios" : [ 2 , 1 ]}) ax1 . plot ( co2 . index , co2 , color = BLUE , linewidth = 1 ) ax1 . set_title ( "CO₂ has risen every decade since 1958" ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) recent = co2 [ "1995" : "1997" ] ax2 . plot ( recent . index , recent , color = BLUE , marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Zoom: 1995-1997" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax2 . tick_params ( axis = "x" , rotation = 45 ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Predict, then reveal Look at the zoomed panel above. In which month of the year is CO₂ highest, and in which is it lowest? (Hint: think about when the forests of the Northern Hemisphere grow leaves.) We check your answer in Part 3. Part 3: Trend, seasonality and decomposition ¶ Most business and natural time series are a mix of a few components : Component Meaning CO₂ example Business example Trend The long-run direction Rising every year Sales growing as a chain opens shops Seasonality A pattern that repeats with a fixed period Peak in spring, dip in autumn, every 12 months More drinks in summer; more calls on Mondays Cycle Longer swings without a fixed period (small here) Economic booms and recessions Noise (residual) What is left: irregular, unpredictable Weather, measurement One-off events, chance In an additive model, value = trend + seasonal + residual: the seasonal swing has the same size in ppm every year. In a multiplicative model, value = trend × seasonal × residual: the swing grows with the level, as with sales that rise 30% every December. The CO₂ swing stays about the same size, so we use additive. seasonal_decompose estimates each component. The trend is a centred 12-month moving average (Part 4), the seasonal part is the average deviation from the trend for each calendar month, and the residual is the rest. parts = seasonal_decompose ( co2 , model = "additive" , period = 12 ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 4 , 1 , figsize = ( 10 , 8 ), sharex = True ) for ax , series , title in zip ( axes , [ co2 , parts . trend , parts . seasonal , parts . resid ], [ "Observed" , "Trend" , "Seasonal" , "Residual (noise)" ], ): ax . plot ( series . index , series , color = BLUE if title != "Residual (noise)" else GREY , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) ax . set_ylabel ( "ppm" ) axes [ - 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) fig . suptitle ( "Additive decomposition of monthly CO₂" , x = 0.02 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () seasonal_effect = parts . seasonal . groupby ( parts . seasonal . index . month ) . mean () seasonal_effect . index = pd . to_datetime ( seasonal_effect . index , format = "%m" ) . strftime ( "%b" ) print ( "Average seasonal effect by calendar month (ppm above or below the trend)" ) print ( seasonal_effect . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Highest month: { seasonal_effect . idxmax () } | lowest month: { seasonal_effect . idxmin () } " ) print ( f "Seasonal swing, highest minus lowest: { seasonal_effect . max () - seasonal_effect . min () : .2f } ppm" ) Average seasonal effect by calendar month (ppm above or below the trend) Jan -0.01 Feb 0.62 Mar 1.40 Apr 2.46 May 2.93 Jun 2.29 Jul 0.75 Aug -1.31 Sep -3.04 Oct -3.14 Nov -2.04 Dec -0.91 Highest month: May | lowest month: Oct Seasonal swing, highest minus lowest: 6.07 ppm Check your prediction against the output above. Plants in the Northern Hemisphere absorb CO₂ as they grow in summer, so concentration falls from late spring to early autumn and rises again over winter. Check your understanding A shop's monthly sales rise by about 2% a year and are 40% higher every December than in an average month. Name the components, and say whether you would use an additive or a multiplicative model. Why are the first and last six months of the trend panel empty? Part 4: Moving averages ¶ A moving average replaces each value with the average of a window of neighbouring values. It smooths out the noise and the seasonal swing so the trend is easier to see. Type Window Use Centred Months before and after Describing the past (the trend line in a decomposition) Trailing The last k months only Forecasting: it uses only what is already known A 12-month window contains exactly one of each calendar month, so the seasonal swing cancels out. window = co2 [ "1990" :] centred = co2 . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean ()[ "1990" :] trailing = co2 . rolling ( 12 ) . mean ()[ "1990" :] fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( window . index , window , color = GREY , linewidth = 1 , label = "Monthly value" ) ax . plot ( centred . index , centred , color = BLUE , linewidth = 2 , label = "Centred 12-month average" ) ax . plot ( trailing . index , trailing , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 , label = "Trailing 12-month average" ) ax . set_title ( "A trailing average runs below a rising series" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () gap = ( window - trailing ) . mean () print ( f "On average, the monthly value is { gap : .2f } ppm above its trailing 12-month average (1990-2001)." ) On average, the monthly value is 0.69 ppm above its trailing 12-month average (1990-2001). The trailing average describes the middle of the last twelve months, about six months ago. When the series has a trend, a forecast that says "next month = average of the last 12 months" will be systematically too low for a rising series (too high for a falling one). Forecasting methods that follow a trend fix this. Part 5: Train and test in time order ¶ How do we know whether a forecast is good before the future arrives? We pretend part of the past is the future: Hide the most recent months: the test period (also called holdout). Fit the model on the earlier months only: the training period. Forecast the test period and compare with what actually happened. Here we hide the last 36 months (1999–2001) and train on everything before. Never shuffle a time series In a random split, the model would train on months after some test months and "see the future". The test must come after the training data, exactly as in real forecasting. HORIZON = 36 train , test = co2 . iloc [: - HORIZON ], co2 . iloc [ - HORIZON :] print ( f "Training: { train . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { train . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } ( { len ( train ) } months)" ) print ( f "Test: { test . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { test . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } ( { len ( test ) } months)" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1990" :] . index , train [ "1990" :], color = BLUE , label = "Training data (the model sees this)" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = ORANGE , label = "Test data (hidden from the model)" ) ax . axvline ( test . index [ 0 ], color = INK , linestyle = ":" , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_title ( "We hide the last three years and try to forecast them" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Training: Mar 1958 to Dec 1998 (490 months) Test: Jan 1999 to Dec 2001 (36 months) Part 6: Measuring forecast error, and baselines ¶ The error for one month is actual minus forecast. Three ways to summarise many errors: Measure Formula, in words Units Read it as MAE , mean absolute error Average of the absolute errors Same as the data (ppm) "On average the forecast is off by … ppm" RMSE , root mean squared error Square the errors, average, take the square root Same as the data Like MAE, but punishes large misses more; always ≥ MAE MAPE , mean absolute percentage error Average of absolute error ÷ actual, in % Per cent "Off by …% on average"; easy to explain, but misleading when actual values are near zero Always compare a model with a baseline : a forecast so simple that a model must beat it to be worth using. Baseline Forecast for every future month Naive The last value seen Seasonal naive The value in the same month one year earlier Average The average of the last 12 months (the trailing moving average) def forecast_errors ( actual , forecast ): """MAE, RMSE and MAPE of a forecast against the actual values.""" error = np . asarray ( actual ) - np . asarray ( forecast ) return { "MAE" : np . mean ( np . abs ( error )), "RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean ( error ** 2 )), "MAPE %" : 100 * np . mean ( np . abs ( error / np . asarray ( actual ))), } forecasts = pd . DataFrame ( index = test . index ) forecasts [ "naive" ] = train . iloc [ - 1 ] forecasts [ "seasonal naive" ] = np . tile ( train . iloc [ - 12 :] . values , HORIZON // 12 ) forecasts [ "12-month average" ] = train . iloc [ - 12 :] . mean () scores = pd . DataFrame ({ name : forecast_errors ( test , forecasts [ name ]) for name in forecasts }) . T scores . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % naive 2.839 3.336 0.766 seasonal naive 2.866 3.109 0.774 12-month average 3.059 3.580 0.825 Predict, then reveal All three baselines are flat or repeat last year. Before you run the next cell, sketch what each one looks like against the rising test data. Which one will at least follow the seasonal zig-zag? fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1997" :] . index , train [ "1997" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) for name , colour in zip ( forecasts . columns , [ BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA ]): ax . plot ( forecasts . index , forecasts [ name ], color = colour , linestyle = "--" , label = name ) ax . set_title ( "Simple baselines miss the trend" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () In the table above, MAPE is well under 1% for every baseline. That looks excellent, but only because the level of CO₂ is large. A fairer yardstick is the size of the changes we care about : the seasonal swing from Part 3 is a few ppm, and the trend adds well over 1 ppm a year. Judge an error against the decision, not only against the level. Check your understanding A forecast of daily sales has a MAPE of 4% on most days but 300% on public holidays, when the shop is almost closed. What causes the 300%, and which measure would you report instead? Part 7: Exponential smoothing ¶ A moving average gives the last 12 months equal weight and everything older no weight. Exponential smoothing gives every past value a weight that shrinks the further back it is. One number, α (alpha, between 0 and 1), sets how quickly the past is forgotten. weights = pd . DataFrame ({ f "alpha = { alpha } " : [ alpha * ( 1 - alpha ) ** k for k in range ( 6 )] for alpha in ( 0.2 , 0.8 ) }, index = [ "latest month" , "1 month ago" ] + [ f " { k } months ago" for k in range ( 2 , 6 )]) print ( "Weight given to each past value" ) weights . round ( 3 ) Weight given to each past value .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } alpha = 0.2 alpha = 0.8 latest month 0.200 0.800 1 month ago 0.160 0.160 2 months ago 0.128 0.032 3 months ago 0.102 0.006 4 months ago 0.082 0.001 5 months ago 0.066 0.000 With a large α, the forecast follows the latest values closely (reacts fast, but also to noise). With a small α, it averages over a long history (stable, but slow to react). The model chooses α by fitting the training data. Method Follows Use when the series has Simple exponential smoothing A level only No trend, no seasonality Holt (double) Level + trend A trend, no seasonality Holt-Winters (triple) Level + trend + seasonality A trend and a repeating season ses = SimpleExpSmoothing ( train , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () holt = ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () holt_winters = ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , seasonal = "add" , seasonal_periods = 12 , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () forecasts [ "simple smoothing" ] = ses . forecast ( HORIZON ) . values forecasts [ "Holt" ] = holt . forecast ( HORIZON ) . values forecasts [ "Holt-Winters" ] = holt_winters . forecast ( HORIZON ) . values print ( f "Simple smoothing: alpha = { ses . params [ 'smoothing_level' ] : .2f } " ) print ( f "Holt-Winters: alpha = { holt_winters . params [ 'smoothing_level' ] : .2f } , " f "trend weight = { holt_winters . params [ 'smoothing_trend' ] : .3f } , " f "seasonal weight = { holt_winters . params [ 'smoothing_seasonal' ] : .2f } " ) for name in [ "simple smoothing" , "Holt" , "Holt-Winters" ]: scores . loc [ name ] = forecast_errors ( test , forecasts [ name ]) scores . round ( 3 ) Simple smoothing: alpha = 1.00 Holt-Winters: alpha = 0.54, trend weight = 0.011, seasonal weight = 0.13 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % naive 2.839 3.336 0.766 seasonal naive 2.866 3.109 0.774 12-month average 3.059 3.580 0.825 simple smoothing 2.839 3.336 0.766 Holt 22.883 26.696 6.190 Holt-Winters 0.810 0.889 0.219 fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1997" :] . index , train [ "1997" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) ax . plot ( forecasts . index , forecasts [ "Holt" ], color = ORANGE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Holt (trend, no season)" ) ax . plot ( forecasts . index , forecasts [ "Holt-Winters" ], color = BLUE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Holt-Winters (trend + season)" ) ax . set_title ( "Holt-Winters follows both the trend and the seasonal swing" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "lower left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () Read the chart and the error table above: Simple smoothing behaves like the naive forecast: it has no trend, so it is flat. Holt has a trend but no season. The training data end in December, in the middle of the yearly climb from the autumn low, when CO₂ rises by more than 1 ppm a month. Holt has no seasonal part, so it reads that seasonal climb as the long-run trend and carries it forward for three years: its forecast shoots far above the actual values. A model that ignores a real pattern can do much worse than a baseline . Holt-Winters models trend and season, and its errors are far smaller than the baselines'. Part 8: The ARIMA idea ¶ ARIMA is the other big family of forecasting models. The name lists its three ingredients: Letter Name Idea in plain words Order AR AutoRegressive This month depends on the last few months' values p I Integrated Model the changes (differences) instead of the levels, to remove the trend d MA Moving Average (of errors) This month corrects for the last few months' forecast errors q It is written ARIMA(p, d, q). Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA) adds the same three ingredients at the seasonal lag, written (P, D, Q, s) with s = 12 for monthly data. Stationarity and differencing ¶ ARIMA needs a stationary series: one whose average and spread do not drift over time. A trending series is not stationary. Differencing fixes this: instead of the CO₂ level, model the change from one month to the next (d = 1). A seasonal difference (D = 1) models the change from the same month last year. first_diff = train . diff () both_diff = train . diff () . diff ( 12 ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 3 , 1 , figsize = ( 10 , 7 ), sharex = True ) for ax , series , title in zip ( axes , [ train , first_diff , both_diff ], [ "Level: trend and season" , "First difference: change from last month (trend removed)" , "First and seasonal difference (trend and season removed)" ], ): ax . plot ( series . index , series , color = BLUE , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) ax . set_ylabel ( "ppm" ) axes [ - 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test checks stationarity with numbers instead of eyes: Null hypothesis The series is not stationary (it has a "unit root", a wandering trend) p-value > 0.05 Not enough evidence of stationarity: difference the series p-value ≤ 0.05 Reject the null: treat the series as stationary We run it on the training data, as levels and after differencing: for label , series in [( "Level" , train ), ( "First difference" , first_diff ), ( "First and seasonal difference" , both_diff )]: statistic , p_value = adfuller ( series . dropna ())[: 2 ] verdict = "stationary" if p_value <= 0.05 else "NOT stationary" print ( f " { label : <31 } ADF statistic = { statistic : 8.3f } p-value = { p_value : .4f } -> { verdict } " ) Level ADF statistic = 2.588 p-value = 0.9991 -> NOT stationary First difference ADF statistic = -3.869 p-value = 0.0023 -> stationary First and seasonal difference ADF statistic = -8.241 p-value = 0.0000 -> stationary Read the p-values above: the level series is not stationary, and differencing makes it stationary. That is why the model below sets d = 1 (and D = 1 for the season). We fit a classic seasonal ARIMA, SARIMA(0, 1, 1)(0, 1, 1, 12), often called the airline model because it was first used for monthly airline passengers. Software chooses the coefficients; your job is to choose a sensible structure, check the errors on the test period and explain the result. sarima = sm . tsa . statespace . SARIMAX ( train , order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 ), seasonal_order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 , 12 )) . fit ( disp = False ) sarima_forecast = sarima . get_forecast ( steps = HORIZON ) forecasts [ "SARIMA" ] = sarima_forecast . predicted_mean . values scores . loc [ "SARIMA" ] = forecast_errors ( test , forecasts [ "SARIMA" ]) scores . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % naive 2.839 3.336 0.766 seasonal naive 2.866 3.109 0.774 12-month average 3.059 3.580 0.825 simple smoothing 2.839 3.336 0.766 Holt 22.883 26.696 6.190 Holt-Winters 0.810 0.889 0.219 SARIMA 1.007 1.098 0.272 Check your understanding A colleague fits ARIMA to monthly sales that grow every year, with d = 0. What problem do you expect, and what would an ADF test have told them? In your own words: what does the "MA" in ARIMA average, and how is that different from a moving average of the values in Part 4? Part 9: Forecast intervals ¶ A point forecast alone suggests more certainty than anyone has. A 95% forecast interval is a range that should contain the actual value in about 95 of 100 similar forecasts. SARIMA gives intervals directly. Predict, then reveal Will the interval for the 36th month ahead be narrower, the same, or wider than the interval for next month? Why? interval_95 = sarima_forecast . conf_int ( alpha = 0.05 ) interval_80 = sarima_forecast . conf_int ( alpha = 0.20 ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1996" :] . index , train [ "1996" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . fill_between ( test . index , interval_95 . iloc [:, 0 ], interval_95 . iloc [:, 1 ], color = BLUE , alpha = 0.15 , label = "95 % i nterval" ) ax . fill_between ( test . index , interval_80 . iloc [:, 0 ], interval_80 . iloc [:, 1 ], color = BLUE , alpha = 0.3 , label = "80 % i nterval" ) ax . plot ( test . index , forecasts [ "SARIMA" ], color = BLUE , linestyle = "--" , label = "SARIMA forecast" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , linewidth = 1.5 , label = "Actual (test)" ) ax . set_title ( "The forecast interval widens as the horizon grows" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () width = interval_95 . iloc [:, 1 ] - interval_95 . iloc [:, 0 ] for months_ahead in ( 1 , 12 , 36 ): print ( f "95% interval width { months_ahead : >2 } months ahead: { width . iloc [ months_ahead - 1 ] : .2f } ppm" ) inside = (( test >= interval_95 . iloc [:, 0 ]) & ( test <= interval_95 . iloc [:, 1 ])) . mean () print ( f "Share of the 36 test months inside the 95% interval: { inside : .0% } " ) 95% interval width 1 months ahead: 1.28 ppm 95% interval width 12 months ahead: 2.99 ppm 95% interval width 36 months ahead: 5.76 ppm Share of the 36 test months inside the 95% interval: 100% Each month ahead adds new, unknown noise on top of the uncertainty already there, so the interval widens with the horizon. Intervals rest on the model's assumptions; a sudden change (a new competitor, a pandemic, a volcano) can push actual values outside them. How to say it to a manager: "We expect about X ppm in December 2001; we are 95% confident it will be between A and B ." Give the point forecast and the range, and say what the range assumes. Part 10: Choosing a model and making the decision ¶ ranking = scores . sort_values ( "RMSE" ) best = ranking . index [ 0 ] shown = ranking . drop ( index = "Holt" ) # Holt's error is off the scale; it stays in the table below fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) ax . barh ( shown . index [:: - 1 ], shown [ "RMSE" ][:: - 1 ], color = [ BLUE if name == best else GREY for name in shown . index [:: - 1 ]]) for i , value in enumerate ( shown [ "RMSE" ][:: - 1 ]): ax . text ( value + 0.05 , i , f " { value : .2f } " , va = "center" , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , shown [ "RMSE" ] . max () * 1.15 ) ax . grid ( axis = "y" , visible = False ) ax . set_title ( f " { best } has the smallest error on the three hidden years" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "RMSE on the 36-month test period (ppm, lower is better); Holt not shown, see table" ) plt . show () ranking . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % Holt-Winters 0.810 0.889 0.219 SARIMA 1.007 1.098 0.272 seasonal naive 2.866 3.109 0.774 naive 2.839 3.336 0.766 simple smoothing 2.839 3.336 0.766 12-month average 3.059 3.580 0.825 Holt 22.883 26.696 6.190 How to choose, in order: Beat the baselines. A model that does not is not worth its complexity. Prefer the smallest test error on the measure that matches the decision (RMSE when large misses are costly, MAE otherwise). Look at the chart , not only the table: does the forecast follow the trend and the season? Close results are a tie. Two models with nearly the same error are equally good on this test; choose the one you can explain, or the one that gives intervals you need. Once a model is chosen, refit it on all the data (training + test) and forecast the real future: final_model = sm . tsa . statespace . SARIMAX ( co2 , order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 ), seasonal_order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 , 12 )) . fit ( disp = False ) future = final_model . get_forecast ( steps = 24 ) future_table = pd . DataFrame ({ "forecast" : future . predicted_mean , "95 % lo w" : future . conf_int ( alpha = 0.05 ) . iloc [:, 0 ], "95 % hi gh" : future . conf_int ( alpha = 0.05 ) . iloc [:, 1 ], }) future_table . index = future_table . index . strftime ( "%b %Y" ) print ( "Forecast for the next 24 months after the data end (ppm)" ) future_table . iloc [[ 0 , 5 , 11 , 17 , 23 ]] . round ( 1 ) Forecast for the next 24 months after the data end (ppm) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } forecast 95% low 95% high Jan 2002 372.0 371.3 372.6 Jun 2002 374.8 373.7 375.9 Dec 2002 372.5 371.1 374.0 Jun 2003 376.4 374.5 378.2 Dec 2003 374.1 372.0 376.3 From forecast to decision ¶ A forecast becomes useful when it is tied to a decision and its cost of being wrong: Decision Which number to use Why Order stock that spoils if unsold Close to the point forecast Over-ordering wastes stock Order stock where running out loses customers Near the upper end of the interval A shortage costs more than spare stock Set a budget Point forecast, with the low end as a risk case Plan on the likely value, prepare for the bad case Promise a delivery date The upper end of the time forecast A broken promise costs trust Remember A forecast assumes the future behaves like the past. Re-check it as new data arrive, and say clearly when something has changed that the history does not contain. Check your understanding LeafLine Tea forecasts 12,000 drinks next month (95% interval 10,500 to 13,800). Tapioca pearls keep for two weeks, and running out on a busy day loses customers to a rival. Which number would you use to plan pearl orders, and what extra information would change your answer? Summary ¶ Idea One-line takeaway Components Trend + seasonality + noise; additive when the swing stays the same size Moving average Centred to describe, trailing to forecast; a trailing average lags a trend Train/test Hide the most recent period; never shuffle a time series Error MAE (typical miss), RMSE (punishes big misses), MAPE (per cent; unsafe near zero) Baselines Naive, seasonal naive, average: a model must beat them Exponential smoothing Weights shrink into the past; Holt adds trend, Holt-Winters adds season ARIMA AR (past values) + I (differencing for stationarity) + MA (past errors); ADF p > 0.05 means difference Intervals Give a range with the forecast; it widens with the horizon Decision Refit on all data; pick the number (point or interval end) that matches the cost of being wrong Quick reference ¶ You want to… Code Weekly to monthly averages series.resample("ME").mean() Decompose seasonal_decompose(series, model="additive", period=12) Moving average series.rolling(12).mean() (trailing), rolling(12, center=True) (centred) Time-ordered split train, test = series.iloc[:-36], series.iloc[-36:] Holt-Winters ExponentialSmoothing(train, trend="add", seasonal="add", seasonal_periods=12).fit().forecast(36) ADF test adfuller(series.dropna())[1] is the p-value SARIMA sm.tsa.statespace.SARIMAX(train, order=(p, d, q), seasonal_order=(P, D, Q, 12)).fit(disp=False) Forecast and interval result.get_forecast(36) , then .predicted_mean and .conf_int(alpha=0.05) Errors mean_absolute_error , mean_squared_error from sklearn.metrics , or the function in Part 6 Closing quiz ¶ Answer in your own words, alone, in about two minutes per question. Name the components of a time series and give a business example of each. Why does a trailing 12-month average forecast fall behind a rising series? Why must the test period come after the training period? Actual values 100, 110, 90; forecasts 105, 100, 90. Compute the MAE and the RMSE by hand. Which is larger, and why? What does α control in exponential smoothing? What happens when α is close to 1? An ADF test on monthly revenue gives p = 0.63. What do you conclude, and what do you do before fitting ARIMA? Why does a forecast interval get wider for later months? A model's MAPE on CO₂ is 0.3%. Is that enough to call it excellent? What else would you compare the error with? This afternoon ¶ Labs: Applied Lab 3: Text mining application and Applied Lab 4: Forecasting (graded, 3% each). In Lab 4 you test stationarity, split the CO₂ series into training and test sets, fit a seasonal ARIMA model and judge its accuracy with RMSE and MAE.

docs.text: Budgets, stock orders, staff rosters and climate policy all rest on a forecast. This lecture shows how to read a time series as trend, seasonality and noise, how to forecast it with moving averages, exponential smoothing and ARIMA models, how to test a forecast honestly on data the model has never seen, and how to report the uncertainty with a forecast interval. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter .
docs.title: Day 3 lecture: Forecasting

docs.text: Describe a time series by its trend , seasonality and noise , and split it with a decomposition . Smooth a series with a moving average and explain why a trailing average lags behind a trend. Split a time series into training and test periods in time order, and explain why it must not be shuffled. Compute and interpret MAE , RMSE and MAPE , and compare models with a baseline . Explain exponential smoothing (simple, Holt and Holt-Winters) as a weighted average that forgets the past. Explain the idea of ARIMA : autoregression, differencing to remove trend ( stationarity ), and moving-average errors; read an ADF test . Produce a forecast interval , explain why it widens with the horizon, and state a forecast for a decision-maker. Reading: TransImpact (n.d.), Forecasting methods: The complete guide . docs.title: What you will be able to do

docs.text: A forecast is an estimate of a future value, made from past data and stated with its uncertainty. It is predictive analytics: it answers what is likely to happen? The decision about what to do with it is prescriptive . Decision Series to forecast Horizon How much milk tea powder to order next month Monthly drinks sold 1 month How many call-centre staff to roster next week Calls per hour 1–2 weeks Next year's budget Monthly revenue 12 months Emission targets Atmospheric CO₂ Years Word Meaning Time series Values of one measure recorded at regular intervals, in time order Horizon How far ahead we forecast (1 month, 12 months, …) Point forecast The single most likely value Forecast interval A range expected to contain the future value with a stated probability, for example 95% Holdout or test period Recent data hidden from the model, used to measure its error The setup cell loads the libraries. Every model in this lecture comes from statsmodels , part of Anaconda. import warnings import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd import statsmodels.api as sm from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing , SimpleExpSmoothing from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller # Recent statsmodels versions print a notice that adfuller's output format will change # in a future release. It does not change any result, so we hide that notice. warnings . filterwarnings ( "ignore" , category = FutureWarning ) BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" # context INK = "#55534e" # notes and labels plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 10 , 4 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , })

docs.text: The Mauna Loa Observatory in Hawaii has measured carbon dioxide (CO₂) in the air since 1958. The measure is the concentration in parts per million (ppm) : how many CO₂ molecules there are in every million molecules of air. The series ships inside statsmodels , so it loads without internet. It is weekly, with some weeks missing; we average it to monthly values, and fill the few months with no measurement by carrying the previous month forward. weekly = sm . datasets . co2 . load_pandas () . data monthly_raw = weekly [ "co2" ] . resample ( "ME" ) . mean () # "ME" = month end co2 = monthly_raw . ffill () print ( "Weekly rows:" , len ( weekly ), "| weeks with no value:" , weekly [ "co2" ] . isna () . sum ()) print ( "Monthly values:" , len ( co2 ), "from" , co2 . index [ 0 ] . strftime ( "%b %Y" ), "to" , co2 . index [ - 1 ] . strftime ( "%b %Y" )) print ( "Months with no measurement, filled from the month before:" , monthly_raw . isna () . sum ()) co2 . head () Weekly rows: 2284 | weeks with no value: 59 Monthly values: 526 from Mar 1958 to Dec 2001 Months with no measurement, filled from the month before: 5 1958-03-31 316.100000 1958-04-30 317.200000 1958-05-31 317.433333 1958-06-30 317.433333 1958-07-31 315.625000 Freq: ME, Name: co2, dtype: float64 fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 13 , 4 ), gridspec_kw = { "width_ratios" : [ 2 , 1 ]}) ax1 . plot ( co2 . index , co2 , color = BLUE , linewidth = 1 ) ax1 . set_title ( "CO₂ has risen every decade since 1958" ) ax1 . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) recent = co2 [ "1995" : "1997" ] ax2 . plot ( recent . index , recent , color = BLUE , marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax2 . set_title ( "Zoom: 1995-1997" ) ax2 . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax2 . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax2 . tick_params ( axis = "x" , rotation = 45 ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Predict, then reveal Look at the zoomed panel above. In which month of the year is CO₂ highest, and in which is it lowest? (Hint: think about when the forests of the Northern Hemisphere grow leaves.) We check your answer in Part 3.
docs.title: Part 2: The data: CO₂ at Mauna Loa

docs.text: Most business and natural time series are a mix of a few components : Component Meaning CO₂ example Business example Trend The long-run direction Rising every year Sales growing as a chain opens shops Seasonality A pattern that repeats with a fixed period Peak in spring, dip in autumn, every 12 months More drinks in summer; more calls on Mondays Cycle Longer swings without a fixed period (small here) Economic booms and recessions Noise (residual) What is left: irregular, unpredictable Weather, measurement One-off events, chance In an additive model, value = trend + seasonal + residual: the seasonal swing has the same size in ppm every year. In a multiplicative model, value = trend × seasonal × residual: the swing grows with the level, as with sales that rise 30% every December. The CO₂ swing stays about the same size, so we use additive. seasonal_decompose estimates each component. The trend is a centred 12-month moving average (Part 4), the seasonal part is the average deviation from the trend for each calendar month, and the residual is the rest. parts = seasonal_decompose ( co2 , model = "additive" , period = 12 ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 4 , 1 , figsize = ( 10 , 8 ), sharex = True ) for ax , series , title in zip ( axes , [ co2 , parts . trend , parts . seasonal , parts . resid ], [ "Observed" , "Trend" , "Seasonal" , "Residual (noise)" ], ): ax . plot ( series . index , series , color = BLUE if title != "Residual (noise)" else GREY , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) ax . set_ylabel ( "ppm" ) axes [ - 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) fig . suptitle ( "Additive decomposition of monthly CO₂" , x = 0.02 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () seasonal_effect = parts . seasonal . groupby ( parts . seasonal . index . month ) . mean () seasonal_effect . index = pd . to_datetime ( seasonal_effect . index , format = "%m" ) . strftime ( "%b" ) print ( "Average seasonal effect by calendar month (ppm above or below the trend)" ) print ( seasonal_effect . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Highest month: { seasonal_effect . idxmax () } | lowest month: { seasonal_effect . idxmin () } " ) print ( f "Seasonal swing, highest minus lowest: { seasonal_effect . max () - seasonal_effect . min () : .2f } ppm" ) Average seasonal effect by calendar month (ppm above or below the trend) Jan -0.01 Feb 0.62 Mar 1.40 Apr 2.46 May 2.93 Jun 2.29 Jul 0.75 Aug -1.31 Sep -3.04 Oct -3.14 Nov -2.04 Dec -0.91 Highest month: May | lowest month: Oct Seasonal swing, highest minus lowest: 6.07 ppm Check your prediction against the output above. Plants in the Northern Hemisphere absorb CO₂ as they grow in summer, so concentration falls from late spring to early autumn and rises again over winter. Check your understanding A shop's monthly sales rise by about 2% a year and are 40% higher every December than in an average month. Name the components, and say whether you would use an additive or a multiplicative model. Why are the first and last six months of the trend panel empty?
docs.title: Part 3: Trend, seasonality and decomposition

docs.text: A moving average replaces each value with the average of a window of neighbouring values. It smooths out the noise and the seasonal swing so the trend is easier to see. Type Window Use Centred Months before and after Describing the past (the trend line in a decomposition) Trailing The last k months only Forecasting: it uses only what is already known A 12-month window contains exactly one of each calendar month, so the seasonal swing cancels out. window = co2 [ "1990" :] centred = co2 . rolling ( 12 , center = True ) . mean ()[ "1990" :] trailing = co2 . rolling ( 12 ) . mean ()[ "1990" :] fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( window . index , window , color = GREY , linewidth = 1 , label = "Monthly value" ) ax . plot ( centred . index , centred , color = BLUE , linewidth = 2 , label = "Centred 12-month average" ) ax . plot ( trailing . index , trailing , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 , label = "Trailing 12-month average" ) ax . set_title ( "A trailing average runs below a rising series" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () gap = ( window - trailing ) . mean () print ( f "On average, the monthly value is { gap : .2f } ppm above its trailing 12-month average (1990-2001)." ) On average, the monthly value is 0.69 ppm above its trailing 12-month average (1990-2001). The trailing average describes the middle of the last twelve months, about six months ago. When the series has a trend, a forecast that says "next month = average of the last 12 months" will be systematically too low for a rising series (too high for a falling one). Forecasting methods that follow a trend fix this.
docs.title: Part 4: Moving averages

docs.text: How do we know whether a forecast is good before the future arrives? We pretend part of the past is the future: Hide the most recent months: the test period (also called holdout). Fit the model on the earlier months only: the training period. Forecast the test period and compare with what actually happened. Here we hide the last 36 months (1999–2001) and train on everything before. Never shuffle a time series In a random split, the model would train on months after some test months and "see the future". The test must come after the training data, exactly as in real forecasting. HORIZON = 36 train , test = co2 . iloc [: - HORIZON ], co2 . iloc [ - HORIZON :] print ( f "Training: { train . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { train . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } ( { len ( train ) } months)" ) print ( f "Test: { test . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { test . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } ( { len ( test ) } months)" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1990" :] . index , train [ "1990" :], color = BLUE , label = "Training data (the model sees this)" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = ORANGE , label = "Test data (hidden from the model)" ) ax . axvline ( test . index [ 0 ], color = INK , linestyle = ":" , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_title ( "We hide the last three years and try to forecast them" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Training: Mar 1958 to Dec 1998 (490 months) Test: Jan 1999 to Dec 2001 (36 months)

docs.text: The error for one month is actual minus forecast. Three ways to summarise many errors: Measure Formula, in words Units Read it as MAE , mean absolute error Average of the absolute errors Same as the data (ppm) "On average the forecast is off by … ppm" RMSE , root mean squared error Square the errors, average, take the square root Same as the data Like MAE, but punishes large misses more; always ≥ MAE MAPE , mean absolute percentage error Average of absolute error ÷ actual, in % Per cent "Off by …% on average"; easy to explain, but misleading when actual values are near zero Always compare a model with a baseline : a forecast so simple that a model must beat it to be worth using. Baseline Forecast for every future month Naive The last value seen Seasonal naive The value in the same month one year earlier Average The average of the last 12 months (the trailing moving average) def forecast_errors ( actual , forecast ): """MAE, RMSE and MAPE of a forecast against the actual values.""" error = np . asarray ( actual ) - np . asarray ( forecast ) return { "MAE" : np . mean ( np . abs ( error )), "RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean ( error ** 2 )), "MAPE %" : 100 * np . mean ( np . abs ( error / np . asarray ( actual ))), } forecasts = pd . DataFrame ( index = test . index ) forecasts [ "naive" ] = train . iloc [ - 1 ] forecasts [ "seasonal naive" ] = np . tile ( train . iloc [ - 12 :] . values , HORIZON // 12 ) forecasts [ "12-month average" ] = train . iloc [ - 12 :] . mean () scores = pd . DataFrame ({ name : forecast_errors ( test , forecasts [ name ]) for name in forecasts }) . T scores . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % naive 2.839 3.336 0.766 seasonal naive 2.866 3.109 0.774 12-month average 3.059 3.580 0.825 Predict, then reveal All three baselines are flat or repeat last year. Before you run the next cell, sketch what each one looks like against the rising test data. Which one will at least follow the seasonal zig-zag? fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1997" :] . index , train [ "1997" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) for name , colour in zip ( forecasts . columns , [ BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA ]): ax . plot ( forecasts . index , forecasts [ name ], color = colour , linestyle = "--" , label = name ) ax . set_title ( "Simple baselines miss the trend" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () In the table above, MAPE is well under 1% for every baseline. That looks excellent, but only because the level of CO₂ is large. A fairer yardstick is the size of the changes we care about : the seasonal swing from Part 3 is a few ppm, and the trend adds well over 1 ppm a year. Judge an error against the decision, not only against the level. Check your understanding A forecast of daily sales has a MAPE of 4% on most days but 300% on public holidays, when the shop is almost closed. What causes the 300%, and which measure would you report instead?
