docs.text: A moving average gives the last 12 months equal weight and everything older no weight. Exponential smoothing gives every past value a weight that shrinks the further back it is. One number, α (alpha, between 0 and 1), sets how quickly the past is forgotten. weights = pd . DataFrame ({ f "alpha = { alpha } " : [ alpha * ( 1 - alpha ) ** k for k in range ( 6 )] for alpha in ( 0.2 , 0.8 ) }, index = [ "latest month" , "1 month ago" ] + [ f " { k } months ago" for k in range ( 2 , 6 )]) print ( "Weight given to each past value" ) weights . round ( 3 ) Weight given to each past value .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } alpha = 0.2 alpha = 0.8 latest month 0.200 0.800 1 month ago 0.160 0.160 2 months ago 0.128 0.032 3 months ago 0.102 0.006 4 months ago 0.082 0.001 5 months ago 0.066 0.000 With a large α, the forecast follows the latest values closely (reacts fast, but also to noise). With a small α, it averages over a long history (stable, but slow to react). The model chooses α by fitting the training data. Method Follows Use when the series has Simple exponential smoothing A level only No trend, no seasonality Holt (double) Level + trend A trend, no seasonality Holt-Winters (triple) Level + trend + seasonality A trend and a repeating season ses = SimpleExpSmoothing ( train , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () holt = ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () holt_winters = ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , seasonal = "add" , seasonal_periods = 12 , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () forecasts [ "simple smoothing" ] = ses . forecast ( HORIZON ) . values forecasts [ "Holt" ] = holt . forecast ( HORIZON ) . values forecasts [ "Holt-Winters" ] = holt_winters . forecast ( HORIZON ) . values print ( f "Simple smoothing: alpha = { ses . params [ 'smoothing_level' ] : .2f } " ) print ( f "Holt-Winters: alpha = { holt_winters . params [ 'smoothing_level' ] : .2f } , " f "trend weight = { holt_winters . params [ 'smoothing_trend' ] : .3f } , " f "seasonal weight = { holt_winters . params [ 'smoothing_seasonal' ] : .2f } " ) for name in [ "simple smoothing" , "Holt" , "Holt-Winters" ]: scores . loc [ name ] = forecast_errors ( test , forecasts [ name ]) scores . round ( 3 ) Simple smoothing: alpha = 1.00 Holt-Winters: alpha = 0.54, trend weight = 0.011, seasonal weight = 0.13 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % naive 2.839 3.336 0.766 seasonal naive 2.866 3.109 0.774 12-month average 3.059 3.580 0.825 simple smoothing 2.839 3.336 0.766 Holt 22.883 26.696 6.190 Holt-Winters 0.810 0.889 0.219 fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1997" :] . index , train [ "1997" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) ax . plot ( forecasts . index , forecasts [ "Holt" ], color = ORANGE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Holt (trend, no season)" ) ax . plot ( forecasts . index , forecasts [ "Holt-Winters" ], color = BLUE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Holt-Winters (trend + season)" ) ax . set_title ( "Holt-Winters follows both the trend and the seasonal swing" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "lower left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () Read the chart and the error table above: Simple smoothing behaves like the naive forecast: it has no trend, so it is flat. Holt has a trend but no season. The training data end in December, in the middle of the yearly climb from the autumn low, when CO₂ rises by more than 1 ppm a month. Holt has no seasonal part, so it reads that seasonal climb as the long-run trend and carries it forward for three years: its forecast shoots far above the actual values. A model that ignores a real pattern can do much worse than a baseline . Holt-Winters models trend and season, and its errors are far smaller than the baselines'.
docs.title: Part 7: Exponential smoothing

docs.text: ARIMA is the other big family of forecasting models. The name lists its three ingredients: Letter Name Idea in plain words Order AR AutoRegressive This month depends on the last few months' values p I Integrated Model the changes (differences) instead of the levels, to remove the trend d MA Moving Average (of errors) This month corrects for the last few months' forecast errors q It is written ARIMA(p, d, q). Seasonal ARIMA (SARIMA) adds the same three ingredients at the seasonal lag, written (P, D, Q, s) with s = 12 for monthly data.
docs.title: Part 8: The ARIMA idea

docs.text: ARIMA needs a stationary series: one whose average and spread do not drift over time. A trending series is not stationary. Differencing fixes this: instead of the CO₂ level, model the change from one month to the next (d = 1). A seasonal difference (D = 1) models the change from the same month last year. first_diff = train . diff () both_diff = train . diff () . diff ( 12 ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 3 , 1 , figsize = ( 10 , 7 ), sharex = True ) for ax , series , title in zip ( axes , [ train , first_diff , both_diff ], [ "Level: trend and season" , "First difference: change from last month (trend removed)" , "First and seasonal difference (trend and season removed)" ], ): ax . plot ( series . index , series , color = BLUE , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) ax . set_ylabel ( "ppm" ) axes [ - 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test checks stationarity with numbers instead of eyes: Null hypothesis The series is not stationary (it has a "unit root", a wandering trend) p-value > 0.05 Not enough evidence of stationarity: difference the series p-value ≤ 0.05 Reject the null: treat the series as stationary We run it on the training data, as levels and after differencing: for label , series in [( "Level" , train ), ( "First difference" , first_diff ), ( "First and seasonal difference" , both_diff )]: statistic , p_value = adfuller ( series . dropna ())[: 2 ] verdict = "stationary" if p_value <= 0.05 else "NOT stationary" print ( f " { label : <31 } ADF statistic = { statistic : 8.3f } p-value = { p_value : .4f } -> { verdict } " ) Level ADF statistic = 2.588 p-value = 0.9991 -> NOT stationary First difference ADF statistic = -3.869 p-value = 0.0023 -> stationary First and seasonal difference ADF statistic = -8.241 p-value = 0.0000 -> stationary Read the p-values above: the level series is not stationary, and differencing makes it stationary. That is why the model below sets d = 1 (and D = 1 for the season). We fit a classic seasonal ARIMA, SARIMA(0, 1, 1)(0, 1, 1, 12), often called the airline model because it was first used for monthly airline passengers. Software chooses the coefficients; your job is to choose a sensible structure, check the errors on the test period and explain the result. sarima = sm . tsa . statespace . SARIMAX ( train , order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 ), seasonal_order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 , 12 )) . fit ( disp = False ) sarima_forecast = sarima . get_forecast ( steps = HORIZON ) forecasts [ "SARIMA" ] = sarima_forecast . predicted_mean . values scores . loc [ "SARIMA" ] = forecast_errors ( test , forecasts [ "SARIMA" ]) scores . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } MAE RMSE MAPE % naive 2.839 3.336 0.766 seasonal naive 2.866 3.109 0.774 12-month average 3.059 3.580 0.825 simple smoothing 2.839 3.336 0.766 Holt 22.883 26.696 6.190 Holt-Winters 0.810 0.889 0.219 SARIMA 1.007 1.098 0.272 Check your understanding A colleague fits ARIMA to monthly sales that grow every year, with d = 0. What problem do you expect, and what would an ADF test have told them? In your own words: what does the "MA" in ARIMA average, and how is that different from a moving average of the values in Part 4?
docs.title: Stationarity and differencing

docs.text: A point forecast alone suggests more certainty than anyone has. A 95% forecast interval is a range that should contain the actual value in about 95 of 100 similar forecasts. SARIMA gives intervals directly. Predict, then reveal Will the interval for the 36th month ahead be narrower, the same, or wider than the interval for next month? Why? interval_95 = sarima_forecast . conf_int ( alpha = 0.05 ) interval_80 = sarima_forecast . conf_int ( alpha = 0.20 ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "1996" :] . index , train [ "1996" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . fill_between ( test . index , interval_95 . iloc [:, 0 ], interval_95 . iloc [:, 1 ], color = BLUE , alpha = 0.15 , label = "95 % i nterval" ) ax . fill_between ( test . index , interval_80 . iloc [:, 0 ], interval_80 . iloc [:, 1 ], color = BLUE , alpha = 0.3 , label = "80 % i nterval" ) ax . plot ( test . index , forecasts [ "SARIMA" ], color = BLUE , linestyle = "--" , label = "SARIMA forecast" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , linewidth = 1.5 , label = "Actual (test)" ) ax . set_title ( "The forecast interval widens as the horizon grows" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "CO₂ concentration (ppm)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () width = interval_95 . iloc [:, 1 ] - interval_95 . iloc [:, 0 ] for months_ahead in ( 1 , 12 , 36 ): print ( f "95% interval width { months_ahead : >2 } months ahead: { width . iloc [ months_ahead - 1 ] : .2f } ppm" ) inside = (( test >= interval_95 . iloc [:, 0 ]) & ( test <= interval_95 . iloc [:, 1 ])) . mean () print ( f "Share of the 36 test months inside the 95% interval: { inside : .0% } " ) 95% interval width 1 months ahead: 1.28 ppm 95% interval width 12 months ahead: 2.99 ppm 95% interval width 36 months ahead: 5.76 ppm Share of the 36 test months inside the 95% interval: 100% Each month ahead adds new, unknown noise on top of the uncertainty already there, so the interval widens with the horizon. Intervals rest on the model's assumptions; a sudden change (a new competitor, a pandemic, a volcano) can push actual values outside them. How to say it to a manager: "We expect about X ppm in December 2001; we are 95% confident it will be between A and B ." Give the point forecast and the range, and say what the range assumes.
docs.title: Part 9: Forecast intervals

Two models with nearly the same error are equally good on this test; choose the one you can explain, or the one that gives intervals you need. docs.title: Part 10: Choosing a model and making the decision

docs.text: A forecast becomes useful when it is tied to a decision and its cost of being wrong: Decision Which number to use Why Order stock that spoils if unsold Close to the point forecast Over-ordering wastes stock Order stock where running out loses customers Near the upper end of the interval A shortage costs more than spare stock Set a budget Point forecast, with the low end as a risk case Plan on the likely value, prepare for the bad case Promise a delivery date The upper end of the time forecast A broken promise costs trust Remember A forecast assumes the future behaves like the past. Re-check it as new data arrive, and say clearly when something has changed that the history does not contain. Check your understanding LeafLine Tea forecasts 12,000 drinks next month (95% interval 10,500 to 13,800). Tapioca pearls keep for two weeks, and running out on a busy day loses customers to a rival. Which number would you use to plan pearl orders, and what extra information would change your answer?
docs.title: From forecast to decision

docs.text: Idea One-line takeaway Components Trend + seasonality + noise; additive when the swing stays the same size Moving average Centred to describe, trailing to forecast; a trailing average lags a trend Train/test Hide the most recent period; never shuffle a time series Error MAE (typical miss), RMSE (punishes big misses), MAPE (per cent; unsafe near zero) Baselines Naive, seasonal naive, average: a model must beat them Exponential smoothing Weights shrink into the past; Holt adds trend, Holt-Winters adds season ARIMA AR (past values) + I (differencing for stationarity) + MA (past errors); ADF p > 0.05 means difference Intervals Give a range with the forecast; it widens with the horizon Decision Refit on all data; pick the number (point or interval end) that matches the cost of being wrong

docs.text: Day 3 lecture: Text mining ¶ Most of what customers tell a business arrives as text: reviews, complaints, chat messages and survey comments. This lecture turns unstructured text into numbers a manager can act on: split it into words, remove the noise, count what people talk about, draw it, score how they feel with the VADER sentiment model, check that score against a second source, and finish with a recommendation. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . What you will be able to do ¶ Explain the difference between structured and unstructured data, and name business sources of text. Tokenise text into words and explain why case, punctuation and numbers need a decision. Remove stopwords , add your own domain stopwords, and explain why stopwords must stay in for sentiment. Count word frequencies , draw them as a bar chart and as a word cloud , and say what each is good for. Score text with VADER : read the compound score, apply the ±0.05 thresholds and explain the rules VADER uses. Check sentiment scores against a second source and name VADER's main blind spots. Turn review text into a decision : which problem to fix first, with evidence and caveats. Reading: Label Your Data (n.d.), Unstructured text in data mining: Unlocking valuable insights . How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Write your guess down first. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words, alone or with the person next to you. Part Topic 1 Unstructured text and the text-mining routine 2 Tokenising 3 Stopwords 4 Word frequency 5 Word clouds and word pairs 6 Sentiment with VADER 7 Checking the scores against star ratings 8 From reviews to a decision Recap: Day 2 ¶ Answer in your own words before we start. Which chart do you choose to compare categories, and why does it beat a pie chart? What is a message title ? Rewrite "Reviews by star rating" as one. Why should a KPI such as "share of unhappy customers" be computed as a ratio of sums across branches? Part 1: Unstructured text and the text-mining routine ¶ Structured data fits a table with fixed columns: an order has a date, a product, a price. Unstructured data has no fixed columns: a review is a free sentence that may mention the price, the staff and the weather at once. Analysts estimate that most of the data organisations hold is unstructured, and most of it is text. Source of text Typical question Product and app reviews What do customers praise and complain about? Customer-service chats and emails Which problems cause most contacts? Survey comments ("anything else?") Why did the satisfaction score drop? Social media posts How do people react to a launch or a crisis? Contracts, reports, job adverts Which clauses, risks or skills appear most often? Text mining is the set of methods that turn text into structured numbers (counts, scores, categories) that can be summarised, charted and joined to the rest of the business data. Every project follows the same routine: Step What happens In this lecture 1. Collect Gather the texts and their context (date, branch, rating) 30 reviews with a branch and a star rating 2. Clean Lowercase, decide what to do with punctuation and numbers Part 2 3. Tokenise Split each text into words ( tokens ) Part 2 4. Filter Remove words that carry no signal ( stopwords ) Part 3 5. Represent Turn tokens into numbers: counts, pairs, scores Parts 4–6 6. Analyse and check Summarise, chart, compare with another source Parts 4–7 7. Decide Recommend an action, with evidence and limits Part 8 The case: LeafLine Tea ¶ LeafLine Tea is a made-up bubble-tea chain with three branches: near a university campus, near a railway station and on a riverside shopping street. Head office has 30 recent customer reviews, each with a star rating from 1 (worst) to 5 (best). The operations manager asks: what should we fix first? The reviews are synthetic : written for teaching, not collected from real customers. Run the two setup cells. The first one tells NLTK, the Natural Language Toolkit, to use the word lists bundled in the data folder, so nothing is downloaded. RangeIndex ( 1 , len ( reviews ) + 1 , name = "review_id" ) print ( "Reviews:" , len ( reviews )) print ( reviews [ "branch" ] . value_counts () . sort_index () . to_string ()) reviews . head () Reviews: 30 branch Campus 10 Riverside 10 Station 10 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } branch stars text review_id 1 Riverside 5 The brown sugar milk tea is delicious and the pearls are perfectly chewy. My new favou... 2 Riverside 2 Waited 35 minutes for one drink. The queue was huge and nobody explained the delay. 3 Riverside 4 Tasty mango tea and friendly staff, but the wait was a bit long at lunchtime. 4 Riverside 1 The app crashed twice while I was paying, and my order was lost. Very frustrating. 5 Riverside 5 Great taste, fair price, quick service. Highly recommend the jasmine green tea. One row is one review : one customer's comment about one visit. The stars column is structured; the text column is unstructured. The rest of the lecture turns the text into columns we can count. Part 2: Tokenising ¶ A computer sees a review as one long string of characters. Tokenising splits it into units, usually words, called tokens . Before that we make a few cleaning decisions: Decision Usual choice Why Upper and lower case Lowercase everything "Great" and "great" should count as one word Punctuation Drop it for counting, keep it for sentiment "!" carries feeling but is not a topic Numbers Drop for word counts "35" is not a topic; "35 minutes" is, as a phrase Contractions ("I've", "don't") Let the tokenizer split them word_tokenize gives "I" + "'ve" and "do" + "n't" Predict, then reveal The next cell splits review 6, "The drink was okay. Not bad, not special." , in two ways: Python's simple split() on spaces, and NLTK's word_tokenize . How many tokens will each give, and what will be different about the commas and full stops? example = reviews . loc [ 6 , "text" ] by_spaces = example . split () by_nltk = word_tokenize ( example . lower ()) print ( "split() on spaces:" , len ( by_spaces ), "tokens" ) print ( by_spaces ) print () print ( "word_tokenize on lowercase text:" , len ( by_nltk ), "tokens" ) print ( by_nltk ) split() on spaces: 8 tokens ['The', 'drink', 'was', 'okay.', 'Not', 'bad,', 'not', 'special.'] word_tokenize on lowercase text: 11 tokens ['the', 'drink', 'was', 'okay', '.', 'not', 'bad', ',', 'not', 'special', '.'] split() leaves punctuation glued to words, so okay. and okay would be counted as different words. word_tokenize separates punctuation into tokens of its own, which we can then drop with one test: keep a token only if token.isalpha() is true (it contains letters only). Now tokenise all 30 reviews at once and keep the alphabetic tokens: reviews [ "tokens" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower () . apply ( word_tokenize ) reviews [ "words" ] = reviews [ "tokens" ] . apply ( lambda tokens : [ t for t in tokens if t . isalpha ()]) all_words = [ w for words in reviews [ "words" ] for w in words ] print ( "Alphabetic tokens in all reviews:" , len ( all_words )) print ( "Different words (the vocabulary):" , len ( set ( all_words ))) print () print ( "Ten most common words so far:" ) print ( Counter ( all_words ) . most_common ( 10 )) Alphabetic tokens in all reviews: 353 Different words (the vocabulary): 172 Ten most common words so far: [('the', 37), ('and', 15), ('app', 9), ('i', 9), ('was', 8), ('tea', 7), ('my', 7), ('drink', 7), ('but', 7), ('is', 6)] Predict, then reveal Look at the ten most common words above. Do they tell the operations manager anything about what to fix? What kind of words are they? Part 3: Stopwords ¶ Most of the top words above are stopwords : very common words such as the , and , is , a that hold sentences together but say nothing about the topic. NLTK ships a list of English stopwords: english_stopwords = set ( stopwords . words ( "english" )) print ( "Stopwords in NLTK's English list:" , len ( english_stopwords )) print ( "A few of them:" , sorted ( english_stopwords )[: 25 ]) print () for word in [ "not" , "no" , "very" , "but" , "too" ]: print ( f "Is ' { word } ' a stopword? { word in english_stopwords } " ) Stopwords in NLTK's English list: 198 A few of them: ['a', 'about', 'above', 'after', 'again', 'against', 'ain', 'all', 'am', 'an', 'and', 'any', 'are', 'aren', "aren't", 'as', 'at', 'be', 'because', 'been', 'before', 'being', 'below', 'between', 'both'] Is 'not' a stopword? True Is 'no' a stopword? True Is 'very' a stopword? True Is 'but' a stopword? True Is 'too' a stopword? True Two things to notice in the output above: The standard list is a starting point. In our reviews, words like tea and drink appear everywhere because every review is about tea. They are domain stopwords : frequent, but they cannot separate one complaint from another. We add them ourselves. not , no , very , but and too are all in the list. For counting topics that is fine. For sentiment it is a disaster: "not good" becomes "good". So we remove stopwords only for word counts, and we always run sentiment on the original text. DOMAIN_STOPWORDS = { "tea" , "drink" , "drinks" , "milk" } stop = english_stopwords | DOMAIN_STOPWORDS reviews [ "content_words" ] = reviews [ "words" ] . apply ( lambda words : [ w for w in words if w not in stop ]) content_words = [ w for words in reviews [ "content_words" ] for w in words ] print ( "Words before removing stopwords:" , len ( all_words )) print ( "Words after:" , len ( content_words )) print ( f "Share of words removed: { 1 - len ( content_words ) / len ( all_words ) : .0% } " ) Words before removing stopwords: 353 Words after: 196 Share of words removed: 44% Check your understanding A hotel analyses 5,000 guest reviews. Name two words you would add as domain stopwords, and one frequent word you would keep even though it is common. Why must "not" stay in the text when you score sentiment? Part 4: Word frequency ¶ With the noise removed, a frequency distribution counts how often each remaining word appears. NLTK's FreqDist is a counter with a most_common method. freq = nltk . FreqDist ( content_words ) top = pd . Series ( dict ( freq . most_common ( 15 )), name = "count" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) ax . barh ( top . index [:: - 1 ], top . values [:: - 1 ], color = BLUE ) for i , value in enumerate ( top . values [:: - 1 ]): ax . text ( value + 0.1 , i , str ( value ), va = "center" , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_title ( "What LeafLine customers write about most" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Number of times the word appears in 30 reviews" ) ax . grid ( axis = "x" , color = "#e6e5e1" ) ax . set_axisbelow ( True ) plt . show () Read the bar chart above as the manager would: which words about the service appear near the top, and which about the product ? Notice that wait and waited are counted as two different words. Grouping word forms is called stemming or lemmatising ; in a short analysis, a hand-made keyword list (Part 8) does the same job more transparently. Word counts are not opinions A frequent word tells you what people talk about, not whether they like it. app can appear in praise ("easy to use") and in complaints ("crashed"). Frequency says where to look ; sentiment and reading the reviews say what is wrong . Part 5: Word clouds and word pairs ¶ A word cloud draws each word with a size proportional to its frequency. We build it from the same counts, with a fixed random_state so the layout is the same each time you run it. cloud = WordCloud ( width = 800 , height = 400 , background_color = "white" , colormap = "viridis" , random_state = 3 ) . generate_from_frequencies ( freq ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 5 )) plt . imshow ( cloud , interpolation = "bilinear" ) plt . axis ( "off" ) plt . title ( "LeafLine reviews as a word cloud (size = frequency)" ) plt . show () Compare the cloud with the bar chart in Part 4, using what you learned on Day 2 about encodings: Word cloud Sorted bar chart Encoding Area and font size (read poorly) Length from a common baseline (read well) Ranking Hard beyond the top two or three words The reading order Exact counts Not shown Labelled Long words Look more important than they are No bias Best use A first impression, a slide that invites discussion Any comparison you will base a decision on Word pairs (bigrams) ¶ Single words lose context: brown and sugar mean more together. A bigram is a pair of neighbouring words. We count pairs within each review, so the last word of one review never pairs with the first word of the next. pairs = Counter () for words in reviews [ "content_words" ]: pairs . update ( nltk . bigrams ( words )) print ( "Most common word pairs (after removing stopwords):" ) for ( first , second ), count in pairs . most_common ( 8 ): print ( f " { first } { second } : { count } " ) Most common word pairs (after removing stopwords): friendly staff: 3 brown sugar: 2 waited minutes: 2 sugar delicious: 1 delicious pearls: 1 pearls perfectly: 1 perfectly chewy: 1 chewy new: 1 Pairs such as a product name ("brown sugar") or a complaint ("long wait") are often more useful than single words. With thousands of reviews, pairs and triples become the main source of key phrases. Check your understanding Your manager wants a word cloud of 10,000 complaints for the board. Give one reason to agree and two things you would add or change so the board is not misled. Part 6: Sentiment with VADER ¶ Sentiment analysis gives a text a score for how positive or negative it is. We use VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner, Hutto and Gilbert, 2014), a lexicon-based model built for short, informal texts such as reviews and posts. How VADER works, in three steps: A lexicon (a dictionary) gives about 7,500 words a rating from about −4 (most negative) to +4 (most positive), averaged from human raters. Rules adjust the ratings: negation ("not good"), intensifiers ("very good"), capital letters ("GOOD"), exclamation marks, and "but" (the part after "but" counts more). The adjusted ratings are added and squashed into a compound score between −1 and +1. The usual reading of the compound score S : Compound score Label S ≥ 0.05 Positive −0.05 < S < 0.05 Neutral S ≤ −0.05 Negative First, a look inside the lexicon: analyzer = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () for word in [ "delicious" , "friendly" , "good" , "okay" , "hate" , "terrible" , "disgusting" , "wait" , "queue" , "watery" ]: rating = analyzer . lexicon . get ( word ) print ( f " { word : <11 } { 'not in the lexicon' if rating is None else rating } " ) delicious 2.7 friendly 2.2 good 1.9 okay 0.9 hate -2.7 terrible -2.1 disgusting -2.4 wait not in the lexicon queue not in the lexicon watery not in the lexicon Predict, then reveal The next cell scores seven short sentences. For each, predict whether the compound score is higher or lower than for plain "The tea is good." sentences = [ "The tea is good." , "The tea is very good." , "The tea is GOOD!" , "The tea is not good." , "The tea is good, but the staff are rude." , "The staff are rude, but the tea is good." , "The tea is watery." , ] rule_demo = pd . DataFrame ( [ analyzer . polarity_scores ( s ) for s in sentences ], index = sentences )[[ "neg" , "neu" , "pos" , "compound" ]] rule_demo .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } neg neu pos compound The tea is good. 0.000 0.508 0.492 0.4404 The tea is very good. 0.000 0.556 0.444 0.4927 The tea is GOOD! 0.000 0.433 0.567 0.6027 The tea is not good. 0.376 0.624 0.000 -0.3412 The tea is good, but the staff are rude. 0.309 0.541 0.151 -0.4678 The staff are rude, but the tea is good. 0.156 0.545 0.300 0.4310 The tea is watery. 0.000 1.000 0.000 0.0000 The neg , neu and pos columns are the shares of the text that are negative, neutral and positive; compound is the overall score. Check your predictions against the output above. Two lessons: The rules matter: emphasis raises the score, negation flips it, and the clause after "but" dominates. watery is a complaint about tea, but it is not in a general-purpose lexicon, so it scores as neutral. A lexicon only knows the words it was given. Now score all 30 reviews, on the original text (with stopwords and punctuation), and label each one: def sentiment_label ( score ): if score >= 0.05 : return "Positive" if score <= - 0.05 : return "Negative" return "Neutral" reviews [ "compound" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . apply ( lambda text : analyzer . polarity_scores ( text )[ "compound" ]) reviews [ "sentiment" ] = reviews [ "compound" ] . apply ( sentiment_label ) LABELS = [ "Positive" , "Neutral" , "Negative" ] counts = reviews [ "sentiment" ] . value_counts () . reindex ( LABELS , fill_value = 0 ) print ( counts . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Average compound score: { reviews [ 'compound' ] . mean () : .3f } " ) reviews [[ "branch" , "stars" , "compound" , "sentiment" , "text" ]] . head ( 8 ) sentiment Positive 19 Neutral 5 Negative 6 Average compound score: 0.254 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } branch stars compound sentiment text review_id 1 Riverside 5 0.8478 Positive The brown sugar milk tea is delicious and the pearls are perfectly chewy. My new favou... 2 Riverside 2 0.0000 Neutral Waited 35 minutes for one drink. The queue was huge and nobody explained the delay. 3 Riverside 4 0.2732 Positive Tasty mango tea and friendly staff, but the wait was a bit long at lunchtime. 4 Riverside 1 -0.6697 Negative The app crashed twice while I was paying, and my order was lost. Very frustrating. 5 Riverside 5 0.8479 Positive Great taste, fair price, quick service. Highly recommend the jasmine green tea. 6 Riverside 3 0.6889 Positive The drink was okay. Not bad, not special. 7 Riverside 2 0.4588 Positive Too sweet even at 30% sugar, and the ice melted before I got back to the office. 8 Riverside 1 0.6249 Positive Great, another 40 minute wait for a lukewarm drink. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 6 , 3.5 )) ax . bar ( counts . index , counts . values , color = [ BLUE , GREY , ORANGE ]) for i , value in enumerate ( counts . values ): ax . text ( i , value + 0.2 , str ( value ), ha = "center" , color = INK ) ax . set_title ( "VADER labels for 30 LeafLine reviews" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of reviews" ) plt . show () Check your understanding A review has a compound score of 0.03. What label does it get, and why might the analyst still want to read it? Why do we run VADER on the original text instead of the cleaned, stopword-free words? Part 7: Checking the scores against star ratings ¶ A model's output is a claim, not a fact. Here we are lucky: every review also has a star rating chosen by the customer. If VADER works well, low-star reviews should have low compound scores. Predict, then reveal Review 8 reads "Great, another 40 minute wait for a lukewarm drink." and has 1 star . Will VADER call it positive, neutral or negative? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 12 ) # fixed seed: the small sideways jitter is the same every run jitter = rng . uniform ( - 0.15 , 0.15 , len ( reviews )) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax . axhspan ( - 0.05 , 0.05 , color = GREY , alpha = 0.4 , label = "Neutral band (-0.05 to 0.05)" ) ax . scatter ( reviews [ "stars" ] + jitter , reviews [ "compound" ], s = 45 , color = BLUE ) ax . set_xticks ([ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ]) ax . set_xlabel ( "Star rating given by the customer (1 = worst, 5 = best)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "VADER compound score (-1 to +1)" ) ax . set_title ( "Higher ratings tend to score higher, with clear exceptions" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () print ( "Average compound score by star rating:" ) print ( reviews . groupby ( "stars" )[ "compound" ] . agg ([ "count" , "mean" ]) . round ( 3 ) . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Correlation between stars and compound score: r = { reviews [ 'stars' ] . corr ( reviews [ 'compound' ]) : .2f } " ) Average compound score by star rating: count mean stars 1 5 -0.256 2 8 0.008 3 4 0.207 4 7 0.422 5 6 0.844 Correlation between stars and compound score: r = 0.79 The chart above shows a clear upward pattern, but some unhappy customers (1 or 2 stars) sit in or above the neutral band. List them: unhappy_not_negative = reviews [( reviews [ "stars" ] <= 2 ) & ( reviews [ "sentiment" ] != "Negative" )] print ( "Reviews with 1-2 stars that VADER does NOT label Negative:" , len ( unhappy_not_negative )) unhappy_not_negative [[ "stars" , "compound" , "sentiment" , "text" ]] Reviews with 1-2 stars that VADER does NOT label Negative: 8 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } stars compound sentiment text review_id 2 2 0.0000 Neutral Waited 35 minutes for one drink. The queue was huge and nobody explained the delay. 7 2 0.4588 Positive Too sweet even at 30% sugar, and the ice melted before I got back to the office. 8 1 0.6249 Positive Great, another 40 minute wait for a lukewarm drink. 10 2 0.1901 Positive The app showed my order as ready but the staff could not find it. I waited another 20 ... 23 2 0.0000 Neutral Convenient location, but the wait times are unpredictable. 25 2 0.0000 Neutral The app kept logging me out, and the queue was very long. 27 1 0.0000 Neutral Overpriced and watery. Never again. 30 2 0.0000 Neutral Waited 30 minutes at the counter while app orders kept jumping the queue. Read each review in the table above and ask why the lexicon missed it. The reasons fall into a few groups: Blind spot Example from the table What to do Domain words missing from the lexicon wait , queue , minutes , watery , lukewarm Add domain words with ratings, or use a keyword list for known problems Sarcasm "Great, another 40 minute wait…" Read a sample; no word-based method handles sarcasm reliably Facts that imply a feeling "I missed my train because the order took 25 minutes" Combine sentiment with topic keywords Mixed reviews Praise and complaint in one review Score sentences separately, or by aspect Other languages Chinese reviews VADER is English only; Chinese text needs its own tokenizer (Chinese has no spaces between words) and its own lexicon Remember Sentiment scores are useful for large volumes and trends (is this month worse than last month?). They are weak evidence about any single review. Always validate against a second source, such as star ratings or a sample read by a person. Part 8: From reviews to a decision ¶ The manager's question was what should we fix first? Topics alone and sentiment alone each fall short, so we combine them. We define a few aspects by keyword lists, flag every review that mentions each aspect, and summarise the reviews in each group. Because VADER misses complaints about waiting, we lead with the star rating and show the compound score next to it. ASPECTS = { "waiting" : { "wait" , "waited" , "queue" , "slow" , "minutes" , "minute" , "long" , "delay" }, "app" : { "app" }, "taste" : { "taste" , "tasty" , "delicious" , "sweet" , "watery" , "pearls" , "fresh" , "lukewarm" }, "staff" : { "staff" , "cashier" , "rude" , "friendly" , "polite" , "kind" , "nobody" }, "price" : { "price" , "cheap" , "expensive" , "overpriced" , "discount" , "paid" , "charged" }, } for aspect , keywords in ASPECTS . items (): reviews [ aspect ] = reviews [ "words" ] . apply ( lambda words : bool ( keywords & set ( words ))) rows = [] for aspect in ASPECTS : group = reviews [ reviews [ aspect ]] rows . append ({ "aspect" : aspect , "reviews" : len ( group ), " % o f all reviews" : 100 * len ( group ) / len ( reviews ), "average stars" : group [ "stars" ] . mean (), "% with 1-2 stars" : 100 * ( group [ "stars" ] <= 2 ) . mean (), "average compound" : group [ "compound" ] . mean (), }) aspects = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . set_index ( "aspect" ) . sort_values ( "% with 1-2 stars" , ascending = False ) aspects . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } reviews % of all reviews average stars % with 1-2 stars average compound aspect waiting 12 40.00 2.58 66.67 0.17 app 9 30.00 2.78 55.56 0.06 staff 9 30.00 3.11 44.44 0.20 price 7 23.33 3.29 28.57 0.28 taste 11 36.67 3.36 27.27 0.45 low_share = aspects [ "% with 1-2 stars" ] . sort_values () worst = low_share . index [ - 1 ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.8 )) ax . barh ( low_share . index , low_share . values , color = [ ORANGE if a == worst else GREY for a in low_share . index ]) for i , ( aspect , value ) in enumerate ( low_share . items ()): ax . text ( value + 1 , i , f " { value : .0f } % (n = { aspects . loc [ aspect , 'reviews' ] } )" , va = "center" , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , 115 ) ax . set_title ( f "Reviews that mention { worst } are the most often unhappy" ) ax . set_xlabel ( " % o f reviews mentioning the aspect that give 1 or 2 stars" ) plt . show () A review can mention several aspects, so the groups overlap and their counts add up to more than 30. The n beside each bar is the number of reviews behind the percentage: with 30 reviews, every group is small. Where does the worst aspect happen? Break it down by branch: by_branch = reviews . groupby ( "branch" ) . agg ( reviews = ( "stars" , "size" ), mention_worst = ( worst , "sum" ), average_stars = ( "stars" , "mean" ), ) by_branch [ f "% mentioning { worst } " ] = 100 * by_branch [ "mention_worst" ] / by_branch [ "reviews" ] by_branch . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } reviews mention_worst average_stars % mentioning waiting branch Campus 10 1 3.6 10.0 Riverside 10 4 2.9 40.0 Station 10 7 2.6 70.0 Writing the recommendation ¶ A recommendation from text mining has four parts. Fill them in from the outputs above: Part Content Finding Which aspect is most often linked to unhappy customers, and in which branches Evidence The share of 1–2 star reviews for that aspect, with n ; two or three quoted reviews Recommendation A specific action the manager controls, for example a separate pick-up counter for app orders and a visible waiting-time display Caveats Synthetic data; only 30 reviews; keyword lists miss synonyms; VADER under-scores waiting complaints; a review is one visit, not one customer Association is not causation Reviews that mention waiting are more often unhappy. That supports fixing waiting times, but it does not prove that shorter waits will raise ratings. A careful manager tests the change in one branch first and compares ratings before and after. Ethics and privacy Real reviews and chat logs can contain names, phone numbers and order numbers. Remove personal details before analysis, store text securely, and report patterns, never individual customers. Check your understanding The app aspect also has many low ratings. Read the app reviews (filter reviews[reviews["app"]] ). Is the problem the same in every review? What would you recommend to the app team? Summary ¶ Idea One-line takeaway Unstructured text Most business feedback is text; text mining turns it into counts, scores and categories Tokenising Lowercase, split with word_tokenize , keep isalpha() tokens for counting Stopwords Remove standard and domain stopwords for topics; never for sentiment ("not") Word frequency Says what people talk about, not what they feel; show it as a sorted bar chart Word cloud A first impression only: area is read poorly; pairs (bigrams) add context VADER Lexicon plus rules gives a compound score from −1 to +1; ±0.05 thresholds Validation Compare with star ratings or a read sample; watch for domain words, sarcasm, mixed reviews, other languages Decision Combine aspects and ratings; finding, evidence, recommendation, caveats Quick reference ¶ You want to… Code Use the bundled NLTK data Run the NLTK setup cell at the top of this notebook Tokenise word_tokenize(text.lower()) Keep words only [t for t in tokens if t.isalpha()] Stopword list set(stopwords.words("english")) , then .update([...]) or \| for your own Count words nltk.FreqDist(words).most_common(10) Word cloud WordCloud(width=800, height=400, background_color="white", random_state=3).generate_from_frequencies(freq) Word pairs Counter(nltk.bigrams(words)) Sentiment SentimentIntensityAnalyzer().polarity_scores(text)["compound"] Closing quiz ¶ Answer in your own words, alone, in about two minutes per question. Give two examples of unstructured data a bank holds, and one business question each could answer. What does word_tokenize("Not bad!") return, and which tokens survive isalpha() ? Why is "the" removed before counting words, but "not" kept before scoring sentiment? A word cloud of hotel reviews shows "room" as the biggest word. What can you conclude, and what can you not? VADER gives "The delivery was slow" a compound score of 0.0. Explain why, using the word "lexicon". What does a compound score of −0.62 mean, and what label does it get? Name two ways to check whether sentiment scores are trustworthy for your data. Write one recommendation sentence for LeafLine that includes a finding, a number from the outputs and a caveat. This afternoon ¶ Lab: Applied Lab 3: Text mining application (graded, 3%). You apply the same routine to customer reviews of a tablet computer: tokenise, remove stopwords, find the key terms, score sentiment with VADER and recommend a product change. The forecasting lecture, Day 3 lecture: Forecasting , prepares you for Applied Lab 4 .
docs.title: Lecture: Text mining

docs.text: Most of what customers tell a business arrives as text: reviews, complaints, chat messages and survey comments. This lecture turns unstructured text into numbers a manager can act on: split it into words, remove the noise, count what people talk about, draw it, score how they feel with the VADER sentiment model, check that score against a second source, and finish with a recommendation. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter .

docs.title: Recap: Day 2

docs.text: Structured data fits a table with fixed columns: an order has a date, a product, a price. Unstructured data has no fixed columns: a review is a free sentence that may mention the price, the staff and the weather at once. Analysts estimate that most of the data organisations hold is unstructured, and most of it is text. Source of text Typical question Product and app reviews What do customers praise and complain about? Customer-service chats and emails Which problems cause most contacts? Survey comments ("anything else?") Why did the satisfaction score drop? Social media posts How do people react to a launch or a crisis? Contracts, reports, job adverts Which clauses, risks or skills appear most often? Text mining is the set of methods that turn text into structured numbers (counts, scores, categories) that can be summarised, charted and joined to the rest of the business data. Every project follows the same routine: Step What happens In this lecture 1. Collect Gather the texts and their context (date, branch, rating) 30 reviews with a branch and a star rating 2. Clean Lowercase, decide what to do with punctuation and numbers Part 2 3. Tokenise Split each text into words ( tokens ) Part 2 4. Filter Remove words that carry no signal ( stopwords ) Part 3 5. Represent Turn tokens into numbers: counts, pairs, scores Parts 4–6 6. Analyse and check Summarise, chart, compare with another source Parts 4–7 7. Decide Recommend an action, with evidence and limits Part 8

docs.text: LeafLine Tea is a made-up bubble-tea chain with three branches: near a university campus, near a railway station and on a riverside shopping street. Head office has 30 recent customer reviews, each with a star rating from 1 (worst) to 5 (best). The operations manager asks: what should we fix first? The reviews are synthetic : written for teaching, not collected from real customers. Run the two setup cells. The first one tells NLTK, the Natural Language Toolkit, to use the word lists bundled in the data folder, so nothing is downloaded. The second loads the other libraries and the reviews. import zipfile from pathlib import Path import nltk NLTK_DIR = Path ( "data/nltk_data" ) . resolve () if not ( NLTK_DIR / "tokenizers" / "punkt_tab" ) . exists (): with zipfile . docs.title: The case: LeafLine Tea

docs.text: A computer sees a review as one long string of characters. Tokenising splits it into units, usually words, called tokens . Before that we make a few cleaning decisions: Decision Usual choice Why Upper and lower case Lowercase everything "Great" and "great" should count as one word Punctuation Drop it for counting, keep it for sentiment "!" carries feeling but is not a topic Numbers Drop for word counts "35" is not a topic; "35 minutes" is, as a phrase Contractions ("I've", "don't") Let the tokenizer split them word_tokenize gives "I" + "'ve" and "do" + "n't" Predict, then reveal The next cell splits review 6, "The drink was okay. Not bad, not special." , in two ways: Python's simple split() on spaces, and NLTK's word_tokenize . How many tokens will each give, and what will be different about the commas and full stops? example = reviews . loc [ 6 , "text" ] by_spaces = example . split () by_nltk = word_tokenize ( example . lower ()) print ( "split() on spaces:" , len ( by_spaces ), "tokens" ) print ( by_spaces ) print () print ( "word_tokenize on lowercase text:" , len ( by_nltk ), "tokens" ) print ( by_nltk ) split() on spaces: 8 tokens ['The', 'drink', 'was', 'okay.', 'Not', 'bad,', 'not', 'special.'] word_tokenize on lowercase text: 11 tokens ['the', 'drink', 'was', 'okay', '.', 'not', 'bad', ',', 'not', 'special', '.'] split() leaves punctuation glued to words, so okay. and okay would be counted as different words. word_tokenize separates punctuation into tokens of its own, which we can then drop with one test: keep a token only if token.isalpha() is true (it contains letters only). Now tokenise all 30 reviews at once and keep the alphabetic tokens: reviews [ "tokens" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower () . apply ( word_tokenize ) reviews [ "words" ] = reviews [ "tokens" ] . apply ( lambda tokens : [ t for t in tokens if t . isalpha ()]) all_words = [ w for words in reviews [ "words" ] for w in words ] print ( "Alphabetic tokens in all reviews:" , len ( all_words )) print ( "Different words (the vocabulary):" , len ( set ( all_words ))) print () print ( "Ten most common words so far:" ) print ( Counter ( all_words ) . most_common ( 10 )) Alphabetic tokens in all reviews: 353 Different words (the vocabulary): 172 Ten most common words so far: [('the', 37), ('and', 15), ('app', 9), ('i', 9), ('was', 8), ('tea', 7), ('my', 7), ('drink', 7), ('but', 7), ('is', 6)] Predict, then reveal Look at the ten most common words above. Do they tell the operations manager anything about what to fix? What kind of words are they?
docs.title: Part 2: Tokenising

docs.text: Most of the top words above are stopwords : very common words such as the , and , is , a that hold sentences together but say nothing about the topic. NLTK ships a list of English stopwords: english_stopwords = set ( stopwords . words ( "english" )) print ( "Stopwords in NLTK's English list:" , len ( english_stopwords )) print ( "A few of them:" , sorted ( english_stopwords )[: 25 ]) print () for word in [ "not" , "no" , "very" , "but" , "too" ]: print ( f "Is ' { word } ' a stopword? { word in english_stopwords } " ) Stopwords in NLTK's English list: 198 A few of them: ['a', 'about', 'above', 'after', 'again', 'against', 'ain', 'all', 'am', 'an', 'and', 'any', 'are', 'aren', "aren't", 'as', 'at', 'be', 'because', 'been', 'before', 'being', 'below', 'between', 'both'] Is 'not' a stopword? True Is 'no' a stopword? True Is 'very' a stopword? True Is 'but' a stopword? True Is 'too' a stopword? True Two things to notice in the output above: The standard list is a starting point. In our reviews, words like tea and drink appear everywhere because every review is about tea. They are domain stopwords : frequent, but they cannot separate one complaint from another. We add them ourselves. not , no , very , but and too are all in the list. For counting topics that is fine. For sentiment it is a disaster: "not good" becomes "good". So we remove stopwords only for word counts, and we always run sentiment on the original text. DOMAIN_STOPWORDS = { "tea" , "drink" , "drinks" , "milk" } stop = english_stopwords | DOMAIN_STOPWORDS reviews [ "content_words" ] = reviews [ "words" ] . apply ( lambda words : [ w for w in words if w not in stop ]) content_words = [ w for words in reviews [ "content_words" ] for w in words ] print ( "Words before removing stopwords:" , len ( all_words )) print ( "Words after:" , len ( content_words )) print ( f "Share of words removed: { 1 - len ( content_words ) / len ( all_words ) : .0% } " ) Words before removing stopwords: 353 Words after: 196 Share of words removed: 44% Check your understanding A hotel analyses 5,000 guest reviews. Name two words you would add as domain stopwords, and one frequent word you would keep even though it is common. Why must "not" stay in the text when you score sentiment?
docs.title: Part 3: Stopwords

docs.text: With the noise removed, a frequency distribution counts how often each remaining word appears. NLTK's FreqDist is a counter with a most_common method. freq = nltk . FreqDist ( content_words ) top = pd . Series ( dict ( freq . most_common ( 15 )), name = "count" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) ax . barh ( top . index [:: - 1 ], top . values [:: - 1 ], color = BLUE ) for i , value in enumerate ( top . values [:: - 1 ]): ax . text ( value + 0.1 , i , str ( value ), va = "center" , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_title ( "What LeafLine customers write about most" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Number of times the word appears in 30 reviews" ) ax . grid ( axis = "x" , color = "#e6e5e1" ) ax . set_axisbelow ( True ) plt . show () Read the bar chart above as the manager would: which words about the service appear near the top, and which about the product ? Notice that wait and waited are counted as two different words. Grouping word forms is called stemming or lemmatising ; in a short analysis, a hand-made keyword list (Part 8) does the same job more transparently. Word counts are not opinions A frequent word tells you what people talk about, not whether they like it. app can appear in praise ("easy to use") and in complaints ("crashed"). Frequency says where to look ; sentiment and reading the reviews say what is wrong .
docs.title: Part 4: Word frequency

docs.text: A word cloud draws each word with a size proportional to its frequency. We build it from the same counts, with a fixed random_state so the layout is the same each time you run it. cloud = WordCloud ( width = 800 , height = 400 , background_color = "white" , colormap = "viridis" , random_state = 3 ) . generate_from_frequencies ( freq ) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 5 )) plt . imshow ( cloud , interpolation = "bilinear" ) plt . axis ( "off" ) plt . title ( "LeafLine reviews as a word cloud (size = frequency)" ) plt . show () Compare the cloud with the bar chart in Part 4, using what you learned on Day 2 about encodings: Word cloud Sorted bar chart Encoding Area and font size (read poorly) Length from a common baseline (read well) Ranking Hard beyond the top two or three words The reading order Exact counts Not shown Labelled Long words Look more important than they are No bias Best use A first impression, a slide that invites discussion Any comparison you will base a decision on
docs.title: Part 5: Word clouds and word pairs

docs.text: Single words lose context: brown and sugar mean more together. A bigram is a pair of neighbouring words. We count pairs within each review, so the last word of one review never pairs with the first word of the next. pairs = Counter () for words in reviews [ "content_words" ]: pairs . update ( nltk . bigrams ( words )) print ( "Most common word pairs (after removing stopwords):" ) for ( first , second ), count in pairs . most_common ( 8 ): print ( f " { first } { second } : { count } " ) Most common word pairs (after removing stopwords): friendly staff: 3 brown sugar: 2 waited minutes: 2 sugar delicious: 1 delicious pearls: 1 pearls perfectly: 1 perfectly chewy: 1 chewy new: 1 Pairs such as a product name ("brown sugar") or a complaint ("long wait") are often more useful than single words. With thousands of reviews, pairs and triples become the main source of key phrases. Check your understanding Your manager wants a word cloud of 10,000 complaints for the board. Give one reason to agree and two things you would add or change so the board is not misled.
docs.title: Word pairs (bigrams)

docs.text: Sentiment analysis gives a text a score for how positive or negative it is. We use VADER (Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner, Hutto and Gilbert, 2014), a lexicon-based model built for short, informal texts such as reviews and posts. How VADER works, in three steps: A lexicon (a dictionary) gives about 7,500 words a rating from about −4 (most negative) to +4 (most positive), averaged from human raters. Rules adjust the ratings: negation ("not good"), intensifiers ("very good"), capital letters ("GOOD"), exclamation marks, and "but" (the part after "but" counts more). The adjusted ratings are added and squashed into a compound score between −1 and +1. The usual reading of the compound score S : Compound score Label S ≥ 0.05 Positive −0.05 < S < 0.05 Neutral S ≤ −0.05 Negative First, a look inside the lexicon: analyzer = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () for word in [ "delicious" , "friendly" , "good" , "okay" , "hate" , "terrible" , "disgusting" , "wait" , "queue" , "watery" ]: rating = analyzer . lexicon . get ( word ) print ( f " { word : <11 } { 'not in the lexicon' if rating is None else rating } " ) delicious 2.7 friendly 2.2 good 1.9 okay 0.9 hate -2.7 terrible -2.1 disgusting -2.4 wait not in the lexicon queue not in the lexicon watery not in the lexicon Predict, then reveal The next cell scores seven short sentences. For each, predict whether the compound score is higher or lower than for plain "The tea is good." sentences = [ "The tea is good." , "The tea is very good." , "The tea is GOOD!" , "The tea is not good." , "The tea is good, but the staff are rude." , "The staff are rude, but the tea is good." , "The tea is watery." , ] rule_demo = pd . DataFrame ( [ analyzer . polarity_scores ( s ) for s in sentences ], index = sentences )[[ "neg" , "neu" , "pos" , "compound" ]] rule_demo .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } neg neu pos compound The tea is good. 0.000 0.508 0.492 0.4404 The tea is very good. 0.000 0.556 0.444 0.4927 The tea is GOOD! 0.000 0.433 0.567 0.6027 The tea is not good. 0.376 0.624 0.000 -0.3412 The tea is good, but the staff are rude. 0.309 0.541 0.151 -0.4678 The staff are rude, but the tea is good. 0.156 0.545 0.300 0.4310 The tea is watery. 0.000 1.000 0.000 0.0000 The neg , neu and pos columns are the shares of the text that are negative, neutral and positive; compound is the overall score. Check your predictions against the output above. Two lessons: The rules matter: emphasis raises the score, negation flips it, and the clause after "but" dominates. watery is a complaint about tea, but it is not in a general-purpose lexicon, so it scores as neutral. A lexicon only knows the words it was given. Now score all 30 reviews, on the original text (with stopwords and punctuation), and label each one: def sentiment_label ( score ): if score >= 0.05 : return "Positive" if score <= - 0.05 : return "Negative" return "Neutral" reviews [ "compound" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . apply ( lambda text : analyzer . polarity_scores ( text )[ "compound" ]) reviews [ "sentiment" ] = reviews [ "compound" ] . apply ( sentiment_label ) LABELS = [ "Positive" , "Neutral" , "Negative" ] counts = reviews [ "sentiment" ] . value_counts () . reindex ( LABELS , fill_value = 0 ) print ( counts . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Average compound score: { reviews [ 'compound' ] . mean () : .3f } " ) reviews [[ "branch" , "stars" , "compound" , "sentiment" , "text" ]] . head ( 8 ) sentiment Positive 19 Neutral 5 Negative 6 Average compound score: 0.254 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } branch stars compound sentiment text review_id 1 Riverside 5 0.8478 Positive The brown sugar milk tea is delicious and the pearls are perfectly chewy. My new favou... 2 Riverside 2 0.0000 Neutral Waited 35 minutes for one drink. The queue was huge and nobody explained the delay. 3 Riverside 4 0.2732 Positive Tasty mango tea and friendly staff, but the wait was a bit long at lunchtime. 4 Riverside 1 -0.6697 Negative The app crashed twice while I was paying, and my order was lost. Very frustrating. 5 Riverside 5 0.8479 Positive Great taste, fair price, quick service. Highly recommend the jasmine green tea. 6 Riverside 3 0.6889 Positive The drink was okay. Not bad, not special. 7 Riverside 2 0.4588 Positive Too sweet even at 30% sugar, and the ice melted before I got back to the office. 8 Riverside 1 0.6249 Positive Great, another 40 minute wait for a lukewarm drink. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 6 , 3.5 )) ax . bar ( counts . index , counts . values , color = [ BLUE , GREY , ORANGE ]) for i , value in enumerate ( counts . values ): ax . text ( i , value + 0.2 , str ( value ), ha = "center" , color = INK ) ax . set_title ( "VADER labels for 30 LeafLine reviews" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of reviews" ) plt . show () Check your understanding A review has a compound score of 0.03. What label does it get, and why might the analyst still want to read it? Why do we run VADER on the original text instead of the cleaned, stopword-free words?
docs.title: Part 6: Sentiment with VADER

docs.text: A model's output is a claim, not a fact. Here we are lucky: every review also has a star rating chosen by the customer. If VADER works well, low-star reviews should have low compound scores. Predict, then reveal Review 8 reads "Great, another 40 minute wait for a lukewarm drink." and has 1 star . Will VADER call it positive, neutral or negative? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 12 ) # fixed seed: the small sideways jitter is the same every run jitter = rng . uniform ( - 0.15 , 0.15 , len ( reviews )) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax . axhspan ( - 0.05 , 0.05 , color = GREY , alpha = 0.4 , label = "Neutral band (-0.05 to 0.05)" ) ax . scatter ( reviews [ "stars" ] + jitter , reviews [ "compound" ], s = 45 , color = BLUE ) ax . set_xticks ([ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ]) ax . set_xlabel ( "Star rating given by the customer (1 = worst, 5 = best)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "VADER compound score (-1 to +1)" ) ax . set_title ( "Higher ratings tend to score higher, with clear exceptions" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () print ( "Average compound score by star rating:" ) print ( reviews . groupby ( "stars" )[ "compound" ] . agg ([ "count" , "mean" ]) . round ( 3 ) . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Correlation between stars and compound score: r = { reviews [ 'stars' ] . corr ( reviews [ 'compound' ]) : .2f } " ) Average compound score by star rating: count mean stars 1 5 -0.256 2 8 0.008 3 4 0.207 4 7 0.422 5 6 0.844 Correlation between stars and compound score: r = 0.79 The chart above shows a clear upward pattern, but some unhappy customers (1 or 2 stars) sit in or above the neutral band. List them: unhappy_not_negative = reviews [( reviews [ "stars" ] <= 2 ) & ( reviews [ "sentiment" ] != "Negative" )] print ( "Reviews with 1-2 stars that VADER does NOT label Negative:" , len ( unhappy_not_negative )) unhappy_not_negative [[ "stars" , "compound" , "sentiment" , "text" ]] Reviews with 1-2 stars that VADER does NOT label Negative: 8 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } stars compound sentiment text review_id 2 2 0.0000 Neutral Waited 35 minutes for one drink. The queue was huge and nobody explained the delay. 7 2 0.4588 Positive Too sweet even at 30% sugar, and the ice melted before I got back to the office. 8 1 0.6249 Positive Great, another 40 minute wait for a lukewarm drink. 10 2 0.1901 Positive The app showed my order as ready but the staff could not find it. I waited another 20 ... 23 2 0.0000 Neutral Convenient location, but the wait times are unpredictable. 25 2 0.0000 Neutral The app kept logging me out, and the queue was very long. 27 1 0.0000 Neutral Overpriced and watery. Never again. 30 2 0.0000 Neutral Waited 30 minutes at the counter while app orders kept jumping the queue. Read each review in the table above and ask why the lexicon missed it. The reasons fall into a few groups: Blind spot Example from the table What to do Domain words missing from the lexicon wait , queue , minutes , watery , lukewarm Add domain words with ratings, or use a keyword list for known problems Sarcasm "Great, another 40 minute wait…" Read a sample; no word-based method handles sarcasm reliably Facts that imply a feeling "I missed my train because the order took 25 minutes" Combine sentiment with topic keywords Mixed reviews Praise and complaint in one review Score sentences separately, or by aspect Other languages Chinese reviews VADER is English only; Chinese text needs its own tokenizer (Chinese has no spaces between words) and its own lexicon Remember Sentiment scores are useful for large volumes and trends (is this month worse than last month?). They are weak evidence about any single review. Always validate against a second source, such as star ratings or a sample read by a person.
docs.title: Part 7: Checking the scores against star ratings

docs.text: The manager's question was what should we fix first? Topics alone and sentiment alone each fall short, so we combine them. We define a few aspects by keyword lists, flag every review that mentions each aspect, and summarise the reviews in each group. Because VADER misses complaints about waiting, we lead with the star rating and show the compound score next to it. ASPECTS = { "waiting" : { "wait" , "waited" , "queue" , "slow" , "minutes" , "minute" , "long" , "delay" }, "app" : { "app" }, "taste" : { "taste" , "tasty" , "delicious" , "sweet" , "watery" , "pearls" , "fresh" , "lukewarm" }, "staff" : { "staff" , "cashier" , "rude" , "friendly" , "polite" , "kind" , "nobody" }, "price" : { "price" , "cheap" , "expensive" , "overpriced" , "discount" , "paid" , "charged" }, } for aspect , keywords in ASPECTS . items (): reviews [ aspect ] = reviews [ "words" ] . apply ( lambda words : bool ( keywords & set ( words ))) rows = [] for aspect in ASPECTS : group = reviews [ reviews [ aspect ]] rows . append ({ "aspect" : aspect , "reviews" : len ( group ), " % o f all reviews" : 100 * len ( group ) / len ( reviews ), "average stars" : group [ "stars" ] . mean (), "% with 1-2 stars" : 100 * ( group [ "stars" ] <= 2 ) . mean (), "average compound" : group [ "compound" ] . mean (), }) aspects = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . set_index ( "aspect" ) . sort_values ( "% with 1-2 stars" , ascending = False ) aspects . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } reviews % of all reviews average stars % with 1-2 stars average compound aspect waiting 12 40.00 2.58 66.67 0.17 app 9 30.00 2.78 55.56 0.06 staff 9 30.00 3.11 44.44 0.20 price 7 23.33 3.29 28.57 0.28 taste 11 36.67 3.36 27.27 0.45 low_share = aspects [ "% with 1-2 stars" ] . sort_values () worst = low_share . index [ - 1 ] fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.8 )) ax . barh ( low_share . index , low_share . values , color = [ ORANGE if a == worst else GREY for a in low_share . index ]) for i , ( aspect , value ) in enumerate ( low_share . items ()): ax . text ( value + 1 , i , f " { value : .0f } % (n = { aspects . loc [ aspect , 'reviews' ] } )" , va = "center" , fontsize = 9 , color = INK ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , 115 ) ax . set_title ( f "Reviews that mention { worst } are the most often unhappy" ) ax . set_xlabel ( " % o f reviews mentioning the aspect that give 1 or 2 stars" ) plt . show () A review can mention several aspects, so the groups overlap and their counts add up to more than 30. The n beside each bar is the number of reviews behind the percentage: with 30 reviews, every group is small. Where does the worst aspect happen? Break it down by branch: by_branch = reviews . groupby ( "branch" ) . agg ( reviews = ( "stars" , "size" ), mention_worst = ( worst , "sum" ), average_stars = ( "stars" , "mean" ), ) by_branch [ f "% mentioning { worst } " ] = 100 * by_branch [ "mention_worst" ] / by_branch [ "reviews" ] by_branch . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } reviews mention_worst average_stars % mentioning waiting branch Campus 10 1 3.6 10.0 Riverside 10 4 2.9 40.0 Station 10 7 2.6 70.0
docs.title: Part 8: From reviews to a decision

docs.text: A recommendation from text mining has four parts. Fill them in from the outputs above: Part Content Finding Which aspect is most often linked to unhappy customers, and in which branches Evidence The share of 1–2 star reviews for that aspect, with n ; two or three quoted reviews Recommendation A specific action the manager controls, for example a separate pick-up counter for app orders and a visible waiting-time display Caveats Synthetic data; only 30 reviews; keyword lists miss synonyms; VADER under-scores waiting complaints; a review is one visit, not one customer Association is not causation Reviews that mention waiting are more often unhappy. That supports fixing waiting times, but it does not prove that shorter waits will raise ratings. A careful manager tests the change in one branch first and compares ratings before and after. Ethics and privacy Real reviews and chat logs can contain names, phone numbers and order numbers. Remove personal details before analysis, store text securely, and report patterns, never individual customers. Check your understanding The app aspect also has many low ratings. Read the app reviews (filter reviews[reviews["app"]] ). Is the problem the same in every review? What would you recommend to the app team?
docs.title: Writing the recommendation

docs.text: Idea One-line takeaway Unstructured text Most business feedback is text; text mining turns it into counts, scores and categories Tokenising Lowercase, split with word_tokenize , keep isalpha() tokens for counting Stopwords Remove standard and domain stopwords for topics; never for sentiment ("not") Word frequency Says what people talk about, not what they feel; show it as a sorted bar chart Word cloud A first impression only: area is read poorly; pairs (bigrams) add context VADER Lexicon plus rules gives a compound score from −1 to +1; ±0.05 thresholds Validation Compare with star ratings or a read sample; watch for domain words, sarcasm, mixed reviews, other languages Decision Combine aspects and ratings; finding, evidence, recommendation, caveats

Part 2: The business report ¶ Write the report in Word (or another editor that saves PDF) for the executive board of UrbanTrend Real Estate Analytics. Use the five headings below exactly , in this order. Write connected paragraphs, not lists of answers; only Section 5 uses bullet points. Quote the numbers you use, with units, and refer to the evidence by name (Figure 1, Table 1, Model B…). 1. Executive Summary ¶ One paragraph. The purpose of the project, the two kinds of data used (structured facts and unstructured agent descriptions), and what the predictive model is for. 2. Exploratory Data Analysis ¶ One or two paragraphs , based on Figures 1 and 2. Describe the relationship between floor area and price in Figure 1: direction, strength, shape. From Figure 2: do more bedrooms always mean a higher median price? How does the spread of prices (the height of the boxes) change from 2 to 5 bedrooms? 3. Text Mining Methodology and Value ¶ One or two paragraphs. Explain, for a non-technical board, what Step 3 did: how a written description became a number between −1 and +1. Using the list of distinct descriptions and their scores: which description scored highest and which lowest? Is the score for the "fixer-upper" description negative, as you might expect? Explain why a general-purpose sentiment lexicon might score it the way it does. Why is it worth turning the descriptions into a number before building a pricing model? Use the comparison of Model A and Model B. 4. Predictive Analytics Results ¶ Two paragraphs , based on Model B (and Model A for comparison). Accuracy: state Model B's test R² and RMSE and explain what they mean for predicting the price of homes the model has not seen. How much did adding the text score improve on Model A? Business drivers: from Model B's coefficients, how much value is associated with one extra bedroom, and how much with each extra year of age, holding the other features fixed? The value of text: the Text Appeal Score runs from −1 to +1, so a change of 1.0 is the jump from a neutral to a highly positive description. Using its coefficient, what is that jump associated with in dollars? Then use the actual scores of the three descriptions to say how large the predicted gap between a "fixer-upper" and a "luxury" description really is. Remember that these are associations, not proof that rewriting a description would raise a price. 5. Strategic Recommendations ¶ Two bullet points , each justified by your results: practical advice for the firm's agents (for example, how much effort to put into descriptions; which features of a home to stress in marketing) or for the firm's modelling team (for example, how to improve the text feature). Good practice from today's lectures Lead with the finding, not the method. Report test results, not training results. Say "is associated with", not "causes". Name the units (dollars, square feet, years).
