Day 5 lab: Applied Lab 5 — Predictive linear regression modelling ¶ Predict a car's fuel efficiency from its engineering specifications the way a data scientist would: separate features from the target, train a multiple linear regression on 80% of the cars, predict the 20% it never saw, measure the error with RMSE, MAE and R², and check the model's health with a residual plot. Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Applied Lab 5 (Predictive linear regression modeling), for local Jupyter without internet access. Graded Yes: 2% of the course grade Outcomes CLO 4 and 5 Tool JupyterLab (Anaconda), with scikit-learn You submit One PDF, YourLastName_DATA300_AppliedLab5.pdf , in the Applied Lab 5 drop-box on GAP (Moodle) Deadline Tuesday 17 November, 23:59 China Standard Time, unless your facilitator says otherwise (see the schedule ) The business scenario ¶ You are a data scientist at an automotive analytics consultancy . A car manufacturer is designing its next models and must meet stricter fuel-efficiency rules. It asks you for a model that predicts a vehicle's fuel efficiency in miles per gallon (MPG) from its engineering specifications alone: Feature Meaning Unit cylinders Number of engine cylinders count displacement Engine size cubic inches horsepower Engine power horsepower weight Vehicle weight pounds acceleration Time from 0 to 60 mph seconds The manufacturer will only trust the model if you prove that it works on vehicles it has never seen. So you hold back a fifth of the cars, train on the rest, and test on the hidden ones. Before you start ¶ Keep this notebook in the course folder, next to the data folder. Save your own copy: File → Save Notebook As… and type YourLastName_Data300_AppliedLab5.ipynb (with your real last name). Work in that copy. The code below works as given. Run each cell in order with Shift + Enter , read the output, and answer the questions in Part 5. You may add cells of your own to check an answer. Part 1: Load the data and choose features and target ¶ In predictive analytics the inputs are the features (X) and the value to predict is the target (y). A few cars have no horsepower recorded; linear regression cannot use a row with a missing value, so we drop those rows and say so. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , mean_squared_error , r2_score from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split # 1. Load the bundled mpg data (no internet needed) df = pd . read_csv ( "data/mpg.csv" ) print ( f "Vehicles in the file: { len ( df ) } " ) print ( "Missing values per column:" , df . isna () . sum ()[ df . isna () . sum () > 0 ] . to_dict ()) # 2. Data cleaning: drop rows with missing values df = df . dropna () # 3. Features (X) and target (y) features = [ "cylinders" , "displacement" , "horsepower" , "weight" , "acceleration" ] X = df [ features ] y = df [ "mpg" ] print ( " 
 --- Dataset snapshot ---" ) print ( df [ features + [ "mpg" ]] . head () . to_string ()) print ( f " 
 Total usable vehicles: { len ( df ) } " ) Vehicles in the file: 398 Missing values per column: {'horsepower': 6} --- Dataset snapshot --- cylinders displacement horsepower weight acceleration mpg 0 8 307.0 130.0 3504 12.0 18.0 1 8 350.0 165.0 3693 11.5 15.0 2 8 318.0 150.0 3436 11.0 18.0 3 8 304.0 150.0 3433 12.0 16.0 4 8 302.0 140.0 3449 10.5 17.0 Total usable vehicles: 392 Part 2: Train/test split and model training ¶ To show that the model predicts rather than memorises, we split the cars at random: the model learns from 80% (the training set) and is then asked about the other 20% (the test set), which it never sees while it learns. random_state=42 fixes the random split so everyone gets the same cars in each set. Coefficients: the business impact of each specification print ( "--- Model coefficients (change in MPG per one-unit increase) ---" ) coefficients = pd . DataFrame ({ "Feature" : features , "Coefficient" : model . coef_ }) print ( coefficients . to_string ( index = False )) print ( f " 
 Intercept: { model . intercept_ : .4f } " ) Training on 313 vehicles... Part 3: Out-of-sample prediction and evaluation ¶ The model now predicts the MPG of the hidden test cars from their specifications, and we compare its predictions with their real MPG: Measure Meaning RMSE , root mean squared error A typical miss, in MPG; large misses count extra MAE , mean absolute error The average size of the miss, in MPG R² on the test set The share of the variation in the test cars' MPG that the model explains In the chart, each dot is one test car. The dashed line marks perfect predictions (predicted = actual): the closer the dots, the better. # 1. Predict the hidden TEST cars y_pred = model . predict ( X_test ) # 2. Evaluation measures rmse = np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( y_test , y_pred )) mae = mean_absolute_error ( y_test , y_pred ) r2_test = r2_score ( y_test , y_pred ) print ( "--- Predictive performance on the TEST data ---" ) print ( f "Root mean squared error (RMSE): { rmse : .2f } MPG" ) print ( f "Mean absolute error (MAE): { mae : .2f } MPG" ) print ( f "Test R-squared (R2): { r2_test : .4f } " ) # 3. Actual vs predicted plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) plt . scatter ( y_test , y_pred , alpha = 0.7 , color = "#2a78d6" ) plt . plot ([ y . min (), y . max ()], [ y . min (), y . max ()], color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Perfect prediction" ) plt . title ( "Predictive accuracy: actual vs. predicted MPG (test cars)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Actual MPG (true values)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Predicted MPG (model)" ) plt . legend () plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () --- Predictive performance on the TEST data --- Root mean squared error (RMSE): 4.24 MPG Mean absolute error (MAE): 3.49 MPG Test R-squared (R2): 0.6485 Use these outputs for questions 2, 3 and 4. Part 4: Residual diagnostics ¶ A residual is actual minus predicted MPG. A healthy linear model leaves residuals that look like a random cloud around zero, equally wide everywhere ( homoscedasticity ). A pattern (a U-shape, an arch, or a funnel that widens: heteroscedasticity ) means the model is systematically wrong for some cars, often because the real relationship is curved. # Residuals: actual minus predicted residuals = y_test - y_pred plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) plt . scatter ( y_pred , residuals , alpha = 0.7 , color = "#1baf7a" ) plt . axhline ( y = 0 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" ) plt . title ( "Residual diagnostic plot (checking for homoscedasticity)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Predicted MPG" ) plt . ylabel ( "Residual (actual - predicted MPG)" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () Use this chart for question 5. Part 5: Questions ¶ Answer all five questions in complete sentences in the answer cell below. Base every answer on the outputs in this notebook, and quote the numbers you use. # Question 1 Coefficients and design. In the Part 2 table, the weight coefficient is about −0.005. Explain in plain words what it means for vehicle design: what happens to predicted MPG for each extra pound, and for an extra 1,000 pounds , with the other specifications held fixed? 2 Predictive performance. State the test R² from Part 3. Because it was measured on cars the model never saw during training, what does it tell the manufacturer about how well the model will predict new vehicles? 3 Error for engineers. State the MAE from Part 3 and explain it in one sentence an engineer would understand, for example: "When the model predicts a car's MPG, it is usually off by about … MPG." 4 Actual vs predicted. In the Part 3 chart, are the dots tightly grouped around the dashed line or widely scattered? Does the model struggle more with low-MPG cars (around 15 MPG) or high-MPG cars (35 MPG or more)? 5 Residuals. In the Part 4 chart, do you see a random cloud around zero, or a U-shape or widening pattern? If there is a pattern, what does it suggest the straight-line model is missing? Writing tips Lead with the answer, then the evidence: "The test R² of … means …" . Keep the units (MPG, pounds). Say "is associated with", not "causes": the coefficients come from past cars, not from an experiment. My answers Name: Your name · Student ID: Your ID 1. The weight coefficient, per pound and per 1,000 pounds: Your answer 2. Test R² and what it says about new vehicles: Your answer 3. MAE, explained for engineers: Your answer 4. Grouping around the line; low- or high-MPG cars: Your answer 5. Residual pattern and what it suggests: Your answer Going further (not graded) ¶ Two ideas a careful analyst would try next. First, the data include each car's model year and origin (USA, Europe, Japan); newer cars and imported cars were more efficient in this period. Second, the residual pattern suggests a curve : MPG falls steeply as weight rises from light cars, then more slowly. Predicting 1 / MPG (gallons per mile, which grows roughly in proportion to weight) is a classic way to straighten it. The cell below compares the models on the same test cars, always reporting the error in MPG. def test_scores ( X_all , target = "mpg" ): """Fit on the same training cars, report R², RMSE and MAE in MPG on the same test cars.""" Xtr , Xte = X_all . loc [ X_train . index ], X_all . loc [ X_test . index ] if target == "mpg" : pred = LinearRegression () . fit ( Xtr , y_train ) . predict ( Xte ) else : # model gallons per mile, then convert the prediction back to MPG pred = 1 / LinearRegression () . fit ( Xtr , 1 / y_train ) . predict ( Xte ) return { "test R²" : r2_score ( y_test , pred ), "RMSE (MPG)" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( y_test , pred )), "MAE (MPG)" : mean_absolute_error ( y_test , pred )} extra = pd . get_dummies ( df [ features + [ "model_year" , "origin" ]], columns = [ "origin" ], drop_first = True , dtype = float ) comparison = pd . DataFrame ({ "Lab model (5 specifications)" : test_scores ( df [ features ]), "+ model year and origin" : test_scores ( extra ), "+ model year and origin, predicting 1/MPG" : test_scores ( extra , target = "inverse" ), }) . Fit the multiple linear regression on the training set only model = LinearRegression () model . fit ( X_train , y_train ) # 3. Coefficients: the business impact of each specification print ( "--- Model coefficients (change in MPG per one-unit increase) ---" ) coefficients = pd . DataFrame ({ "Feature" : features , "Coefficient" : model . coef_ }) print ( coefficients . to_string ( index = False )) print ( f " \n Intercept: { model . intercept_ : .4f } " ) Training on 313 vehicles... Testing on 79 vehicles (hidden during training)... --- Model coefficients (change in MPG per one-unit increase) --- Feature Coefficient cylinders -0.175808 displacement -0.006713 horsepower -0.048908 weight -0.004992 acceleration -0.060449 Intercept: 46.8371 Use this table for question 1.

docs.text: The model now predicts the MPG of the hidden test cars from their specifications, and we compare its predictions with their real MPG: Measure Meaning RMSE , root mean squared error A typical miss, in MPG; large misses count extra MAE , mean absolute error The average size of the miss, in MPG R² on the test set The share of the variation in the test cars' MPG that the model explains In the chart, each dot is one test car. The dashed line marks perfect predictions (predicted = actual): the closer the dots, the better. # 1. Predict the hidden TEST cars y_pred = model . predict ( X_test ) # 2. Evaluation measures rmse = np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( y_test , y_pred )) mae = mean_absolute_error ( y_test , y_pred ) r2_test = r2_score ( y_test , y_pred ) print ( "--- Predictive performance on the TEST data ---" ) print ( f "Root mean squared error (RMSE): { rmse : .2f } MPG" ) print ( f "Mean absolute error (MAE): { mae : .2f } MPG" ) print ( f "Test R-squared (R2): { r2_test : .4f } " ) # 3. Actual vs predicted plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) plt . scatter ( y_test , y_pred , alpha = 0.7 , color = "#2a78d6" ) plt . plot ([ y . min (), y . max ()], [ y . min (), y . max ()], color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" , linewidth = 2 , label = "Perfect prediction" ) plt . title ( "Predictive accuracy: actual vs. predicted MPG (test cars)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Actual MPG (true values)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Predicted MPG (model)" ) plt . legend () plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () --- Predictive performance on the TEST data --- Root mean squared error (RMSE): 4.24 MPG Mean absolute error (MAE): 3.49 MPG Test R-squared (R2): 0.6485 Use these outputs for questions 2, 3 and 4.

docs.text: A residual is actual minus predicted MPG. A healthy linear model leaves residuals that look like a random cloud around zero, equally wide everywhere ( homoscedasticity ). A pattern (a U-shape, an arch, or a funnel that widens: heteroscedasticity ) means the model is systematically wrong for some cars, often because the real relationship is curved. # Residuals: actual minus predicted residuals = y_test - y_pred plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 6 )) plt . scatter ( y_pred , residuals , alpha = 0.7 , color = "#1baf7a" ) plt . axhline ( y = 0 , color = "#eb6834" , linestyle = "--" ) plt . title ( "Residual diagnostic plot (checking for homoscedasticity)" ) plt . xlabel ( "Predicted MPG" ) plt . ylabel ( "Residual (actual - predicted MPG)" ) plt . grid ( True , linestyle = "--" , alpha = 0.5 ) plt . show () Use this chart for question 5.

docs.text: Two ideas a careful analyst would try next. First, the data include each car's model year and origin (USA, Europe, Japan); newer cars and imported cars were more efficient in this period. Second, the residual pattern suggests a curve : MPG falls steeply as weight rises from light cars, then more slowly. Predicting 1 / MPG (gallons per mile, which grows roughly in proportion to weight) is a classic way to straighten it. The cell below compares the models on the same test cars, always reporting the error in MPG. def test_scores ( X_all , target = "mpg" ): """Fit on the same training cars, report R², RMSE and MAE in MPG on the same test cars.""" Xtr , Xte = X_all . loc [ X_train . index ], X_all . loc [ X_test . index ] if target == "mpg" : pred = LinearRegression () . fit ( Xtr , y_train ) . predict ( Xte ) else : # model gallons per mile, then convert the prediction back to MPG pred = 1 / LinearRegression () . fit ( Xtr , 1 / y_train ) . predict ( Xte ) return { "test R²" : r2_score ( y_test , pred ), "RMSE (MPG)" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( y_test , pred )), "MAE (MPG)" : mean_absolute_error ( y_test , pred )} extra = pd . get_dummies ( df [ features + [ "model_year" , "origin" ]], columns = [ "origin" ], drop_first = True , dtype = float ) comparison = pd . DataFrame ({ "Lab model (5 specifications)" : test_scores ( df [ features ]), "+ model year and origin" : test_scores ( extra ), "+ model year and origin, predicting 1/MPG" : test_scores ( extra , target = "inverse" ), }) . T print ( comparison . round ( 3 ) . to_string ()) test R² RMSE (MPG) MAE (MPG) Lab model (5 specifications) 0.649 4.235 3.486 + model year and origin 0.792 3.256 2.462 + model year and origin, predicting 1/MPG 0.850 2.766 2.110 Which change helps more: the extra features, or the change of target? Plot the residuals of the best model the same way as in Part 4: has the pattern gone? Remember that adding model_year changes the meaning of the question: the manufacturer asked about engineering specifications only, and a future car's model year is not a design choice.

docs.text: Day 5 lecture: Financial modelling and spreadsheet simulation ¶ Every business plan rests on numbers nobody knows for sure: how many customers will come, what supplies will cost. This lecture shows how to build a clear financial model in Excel, explore it with what-if tables and scenarios, replace single guesses with random inputs in a Monte Carlo simulation, and turn thousands of simulated outcomes into risk measures a manager can act on. Python checks every idea along the way. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Keep Microsoft Excel open next to it: most parts end with steps to do in Excel. Recap quiz ¶ Before we start, answer the closing quizzes at the end of yesterday's lectures on predictive analytics and regression and data mining with text features . Write short answers; we discuss them together. What you will be able to do ¶ Lay out a financial model with separate inputs, calculations and outputs, and follow good spreadsheet practice. Run what-if analysis in Excel: one-way and two-way Data Tables , Goal Seek and the Scenario Manager . Generate random inputs in Excel with RAND() , RANDBETWEEN() and NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) , and explain how they work. Build a Monte Carlo simulation in Excel and check it with numpy. Summarise a simulation with risk measures : expected value, spread, probability of loss, percentiles and the average of the worst cases. Explain why the profit at average inputs is not the average profit (the flaw of averages), and how many trials a simulation needs. Compare two decisions under uncertainty and report the result honestly. Reading: Wall Street Prep (n.d.), Financial modeling guide ; Workday (n.d.), Financial forecasting in Excel made easy . How to use the questions in this notebook Predict, then reveal boxes ask you to guess before running the next cell. Check your understanding boxes are short questions to answer in your own words. In Excel boxes are numbered steps to do on your computer. Practice workbook data/leafline_simulation_practice.xlsx , in the course folder, holds the model from this lecture, ready-made: a Model sheet, a frame for a Data Table, and a Simulation sheet with 1,000 trials. Build the model yourself first (Part 2); use the workbook to check your work or to catch up. Part Topic 1 What a financial model is 2 The case: a new LeafLine Tea branch 3 What-if analysis: Data Tables and Goal Seek 4 Scenarios 5 Random inputs in Excel and Python 6 Monte Carlo simulation 7 Risk measures 8 How many trials? 9 The flaw of averages 10 Comparing two decisions 11 Reporting a simulation Part 1: What a financial model is ¶ A financial model is a set of linked calculations that turns assumptions about the business into financial results : revenue, costs, profit, cash. Managers use it to answer "what happens if…?" before they commit money. Layer Contents Example Inputs (assumptions) Numbers someone must estimate or decide Cups sold per year, price per cup, rent Calculations Formulas that link inputs Revenue = cups × price Outputs The results decisions depend on Profit, break-even point A model is deterministic when each input has one value: it gives one answer. A simulation model lets uncertain inputs vary at random and gives a distribution of answers. Good spreadsheet practice ¶ Rule Why Put every input in its own labelled cell , in one place, and colour input cells (for example blue) Anyone can see and change the assumptions Never type a number inside a formula : refer to the input cell One change updates the whole model; no hidden assumptions Use absolute references ( $B$5 ) for inputs that formulas copied down or across must keep Copied formulas still point at the right input Work left to right, top to bottom : inputs, then calculations, then outputs The model reads like a story Write the units in the label (per cup, per year) Avoids mixing months and years, or cups and cartons Add checks (for example, cups sold never exceed capacity) Errors are caught early The setup cell loads the libraries. Everything here uses numpy, pandas and matplotlib; statistics.NormalDist comes with Python itself. from statistics import NormalDist import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" INK = "#55534e" plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 9 , 4.5 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) pd . set_option ( "display.width" , 120 ) Part 2: The case: a new LeafLine Tea branch ¶ About the case LeafLine Tea is the synthetic milk-tea chain from the Day 3 text-mining lecture. All numbers are invented for teaching. Amounts are in neutral currency units . LeafLine Tea is deciding whether to open a new branch. The finance team's first-year assumptions: Input Base value Unit Expected demand 60,000 cups per year Price 18 currency units per cup Variable cost (tea, milk, cups, packaging) 7.5 currency units per cup Fixed costs (rent, staff, equipment) 500,000 currency units per year Capacity 75,000 cups per year the branch can make The calculations: Cups sold = the smaller of demand and capacity Revenue = cups sold × price Variable costs = cups sold × variable cost per cup Profit = revenue − variable costs − fixed costs Break-even demand = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per cup): the cups needed for zero profit. Price − variable cost is the contribution margin per cup. BASE = { "demand" : 60_000 , "price" : 18.0 , "variable_cost" : 7.5 , "fixed_costs" : 500_000 , "capacity" : 75_000 } def profit ( demand , price , variable_cost , fixed_costs , capacity ): """Year-1 profit of the branch. Works on single numbers and on whole numpy arrays.""" cups_sold = np . minimum ( demand , capacity ) return cups_sold * ( price - variable_cost ) - fixed_costs base_profit = profit ( ** BASE ) break_even = BASE [ "fixed_costs" ] / ( BASE [ "price" ] - BASE [ "variable_cost" ]) print ( f "Base-case profit: { base_profit : ,.0f } currency units" ) print ( f "Break-even demand: { break_even : ,.0f } cups per year" ) print ( f "Safety margin: demand can fall { 1 - break_even / BASE [ 'demand' ] : .0% } below the base case before a loss" ) Base-case profit: 130,000 currency units Break-even demand: 47,619 cups per year Safety margin: demand can fall 21% below the base case before a loss In Excel: build the base model (about 10 minutes) Open a blank workbook. Rename Sheet1 to Model (double-click the tab). In A4:A8 type the five input labels from the table above; in B4:B8 type the base values. Fill B4:B8 blue ( Home → Fill Color ). In D4:D8 type the labels Cups sold , Revenue , Variable costs , Profit , Break-even demand . In E4 type =MIN(B4,B8) ; in E5 =E4*B5 ; in E6 =E4*B6 ; in E7 =E5-E6-B7 ; in E8 =B7/(B5-B6) . Format money cells with Home → Number Format → Number and the thousands separator. Check: E7 and E8 must match the Python output above. Part 3: What-if analysis: Data Tables and Goal Seek ¶ What-if analysis changes inputs and watches the outputs. Its simplest form is a one-way sensitivity table : vary one input, hold the others at their base values. Predict, then reveal Demand falls from 60,000 to 40,000 cups. Will profit fall by a third, by about half, or by more than that? demands = np . arange ( 30_000 , 90_001 , 10_000 ) one_way = pd . DataFrame ({ "demand (cups)" : demands , "profit" : profit ( demands , BASE [ "price" ], BASE [ "variable_cost" ], BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ])}) print ( one_way . to_string ( index = False , formatters = { "profit" : " {:,.0f} " . format , "demand (cups)" : " {:,} " . format })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( one_way [ "demand (cups)" ], one_way [ "profit" ], marker = "o" , color = BLUE ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . axvline ( break_even , color = ORANGE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Break-even demand" ) ax . axvline ( BASE [ "capacity" ], color = GREY , linestyle = ":" , label = "Capacity" ) ax . set_title ( "Profit rises with demand until the branch reaches capacity" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Demand (cups per year)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Profit (currency units)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () demand (cups) profit 30,000 -185,000 40,000 -80,000 50,000 25,000 60,000 130,000 70,000 235,000 80,000 287,500 90,000 287,500 Profit falls much faster than demand, because the fixed costs do not shrink when customers stay away. This is operating leverage : high fixed costs make profit sensitive to volume. Beyond capacity, extra demand adds nothing. Two-way Data Table ¶ A two-way Data Table varies two inputs at once and shows the output for every combination. Here: demand down the side, price across the top. prices = np . array ([ 14 , 16 , 18 , 20 , 22 ]) grid = pd . DataFrame ( [[ profit ( d , p , BASE [ "variable_cost" ], BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) for p in prices ] for d in demands ], index = pd . Index ( demands , name = "demand" ), columns = pd . Index ( prices , name = "price" ), ) print ( "Profit (currency units) by demand (rows) and price per cup (columns)" ) print ( grid . to_string ( float_format = " {:,.0f} " . format )) Profit (currency units) by demand (rows) and price per cup (columns) price 14 16 18 20 22 demand 30000 -305,000 -245,000 -185,000 -125,000 -65,000 40000 -240,000 -160,000 -80,000 0 80,000 50000 -175,000 -75,000 25,000 125,000 225,000 60000 -110,000 10,000 130,000 250,000 370,000 70000 -45,000 95,000 235,000 375,000 515,000 80000 -12,500 137,500 287,500 437,500 587,500 90000 -12,500 137,500 287,500 437,500 587,500 Read the table above: which combinations make a loss? Notice that a higher price helps a lot if demand holds . The table cannot say whether demand would hold at a higher price; that is a question for market research or an experiment, not for the spreadsheet. In Excel: two-way Data Table (Excel calls it Data Table ; in Chinese Excel 模拟运算表) On the Model sheet, in B17 type =E7 (the output you want to see). This must be the top-left corner of the table. In C17:G17 type the prices 14, 16, 18, 20, 22 (across). In B18:B24 type the demands 30000 to 90000 in steps of 10000 (down). Select the whole block B17:G24 . Data → What-If Analysis → Data Table… (数据 → 模拟分析 → 模拟运算表). Row input cell: B5 (price, because the prices run along the row). Column input cell: B4 (demand, because the demands run down the column). Click OK . Select C18:G24 → Home → Conditional Formatting → Color Scales so losses stand out. Check: your table must match the Python output above. Two traps The input cells must be on the same sheet as the Data Table. If you point to an input on another sheet, Excel refuses with "Input cell reference is not valid". Keep the table on the Model sheet, or link the inputs. Data Tables recalculate every time anything changes and can make a big workbook slow. Formulas → Calculation Options → Automatic except for Data Tables helps; press F9 to update. Goal Seek ¶ Goal Seek works backwards: "which value of this input gives that output?" In Excel: Goal Seek (单变量求解) Data → What-If Analysis → Goal Seek… Set cell: E7 (profit). To value: 0 . By changing cell: B4 (demand). Click OK . Excel finds the break-even demand. Compare it with E8, then click Cancel to keep the original demand. Check your understanding Use the Data Table above: at a price of 16, roughly what demand does the branch need to break even? Check with the break-even formula. Part 4: Scenarios ¶ A scenario changes several inputs together to tell one consistent story. Most plans show three: Scenario Story Demand Variable cost Fixed costs Worst case A rival opens nearby; milk prices rise 42,000 8.5 520,000 Base case The finance team's plan 60,000 7.5 500,000 Best case Strong launch; a supplier discount 75,000 6.5 500,000 scenarios = pd . DataFrame ({ "worst case" : { "demand" : 42_000 , "variable_cost" : 8.5 , "fixed_costs" : 520_000 }, "base case" : { "demand" : 60_000 , "variable_cost" : 7.5 , "fixed_costs" : 500_000 }, "best case" : { "demand" : 75_000 , "variable_cost" : 6.5 , "fixed_costs" : 500_000 }, }) . T scenarios [ "profit" ] = profit ( scenarios [ "demand" ], BASE [ "price" ], scenarios [ "variable_cost" ], scenarios [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) print ( scenarios . to_string ( formatters = { "demand" : " {:,.0f} " . format , "fixed_costs" : " {:,.0f} " . format , "profit" : " {:,.0f} " . format })) demand variable_cost fixed_costs profit worst case 42,000 8.5 520,000 -121,000 base case 60,000 7.5 500,000 130,000 best case 75,000 6.5 500,000 362,500 In Excel: Scenario Manager (方案管理器) Data → What-If Analysis → Scenario Manager… → Add . Name it Worst case . Changing cells: B4,B6,B7 (hold Ctrl to pick several). Click OK , then type the three worst-case values. Click OK . Repeat for Base case and Best case . Click Summary… , choose Scenario summary , Result cells: E7 . Excel adds a new sheet comparing the scenarios. Scenarios are easy to explain, but they have two weaknesses: They say nothing about how likely each story is. Is the worst case a 1-in-3 or a 1-in-1,000 event? The real outcome is almost never exactly one of the three. Inputs combine in countless ways. A simulation fixes both. Part 5: Random inputs in Excel and Python ¶ Instead of one guess for demand, we describe it with a probability distribution : the range of values it could take and how likely each is. Distribution Use when Excel numpy Uniform between 0 and 1 The building block for all others =RAND() rng.uniform(0, 1) Uniform between a and b Only a range is known; every value equally likely =a+(b-a)*RAND() rng.uniform(a, b) Whole numbers between a and b Counts, equally likely =RANDBETWEEN(a,b) rng.integers(a, b + 1) Normal with mean m and standard deviation s A typical value with symmetric uncertainty around it =NORM.INV(RAND(),m,s) rng.normal(m, s) Yes/no with probability p An event that may happen (a rival opens) =IF(RAND()<p,1,0) rng.uniform() < p For LeafLine Tea the team chooses: Demand: normal, mean 60,000 cups, standard deviation 12,000 (about two times in three, demand lands between 48,000 and 72,000). Variable cost per cup: uniform between 6 and 9 (milk and tea prices could move anywhere in that range). Price, fixed costs and capacity stay fixed: the company sets them. How NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) works ¶ RAND() gives a random probability between 0 and 1. NORM.INV turns a probability into the value with that much of the normal distribution below it. A RAND() of 0.5 gives the mean; 0.84 gives about mean + 1 sd; 0.025 gives about mean − 2 sd. Because RAND() is equally likely to land anywhere between 0 and 1, the results follow the normal shape. This is called the inverse transform method. Python's NormalDist(...).inv_cdf is the same function as Excel's NORM.INV , so we can check the method directly. demand_dist = NormalDist ( mu = 60_000 , sigma = 12_000 ) for u in [ 0.025 , 0.16 , 0.5 , 0.84 , 0.975 ]: print ( f "RAND() = { u : <5 } -> NORM.INV gives { demand_dist . inv_cdf ( u ) : >8,.0f } cups" ) rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 17 ) u = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , 10_000 ) # 10,000 "RAND()" values via_inverse = np . array ([ demand_dist . inv_cdf ( x ) for x in u ]) # Excel's way: NORM.INV(RAND(), 60000, 12000) direct = rng . normal ( 60_000 , 12_000 , 10_000 ) # numpy's way print ( f " \n { '' : <28 }{ 'mean' : >10 }{ 'std dev' : >10 } " ) print ( f " { 'NORM.INV(RAND(), ...)' : <28 }{ via_inverse . mean () : >10,.0f }{ via_inverse . std ( ddof = 1 ) : >10,.0f } " ) print ( f " { 'rng.normal(...)' : <28 }{ direct . mean () : >10,.0f }{ direct . std ( ddof = 1 ) : >10,.0f } " ) RAND() = 0.025 -> NORM.INV gives 36,480 cups RAND() = 0.16 -> NORM.INV gives 48,067 cups RAND() = 0.5 -> NORM.INV gives 60,000 cups RAND() = 0.84 -> NORM.INV gives 71,933 cups RAND() = 0.975 -> NORM.INV gives 83,520 cups mean std dev NORM.INV(RAND(), ...) 59,800 12,018 rng.normal(...) 59,930 12,143 fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 )) axes [ 0 ] . hist ( u , bins = 20 , color = GREY , edgecolor = "white" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "10,000 values of RAND(): flat" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "RAND() value (probability)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Number of draws" ) axes [ 1 ] . hist ( via_inverse , bins = 40 , color = BLUE , edgecolor = "white" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "After NORM.INV: bell-shaped demand" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Simulated demand (cups per year)" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylabel ( "Number of draws" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Both methods give a mean close to 60,000 and a standard deviation close to 12,000 (output above). They are not identical, because they are different random draws. Seeds: Python yes, Excel no numpy's default_rng(seed=…) makes the "random" numbers repeat exactly, so everyone in the room gets the same output. Excel's RAND() has no seed : it draws new numbers every time the sheet recalculates (any edit, or F9 ). Your Excel results will differ slightly from your neighbour's and from Python. That is expected. To freeze one set of draws, copy the cells and use Home → Paste → Paste Special → Values (选择性粘贴 → 数值). A normal distribution has no floor NORM.INV can return negative demand when the standard deviation is large compared with the mean. Wrap it: =MAX(0, NORM.INV(RAND(), 60000, 12000)) . Here negative values are practically impossible, but the guard costs nothing. Part 6: Monte Carlo simulation ¶ A Monte Carlo simulation runs the model many times. In each trial it draws a random value for every uncertain input, computes the output, and records it. The collection of outputs shows the range of possible results and how likely each is. Describe each uncertain input with a distribution. For trial 1, draw the inputs and compute profit. Repeat for thousands of trials. Summarise the profits: a histogram and risk measures. In numpy, the profit function already works on whole arrays, so 10,000 trials take one line. N = 10_000 rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 2026 ) sim = pd . DataFrame ({ "demand" : np . maximum ( 0 , rng . normal ( 60_000 , 12_000 , N )), "variable_cost" : rng . uniform ( 6 , 9 , N ), }) sim [ "profit" ] = profit ( sim [ "demand" ], BASE [ "price" ], sim [ "variable_cost" ], BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) print ( "First five trials:" ) print ( sim . head () . to_string ( formatters = { "demand" : " {:,.0f} " . format , "variable_cost" : " {:.2f} " . format , "profit" : " {:,.0f} " . format })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . hist ( sim [ "profit" ], bins = 60 , color = BLUE , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 , label = "Zero profit" ) ax . axvline ( sim [ "profit" ] . mean (), color = INK , linestyle = "--" , label = "Average profit" ) ax . set_title ( "10,000 simulated first years: mostly profitable, sometimes not" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year-1 profit (currency units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of trials" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () First five trials: demand variable_cost profit 0 50,483 7.28 41,164 1 62,887 6.67 212,327 2 37,244 8.86 -159,717 3 76,749 6.02 398,718 4 67,660 8.95 112,118 The histogram is not a perfect bell: its right side is cut short. That is the capacity limit. When demand is high, the branch cannot sell more than 75,000 cups, so the best outcomes are capped while the bad outcomes are not. In Excel: build the simulation (about 15 minutes; the Simulation sheet of the practice workbook shows the finished version) Add a sheet named Simulation . In A1:E1 type Trial , Demand , Variable cost per cup , Cups sold , Profit . On the Model sheet, add the uncertainty inputs: B11 demand standard deviation (12000), B12 lowest cost (6), B13 highest cost (9). In A2 type 1, in A3 type 2, select both and drag the fill handle down to A1001 (1,000 trials). In B2 : =MAX(0,NORM.INV(RAND(),Model!$B$4,Model!$B$11)) In C2 : =Model!$B$12+(Model!$B$13-Model!$B$12)*RAND() In D2 : =MIN(B2,Model!$B$8) In E2 : =D2*(Model!$B$5-C2)-Model!$B$7 Select B2:E2 and double-click the fill handle (the small square at the bottom right) to copy the formulas down to row 1001. The $ signs keep every formula pointing at the same inputs. Select E2:E1001 → Insert → Charts → Histogram (插入 → 图表 → 直方图). Press F9 a few times: the histogram moves a little each time. That is the simulation working. Part 7: Risk measures ¶ A histogram is the full picture. Managers also need a few numbers. Measure Question it answers Excel (profits in E2:E1001) pandas Expected profit What do we get on average? =AVERAGE(E2:E1001) .mean() Standard deviation How spread out are the outcomes? =STDEV.S(E2:E1001) .std() Minimum, maximum The extremes seen in this run =MIN(…) , =MAX(…) .min() , .max() Probability of a loss How often do we lose money? =COUNTIF(E2:E1001,"<0")/1000 (profit < 0).mean() 5th percentile (P5) A bad year: only 1 trial in 20 is worse =PERCENTILE.INC(E2:E1001,0.05) .quantile(0.05) 95th percentile (P95) A good year: only 1 in 20 is better =PERCENTILE.INC(E2:E1001,0.95) .quantile(0.95) Average of the worst 5% (expected shortfall) When things go badly, how bad on average? =AVERAGEIF(E2:E1001,"<="&P5cell) profit[profit <= p5].mean() The P5 is often called the value at risk at 95%: "in 95% of years, we do at least this well". def risk_summary ( profits ): """Risk measures of a set of simulated profits.""" profits = pd . Series ( profits ) p5 = profits . quantile ( 0.05 ) return pd . Series ({ "trials" : len ( profits ), "expected profit" : profits . mean (), "standard deviation" : profits . std (), "minimum" : profits . min (), "maximum" : profits . max (), "probability of a loss" : ( profits < 0 ) . mean (), "5th percentile (P5)" : p5 , "95th percentile (P95)" : profits . quantile ( 0.95 ), "average of worst 5%" : profits [ profits <= p5 ] . mean (), }) summary = risk_summary ( sim [ "profit" ]) for name , value in summary . items (): shown = f " { value : .1% } " if name == "probability of a loss" else f " { value : ,.0f } " print ( f " { name : <24 }{ shown : >12 } " ) trials 10,000 expected profit 123,974 standard deviation 126,834 minimum -357,645 maximum 399,842 probability of a loss 17.3% 5th percentile (P5) -87,827 95th percentile (P95) 329,550 average of worst 5% -140,884 How to read the output above for the board: "On average we expect a first-year profit of about the expected profit , but the outcome is uncertain: in a bad year (1 in 20) profit falls to about the P5 or below." "There is about a probability of a loss chance that the branch loses money in its first year." "When it does go badly, the worst 5% of years average the average of worst 5% ." Check your understanding Two projects have the same expected profit. Project X has P5 = 50,000; project Y has P5 = −300,000. Which would a cautious owner prefer, and which number would you put first in your report? Part 8: How many trials? ¶ A simulation estimates the true risk measures; more trials give a more precise estimate. To see how precise, we repeat the whole simulation 200 times with 50 trials each, and again with 1,000 and 10,000 trials, and look at how much the estimated probability of a loss moves from run to run. Predict, then reveal With only 50 trials, could two students' estimates of the probability of a loss differ by 10 percentage points or more? rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 8 ) spread = {} estimates = {} for trials in [ 50 , 1_000 , 10_000 ]: runs = [] for _ in range ( 200 ): d = np . maximum ( 0 , rng . normal ( 60_000 , 12_000 , trials )) c = rng . uniform ( 6 , 9 , trials ) runs . append (( profit ( d , BASE [ "price" ], c , BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) < 0 ) . mean ()) estimates [ trials ] = np . array ( runs ) spread [ f " { trials : , } trials" ] = { "lowest estimate" : min ( runs ), "highest estimate" : max ( runs ), "middle 95 % o f runs" : f " { np . quantile ( runs , 0.025 ) : .1% } to { np . quantile ( runs , 0.975 ) : .1% } " } print ( "Probability of a loss, estimated in 200 separate runs" ) print ( pd . DataFrame ( spread ) . T . to_string ( formatters = { "lowest estimate" : " {:.1%} " . format , "highest estimate" : " {:.1%} " . format })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () jitter = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 1 ) for row , t in enumerate ( estimates , start = 1 ): ax . scatter ( estimates [ t ], row + jitter . uniform ( - 0.15 , 0.15 , len ( estimates [ t ])), s = 10 , alpha = 0.5 , color = BLUE ) ax . set_yticks ([ 1 , 2 , 3 ], [ f " { t : , } trials" for t in estimates ]) ax . grid ( axis = "y" , visible = False ) ax . set_title ( "Few trials give a wobbly estimate" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Estimated probability of a loss in one run" ) plt . show () Probability of a loss, estimated in 200 separate runs lowest estimate highest estimate middle 95% of runs 50 trials 2.0% 34.0% 6.0% to 26.0% 1,000 trials 13.9% 19.6% 14.9% to 19.1% 10,000 trials 16.2% 18.2% 16.4% to 17.8% With 50 trials the estimate jumps around a lot from run to run (see the range above); with 10,000 it barely moves. A rough rule: the uncertainty in an estimated probability p from n trials is about √( p (1 − p ) ÷ n ). Quadrupling the trials halves the uncertainty. Situation Trials Classroom demonstration, quick check 50–500 A decision in a normal spreadsheet 1,000–5,000 Rare events (probabilities of 1% or less) or a big decision 10,000 or more, usually in Python or a dedicated tool When you press F9 in a 50-trial Excel model, expect the probability of a loss to change noticeably. Report it as an approximate figure, and use more trials before a real decision. Part 9: The flaw of averages ¶ A tempting shortcut: put the average of each input into the model and read off the profit. The result is the profit at average inputs . Is it the same as the average profit over all the simulated years? Predict, then reveal Will the profit at average inputs be higher, the same, or lower than the average simulated profit? at_average = profit ( 60_000 , BASE [ "price" ], 7.5 , BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) print ( f "Profit at average inputs (demand 60,000, cost 7.5): { at_average : >10,.0f } " ) print ( f "Average simulated profit: { sim [ 'profit' ] . mean () : >10,.0f } " ) no_cap = profit ( sim [ "demand" ], BASE [ "price" ], sim [ "variable_cost" ], BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], np . inf ) print ( f "Average simulated profit with NO capacity limit: { no_cap . mean () : >10,.0f } " ) Profit at average inputs (demand 60,000, cost 7.5): 130,000 Average simulated profit: 123,974 Average simulated profit with NO capacity limit: 130,111 Read the output above. With the capacity limit, the average simulated profit is lower than the profit at average inputs. In good years the branch hits capacity and cannot earn the extra profit, while in bad years it bears the full loss. Without the limit, the two numbers are close, because profit is then a straight-line function of demand. This is the flaw of averages : whenever the model contains a limit, a threshold or anything non-linear (capacity, stock-outs, tax bands, minimum orders), plugging in average inputs gives the wrong average output. A simulation does not have this problem. Part 10: Comparing two decisions ¶ LeafLine Tea has a second option: a site in a shopping mall. More customers pass by, but the rent is higher and the footfall is less predictable. Input Street site (A) Mall site (B) Demand normal, mean 60,000, sd 12,000 normal, mean 85,000, sd 20,000 Fixed costs 500,000 700,000 Capacity 75,000 100,000 Price, variable cost 18; uniform 6 to 9 same We simulate both with the same random numbers (the same standard-normal and uniform draws, scaled to each site). This is called common random numbers : differences between the two results then come from the decision, not from luck in the draws. rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 99 ) z = rng . standard_normal ( N ) # shared "how good a year is it" draw cost = rng . uniform ( 6 , 9 , N ) # shared cost draw street = profit ( np . maximum ( 0 , 60_000 + 12_000 * z ), BASE [ "price" ], cost , 500_000 , 75_000 ) mall = profit ( np . maximum ( 0 , 85_000 + 20_000 * z ), BASE [ "price" ], cost , 700_000 , 100_000 ) comparison = pd . DataFrame ({ "A: street site" : risk_summary ( street ), "B: mall site" : risk_summary ( mall )}) print ( comparison . drop ( index = "trials" ) . to_string ( formatters = { c : ( lambda v : f " { v : ,.3f } " if abs ( v ) < 1 else f " { v : ,.0f } " ) for c in comparison . columns })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () bins = np . linspace ( min ( street . min (), mall . min ()), max ( street . max (), mall . max ()), 70 ) ax . hist ( street , bins = bins , alpha = 0.6 , color = BLUE , label = "A: street site" ) ax . hist ( mall , bins = bins , alpha = 0.6 , color = ORANGE , label = "B: mall site" ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_title ( "The mall site: a higher average, but a wider range" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year-1 profit (currency units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of trials" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () A: street site B: mall site expected profit 123,308 164,534 standard deviation 126,722 185,781 minimum -328,707 -552,117 maximum 399,999 499,999 probability of a loss 0.174 0.199 5th percentile (P5) -86,310 -161,594 95th percentile (P95) 330,575 447,112 average of worst 5% -139,030 -248,374 Read the comparison table above. Neither site wins on every measure: the mall has the higher expected profit, the street site the smaller chance of a loss and the better bad year. The choice depends on the owner's risk appetite : a chain with cash reserves may accept more risk for a higher average; a new owner who cannot survive a bad first year should care more about the P5 and the probability of a loss. The simulation does not make the decision. It makes the trade-off visible , so the decision-maker can choose knowingly. Check your understanding The mall landlord offers a lower rent of 600,000 if LeafLine signs for five years. Which line of code would you change to test this, and which two measures would you compare first? Part 11: Reporting a simulation ¶ Do Don't Give a range and a probability: "expected profit about …; 1 year in 20 below …; about …% chance of a loss" Report one number as if it were certain List every assumption and distribution in a table, with its source Hide the inputs in formulas Say how many trials you ran and that results vary slightly between runs Quote results to the last unit Show the histogram Show only the average Test what happens if a key assumption is wrong (for example a larger demand standard deviation) Treat the distributions as facts Ethics: who carries the risk? A plan built only on the best case can push risk onto people who did not choose it: staff who lose jobs when a branch closes, suppliers who are not paid, customers left without service. Simulating uncertainty, and reporting the bad outcomes honestly, is part of responsible decision-making. Tomorrow's lab takes this further with a supply-chain decision that has an ethical side. Summary ¶ Idea One-line takeaway Financial model Inputs → calculations → outputs; inputs in labelled cells, never inside formulas Data Table Varies one or two inputs and shows an output for every value; input cells on the same sheet Goal Seek Finds the input value that gives a target output (for example break-even) Scenarios Consistent stories (worst, base, best); no probabilities Random inputs RAND() , RANDBETWEEN() , NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) ; Excel has no seed, numpy does Monte Carlo Draw inputs, compute the output, repeat thousands of times, summarise Risk measures Expected value, standard deviation, probability of a loss, P5/P95, average of the worst 5% Number of trials 50 trials give a rough estimate; use thousands for decisions Flaw of averages With limits or thresholds, profit at average inputs ≠ average profit Comparing options Same random numbers for both; the choice depends on risk appetite Excel reference ¶ Task English Excel Chinese Excel (labels may vary slightly by version) Data Table Data → What-If Analysis → Data Table 数据 → 模拟分析 → 模拟运算表 Goal Seek Data → What-If Analysis → Goal Seek 数据 → 模拟分析 → 单变量求解 Scenario Manager Data → What-If Analysis → Scenario Manager 数据 → 模拟分析 → 方案管理器 Histogram chart Insert → Charts → Histogram 插入 → 图表 → 直方图 Freeze random numbers Copy, then Paste Special → Values 复制，然后 选择性粘贴 → 数值 Recalculate F9 F9 Calculation options Formulas → Calculation Options 公式 → 计算选项 Function names ( RAND , NORM.INV , COUNTIF , PERCENTILE.INC …) are the same in English and Chinese Excel. Closing quiz ¶ Name the three layers of a financial model and give one example of each for a coffee cart. Why should a formula refer to an input cell instead of containing the number itself? In a two-way Data Table, the prices run across row 17 and the demands down column B. Which input cell goes in the Row input cell box? What does =NORM.INV(RAND(), 500, 80) produce, and why does the result change when you press F9? A simulation of 1,000 trials gives 87 trials with a loss. What is the estimated probability of a loss, and roughly how precise is it? Explain the P5 of a profit distribution to a manager in one sentence. A model has a capacity limit. Why is the profit at average demand higher than the average simulated profit? Why is it risky, for the company and for others, to plan only on the best case? You predict cars' fuel efficiency from their specifications with the regression workflow from yesterday's lecture. docs.text: Every business plan rests on numbers nobody knows for sure: how many customers will come, what supplies will cost. This lecture shows how to build a clear financial model in Excel, explore it with what-if tables and scenarios, replace single guesses with random inputs in a Monte Carlo simulation, and turn thousands of simulated outcomes into risk measures a manager can act on. Python checks every idea along the way. Open this notebook in JupyterLab from the course folder and run each cell from top to bottom with Shift + Enter . Keep Microsoft Excel open next to it: most parts end with steps to do in Excel.

Explain why the profit at average inputs is not the average profit (the flaw of averages), and how many trials a simulation needs. docs.text: A financial model is a set of linked calculations that turns assumptions about the business into financial results : revenue, costs, profit, cash. Managers use it to answer "what happens if…?" before they commit money. Layer Contents Example Inputs (assumptions) Numbers someone must estimate or decide Cups sold per year, price per cup, rent Calculations Formulas that link inputs Revenue = cups × price Outputs The results decisions depend on Profit, break-even point A model is deterministic when each input has one value: it gives one answer. A simulation model lets uncertain inputs vary at random and gives a distribution of answers.
docs.title: Part 1: What a financial model is

docs.text: Rule Why Put every input in its own labelled cell , in one place, and colour input cells (for example blue) Anyone can see and change the assumptions Never type a number inside a formula : refer to the input cell One change updates the whole model; no hidden assumptions Use absolute references ( $B$5 ) for inputs that formulas copied down or across must keep Copied formulas still point at the right input Work left to right, top to bottom : inputs, then calculations, then outputs The model reads like a story Write the units in the label (per cup, per year) Avoids mixing months and years, or cups and cartons Add checks (for example, cups sold never exceed capacity) Errors are caught early The setup cell loads the libraries. Everything here uses numpy, pandas and matplotlib; statistics.NormalDist comes with Python itself. from statistics import NormalDist import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" INK = "#55534e" plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 9 , 4.5 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) pd . set_option ( "display.width" , 120 )
docs.title: Good spreadsheet practice

docs.text: About the case LeafLine Tea is the synthetic milk-tea chain from the Day 3 text-mining lecture. All numbers are invented for teaching. Amounts are in neutral currency units . LeafLine Tea is deciding whether to open a new branch. The finance team's first-year assumptions: Input Base value Unit Expected demand 60,000 cups per year Price 18 currency units per cup Variable cost (tea, milk, cups, packaging) 7.5 currency units per cup Fixed costs (rent, staff, equipment) 500,000 currency units per year Capacity 75,000 cups per year the branch can make The calculations: Cups sold = the smaller of demand and capacity Revenue = cups sold × price Variable costs = cups sold × variable cost per cup Profit = revenue − variable costs − fixed costs Break-even demand = fixed costs ÷ (price − variable cost per cup): the cups needed for zero profit. Price − variable cost is the contribution margin per cup. BASE = { "demand" : 60_000 , "price" : 18.0 , "variable_cost" : 7.5 , "fixed_costs" : 500_000 , "capacity" : 75_000 } def profit ( demand , price , variable_cost , fixed_costs , capacity ): """Year-1 profit of the branch. Works on single numbers and on whole numpy arrays.""" cups_sold = np . minimum ( demand , capacity ) return cups_sold * ( price - variable_cost ) - fixed_costs base_profit = profit ( ** BASE ) break_even = BASE [ "fixed_costs" ] / ( BASE [ "price" ] - BASE [ "variable_cost" ]) print ( f "Base-case profit: { base_profit : ,.0f } currency units" ) print ( f "Break-even demand: { break_even : ,.0f } cups per year" ) print ( f "Safety margin: demand can fall { 1 - break_even / BASE [ 'demand' ] : .0% } below the base case before a loss" ) Base-case profit: 130,000 currency units Break-even demand: 47,619 cups per year Safety margin: demand can fall 21% below the base case before a loss In Excel: build the base model (about 10 minutes) Open a blank workbook. Rename Sheet1 to Model (double-click the tab). In A4:A8 type the five input labels from the table above; in B4:B8 type the base values. Fill B4:B8 blue ( Home → Fill Color ). In D4:D8 type the labels Cups sold , Revenue , Variable costs , Profit , Break-even demand . In E4 type =MIN(B4,B8) ; in E5 =E4*B5 ; in E6 =E4*B6 ; in E7 =E5-E6-B7 ; in E8 =B7/(B5-B6) . Format money cells with Home → Number Format → Number and the thousands separator. Check: E7 and E8 must match the Python output above.
docs.title: Part 2: The case: a new LeafLine Tea branch

docs.text: What-if analysis changes inputs and watches the outputs. Its simplest form is a one-way sensitivity table : vary one input, hold the others at their base values. Predict, then reveal Demand falls from 60,000 to 40,000 cups. Will profit fall by a third, by about half, or by more than that? demands = np . arange ( 30_000 , 90_001 , 10_000 ) one_way = pd . DataFrame ({ "demand (cups)" : demands , "profit" : profit ( demands , BASE [ "price" ], BASE [ "variable_cost" ], BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ])}) print ( one_way . to_string ( index = False , formatters = { "profit" : " {:,.0f} " . format , "demand (cups)" : " {:,} " . format })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( one_way [ "demand (cups)" ], one_way [ "profit" ], marker = "o" , color = BLUE ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 0.8 ) ax . axvline ( break_even , color = ORANGE , linestyle = "--" , label = "Break-even demand" ) ax . axvline ( BASE [ "capacity" ], color = GREY , linestyle = ":" , label = "Capacity" ) ax . set_title ( "Profit rises with demand until the branch reaches capacity" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Demand (cups per year)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Profit (currency units)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () demand (cups) profit 30,000 -185,000 40,000 -80,000 50,000 25,000 60,000 130,000 70,000 235,000 80,000 287,500 90,000 287,500 Profit falls much faster than demand, because the fixed costs do not shrink when customers stay away. This is operating leverage : high fixed costs make profit sensitive to volume. Beyond capacity, extra demand adds nothing.

docs.text: A two-way Data Table varies two inputs at once and shows the output for every combination. Here: demand down the side, price across the top. prices = np . array ([ 14 , 16 , 18 , 20 , 22 ]) grid = pd . DataFrame ( [[ profit ( d , p , BASE [ "variable_cost" ], BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) for p in prices ] for d in demands ], index = pd . Index ( demands , name = "demand" ), columns = pd . Index ( prices , name = "price" ), ) print ( "Profit (currency units) by demand (rows) and price per cup (columns)" ) print ( grid . to_string ( float_format = " {:,.0f} " . format )) Profit (currency units) by demand (rows) and price per cup (columns) price 14 16 18 20 22 demand 30000 -305,000 -245,000 -185,000 -125,000 -65,000 40000 -240,000 -160,000 -80,000 0 80,000 50000 -175,000 -75,000 25,000 125,000 225,000 60000 -110,000 10,000 130,000 250,000 370,000 70000 -45,000 95,000 235,000 375,000 515,000 80000 -12,500 137,500 287,500 437,500 587,500 90000 -12,500 137,500 287,500 437,500 587,500 Read the table above: which combinations make a loss? Notice that a higher price helps a lot if demand holds . The table cannot say whether demand would hold at a higher price; that is a question for market research or an experiment, not for the spreadsheet. In Excel: two-way Data Table (Excel calls it Data Table ; in Chinese Excel 模拟运算表) On the Model sheet, in B17 type =E7 (the output you want to see). This must be the top-left corner of the table. In C17:G17 type the prices 14, 16, 18, 20, 22 (across). In B18:B24 type the demands 30000 to 90000 in steps of 10000 (down). Select the whole block B17:G24 . Data → What-If Analysis → Data Table… (数据 → 模拟分析 → 模拟运算表). Row input cell: B5 (price, because the prices run along the row). Column input cell: B4 (demand, because the demands run down the column). Click OK . Select C18:G24 → Home → Conditional Formatting → Color Scales so losses stand out. Check: your table must match the Python output above. Two traps The input cells must be on the same sheet as the Data Table. If you point to an input on another sheet, Excel refuses with "Input cell reference is not valid". Keep the table on the Model sheet, or link the inputs. Data Tables recalculate every time anything changes and can make a big workbook slow. Formulas → Calculation Options → Automatic except for Data Tables helps; press F9 to update.

docs.text: Goal Seek works backwards: "which value of this input gives that output?" In Excel: Goal Seek (单变量求解) Data → What-If Analysis → Goal Seek… Set cell: E7 (profit). To value: 0 . By changing cell: B4 (demand). Click OK . Excel finds the break-even demand. Compare it with E8, then click Cancel to keep the original demand. Check your understanding Use the Data Table above: at a price of 16, roughly what demand does the branch need to break even? Check with the break-even formula.

docs.text: A scenario changes several inputs together to tell one consistent story. Most plans show three: Scenario Story Demand Variable cost Fixed costs Worst case A rival opens nearby; milk prices rise 42,000 8.5 520,000 Base case The finance team's plan 60,000 7.5 500,000 Best case Strong launch; a supplier discount 75,000 6.5 500,000 scenarios = pd . DataFrame ({ "worst case" : { "demand" : 42_000 , "variable_cost" : 8.5 , "fixed_costs" : 520_000 }, "base case" : { "demand" : 60_000 , "variable_cost" : 7.5 , "fixed_costs" : 500_000 }, "best case" : { "demand" : 75_000 , "variable_cost" : 6.5 , "fixed_costs" : 500_000 }, }) . T scenarios [ "profit" ] = profit ( scenarios [ "demand" ], BASE [ "price" ], scenarios [ "variable_cost" ], scenarios [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) print ( scenarios . to_string ( formatters = { "demand" : " {:,.0f} " . format , "fixed_costs" : " {:,.0f} " . format , "profit" : " {:,.0f} " . format })) demand variable_cost fixed_costs profit worst case 42,000 8.5 520,000 -121,000 base case 60,000 7.5 500,000 130,000 best case 75,000 6.5 500,000 362,500 In Excel: Scenario Manager (方案管理器) Data → What-If Analysis → Scenario Manager… → Add . Name it Worst case . Changing cells: B4,B6,B7 (hold Ctrl to pick several). Click OK , then type the three worst-case values. Click OK . Repeat for Base case and Best case . Click Summary… , choose Scenario summary , Result cells: E7 . Excel adds a new sheet comparing the scenarios. Scenarios are easy to explain, but they have two weaknesses: They say nothing about how likely each story is. Is the worst case a 1-in-3 or a 1-in-1,000 event? The real outcome is almost never exactly one of the three. Inputs combine in countless ways. A simulation fixes both.
docs.title: Part 4: Scenarios

docs.text: Instead of one guess for demand, we describe it with a probability distribution : the range of values it could take and how likely each is. Distribution Use when Excel numpy Uniform between 0 and 1 The building block for all others =RAND() rng.uniform(0, 1) Uniform between a and b Only a range is known; every value equally likely =a+(b-a)*RAND() rng.uniform(a, b) Whole numbers between a and b Counts, equally likely =RANDBETWEEN(a,b) rng.integers(a, b + 1) Normal with mean m and standard deviation s A typical value with symmetric uncertainty around it =NORM.INV(RAND(),m,s) rng.normal(m, s) Yes/no with probability p An event that may happen (a rival opens) =IF(RAND()<p,1,0) rng.uniform() < p For LeafLine Tea the team chooses: Demand: normal, mean 60,000 cups, standard deviation 12,000 (about two times in three, demand lands between 48,000 and 72,000). Variable cost per cup: uniform between 6 and 9 (milk and tea prices could move anywhere in that range). Price, fixed costs and capacity stay fixed: the company sets them.
docs.title: Part 5: Random inputs in Excel and Python

docs.text: RAND() gives a random probability between 0 and 1. NORM.INV turns a probability into the value with that much of the normal distribution below it. A RAND() of 0.5 gives the mean; 0.84 gives about mean + 1 sd; 0.025 gives about mean − 2 sd. Because RAND() is equally likely to land anywhere between 0 and 1, the results follow the normal shape. This is called the inverse transform method. Python's NormalDist(...).inv_cdf is the same function as Excel's NORM.INV , so we can check the method directly. demand_dist = NormalDist ( mu = 60_000 , sigma = 12_000 ) for u in [ 0.025 , 0.16 , 0.5 , 0.84 , 0.975 ]: print ( f "RAND() = { u : <5 } -> NORM.INV gives { demand_dist . inv_cdf ( u ) : >8,.0f } cups" ) rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 17 ) u = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , 10_000 ) # 10,000 "RAND()" values via_inverse = np . array ([ demand_dist . inv_cdf ( x ) for x in u ]) # Excel's way: NORM.INV(RAND(), 60000, 12000) direct = rng . normal ( 60_000 , 12_000 , 10_000 ) # numpy's way print ( f " \n { '' : <28 }{ 'mean' : >10 }{ 'std dev' : >10 } " ) print ( f " { 'NORM.INV(RAND(), ...)' : <28 }{ via_inverse . mean () : >10,.0f }{ via_inverse . std ( ddof = 1 ) : >10,.0f } " ) print ( f " { 'rng.normal(...)' : <28 }{ direct . mean () : >10,.0f }{ direct . std ( ddof = 1 ) : >10,.0f } " ) RAND() = 0.025 -> NORM.INV gives 36,480 cups RAND() = 0.16 -> NORM.INV gives 48,067 cups RAND() = 0.5 -> NORM.INV gives 60,000 cups RAND() = 0.84 -> NORM.INV gives 71,933 cups RAND() = 0.975 -> NORM.INV gives 83,520 cups mean std dev NORM.INV(RAND(), ...) 59,800 12,018 rng.normal(...) 59,930 12,143 fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 )) axes [ 0 ] . hist ( u , bins = 20 , color = GREY , edgecolor = "white" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "10,000 values of RAND(): flat" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "RAND() value (probability)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Number of draws" ) axes [ 1 ] . hist ( via_inverse , bins = 40 , color = BLUE , edgecolor = "white" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "After NORM.INV: bell-shaped demand" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Simulated demand (cups per year)" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylabel ( "Number of draws" ) fig . tight_layout () plt . show () Both methods give a mean close to 60,000 and a standard deviation close to 12,000 (output above). They are not identical, because they are different random draws. Seeds: Python yes, Excel no numpy's default_rng(seed=…) makes the "random" numbers repeat exactly, so everyone in the room gets the same output. Excel's RAND() has no seed : it draws new numbers every time the sheet recalculates (any edit, or F9 ). Your Excel results will differ slightly from your neighbour's and from Python. That is expected. To freeze one set of draws, copy the cells and use Home → Paste → Paste Special → Values (选择性粘贴 → 数值). A normal distribution has no floor NORM.INV can return negative demand when the standard deviation is large compared with the mean. Wrap it: =MAX(0, NORM.INV(RAND(), 60000, 12000)) . Here negative values are practically impossible, but the guard costs nothing.
docs.title: How NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) works

docs.text: A Monte Carlo simulation runs the model many times. In each trial it draws a random value for every uncertain input, computes the output, and records it. The collection of outputs shows the range of possible results and how likely each is. Describe each uncertain input with a distribution. For trial 1, draw the inputs and compute profit. Repeat for thousands of trials. Summarise the profits: a histogram and risk measures. In numpy, the profit function already works on whole arrays, so 10,000 trials take one line. N = 10_000 rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 2026 ) sim = pd . DataFrame ({ "demand" : np . maximum ( 0 , rng . normal ( 60_000 , 12_000 , N )), "variable_cost" : rng . uniform ( 6 , 9 , N ), }) sim [ "profit" ] = profit ( sim [ "demand" ], BASE [ "price" ], sim [ "variable_cost" ], BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) print ( "First five trials:" ) print ( sim . head () . to_string ( formatters = { "demand" : " {:,.0f} " . format , "variable_cost" : " {:.2f} " . format , "profit" : " {:,.0f} " . format })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . hist ( sim [ "profit" ], bins = 60 , color = BLUE , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 , label = "Zero profit" ) ax . axvline ( sim [ "profit" ] . mean (), color = INK , linestyle = "--" , label = "Average profit" ) ax . set_title ( "10,000 simulated first years: mostly profitable, sometimes not" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year-1 profit (currency units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of trials" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () First five trials: demand variable_cost profit 0 50,483 7.28 41,164 1 62,887 6.67 212,327 2 37,244 8.86 -159,717 3 76,749 6.02 398,718 4 67,660 8.95 112,118 The histogram is not a perfect bell: its right side is cut short. That is the capacity limit. When demand is high, the branch cannot sell more than 75,000 cups, so the best outcomes are capped while the bad outcomes are not. In Excel: build the simulation (about 15 minutes; the Simulation sheet of the practice workbook shows the finished version) Add a sheet named Simulation . In A1:E1 type Trial , Demand , Variable cost per cup , Cups sold , Profit . On the Model sheet, add the uncertainty inputs: B11 demand standard deviation (12000), B12 lowest cost (6), B13 highest cost (9). In A2 type 1, in A3 type 2, select both and drag the fill handle down to A1001 (1,000 trials). In B2 : =MAX(0,NORM.INV(RAND(),Model!$B$4,Model!$B$11)) In C2 : =Model!$B$12+(Model!$B$13-Model!$B$12)*RAND() In D2 : =MIN(B2,Model!$B$8) In E2 : =D2*(Model!$B$5-C2)-Model!$B$7 Select B2:E2 and double-click the fill handle (the small square at the bottom right) to copy the formulas down to row 1001. The $ signs keep every formula pointing at the same inputs. Select E2:E1001 → Insert → Charts → Histogram (插入 → 图表 → 直方图). Press F9 a few times: the histogram moves a little each time. That is the simulation working.
docs.title: Part 6: Monte Carlo simulation

docs.text: A histogram is the full picture. Managers also need a few numbers. Measure Question it answers Excel (profits in E2:E1001) pandas Expected profit What do we get on average? =AVERAGE(E2:E1001) .mean() Standard deviation How spread out are the outcomes? =STDEV.S(E2:E1001) .std() Minimum, maximum The extremes seen in this run =MIN(…) , =MAX(…) .min() , .max() Probability of a loss How often do we lose money? =COUNTIF(E2:E1001,"<0")/1000 (profit < 0).mean() 5th percentile (P5) A bad year: only 1 trial in 20 is worse =PERCENTILE.INC(E2:E1001,0.05) .quantile(0.05) 95th percentile (P95) A good year: only 1 in 20 is better =PERCENTILE.INC(E2:E1001,0.95) .quantile(0.95) Average of the worst 5% (expected shortfall) When things go badly, how bad on average? =AVERAGEIF(E2:E1001,"<="&P5cell) profit[profit <= p5].mean() The P5 is often called the value at risk at 95%: "in 95% of years, we do at least this well". def risk_summary ( profits ): """Risk measures of a set of simulated profits.""" profits = pd . Series ( profits ) p5 = profits . quantile ( 0.05 ) return pd . Series ({ "trials" : len ( profits ), "expected profit" : profits . mean (), "standard deviation" : profits . std (), "minimum" : profits . min (), "maximum" : profits . max (), "probability of a loss" : ( profits < 0 ) . mean (), "5th percentile (P5)" : p5 , "95th percentile (P95)" : profits . quantile ( 0.95 ), "average of worst 5%" : profits [ profits <= p5 ] . mean (), }) summary = risk_summary ( sim [ "profit" ]) for name , value in summary . items (): shown = f " { value : .1% } " if name == "probability of a loss" else f " { value : ,.0f } " print ( f " { name : <24 }{ shown : >12 } " ) trials 10,000 expected profit 123,974 standard deviation 126,834 minimum -357,645 maximum 399,842 probability of a loss 17.3% 5th percentile (P5) -87,827 95th percentile (P95) 329,550 average of worst 5% -140,884 How to read the output above for the board: "On average we expect a first-year profit of about the expected profit , but the outcome is uncertain: in a bad year (1 in 20) profit falls to about the P5 or below." "There is about a probability of a loss chance that the branch loses money in its first year." "When it does go badly, the worst 5% of years average the average of worst 5% ." Check your understanding Two projects have the same expected profit. Project X has P5 = 50,000; project Y has P5 = −300,000. Which would a cautious owner prefer, and which number would you put first in your report?
docs.title: Part 7: Risk measures

docs.text: A simulation estimates the true risk measures; more trials give a more precise estimate. To see how precise, we repeat the whole simulation 200 times with 50 trials each, and again with 1,000 and 10,000 trials, and look at how much the estimated probability of a loss moves from run to run. Predict, then reveal With only 50 trials, could two students' estimates of the probability of a loss differ by 10 percentage points or more? rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 8 ) spread = {} estimates = {} for trials in [ 50 , 1_000 , 10_000 ]: runs = [] for _ in range ( 200 ): d = np . maximum ( 0 , rng . normal ( 60_000 , 12_000 , trials )) c = rng . uniform ( 6 , 9 , trials ) runs . append (( profit ( d , BASE [ "price" ], c , BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) < 0 ) . mean ()) estimates [ trials ] = np . array ( runs ) spread [ f " { trials : , } trials" ] = { "lowest estimate" : min ( runs ), "highest estimate" : max ( runs ), "middle 95 % o f runs" : f " { np . quantile ( runs , 0.025 ) : .1% } to { np . quantile ( runs , 0.975 ) : .1% } " } print ( "Probability of a loss, estimated in 200 separate runs" ) print ( pd . DataFrame ( spread ) . T . to_string ( formatters = { "lowest estimate" : " {:.1%} " . format , "highest estimate" : " {:.1%} " . format })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () jitter = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 1 ) for row , t in enumerate ( estimates , start = 1 ): ax . scatter ( estimates [ t ], row + jitter . uniform ( - 0.15 , 0.15 , len ( estimates [ t ])), s = 10 , alpha = 0.5 , color = BLUE ) ax . set_yticks ([ 1 , 2 , 3 ], [ f " { t : , } trials" for t in estimates ]) ax . grid ( axis = "y" , visible = False ) ax . set_title ( "Few trials give a wobbly estimate" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Estimated probability of a loss in one run" ) plt . show () Probability of a loss, estimated in 200 separate runs lowest estimate highest estimate middle 95% of runs 50 trials 2.0% 34.0% 6.0% to 26.0% 1,000 trials 13.9% 19.6% 14.9% to 19.1% 10,000 trials 16.2% 18.2% 16.4% to 17.8% With 50 trials the estimate jumps around a lot from run to run (see the range above); with 10,000 it barely moves. A rough rule: the uncertainty in an estimated probability p from n trials is about √( p (1 − p ) ÷ n ). Quadrupling the trials halves the uncertainty. Situation Trials Classroom demonstration, quick check 50–500 A decision in a normal spreadsheet 1,000–5,000 Rare events (probabilities of 1% or less) or a big decision 10,000 or more, usually in Python or a dedicated tool When you press F9 in a 50-trial Excel model, expect the probability of a loss to change noticeably. Report it as an approximate figure, and use more trials before a real decision.
docs.title: Part 8: How many trials?

docs.text: A tempting shortcut: put the average of each input into the model and read off the profit. The result is the profit at average inputs . Is it the same as the average profit over all the simulated years? Predict, then reveal Will the profit at average inputs be higher, the same, or lower than the average simulated profit? at_average = profit ( 60_000 , BASE [ "price" ], 7.5 , BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], BASE [ "capacity" ]) print ( f "Profit at average inputs (demand 60,000, cost 7.5): { at_average : >10,.0f } " ) print ( f "Average simulated profit: { sim [ 'profit' ] . mean () : >10,.0f } " ) no_cap = profit ( sim [ "demand" ], BASE [ "price" ], sim [ "variable_cost" ], BASE [ "fixed_costs" ], np . inf ) print ( f "Average simulated profit with NO capacity limit: { no_cap . mean () : >10,.0f } " ) Profit at average inputs (demand 60,000, cost 7.5): 130,000 Average simulated profit: 123,974 Average simulated profit with NO capacity limit: 130,111 Read the output above. With the capacity limit, the average simulated profit is lower than the profit at average inputs. In good years the branch hits capacity and cannot earn the extra profit, while in bad years it bears the full loss. Without the limit, the two numbers are close, because profit is then a straight-line function of demand. This is the flaw of averages : whenever the model contains a limit, a threshold or anything non-linear (capacity, stock-outs, tax bands, minimum orders), plugging in average inputs gives the wrong average output. A simulation does not have this problem.
docs.title: Part 9: The flaw of averages

docs.text: LeafLine Tea has a second option: a site in a shopping mall. More customers pass by, but the rent is higher and the footfall is less predictable. Input Street site (A) Mall site (B) Demand normal, mean 60,000, sd 12,000 normal, mean 85,000, sd 20,000 Fixed costs 500,000 700,000 Capacity 75,000 100,000 Price, variable cost 18; uniform 6 to 9 same We simulate both with the same random numbers (the same standard-normal and uniform draws, scaled to each site). This is called common random numbers : differences between the two results then come from the decision, not from luck in the draws. rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 99 ) z = rng . standard_normal ( N ) # shared "how good a year is it" draw cost = rng . uniform ( 6 , 9 , N ) # shared cost draw street = profit ( np . maximum ( 0 , 60_000 + 12_000 * z ), BASE [ "price" ], cost , 500_000 , 75_000 ) mall = profit ( np . maximum ( 0 , 85_000 + 20_000 * z ), BASE [ "price" ], cost , 700_000 , 100_000 ) comparison = pd . DataFrame ({ "A: street site" : risk_summary ( street ), "B: mall site" : risk_summary ( mall )}) print ( comparison . drop ( index = "trials" ) . to_string ( formatters = { c : ( lambda v : f " { v : ,.3f } " if abs ( v ) < 1 else f " { v : ,.0f } " ) for c in comparison . columns })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () bins = np . linspace ( min ( street . min (), mall . min ()), max ( street . max (), mall . max ()), 70 ) ax . hist ( street , bins = bins , alpha = 0.6 , color = BLUE , label = "A: street site" ) ax . hist ( mall , bins = bins , alpha = 0.6 , color = ORANGE , label = "B: mall site" ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = INK , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_title ( "The mall site: a higher average, but a wider range" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Year-1 profit (currency units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of trials" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () A: street site B: mall site expected profit 123,308 164,534 standard deviation 126,722 185,781 minimum -328,707 -552,117 maximum 399,999 499,999 probability of a loss 0.174 0.199 5th percentile (P5) -86,310 -161,594 95th percentile (P95) 330,575 447,112 average of worst 5% -139,030 -248,374 Read the comparison table above. Neither site wins on every measure: the mall has the higher expected profit, the street site the smaller chance of a loss and the better bad year. The choice depends on the owner's risk appetite : a chain with cash reserves may accept more risk for a higher average; a new owner who cannot survive a bad first year should care more about the P5 and the probability of a loss. The simulation does not make the decision. It makes the trade-off visible , so the decision-maker can choose knowingly. Check your understanding The mall landlord offers a lower rent of 600,000 if LeafLine signs for five years. Which line of code would you change to test this, and which two measures would you compare first?
docs.title: Part 10: Comparing two decisions

docs.text: Do Don't Give a range and a probability: "expected profit about …; 1 year in 20 below …; about …% chance of a loss" Report one number as if it were certain List every assumption and distribution in a table, with its source Hide the inputs in formulas Say how many trials you ran and that results vary slightly between runs Quote results to the last unit Show the histogram Show only the average Test what happens if a key assumption is wrong (for example a larger demand standard deviation) Treat the distributions as facts Ethics: who carries the risk? A plan built only on the best case can push risk onto people who did not choose it: staff who lose jobs when a branch closes, suppliers who are not paid, customers left without service. Simulating uncertainty, and reporting the bad outcomes honestly, is part of responsible decision-making. Tomorrow's lab takes this further with a supply-chain decision that has an ethical side.
docs.title: Part 11: Reporting a simulation

docs.text: Idea One-line takeaway Financial model Inputs → calculations → outputs; inputs in labelled cells, never inside formulas Data Table Varies one or two inputs and shows an output for every value; input cells on the same sheet Goal Seek Finds the input value that gives a target output (for example break-even) Scenarios Consistent stories (worst, base, best); no probabilities Random inputs RAND() , RANDBETWEEN() , NORM.INV(RAND(), mean, sd) ; Excel has no seed, numpy does Monte Carlo Draw inputs, compute the output, repeat thousands of times, summarise Risk measures Expected value, standard deviation, probability of a loss, P5/P95, average of the worst 5% Number of trials 50 trials give a rough estimate; use thousands for decisions Flaw of averages With limits or thresholds, profit at average inputs ≠ average profit Comparing options Same random numbers for both; the choice depends on risk appetite
