docs.text: Assignment 3 — Spreadsheet simulation and decision model ¶ Act as the analytics planner for a smart-thermostat launch: simulate twelve months of uncertain demand in Excel for two marketing strategies, freeze the simulation, chart both strategies' monthly profit in Tableau, and write a short executive report that recommends a strategy and explains why simulating uncertainty is safer than planning on a single number. Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Assignment 3 (Spreadsheet simulation and decision model). Brief rewritten for this classroom; the work is done in Microsoft Excel and Tableau, and this notebook adds optional checks. Graded work: Assignment 3 (6%, CLO 3, 4 and 5) Set: Wednesday 18 November (Day 6), after the briefing in the lecture. Due: Sunday 22 November 2026, 23:59 China Standard Time . Submit: two files to the DATA 300: Assignment 3 drop-box on GAP (Moodle) : your locked workbook YourLastName_DATA300_Assignment3.xlsx and your report YourLastName_Assignment3_Report.pdf . Work: individual. Online support is available during the post-class week. This notebook is the brief (read it all first) and a set of starter checks you can run on your own workbook. The graded work is the Excel file and the PDF report; you do not submit this notebook. The scenario ¶ You are an analytics planner at SmartHome Tech (a fictional company), which is about to launch an AI-powered thermostat. Earlier data mining by your team found two facts that the plan must respect: Baseline demand is about 1,000 units per month , but market volatility moves it up or down at random by up to 150 units in any month. Every thermostat sold earns a fixed profit margin of 100 US dollars . Management must choose one of two marketing strategies for the first year: Strategy Marketing cost Effect on demand A: Standard 10,000 US dollars per month (fixed) Baseline demand plus volatility B: Aggressive 25,000 US dollars per month (fixed) 1.4 times the Standard demand Your simulation runs twelve months under the same random market conditions for both strategies, so that the comparison is fair. What you must do ¶ Part Tool Task 1 Excel Build the 12-month simulation, then lock the random numbers 2 Tableau Chart both strategies' monthly profit as two lines; export the chart as an image 3 Word Write a short executive report with the chart, answering two questions 4 GAP Submit the locked workbook and the PDF report Part 1: The simulation in Excel ¶ Open a blank workbook and save it straight away as YourLastName_DATA300_Assignment3.xlsx . Work on the first sheet and do not rename it (Tableau will show it as Sheet1 , or 工作表1 in Chinese Excel). Step 1: Headers ¶ In row 1, from A1 to G1 , type exactly: Month , Baseline_Demand , Market_Volatility , Standard_Demand , Aggressive_Demand , Standard_Profit , Aggressive_Profit . The underscores matter: Tableau uses these names as field names. Step 2: Formulas ¶ Column Rows 2–13 What it means A Month Type 1 to 12 The month of the first year B Baseline_Demand Type 1000 in every row The demand the data mining found C Market_Volatility In C2: =RANDBETWEEN(-150,150) , then fill down to C13 A random monthly swing between −150 and +150 units D Standard_Demand In D2: =B2+C2 , fill down Units sold with the Standard strategy E Aggressive_Demand In E2: =ROUND((B2+C2)*1.4,0) , fill down 1.4 times the Standard demand, rounded to whole units F Standard_Profit In F2: =(D2*100)-10000 , fill down Units × 100 dollars margin − 10,000 dollars marketing G Aggressive_Profit In G2: =(E2*100)-25000 , fill down Units × 100 dollars margin − 25,000 dollars marketing To fill a formula down, select the cell and double-click the small square at its bottom-right corner (the fill handle), or drag it to row 13. Press F9 a couple of times and watch columns C to G change: that is the simulation running. Good practice (optional, not required for marks) Day 5 taught you to keep inputs out of formulas. You may put the margin, the two marketing costs and the 1.4 multiplier in labelled cells to the right of the table (for example in column J) and refer to them with $ references. Keep columns A to G exactly as named above. Step 3: Lock the simulation ¶ RANDBETWEEN draws new numbers every time Excel recalculates. Tableau reads the values saved in the file, and your report must describe the same twelve months your chart shows, so you must freeze them: Select A1:G13 and copy ( Ctrl + C ). Without moving the selection, right-click A1 → Paste Special → Values (选择性粘贴 → 数值; the clipboard icon with 123 ). Click any cell in column C: the formula bar must now show a number , not =RANDBETWEEN(…) . Save and close Excel. Part 2: Decision chart in Tableau ¶ Open Tableau Desktop . Under Connect → To a File , click Microsoft Excel and open your workbook. Drag your sheet onto the canvas if it is not there already, then click the Sheet 1 worksheet tab at the bottom. Drag Month to the Columns shelf. Right-click the Month pill and choose Dimension , so that each month is a separate point instead of one sum. Drag Measure Values (at the bottom of the Data pane) to the Rows shelf. In the Measure Values card that appears below the Marks card, remove every measure except SUM(Standard Profit) and SUM(Aggressive Profit) (right-click → Remove ). On the Marks card, change the mark type from Automatic to Line . Drag Measure Names onto Color in the Marks card, so each strategy has its own coloured line and a legend. Give the sheet a message title (double-click the title), label the y-axis with its unit (US dollars per month), and check that the colours are easy to tell apart. Worksheet → Export → Image… , save the picture as PNG or JPEG, and insert it into a blank Word document. Part 3: The executive report ¶ Write a short executive report (about one to two pages) for SmartHome Tech's management in the Word document that holds your Tableau chart. Put your name and student ID at the top. Lead with your recommendation, then answer the two questions in connected paragraphs, quoting numbers from your locked simulation with units. # Question 1 Strategic decision. Using your Tableau chart, which marketing strategy gives the higher profit, and which gives the more consistent profit across the twelve months? In your simulation, was there any month in which the Aggressive strategy earned less than the Standard strategy because of its higher fixed cost in a weak month? docs.text: Day 6 lab: Applied Lab 6 — Advanced spreadsheet simulation ¶ Build a decision model in Microsoft Excel for a car maker's electric-vehicle launch: a base profit model, a two-way Data Table that shows profit for 25 combinations of demand and cost, and a 50-trial Monte Carlo simulation that estimates the risk of a loss. Then use the model to weigh an ethical sourcing decision. This notebook gives the Excel steps and checks your numbers in Python. Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Applied Lab 6 (Advanced spreadsheet simulation). Instructions rewritten for this classroom; the Data Table layout is corrected so that it works in Excel (see below). Graded Yes: 2% of the course grade Outcomes CLO 4 and 5 Tools Microsoft Excel (the graded work); this notebook in JupyterLab to check your numbers You submit Two files in the Applied Lab 6 drop-box on GAP (Moodle) : your workbook YourLastName_DATA300_Lab6.xlsx and your answers YourLastName_Lab6_Answers.pdf Deadline Wednesday 18 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , unless your facilitator says otherwise (see the schedule ) Two corrections to the syllabus version The Data Table's input cells must be on the same sheet as the table. Excel refuses an input cell on another sheet with the message "Input cell reference is not valid" . The syllabus puts the table on a What-If Analysis sheet and its input cells on the Base Model sheet, which fails. In this version the What-If Analysis sheet has its own two driver cells for demand and cost, and the table uses those. The formula must sit in the top-left corner of the selected range. In a two-way Data Table the corner cell holds the formula, the row values run to its right and the column values run below it. So the demand values go in B3:B7 , directly under the formula in B2, and you select B2:G7 . The results land in the same cells as in the syllabus (C3:G7), and every question is unchanged. The business scenario ¶ You are a financial analyst at EcoDrive Motors , a fictional company preparing to launch an affordable electric vehicle (EV). Two things make the launch's profit uncertain: the cost of battery materials, and how many customers will buy. The board is also split on the battery supply chain: Option Battery supplier Extra cost Cheaper A supplier known for severe labour violations none Ethical A supplier with ethical certification 500 US dollars per vehicle Your job: build an Excel model that projects the financial result, measures the risk of a loss, and shows what the ethical choice costs, so the board can decide knowingly. The plan uses the ethical supplier. Before you start ¶ Open a blank Excel workbook and save it straight away as YourLastName_DATA300_Lab6.xlsx (with your real last name). Save again after each part. Keep this notebook open next to Excel. Run its cells with Shift + Enter : each part ends with a Python check of the numbers your workbook should show. Excel menus are given in English, with the Chinese labels where they help (labels may vary slightly by Excel version). The setup cell loads the libraries and stores the plan's assumptions. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" INK = "#55534e" plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 9 , 4.5 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) # The plan's assumptions (Base Model sheet, B2:B6), in US dollars DEMAND = 15_000 # B2 expected unit sales PRICE = 35_000 # B3 sale price per vehicle BASE_COST = 28_000 # B4 base manufacturing cost per vehicle PREMIUM = 500 # B5 ethical sourcing premium per vehicle OVERHEAD = 50_000_000 # B6 fixed overhead costs def net_profit ( demand , base_cost = BASE_COST , premium = PREMIUM , price = PRICE , overhead = OVERHEAD ): """Net profit = revenue - variable costs - fixed overhead. Works on numbers and numpy arrays.""" revenue = demand * price variable_costs = demand * ( base_cost + premium ) return revenue - variable_costs - overhead Part 1: The base (deterministic) model ¶ A deterministic model gives one answer from one set of assumptions. It is the core that the Data Table and the simulation re-use, so every assumption goes in its own labelled cell and every formula refers to those cells. In Excel: assumptions (sheet Base Model ) Double-click the Sheet1 tab and rename it Base Model . Type these labels in column A and values in column B: Cell Label (column A) Value (column B) A1 Scenario Assumptions A2 / B2 Expected Unit Sales (Demand) 15000 A3 / B3 EV Sale Price (Per Unit) 35000 A4 / B4 Base Manufacturing Cost (Per Unit) 28000 A5 / B5 Ethical Sourcing Premium (Per Unit) 500 A6 / B6 Fixed Overhead Costs 50000000 Select B3:B6 and format them as currency: Home → Number Format → Currency (开始 → 数字格式 → 货币). In Excel: outputs In D1:D4 type the labels Financial Projections , Total Revenue , Total Variable Costs , Net Profit . In E2 type =B2*B3 (demand × price). In E3 type =B2*(B4+B5) (demand × (base cost + ethical premium)). In E4 type =E2-E3-B6 (revenue − variable costs − fixed overhead). docs.text: Build a decision model in Microsoft Excel for a car maker's electric-vehicle launch: a base profit model, a two-way Data Table that shows profit for 25 combinations of demand and cost, and a 50-trial Monte Carlo simulation that estimates the risk of a loss. Then use the model to weigh an ethical sourcing decision. This notebook gives the Excel steps and checks your numbers in Python. Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Applied Lab 6 (Advanced spreadsheet simulation). Instructions rewritten for this classroom; the Data Table layout is corrected so that it works in Excel (see below). Graded Yes: 2% of the course grade Outcomes CLO 4 and 5 Tools Microsoft Excel (the graded work); this notebook in JupyterLab to check your numbers You submit Two files in the Applied Lab 6 drop-box on GAP (Moodle) : your workbook YourLastName_DATA300_Lab6.xlsx and your answers YourLastName_Lab6_Answers.pdf Deadline Wednesday 18 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , unless your facilitator says otherwise (see the schedule ) Two corrections to the syllabus version The Data Table's input cells must be on the same sheet as the table. Excel refuses an input cell on another sheet with the message "Input cell reference is not valid" . The syllabus puts the table on a What-If Analysis sheet and its input cells on the Base Model sheet, which fails. In this version the What-If Analysis sheet has its own two driver cells for demand and cost, and the table uses those. The formula must sit in the top-left corner of the selected range. In a two-way Data Table the corner cell holds the formula, the row values run to its right and the column values run below it. So the demand values go in B3:B7 , directly under the formula in B2, and you select B2:G7 . The results land in the same cells as in the syllabus (C3:G7), and every question is unchanged.

docs.text: You are a financial analyst at EcoDrive Motors , a fictional company preparing to launch an affordable electric vehicle (EV). Two things make the launch's profit uncertain: the cost of battery materials, and how many customers will buy. The board is also split on the battery supply chain: Option Battery supplier Extra cost Cheaper A supplier known for severe labour violations none Ethical A supplier with ethical certification 500 US dollars per vehicle Your job: build an Excel model that projects the financial result, measures the risk of a loss, and shows what the ethical choice costs, so the board can decide knowingly. The plan uses the ethical supplier.
docs.title: The business scenario

docs.text: Open a blank Excel workbook and save it straight away as YourLastName_DATA300_Lab6.xlsx (with your real last name). Save again after each part. Keep this notebook open next to Excel. Run its cells with Shift + Enter : each part ends with a Python check of the numbers your workbook should show. Excel menus are given in English, with the Chinese labels where they help (labels may vary slightly by Excel version). The setup cell loads the libraries and stores the plan's assumptions. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" INK = "#55534e" plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 9 , 4.5 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) # The plan's assumptions (Base Model sheet, B2:B6), in US dollars DEMAND = 15_000 # B2 expected unit sales PRICE = 35_000 # B3 sale price per vehicle BASE_COST = 28_000 # B4 base manufacturing cost per vehicle PREMIUM = 500 # B5 ethical sourcing premium per vehicle OVERHEAD = 50_000_000 # B6 fixed overhead costs def net_profit ( demand , base_cost = BASE_COST , premium = PREMIUM , price = PRICE , overhead = OVERHEAD ): """Net profit = revenue - variable costs - fixed overhead. Works on numbers and numpy arrays.""" revenue = demand * price variable_costs = demand * ( base_cost + premium ) return revenue - variable_costs - overhead

As in the syllabus, demand is equally likely to be any whole number from 8,000 to 22,000 vehicles, and every other assumption stays at its Base Model value. In Excel: build the simulation (sheet Risk Simulation ) Add a sheet and rename it Risk Simulation . In A1 , B1 , C1 type Trial Number , Simulated Demand , Simulated Net Profit . Trial numbers: in A2 type 1 and in A3 type 2, select both and drag the fill handle down to A51 (trials 1 to 50). In B2 type =RANDBETWEEN(8000,22000) : a random whole-number demand. In C2 type =(B2*'Base Model'!$B$3)-(B2*('Base Model'!$B$4+'Base Model'!$B$5))-'Base Model'!$B$6 This is the Base Model's profit formula with the random demand. The $ signs keep every row pointing at the same assumptions. (Cross-sheet references are fine here: only Data Tables need their input cells on the same sheet.) Select B2:C2 and drag the fill handle down to row 51 . Summary box: Label Formula E1 Average Expected Profit F1 =AVERAGE(C2:C51) E2 Minimum Profit (Worst Case) F2 =MIN(C2:C51) E3 Maximum Profit (Best Case) F3 =MAX(C2:C51) E4 Probability of Loss F4 =COUNTIF(C2:C51,"<0")/50 Format C2:C51 and F1:F3 as currency and F4 as a percentage ( Home → % ). Press F9 several times. The numbers change each time: Excel's RANDBETWEEN draws new values on every recalculation. Write down the average profit and the probability of a loss from at least five recalculations, for question 2. Your Excel numbers will differ from the Python run below and from your neighbour's: Excel has no seed. The Python check uses a fixed seed so that everyone in the room sees the same reference run, then repeats the 50-trial simulation 1,000 times to show how much a 50-trial result can move when you press F9. rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 2026 ) N_TRIALS = 50 # One 50-trial run, like your Risk Simulation sheet sim = pd . DataFrame ({ "Trial Number" : np . arange ( 1 , N_TRIALS + 1 ), "Simulated Demand" : rng . integers ( 8_000 , 22_001 , N_TRIALS )}) # = RANDBETWEEN(8000, 22000) sim [ "Simulated Net Profit" ] = net_profit ( sim [ "Simulated Demand" ]) print ( "First five trials of the reference run:" ) print ( sim . head () . to_string ( index = False , formatters = { "Simulated Demand" : " {:,} " . format , "Simulated Net Profit" : " {:,.0f} " . format })) print ( " \n Summary box of the reference run (US dollars)" ) print ( f " F1 Average Expected Profit: { sim [ 'Simulated Net Profit' ] . mean () : >14,.0f } " ) print ( f " F2 Minimum Profit (Worst Case): { sim [ 'Simulated Net Profit' ] . min () : >14,.0f } " ) print ( f " F3 Maximum Profit (Best Case): { sim [ 'Simulated Net Profit' ] . max () : >14,.0f } " ) print ( f " F4 Probability of Loss: { ( sim [ 'Simulated Net Profit' ] < 0 ) . mean () : >14.0% } " ) # What pressing F9 does: 1,000 separate 50-trial runs runs = net_profit ( rng . integers ( 8_000 , 22_001 , ( 1_000 , N_TRIALS ))) run_means = runs . mean ( axis = 1 ) run_loss = ( runs < 0 ) . mean ( axis = 1 ) print ( " \n Across 1,000 separate 50-trial runs (like pressing F9 1,000 times):" ) print ( f " average profit ranged from { run_means . min () : ,.0f } to { run_means . max () : ,.0f } " ) print ( f " middle 95% of runs: { np . quantile ( run_means , 0.025 ) : ,.0f } to { np . quantile ( run_means , 0.975 ) : ,.0f } " ) print ( f " probability of loss ranged from { run_loss . min () : .0% } to { run_loss . max () : .0% } " ) First five trials of the reference F1 Average Expected Profit: 46,552,430 F2 Minimum Profit (Worst Case): 3,163,500 F3 Maximum Profit (Best Case): 89,997,000 F4 Probability of Loss: 0% Across 1,000 separate 50-trial runs (like pressing BASE_COST - PREMIUM ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . hist ( sim [ "Simulated Net Profit" ] / 1e6 , bins = 12 , color = BLUE , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 , label = "Zero profit" ) ax . axvline ( sim [ "Simulated Net Profit" ] . mean () / 1e6 , color = INK , linestyle = "--" , label = "Average of the 50 trials" ) ax . set_title ( "50 simulated launch the Base Model's cost and premium: { break_even_demand : ,.0f } vehicles" ) print ( "Lowest demand the simulation can draw: 8,000 vehicles" ) Break-even demand at the Base Model's cost and premium: Put your name and student ID at the top, number your answers 1–4, and quote the numbers you use, with units. Write in complete sentences. # Outcome Question 1 CLO 4 Break-even under a cost shock. Supply shortages push the base manufacturing cost to 32,000 US dollars per vehicle. Using your Data Table, what is the smallest demand EcoDrive must reach to avoid a loss? Show how you confirmed it with a calculation (fixed overhead ÷ profit per vehicle). 2 CLO 4 How risky is the launch? Press F9 several times on the Risk Simulation sheet. Report the probability of a loss and the average expected profit you observed (a range is fine), and explain how risky the launch looks and why. 3 CLO 5 The ethical dilemma. On the Base Model, change the Ethical Sourcing Premium (B5) from 500 to 0 : this is the cheaper supplier with severe labour violations. (a) By how much does net profit rise? (b) As the analytics manager, write a 3–4 sentence recommendation to the board for keeping the 500-dollar premium even though it lowers immediate profit. Consider long-term brand reputation, the people affected, and corporate responsibility. Then set B5 back to 500 . 4 CLO 5 The societal value of BI tools. How does a spreadsheet simulation like this help EcoDrive bring an affordable EV to market responsibly ? Why is it dangerous, financially and for society, to set prices and plans from a single best-case scenario instead of simulating uncertainty? Writing tips Lead with the answer, then the evidence: "At a cost of 32,000 dollars, EcoDrive must sell at least … vehicles, because …" . In question 3, use today's lecture: put a number on the ethical choice, then weigh what the spreadsheet does not contain (fines, boycotts, import rules, workers' welfare). docs.text: The syllabus simulation lets only demand vary. In reality the base manufacturing cost is uncertain too: that is exactly what worried the board. Suppose the cost per vehicle follows a normal distribution with mean 28,000 and standard deviation 1,500 dollars. In Excel, add a column to the Risk Simulation sheet: in D1 Simulated Base Cost , in D2 =NORM.INV(RAND(),28000,1500) , fill down to row 51, and change C2 to use D2 instead of 'Base Model'!$B$4 . Press F9: what happens to the probability of a loss? The cell below runs the same idea with 10,000 trials (more trials give a steadier estimate, as you saw on Day 5). rng = np . random . default_rng ( seed = 7 ) N = 10_000 demand_draws = rng . integers ( 8_000 , 22_001 , N ) for label , cost_draws in [( "demand varies, cost fixed at 28,000" , np . full ( N , BASE_COST )), ( "demand varies, cost ~ normal(28,000, 1,500)" , rng . normal ( 28_000 , 1_500 , N ))]: profits = net_profit ( demand_draws , base_cost = cost_draws ) print ( f " { label : <46 } average { profits . mean () : >13,.0f } P(loss) { ( profits < 0 ) . mean () : >6.1% } " f "P5 { np . quantile ( profits , 0.05 ) : >13,.0f } " ) demand varies, cost fixed at 28,000 average 47,449,074 P(loss) 0.0% P5 6,855,175 demand varies, cost ~ normal(28,000, 1,500) average 47,437,440 P(loss) 6.3% P5 -1,996,400 Two more ideas to try in Excel: Goal Seek for question 1: on the Base Model, set B4 to 32000, then Data → What-If Analysis → Goal Seek (单变量求解) with Set cell E4 , To value 0 , By changing cell B2 . Then press Ctrl + Z to undo, and set B4 back to 28000. More trials: extend the Risk Simulation to 1,000 rows and change the 50 in F4 to COUNT(C2:C1001) . Does the average expected profit still move as much when you press F9? Stuck? "Input cell reference is not valid" : your row or column input cell is on another sheet; use J3 and J2 on the What-If Analysis sheet. Every cell of the table shows the same number : the corner formula in B2 does not use J2 and J3. The numbers do not match the Part 2 check : the row and column input cells are swapped (row input J3, column input J2). #NAME? : a function name or sheet name is mistyped; sheet names with spaces need single quotes, as in 'Base Model'!B3 . For anything else, take a screenshot and ask your facilitator.

docs.text: Day 6 lab: Applied Lab 7 — BI case study implementation ¶ Continue the EcoDrive Motors case from Lab 6. Forecast the cost of electric-vehicle batteries with Excel's Forecast Sheet, carry the worst-case forecast into a case-study dashboard that compares three sourcing strategies, and write a managerial report that weighs profit against ethical and social impact. This notebook gives the Excel steps and cross-checks the forecast in Python. Adapted from the DATA 300 syllabus, Applied Lab 7 (BI case study implementation). Instructions rewritten for this classroom; the data come bundled with the course. Graded Yes: 2% of the course grade Outcomes CLO 4 and 5 Tools Microsoft Excel (Forecast Sheet; the graded work); this notebook in JupyterLab to check your forecast You submit Two files in the Applied Lab 7 drop-box on GAP (Moodle) : your workbook YourLastName_DATA300_Lab7.xlsx and your report YourLastName_Lab7_Report.pdf Deadline Wednesday 18 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , unless your facilitator says otherwise (see the schedule ) Three notes on the syllabus version Eleven quarters, not twelve. The history runs from Q1-2023 to Q3-2025: 11 values, in rows 2–12 (not 2–13). A numeric timeline. Excel's Forecast Sheet needs the timeline to be numbers or dates at equal steps; labels such as "Q1-2023" are text. The bundled workbook therefore numbers the quarters 1–11 in column A and keeps the labels in column C. Five steps ahead. From period 11 (Q3-2025), Q4-2026 is period 16 , five quarters ahead, so the forecast must end at 16. The business scenario ¶ After your Lab 6 simulation, the EcoDrive Motors ( fictional ) board has a new worry. Shortages of lithium and cobalt have pushed the cost of EV batteries up and down over the last three years. Before committing to the 500-dollar ethical sourcing premium for next year's launch, the chief financial officer (CFO) wants to know where battery costs are heading, and what each sourcing strategy would earn if costs end up at the high end of the forecast. Your three tasks: Predict: forecast the battery cost per vehicle to Q4-2026 with Excel's exponential smoothing (ETS) forecast. Compare: build a case-study dashboard of three sourcing strategies under the worst-case forecast cost. Recommend: write a managerial report that weighs the money against the ethical and social impacts. Before you start ¶ In the course folder, open data/ecodrive_battery_costs.xlsx in Excel and immediately File → Save As YourLastName_DATA300_Lab7.xlsx in your own folder. Its sheet Historical Data already holds the 11 quarters. (You may instead type the data into a blank workbook: same layout, sheet named Historical Data .) Keep this notebook open next to Excel and run its cells with Shift + Enter . The first cell loads the same data in Python. import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import numpy as np import pandas as pd from statsmodels.tsa.exponential_smoothing.ets import ETSModel BLUE , ORANGE , AQUA = "#2a78d6" , "#eb6834" , "#1baf7a" GREY = "#c9c7c1" INK = "#55534e" plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.figsize" : ( 9 , 4.5 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.grid" : True , "axes.axisbelow" : True , "grid.color" : "#e6e5e1" , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlelocation" : "left" , }) history = pd . read_excel ( "data/ecodrive_battery_costs.xlsx" , sheet_name = "Historical Data" , usecols = "A:C" ) print ( history . to_string ( index = False )) Period Battery Cost per EV ($) Quarter 1 7500 Q1-2023 2 7650 Q2-2023 3 7900 Q3-2023 4 8100 Q4-2023 5 8000 Q1-2024 6 8350 Q2-2024 7 8600 Q3-2024 8 8900 Q4-2024 9 8800 Q1-2025 10 9200 Q2-2025 11 9550 Q3-2025 Part 1: Time series forecasting in Excel (CLO 4) ¶ Excel's Forecast Sheet fits an exponential smoothing (ETS) model: it gives recent quarters more weight than old ones, follows the trend , and, if it finds one, a repeating seasonal pattern. It also draws a 95% confidence interval : a lower and an upper bound around each forecast. In Excel: create the forecast (sheet Historical Data ) Check the layout: A1 Period , B1 Battery Cost per EV ($) , C1 Quarter ; periods 1–11 in A2:A12 , costs in B2:B12 . Format B2:B12 as currency if it is not already. Select A1:B12 (the timeline and the values, with their headers). Data → Forecast Sheet (数据 → 预测工作表), in the Forecast group at the right of the Data tab. In the preview window choose the line chart , then set Forecast End to 16 (period 16 = Q4-2026). Click Options and check: Confidence Interval 95% ; Seasonality Detect automatically ; Timeline Range A2:A12 ; Values Range B2:B12 . Click Create . Excel adds a new sheet with a table and a chart: the history, the Forecast , the Lower Confidence Bound and the Upper Confidence Bound for periods 12–16. Rename the new sheet Predictive Forecast . Find the row for period 16 (usually row 17) and write down three numbers for your report: the forecast, the lower bound and the upper bound. Note which cell holds the upper bound (usually E17 ); Part 2 links to it. If Forecast Sheet is greyed out or missing It needs Excel 2016 or later. Click a cell inside the data first. If Excel complains about the timeline, check that column A holds numbers 1–11 with no gaps and no text. Python cross-check ¶ Excel chooses its ETS settings automatically, so its numbers depend on whether it detects a 4-quarter seasonal pattern. The cell below fits the two most likely versions with the same method (additive ETS) and prints their forecasts and 95% bounds. Your Excel results should be close to one of the two , but they will not match exactly: Excel's fitting procedure is not identical. In your report, quote Excel's numbers. Predict, then reveal Will the forecast for Q4-2026 be above or below 10,000 dollars? And the upper bound? y = history [ "Battery Cost per EV ($)" ] . astype ( float ) future_periods = np . arange ( 12 , 17 ) # Q4-2025 ... Q4-2026 future_labels = [ "Q4-2025" , "Q1-2026" , "Q2-2026" , "Q3-2026" , "Q4-2026" ] fits = { "trend only" : ETSModel ( y , error = "add" , trend = "add" ) . fit ( disp = False ), "trend + 4-quarter season" : ETSModel ( y , error = "add" , trend = "add" , seasonal = "add" , seasonal_periods = 4 ) . fit ( disp = False ), } forecasts = {} for name , fit in fits . items (): frame = fit . get_prediction ( start = len ( y ), end = len ( y ) + 4 ) . summary_frame ( alpha = 0.05 ) frame . index = pd . Index ( future_periods , name = "period" ) frame . insert ( 0 , "quarter" , future_labels ) forecasts [ name ] = frame . rename ( columns = { "mean" : "forecast" , "pi_lower" : "lower bound" , "pi_upper" : "upper bound" }) print ( f "--- ETS, { name } (US dollars per vehicle) ---" ) print ( forecasts [ name ] . to_string ( formatters = { c : " {:,.0f} " . format for c in [ "forecast" , "lower bound" , "upper bound" ]})) print () --- ETS, trend only (US dollars per vehicle) --- quarter forecast lower bound upper bound period 12 Q4-2025 9,578 9,356 9,801 13 Q1-2026 9,772 9,550 9,995 14 Q2-2026 9,966 9,744 10,189 15 Q3-2026 10,161 9,938 10,383 16 Q4-2026 10,355 10,132 10,577 --- ETS, trend + 4-quarter season (US dollars per vehicle) --- quarter forecast lower bound upper bound period 12 Q4-2025 9,800 9,672 9,927 13 Q1-2026 9,700 9,520 9,881 14 Q2-2026 10,000 9,779 10,221 15 Q3-2026 10,283 10,028 10,539 16 Q4-2026 10,533 10,247 10,818 fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 10 , 4.5 )) ax . plot ( history [ "Period" ], y , marker = "o" , color = INK , linewidth = 2 , label = "History" ) for ( name , frame ), colour in zip ( forecasts . items (), [ BLUE , ORANGE ]): ax . plot ( frame . index , frame [ "forecast" ], marker = "o" , color = colour , linewidth = 2 , label = f "Forecast: { name } " ) ax . fill_between ( frame . index , frame [ "lower bound" ], frame [ "upper bound" ], color = colour , alpha = 0.15 ) ax . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , 17 ), list ( history [ "Quarter" ]) + future_labels , rotation = 45 ) ax . set_title ( "Battery costs are forecast to keep rising; the band shows the 95 % r ange" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Quarter" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Battery cost per EV (US dollars)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Read the chart above: the line continues the upward trend, and the shaded band is the range in which the model expects the true cost to fall 95% of the time. Your Excel chart should look similar. Use your Excel Predictive Forecast sheet for questions 1 and 2. Part 2: The case-study dashboard ¶ The CFO wants to plan for the worst case the forecast considers plausible: the upper confidence bound for Q4-2026. Three sourcing strategies are on the table: Strategy Ethical premium per vehicle 1. Profit-maximised (no ethical sourcing) 0 2. Hybrid sourcing (half the batteries certified) 250 3. Fully ethical (all batteries certified) 500 In Excel: constants and the forecast link (sheet Case Study Dashboard ) Add a sheet and rename it Case Study Dashboard . Type the constants: Cell Label (column A) Value (column B) A1 / B1 Expected EV Demand 15000 A2 / B2 EV Sale Price 35000 A3 / B3 Non-Battery Manufacturing Cost 18000 A4 / B4 Fixed Overhead Costs 50000000 In A6 type Projected Battery Cost (Upper Confidence Bound, Q4-2026) . In B6 type = , click the Predictive Forecast tab, click the cell with the upper bound for period 16 , and press Enter . B6 now shows a formula such as ='Predictive Forecast'!E17 . Check that the value is the number you wrote down in Part 1. In Excel: compare the three strategies Row 8, headings: A8 Strategy , B8 1. Profit-Maximized (No Ethics) , C8 2. Hybrid Sourcing (50% Ethical) , D8 3. Fully Ethical (100% Certified) . Row 9, premium: A9 Ethical Premium ; B9 0 , C9 250 , D9 500 . Row 10, cost per vehicle: A10 Total Variable Cost ; in B10 type =$B$3+$B$6+B9 and copy it to C10:D10 . The $ signs keep the non-battery cost and the battery cost fixed while the premium column changes. Row 11, profit: A11 Projected Net Profit ; in B11 type =($B$1*$B$2)-($B$1*B10)-$B$4 and copy it to C11:D11 . Format B9:D11 as currency. Recommended: select B8:D8 , hold Ctrl and select B11:D11 , then Insert → Column Chart (插入 → 柱形图). Give the chart a message title, for example the profit gap between strategies 1 and 3. The cell below computes the dashboard with each Python upper bound, so you can check your formulas. Your row 11 will differ a little, because your B6 comes from Excel's forecast; the gaps between strategies must match exactly. Work out why. DEMAND , PRICE , NON_BATTERY , OVERHEAD = 15_000 , 35_000 , 18_000 , 50_000_000 PREMIUMS = { "1. Profit-Maximized (No Ethics)" : 0 , "2. Hybrid Sourcing (50 % E thical)" : 250 , "3. Fully Ethical (100% Certified)" : 500 } def dashboard ( battery_cost ): """Rows 9-11 of the Case Study Dashboard for a given battery cost per vehicle (cell B6).""" rows = {} for strategy , premium in PREMIUMS . items (): variable = NON_BATTERY + battery_cost + premium rows [ strategy . split ( " (" )[ 0 ]] = { "premium (row 9)" : premium , "variable cost (row 10)" : variable , "net profit (row 11)" : DEMAND * PRICE - DEMAND * variable - OVERHEAD } return pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . T for name , frame in forecasts . items (): upper = frame . loc [ 16 , "upper bound" ] print ( f "--- B6 = { upper : ,.0f } (upper bound for Q4-2026, ETS { name } ) ---" ) print ( dashboard ( upper ) . map ( " {:,.0f} " . format ) . to_string ()) print () --- B6 = 10,577 (upper bound for Q4-2026, ETS trend only) --- premium (row 9) variable cost (row 10) net profit (row 11) 1. Profit-Maximized 0 28,577 46,343,926 2. Hybrid Sourcing 250 28,827 42,593,926 3. Fully Ethical 500 29,077 38,843,926 --- B6 = 10,818 (upper bound for Q4-2026, ETS trend + 4-quarter season) --- premium (row 9) variable cost (row 10) net profit (row 11) 1. Profit-Maximized 0 28,818 42,722,534 2. Hybrid Sourcing 250 29,068 38,972,534 3. Fully Ethical 500 29,318 35,222,534 Part 3: Managerial report ¶ Write a short, professional managerial report in Word for the CFO and the board. Use the two section headings below, put your name and student ID at the top, and answer every question in complete sentences, quoting your Excel numbers with units. You may paste your forecast chart and dashboard into the report as pictures (copy them from Excel). Section 1: Predictive modelling analysis (CLO 4) ¶ # Question 1 Trend. Describe the history of battery costs shown on your Predictive Forecast sheet: direction, rough size of the change, and any repeating pattern within the year. What is the forecast (baseline) battery cost for Q4-2026? 2 Confidence intervals. Explain, in your own words, what the lower and upper confidence bounds mean in a forecast. Why does the dashboard use the upper bound rather than the baseline forecast? Section 2: Ethical impact and BI evaluation (CLO 5) ¶ # Question 3 The cost of ethics. If the worst-case battery cost for Q4-2026 comes true, what is the projected net profit of Strategy 1 (no ethics) and of Strategy 3 (fully ethical)? How large is the difference, in dollars and as a share of Strategy 1's profit? 4 Recommendation. EcoDrive markets itself as a "green and responsible" company, yet full ethical sourcing plus rising battery costs cuts its margins. As an analytics consultant, write one or two paragraphs recommending one of the three strategies. Justify it by weighing the numbers (profit, costs) against the societal impacts: brand reputation, human rights in the supply chain, and corporate social responsibility. 5 The value of BI. Why does combining a time series forecast with a dashboard of several strategies support a better decision than simply looking at last year's battery costs? Writing tips Start Section 2 with your recommendation in one sentence. Quote the profit gap in dollars and in per cent. A strong recommendation names what the spreadsheet leaves out (fines, import bans on goods linked to forced labour, boycotts, staff and investor reactions) and says what you would monitor after the decision. "Hybrid" is not automatically the safe middle: if you choose it, explain what happens to the uncertified half. Part 4: Save and submit ¶ Check the workbook has the sheets Historical Data , Predictive Forecast and Case Study Dashboard , and that B6 on the dashboard is a link to the forecast sheet (click it: the formula bar shows ='Predictive Forecast'!… ). Save it as YourLastName_DATA300_Lab7.xlsx . Save the report as PDF: File → Save As → PDF (文件 → 另存为 → PDF), named YourLastName_Lab7_Report.pdf . Log in to GAP (Moodle) , open the DATA 300: Applied Lab 7 drop-box, upload both files and click Submit by 23:59 China Standard Time today . Paste any charts into the Word report before you save it as PDF, so the report is a single file. If you end up with two PDFs, combine them as shown in Combining PDFs without internet . Checklist before you upload ¶ Predictive Forecast sheet created by Forecast Sheet, ending at period 16, with lower and upper bounds. Case Study Dashboard: B6 links to the period-16 upper bound; rows 9–11 complete and formatted as currency. The gaps between strategies match the Part 2 check. Report: two sections, five numbered answers, Excel numbers quoted with units, one clear recommendation. Files named YourLastName_DATA300_Lab7.xlsx and YourLastName_Lab7_Report.pdf , both uploaded to the Applied Lab 7 drop-box on GAP (Moodle). How it is marked ¶ The lab uses the course's Lab 7 rubric: CLO 4 (developing predictive models such as time series forecasts to project outcomes, 40 points), CLO 5 (evaluating BI tools in a case and writing managerial reports that consider ethical and societal contexts, 40 points), professional formatting (10 points) and clear academic writing (10 points). In practice: a working forecast and dashboard linked by formula, a correct reading of the confidence bounds, profit figures quoted correctly, and a recommendation that weighs money and ethics instead of mentioning ethics in passing. Going further (not graded) ¶ The dashboard uses one battery cost. A one-way Data Table shows how the three profits respond to any battery cost. Because a Data Table's input cell must be on its own sheet, build it on the Case Study Dashboard itself, where B6 lives: In F2:F8 type battery costs from 9,000 to 12,000 in steps of 500 (down a column). docs.text: Excel's Forecast Sheet fits an exponential smoothing (ETS) model: it gives recent quarters more weight than old ones, follows the trend , and, if it finds one, a repeating seasonal pattern. It also draws a 95% confidence interval : a lower and an upper bound around each forecast. Click Options and check: Confidence Interval 95% ; Seasonality Detect automatically ; Timeline Range A2:A12 ; Values Range B2:B12 . Click Create . Excel adds a new sheet with a table and a chart: the history, the Forecast , the Lower Confidence Bound and the Upper Confidence Bound for periods 12–16. Rename the new sheet Predictive Forecast .
