docs.text: Explain what the kernel is and why the order in which cells run matters. Use Python numbers, text, true/false values, lists and dictionaries. Build, load and inspect a pandas DataFrame : size, types, missing values, summary statistics. Select, filter, add columns, group and pivot , and draw a labelled chart. Read a Python error from the bottom up and fix the usual causes. Say which level of the analytics hierarchy a result belongs to before you act on it. How the course uses code Most notebooks give you working code. You read it, run it, predict what it will show, then change a line or two. Writing long programs from scratch is not the aim; reading output carefully is. Part Topic 1 Notebooks, cells and the kernel 2 Python values 3 Lists and dictionaries 4 DataFrames with pandas 5 Describe, group, pivot and plot 6 Reading errors 7 Practice on the penguins data (Core, Stretch, Challenge) 8 Business case, quiz and summary Reading Read Chapter 1 of the course reading packet for the four levels of analytics (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive) and for what describe() , isnull().sum() , groupby() and correlation can and cannot tell you. This notebook practises exactly those calls.
docs.title: What you will be able to do

docs.text: A notebook is a page of cells . A Markdown cell holds text like this one. A code cell holds Python; when you run it, the result appears underneath. Behind the page sits the kernel : the Python process that actually runs your code and remembers every name you have created. The page and the kernel are separate. The page shows what you typed ; the kernel knows what you ran , and in which order. You see It means [3] to the left of a cell This cell was the third one run in this session [ ] Not run yet in this session [*] Running now; wait Kernel status "Idle" Ready for the next cell
docs.title: Part 1: Notebooks, cells and the kernel

docs.text: Key Action Shift + Enter Run the cell, move to the next Esc , then A / B Add a cell above / below Esc , then M / Y Make the cell Markdown / code Ctrl + S (Cmd + S) Save cups_sold = 40 price_per_cup = 18 cups_sold * price_per_cup 720 The last line of a cell is shown automatically. Everything else needs print(...) . Predict, then run Suppose you scroll up, change cups_sold = 40 to cups_sold = 55 , but do not run that cell. Then you run the cell below. Which number will it print? Write your guess, try it, then put the value back. print ( "The kernel currently remembers cups_sold =" , cups_sold ) The kernel currently remembers cups_sold = 40 The kernel only knows what has run . Editing a cell changes the page, not the kernel's memory. Misconception: "the notebook runs from top to bottom" It does not, unless you make it. You can run cells in any order, and the kernel keeps whatever ran last. A notebook that "worked yesterday" can fail today because, yesterday, cells ran in a different order. The cure is Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells : Python forgets everything and runs the page top to bottom. Do this before every export or submission, so the PDF shows outputs that match the code. Check your understanding A classmate's PDF shows [7] , [3] , [12] beside three consecutive cells. What does that tell you about how the notebook was run, and what should they do before submitting?
docs.title: Keys to learn first

docs.text: Every value has a type , and the type decides what you can do with it. Type Example Used for int 42 Whole numbers: counts float 18.5 Decimal numbers: prices, measurements str "Iced tea" Text, always in quotes bool True , False Answers to yes/no questions NoneType None "No value" shop = "Harbour Lane Cafe" open_days = 7 average_ticket = 23.5 takes_cards = True print ( type ( shop ), type ( open_days ), type ( average_ticket ), type ( takes_cards )) print ( f " { shop } opens { open_days } days a week; the average ticket is { average_ticket : .2f } currency units." ) <class 'str'> <class 'int'> <class 'float'> <class 'bool'> Harbour Lane Cafe opens 7 days a week; the average ticket is 23.50 currency units. An f-string (text starting with f ) puts values into text inside { } ; :.2f shows two decimals.
docs.title: Part 2: Python values

docs.text: One = stores a value. Two, == , asks whether two values are equal. Filters in pandas are built from exactly these questions. print ( open_days == 6 ) # a question: is it 6? print ( average_ticket > 25 ) # is it above 25? print ( takes_cards and open_days >= 5 ) False False True Predict, then run: text that looks like a number "3" is text and 3 is a number. What happens when you add "3" + "4" ? What about int("3") + 4 ? Guess both, then run. print ( "3" + "4" ) # joining two pieces of text print ( int ( "3" ) + 4 ) # converting text to a number first 34 7 Joining text is not arithmetic. When a column of numbers has been read as text (one stray letter is enough), sums and means fail or behave strangely, so always check the types of a new table. Misconception: "the computer does exact decimal arithmetic" Decimals are stored in binary, so tiny rounding gaps appear. Run the next cell. This never matters for business reporting as long as you round when you display , and never test decimals with == . print ( 0.1 + 0.2 ) print ( round ( 0.1 + 0.2 , 2 )) 0.30000000000000004 0.3
docs.title: Comparisons give True or False

docs.text: A list holds values in order, inside [ ] . Positions count from 0 , and -1 means the last one. A slice [a:b] takes positions a up to, but not including, b . weekly_cups = [ 210 , 185 , 240 , 260 , 198 , 305 ] # six weeks print ( "First week:" , weekly_cups [ 0 ]) print ( "Last week:" , weekly_cups [ - 1 ]) print ( "Weeks 2 to 4:" , weekly_cups [ 1 : 4 ]) print ( "Total:" , sum ( weekly_cups ), "| weeks:" , len ( weekly_cups ), "| average:" , round ( sum ( weekly_cups ) / len ( weekly_cups ), 1 )) First week: 210 Last week: 305 Weeks 2 to 4: [185, 240, 260] Total: 1398 | weeks: 6 | average: 233.0 A dictionary pairs keys with values , inside { } , so you look things up by name instead of by position. menu = { "Latte" : 18 , "Iced tea" : 15 , "Hot chocolate" : 16 } print ( "Price of iced tea:" , menu [ "Iced tea" ]) menu [ "Lemonade" ] = 14 # add an item print ( "Items:" , list ( menu )) print ( "Cheapest first:" , sorted ( menu , key = menu . get )) Price of iced tea: 15 Items: ['Latte', 'Iced tea', 'Hot chocolate', 'Lemonade'] Cheapest first: ['Lemonade', 'Iced tea', 'Hot chocolate', 'Latte'] A table is just these two ideas combined: a list of rows , where each row is a dictionary of column values. pandas turns that into a DataFrame in one step. import pandas as pd rows = [ { "drink" : "Latte" , "cups" : 31 , "price" : 18 }, { "drink" : "Iced tea" , "cups" : 22 , "price" : 15 }, { "drink" : "Hot chocolate" , "cups" : 9 , "price" : 16 }, ] small = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) small [ "revenue" ] = small [ "cups" ] * small [ "price" ] small .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } drink cups price revenue 0 Latte 31 18 558 1 Iced tea 22 15 330 2 Hot chocolate 9 16 144 Check your understanding What does weekly_cups[2] return, and why is it not 185 ? In the small table, what does one row represent? (This is the table's grain , and it decides what counting means.)
docs.title: Part 3: Lists and dictionaries

docs.text: To practise on something bigger without touching any graded dataset, the next cell generates six weeks of sales for an imaginary café: one row per drink per day. The data is synthetic (made up by a seeded random generator, so it is identical every time). Money is in neutral currency units . import numpy as np rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) dates = pd . date_range ( "2026-09-07" , periods = 42 , freq = "D" ) # six weeks, Monday to Sunday temperature = np . round ( rng . normal ( 24 , 4 , len ( dates )), 1 ) # daily high, degrees Celsius prices = { "Latte" : 18 , "Iced tea" : 15 , "Hot chocolate" : 16 } records = [] for day , temp in zip ( dates , temperature ): weekend = day . dayofweek >= 5 base = { "Latte" : 30 , "Iced tea" : 6 + 1.6 * ( temp - 18 ), "Hot chocolate" : 22 - 0.9 * ( temp - 18 )} for drink , mean_cups in base . items (): mean_cups = max ( mean_cups , 2 ) * ( 1.4 if weekend else 1.0 ) records . append ({ "date" : day , "weekday" : day . day_name (), "weekend" : weekend , "temp_c" : temp , "drink" : drink , "cups" : int ( rng . poisson ( mean_cups )), "price" : prices [ drink ], }) cafe = pd . DataFrame ( records ) cafe . loc [[ 17 , 88 ], "cups" ] = np . nan # two days where the till record was lost cafe . head () .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } date weekday weekend temp_c drink cups price 0 2026-09-07 Monday False 20.8 Latte 25.0 18 1 2026-09-07 Monday False 20.8 Iced tea 11.0 15 2 2026-09-07 Monday False 20.8 Hot chocolate 23.0 16 3 2026-09-08 Tuesday False 25.0 Latte 32.0 18 4 2026-09-08 Tuesday False 25.0 Iced tea 16.0 15
docs.title: Part 4: DataFrames with pandas

docs.text: Four questions to ask of every new table, in this order: How big is it? shape What type is each column? dtypes Where is data missing? isnull().sum() What do the numbers look like? describe() print ( "Rows, columns:" , cafe . shape ) print () print ( cafe . dtypes ) Rows, columns: (126, 7) date datetime64[ns] weekday object weekend bool temp_c float64 drink object cups float64 price int64 dtype: object int64 is whole numbers, float64 decimals, object text, bool true/false and datetime64 dates. Notice that cups is float64 although cups are whole: pandas stores a missing number as NaN ("not a number"), which is a float, so the whole column becomes float. cafe . isnull () . sum () date 0 weekday 0 weekend 0 temp_c 0 drink 0 cups 2 price 0 dtype: int64 cafe . describe () . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } date temp_c cups price count 126 126.0 124.0 126.0 mean 2026-09-27 12:00:00 24.2 23.0 16.3 min 2026-09-07 00:00:00 16.4 0.0 15.0 25% 2026-09-17 00:00:00 22.1 16.0 15.0 50% 2026-09-27 12:00:00 23.7 22.0 16.0 75% 2026-10-08 00:00:00 26.6 29.0 18.0 max 2026-10-18 00:00:00 31.3 56.0 18.0 std NaN 3.2 10.0 1.3 Predict, then run The table has 126 rows. What will the count row of describe() show for cups , and why? Check your prediction against the output above. describe() silently skips missing values. The mean of cups is a real number, but it describes fewer rows than the table holds. That is why isnull().sum() comes first. Misconception: "a missing value is zero" A lost till record does not mean nobody bought a drink. Filling NaN with 0 would drag every average down. In this course a missing value is not available , never 0, unless you have evidence it really was zero.

docs.text: An overall average blends groups that may behave very differently. groupby splits the table into groups and summarises each one. Each line inside agg reads new name = (column, summary) . by_drink = cafe . groupby ( "drink" ) . agg ( days = ( "cups" , "count" ), average_cups = ( "cups" , "mean" ), total_revenue = ( "revenue" , "sum" ), ) . round ( 1 ) by_drink .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } days average_cups total_revenue drink Hot chocolate 41 18.7 12240.0 Iced tea 41 17.8 10950.0 Latte 42 32.5 24534.0 The days column counts non-missing values, so it shows directly where the two lost records were.

docs.text: A pivot table puts one category down the side and another across the top, like a pivot table in Excel. cafe [ "weather" ] = np . where ( cafe [ "temp_c" ] >= 25 , "Warm (25 °C or more)" , "Cool (below 25 °C)" ) pd . pivot_table ( cafe , index = "drink" , columns = "weather" , values = "cups" , aggfunc = "mean" ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } weather Cool (below 25 °C) Warm (25 °C or more) drink Hot chocolate 21.8 14.2 Iced tea 15.0 21.7 Latte 32.9 31.8 Predict, then run Before looking closely at the pivot table: which drink do you expect to sell more on warm days and which less ? docs.text: A chart needs a title that states the message, labelled axes with units , and ends with plt.show() . Choose the chart for the question: Question Chart How is one number spread out? Histogram How do groups compare? Bar chart Do two numbers move together? Scatter plot How does a number change over time? Line chart import matplotlib.pyplot as plt daily = cafe . groupby ( "date" ) . agg ( cups = ( "cups" , "sum" ), temp_c = ( "temp_c" , "first" )) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) ax . plot ( daily . index , daily [ "cups" ], color = "#2a78d6" , marker = "o" , markersize = 3 ) ax . set_title ( "Daily cups sold rise and fall every week (synthetic cafe data)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Date" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Cups sold per day (all drinks)" ) fig . autofmt_xdate () plt . show () colours = { "Latte" : "#2a78d6" , "Iced tea" : "#eb6834" , "Hot chocolate" : "#1baf7a" } fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4.5 )) for drink , group in cafe . groupby ( "drink" ): ax . scatter ( group [ "temp_c" ], group [ "cups" ], label = drink , color = colours [ drink ], alpha = 0.7 , s = 25 ) ax . set_title ( "Iced tea sells more and hot chocolate less on warmer days" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Daily high temperature (°C)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Cups sold that day" ) ax . legend ( title = "Drink" ) plt . show ()

docs.text: The correlation coefficient r runs from −1 to +1 and measures how closely two numbers move together along a straight line. for drink , group in cafe . groupby ( "drink" ): r = group [ "temp_c" ] . corr ( group [ "cups" ]) print ( f " { drink : <14 } r(temperature, cups) = { r : +.2f } " ) Hot chocolate r(temperature, cups) = -0.69 Iced tea r(temperature, cups) = +0.63 Latte r(temperature, cups) = +0.07 From statistic to insight: a worked example The manager asks: "Should we prepare more iced tea on warm days?" Descriptive (what happened): the pivot table and the scatter plot show iced tea sales were higher on warm days in these six weeks. Diagnostic (why): warmer weather is a plausible reason, but weekends also lift sales. If warm days happened to fall on weekends, part of the "temperature effect" would really be a weekend effect. Check by comparing warm and cool days within weekdays only. Predictive (what next): tomorrow's forecast high could be used to estimate tomorrow's iced tea sales. Prescriptive (what to do): prepare more iced tea when the forecast is warm, and less hot chocolate, then measure whether waste falls. The numbers above only answer step 1. Each later step needs more work, and that is the path this course follows. weekdays_only = cafe [ ~ cafe [ "weekend" ]] pd . pivot_table ( weekdays_only , index = "drink" , columns = "weather" , values = "cups" , aggfunc = "mean" ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } weather Cool (below 25 °C) Warm (25 °C or more) drink Hot chocolate 18.8 13.8 Iced tea 11.4 19.8 Latte 28.1 29.9 Misconception: "a strong correlation proves one thing causes the other" Correlation describes how two columns moved together in this data. A third factor (here, the weekend) can push both, and a categorical factor never appears in a correlation at all because it is not a number. Always ask what else changed at the same time. Check your understanding Compare the weekday-only pivot table with the full one. Does the warm-versus-cool difference for iced tea survive when weekends are removed? What does your answer say about the manager's question?

docs.text: Errors are normal and informative. A Python error message (a traceback ) reads from the bottom up : The last line names the error type and the problem. The lines above show where it happened; the arrow points to the line in your cell. Normally an error stops the cell. So that this page runs without stopping, the next cells catch each error and print its last line, which is exactly the line you would read first. try : cafe [ "Cups" ] . mean () # capital C except KeyError as error : print ( "KeyError:" , error ) print ( "The real column names are:" , list ( cafe . columns )) KeyError: 'Cups' The real column names are: ['date', 'weekday', 'weekend', 'temp_c', 'drink', 'cups', 'price', 'revenue', 'weather'] try : "Revenue: " + 250 except TypeError as error : print ( "TypeError:" , error ) print ( "Fixed:" , "Revenue: " + str ( 250 )) TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str Fixed: Revenue: 250 try : pd . read_csv ( "data/penguin.csv" ) # missing an 's' except FileNotFoundError as error : print ( "FileNotFoundError:" , error ) FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'data/penguin.csv' Error (last line) Usual cause Fix NameError: name 'x' is not defined The cell that creates x has not run in this session Run the earlier cells, or restart and run all KeyError: 'Cups' A column or key spelled differently; capitals count Check df.columns and copy the exact name TypeError: can only concatenate str … Mixing text and numbers Convert with str() , int() or float() SyntaxError A missing bracket, quote or comma Look at the line the caret ^ points to FileNotFoundError Wrong file name, or the notebook is not next to data Check the spelling; save the notebook in DATA300_GAP ModuleNotFoundError The package is not installed in this session Route A: run the %pip install cell. Route B: tell your facilitator Warnings are not errors A pink box that starts with FutureWarning or UserWarning is advice, and the cell still ran. Read it, but do not panic.

docs.text: The kernel remembers what ran , not what is written. Restart and run all before exporting. Types matter: text that looks like a number is still text; decimals need rounding for display. docs.text:
Day 1 lecture: Exploring data ¶ Periods 4 to 6 of Day 1, and the bridge to Lab 1. A routine for meeting a new dataset: structure and quality checks, missing values and what to do about them, distributions and skew, pivot tables and grouped summaries, correlation and its limits, confounding and Simpson's paradox, and charts that still work with tens of thousands of points. Run each code cell with Shift + Enter , in order. The examples use the mpg car data, a real university admissions table and synthetic data. Lab 1 uses the diamonds data; this lecture deliberately does not , so that you practise each skill here and apply it yourself in the lab. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder; everything loads from data/ . Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook and data/mpg.csv , run %pip install seaborn in a first cell, and change "data/mpg.csv" to "mpg.csv" in Part 2. What you will be able to do ¶ Run a fixed exploration routine on any new table and report what you find. Find missing, duplicated and impossible values, and explain why the reason for missingness matters. Describe a distribution by its centre, spread and shape , and say when the median is the better summary. Build and read pivot tables , always with the counts behind each cell. Read a correlation matrix and explain five ways a correlation can mislead. Recognise confounding and Simpson's paradox , and make a fairer comparison. Choose a chart that still works when points overlap ( over-plotting ). Part Topic Period 1 The exploration routine P4 2 Structure, data quality and missing values P4 3 Distributions and skew P4–P5 4 Pivot tables and grouped summaries P5 5 Correlation and its limits P5 6 Confounding and Simpson's paradox P6 7 Over-plotting and its fixes P6 8 Lab 1 briefing P6 9 Business case, practice, quiz and summary Self-study Reading Read Chapter 1 of the course reading packet, Section 1.5 especially, for what describe() , isnull().sum() , groupby() and corr() each reveal and the two easy mistakes with corr() . This lecture adds distributions, missingness, Simpson's paradox and over-plotting. Part 1: The exploration routine ¶ This morning ended with a rule: summarise and plot . This afternoon turns it into a routine you can run on any table, in this order. Each step answers a question the next step depends on. Step Question Code 1 What is one row? (the grain ) Read the source; head() 2 How big is it? shape 3 What type is each column? info() , dtypes 4 What is missing? isnull().sum() 5 Anything duplicated or impossible? duplicated().sum() , describe() min and max 6 What do the categories look like? value_counts() 7 How is each number distributed? describe() , histogram, box or violin plot 8 How do groups compare? groupby , pivot_table , with counts 9 How do numbers move together? corr() , heatmap, scatter or hexbin 10 What else could explain it? Split by a third variable Steps 1–6 are about trust : can these numbers be used at all? Steps 7–10 are about patterns . Skipping the first half is how good charts of bad data get made. Part 2: Structure, data quality and missing values ¶ The mpg data describes 398 car models sold in the 1970s and early 1980s: fuel economy in miles per US gallon, engine size, power, weight in pounds, acceleration, model year and region of origin. One row is one car model in one model year . (Day 5's Lab 5 builds a regression on it; today we only explore.) import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns cars = pd . read_csv ( "data/mpg.csv" ) # Route A: "mpg.csv" print ( "Rows, columns:" , cars . shape ) cars . head () Rows, columns: (398, 9) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mpg cylinders displacement horsepower weight acceleration model_year origin name 0 18.0 8 307.0 130.0 3504 12.0 70 usa chevrolet chevelle malibu 1 15.0 8 350.0 165.0 3693 11.5 70 usa buick skylark 320 2 18.0 8 318.0 150.0 3436 11.0 70 usa plymouth satellite 3 16.0 8 304.0 150.0 3433 12.0 70 usa amc rebel sst 4 17.0 8 302.0 140.0 3449 10.5 70 usa ford torino cars . info () <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> RangeIndex: 398 entries, 0 to 397 Data columns (total 9 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 mpg 398 non-null float64 1 cylinders 398 non-null int64 2 displacement 398 non-null float64 3 horsepower 392 non-null float64 4 weight 398 non-null int64 5 acceleration 398 non-null float64 6 model_year 398 non-null int64 7 origin 398 non-null object 8 name 398 non-null object dtypes: float64(4), int64(3), object(2) memory usage: 28.1+ KB info() gives three things at once: the column types , the non-null count per column, and the memory used. Compare each non-null count with the number of rows: any column with fewer has missing values. Predict, then run From the info() output alone, which column has missing values, and how many? Write your answer, then check it with the next cell. print ( "Missing values per column:" ) print ( cars . isnull () . sum ()) print ( " 
 Fully duplicated rows:" , cars . duplicated () . sum ()) Missing values per column: mpg 0 cylinders 0 displacement 0 horsepower 6 weight 0 acceleration 0 model_year 0 origin 0 name 0 dtype: int64 Fully duplicated rows: 0 cars [ cars [ "horsepower" ] . isnull ()][[ "name" , "model_year" , "cylinders" , "weight" , "horsepower" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } name model_year cylinders weight horsepower 32 ford pinto 71 4 2046 NaN 126 ford maverick 74 6 2875 NaN 330 renault lecar deluxe 80 4 1835 NaN 336 ford mustang cobra 80 4 2905 NaN 354 renault 18i 81 4 2320 NaN 374 amc concord dl 82 4 3035 NaN Looking at the missing rows themselves, not just the count, is a habit worth keeping: here they are ordinary cars from several years, which suggests the values were simply not recorded, not that some kind of car is missing. Validity: ranges and codes ¶ cars . describe () . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mpg cylinders displacement horsepower weight acceleration model_year count 398.0 398.0 398.0 392.0 398.0 398.0 398.0 mean 23.5 5.5 193.4 104.5 2970.4 15.6 76.0 std 7.8 1.7 104.3 38.5 846.8 2.8 3.7 min 9.0 3.0 68.0 46.0 1613.0 8.0 70.0 25% 17.5 4.0 104.2 75.0 2223.8 13.8 73.0 50% 23.0 4.0 148.5 93.5 2803.5 15.5 76.0 75% 29.0 8.0 262.0 126.0 3608.0 17.2 79.0 max 46.6 8.0 455.0 230.0 5140.0 24.8 82.0 print ( cars [ "origin" ] . value_counts ()) print () print ( cars [ "cylinders" ] . value_counts () . sort_index ()) origin usa 249 japan 79 europe 70 Name: count, dtype: int64 cylinders 3 4 4 204 5 3 6 84 8 103 Name: count, dtype: int64 Check your understanding model_year runs from 70 to 82. What does a value of 76 mean, and why is this a validity and consistency risk if this table were joined to one that stores years as 1976? Only a handful of cars have 3 or 5 cylinders. What does that mean for any average calculated for those groups? Why the reason for missingness matters ¶ What you may do with a missing value depends on why it is missing. Kind Meaning Business example Is dropping the rows safe? Missing completely at random Missingness has nothing to do with any value A till lost records on random days because of a power cut Usually: you lose rows, not truth Missing at random (given other columns) Missingness depends on something you have recorded Older stores do not record loyalty IDs; store age is in the data Only if you compare within groups of that column Missing not at random Missingness depends on the missing value itself High earners skip the income question; unhappy customers skip the survey No: the remaining rows are biased The next cell simulates the third kind: a salary survey of 2,000 employees where the higher someone's salary, the more likely they leave the question blank. Salaries are in neutral currency units per month. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 1012 ) true_salary = rng . lognormal ( np . log ( 9000 ), 0.4 , 2000 ) . round ( - 1 ) skip_chance = np . clip (( true_salary - 6000 ) / 20000 , 0.02 , 0.9 ) # richer people skip more often answered = rng . random ( 2000 ) > skip_chance survey = pd . DataFrame ({ "salary" : np . where ( answered , true_salary , np . nan )}) print ( f "Answered: { answered . sum () } of 2000" ) print ( f "True mean salary (known only in a simulation): { true_salary . mean () : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Mean of the answers that were given: { survey [ 'salary' ] . mean () : ,.0f } " ) filled = survey [ "salary" ] . fillna ( survey [ "salary" ] . mean ()) print ( f " 
 Standard deviation of the answers: { survey [ 'salary' ] . std () : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Standard deviation after filling with the mean: { filled . std () : ,.0f } " ) Answered: 1622 of 2000 True mean salary (known only in a simulation): 9,718 Mean of the answers that were given: 8,820 Standard deviation of the answers: 3,170 Standard deviation after filling with the mean: 2,854 Two lessons: When missingness depends on the value, the observed mean is biased , and no amount of data fixes it. Only a better collection method does (for example, salary bands instead of an exact figure). Filling gaps with the mean ( mean imputation ) keeps the row count but shrinks the spread , because hundreds of identical values are added in the middle. It also keeps the bias. Use it only when few values are missing, and say that you did. Misconception: "no missing values means the data is complete" A column can have no NaN and still be incomplete: a missing measurement is sometimes stored as 0, −1, 999 or an empty string. Always read the min and max in describe() and ask whether each extreme value is physically possible. Part 3: Distributions and skew ¶ A distribution is how the values of one column are spread out. Describe it with three words: Aspect Measures Question Centre Mean, median, mode What is a typical value? Spread Standard deviation, interquartile range (IQR), range How different are the values from each other? Shape Skewness, number of peaks, tails, gaps Is it symmetric? Is it really one group? Right skew (positive skew) means a long tail of large values: most values are modest, a few are very large. Money is almost always right-skewed: incomes, house prices, order values, claims. In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled toward the tail, so mean > median . The next cell generates 5,000 online orders for an imaginary home-goods shop, in currency units. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) shop = pd . Intuitively, it averages, over all rows, "how far above or below its mean is x, times how far above or below its mean is y", after putting both on the same scale. |r| Usual reading below 0.3 weak 0.3 to 0.7 moderate above 0.7 strong These cut-offs are conventions, not laws: in some fields an r of 0.3 is valuable. numeric = cars . select_dtypes ( include = "number" ) corr_matrix = numeric . corr () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 )) sns . heatmap ( corr_matrix , annot = True , fmt = ".2f" , cmap = "RdBu_r" , vmin =- 1 , vmax = 1 , linewidths = 0.5 , cbar_kws = { "label" : "Correlation coefficient r" }, ax = ax ) ax . set_title ( "Correlations between the numeric columns of the mpg data" ) plt . show () How to read a correlation heatmap: The diagonal is always 1: each column with itself. Misconception: "correlation means causation" (and its opposite) A correlation is a description of how two columns moved together in this data. It can arise from a cause, a reverse cause, a third factor, selection, a shared trend or chance. The opposite mistake is just as common: " r is near 0, so there is no relationship" (panel 1). Part 6: Confounding and Simpson's paradox ¶ A confounder is a third variable that affects both the thing you compare by and the thing you measure , so that the comparison mixes two effects. Written as arrows: Z → X and Z → Y. Comparing Y across X then shows partly the effect of Z. In Part 4, US cars had lower average mpg and far more 8-cylinder engines. Is "US-made" the reason for lower fuel economy, or is engine size? Engine size is a candidate confounder: it differs between regions and it affects fuel use. Simpson's paradox: a real case ¶ The most famous example comes from graduate admissions at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1973. The table below is the widely published version for the six largest departments (Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell, 1975). admissions = pd . DataFrame ({ "department" : list ( "AABBCCDDEEFF" ), "gender" : [ "Men" , "Women" ] * 6 , "applicants" : [ 825 , 108 , 560 , 25 , 325 , 593 , 417 , 375 , 191 , 393 , 373 , 341 ], "admitted" : [ 512 , 89 , 353 , 17 , 120 , 202 , 138 , 131 , 53 , 94 , 22 , 24 ], }) overall = admissions . groupby ( "gender" )[[ "applicants" , "admitted" ]] . sum () overall [ "admitted (%)" ] = ( 100 * overall [ "admitted" ] / overall [ "applicants" ]) . round ( 1 ) print ( "All six departments together" ) print ( overall ) All six departments together applicants admitted admitted (%) gender Men 2691 1198 44.5 Women 1835 557 30.4 Predict, then run Overall, men were admitted at a clearly higher rate. Predict: in how many of the six departments will men have the higher admission rate? admissions [ "admitted (%)" ] = ( 100 * admissions [ "admitted" ] / admissions [ "applicants" ]) . round ( 1 ) by_dept = admissions . pivot_table ( index = "department" , columns = "gender" , values = [ "admitted (%)" , "applicants" ]) by_dept .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead tr th { text-align: left; } .dataframe thead tr:last-of-type th { text-align: right; } admitted (%) applicants gender Men Women Men Women department A 62.1 82.4 825.0 108.0 B 63.0 68.0 560.0 25.0 C 36.9 34.1 325.0 593.0 D 33.1 34.9 417.0 375.0 E 27.7 23.9 191.0 393.0 F 5.9 7.0 373.0 341.0 In most departments women were admitted at a rate similar to or higher than men, yet overall they were admitted less often. Look at the applicant counts: most women applied to departments C–F, which admitted few applicants of either gender; most men applied to A and B, which admitted most applicants. The department is the confounder: it affects both who applied (gender mix) and the chance of admission. Simpson's paradox is the name for a trend that appears in every group, or most groups, and reverses (or disappears) when the groups are combined. It happens when the groups differ in size and in their baseline rate. A business version, and a fairer comparison ¶ Two support teams resolve customer tickets. Team North handles many hard tickets (technical faults); Team South mostly easy ones (password resets). Synthetic numbers: tickets = pd . DataFrame ({ "team" : [ "North" , "North" , "South" , "South" ], "ticket_type" : [ "Easy" , "Hard" , "Easy" , "Hard" ], "tickets" : [ 300 , 700 , 900 , 100 ], "resolved_first_time" : [ 282 , 420 , 801 , 52 ], }) tickets [ "rate (%)" ] = ( 100 * tickets [ "resolved_first_time" ] / tickets [ "tickets" ]) . round ( 1 ) print ( tickets . pivot_table ( index = "team" , columns = "ticket_type" , values = "rate (%)" )) team_total = tickets . groupby ( "team" )[[ "tickets" , "resolved_first_time" ]] . sum () team_total [ "rate (%)" ] = ( 100 * team_total [ "resolved_first_time" ] / team_total [ "tickets" ]) . round ( 1 ) print () print ( team_total ) ticket_type Easy Hard team North 94.0 60.0 South 89.0 52.0 tickets resolved_first_time rate (%) team North 1000 702 70.2 South 1000 853 85.3 North is better at both kinds of ticket and worse overall, because it carries most of the hard work. A manager who ranked teams on the overall rate would reward the wrong team. The fix is to compare like with like. Standardisation applies one common ticket mix to both teams' rates, so the mix no longer differs: common_mix = tickets . groupby ( "ticket_type" )[ "tickets" ] . sum () / tickets [ "tickets" ] . sum () print ( "Common mix:" , ( common_mix * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) . to_dict (), "( % o f all tickets)" ) rates = tickets . pivot_table ( index = "team" , columns = "ticket_type" , values = "rate (%)" ) standardised = ( rates * common_mix ) . sum ( axis = 1 ) . round ( 1 ) print ( " 
 First-time resolution (%) if both teams had the same ticket mix:" ) print ( standardised ) Common mix: {'Easy': 60.0, 'Hard': 40.0} (% of all tickets) First-time resolution (%) if both teams had the same ticket mix: team North 80.4 South 74.2 dtype: float64 How to look for confounding ¶ Ask: what else differs between the groups I am comparing? (Size, mix, location, time, who chose to be in them.) Split by that variable (pivot with it as a second dimension) and compare within each level. Show the counts , so you see where each group's weight lies. If the groups differ in mix, standardise or compare like with like. Remember that you can only split by confounders you have recorded . The strongest protection is a designed comparison, such as a randomised trial. Misconception: "with enough data, the confounding goes away" Berkeley had over 4,500 applicants. More rows make each rate more precise, but they make a confounded comparison precisely wrong. Only splitting, standardising or a better design helps. Part 9: Business case, practice, quiz and summary ¶ Business case for discussion: the hospital league table ¶ A health authority publishes a league table of hospitals ranked by the share of patients who die within 30 days of surgery. Hospital R, a large regional centre, ranks near the bottom; several small local hospitals rank near the top. A newspaper calls Hospital R "the most dangerous in the region". Discuss in groups (15 minutes): Large regional centres often receive the most complex cases, referred from smaller hospitals. Draw the confounding arrows (Z → X, Z → Y). What is Z? What table would you ask for before agreeing with the newspaper? Name its rows, columns and the counts you would want to see. A small hospital performed 40 operations and had no deaths. How confident can anyone be that its true rate is 0%? Which part of today's lecture warned about this? Some hospitals transfer their sickest patients elsewhere before day 30. Which data quality dimension, and which framing element (Part 4 of the morning lecture), does that affect? Propose a fairer league table, in one paragraph. Practice ¶ Core ¶ Core 1. Run the cell below. Which origin has the heaviest cars on average? Add a line for the median weight. Are mean and median close for each region? What does that say about skew? cars . groupby ( "origin" ) . agg ( car_models = ( "weight" , "size" ), mean_weight_lb = ( "weight" , "mean" )) . round ( 0 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } car_models mean_weight_lb origin europe 70 2423.0 japan 79 2221.0 usa 249 3362.0 Core 2. Draw a histogram of mpg with 30 bins, a title and labelled axes (with units). Describe its centre, spread and shape in three sentences, and say whether you would report the mean or the median. Core 3. In the survey data from Part 2, how many values are missing? Explain to a manager, in two sentences and without the word "MNAR", why the average of the answers is too low. Stretch ¶ Stretch 1. Is the region gap in mpg confounded by weight? Create weight bands with pd.cut(cars["weight"], bins=[0, 2500, 3000, 3500, 6000]) and build a pivot table of mean mpg by origin (rows) and weight band (columns), with a count table . Does the US gap shrink within bands? Where are the empty or tiny cells, and what do they mean? Stretch 2. In the taxi data, redraw the hexbin without bins="log" . What happens to the airport cluster? When would you choose each version? Stretch 3. In the ticket example, change Team North's hard-ticket count to 400 (and its resolved count to 240). Does the paradox remain? Explain using the mix. Challenge ¶ Challenge 1. Using the penguins data ( data/penguins.csv ), compute the correlation between flipper_length_mm and bill_depth_mm for all penguins, then within each species. Explain the difference using the word confounder , and draw the chart that shows it. Challenge 2. Write a function explore(df) that prints the routine's steps 2–6 for any DataFrame: shape, types, missing values per column, duplicated rows, and the value_counts() of every text column. Test it on cars and on signups -style messy data you make yourself. Quiz ¶ List the first six steps of the exploration routine. Why do they come before any chart? A column has no missing values but its minimum is −999. What might that mean, and what do you check? In a right-skewed distribution, which is larger, the mean or the median? Name two business variables that are usually right-skewed. What does the "All" margin of a pivot table weight by, and why does an average of group averages differ from it? r = 0.05 between temperature and complaints. Can you conclude there is no relationship? Why or why not? Define Simpson's paradox in one sentence and give the Berkeley confounder. Name three fixes for over-plotting and one risk of each. On a hexbin plot, what does the darkest hexagon tell you? Quick reference ¶ You want to… Code Size, types and non-null counts df.shape , df.info() Missing values per column df.isnull().sum() Duplicated rows df.duplicated().sum() Summary of numeric columns df.describe() Counts of each category df["col"].value_counts() Skewness df["col"].skew() Pivot table, with counts pd.pivot_table(df, index=..., columns=..., values=..., aggfunc="mean") , then aggfunc="count" Several summaries per group df.groupby("g").agg(name=("col", "mean"), ...) Shares within each row pd.crosstab(df["a"], df["b"], normalize="index") Correlation matrix and heatmap df.select_dtypes(include="number").corr() , sns.heatmap(..., vmin=-1, vmax=1) Rank correlation df["x"].corr(df["y"], method="spearman") Violin plot sns.violinplot(data=df, x="group", y="value", cut=0) Hexbin plt.hexbin(x, y, gridsize=40, mincnt=1) Summary ¶ Idea Remember Routine Trust first (grain, size, types, missing, duplicates, codes), then patterns Missing values Ask why they are missing; dropping or filling can bias results Distributions Centre, spread, shape; for skewed money data, report the median too Pivot tables Always show the counts; beware averages of averages; set the category order Correlation Straight lines only; sensitive to outliers, selection and trends; not a slope, not a cause Confounding Ask what else differs; split, show counts, standardise Over-plotting Transparency, sampling, hexbin, jitter, panels Reference: Bickel, P. docs.title: What you will be able to do

docs.text: This morning ended with a rule: summarise and plot . This afternoon turns it into a routine you can run on any table, in this order. Each step answers a question the next step depends on. Step Question Code 1 What is one row? (the grain ) Read the source; head() 2 How big is it? shape 3 What type is each column? info() , dtypes 4 What is missing? isnull().sum() 5 Anything duplicated or impossible? duplicated().sum() , describe() min and max 6 What do the categories look like? value_counts() 7 How is each number distributed? describe() , histogram, box or violin plot 8 How do groups compare? groupby , pivot_table , with counts 9 How do numbers move together? corr() , heatmap, scatter or hexbin 10 What else could explain it? Split by a third variable Steps 1–6 are about trust : can these numbers be used at all? Steps 7–10 are about patterns . Skipping the first half is how good charts of bad data get made.
docs.title: Part 1: The exploration routine

docs.text: The mpg data describes 398 car models sold in the 1970s and early 1980s: fuel economy in miles per US gallon, engine size, power, weight in pounds, acceleration, model year and region of origin. One row is one car model in one model year . (Day 5's Lab 5 builds a regression on it; today we only explore.) import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import seaborn as sns cars = pd . read_csv ( "data/mpg.csv" ) # Route A: "mpg.csv" print ( "Rows, columns:" , cars . shape ) cars . head () Rows, columns: (398, 9) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } mpg cylinders displacement horsepower weight acceleration model_year origin name 0 18.0 8 307.0 130.0 3504 12.0 70 usa chevrolet chevelle malibu 1 15.0 8 350.0 165.0 3693 11.5 70 usa buick skylark 320 2 18.0 8 318.0 150.0 3436 11.0 70 usa plymouth satellite 3 16.0 8 304.0 150.0 3433 12.0 70 usa amc rebel sst 4 17.0 8 302.0 140.0 3449 10.5 70 usa ford torino cars . info () <class 'pandas.core.frame.DataFrame'> RangeIndex: 398 entries, 0 to 397 Data columns (total 9 columns): # Column Non-Null Count Dtype --- ------ -------------- ----- 0 mpg 398 non-null float64 1 cylinders 398 non-null int64 2 displacement 398 non-null float64 3 horsepower 392 non-null float64 4 weight 398 non-null int64 5 acceleration 398 non-null float64 6 model_year 398 non-null int64 7 origin 398 non-null object 8 name 398 non-null object dtypes: float64(4), int64(3), object(2) memory usage: 28.1+ KB info() gives three things at once: the column types , the non-null count per column, and the memory used. Compare each non-null count with the number of rows: any column with fewer has missing values. Predict, then run From the info() output alone, which column has missing values, and how many? Write your answer, then check it with the next cell. print ( "Missing values per column:" ) print ( cars . isnull () . sum ()) print ( " \n Fully duplicated rows:" , cars . duplicated () . sum ()) Missing values per column: mpg 0 cylinders 0 displacement 0 horsepower 6 weight 0 acceleration 0 model_year 0 origin 0 name 0 dtype: int64 Fully duplicated rows: 0 cars [ cars [ "horsepower" ] . isnull ()][[ "name" , "model_year" , "cylinders" , "weight" , "horsepower" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } name model_year cylinders weight horsepower 32 ford pinto 71 4 2046 NaN 126 ford maverick 74 6 2875 NaN 330 renault lecar deluxe 80 4 1835 NaN 336 ford mustang cobra 80 4 2905 NaN 354 renault 18i 81 4 2320 NaN 374 amc concord dl 82 4 3035 NaN Looking at the missing rows themselves, not just the count, is a habit worth keeping: here they are ordinary cars from several years, which suggests the values were simply not recorded, not that some kind of car is missing.

docs.title: Validity: ranges and codes

docs.text: What you may do with a missing value depends on why it is missing. Kind Meaning Business example Is dropping the rows safe? Missing completely at random Missingness has nothing to do with any value A till lost records on random days because of a power cut Usually: you lose rows, not truth Missing at random (given other columns) Missingness depends on something you have recorded Older stores do not record loyalty IDs; store age is in the data Only if you compare within groups of that column Missing not at random Missingness depends on the missing value itself High earners skip the income question; unhappy customers skip the survey No: the remaining rows are biased The next cell simulates the third kind: a salary survey of 2,000 employees where the higher someone's salary, the more likely they leave the question blank. Salaries are in neutral currency units per month. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 1012 ) true_salary = rng . lognormal ( np . log ( 9000 ), 0.4 , 2000 ) . round ( - 1 ) skip_chance = np . clip (( true_salary - 6000 ) / 20000 , 0.02 , 0.9 ) # richer people skip more often answered = rng . random ( 2000 ) > skip_chance survey = pd . DataFrame ({ "salary" : np . where ( answered , true_salary , np . nan )}) print ( f "Answered: { answered . sum () } of 2000" ) print ( f "True mean salary (known only in a simulation): { true_salary . mean () : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Mean of the answers that were given: { survey [ 'salary' ] . mean () : ,.0f } " ) filled = survey [ "salary" ] . fillna ( survey [ "salary" ] . mean ()) print ( f " \n Standard deviation of the answers: { survey [ 'salary' ] . std () : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "Standard deviation after filling with the mean: { filled . std () : ,.0f } " ) Answered: 1622 of 2000 True mean salary (known only in a simulation): 9,718 Mean of the answers that were given: 8,820 Standard deviation of the answers: 3,170 Standard deviation after filling with the mean: 2,854 Two lessons: When missingness depends on the value, the observed mean is biased , and no amount of data fixes it. Only a better collection method does (for example, salary bands instead of an exact figure). Filling gaps with the mean ( mean imputation ) keeps the row count but shrinks the spread , because hundreds of identical values are added in the middle. It also keeps the bias. Use it only when few values are missing, and say that you did. Misconception: "no missing values means the data is complete" A column can have no NaN and still be incomplete: a missing measurement is sometimes stored as 0, −1, 999 or an empty string. Always read the min and max in describe() and ask whether each extreme value is physically possible.
docs.title: Why the reason for missingness matters

docs.text: A distribution is how the values of one column are spread out. Describe it with three words: Aspect Measures Question Centre Mean, median, mode What is a typical value? Spread Standard deviation, interquartile range (IQR), range How different are the values from each other? Shape Skewness, number of peaks, tails, gaps Is it symmetric? Is it really one group? Right skew (positive skew) means a long tail of large values: most values are modest, a few are very large. Money is almost always right-skewed: incomes, house prices, order values, claims. In a right-skewed distribution the mean is pulled toward the tail, so mean > median . The next cell generates 5,000 online orders for an imaginary home-goods shop, in currency units. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) shop = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_value" : rng . lognormal ( np . log ( 60 ), 0.75 , 5000 ) . round ( 2 )}) value = shop [ "order_value" ] print ( f "Mean: { value . mean () : 8.2f } " ) print ( f "Median: { value . median () : 8.2f } " ) print ( f "Skewness: { value . skew () : 8.2f } (0 = symmetric; above 1 = strongly right-skewed)" ) print ( f "Share of orders below the mean: { ( value < value . mean ()) . mean () * 100 : .0f } %" ) Mean: 79.05 Median: 60.80 Skewness: 3.09 (0 = symmetric; above 1 = strongly right-skewed) Share of orders below the mean: 64% Predict, then run The mean is called the "average order". What share of customers actually spent less than it? Check the last line above. Would you report the mean or the median to a manager asking "what does a typical customer spend?" fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) ax . hist ( value , bins = 60 , color = "#2a78d6" , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . axvline ( value . median (), color = "#eb6834" , linewidth = 2 , label = f "Median { value . median () : .0f } " ) ax . axvline ( value . mean (), color = "#1baf7a" , linewidth = 2 , linestyle = "--" , label = f "Mean { value . mean () : .0f } " ) ax . set_title ( "Most orders are modest; a long right tail pulls the mean above the median" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Order value (currency units)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of orders" ) ax . legend () plt . show ()
docs.title: Part 3: Distributions and skew

docs.text: Predict, then run The next cell draws the same data with 6 bins and with 150 bins. Which one will look smoother? Which one could hide a second peak? fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.8 ), sharey = False ) for ax , bins in zip ( axes , [ 6 , 150 ]): ax . hist ( value , bins = bins , color = "#2a78d6" , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . set_title ( f " { bins } bins" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Order value (currency units)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Number of orders" ) fig . suptitle ( "Same data, different bins: too few hide detail, too many show noise" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show ()
docs.title: The number of bins changes the story

docs.text: On a log scale each step is a multiplication (10, 100, 1,000), so a right-skewed variable often looks symmetric. A box plot shows the median (line), the middle half of the data (the box, from the 25th to the 75th percentile: the IQR), whiskers to the furthest points within 1.5 IQR, and dots beyond that. q1 , q3 = value . quantile ([ 0.25 , 0.75 ]) iqr = q3 - q1 upper_fence = q3 + 1.5 * iqr print ( f "IQR: { iqr : .2f } | upper fence: { upper_fence : .2f } | orders beyond it: { ( value > upper_fence ) . sum () } " ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.8 )) axes [ 0 ] . hist ( value , bins = np . logspace ( np . log10 ( value . min ()), np . log10 ( value . max ()), 50 ), color = "#2a78d6" , edgecolor = "white" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xscale ( "log" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Log scale: the skewed data looks roughly symmetric" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "Order value (currency units, log scale)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Number of orders" ) sns . boxplot ( x = value , color = "#9cc3ef" , width = 0.5 , ax = axes [ 1 ]) # a horizontal box plot axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Box plot: the dots are orders beyond 1.5 IQR" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Order value (currency units)" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () IQR: 64.13 | upper fence: 195.80 | orders beyond it: 278 Misconception: "the dots on a box plot are errors to delete" In skewed data, points beyond the whisker are expected: here they are the shop's biggest customers. A value is an error only if it is impossible (a negative price, a weight of 0). A value that is merely unusual is information.
docs.title: Two remedies for skew: a log scale, and the box plot

docs.text: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.8 )) ax . hist ( cars [ "displacement" ], bins = 40 , color = "#2a78d6" , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . set_title ( "Engine size has several peaks: the cars are not one group" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Engine displacement (cubic inches)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of car models" ) plt . show () Predict, then run Which column in cars do you think explains the separate peaks? Make a guess, then run the next cell, which draws one violin per number of cylinders. A violin plot is a box plot's richer cousin: its width at each height shows how many values sit there, so it shows several peaks and long tails that a box hides. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) sns . violinplot ( data = cars , x = "cylinders" , y = "displacement" , color = "#9cc3ef" , cut = 0 , ax = ax ) counts = cars [ "cylinders" ] . value_counts () . sort_index () ax . set_xticks ( range ( len ( counts ))) ax . set_xticklabels ([ f " { c } \n (n= { n } )" for c , n in counts . items ()]) ax . set_title ( "Each cylinder count has its own range of engine sizes" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Number of cylinders (number of car models)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Engine displacement (cubic inches)" ) plt . show () Writing the count under each violin matters: a violin drawn from four cars looks as confident as one drawn from two hundred. Software note: violins and colour Here every violin has one colour ( color= ). To give each category its own colour, newer seaborn (0.13 and later) uses hue= set to the same column plus legend=False . Older versions ignore legend=False and draw thin, shifted violins. The Lab 1 guide's pitfalls table explains the fix.
docs.title: More than one peak usually means more than one group

docs.text: A pivot table puts one category down the side, another across the top, and a summary of a number in each cell. It is the workhorse of descriptive and diagnostic analytics, in Python, Excel and Tableau alike. Predict, then run Before running: will European, Japanese or US cars have the highest average mpg? And among 4-cylinder cars only? mpg_pivot = pd . pivot_table ( cars , index = "origin" , columns = "cylinders" , values = "mpg" , aggfunc = "mean" ) count_pivot = pd . pivot_table ( cars , index = "origin" , columns = "cylinders" , values = "mpg" , aggfunc = "count" ) print ( "Average mpg by origin and cylinders (NaN = no such cars)" ) print ( mpg_pivot . round ( 1 )) print ( " \n Number of car models behind each average" ) print ( count_pivot . fillna ( 0 ) . astype ( int )) Average mpg by origin and cylinders (NaN = no such cars) cylinders 3 4 5 6 8 origin europe NaN 28.4 27.4 20.1 NaN japan 20.6 31.6 NaN 23.9 NaN usa NaN 27.8 NaN 19.7 15.0 Number of car models behind each average cylinders 3 4 5 6 8 origin europe 0 63 3 4 0 japan 4 69 0 6 0 usa 0 72 0 74 103 Read the count table first. Several cells are empty ( NaN ) because the combination does not exist in this data: no US car here has 3 or 5 cylinders, and only US cars have 8. Other cells rest on three or four cars and should not be compared with cells resting on a hundred.
docs.title: Part 4: Pivot tables and grouped summaries

docs.text: margins=True adds an "All" row and column. Those margins are calculated from the rows , so they are weighted by how many cars each group has. Averaging the cell averages instead gives a different, usually wrong, number. with_margins = pd . pivot_table ( cars , index = "origin" , values = "mpg" , aggfunc = [ "mean" , "count" ], margins = True ) print ( with_margins . round ( 2 )) region_means = cars . groupby ( "origin" )[ "mpg" ] . mean () print ( f " \n Mean of all cars: { cars [ 'mpg' ] . mean () : .2f } " ) print ( f "Average of the three region averages: { region_means . mean () : .2f } " ) mean count mpg mpg origin europe 27.89 70 japan 30.45 79 usa 20.08 249 All 23.51 398 Mean of all cars: 23.51 Average of the three region averages: 26.14 Check your understanding Why is the average of the three region averages higher than the mean of all cars? (Hint: look at the counts.) Which number answers "what was the average fuel economy of a car model on sale"?
docs.title: Margins, and the average-of-averages trap

docs.text: groupby().agg() gives the same numbers as a one-way pivot, with several summaries side by side. crosstab(..., normalize="index") turns counts into shares of each row , which is how you compare groups of different sizes. cars . groupby ( "origin" ) . agg ( car_models = ( "mpg" , "size" ), mean_mpg = ( "mpg" , "mean" ), median_mpg = ( "mpg" , "median" ), mean_weight_lb = ( "weight" , "mean" ), ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } car_models mean_mpg median_mpg mean_weight_lb origin europe 70 27.9 26.5 2423.3 japan 79 30.5 31.6 2221.2 usa 249 20.1 18.5 3361.9 ( pd . crosstab ( cars [ "origin" ], cars [ "cylinders" ], normalize = "index" ) * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } cylinders 3 4 5 6 8 origin europe 0.0 90.0 4.3 5.7 0.0 japan 5.1 87.3 0.0 7.6 0.0 usa 0.0 28.9 0.0 29.7 41.4 Predict, then run In the share table, about what share of US car models had 8 cylinders, and of Japanese models? Keep this in mind for Part 6: if 8-cylinder cars use more fuel, how could that alone affect the region comparison?
docs.title: The same summary with groupby, and shares with crosstab

docs.text: Pivot tables sort text categories alphabetically , which is rarely the order a reader expects ("Average", "Good", "Poor" instead of Poor → Average → Good). Fix it with reindex on the result, or by making the column an ordered category before you pivot. cars [ "era" ] = pd . cut ( cars [ "model_year" ], bins = [ 69 , 73 , 77 , 82 ], labels = [ "1970-73" , "1974-77" , "1978-82" ]) era_order = [ "1978-82" , "1974-77" , "1970-73" ] # newest first, chosen on purpose pd . pivot_table ( cars , index = "era" , columns = "origin" , values = "mpg" , aggfunc = "mean" , observed = True ) . reindex ( era_order ) . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } origin europe japan usa era 1978-82 32.5 33.5 25.3 1974-77 25.8 28.1 19.0 1970-73 24.7 24.7 16.0
docs.title: Ordering categories

docs.text: The Pearson correlation coefficient r measures how closely two numbers follow a straight line together. It runs from −1 (perfect downward line) through 0 (no straight-line pattern) to +1 (perfect upward line). Intuitively, it averages, over all rows, "how far above or below its mean is x, times how far above or below its mean is y", after putting both on the same scale. |r| Usual reading below 0.3 weak 0.3 to 0.7 moderate above 0.7 strong These cut-offs are conventions, not laws: in some fields an r of 0.3 is valuable. numeric = cars . select_dtypes ( include = "number" ) corr_matrix = numeric . corr () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 6.5 )) sns . heatmap ( corr_matrix , annot = True , fmt = ".2f" , cmap = "RdBu_r" , vmin =- 1 , vmax = 1 , linewidths = 0.5 , cbar_kws = { "label" : "Correlation coefficient r" }, ax = ax ) ax . set_title ( "Correlations between the numeric columns of the mpg data" ) plt . show () How to read a correlation heatmap: The diagonal is always 1: each column with itself. The matrix is symmetric, so read only one triangle. Fix the colour scale at −1 to +1 ( vmin , vmax ), with a diverging palette centred on 0, so that colours mean the same thing on every chart. Look for blocks : here cylinders, displacement, horsepower and weight are all strongly related to each other. They largely measure one thing, "how big the car is". Day 4 calls this multicollinearity . origin and name are not in the matrix: they are text. A categorical column can matter a great deal and still never appear in corr() . Use groupby for it. Check your understanding Which pair of different columns has the strongest correlation in this matrix? Is it positive or negative, and what does that mean in words?
docs.title: Part 5: Correlation and its limits

docs.text: The next cell builds four small synthetic datasets, each designed to break the naive reading of r . rng = np . random . default_rng ( 55 ) n = 200 # 1. A strong curved relationship: temperature and comfort complaints temp = rng . uniform ( 10 , 34 , n ) complaints = ( temp - 22 ) ** 2 / 6 + rng . normal ( 0 , 1.5 , n ) # 2. No relationship, plus one extreme point x_noise = rng . normal ( 50 , 10 , n ) y_noise = rng . normal ( 50 , 10 , n ) x_out = np . append ( x_noise , 160 ) y_out = np . append ( y_noise , 170 ) # 3. Restricted range: a test score and job performance, but only high scorers were hired score = rng . normal ( 70 , 12 , 2000 ) performance = 0.6 * score + rng . normal ( 0 , 8 , 2000 ) hired = score > 85 # 4. The same r, different slopes x_s = rng . uniform ( 0 , 10 , n ) y_gentle = 1 * x_s + rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n ) y_steep = 10 * x_s + rng . normal ( 0 , 10 , n ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 4 , figsize = ( 16 , 3.8 )) axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( temp , complaints , s = 10 , color = "#2a78d6" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( f "1. Curve: r = { np . corrcoef ( temp , complaints )[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } " ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "Office temperature (°C)" ); axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Complaints" ) axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( x_out , y_out , s = 10 , color = "#2a78d6" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( f "2. Outlier: r = { np . corrcoef ( x_out , y_out )[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } " f "(without it { np . corrcoef ( x_noise , y_noise )[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } )" , fontsize = 10 ) axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( score , performance , s = 4 , color = "#c9c9c9" , label = "Not hired" ) axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( score [ hired ], performance [ hired ], s = 6 , color = "#2a78d6" , label = "Hired" ) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( f "3. Range: all r = { np . corrcoef ( score , performance )[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } , " f "hired r = { np . corrcoef ( score [ hired ], performance [ hired ])[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } " , fontsize = 10 ) axes [ 2 ] . set_xlabel ( "Test score" ); axes [ 2 ] . set_ylabel ( "Performance" ); axes [ 2 ] . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) axes [ 3 ] . scatter ( x_s , y_gentle , s = 10 , color = "#2a78d6" , label = "gentle" ) axes [ 3 ] . scatter ( x_s , y_steep , s = 10 , color = "#eb6834" , label = "steep" ) axes [ 3 ] . set_title ( f "4. r = { np . corrcoef ( x_s , y_gentle )[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } and { np . corrcoef ( x_s , y_steep )[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } " , fontsize = 10 ) axes [ 3 ] . legend ( fontsize = 8 ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Panel Trap Lesson 1 A strong pattern, r near 0 r measures straight-line patterns only; plot first 2 One point creates a correlation Check outliers; Spearman's rank correlation (below) is less sensitive 3 The correlation shrinks inside a selected group Looking only at hired staff, customers who stayed, or products that survived understates the relationship 4 Same r , ten times the slope r says how tight the line is, not how much y changes per unit of x; that is the slope (Day 4) The fifth trap needs time: two things that both grow over time correlate , whatever they are. years = np . arange ( 2010 , 2026 ) rng = np . random . default_rng ( 7 ) phones_sold = 100 + 9 * ( years - 2010 ) + rng . normal ( 0 , 4 , len ( years )) # invented series cinema_tickets = 50 + 3 * ( years - 2010 ) + rng . normal ( 0 , 3 , len ( years )) # invented series print ( f "r between the two yearly totals: { np . corrcoef ( phones_sold , cinema_tickets )[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } " ) print ( f "r between their year-on-year changes: { np . corrcoef ( np . diff ( phones_sold ), np . diff ( cinema_tickets ))[ 0 , 1 ] : +.2f } " ) rank_r = pd . Series ( x_out ) . corr ( pd . Series ( y_out ), method = "spearman" ) print ( f " \n Panel 2 again, Spearman rank correlation: { rank_r : +.2f } " ) r between the two yearly totals: +0.98 r between their year-on-year changes: -0.20 Panel 2 again, Spearman rank correlation: +0.02 Two series that both trend upward correlate strongly even when they have nothing to do with each other. Comparing the changes removes the shared trend, and the correlation largely disappears. Day 3's forecasting lecture returns to this. Misconception: "correlation means causation" (and its opposite) A correlation is a description of how two columns moved together in this data. It can arise from a cause, a reverse cause, a third factor, selection, a shared trend or chance. The opposite mistake is just as common: " r is near 0, so there is no relationship" (panel 1).
docs.title: Five ways a correlation misleads

docs.text: A confounder is a third variable that affects both the thing you compare by and the thing you measure , so that the comparison mixes two effects. Written as arrows: Z → X and Z → Y. Comparing Y across X then shows partly the effect of Z. In Part 4, US cars had lower average mpg and far more 8-cylinder engines. Is "US-made" the reason for lower fuel economy, or is engine size? Engine size is a candidate confounder: it differs between regions and it affects fuel use.
docs.title: Part 6: Confounding and Simpson's paradox

docs.text: The most famous example comes from graduate admissions at the University of California, Berkeley, in 1973. The table below is the widely published version for the six largest departments (Bickel, Hammel & O'Connell, 1975). admissions = pd . DataFrame ({ "department" : list ( "AABBCCDDEEFF" ), "gender" : [ "Men" , "Women" ] * 6 , "applicants" : [ 825 , 108 , 560 , 25 , 325 , 593 , 417 , 375 , 191 , 393 , 373 , 341 ], "admitted" : [ 512 , 89 , 353 , 17 , 120 , 202 , 138 , 131 , 53 , 94 , 22 , 24 ], }) overall = admissions . groupby ( "gender" )[[ "applicants" , "admitted" ]] . sum () overall [ "admitted (%)" ] = ( 100 * overall [ "admitted" ] / overall [ "applicants" ]) . round ( 1 ) print ( "All six departments together" ) print ( overall ) All six departments together applicants admitted admitted (%) gender Men 2691 1198 44.5 Women 1835 557 30.4 Predict, then run Overall, men were admitted at a clearly higher rate. Predict: in how many of the six departments will men have the higher admission rate? admissions [ "admitted (%)" ] = ( 100 * admissions [ "admitted" ] / admissions [ "applicants" ]) . round ( 1 ) by_dept = admissions . pivot_table ( index = "department" , columns = "gender" , values = [ "admitted (%)" , "applicants" ]) by_dept .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead tr th { text-align: left; } .dataframe thead tr:last-of-type th { text-align: right; } admitted (%) applicants gender Men Women Men Women department A 62.1 82.4 825.0 108.0 B 63.0 68.0 560.0 25.0 C 36.9 34.1 325.0 593.0 D 33.1 34.9 417.0 375.0 E 27.7 23.9 191.0 393.0 F 5.9 7.0 373.0 341.0 In most departments women were admitted at a rate similar to or higher than men, yet overall they were admitted less often. Look at the applicant counts: most women applied to departments C–F, which admitted few applicants of either gender; most men applied to A and B, which admitted most applicants. The department is the confounder: it affects both who applied (gender mix) and the chance of admission. Simpson's paradox is the name for a trend that appears in every group, or most groups, and reverses (or disappears) when the groups are combined. It happens when the groups differ in size and in their baseline rate.
docs.title: Simpson's paradox: a real case

docs.text: Two support teams resolve customer tickets. Team North handles many hard tickets (technical faults); Team South mostly easy ones (password resets). Synthetic numbers: tickets = pd . DataFrame ({ "team" : [ "North" , "North" , "South" , "South" ], "ticket_type" : [ "Easy" , "Hard" , "Easy" , "Hard" ], "tickets" : [ 300 , 700 , 900 , 100 ], "resolved_first_time" : [ 282 , 420 , 801 , 52 ], }) tickets [ "rate (%)" ] = ( 100 * tickets [ "resolved_first_time" ] / tickets [ "tickets" ]) . round ( 1 ) print ( tickets . pivot_table ( index = "team" , columns = "ticket_type" , values = "rate (%)" )) team_total = tickets . groupby ( "team" )[[ "tickets" , "resolved_first_time" ]] . sum () team_total [ "rate (%)" ] = ( 100 * team_total [ "resolved_first_time" ] / team_total [ "tickets" ]) . round ( 1 ) print () print ( team_total ) ticket_type Easy Hard team North 94.0 60.0 South 89.0 52.0 tickets resolved_first_time rate (%) team North 1000 702 70.2 South 1000 853 85.3 North is better at both kinds of ticket and worse overall, because it carries most of the hard work. A manager who ranked teams on the overall rate would reward the wrong team. The fix is to compare like with like. Standardisation applies one common ticket mix to both teams' rates, so the mix no longer differs: common_mix = tickets . groupby ( "ticket_type" )[ "tickets" ] . sum () / tickets [ "tickets" ] . sum () print ( "Common mix:" , ( common_mix * 100 ) . round ( 1 ) . to_dict (), "( % o f all tickets)" ) rates = tickets . pivot_table ( index = "team" , columns = "ticket_type" , values = "rate (%)" ) standardised = ( rates * common_mix ) . sum ( axis = 1 ) . round ( 1 ) print ( " \n First-time resolution (%) if both teams had the same ticket mix:" ) print ( standardised ) Common mix: {'Easy': 60.0, 'Hard': 40.0} (% of all tickets) First-time resolution (%) if both teams had the same ticket mix: team North 80.4 South 74.2 dtype: float64
docs.title: A business version, and a fairer comparison

docs.text: Ask: what else differs between the groups I am comparing? (Size, mix, location, time, who chose to be in them.) Split by that variable (pivot with it as a second dimension) and compare within each level. Show the counts , so you see where each group's weight lies. If the groups differ in mix, standardise or compare like with like. Remember that you can only split by confounders you have recorded . The strongest protection is a designed comparison, such as a randomised trial. Misconception: "with enough data, the confounding goes away" Berkeley had over 4,500 applicants. More rows make each rate more precise, but they make a confounded comparison precisely wrong. Only splitting, standardising or a better design helps.
docs.title: How to look for confounding

docs.text: With a few hundred points a scatter plot is honest. With tens of thousands, points pile on top of each other and the densest region looks no darker than a sparse one: over-plotting . The next cell generates 80,000 synthetic taxi trips, distance against fare, including a flat-fare airport route. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 80 ) n_city = 76000 distance = rng . gamma ( 1.8 , 3.0 , n_city ) fare = 12 + 2.4 * distance + rng . normal ( 0 , 3 , n_city ) airport_distance = rng . normal ( 28 , 2.5 , 4000 ) airport_fare = rng . normal ( 95 , 2 , 4000 ) # a flat fare, whatever the distance trips = pd . DataFrame ({ "distance_km" : np . concatenate ([ distance , airport_distance ]), "fare" : np . concatenate ([ fare , airport_fare ])}) trips = trips [( trips [ "distance_km" ] > 0 ) & ( trips [ "fare" ] > 0 )] print ( "Trips:" , len ( trips )) Trips: 80000 Predict, then run 4,000 trips (5%) are airport trips at a flat fare of about 95; the other 76,000 are city trips. In a plain scatter plot, will the airport group look small or large compared with the city trips? In which of the four panels can you see that the city trips are about nineteen times as many, and where most of them lie? fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 8.5 ), sharex = True , sharey = True ) axes [ 0 , 0 ] . scatter ( trips [ "distance_km" ], trips [ "fare" ], s = 6 , color = "#2a78d6" ) axes [ 0 , 0 ] . set_title ( "1. Plain scatter: one solid blob" ) axes [ 0 , 1 ] . scatter ( trips [ "distance_km" ], trips [ "fare" ], s = 2 , alpha = 0.05 , color = "#2a78d6" ) axes [ 0 , 1 ] . set_title ( "2. Small, transparent points: density appears" ) sample = trips . sample ( 3000 , random_state = 1 ) axes [ 1 , 0 ] . scatter ( sample [ "distance_km" ], sample [ "fare" ], s = 6 , alpha = 0.5 , color = "#2a78d6" ) axes [ 1 , 0 ] . set_title ( "3. A random sample of 3,000 trips" ) hb = axes [ 1 , 1 ] . hexbin ( trips [ "distance_km" ], trips [ "fare" ], gridsize = 45 , cmap = "Blues" , mincnt = 1 , bins = "log" ) fig . colorbar ( hb , ax = axes [ 1 , 1 ], label = "Trips per hexagon (log scale)" ) axes [ 1 , 1 ] . set_title ( "4. Hexbin with a log colour scale" ) for ax in axes [ 1 ]: ax . set_xlabel ( "Trip distance (km)" ) for ax in axes [:, 0 ]: ax . set_ylabel ( "Fare (currency units)" ) fig . suptitle ( "80,000 synthetic taxi trips, four ways" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Fix When to use it Watch out for Smaller points, transparency ( s , alpha ) Up to about 100,000 points Very rare points can vanish Random sample Very large data, quick look Rare groups may be missed; set random_state so it repeats Hexbin or 2-D histogram Any size; shows where points concentrate Choose gridsize ; a log colour scale stops the densest cell dominating Density contours ( sns.kdeplot ) Smooth overview of a few groups Can invent smoothness where data is sparse Jitter (small random shift) When one axis is a count or category Never use jittered values for calculations Split into panels or colour by group When a third variable separates the cloud Too many colours become unreadable A hexbin divides the plane into hexagons and colours each by how many points fall inside it. mincnt=1 leaves empty hexagons blank. Reading it: the darkest region is where most rows lie, and its position on both axes describes the "typical" combination.
docs.title: Part 7: Over-plotting and its fixes

docs.text: fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 ), sharey = True ) axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( cars [ "cylinders" ], cars [ "mpg" ], s = 14 , color = "#2a78d6" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Without jitter: points stack in five columns" ) jitter = np . random . default_rng ( 3 ) . uniform ( - 0.25 , 0.25 , len ( cars )) # a small random shift, seeded axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( cars [ "cylinders" ] + jitter , cars [ "mpg" ], s = 14 , alpha = 0.7 , color = "#2a78d6" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "With jitter: each car model is visible" ) for ax in axes : ax . set_xlabel ( "Number of cylinders" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Fuel economy (miles per gallon)" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show ()
