docs.text: Day 1 lecture: Foundations of data-driven decisions ¶ The first three periods of Day 1. Why organisations decide with data and how famous decisions went right and wrong; the four levels of analytics, from describing the past to recommending an action; how to turn a vague business question into something data can answer; what "good data" means; and why a table of summary statistics is never enough on its own. Run each code cell with Shift + Enter , in order. The notebook makes its own synthetic data, except Part 6, which reads data/datasaurus_dozen.csv . Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder; everything loads from data/ . Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook and data/datasaurus_dozen.csv , run %pip install seaborn in a first cell, and change "data/datasaurus_dozen.csv" to "datasaurus_dozen.csv" in Part 6. What you will be able to do ¶ Explain, with real cases, what data adds to a decision, and name the ways data-driven decisions fail. Place any business question on the analytics hierarchy (descriptive, diagnostic, predictive, prescriptive) and say what each level can and cannot tell you. Frame a decision: name the decision, the population, the period and the measure, and show how each choice changes the answer. Check a table against six data quality dimensions with short pandas tests. Explain, using Anscombe's quartet and the Datasaurus Dozen, why you must always plot data before trusting its summary. Part Topic Period 1 Welcome: the course on one page P1 2 Why decide with data, and how it goes wrong P1 3 The analytics hierarchy, with a worked example P2 4 Framing a decision: decision, population, period, measure P3 5 Data quality dimensions P3 6 Why summary statistics are not enough P3 7 Business case, practice, quiz and summary P3 and self-study Reading Read Chapter 1 of the course reading packet for the four levels of analytics carried through a single worked example, for how to read a page of industry statistics with healthy suspicion, and for what describe() , isnull().sum() , groupby() and correlation each reveal. This lecture goes further on cases, framing and data quality. Part 1: Welcome: the course on one page ¶ DATA 300 is about one habit: before you act, ask what the evidence says, and how sure you can be . You will practise it in three programs, each graded: Program Used for Days JupyterLab (Python) Exploring data, text mining, forecasting, regression 1, 3, 4, 5 Tableau Desktop Dashboards and visual communication 2, 6 Microsoft Excel Spreadsheet models, What-If tables, simulation, forecast sheets 5, 6 How each day works: theory in the morning, a lab in the afternoon that you submit on GAP the same day . Today's lab is Lab 1, data exploration on a dataset of diamonds. The overview lists every graded item and its weight; the timetable shows each period. Three habits save more marks than any formula: Restart and run all before you export, so the PDF matches the code. Export a PDF before closing a Try JupyterLab tab; the session lives only in the browser. Write the unit with every number: US dollars, grams, minutes, per cent. Check your understanding Which of the three programs keeps your work only as long as a browser tab is open, and what do you do about it? Part 2: Why decide with data, and how it goes wrong ¶ Every organisation already decides. The question is what the decision rests on: habit, the loudest voice in the room, a competitor's move, or evidence. Data helps in three ways: It replaces memory with records . People remember vivid events (the one angry customer, the record sales day) and forget ordinary ones. A table remembers them all equally. It makes a claim checkable . "Sales are down in the north" can be tested; "I have a feeling" cannot. It scales judgement . A rule that worked for one store manager can be applied to 500 stores, and its results measured. Data does not replace judgement. People still choose which question matters, decide whether a strange number is an error or a discovery, weigh values that no column records (fairness, safety, reputation) and take responsibility for the action. Biases that data can correct, if it is used honestly ¶ Bias What it looks like How data helps Availability Judging by the examples that come to mind most easily Count all the cases, not the memorable ones Confirmation Looking only for evidence that supports what you already believe Decide the test before you look at the result Survivorship Studying only the cases that "made it" Ask which cases are missing from the table, and why Anchoring Sticking to the first number you heard Compare against a baseline chosen in advance Overconfidence Treating one good quarter as a law Look at variation over many periods Cases: when data helped, and when it failed ¶ These are well-known, widely reported cases, summarised in our own words. Details differ between sources; the references at the end of this notebook give a place to start. Case What happened Level of analytics Lesson Walmart before a hurricane (2004) Analysts looked at sales records from earlier storms and found that, besides water and torches, some unexpected items (a breakfast pastry, beer) sold far above normal. Stores in the storm's path were stocked accordingly Descriptive, used for prediction Past records can reveal demand nobody would guess Parcel route planning (UPS ORION, 2010s) An optimisation system proposes the order of each driver's stops; the company reports large savings in miles and fuel each year Prescriptive Recommending an action needs a good model of costs and constraints Airline revenue management (1980s onward) Airlines forecast demand for each fare class and decide how many seats to sell at each price Predictive and prescriptive A forecast becomes valuable when it changes a decision A 1936 US election poll ( Literary Digest ) Over two million mailed ballots predicted a clear win for the challenger; the president won in a landslide. The mailing lists favoured wealthier households, and those who replied differed from those who did not Descriptive, wrongly generalised A huge sample from the wrong population is still wrong Damage to returning aircraft (Second World War) Planners proposed armour where returning planes had the most bullet holes. The statistician Abraham Wald argued the opposite: planes hit elsewhere had not come back Diagnostic The data you cannot see (survivorship) can reverse the conclusion Space Shuttle Challenger (1986) Before launch, engineers discussed O-ring damage against temperature using only flights that had damage. Including the flights with no damage shows the cold-weather risk much more clearly Diagnostic Leaving out "nothing happened" cases hides the pattern Google Flu Trends (2008–2015) Search terms were used to estimate flu levels. In the 2012–13 season the estimates were roughly double the official figures Predictive Correlation without a mechanism drifts; check predictions against reality A home-buying algorithm (Zillow Offers, 2021) A company bought homes based on price forecasts, then closed the business after the forecasts and the market moved apart, with large losses and job cuts Predictive, acted on at scale A model is only as good as its fit to today's conditions Amazon's CV-screening tool (reported 2018) A tool trained on ten years of past hiring learned to mark down CVs that mentioned women's activities, and was dropped Predictive History records past decisions, including biased ones Discuss in pairs (5 minutes) Pick one failure from the table. Which one question, asked before the decision, might have caught the problem? Keep your answer: by the end of Part 4 you will see that most of these questions are about the population , the period or the measure . Part 3: The analytics hierarchy ¶ Analytics questions come in four kinds. Each one needs the answer to the one before it. Level Question Typical output Typical methods In this course Descriptive What happened? Totals, averages, rates, charts, dashboards Summaries, pivot tables, histograms Days 1–2, Labs 1–2, Assignment 1 Diagnostic Why did it happen? Breakdowns, comparisons, drivers Grouping, segmentation, correlation, controlled comparisons Days 1–3 Predictive What is likely to happen? Forecasts, probabilities, scores Time series, regression, text features Days 3–5, Labs 4–5, Assignment 2 Prescriptive What should we do? Which customers to target within the budget Misconception: "descriptive analytics is the easy, low-value level" Every later level is built on it. A forecast trained on wrongly described history is wrong, and a recommendation built on a wrong forecast is wrong with confidence. Most of the failures in Part 2 were descriptive or framing errors, not modelling errors. Misconception: "a predictive model explains why" A model can predict well using a column that has nothing to do with the cause (Google Flu Trends used search habits, not infections). Prediction answers what next , not why . Diagnosis and experiments answer why . The hierarchy is also a loop , not a ladder you climb once: a prescription is acted on, the result is measured (descriptive again), and the model is corrected. Before a full rollout, the honest next step is a trial : add riders on some rainy dinners and not others, and measure the difference. That is the loop from prescriptive back to descriptive, and it is how Days 5 and 6 treat uncertainty. Statistic, insight, decision Statistic: "x% of rainy dinner orders were late." Insight: "Rain at dinner time is where lateness concentrates, and a late order costs us about 25 units." Decision: "Trial standby riders on rainy dinners for four weeks, and keep them if the late rate falls by at least a third." A statistic is a number. An insight says what it means for the business. A decision says what we will do, and how we will know if it worked. Part 4: Framing a decision ¶ Most analysis goes wrong before any code runs, because the question was vague. "How are our branches doing?" cannot be answered; it can only be argued about. A framed question names four things: Element Ask Example Decision What will someone do differently depending on the answer? Move the senior barista to the weaker branch, or not Population Which rows count? Who or what is in, and who is out? Customer orders only: no staff meals, no test orders, no refunds Period Which time window, and why that one? The last eight full weeks, after the menu change Measure Which number, calculated how? Median order value in currency units, per order Add a comparison (against what? last year, a target, another branch) and a threshold (how big a difference would change the decision?), and the question is ready. Reframing vague questions ¶ Vague Framed Are customers happy? Should we fix delivery packaging first? Compare the share of 1–2 star reviews mentioning packaging versus delivery time, for reviews of orders placed in September–October, app orders only Is the promotion working? Should we extend the promotion to all stores? Compare weekly units sold per store in the 10 promotion stores and 10 similar stores without it, for the four weeks before and the four weeks during the promotion Who are our best customers? Which customers should get a loyalty invitation? Rank active customers (ordered in the last 90 days) by gross margin over the last 12 months; invite the top 5% Every choice changes the answer ¶ The next cell generates twelve weeks of orders for two branches of an imaginary bakery chain. They answer different questions: The population choice (dropping test orders) removes rows that are not customers at all, and moves both means. The measure choice (mean or median) decides how much three huge catering orders count: compare the size of East's lead under each. The period choice (from week 5) removes the refurbishment, when the West branch was not trading normally, and here it reverses the answer. None of these choices is automatically right. If the decision is about catering sales, the mean with catering orders is exactly what you want. That is why framing starts from the decision . Misconception: "the data will tell us which number to use" It will not. The decision tells you which number to use. Choose the population, period and measure before looking at the result, and write them down; otherwise it is easy to pick, without meaning to, the version that supports what you already believed (confirmation bias from Part 2). Part 5: Data quality dimensions ¶ "Is the data good?" is another vague question. Data quality is usually split into dimensions, each with its own test. Data is never perfect; the question is whether it is fit for this decision . Dimension Question Typical pandas check Completeness Is anything missing? df.isnull().sum() Uniqueness Is anything counted twice? df.duplicated().sum() , or duplicates on an ID column Validity Are values allowed and in range? describe() min and max; a filter for impossible values Consistency Is the same thing written the same way everywhere? value_counts() on text columns Accuracy Do values match reality? Compare with a trusted source; spot-check rows Timeliness Is it recent enough for the decision? max() of the date column against today Here is a tiny customer sign-up table with problems planted in it. docs.text: Every organisation already decides. The question is what the decision rests on: habit, the loudest voice in the room, a competitor's move, or evidence. Data helps in three ways: It replaces memory with records . People remember vivid events (the one angry customer, the record sales day) and forget ordinary ones. A table remembers them all equally. It makes a claim checkable . "Sales are down in the north" can be tested; "I have a feeling" cannot. It scales judgement . A rule that worked for one store manager can be applied to 500 stores, and its results measured. Data does not replace judgement. People still choose which question matters, decide whether a strange number is an error or a discovery, weigh values that no column records (fairness, safety, reputation) and take responsibility for the action.
docs.title: Part 2: Why decide with data, and how it goes wrong

docs.text: Bias What it looks like How data helps Availability Judging by the examples that come to mind most easily Count all the cases, not the memorable ones Confirmation Looking only for evidence that supports what you already believe Decide the test before you look at the result Survivorship Studying only the cases that "made it" Ask which cases are missing from the table, and why Anchoring Sticking to the first number you heard Compare against a baseline chosen in advance Overconfidence Treating one good quarter as a law Look at variation over many periods
docs.title: Biases that data can correct, if it is used honestly

docs.text: These are well-known, widely reported cases, summarised in our own words. Details differ between sources; the references at the end of this notebook give a place to start. Case What happened Level of analytics Lesson Walmart before a hurricane (2004) Analysts looked at sales records from earlier storms and found that, besides water and torches, some unexpected items (a breakfast pastry, beer) sold far above normal. Stores in the storm's path were stocked accordingly Descriptive, used for prediction Past records can reveal demand nobody would guess Parcel route planning (UPS ORION, 2010s) An optimisation system proposes the order of each driver's stops; the company reports large savings in miles and fuel each year Prescriptive Recommending an action needs a good model of costs and constraints Airline revenue management (1980s onward) Airlines forecast demand for each fare class and decide how many seats to sell at each price Predictive and prescriptive A forecast becomes valuable when it changes a decision A 1936 US election poll ( Literary Digest ) Over two million mailed ballots predicted a clear win for the challenger; the president won in a landslide. The mailing lists favoured wealthier households, and those who replied differed from those who did not Descriptive, wrongly generalised A huge sample from the wrong population is still wrong Damage to returning aircraft (Second World War) Planners proposed armour where returning planes had the most bullet holes. The statistician Abraham Wald argued the opposite: planes hit elsewhere had not come back Diagnostic The data you cannot see (survivorship) can reverse the conclusion Space Shuttle Challenger (1986) Before launch, engineers discussed O-ring damage against temperature using only flights that had damage. Including the flights with no damage shows the cold-weather risk much more clearly Diagnostic Leaving out "nothing happened" cases hides the pattern Google Flu Trends (2008–2015) Search terms were used to estimate flu levels. In the 2012–13 season the estimates were roughly double the official figures Predictive Correlation without a mechanism drifts; check predictions against reality A home-buying algorithm (Zillow Offers, 2021) A company bought homes based on price forecasts, then closed the business after the forecasts and the market moved apart, with large losses and job cuts Predictive, acted on at scale A model is only as good as its fit to today's conditions Amazon's CV-screening tool (reported 2018) A tool trained on ten years of past hiring learned to mark down CVs that mentioned women's activities, and was dropped Predictive History records past decisions, including biased ones Discuss in pairs (5 minutes) Pick one failure from the table. Which one question, asked before the decision, might have caught the problem? Keep your answer: by the end of Part 4 you will see that most of these questions are about the population , the period or the measure .
docs.title: Cases: when data helped, and when it failed

docs.text: Analytics questions come in four kinds. Each one needs the answer to the one before it. Level Question Typical output Typical methods In this course Descriptive What happened? Totals, averages, rates, charts, dashboards Summaries, pivot tables, histograms Days 1–2, Labs 1–2, Assignment 1 Diagnostic Why did it happen? Breakdowns, comparisons, drivers Grouping, segmentation, correlation, controlled comparisons Days 1–3 Predictive What is likely to happen? Forecasts, probabilities, scores Time series, regression, text features Days 3–5, Labs 4–5, Assignment 2 Prescriptive What should we do? A recommended action, with its expected result and risk Optimisation, simulation, What-If analysis Days 5–6, Labs 6–7, Assignment 3 Value usually rises up the table, and so do difficulty and the number of assumptions you must make. A descriptive number can be checked against the records; a prescription rests on a model of how the world will respond.
docs.title: Part 3: The analytics hierarchy

docs.text: Function Descriptive Diagnostic Predictive Prescriptive Retail Sales by store last month Why did the new store under-perform? Demand per product next week How much of each product to order Human resources Staff turnover rate by team Which factors go with people leaving? Who is likely to resign this year? Which retention offer to make, to whom Finance Overdue invoices by customer Which customer types pay late, and when? Probability that an invoice is paid late Which customers get credit, and how much Operations Average delivery time Where in the process do delays build up? Delay risk for tomorrow's routes How many drivers to roster per shift Marketing Campaign click rate Which audience and message drove the clicks? Who will respond to the next campaign? Which customers to target within the budget Misconception: "descriptive analytics is the easy, low-value level" Every later level is built on it. A forecast trained on wrongly described history is wrong, and a recommendation built on a wrong forecast is wrong with confidence. Most of the failures in Part 2 were descriptive or framing errors, not modelling errors. Misconception: "a predictive model explains why" A model can predict well using a column that has nothing to do with the cause (Google Flu Trends used search habits, not infections). Prediction answers what next , not why . Diagnosis and experiments answer why . The hierarchy is also a loop , not a ladder you climb once: a prescription is acted on, the result is measured (descriptive again), and the model is corrected.

docs.title: A worked example: late deliveries at a food delivery firm

docs.text: Most analysis goes wrong before any code runs, because the question was vague. "How are our branches doing?" cannot be answered; it can only be argued about. A framed question names four things: Element Ask Example Decision What will someone do differently depending on the answer? Move the senior barista to the weaker branch, or not Population Which rows count? Who or what is in, and who is out? Customer orders only: no staff meals, no test orders, no refunds Period Which time window, and why that one? The last eight full weeks, after the menu change Measure Which number, calculated how? Median order value in currency units, per order Add a comparison (against what? last year, a target, another branch) and a threshold (how big a difference would change the decision?), and the question is ready.
docs.title: Part 4: Framing a decision

docs.text: Vague Framed Are customers happy? Should we fix delivery packaging first? Compare the share of 1–2 star reviews mentioning packaging versus delivery time, for reviews of orders placed in September–October, app orders only Is the promotion working? Should we extend the promotion to all stores? Compare weekly units sold per store in the 10 promotion stores and 10 similar stores without it, for the four weeks before and the four weeks during the promotion Who are our best customers? Which customers should get a loyalty invitation? Rank active customers (ordered in the last 90 days) by gross margin over the last 12 months; invite the top 5%
docs.title: Reframing vague questions

docs.text: The next cell generates twelve weeks of orders for two branches of an imaginary bakery chain. The East branch had three big catering orders early on; both branches have some test orders placed by staff, and the West branch was refurbished in weeks 1–4, when it sold a reduced menu and staff placed many test orders on the new tills. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 11 ) frames = [] for branch in [ "East" , "West" ]: for week in range ( 1 , 13 ): refurbishing = branch == "West" and week <= 4 # West branch weeks 1-4 n = 150 if refurbishing else 160 typical = 44 if branch == "East" else ( 28 if refurbishing else 47 ) value = rng . lognormal ( np . log ( typical ), 0.45 , n ) test = rng . random ( n ) < ( 0.25 if refurbishing else 0.03 ) # staff tested the new tills frames . append ( pd . DataFrame ({ "branch" : branch , "week" : week , "order_value" : value . round ( 2 ), "test_order" : test })) bakery = pd . concat ( frames , ignore_index = True ) catering = pd . DataFrame ({ "branch" : "East" , "week" : [ 1 , 2 , 3 ], "order_value" : [ 2400.0 , 3100.0 , 2750.0 ], "test_order" : False }) bakery = pd . concat ([ bakery , catering ], ignore_index = True ) bakery . loc [ bakery [ "test_order" ], "order_value" ] = 0.01 # staff test orders are recorded at 0.01 print ( "Rows:" , len ( bakery )) bakery . groupby ( "branch" )[ "order_value" ] . describe () . round ( 2 ) Rows: 3803 .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } count mean std min 25% 50% 75% max branch East 1923.0 51.79 110.01 0.01 31.97 43.46 58.94 3100.0 West 1880.0 43.35 27.81 0.01 25.65 39.81 56.88 204.9 The manager asks: "Which branch has the higher average order value?" Here are four defensible answers to that one question. Predict, then run Before running: which branch do you think "wins" if we use the plain mean over all twelve weeks? Will it still win with the median, or when we use only the weeks in which both branches traded normally? customers_only = bakery [ ~ bakery [ "test_order" ]] recent = customers_only [ customers_only [ "week" ] >= 5 ] answers = pd . DataFrame ({ "Mean, all rows, 12 weeks" : bakery . groupby ( "branch" )[ "order_value" ] . mean (), "Mean, customers only, 12 weeks" : customers_only . groupby ( "branch" )[ "order_value" ] . mean (), "Median, customers only, 12 weeks" : customers_only . groupby ( "branch" )[ "order_value" ] . median (), "Median, customers only, weeks 5-12" : recent . groupby ( "branch" )[ "order_value" ] . median (), }) . T . round ( 2 ) answers [ "higher" ] = np . where ( answers [ "East" ] > answers [ "West" ], "East" , "West" ) answers .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } branch East West higher Mean, all rows, 12 weeks 51.79 43.35 East Mean, customers only, 12 weeks 53.34 47.33 East Median, customers only, 12 weeks 44.28 42.10 East Median, customers only, weeks 5-12 44.66 48.06 West Every number in that table is correct . They answer different questions: The population choice (dropping test orders) removes rows that are not customers at all, and moves both means. The measure choice (mean or median) decides how much three huge catering orders count: compare the size of East's lead under each. The period choice (from week 5) removes the refurbishment, when the West branch was not trading normally, and here it reverses the answer. None of these choices is automatically right. If the decision is about catering sales, the mean with catering orders is exactly what you want. That is why framing starts from the decision . Misconception: "the data will tell us which number to use" It will not. The decision tells you which number to use. Choose the population, period and measure before looking at the result, and write them down; otherwise it is easy to pick, without meaning to, the version that supports what you already believed (confirmation bias from Part 2). docs.title: Every choice changes the answer

docs.text:
"Is the data good?" is another vague question. Data quality is usually split into dimensions, each with its own test. Data is never perfect; the question is whether it is fit for this decision . Dimension Question Typical pandas check Completeness Is anything missing? df.isnull().sum() Uniqueness Is anything counted twice? df.duplicated().sum() , or duplicates on an ID column Validity Are values allowed and in range? describe() min and max; a filter for impossible values Consistency Is the same thing written the same way everywhere? value_counts() on text columns Accuracy Do values match reality? Compare with a trusted source; spot-check rows Timeliness Is it recent enough for the decision? max() of the date column against today Here is a tiny customer sign-up table with problems planted in it. docs.text:
Day 2 lecture: Tableau concepts and dashboards ¶ Periods 5 and 6 of Day 2, plus the Assignment 1 briefing in period 9. The ideas that make Tableau behave the way it does: dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous fields, aggregation and level of detail, the Marks card, filters and the order in which Tableau applies them, calculated fields, maps and dashboard actions. Each idea is explained in Tableau terms and then mirrored in Python, so you can see exactly what Tableau computes. Tableau is a tool you learn by clicking, so this lecture is meant to be taught with Tableau Desktop open on the projector. The Python mirrors use a synthetic bookshop chain , "Harbour Books", made inside the notebook, and the penguins data. Lab 2 uses Tableau's Sample – Superstore; this lecture deliberately does not , and asks different questions, so that you build and read your own dashboard in the lab. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder. Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook and data/penguins.csv , run %pip install seaborn in a first cell, and change "data/penguins.csv" to "penguins.csv" . What you will be able to do ¶ Explain the difference between dimensions and measures , and between discrete (blue) and continuous (green) fields, and predict what each does to a view. Explain aggregation and the level of detail of a view, and when a number changes because the level of detail changed. Use the Marks card (mark type, Color, Size, Label, Detail, Tooltip) on purpose. Apply filters and explain Tableau's order of operations , including why a Top N filter can give a surprising answer. Write calculated fields at row level and aggregate level, and use table calculations . Build a dashboard with filter and highlight actions , and check it against a design checklist . Read a box plot and a regression line in words a manager understands (for Assignment 1). Part Topic Period 1 Tableau's building blocks P5 2 Dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous P5 3 Aggregation and level of detail P5 4 The Marks card P5 5 Filters and the order of operations P6 6 Calculated fields and table calculations P6 7 Maps P6 8 Dashboards, actions and a design checklist P6 9 Lab 2 briefing P6 10 Assignment 1 briefing: reading box plots and regression lines P9 11 Practice, quiz and summary Self-study Reading Read Chapter 2 of the course reading packet on dual encoding (a chart that carries two variables at once) and on what changes when static charts become a linked, interactive dashboard. Its review questions 3 and 4 are good preparation for Lab 2. Part 1: Tableau's building blocks ¶ Tableau object What it is Python mirror Data source A connection to a file or database (Excel, CSV, a server), with any joins or relationships between tables pd.read_csv(...) , merge Live or extract Query the source each time, or take a fast snapshot ( .hyper ) Reading the file again, or keeping a DataFrame in memory Worksheet One view (chart or table) built by dragging fields onto shelves One groupby plus one plot Dashboard Several worksheets (plus text, images, filters) arranged on one canvas, optionally linked by actions A figure with several panels and a function that redraws them Story A sequence of sheets or dashboards with captions, like slides A report Workbook The file holding all of the above: .twb (no data) or .twbx ( packaged , data included) The notebook The workspace has the Data pane on the left (fields), the Columns and Rows shelves at the top, the Marks card and the Filters and Pages shelves beside the view, Show Me at the top right, and tabs at the bottom for sheets, dashboards and stories. Save as .twbx when you send a workbook to someone else, so the data travels with it. Below is the synthetic data that the Python mirrors use. One row is one order line : one product sub-category in one order. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import matplotlib.colors as mcolors import matplotlib.dates as mdates import seaborn as sns plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.dpi" : 100 , "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlesize" : 11 }) OI = { "orange" : "#E69F00" , "sky" : "#56B4E9" , "green" : "#009E73" , "blue" : "#0072B2" , "vermillion" : "#D55E00" , "purple" : "#CC79A7" } GREY = "#B0B0B0" # Harbour Books: a fictional chain of 12 bookshops in four regions (synthetic data) rng = np . random . default_rng ( 300 ) stores = pd . } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_date customer_id region store category sub_category quantity discount sales profit 0 2023-01-01 261 South Riverbend Stationery Notebooks 3 0.0 18.0 9.90 1 2023-01-01 47 West Sunsetvale Books Children's 4 0.0 44.0 18.48 2 2023-01-01 654 East Eastmere Books Fiction 1 0.0 14.0 5.32 3 2023-01-01 67 North Frostford Books Fiction 2 0.0 28.0 10.64 4 2023-01-01 1301 West Westfall Stationery Art supplies 2 0.0 30.0 13.50 Part 2: Dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous ¶ Dimensions and measures ¶ When Tableau connects to data it sorts each field into one of two roles: A dimension is a field you group or slice by : region, store, category, order date. Dimensions set how many marks the view has. A measure is a field you aggregate : sales, profit, quantity. Measures are summed (or averaged, counted…) within each group. Dragging Region to Rows and Sales to Columns gives a bar per region showing SUM(Sales) . That is exactly a groupby : # Tableau: Region on Rows, SUM(Sales) on Columns by_region = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum () . sort_values () print ( by_region . round ( 0 )) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 2.8 )) ax . barh ( by_region . index , by_region . values , color = GREY ) ax . set_xlabel ( "SUM(Sales), US dollars" ) ax . set_title ( "Region on Rows, SUM(Sales) on Columns" ) plt . show () region West 50648.0 North 50959.0 East 50985.0 South 53836.0 Name: sales, dtype: float64 The role is a default , not a law. A number such as a store's postcode or a customer ID is stored as a number but is really a label: convert it to a dimension (drag it above the line in the Data pane, or right-click → Convert to Dimension ). The rule of thumb: if adding it up makes no sense, it is a dimension. Discrete (blue) and continuous (green) ¶ The pill colour tells you something different from the role: Discrete (blue) values are separate and distinct. On a shelf, a discrete field creates headers (a label for each value), and on Color it creates a categorical palette. Continuous (green) values form an unbroken range. On a shelf, a continuous field creates an axis , and on Color a gradient . Discrete (blue) Continuous (green) Dimension Region, Category; date parts such as MONTH(Order Date) = "May" Date values such as MONTH(Order Date) = "May 2024"; a numeric dimension made continuous Measure SUM(Sales) turned discrete: a header per value, like a text table SUM(Sales): an axis (the usual case) The most important case in practice is the date . Right-click a date pill and you see two lists of Year, Quarter, Month…: the upper list gives date parts (discrete), which combine the same month from every year into one header; the lower list gives date values (continuous), which keep each month of each year as its own point on a timeline. Compare them on our synthetic data: fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 13 , 3.8 )) # Discrete date part: MONTH(Order Date) as a blue pill -> 12 headers, every year combined part = orders . groupby ( orders [ "order_date" ] . dt . month )[ "sales" ] . sum () axes [ 0 ] . bar ( pd . to_datetime ( part . index , format = "%m" ) . strftime ( "%b" ), part . values / 1000 , color = OI [ "sky" ]) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Discrete MONTH: 12 headers, all years added together" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand USD)" ) # Continuous date value: MONTH(Order Date) as a green pill -> 36 points on a timeline value = orders . set_index ( "order_date" )[ "sales" ] . resample ( "MS" ) . sum () axes [ 1 ] . plot ( value . index , value . values / 1000 , color = OI [ "blue" ], lw = 2 ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Continuous MONTH: one point per month of each year" ) axes [ 1 ] . xaxis . set_major_locator ( mdates . YearLocator ()) axes [ 1 ] . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( mdates . DateFormatter ( "%Y" )) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Both are correct answers to different questions. The left chart answers "Which month of the year is usually strongest?" (seasonality); the right chart answers "How did sales move over time?" (trend, and when something unusual happened). A trend line needs the continuous version: with the discrete version, an unusual month in one year is diluted by adding it to the same month of the other years. Predict, then run. If you put discrete YEAR and discrete MONTH next to each other on Columns, what would the chart look like, and how would it differ from the continuous version? (Hint: headers, not an axis.) Misconceptions ¶ Misconception Better view "Blue means dimension, green means measure." Blue means discrete , green means continuous . Most dimensions are discrete and most measures continuous, which is why the two get confused. "Dates are always continuous." A date can be either; you choose with the pill's menu. "Numbers are measures." IDs, postcodes and years are numbers you group by, so they are dimensions. Part 3: Aggregation and level of detail ¶ Aggregation ¶ A measure on a shelf is always aggregated: SUM by default, changeable from the pill's menu to AVG, MEDIAN, COUNT, COUNTD (count distinct), MIN, MAX and others. Each answers a different question: summary = orders . groupby ( "region" ) . agg ( SUM_sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), AVG_sales_per_line = ( "sales" , "mean" ), MEDIAN_sales_per_line = ( "sales" , "median" ), COUNT_lines = ( "sales" , "size" ), COUNTD_customers = ( "customer_id" , "nunique" ), ) . round ( 2 ) print ( summary . to_string ()) SUM_sales AVG_sales_per_line MEDIAN_sales_per_line COUNT_lines COUNTD_customers region East 50984.7 33.81 28.0 1508 1019 North 50959.1 34.78 28.0 1465 1026 South 53836.2 35.44 28.0 1519 1014 West 50648.3 34.50 28.0 1468 994 AVG(Sales) is the average order line , not the average order or the average customer: an aggregate always averages over the rows of the data source. If you need "sales per customer", that is SUM(Sales) / COUNTD(Customer ID) , which is a different number again. Level of detail ¶ The level of detail (LOD) of a view is set by the dimensions in it (on Rows, Columns and the Marks card). Every aggregate is computed once per combination of those dimensions. Add a dimension and each mark splits into several smaller marks; the totals are re-cut, not changed. lod_1 = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "profit" ] . sum () lod_2 = orders . groupby ([ "region" , "category" ])[ "profit" ] . sum () . unstack () print ( "Level of detail = Region:
