Unticking Analysis → Aggregate Measures shows every row as its own mark, which is what you want for a scatter of individual records. Here, discount against profit per order line: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) jit = np . random . default_rng ( 1 ) . uniform ( - 0.012 , 0.012 , len ( orders )) ax . scatter ( orders [ "discount" ] + jit , orders [ "profit" ], s = 5 , alpha = 0.25 , color = OI [ "blue" ]) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.8 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Discount (share of list price)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Profit per order line (USD)" ) ax . set_title ( "Disaggregated: one mark per order line" ) plt . show () Level of detail expressions ¶ Sometimes you need a number computed at a different level from the view. Tableau's LOD expressions do this: {FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])} : each customer's first order date, whatever the view shows. {INCLUDE [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])} : compute per customer, then aggregate up to the view (for example the average customer's spend per region). {EXCLUDE [Category] : SUM([Sales])} : ignore a dimension that is in the view (for example a region total next to each category). In pandas, FIXED is a groupby(...).transform(...) : a group result written back to every row. # {FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])} -> first-order year (a cohort) on every row orders [ "first_order_year" ] = orders . groupby ( "customer_id" )[ "order_date" ] . transform ( "min" ) . dt . year # {INCLUDE [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])}, then AVG in the view: average spend per customer, by region per_customer = orders . groupby ([ "region" , "customer_id" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () print ( "Average 3-year spend per customer in each region (USD):" ) print ( per_customer . groupby ( "region" ) . mean () . round ( 2 )) print ( " 
 Customers by the year of their first order:" ) print ( orders . drop_duplicates ( "customer_id" )[ "first_order_year" ] . value_counts () . sort_index ()) Average 3-year spend per customer in each region (USD): region East 50.03 North 49.67 South 53.09 West 50.95 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Customers by the year of their first order: first_order_year 2023 1183 2024 407 2025 135 Name: count, dtype: int64 Misconception Better view "AVG(Sales) is the average sale per customer." It is the average per row of the data source, here per order line. "Adding a dimension changes the totals." It splits marks; the grand total is the same unless a filter or LOD calculation changes it. Part 4: The Marks card ¶ The Marks card controls how each mark looks. Its parts map directly onto the encodings from this morning's lecture: Marks card What it encodes matplotlib / seaborn mirror Mark type (Automatic, Bar, Line, Area, Circle, Square, Shape, Text, Map, Pie, Gantt bar, Polygon, Density) The kind of mark bar , plot , scatter , text … Color A dimension (categorical palette) or a measure (sequential or diverging gradient) hue= , c= with a colormap Size A measure, as mark area size= , s= Label Text on each mark ax.text , bar_label Detail Splits marks by a dimension without encoding it visually Adding a column to groupby Tooltip Text shown on hover (no static equivalent) Shape , Path , Angle Shape per category; drawing order of a line; pie slice angle marker= , sort order, pie Automatic chooses a mark type from the fields: a date on Columns gives a line, a dimension and a measure give bars, two measures give circles, a geographic field gives a map. Automatic is a guess; choose deliberately. Here is one view with Color, Size, Detail and Label all in use, on the penguins data: penguins = pd . read_csv ( "data/penguins.csv" ) . dropna () # Route A: "penguins.csv" # Detail = island and species: one mark per island-species pair (no visual encoding of island itself) marks = penguins . groupby ([ "species" , "island" ]) . agg ( flipper = ( "flipper_length_mm" , "mean" ), mass = ( "body_mass_g" , "mean" ), birds = ( "body_mass_g" , "size" )) . reset_index () sp_col = { "Adelie" : OI [ "orange" ], "Chinstrap" : OI [ "purple" ], "Gentoo" : OI [ "green" ]} fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax . scatter ( marks [ "flipper" ], marks [ "mass" ], s = marks [ "birds" ] * 6 , # Size = COUNT color = marks [ "species" ] . map ( sp_col ), alpha = 0.8 ) # Color = species offsets = { "Biscoe" : ( - 12 , 14 ), "Dream" : ( 4 , - 18 ), "Torgersen" : ( 12 , 6 )} # keep labels apart for _ , r in marks . iterrows (): # Label = island ax . annotate ( r [ "island" ], ( r [ "flipper" ], r [ "mass" ]), xytext = offsets [ r [ "island" ]], textcoords = "offset points" , fontsize = 8 ) for sp , c in sp_col . items (): ax . scatter ([], [], color = c , label = sp ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , title = "Color: species" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "AVG(Flipper length), mm" ); ax . set_ylabel ( "AVG(Body mass), g" ) ax . set_title ( "Marks: Color = species, Size = number of birds, Label = island" ) ax . set_xlim ( 185 , 222 ); ax . set_ylim ( 3550 , 5350 ) plt . show () Read the encodings in order of strength: position (x and y) first, then colour, then size. The three Adelie marks sit close together; the Detail field (island) is what split them into three. Size shows that the marks rest on very different numbers of birds, a reminder from Day 1 to show counts. Colour from a measure. When a measure such as profit goes on Color, Tableau uses a continuous gradient . For a measure with a meaningful zero (profit, change), use a diverging palette and make sure its centre is at zero : in Tableau, Color → Edit Colors → Advanced → Center: 0 . Otherwise the neutral colour sits at the middle of the data range and a small profit can look like a loss. The mirror in matplotlib is TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0) ; Part 8 uses it. Part 5: Filters and the order of operations ¶ Kinds of filter ¶ Filter How you make it What it does Extract filter When creating an extract Leaves rows out of the extract entirely Data source filter Data Source page → Filters → Add Applies to every sheet using the source Context filter Right-click a filter → Add to Context (turns grey) Applied first; later filters and Top N work inside it Dimension filter Drag a dimension to Filters Keeps chosen members (or a Top N, a wildcard, a condition) Measure filter Drag a measure to Filters Keeps marks whose aggregate is in a range Table calculation filter Filter on a table calculation Hides marks after everything is computed Showing a filter ( Show Filter ) adds a control for the reader; on a dashboard, filters can apply to one sheet, several, or all sheets using the source. Order of operations ¶ Tableau applies operations in a fixed order. Simplified: Extract filters Data source filters Context filters FIXED LOD expressions, sets, Top N and conditions Dimension filters INCLUDE and EXCLUDE LOD expressions Measure filters Table calculations, then table calculation filters The order matters because a step can only see what the earlier steps left. The classic surprise is Top N with another filter . Say you want the top 3 stores by sales in the West . You add a Top 3 filter on Store and a filter Region = West. Both are dimension filters, so Tableau computes the Top 3 over all regions and then intersects with West: store_sales = orders . groupby ([ "region" , "store" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . reset_index () # Both filters at the same step: Top 3 computed on ALL stores, then intersected with West top3_all = store_sales . nlargest ( 3 , "sales" ) print ( "Top 3 stores overall: 
 " , top3_all . to_string ( index = False ), " 
 " ) print ( "Top 3 filter AND Region = West (same step):" ) in_west = top3_all [ top3_all [ "region" ] == "West" ] print ( in_west . to_string ( index = False ) if len ( in_west ) else " (no rows: none of the overall top 3 is in the West)" ) # Region = West as a CONTEXT filter: applied first, so Top 3 is computed inside the West west = store_sales [ store_sales [ "region" ] == "West" ] print ( " 
 Region = West in context, then Top 3:" ) print ( west . nlargest ( 3 , "sales" ) . to_string ( index = False )) Top 3 stores overall: region store sales South Riverbend 19658.5 North Frostford 18022.4 East Dawnport 17953.8 Top 3 filter AND Region = West (same step): (no rows: none of the overall top 3 is in the West) Region = West in context, then Top 3: region store sales West Sunsetvale 17195.4 West Cliffton 16787.6 West Westfall 16665.3 Predict, then run (above). Before running, guess how many stores the first approach returns. Whatever the count, it answers a different question ("which of the chain's top 3 are in the West?"). Add to Context makes the region filter run first, so the Top 3 is chosen within the West. Dimension filter on a measure, or measure filter? ¶ A second classic surprise: "show me the loss-making sub-categories". Two different filters give two different answers. # Measure filter: aggregate first (SUM(Profit) per sub-category), then keep the negative ones sub = orders . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "profit" ] . sum () print ( "Sub-categories whose TOTAL profit is negative (measure filter on SUM):" ) print ( sub [ sub < 0 ] . round ( 0 ) . to_string () or " none" , " 
 " ) # Row-level filter: keep only loss-making order lines, then aggregate loss_rows = orders [ orders [ "profit" ] < 0 ] . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "profit" ] . sum () print ( "Sub-categories with ANY loss-making order lines (row filter, then SUM):" ) print ( loss_rows . round ( 0 ) . sort_values () . to_string ()) Sub-categories whose TOTAL profit is negative (measure filter on SUM): sub_category Board games -168.0 Sub-categories with ANY loss-making order lines (row filter, then SUM): sub_category Board games -2279.0 The first answers "which sub-categories lose money overall?"; the second answers "where do loss-making lines occur, and how much do they lose?". In Tableau, dragging a measure to Filters asks how to aggregate it ( Sum gives the first; All values filters rows and gives the second). Say which one you mean. Misconception Better view "Filters are applied in the order I add them." Tableau applies them by type , in the fixed order above. "Top N always gives me the top N of what I see." Only if the other filters are in context . "Filtering never changes a percentage of total." Percent of total is a table calculation, computed after filters, so it re-bases to what is left. Part 6: Calculated fields and table calculations ¶ Analysis → Create Calculated Field (or right-click in the Data pane) opens the editor. A calculation is either row-level (computed for each row, then aggregated like any field) or aggregate (computed from aggregates, at the level of detail of the view). You cannot mix the two in one expression without aggregating everything: Tableau will report that it cannot mix aggregate and non-aggregate arguments . Profit ratio: the morning's ratio problem again ¶ Calculation Type What it gives [Profit] / [Sales] then AVG Row-level, then averaged The mean of the line-by-line margins: every line counts equally SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) Aggregate Total profit ÷ total sales: every dollar counts equally orders [ "line_margin" ] = orders [ "profit" ] / orders [ "sales" ] # row-level calculated field g = orders . groupby ( "category" ) compare = pd . DataFrame ({ "AVG([Profit]/[Sales])" : g [ "line_margin" ] . mean (), "SUM([Profit])/SUM([Sales])" : g [ "profit" ] . sum () / g [ "sales" ] . sum (), }) print ( compare . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) . to_string ()) AVG([Profit]/[Sales]) SUM([Profit])/SUM([Sales]) category Books 36.8% 37.0% Gifts 43.4% 25.6% Stationery 51.7% 48.0% The usual business definition of profit ratio is the aggregate one, SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) : a large order matters more than a small one. Format it as a percentage (right-click → Default Properties → Number Format ). Logic, dates and strings ¶ Three more patterns you will use often, with their pandas mirrors: // Discount band (row-level, a new dimension) IF [Discount] = 0 THEN "None" ELSEIF [Discount] <= 0.2 THEN "Up to 20%" ELSE "Over 20%" END // Days since the customer's first order (an LOD inside a row-level calculation) DATEDIFF('day', {FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])}, [Order Date]) // Profitable? (aggregate, at the level of the view) IF SUM([Profit]) >= 0 THEN "Profit" ELSE "Loss" END orders [ "discount_band" ] = pd . cut ( orders [ "discount" ], [ - 0.01 , 0 , 0.2 , 1 ], labels = [ "None" , "Up to 20%" , "Over 20%" ]) first = orders . groupby ( "customer_id" )[ "order_date" ] . transform ( "min" ) orders [ "days_since_first" ] = ( orders [ "order_date" ] - first ) . dt . days band = orders . groupby ( "discount_band" , observed = True ) . agg ( lines = ( "sales" , "size" ), sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" )) band [ "profit_ratio" ] = band [ "profit" ] / band [ "sales" ] print ( band . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) lines sales profit profit_ratio discount_band None 3989 138470.0 58209.77 0.42 Up to 20% 1808 56783.9 18004.89 0.32 Over 20% 163 11174.4 -2279.04 -0.20 Table calculations ¶ A table calculation is computed on the aggregated table in the view , after filters: running totals, differences, percent of total, rank, moving average. Right-click a measure pill → Quick Table Calculation . The key setting is Compute Using (Table across, Table down, Pane, or a specific dimension): it decides which marks are added up or compared. A wrong Compute Using is the most common table-calculation error. monthly = orders . set_index ( "order_date" )[ "sales" ] . resample ( "MS" ) . sum () . to_frame ( "sales" ) monthly [ "running_total" ] = monthly [ "sales" ] . groupby ( monthly . index . year ) . cumsum () # Running total, restarting each year monthly [ "pct_of_year" ] = monthly [ "sales" ] / monthly [ "sales" ] . groupby ( monthly . index . year ) . transform ( "sum" ) # Percent of total monthly [ "yoy_change" ] = monthly [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( 12 ) # Percent difference from a year earlier print ( monthly . tail ( 6 ) . round ( 3 ) . to_string ()) sales running_total pct_of_year yoy_change order_date 2025-07-01 5267.5 35941.8 0.080 -0.083 2025-08-01 5158.9 41100.7 0.078 0.006 2025-09-01 5819.8 46920.5 0.088 -0.148 2025-10-01 4598.5 51519.0 0.070 -0.212 2025-11-01 5297.8 56816.8 0.080 -0.070 2025-12-01 9227.2 66044.0 0.140 0.251 Each of these is a choice of what to compute along (here, months within a year) and what to restart on (each year). In Tableau that choice is Compute Using . Misconception Better view "A calculated field is computed on the chart." Row-level calculations are computed on the data rows; only aggregate calculations and table calculations work on the view. "Percent of total is fixed." It is a table calculation: it changes when you filter or change Compute Using . Part 7: Maps ¶ Tableau recognises fields with a geographic role (Country/Region, State/Province, City, Postal Code…) and shows a globe icon next to them. Double-clicking a geographic field creates a map with Latitude and Longitude (generated) on the shelves. A symbol map (mark type Circle or Automatic) puts a dot on each location; size can show a total. A filled map (mark type Map ) shades each area; colour shows a measure. Field names change between Tableau versions and data sources: the same field may be called State in one and State/Province in another, and Country or Country/Region . If a field has no globe icon, right-click it → Geographic Role and choose the right role. If Tableau cannot place some names, an indicator such as "3 unknown" appears at the bottom right of the map; click it to fix or filter them. Two cautions from this morning: A filled map gives large areas more visual weight regardless of their values, and small areas (city states, small provinces) almost disappear. Pair a map with a sorted bar chart when exact comparison matters. A filled map of totals is often just a map of population or of store count. For a fair comparison, map a rate (profit ratio, sales per store, complaints per customer). Part 8: Dashboards, actions and a design checklist ¶ Building a dashboard ¶ New Dashboard (the icon next to New Worksheet at the bottom). Set Size : Fixed size (a set width and height; predictable when printing or sharing), Automatic (fills whatever window it is in) or Range (between a minimum and maximum). Recent versions start with a fixed size. Drag sheets from the Sheets list onto the canvas. By default objects are tiled into layout containers; hold Shift or choose Floating to place an object freely. Add text (a title that states the purpose, an instruction such as "Click a region to filter"), and remove legends and filter cards you do not need. Actions: making views talk to each other ¶ Dashboard → Actions → Add Action creates links between sheets: Action What it does Typical use Filter Selecting marks in a source sheet filters target sheets Click a region → the trend and bar charts show only that region Highlight Selecting marks highlights related marks elsewhere, greying the rest Keep the context visible while emphasising one item Go to URL / Go to Sheet Opens a web page or another sheet Drill to a detail dashboard Change Parameter / Change Set Values Updates a parameter or set from a selection More advanced what-if and comparison designs Each action has a source sheet, target sheets, a trigger ( Hover , Select or Menu ), and a rule for what happens when the selection is cleared : Keep filtered values , Show all values or Exclude all values . The quick way to make a filter action: click a sheet on the dashboard, then click the Use as Filter icon (a small funnel) on the sheet's border. That creates a filter action from that sheet to all others on the dashboard, run on Select , showing all values when cleared. Check it under Dashboard → Actions . A Python mirror of a filter action ¶ The function below plays the role of a dashboard: three linked views of Harbour Books. Calling it with a region is like clicking that region in a source sheet. Note the diverging colour scale centred at zero for profit. def harbour_dashboard ( region = None ): data = orders if region is None else orders [ orders [ "region" ] == region ] label = "All regions" if region is None else region fig = plt . figure ( figsize = ( 13 , 5.5 )) gs = fig . add_gridspec ( 2 , 2 , width_ratios = [ 1 , 1.15 ], hspace = 0.55 , wspace = 0.35 ) # View 1: the source sheet (regions), with the selection highlighted ax = fig . add_subplot ( gs [ 0 , 0 ]) reg = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum () . sort_values () ax . barh ( reg . index , reg . values / 1000 , color = [ OI [ "blue" ] if ( region is None or r == region ) else "#E5E5E5" for r in reg . index ]) ax . set_title ( "Sales by region (click to filter)" ); ax . set_xlabel ( "Sales (thousand USD)" ) # View 2: monthly trend, continuous month ax = fig . add_subplot ( gs [ 1 , 0 ]) trend = data . set_index ( "order_date" )[ "sales" ] . resample ( "MS" ) . sum () ax . plot ( trend . index , trend . values / 1000 , color = OI [ "blue" ]) ax . set_title ( f "Monthly sales: { label } " ); ax . set_ylabel ( "Thousand USD" ) ax . xaxis . set_major_locator ( mdates . YearLocator ()) ax . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( mdates . DateFormatter ( "%Y" )) # View 3: sales by sub-category (length), coloured by profit (diverging, centred at 0) ax = fig . add_subplot ( gs [:, 1 ]) sub = data . groupby ( "sub_category" ) . agg ( sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" )) . sort_values ( "sales" ) lim = max ( abs ( sub [ "profit" ] . min ()), abs ( sub [ "profit" ] . max ())) norm = mcolors . TwoSlopeNorm ( vmin =- lim , vcenter = 0 , vmax = lim ) cmap = plt . get_cmap ( "PuOr" ) ax . barh ( sub . index , sub [ "sales" ] / 1000 , color = cmap ( norm ( sub [ "profit" ]))) ax . set_title ( f "Sales by sub-category, coloured by profit: { label } " ); ax . set_xlabel ( "Sales (thousand USD)" ) sm = plt . cm . ScalarMappable ( norm = norm , cmap = cmap ) fig . colorbar ( sm , ax = ax , label = "SUM(Profit), USD (orange = loss)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Harbour Books dashboard (synthetic data)" , x = 0.02 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) plt . show () harbour_dashboard () harbour_dashboard ( "East" ) # like clicking East in the region view Discuss. In the right-hand chart, bar length shows sales and colour shows profit. What can a manager see with both encodings that they could not see from length alone? Which encoding will a hurried reader look at first, and what might they miss? (This morning's lecture, Part 2, and the reading packet's section on dual encoding will help.) Notice also: after filtering, the colour scale was recomputed from the filtered data, so the same shade can mean different amounts in the two pictures. Tableau behaves the same way unless you fix the colour range ( Edit Colors → Advanced → Start / End ). When comparing filtered views, read the values (tooltip or labels), not just the shade. Dashboard design checklist ¶ Before you publish or print a dashboard, check: Purpose: one sentence says who it is for and which decision it supports; the title says it. Priority: the most important view or KPI is top-left; overview first, detail below. Few views: three to five, each with a message title. Chart choice: each view matches its question (Part 1 of the morning lecture); bars sorted when ranking. Colour: one meaning per colour across the dashboard; diverging measures centred at zero; colour-blind safe; never colour alone. Numbers: units and formats (US dollars, percentages) set in Default Properties ; sensible rounding. Interactivity: actions tested; the instruction ("click a state…") is visible; clearing a selection returns to the full view. Tooltips: edited to read like a sentence, with units. Size: fixed size when the output is a PDF or a slide; checked at the size readers will use. Static state: before printing or exporting, the selection is cleared so the output shows the intended (usually unfiltered) view. Test: someone who did not build it can answer the intended question in under a minute. Part 9: Lab 2 briefing ¶ In Lab 2 (periods 7 and 8) you build an executive summary dashboard in Tableau Desktop from Sample – Superstore : a monthly sales trend, a filled map of profit by state, and sales by sub-category coloured by profit, linked so that clicking a state filters the other two. You then use it to answer GAP's questions in a separate document and submit one combined PDF. What from this lecture you will need: Lab step Concept The trend uses the second Month option, and the pill turns green Part 2: continuous date values make a timeline The map uses the Map mark type with Profit on Color Parts 4 and 7: filled map, diverging colour centred at zero Bars sorted, Profit on Color Morning Part 1 (sorting) and Part 2 (two encodings) The map becomes a filter for the other sheets Part 8: Use as Filter creates a filter action Print with nothing selected Part 8 checklist: clear the selection The Lab 2 guide lists the steps, the version differences in Superstore (for example State or State/Province ) and the known pitfalls. Your answers must come from your own dashboard: Superstore's figures differ between Tableau versions. Part 10: Assignment 1 briefing: reading box plots and regression lines ¶ Assignment 1 (periods 9 and 10, due Sunday 15 November) asks you to run a given script on a restaurant's transaction data and write a four-section business report about its tables and three figures: a bar chart, a box plot and a scatter plot with a regression line . The Assignment 1 guide gives the structure and report-writing advice. Here we practise the two harder readings on penguins, so the skill transfers but the answers do not. Reading a box plot in sentences ¶ fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.8 )) sns . boxplot ( data = penguins , x = "species" , y = "flipper_length_mm" , order = [ "Adelie" , "Chinstrap" , "Gentoo" ], color = OI [ "sky" ], width = 0.5 , ax = ax ) ax . set_xlabel ( "" ); ax . set_ylabel ( "Flipper length (mm)" ) ax . set_title ( "Flipper length by species" ) plt . show () stats = penguins . groupby ( "species" )[ "flipper_length_mm" ] . describe ()[[ "count" , "25%" , "50%" , "75%" ]] stats [ "IQR" ] = stats [ "75%" ] - stats [ "25%" ] print ( stats . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) count 25% 50% 75% IQR species Adelie 146.0 186.0 190.0 195.0 9.0 Chinstrap 68.0 191.0 196.0 201.0 10.0 Gentoo 119.0 212.0 216.0 221.5 9.5 A model paragraph (notice the numbers, the units and the comparison): The typical Gentoo penguin has a flipper about 25 mm longer than the typical Adelie (medians of 216 mm and 190 mm). The middle half of each species spans only about 9 to 10 mm (the interquartile ranges), so the boxes do not overlap and flipper length alone separates Gentoo from the other two species well. Chinstrap and Adelie overlap heavily and could not be told apart by this measure. A few birds lie beyond the whiskers; they are unusual for their species rather than errors. The checklist behind it: (1) compare the medians with units; (2) compare the spreads (IQR, whisker length); (3) say whether the boxes overlap and what that means for the decision; (4) mention outliers and what they might be; (5) say how many observations each box rests on if they differ a lot. Reading a regression line in sentences ¶ gentoo = penguins [ penguins [ "species" ] == "Gentoo" ] slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( gentoo [ "flipper_length_mm" ], gentoo [ "body_mass_g" ], 1 ) r = gentoo [ "flipper_length_mm" ] . corr ( gentoo [ "body_mass_g" ]) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) sns . regplot ( data = gentoo , x = "flipper_length_mm" , y = "body_mass_g" , ax = ax , seed = 0 , # seed: the band is bootstrapped scatter_kws = { "alpha" : 0.5 , "color" : OI [ "green" ]}, line_kws = { "color" : "black" }) ax . set_xlabel ( "Flipper length (mm)" ); ax . set_ylabel ( "Body mass (g)" ) ax . set_title ( "Gentoo penguins: longer flippers, heavier birds" ) plt . show () print ( f "slope = { slope : .1f } g per mm, intercept = { intercept : .0f } g, r = { r : .2f } , n = { len ( gentoo ) } " ) slope = 54.2 g per mm, intercept = -6674 g, r = 0.71, n = 119 A model paragraph: Among Gentoo penguins, each extra millimetre of flipper length goes with about 54 g more body mass on average (the slope of the fitted line), across flippers from about 205 to 230 mm. The points scatter widely around the line (r ≈ 0.7), so flipper length gives a useful but rough guide to an individual bird's mass. The relationship is an association: it does not show that longer flippers cause extra weight; both grow with the bird's overall size. The checklist: (1) state the slope in words with both units ("per mm", "per dollar"); (2) give the range of x over which it holds; do not extrapolate far beyond it; (3) say how tightly the points follow the line (r, or "wide scatter"); (4) say association, not causation , and name what else could explain it; (5) the shaded band around a seaborn regression line is a confidence band for the line , not a range for individual points. If the script you are given does not print the slope, you can read it from the chart: pick two points on the line far apart and divide the rise by the run. Do not copy these paragraphs into Assignment 1: they are about penguins. Use the checklists on your own figures. Part 11: Practice, quiz and summary ¶ Practice ¶ Core ¶ Core 1. In Tableau with any data source (Superstore is fine for practice; do this after Lab 2), make the same view twice: once with discrete MONTH(Order Date) and once with continuous MONTH(Order Date). Write one question each view answers. Core 2. Using orders , compute total sales and profit ratio ( SUM/SUM ) for each category within each region (level of detail = region × category). Which combination has the lowest profit ratio? Core 3. Using orders , find the top 2 sub-categories by sales within the South (filter first, then rank, as a context filter would), and compare them with the top 2 for the whole chain. Stretch ¶ Stretch 1. Write the Tableau calculation for "share of a region's sales that came from discounted lines" and mirror it in pandas. Stretch 2. Change harbour_dashboard so that the colour scale is fixed across all regions (compute lim from the full data). Compare the East view with the one above. Stretch 3. Mirror an EXCLUDE expression: for each region × category mark, show the region's total sales next to the category's sales, and the category's share of its region. Challenge ¶ Challenge 1. Using first_order_year , build a cohort table: rows are the first-order year, columns are order years, values are distinct customers who ordered. What does the table say about customer retention at Harbour Books? Challenge 2. Add a highlight behaviour to harbour_dashboard : instead of filtering the trend to one region, draw all four regions' trends in grey and the selected one in colour. When is highlight better than filter for a manager? Quiz ¶ What is the difference between a dimension and a measure? Give one numeric field that should be a dimension. What do blue and green pills mean? What does each create on the Columns shelf? A line chart of monthly sales shows only 12 points for three years of data. What happened, and how do you fix it? What sets the level of detail of a view? What happens to the marks when you drag a dimension onto Detail? Why might AVG([Sales]) not answer "what does an average customer spend?" In which order does Tableau apply context filters, dimension filters and measure filters? Why does this matter for Top N? Write the aggregate calculation for profit ratio, and explain why it differs from AVG([Profit]/[Sales]) . What does Compute Using control in a table calculation? What does the Use as Filter icon create, and where can you edit it? Give two reasons to clear the selection and use a fixed size before printing a dashboard to PDF. In one sentence each, describe what the slope of a regression line and the box of a box plot tell a manager. Summary ¶ Idea Remember Building blocks Data source → worksheets → dashboard → story; save .twbx to share Roles Dimensions group, measures aggregate; IDs and years are usually dimensions Pill colour Blue = discrete → headers; green = continuous → axis. Date parts vs date values Aggregation SUM by default; AVG is per row; COUNTD for distinct customers Level of detail Set by the dimensions in the view; FIXED / INCLUDE / EXCLUDE change it for one calculation Marks Mark type, Color, Size, Label, Detail, Tooltip; diverging colour centred at zero Filters Extract → data source → context → FIXED/Top N → dimension → INCLUDE/EXCLUDE → measure → table calcs Calculations Row-level vs aggregate; profit ratio = SUM/SUM; table calculations depend on Compute Using Maps Geographic roles; field names vary by version; filled maps favour big areas; map rates Dashboards Few views, clear purpose, visible instructions; filter and highlight actions; clear the selection before export Reports Box plot: medians, IQR, overlap, outliers. Regression: slope with units, range, scatter, association not cause Next: the Lab 2 guide (periods 7 and 8) and the Assignment 1 guide (periods 9 and 10). Earlier today: Visualising and communicating data . For the facilitator ¶ This notebook fills periods P5–P6 of Day 2 and the Assignment 1 briefing in P9. It is best taught with Tableau Desktop on the projector: demonstrate each concept in Tableau on a data source other than Superstore (for example a CSV of the orders table, exported with orders.to_csv("harbour_books.csv", index=False) ), then show the Python mirror. No Lab 2 or Assignment 1 answers are given here. Period Minutes Content Notes P5 10 Part 1: building blocks and the workspace Open Tableau; name each area of the screen P5 15 Part 2: dimensions, measures, discrete and continuous dates Build both date views live; ask the prediction about YEAR + MONTH as headers P5 10 Part 3: aggregation, level of detail, LOD expressions Change SUM to AVG and COUNTD live; drag a dimension to Detail P5 10 Part 4: the Marks card Set the profit colour centre to 0 live P6 12 Part 5: filters and the Top N surprise Show the empty or short result, then Add to Context P6 10 Part 6: calculated fields, profit ratio, table calculations Trigger the "cannot mix aggregate" error on purpose P6 5 Part 7: maps and geographic roles Mention State vs State/Province P6 10 Part 8: dashboard, Use as Filter, checklist Build a two-sheet dashboard with an action in five minutes P6 8 Part 9: Lab 2 briefing Walk through the guide's pitfalls; check every student has Tableau activated P7–P8 90 Lab 2 Circulate; check the green Month pill, the Map mark type and the filter action P9 30 Part 10: Assignment 1 briefing, box plots and regression lines Read the two penguin paragraphs aloud; students mark the checklist items in them P9 15 The Assignment 1 guide : headings, routes, pitfalls Everyone runs Route A or B before P10 P10 45 Assignment 1 studio Students draft their outline using the four headings; answer questions without giving values Practice and quiz are for self-study or faster groups.
docs.title: Lecture: Tableau concepts and dashboards

docs.text: Periods 5 and 6 of Day 2, plus the Assignment 1 briefing in period 9. The ideas that make Tableau behave the way it does: dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous fields, aggregation and level of detail, the Marks card, filters and the order in which Tableau applies them, calculated fields, maps and dashboard actions. Each idea is explained in Tableau terms and then mirrored in Python, so you can see exactly what Tableau computes. Tableau is a tool you learn by clicking, so this lecture is meant to be taught with Tableau Desktop open on the projector. The Python mirrors use a synthetic bookshop chain , "Harbour Books", made inside the notebook, and the penguins data. Lab 2 uses Tableau's Sample – Superstore; this lecture deliberately does not , and asks different questions, so that you build and read your own dashboard in the lab. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder. Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook and data/penguins.csv , run %pip install seaborn in a first cell, and change "data/penguins.csv" to "penguins.csv" .
docs.title: Day 2 lecture: Tableau concepts and dashboards

docs.text: Explain the difference between dimensions and measures , and between discrete (blue) and continuous (green) fields, and predict what each does to a view. Explain aggregation and the level of detail of a view, and when a number changes because the level of detail changed. Use the Marks card (mark type, Color, Size, Label, Detail, Tooltip) on purpose. Apply filters and explain Tableau's order of operations , including why a Top N filter can give a surprising answer. Write calculated fields at row level and aggregate level, and use table calculations . Build a dashboard with filter and highlight actions , and check it against a design checklist . Read a box plot and a regression line in words a manager understands (for Assignment 1). Part Topic Period 1 Tableau's building blocks P5 2 Dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous P5 3 Aggregation and level of detail P5 4 The Marks card P5 5 Filters and the order of operations P6 6 Calculated fields and table calculations P6 7 Maps P6 8 Dashboards, actions and a design checklist P6 9 Lab 2 briefing P6 10 Assignment 1 briefing: reading box plots and regression lines P9 11 Practice, quiz and summary Self-study Reading Read Chapter 2 of the course reading packet on dual encoding (a chart that carries two variables at once) and on what changes when static charts become a linked, interactive dashboard. Its review questions 3 and 4 are good preparation for Lab 2.
docs.title: What you will be able to do

docs.text: Tableau object What it is Python mirror Data source A connection to a file or database (Excel, CSV, a server), with any joins or relationships between tables pd.read_csv(...) , merge Live or extract Query the source each time, or take a fast snapshot ( .hyper ) Reading the file again, or keeping a DataFrame in memory Worksheet One view (chart or table) built by dragging fields onto shelves One groupby plus one plot Dashboard Several worksheets (plus text, images, filters) arranged on one canvas, optionally linked by actions A figure with several panels and a function that redraws them Story A sequence of sheets or dashboards with captions, like slides A report Workbook The file holding all of the above: .twb (no data) or .twbx ( packaged , data included) The notebook The workspace has the Data pane on the left (fields), the Columns and Rows shelves at the top, the Marks card and the Filters and Pages shelves beside the view, Show Me at the top right, and tabs at the bottom for sheets, dashboards and stories. Save as .twbx when you send a workbook to someone else, so the data travels with it. Below is the synthetic data that the Python mirrors use. One row is one order line : one product sub-category in one order. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import matplotlib.colors as mcolors import matplotlib.dates as mdates import seaborn as sns plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.dpi" : 100 , "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlesize" : 11 }) OI = { "orange" : "#E69F00" , "sky" : "#56B4E9" , "green" : "#009E73" , "blue" : "#0072B2" , "vermillion" : "#D55E00" , "purple" : "#CC79A7" } GREY = "#B0B0B0" # Harbour Books: a fictional chain of 12 bookshops in four regions (synthetic data) rng = np . random . default_rng ( 300 ) stores = pd . DataFrame ({ "region" : np . repeat ([ "North" , "South" , "East" , "West" ], 3 ), "store" : [ "Pinefield" , "Stonebridge" , "Frostford" , "Palmhaven" , "Suncove" , "Riverbend" , "Dawnport" , "Eastmere" , "Harbourside" , "Westfall" , "Sunsetvale" , "Cliffton" ], }) products = pd . DataFrame ({ "category" : [ "Books" ] * 3 + [ "Stationery" ] * 3 + [ "Gifts" ] * 3 , "sub_category" : [ "Fiction" , "Non-fiction" , "Children's" , "Notebooks" , "Pens" , "Art supplies" , "Board games" , "Mugs" , "Cards" ], "unit_price" : [ 14 , 18 , 11 , 6 , 3 , 15 , 32 , 12 , 4 ], "cost_share" : [ 0.62 , 0.60 , 0.58 , 0.45 , 0.40 , 0.55 , 0.78 , 0.50 , 0.35 ], "weight" : [ 22 , 14 , 14 , 10 , 8 , 6 , 6 , 8 , 12 ], }) n = 9000 dates = pd . to_datetime ( "2023-01-01" ) + pd . to_timedelta ( rng . integers ( 0 , 1096 , n ), unit = "D" ) season = 1 + 0.6 * ( dates . month == 12 ) + 0.25 * ( dates . month == 9 ) # December and back-to-school keep = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1.6 , n ) < season orders = pd . DataFrame ({ "order_date" : dates [ keep ]}) m = len ( orders ) orders [ "customer_id" ] = rng . integers ( 1 , 1801 , m ) orders = orders . join ( stores . sample ( m , replace = True , random_state = 1 ) . reset_index ( drop = True )) prod = products . sample ( m , replace = True , weights = "weight" , random_state = 2 ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) orders = orders . join ( prod [[ "category" , "sub_category" , "unit_price" , "cost_share" ]]) orders [ "quantity" ] = rng . integers ( 1 , 6 , m ) games = orders [ "sub_category" ] == "Board games" orders [ "discount" ] = np . where ( games , rng . choice ([ 0 , 0.2 , 0.3 , 0.4 ], m , p = [ 0.3 , 0.2 , 0.25 , 0.25 ]), rng . choice ([ 0 , 0.1 , 0.2 ], m , p = [ 0.7 , 0.2 , 0.1 ])) list_value = orders [ "quantity" ] * orders [ "unit_price" ] orders [ "sales" ] = ( list_value * ( 1 - orders [ "discount" ])) . round ( 2 ) # US dollars orders [ "profit" ] = ( orders [ "sales" ] - list_value * orders [ "cost_share" ]) . round ( 2 ) # US dollars orders = orders . drop ( columns = [ "unit_price" , "cost_share" ]) . sort_values ( "order_date" ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) print ( orders . shape ) orders . head () (5960, 10) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } order_date customer_id region store category sub_category quantity discount sales profit 0 2023-01-01 261 South Riverbend Stationery Notebooks 3 0.0 18.0 9.90 1 2023-01-01 47 West Sunsetvale Books Children's 4 0.0 44.0 18.48 2 2023-01-01 654 East Eastmere Books Fiction 1 0.0 14.0 5.32 3 2023-01-01 67 North Frostford Books Fiction 2 0.0 28.0 10.64 4 2023-01-01 1301 West Westfall Stationery Art supplies 2 0.0 30.0 13.50
docs.title: Part 1: Tableau's building blocks
Part 2: Dimensions and measures, discrete and continuous

docs.text: When Tableau connects to data it sorts each field into one of two roles: A dimension is a field you group or slice by : region, store, category, order date. Dimensions set how many marks the view has. A measure is a field you aggregate : sales, profit, quantity. Measures are summed (or averaged, counted…) within each group. Dragging Region to Rows and Sales to Columns gives a bar per region showing SUM(Sales) . That is exactly a groupby : # Tableau: Region on Rows, SUM(Sales) on Columns by_region = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum () . sort_values () print ( by_region . round ( 0 )) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 2.8 )) ax . barh ( by_region . index , by_region . values , color = GREY ) ax . set_xlabel ( "SUM(Sales), US dollars" ) ax . set_title ( "Region on Rows, SUM(Sales) on Columns" ) plt . show () region West 50648.0 North 50959.0 East 50985.0 South 53836.0 Name: sales, dtype: float64 The role is a default , not a law. A number such as a store's postcode or a customer ID is stored as a number but is really a label: convert it to a dimension (drag it above the line in the Data pane, or right-click → Convert to Dimension ). The rule of thumb: if adding it up makes no sense, it is a dimension.
docs.title: Dimensions and measures

docs.text: The pill colour tells you something different from the role: Discrete (blue) values are separate and distinct. On a shelf, a discrete field creates headers (a label for each value), and on Color it creates a categorical palette. Continuous (green) values form an unbroken range. On a shelf, a continuous field creates an axis , and on Color a gradient . Discrete (blue) Continuous (green) Dimension Region, Category; date parts such as MONTH(Order Date) = "May" Date values such as MONTH(Order Date) = "May 2024"; a numeric dimension made continuous Measure SUM(Sales) turned discrete: a header per value, like a text table SUM(Sales): an axis (the usual case) The most important case in practice is the date . Right-click a date pill and you see two lists of Year, Quarter, Month…: the upper list gives date parts (discrete), which combine the same month from every year into one header; the lower list gives date values (continuous), which keep each month of each year as its own point on a timeline. Compare them on our synthetic data: fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 13 , 3.8 )) # Discrete date part: MONTH(Order Date) as a blue pill -> 12 headers, every year combined part = orders . groupby ( orders [ "order_date" ] . dt . month )[ "sales" ] . sum () axes [ 0 ] . bar ( pd . to_datetime ( part . index , format = "%m" ) . strftime ( "%b" ), part . values / 1000 , color = OI [ "sky" ]) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Discrete MONTH: 12 headers, all years added together" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand USD)" ) # Continuous date value: MONTH(Order Date) as a green pill -> 36 points on a timeline value = orders . set_index ( "order_date" )[ "sales" ] . resample ( "MS" ) . sum () axes [ 1 ] . plot ( value . index , value . values / 1000 , color = OI [ "blue" ], lw = 2 ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Continuous MONTH: one point per month of each year" ) axes [ 1 ] . xaxis . set_major_locator ( mdates . YearLocator ()) axes [ 1 ] . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( mdates . DateFormatter ( "%Y" )) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Both are correct answers to different questions. The left chart answers "Which month of the year is usually strongest?" (seasonality); the right chart answers "How did sales move over time?" (trend, and when something unusual happened). A trend line needs the continuous version: with the discrete version, an unusual month in one year is diluted by adding it to the same month of the other years. Predict, then run. If you put discrete YEAR and discrete MONTH next to each other on Columns, what would the chart look like, and how would it differ from the continuous version? (Hint: headers, not an axis.)
docs.title: Discrete (blue) and continuous (green)

docs.text: Misconception Better view "Blue means dimension, green means measure." Blue means discrete , green means continuous . Most dimensions are discrete and most measures continuous, which is why the two get confused. "Dates are always continuous." A date can be either; you choose with the pill's menu. "Numbers are measures." IDs, postcodes and years are numbers you group by, so they are dimensions.
docs.title: Misconceptions
Part 3: Aggregation and level of detail

docs.text: A measure on a shelf is always aggregated: SUM by default, changeable from the pill's menu to AVG, MEDIAN, COUNT, COUNTD (count distinct), MIN, MAX and others. Each answers a different question: summary = orders . groupby ( "region" ) . agg ( SUM_sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), AVG_sales_per_line = ( "sales" , "mean" ), MEDIAN_sales_per_line = ( "sales" , "median" ), COUNT_lines = ( "sales" , "size" ), COUNTD_customers = ( "customer_id" , "nunique" ), ) . round ( 2 ) print ( summary . to_string ()) SUM_sales AVG_sales_per_line MEDIAN_sales_per_line COUNT_lines COUNTD_customers region East 50984.7 33.81 28.0 1508 1019 North 50959.1 34.78 28.0 1465 1026 South 53836.2 35.44 28.0 1519 1014 West 50648.3 34.50 28.0 1468 994 AVG(Sales) is the average order line , not the average order or the average customer: an aggregate always averages over the rows of the data source. If you need "sales per customer", that is SUM(Sales) / COUNTD(Customer ID) , which is a different number again.
docs.title: Aggregation

docs.text:
The level of detail (LOD) of a view is set by the dimensions in it (on Rows, Columns and the Marks card). Every aggregate is computed once per combination of those dimensions. Add a dimension and each mark splits into several smaller marks; the totals are re-cut, not changed. lod_1 = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "profit" ] . sum () lod_2 = orders . groupby ([ "region" , "category" ])[ "profit" ] . sum () . unstack () print ( "Level of detail = Region: 
 " , lod_1 . round ( 0 ), " 
 " ) print ( "Level of detail = Region x Category: 
 " , lod_2 . round ( 0 )) print ( " 
 Row sums of the second table equal the first:" , np . allclose ( lod_2 . sum ( axis = 1 ), lod_1 )) Level of detail = Region: region East 18434.0 North 18264.0 South 19252.0 West 17986.0 Name: profit, dtype: float64 Level of detail = Region x Category: category Books Gifts Stationery region East 11739.0 3333.0 3363.0 North 11559.0 3095.0 3610.0 South 12032.0 3420.0 3800.0 West 11623.0 3031.0 3332.0 Row sums of the second table equal the first: True Disaggregating. Unticking Analysis → Aggregate Measures shows every row as its own mark, which is what you want for a scatter of individual records. Here, discount against profit per order line: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) jit = np . random . default_rng ( 1 ) . uniform ( - 0.012 , 0.012 , len ( orders )) ax . scatter ( orders [ "discount" ] + jit , orders [ "profit" ], s = 5 , alpha = 0.25 , color = OI [ "blue" ]) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.8 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Discount (share of list price)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Profit per order line (USD)" ) ax . set_title ( "Disaggregated: one mark per order line" ) plt . show ()
docs.title: Level of detail

docs.text: Sometimes you need a number computed at a different level from the view. Tableau's LOD expressions do this: {FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])} : each customer's first order date, whatever the view shows. {INCLUDE [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])} : compute per customer, then aggregate up to the view (for example the average customer's spend per region). {EXCLUDE [Category] : SUM([Sales])} : ignore a dimension that is in the view (for example a region total next to each category). In pandas, FIXED is a groupby(...).transform(...) : a group result written back to every row. # {FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])} -> first-order year (a cohort) on every row orders [ "first_order_year" ] = orders . groupby ( "customer_id" )[ "order_date" ] . transform ( "min" ) . dt . year # {INCLUDE [Customer ID] : SUM([Sales])}, then AVG in the view: average spend per customer, by region per_customer = orders . groupby ([ "region" , "customer_id" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () print ( "Average 3-year spend per customer in each region (USD):" ) print ( per_customer . groupby ( "region" ) . mean () . round ( 2 )) print ( " \n Customers by the year of their first order:" ) print ( orders . drop_duplicates ( "customer_id" )[ "first_order_year" ] . value_counts () . sort_index ()) Average 3-year spend per customer in each region (USD): region East 50.03 North 49.67 South 53.09 West 50.95 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Customers by the year of their first order: first_order_year 2023 1183 2024 407 2025 135 Name: count, dtype: int64 Misconception Better view "AVG(Sales) is the average sale per customer." It is the average per row of the data source, here per order line. "Adding a dimension changes the totals." It splits marks; the grand total is the same unless a filter or LOD calculation changes it.
docs.title: Level of detail expressions

docs.text: The Marks card controls how each mark looks. Its parts map directly onto the encodings from this morning's lecture: Marks card What it encodes matplotlib / seaborn mirror Mark type (Automatic, Bar, Line, Area, Circle, Square, Shape, Text, Map, Pie, Gantt bar, Polygon, Density) The kind of mark bar , plot , scatter , text … Color A dimension (categorical palette) or a measure (sequential or diverging gradient) hue= , c= with a colormap Size A measure, as mark area size= , s= Label Text on each mark ax.text , bar_label Detail Splits marks by a dimension without encoding it visually Adding a column to groupby Tooltip Text shown on hover (no static equivalent) Shape , Path , Angle Shape per category; drawing order of a line; pie slice angle marker= , sort order, pie Automatic chooses a mark type from the fields: a date on Columns gives a line, a dimension and a measure give bars, two measures give circles, a geographic field gives a map. Automatic is a guess; choose deliberately. Here is one view with Color, Size, Detail and Label all in use, on the penguins data: penguins = pd . read_csv ( "data/penguins.csv" ) . dropna () # Route A: "penguins.csv" # Detail = island and species: one mark per island-species pair (no visual encoding of island itself) marks = penguins . groupby ([ "species" , "island" ]) . agg ( flipper = ( "flipper_length_mm" , "mean" ), mass = ( "body_mass_g" , "mean" ), birds = ( "body_mass_g" , "size" )) . reset_index () sp_col = { "Adelie" : OI [ "orange" ], "Chinstrap" : OI [ "purple" ], "Gentoo" : OI [ "green" ]} fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) ax . scatter ( marks [ "flipper" ], marks [ "mass" ], s = marks [ "birds" ] * 6 , # Size = COUNT color = marks [ "species" ] . map ( sp_col ), alpha = 0.8 ) # Color = species offsets = { "Biscoe" : ( - 12 , 14 ), "Dream" : ( 4 , - 18 ), "Torgersen" : ( 12 , 6 )} # keep labels apart for _ , r in marks . iterrows (): # Label = island ax . annotate ( r [ "island" ], ( r [ "flipper" ], r [ "mass" ]), xytext = offsets [ r [ "island" ]], textcoords = "offset points" , fontsize = 8 ) for sp , c in sp_col . items (): ax . scatter ([], [], color = c , label = sp ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , title = "Color: species" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "AVG(Flipper length), mm" ); ax . set_ylabel ( "AVG(Body mass), g" ) ax . set_title ( "Marks: Color = species, Size = number of birds, Label = island" ) ax . set_xlim ( 185 , 222 ); ax . set_ylim ( 3550 , 5350 ) plt . show () Read the encodings in order of strength: position (x and y) first, then colour, then size. The three Adelie marks sit close together; the Detail field (island) is what split them into three. Size shows that the marks rest on very different numbers of birds, a reminder from Day 1 to show counts. Colour from a measure. When a measure such as profit goes on Color, Tableau uses a continuous gradient . For a measure with a meaningful zero (profit, change), use a diverging palette and make sure its centre is at zero : in Tableau, Color → Edit Colors → Advanced → Center: 0 . Otherwise the neutral colour sits at the middle of the data range and a small profit can look like a loss. The mirror in matplotlib is TwoSlopeNorm(vcenter=0) ; Part 8 uses it.
docs.title: Part 4: The Marks card
Part 5: Filters and the order of operations

docs.text: Filter How you make it What it does Extract filter When creating an extract Leaves rows out of the extract entirely Data source filter Data Source page → Filters → Add Applies to every sheet using the source Context filter Right-click a filter → Add to Context (turns grey) Applied first; later filters and Top N work inside it Dimension filter Drag a dimension to Filters Keeps chosen members (or a Top N, a wildcard, a condition) Measure filter Drag a measure to Filters Keeps marks whose aggregate is in a range Table calculation filter Filter on a table calculation Hides marks after everything is computed Showing a filter ( Show Filter ) adds a control for the reader; on a dashboard, filters can apply to one sheet, several, or all sheets using the source.
docs.title: Kinds of filter

docs.text:
Tableau applies operations in a fixed order. Simplified: Extract filters Data source filters Context filters FIXED LOD expressions, sets, Top N and conditions Dimension filters INCLUDE and EXCLUDE LOD expressions Measure filters Table calculations, then table calculation filters The order matters because a step can only see what the earlier steps left. The classic surprise is Top N with another filter . Say you want the top 3 stores by sales in the West . You add a Top 3 filter on Store and a filter Region = West. Both are dimension filters, so Tableau computes the Top 3 over all regions and then intersects with West: store_sales = orders . groupby ([ "region" , "store" ])[ "sales" ] . sum () . reset_index () # Both filters at the same step: Top 3 computed on ALL stores, then intersected with West top3_all = store_sales . nlargest ( 3 , "sales" ) print ( "Top 3 stores overall: 
 " , top3_all . to_string ( index = False ), " 
 " ) print ( "Top 3 filter AND Region = West (same step):" ) in_west = top3_all [ top3_all [ "region" ] == "West" ] print ( in_west . to_string ( index = False ) if len ( in_west ) else " (no rows: none of the overall top 3 is in the West)" ) # Region = West as a CONTEXT filter: applied first, so Top 3 is computed inside the West west = store_sales [ store_sales [ "region" ] == "West" ] print ( " 
 Region = West in context, then Top 3:" ) print ( west . nlargest ( 3 , "sales" ) . to_string ( index = False )) Top 3 stores overall: region store sales South Riverbend 19658.5 North Frostford 18022.4 East Dawnport 17953.8 Top 3 filter AND Region = West (same step): (no rows: none of the overall top 3 is in the West) Region = West in context, then Top 3: region store sales West Sunsetvale 17195.4 West Cliffton 16787.6 West Westfall 16665.3 Predict, then run (above). Before running, guess how many stores the first approach returns. Whatever the count, it answers a different question ("which of the chain's top 3 are in the West?"). Add to Context makes the region filter run first, so the Top 3 is chosen within the West.
docs.title: Order of operations

docs.text: A second classic surprise: "show me the loss-making sub-categories". Two different filters give two different answers. # Measure filter: aggregate first (SUM(Profit) per sub-category), then keep the negative ones sub = orders . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "profit" ] . sum () print ( "Sub-categories whose TOTAL profit is negative (measure filter on SUM):" ) print ( sub [ sub < 0 ] . round ( 0 ) . to_string () or " none" , " \n " ) # Row-level filter: keep only loss-making order lines, then aggregate loss_rows = orders [ orders [ "profit" ] < 0 ] . groupby ( "sub_category" )[ "profit" ] . sum () print ( "Sub-categories with ANY loss-making order lines (row filter, then SUM):" ) print ( loss_rows . round ( 0 ) . sort_values () . to_string ()) Sub-categories whose TOTAL profit is negative (measure filter on SUM): sub_category Board games -168.0 Sub-categories with ANY loss-making order lines (row filter, then SUM): sub_category Board games -2279.0 The first answers "which sub-categories lose money overall?"; the second answers "where do loss-making lines occur, and how much do they lose?". In Tableau, dragging a measure to Filters asks how to aggregate it ( Sum gives the first; All values filters rows and gives the second). Say which one you mean. Misconception Better view "Filters are applied in the order I add them." Tableau applies them by type , in the fixed order above. "Top N always gives me the top N of what I see." Only if the other filters are in context . "Filtering never changes a percentage of total." Percent of total is a table calculation, computed after filters, so it re-bases to what is left.
docs.title: Dimension filter on a measure, or measure filter?

docs.text: Analysis → Create Calculated Field (or right-click in the Data pane) opens the editor. A calculation is either row-level (computed for each row, then aggregated like any field) or aggregate (computed from aggregates, at the level of detail of the view). You cannot mix the two in one expression without aggregating everything: Tableau will report that it cannot mix aggregate and non-aggregate arguments .
docs.title: Part 6: Calculated fields and table calculations

docs.text: Calculation Type What it gives [Profit] / [Sales] then AVG Row-level, then averaged The mean of the line-by-line margins: every line counts equally SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) Aggregate Total profit ÷ total sales: every dollar counts equally orders [ "line_margin" ] = orders [ "profit" ] / orders [ "sales" ] # row-level calculated field g = orders . groupby ( "category" ) compare = pd . DataFrame ({ "AVG([Profit]/[Sales])" : g [ "line_margin" ] . mean (), "SUM([Profit])/SUM([Sales])" : g [ "profit" ] . sum () / g [ "sales" ] . sum (), }) print ( compare . map ( " {:.1%} " . format ) . to_string ()) AVG([Profit]/[Sales]) SUM([Profit])/SUM([Sales]) category Books 36.8% 37.0% Gifts 43.4% 25.6% Stationery 51.7% 48.0% The usual business definition of profit ratio is the aggregate one, SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) : a large order matters more than a small one. Format it as a percentage (right-click → Default Properties → Number Format ).
docs.title: Profit ratio: the morning's ratio problem again

docs.text: Three more patterns you will use often, with their pandas mirrors: // Discount band (row-level, a new dimension) IF [Discount] = 0 THEN "None" ELSEIF [Discount] <= 0.2 THEN "Up to 20%" ELSE "Over 20%" END // Days since the customer's first order (an LOD inside a row-level calculation) DATEDIFF('day', {FIXED [Customer ID] : MIN([Order Date])}, [Order Date]) // Profitable? (aggregate, at the level of the view) IF SUM([Profit]) >= 0 THEN "Profit" ELSE "Loss" END orders [ "discount_band" ] = pd . cut ( orders [ "discount" ], [ - 0.01 , 0 , 0.2 , 1 ], labels = [ "None" , "Up to 20%" , "Over 20%" ]) first = orders . groupby ( "customer_id" )[ "order_date" ] . transform ( "min" ) orders [ "days_since_first" ] = ( orders [ "order_date" ] - first ) . dt . days band = orders . groupby ( "discount_band" , observed = True ) . agg ( lines = ( "sales" , "size" ), sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" )) band [ "profit_ratio" ] = band [ "profit" ] / band [ "sales" ] print ( band . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) lines sales profit profit_ratio discount_band None 3989 138470.0 58209.77 0.42 Up to 20% 1808 56783.9 18004.89 0.32 Over 20% 163 11174.4 -2279.04 -0.20
docs.title: Logic, dates and strings

docs.text: A table calculation is computed on the aggregated table in the view , after filters: running totals, differences, percent of total, rank, moving average. Right-click a measure pill → Quick Table Calculation . The key setting is Compute Using (Table across, Table down, Pane, or a specific dimension): it decides which marks are added up or compared. A wrong Compute Using is the most common table-calculation error. monthly = orders . set_index ( "order_date" )[ "sales" ] . resample ( "MS" ) . sum () . to_frame ( "sales" ) monthly [ "running_total" ] = monthly [ "sales" ] . groupby ( monthly . index . year ) . cumsum () # Running total, restarting each year monthly [ "pct_of_year" ] = monthly [ "sales" ] / monthly [ "sales" ] . groupby ( monthly . index . year ) . transform ( "sum" ) # Percent of total monthly [ "yoy_change" ] = monthly [ "sales" ] . pct_change ( 12 ) # Percent difference from a year earlier print ( monthly . tail ( 6 ) . round ( 3 ) . to_string ()) sales running_total pct_of_year yoy_change order_date 2025-07-01 5267.5 35941.8 0.080 -0.083 2025-08-01 5158.9 41100.7 0.078 0.006 2025-09-01 5819.8 46920.5 0.088 -0.148 2025-10-01 4598.5 51519.0 0.070 -0.212 2025-11-01 5297.8 56816.8 0.080 -0.070 2025-12-01 9227.2 66044.0 0.140 0.251 Each of these is a choice of what to compute along (here, months within a year) and what to restart on (each year). In Tableau that choice is Compute Using . Misconception Better view "A calculated field is computed on the chart." Row-level calculations are computed on the data rows; only aggregate calculations and table calculations work on the view. "Percent of total is fixed." It is a table calculation: it changes when you filter or change Compute Using .
docs.title: Table calculations

docs.text: Tableau recognises fields with a geographic role (Country/Region, State/Province, City, Postal Code…) and shows a globe icon next to them. Double-clicking a geographic field creates a map with Latitude and Longitude (generated) on the shelves. A symbol map (mark type Circle or Automatic) puts a dot on each location; size can show a total. A filled map (mark type Map ) shades each area; colour shows a measure. Field names change between Tableau versions and data sources: the same field may be called State in one and State/Province in another, and Country or Country/Region . If a field has no globe icon, right-click it → Geographic Role and choose the right role. If Tableau cannot place some names, an indicator such as "3 unknown" appears at the bottom right of the map; click it to fix or filter them. Two cautions from this morning: A filled map gives large areas more visual weight regardless of their values, and small areas (city states, small provinces) almost disappear. Pair a map with a sorted bar chart when exact comparison matters. A filled map of totals is often just a map of population or of store count. For a fair comparison, map a rate (profit ratio, sales per store, complaints per customer).
docs.title: Part 7: Maps
Part 8: Dashboards, actions and a design checklist

docs.text: New Dashboard (the icon next to New Worksheet at the bottom). Set Size : Fixed size (a set width and height; predictable when printing or sharing), Automatic (fills whatever window it is in) or Range (between a minimum and maximum). Recent versions start with a fixed size. Drag sheets from the Sheets list onto the canvas. By default objects are tiled into layout containers; hold Shift or choose Floating to place an object freely. Add text (a title that states the purpose, an instruction such as "Click a region to filter"), and remove legends and filter cards you do not need.
docs.title: Building a dashboard

docs.text: Dashboard → Actions → Add Action creates links between sheets: Action What it does Typical use Filter Selecting marks in a source sheet filters target sheets Click a region → the trend and bar charts show only that region Highlight Selecting marks highlights related marks elsewhere, greying the rest Keep the context visible while emphasising one item Go to URL / Go to Sheet Opens a web page or another sheet Drill to a detail dashboard Change Parameter / Change Set Values Updates a parameter or set from a selection More advanced what-if and comparison designs Each action has a source sheet, target sheets, a trigger ( Hover , Select or Menu ), and a rule for what happens when the selection is cleared : Keep filtered values , Show all values or Exclude all values . The quick way to make a filter action: click a sheet on the dashboard, then click the Use as Filter icon (a small funnel) on the sheet's border. That creates a filter action from that sheet to all others on the dashboard, run on Select , showing all values when cleared. Check it under Dashboard → Actions .
docs.title: Actions: making views talk to each other

docs.text: The function below plays the role of a dashboard: three linked views of Harbour Books. Calling it with a region is like clicking that region in a source sheet. Note the diverging colour scale centred at zero for profit. def harbour_dashboard ( region = None ): data = orders if region is None else orders [ orders [ "region" ] == region ] label = "All regions" if region is None else region fig = plt . figure ( figsize = ( 13 , 5.5 )) gs = fig . add_gridspec ( 2 , 2 , width_ratios = [ 1 , 1.15 ], hspace = 0.55 , wspace = 0.35 ) # View 1: the source sheet (regions), with the selection highlighted ax = fig . add_subplot ( gs [ 0 , 0 ]) reg = orders . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . sum () . sort_values () ax . barh ( reg . index , reg . values / 1000 , color = [ OI [ "blue" ] if ( region is None or r == region ) else "#E5E5E5" for r in reg . index ]) ax . set_title ( "Sales by region (click to filter)" ); ax . set_xlabel ( "Sales (thousand USD)" ) # View 2: monthly trend, continuous month ax = fig . add_subplot ( gs [ 1 , 0 ]) trend = data . set_index ( "order_date" )[ "sales" ] . resample ( "MS" ) . sum () ax . plot ( trend . index , trend . values / 1000 , color = OI [ "blue" ]) ax . set_title ( f "Monthly sales: { label } " ); ax . set_ylabel ( "Thousand USD" ) ax . xaxis . set_major_locator ( mdates . YearLocator ()) ax . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( mdates . DateFormatter ( "%Y" )) # View 3: sales by sub-category (length), coloured by profit (diverging, centred at 0) ax = fig . add_subplot ( gs [:, 1 ]) sub = data . groupby ( "sub_category" ) . agg ( sales = ( "sales" , "sum" ), profit = ( "profit" , "sum" )) . sort_values ( "sales" ) lim = max ( abs ( sub [ "profit" ] . min ()), abs ( sub [ "profit" ] . max ())) norm = mcolors . TwoSlopeNorm ( vmin =- lim , vcenter = 0 , vmax = lim ) cmap = plt . get_cmap ( "PuOr" ) ax . barh ( sub . index , sub [ "sales" ] / 1000 , color = cmap ( norm ( sub [ "profit" ]))) ax . set_title ( f "Sales by sub-category, coloured by profit: { label } " ); ax . set_xlabel ( "Sales (thousand USD)" ) sm = plt . cm . ScalarMappable ( norm = norm , cmap = cmap ) fig . colorbar ( sm , ax = ax , label = "SUM(Profit), USD (orange = loss)" ) fig . suptitle ( "Harbour Books dashboard (synthetic data)" , x = 0.02 , ha = "left" , fontweight = "bold" ) plt . show () harbour_dashboard () harbour_dashboard ( "East" ) # like clicking East in the region view Discuss. In the right-hand chart, bar length shows sales and colour shows profit. What can a manager see with both encodings that they could not see from length alone? Which encoding will a hurried reader look at first, and what might they miss? (This morning's lecture, Part 2, and the reading packet's section on dual encoding will help.) Notice also: after filtering, the colour scale was recomputed from the filtered data, so the same shade can mean different amounts in the two pictures. Tableau behaves the same way unless you fix the colour range ( Edit Colors → Advanced → Start / End ). When comparing filtered views, read the values (tooltip or labels), not just the shade.
docs.title: A Python mirror of a filter action

docs.text: Before you publish or print a dashboard, check: Purpose: one sentence says who it is for and which decision it supports; the title says it. Priority: the most important view or KPI is top-left; overview first, detail below. Few views: three to five, each with a message title. Chart choice: each view matches its question (Part 1 of the morning lecture); bars sorted when ranking. Colour: one meaning per colour across the dashboard; diverging measures centred at zero; colour-blind safe; never colour alone. Numbers: units and formats (US dollars, percentages) set in Default Properties ; sensible rounding. Interactivity: actions tested; the instruction ("click a state…") is visible; clearing a selection returns to the full view. Tooltips: edited to read like a sentence, with units. Size: fixed size when the output is a PDF or a slide; checked at the size readers will use. Static state: before printing or exporting, the selection is cleared so the output shows the intended (usually unfiltered) view. Test: someone who did not build it can answer the intended question in under a minute.
docs.title: Dashboard design checklist

docs.text: fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.8 )) sns . boxplot ( data = penguins , x = "species" , y = "flipper_length_mm" , order = [ "Adelie" , "Chinstrap" , "Gentoo" ], color = OI [ "sky" ], width = 0.5 , ax = ax ) ax . set_xlabel ( "" ); ax . set_ylabel ( "Flipper length (mm)" ) ax . set_title ( "Flipper length by species" ) plt . show () stats = penguins . groupby ( "species" )[ "flipper_length_mm" ] . describe ()[[ "count" , "25%" , "50%" , "75%" ]] stats [ "IQR" ] = stats [ "75%" ] - stats [ "25%" ] print ( stats . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) count 25% 50% 75% IQR species Adelie 146.0 186.0 190.0 195.0 9.0 Chinstrap 68.0 191.0 196.0 201.0 10.0 Gentoo 119.0 212.0 216.0 221.5 9.5 A model paragraph (notice the numbers, the units and the comparison): The typical Gentoo penguin has a flipper about 25 mm longer than the typical Adelie (medians of 216 mm and 190 mm). The middle half of each species spans only about 9 to 10 mm (the interquartile ranges), so the boxes do not overlap and flipper length alone separates Gentoo from the other two species well. Chinstrap and Adelie overlap heavily and could not be told apart by this measure. A few birds lie beyond the whiskers; they are unusual for their species rather than errors. The checklist behind it: (1) compare the medians with units; (2) compare the spreads (IQR, whisker length); (3) say whether the boxes overlap and what that means for the decision; (4) mention outliers and what they might be; (5) say how many observations each box rests on if they differ a lot.
docs.title: Reading a box plot in sentences

docs.text: gentoo = penguins [ penguins [ "species" ] == "Gentoo" ] slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( gentoo [ "flipper_length_mm" ], gentoo [ "body_mass_g" ], 1 ) r = gentoo [ "flipper_length_mm" ] . corr ( gentoo [ "body_mass_g" ]) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) sns . regplot ( data = gentoo , x = "flipper_length_mm" , y = "body_mass_g" , ax = ax , seed = 0 , # seed: the band is bootstrapped scatter_kws = { "alpha" : 0.5 , "color" : OI [ "green" ]}, line_kws = { "color" : "black" }) ax . set_xlabel ( "Flipper length (mm)" ); ax . set_ylabel ( "Body mass (g)" ) ax . set_title ( "Gentoo penguins: longer flippers, heavier birds" ) plt . show () print ( f "slope = { slope : .1f } g per mm, intercept = { intercept : .0f } g, r = { r : .2f } , n = { len ( gentoo ) } " ) slope = 54.2 g per mm, intercept = -6674 g, r = 0.71, n = 119 A model paragraph: Among Gentoo penguins, each extra millimetre of flipper length goes with about 54 g more body mass on average (the slope of the fitted line), across flippers from about 205 to 230 mm. The points scatter widely around the line (r ≈ 0.7), so flipper length gives a useful but rough guide to an individual bird's mass. The relationship is an association: it does not show that longer flippers cause extra weight; both grow with the bird's overall size. The checklist: (1) state the slope in words with both units ("per mm", "per dollar"); (2) give the range of x over which it holds; do not extrapolate far beyond it; (3) say how tightly the points follow the line (r, or "wide scatter"); (4) say association, not causation , and name what else could explain it; (5) the shaded band around a seaborn regression line is a confidence band for the line , not a range for individual points. If the script you are given does not print the slope, you can read it from the chart: pick two points on the line far apart and divide the rise by the run. Do not copy these paragraphs into Assignment 1: they are about penguins. Use the checklists on your own figures.
