docs.text: Day 2 lecture: Visualising and communicating data ¶ Periods 1 to 4 of Day 2. How to choose a chart for the question being asked, why the eye reads some charts more accurately than others, how colour helps or excludes readers, how honest data can be drawn dishonestly and how to rebuild it, and how to turn a finding into a message, a KPI, a dashboard and a marketing decision. Run each code cell with Shift + Enter , in order. The examples use the penguins and mpg data and synthetic data made inside the notebook. Lab 2 uses Tableau's Superstore data and Assignment 1 uses the restaurant tips data; this lecture uses neither , so that you practise the ideas here and apply them yourself in the graded work. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder; everything loads from data/ . Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook, data/penguins.csv and data/mpg.csv , run %pip install seaborn in a first cell, and remove data/ from the two file paths in the setup cell. What you will be able to do ¶ Choose a chart from the shape of the question (rank, change, distribution, relationship, part-to-whole, deviation) and defend it against an alternative. Explain why position and length beat angle, area and colour, and use pre-attentive attributes and Gestalt grouping to direct the reader's eye. Remove clutter ( data-ink ) and choose colour that is meaningful and readable by colour-blind readers. Spot six common misleading charts and rebuild each one honestly. Write a big idea , structure a short report as situation, complication, resolution , and title charts with the message, not the topic. Design a KPI correctly, including the difference between a ratio of sums and a mean of ratios , and lay out a dashboard . Calculate and interpret the core marketing metrics : funnel conversion, CTR, CPC, CPA, ROAS, CLV, and explain the limits of attribution . Part Topic Period 1 Choosing a chart for the question P1 2 Perception: encodings, pre-attentive attributes, Gestalt, data-ink P1–P2 3 Colour and accessibility P2 4 Misleading charts and their rebuilds P2 5 Communicating results: audience, big idea, structure, titles, annotation P3 6 KPIs and dashboards P3 7 Marketing analytics P4 8 Two real cases P4 9 Practice, quiz and summary Self-study Reading Read Chapter 2 of the course reading packet for the four question shapes and their charts, why position and length are read more accurately than colour and area, dual encoding, and leading with the finding. Its summaries of Gordon's Chapter 5 ( Communicating Analytical Results ) and Chapter 6 ( Marketing Analytics ) frame Parts 5 to 7. This lecture adds perception research, colour and accessibility, misleading charts, KPI arithmetic and the marketing metrics. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import matplotlib.colors as mcolors import seaborn as sns penguins = pd . read_csv ( "data/penguins.csv" ) . dropna () # Route A: "penguins.csv" cars = pd . read_csv ( "data/mpg.csv" ) # Route A: "mpg.csv" # One colour-blind-safe palette (Okabe and Ito) and a neutral grey, used all day OI = { "orange" : "#E69F00" , "sky" : "#56B4E9" , "green" : "#009E73" , "yellow" : "#F0E442" , "blue" : "#0072B2" , "vermillion" : "#D55E00" , "purple" : "#CC79A7" , "black" : "#000000" } GREY = "#B0B0B0" plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.dpi" : 100 , "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlesize" : 11 }) print ( "penguins:" , penguins . shape , " cars:" , cars . shape ) penguins: (333, 7) cars: (398, 9) Part 1: Choosing a chart for the question ¶ A chart is an answer to a question. The most common chart mistake is not ugliness but a mismatch: a pie chart asked to show change over time, or a line drawn through categories that have no order. So start with the shape of the question , then pick the form. Question shape Typical words First choice Good alternatives Avoid Rank or compare categories "which is biggest", "top 10" Bar chart, sorted , often horizontal Dot plot, lollipop Unsorted bars, pie with many slices Change over time "trend", "since", "per month" Line chart Column chart for few periods, area for totals Pie per year, unequal time gaps Distribution of one number "typical", "spread", "outliers" Histogram, box plot Violin, strip (dots), density A bar of the mean alone Relationship between two numbers "does X go with Y" Scatter plot Hexbin for many points, bubble for a third number Two lines on two axes Part-to-whole "share", "mix", "of the total" Sorted bar of shares, or one stacked bar Pie with 2–3 slices, treemap, waffle Pie with many similar slices, 3-D pie Deviation from a reference "vs target", "above or below" Diverging bar around zero Bullet chart, line with a target line Separate bars for actual and target Geography "where", "by region" Filled (choropleth) map of a rate Symbol map of totals, sorted bar A filled map of raw totals Flow or process "where do we lose people" Funnel (stage bars) Sankey Pie of stages Two tests before you draw anything: Write the question as a sentence ending in a question mark. If you cannot, you are not ready to chart. Say what the reader should compare. Bars next to each other? A line against its own past? A point against a target? The chart should put those things side by side, on the same scale. Example 1: rank, with sorting ¶ Which manufacturers have the most models in the mpg data? The manufacturer is the first word of each car's name. cars [ "maker" ] = cars [ "name" ] . str . split () . str [ 0 ] counts = cars [ "maker" ] . value_counts () . head ( 12 ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 )) alpha_order = counts . sort_index () axes [ 0 ] . bar ( alpha_order . index , alpha_order . values , color = GREY ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Default: alphabetical, vertical" ) axes [ 0 ] . tick_params ( axis = "x" , rotation = 60 ) ranked = counts . sort_values () axes [ 1 ] . barh ( ranked . index , ranked . values , color = GREY ) axes [ 1 ] . barh ( ranked . index [ - 1 ], ranked . values [ - 1 ], color = OI [ "blue" ]) for y , v in enumerate ( ranked . values ): axes [ 1 ] . text ( v + 0.5 , y , str ( v ), va = "center" , fontsize = 9 ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Sorted, horizontal, labelled, one bar highlighted" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Number of car models" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Both charts hold the same twelve numbers. On the left, the reader must hunt for the longest bar and tilt their head to read the names. On the right, rank is the order , names read horizontally, and the labels make the gridlines unnecessary. Look closer. Scroll through cars["maker"].value_counts() . You will find spellings such as chevy and chevroelt next to chevrolet , and vw next to volkswagen . A chart of counts is only as good as the category labels: data quality (Day 1) comes before chart design. Example 2: change over time ¶ How did fuel economy change across model years, by region of origin? A line chart, because the x-axis is ordered time and the eye reads slopes. trend = cars . groupby ([ "model_year" , "origin" ])[ "mpg" ] . median () . unstack () colours = { "usa" : OI [ "vermillion" ], "europe" : OI [ "blue" ], "japan" : OI [ "green" ]} fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 4 )) for region in trend . columns : ax . plot ( 1900 + trend . index , trend [ region ], color = colours [ region ], lw = 2 ) ax . text ( 1900 + trend . index [ - 1 ] + 0.3 , trend [ region ] . iloc [ - 1 ], region . upper (), color = colours [ region ], va = "center" , fontweight = "bold" ) ax . set_title ( "Median fuel economy rose for cars from every region, 1970-1982" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Median miles per US gallon" ) ax . set_xlim ( 1969.5 , 1984 ) plt . show () Notice three choices: the title states the finding ; each line is labelled directly at its end, so there is no legend to decode; and the colours come from a colour-blind-safe palette. The y-axis does not start at zero: for a line chart that is acceptable, because the eye reads position and slope , not length. (Bars are different; see Part 4.) Predict, then run. Would a pie chart per year show the same story? Try to picture thirteen pies side by side. What could a reader compare, and what could they not? Example 3: distribution, and why a bar of the mean is not enough ¶ fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4 ), sharey = True ) means = penguins . groupby ( "species" )[ "body_mass_g" ] . mean () axes [ 0 ] . bar ( means . index , means . values , color = GREY ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Only the means" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Body mass (g)" ) order = [ "Adelie" , "Chinstrap" , "Gentoo" ] sns . boxplot ( data = penguins , x = "species" , y = "body_mass_g" , order = order , color = "white" , width = 0.5 , showfliers = False , ax = axes [ 1 ]) rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2 ) for i , sp in enumerate ( order ): vals = penguins . loc [ penguins [ "species" ] == sp , "body_mass_g" ] axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( i + rng . uniform ( - 0.18 , 0.18 , len ( vals )), vals , s = 8 , alpha = 0.5 , color = OI [ "blue" ]) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Box plot with every penguin shown" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () The bar chart says "Gentoo are heavier". The box-and-dots chart says how much heavier, how much the groups overlap , and how many birds stand behind each box. If a decision depends on individuals (which penguin, which customer, which order), show the distribution, not just the average. Reading a box plot (you will need this for Assignment 1): the line inside the box is the median ; the box spans the middle half of the data, from the first quartile (Q1) to the third (Q3), so its height is the interquartile range (IQR) ; the whiskers reach the furthest points within 1.5 × IQR of the box; points beyond the whiskers are drawn separately as outliers . An outlier is unusual, not necessarily wrong. Example 4: relationship ¶ Do penguins with longer flippers weigh more? Two numbers per individual: a scatter plot. fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4.5 )) sp_col = { "Adelie" : OI [ "orange" ], "Chinstrap" : OI [ "purple" ], "Gentoo" : OI [ "green" ]} for sp , grp in penguins . groupby ( "species" ): ax . scatter ( grp [ "flipper_length_mm" ], grp [ "body_mass_g" ], s = 14 , alpha = 0.7 , color = sp_col [ sp ]) label_at = { "Adelie" : ( 172 , 4300 ), "Chinstrap" : ( 204 , 3150 ), "Gentoo" : ( 231 , 5100 )} for sp , ( lx , ly ) in label_at . items (): ax . text ( lx , ly , sp , color = sp_col [ sp ], fontweight = "bold" , va = "center" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Flipper length (mm)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Body mass (g)" ) ax . set_title ( "Longer flippers go with heavier penguins, within and across species" ) ax . set_xlim ( 170 , 245 ) plt . show () Example 5: part-to-whole, the pie problem ¶ Five brands share a market. Predict, then run: before you look at the labels, rank the five slices of the pie from largest to smallest. shares = pd . Misconceptions about chart choice ¶ Misconception Better view "The chart that looks most impressive is best." The best chart makes the intended comparison easiest. Impressive often means harder to read. "Every chart needs a legend." Direct labels are usually faster; a legend forces the eye to travel back and forth. "Lines and bars are interchangeable." Lines imply continuity and order; use them for time or ordered values, not unordered categories. "A pie is the chart for shares." Only for two or three parts. Otherwise a sorted bar of percentages is clearer. "Show all the data, always." Show the data the decision needs, in the form the reader needs; keep the rest available. Part 2: Perception ¶ Encodings and how accurately we read them ¶ A chart encodes each number as a visual property: a position, a length, an angle, an area, a shade. In experiments where people estimated ratios from charts, Cleveland and McGill (1984) found a consistent ranking of how accurately each encoding is read: Most accurate Least accurate Position on a common scale Position on separate, aligned scales Length, direction, angle Area Volume, colour saturation, colour hue The practical rule: put the most important comparison on position or length ; use colour and area for secondary information or rough groups. A second finding from perception research (Stevens' power law) explains why bubbles mislead: people tend to underestimate differences in area, so a circle with twice the area looks less than twice as big. Most people estimate the bars well, the pie roughly, and the circles and shades badly (usually too low for the circles). Nothing in the data changed; only the encoding did. Pre-attentive attributes: what the eye sees before it reads ¶ Some visual differences are picked up in a fraction of a second, before any conscious search. These pre-attentive attributes include colour hue, intensity, size, orientation, shape, enclosure and added marks. You can use them to send the reader's eye straight to the point, or, by using too many at once, to send it everywhere. Predict, then run. In each panel there is one odd point. Which panel will take you longest to find it in? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 11 ) n = 70 x , y = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , n ), rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , n ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 13 , 3.8 )) axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( x [ 1 :], y [ 1 :], color = GREY , s = 40 ) axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( x [ 0 ], y [ 0 ], color = OI [ "vermillion" ], s = 40 ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Colour: one point differs" ) axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( x [ 1 :], y [ 1 :], color = GREY , s = 40 , marker = "o" ) axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( x [ 0 ], y [ 0 ], color = GREY , s = 40 , marker = "s" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Shape: one point differs" ) half = n // 2 axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( x [ 1 : half ], y [ 1 : half ], color = OI [ "vermillion" ], s = 40 , marker = "s" ) axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( x [ half :], y [ half :], color = GREY , s = 40 , marker = "o" ) axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( x [ 0 ], y [ 0 ], color = OI [ "vermillion" ], s = 40 , marker = "o" ) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "Colour AND shape: the red circle" ) for ax in axes : ax . set_xticks ([]); ax . set_yticks ([]) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () The red point on the left "pops out". The square in the middle takes longer: shape is a weaker pre-attentive cue than colour. The right panel is slowest because the target differs only in a combination of colour and shape, which the eye has to search for point by point. Lesson for dashboards: one highlight colour against grey is powerful; five bright colours cancel each other out. Gestalt principles: how the eye groups things ¶ Gestalt psychology describes how we see marks as groups. Four principles matter most for charts: fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 4 , figsize = ( 14 , 3.2 )) xs = np . arange ( 6 ) axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( np . r_ [ xs [: 3 ], xs [ 3 :] + 1.2 ], np . zeros ( 6 ), s = 120 , color = GREY ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Proximity: two groups by spacing" ) axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( xs , np . zeros ( 6 ), s = 120 , color = [ OI [ "blue" ] if i % 2 else GREY for i in xs ]) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Similarity: grouped by colour" ) axes [ 2 ] . add_patch ( plt . Rectangle (( 1.6 , - 0.4 ), 2.8 , 0.8 , color = OI [ "sky" ], alpha = 0.25 )) axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( xs , np . zeros ( 6 ), s = 120 , color = GREY ) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "Enclosure: a shaded band" ) axes [ 3 ] . scatter ( xs , np . zeros ( 6 ), s = 120 , color = GREY ) axes [ 3 ] . plot ([ 1 , 2 ], [ 0 , 0 ], color = "black" ); axes [ 3 ] . plot ([ 3 , 4 ], [ 0 , 0 ], color = "black" ) axes [ 3 ] . set_title ( "Connection: joined by lines" ) for ax in axes : ax . set_ylim ( - 1 , 1 ); ax . set_xlim ( - 0.8 , 7.5 ); ax . axis ( "off" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Principle What the eye does Use it in a chart Proximity Treats close marks as a group Put bars that should be compared next to each other; leave gaps between groups Similarity Treats same-coloured or same-shaped marks as a group Give one series one colour everywhere on the dashboard Enclosure Treats marks inside a boundary as a group Shade a period (a promotion, a recession) or box related KPIs together Connection Treats joined marks as a sequence Lines connect time points; do not connect unordered categories Continuity, closure Follows smooth paths, completes shapes Light gridlines are enough; the eye completes the alignment Data-ink: remove what does not carry data ¶ Edward Tufte's data-ink ratio is the share of a chart's ink that shows data. Heavy borders, dark gridlines, shadows, 3-D effects, repeated labels and decorative images ("chart junk") use ink without adding information and compete with the data for attention. The aim is not minimalism for its own sake but attention on the data . quarters = [ "Q1" , "Q2" , "Q3" , "Q4" ] regions = { "North" : [ 42 , 45 , 47 , 50 ], "South" : [ 38 , 37 , 35 , 31 ], "East" : [ 40 , 43 , 44 , 46 ], "West" : [ 36 , 38 , 40 , 41 ]} fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 13 , 4.2 )) ax = axes [ 0 ] bright = [ "red" , "lime" , "blue" , "magenta" ] for ( name , vals ), col in zip ( regions . items (), bright ): ax . plot ( quarters , vals , marker = "o" , lw = 3 , color = col , label = name ) for q , v in zip ( quarters , vals ): ax . text ( q , v + 0.6 , f " { v : .2f } " , fontsize = 7 , ha = "center" ) ax . grid ( True , color = "black" , lw = 1 ) for side in [ "top" , "right" ]: ax . spines [ side ] . set_visible ( True ); ax . spines [ side ] . set_linewidth ( 2 ) ax . set_facecolor ( "#EFEFD0" ) ax . legend ( loc = "lower left" , fontsize = 8 , frameon = True , shadow = True ) ax . set_title ( "SALES BY REGION BY QUARTER (USD THOUSANDS)" ) ax = axes [ 1 ] for name , vals in regions . items (): col = OI [ "vermillion" ] if name == "South" else GREY ax . plot ( quarters , vals , lw = 2.5 if name == "South" else 1.5 , color = col ) ax . text ( 3.1 , vals [ - 1 ], name , color = col , va = "center" , fontweight = "bold" if name == "South" else None ) ax . set_title ( "South is the only region whose sales fell this year" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_xlim ( - 0.2 , 3.6 ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () The left chart is not wrong; it is just loud. The right chart removes the frame, the dark grid, the background, the legend and sixteen over-precise labels, puts one region in colour and three in grey, and says the finding in the title. Decluttering checklist: remove borders and backgrounds; lighten or drop gridlines; label directly instead of a legend; round numbers to what the decision needs; one accent colour; no 3-D, shadows or images inside the plot area. Misconception Better view "Maximise data-ink: delete everything." Keep what helps reading: axis labels with units, a light grid for precise lookups, a source note. "More colours make a chart more informative." Each extra colour weakens the others. Use grey for context and colour for the point. Part 3: Colour and accessibility ¶ Three kinds of palette ¶ Choose the palette from the kind of variable , not from taste: Sequential (light to dark, one hue): ordered values from low to high, such as sales or population. Diverging (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint): values above and below a meaningful centre, such as profit (around zero) or change versus last year. The midpoint must be set at that centre. Categorical (distinct hues, similar lightness): unordered groups such as regions or brands. Keep to about six; beyond that, group the rest as "Other" or use labels. fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 3 , 1 , figsize = ( 9 , 2.6 )) grad = np . linspace ( 0 , 1 , 256 )[ None , :] axes [ 0 ] . imshow ( grad , aspect = "auto" , cmap = "Blues" ); axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Sequential (Blues): low to high" , fontsize = 9 ) axes [ 1 ] . imshow ( grad , aspect = "auto" , cmap = "PuOr" ); axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Diverging (PuOr): below and above a centre" , fontsize = 9 ) cat = list ( OI . values ())[: 7 ] axes [ 2 ] . imshow ( np . arange ( 7 )[ None , :], aspect = "auto" , cmap = mcolors . ListedColormap ( cat )) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "Categorical (Okabe-Ito): distinct groups" , fontsize = 9 ) for ax in axes : ax . set_xticks ([]); ax . set_yticks ([]) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Why the rainbow palette misleads ¶ The classic rainbow ("jet") palette changes lightness up and down as it changes hue, so the eye sees bands and edges that are not in the data, and the order of colours is not intuitive. Perceptually uniform palettes such as viridis get steadily lighter from one end to the other. The next cell measures the lightness of each palette along its length. def lightness ( cmap_name , n = 256 ): """Approximate perceived lightness (relative luminance) along a colormap.""" rgb = plt . get_cmap ( cmap_name )( np . linspace ( 0 , 1 , n ))[:, : 3 ] lin = np . where ( rgb <= 0.04045 , rgb / 12.92 , (( rgb + 0.055 ) / 1.055 ) ** 2.4 ) return lin @ np . array ([ 0.2126 , 0.7152 , 0.0722 ]) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.2 )) ax . plot ( lightness ( "jet" ), color = OI [ "vermillion" ], label = "jet (rainbow)" ) ax . plot ( lightness ( "viridis" ), color = OI [ "blue" ], label = "viridis" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Position along the palette (low value to high value)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Relative luminance" ) ax . set_title ( "Viridis brightens steadily; the rainbow rises and falls" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () Colour vision deficiency ¶ Roughly 1 in 12 men and 1 in 200 women of Northern European ancestry have some form of colour vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green ; rates are somewhat lower but still substantial in East Asian populations. In a class of forty, expect at least one or two readers who cannot separate a red–green "bad/good" palette. The next cell simulates deuteranopia (missing green-sensitive cones) using the matrix published by Machado, Oliveira and Fernandes (2009). It is an approximation, but good enough to test a palette. DEUTAN = np . array ([[ 0.367322 , 0.860646 , - 0.227968 ], [ 0.280085 , 0.672501 , 0.047413 ], [ - 0.011820 , 0.042940 , 0.968881 ]]) def simulate_deutan ( hex_colours ): rgb = np . array ([ mcolors . to_rgb ( h ) for h in hex_colours ]) lin = np . where ( rgb <= 0.04045 , rgb / 12.92 , (( rgb + 0.055 ) / 1.055 ) ** 2.4 ) sim = np . clip ( lin @ DEUTAN . T , 0 , 1 ) return np . where ( sim <= 0.0031308 , sim * 12.92 , 1.055 * sim ** ( 1 / 2.4 ) - 0.055 ) palettes = { "Red / green (traffic light)" : [ "#D62728" , "#FFBF00" , "#2CA02C" ], "Orange / blue (Okabe-Ito)" : [ OI [ "vermillion" ], OI [ "yellow" ], OI [ "blue" ]]} fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 2 , figsize = ( 9 , 2.8 )) for row , ( name , pal ) in enumerate ( palettes . items ()): axes [ row , 0 ] . imshow ( np . array ([[ mcolors . to_rgb ( c ) for c in pal ]])) axes [ row , 1 ] . imshow ( simulate_deutan ( pal )[ None , :, :]) axes [ row , 0 ] . set_ylabel ( name , rotation = 0 , ha = "right" , va = "center" , fontsize = 9 ) axes [ 0 , 0 ] . set_title ( "As most people see it" , fontsize = 9 ) axes [ 0 , 1 ] . set_title ( "Simulated deuteranopia" , fontsize = 9 ) for ax in axes . ravel (): ax . set_xticks ([]); ax . set_yticks ([]) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () In the simulation the red and green of the traffic-light palette collapse into similar brownish tones, while the orange–blue pair stays distinct. This is one reason Tableau's default for a measure such as profit is an orange–blue diverging palette rather than red–green. Accessibility rules worth keeping ¶ Never rely on colour alone. Add a label, a sign (+/−), a position above or below a line, or a shape. Use colour-blind-safe palettes (Okabe-Ito, viridis, Tableau's Color Blind palette) and check with a simulator. Keep contrast high for text: dark text on a light background; the WCAG guideline for normal text is a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1. Keep colour meanings consistent across every chart on a page: if the South is orange in one chart, it is orange in all of them. Make text large enough to read when projected or printed, and write a one-sentence alt text or caption that states the message for readers who cannot see the chart. Part 4: Misleading charts and their rebuilds ¶ A chart can be built from correct numbers and still lead a reader to a wrong conclusion. Each example below shows a misleading version (left) and an honest rebuild (right), all on synthetic data. 1. The truncated bar axis ¶ Two products' satisfaction scores are 81.2 and 82.9 out of 100. scores = pd . Series ({ "Product X" : 81.2 , "Product Y" : 82.9 }) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 10 , 3.6 )) axes [ 0 ] . bar ( scores . index , scores . values , color = [ GREY , OI [ "blue" ]]) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylim ( 80.8 , 83.2 ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Misleading: Y looks five times better" ) axes [ 1 ] . bar ( scores . index , scores . values , color = [ GREY , OI [ "blue" ]]) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylim ( 0 , 100 ) for i , v in enumerate ( scores . values ): axes [ 1 ] . text ( i , v + 2 , f " { v } " , ha = "center" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Honest: a 1.7-point difference out of 100" ) for ax in axes : ax . set_ylabel ( "Satisfaction score (0-100)" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Rule: a bar's length encodes its value, so bars must start at zero. If the small difference is what matters, show the difference itself (a dot plot, or a bar of "Y minus X") rather than cutting the axis. Line charts and dot plots may start elsewhere, because they encode position. 2. A cumulative line that hides a decline ¶ new_signups = np . array ([ 520 , 560 , 610 , 640 , 600 , 560 , 520 , 470 , 430 , 400 , 380 , 350 ]) m = pd . period_range ( "2025-01" , periods = 12 , freq = "M" ) . strftime ( "%b" ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.6 )) axes [ 0 ] . plot ( m , new_signups . cumsum (), color = OI [ "blue" ], lw = 2 ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Misleading: 'steady growth all year'" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Total sign-ups to date" ) axes [ 1 ] . bar ( m , new_signups , color = [ GREY ] * 4 + [ OI [ "vermillion" ]] * 8 ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Honest: new sign-ups fell every month since April" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylabel ( "New sign-ups in the month" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () A running total can only go up (as long as the monthly values are positive), so it disguises a slowdown. Show the monthly flow alongside, or instead. Five questions to ask any chart ¶ Where does each axis start, and is the encoding length (needs zero) or position (does not)? Is there more than one scale, and who chose it? Why this time window, this filter, these categories? What was left out? Totals or rates? Should the numbers be divided by something? Does the title claim more than the chart shows, for example a cause where the chart shows only an association? Misconception Better view "Every y-axis must start at zero." Bars must. Lines and dots may zoom in, but say so and do not exaggerate small noise. "If the numbers are correct, the chart is honest." Scale, window, base and title choices can mislead with correct numbers. Part 5: Communicating results ¶ Exploratory and explanatory charts ¶ So far today, most charts have been explanatory : built to show one finding to someone else. On Day 1 you made exploratory charts: many quick views to find out what is in the data. Both are necessary, but they are different products. The common failure in reports is to paste exploratory charts (defaults, every variable, no message) into a document meant for a decision maker. Start with the audience ¶ Gordon's Chapter 5 starts communication from the audience and the decision , not from the software's default chart. Before you design anything, answer four questions: Question Example answer Who is the reader, and what do they already know? A regional operations manager; knows the stores well, not statistics What decision are they making, and when? Whether to extend weekend opening hours, at Friday's meeting What do they believe now? What might they push back on? That weekends are quiet; they will ask whether last month was unusual What should they do or think after reading? Approve a three-month trial in two stores The big idea ¶ Cole Nussbaumer Knaflic ( Storytelling with Data , 2015) suggests writing your big idea before making any slide: one complete sentence that states your point of view and what is at stake . If you cannot write it, you do not yet know what you are saying. Weak (a topic) Strong (a big idea) "Weekend sales analysis." "Weekend afternoons now bring a third of our sales but get a fifth of our staff hours, so we are losing sales to queues; a trial of two extra staff in two stores would test the fix at low cost." "Customer survey results." "Delivery speed, not price, is what our lapsed customers complain about most, so the planned discount campaign is unlikely to win them back." Situation, complication, resolution ¶ Barbara Minto's pyramid principle says: lead with the answer, then give the supporting arguments, then the detail. A short way to structure the opening of any report or presentation is SCR : Situation: what the reader already knows and agrees with. "We open all stores 9:00–18:00 every day, with the same staff all week." Complication: what has changed or what is wrong. "Since spring, Saturday and Sunday afternoons bring far more customers than weekdays; queue times on those afternoons have doubled and abandoned baskets are rising." Resolution: what you recommend, and the evidence for it. "Move two staff shifts from Tuesday mornings to weekend afternoons in two pilot stores for three months, and measure queue time and sales." The order matters. A report written in the order the work was done (data, cleaning, methods, results, conclusion) makes a busy reader wait until the end for the only part they need. Finding first, method later (or in an appendix). Titles that say the message ¶ Topic title (what the chart is about) Message title (what the chart shows) "Sales by region, 2025" "South was the only region whose sales fell in 2025" "Monthly complaints" "Complaints doubled after the courier changed in June" "Conversion by channel" "Email converts four times better than social, at a tenth of the cost" A message title must be true to the chart and specific (with a number where possible). If you are not sure enough to write the claim, the chart is not ready to present. Worked example: from an exploratory default to an explanatory chart ¶ A delivery company changed its courier in the North region in week 23. Here are weekly complaints for four regions. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 23 ) weeks = np . arange ( 1 , 41 ) base = { "North" : 60 , "South" : 55 , "East" : 50 , "West" : 45 } comp = pd . DataFrame ({ r : b + rng . normal ( 0 , 4 , len ( weeks )) for r , b in base . items ()}, index = weeks ) comp . loc [ 23 :, "North" ] += np . linspace ( 25 , 45 , len ( weeks ) - 22 ) comp = comp . round () fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 13 , 4.2 )) comp . plot ( ax = axes [ 0 ]) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "complaints" ) ax = axes [ 1 ] for r in comp . columns : ax . plot ( comp . index , comp [ r ], color = OI [ "vermillion" ] if r == "North" else GREY , lw = 2.5 if r == "North" else 1.2 ) ax . axvline ( 23 , color = "black" , lw = 0.8 , ls = "--" ) ax . text ( 23.5 , comp . values . max (), "New courier \n in North (week 23)" , va = "top" , fontsize = 9 ) ax . text ( 40.5 , comp [ "North" ] . iloc [ - 1 ], "North" , color = OI [ "vermillion" ], fontweight = "bold" , va = "center" ) ax . text ( 40.5 , comp [[ "South" , "East" , "West" ]] . iloc [ - 1 ] . mean (), "Other \n regions" , color = "grey" , va = "center" ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , 45 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Week of 2025" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Complaints per week" ) ax . set_title ( "North complaints rose by about two-thirds after the courier change" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () before = comp . loc [ 11 : 22 , "North" ] . mean (); after = comp . loc [ 29 : 40 , "North" ] . mean () print ( f "North, mean complaints per week: weeks 11-22 = { before : .0f } , weeks 29-40 = { after : .0f } , change = { after / before - 1 : +.0% } " ) North, mean complaints per week: weeks 11-22 = 60, weeks 29-40 = 99, change = +66% Five changes turned the left chart into the right one: (1) a message title with a number, checked by the printed calculation; (2) one accent colour for the series that matters and grey for context; (3) an annotation that marks the event and explains it; (4) direct labels instead of a legend; (5) axis labels with units . The data did not change. Note the honest wording: the chart shows that complaints rose after the change. It does not prove the courier caused it (Day 1's confounding questions still apply: did anything else change in the North in week 23?). A good title claims exactly what the evidence supports. Writing numbers for a reader ¶ Always give units : "US$4.20 per order", "12 percentage points", "3.1 days". Give a comparison : versus last year, versus target, versus the other group. A number alone means little. Round to what the decision needs: "about 38%" rather than "37.846%". Distinguish percent from percentage points : a rate going from 10% to 12% is a rise of 2 percentage points, or 20%. State the base and period : "of 1,240 orders in March", "per 10,000 customers". Misconception Better view "Storytelling means making things up or dramatising." It means ordering true evidence so the reader can follow it to a decision. "Put every chart in, to show the work." Put in the charts the argument needs; the rest go in an appendix. "The title should be neutral." It should be accurate. A specific, true message is more useful than a neutral label. Part 6: KPIs and dashboards ¶ What makes a KPI ¶ A metric is any number you can measure. A key performance indicator (KPI) is a metric chosen because it tracks progress towards an objective someone is responsible for. A useful KPI is: Defined precisely: numerator, denominator, period, filters, and who owns it ("orders delivered within 48 hours ÷ all orders delivered, per calendar week, excluding cancellations"). Tied to a decision or objective: if it moves, someone knows what to do. Compared with something: a target, last period, or a benchmark. Hard to game , or paired with a balancing metric. Goodhart's law: when a measure becomes a target, it tends to stop being a good measure. Call-centre "average handling time" falls if agents hang up early; pair it with "issue resolved on first call". Leading indicators move before the result (website visits, sales pipeline, staff training hours); lagging indicators record the result (revenue, churn). Vanity metrics look impressive but do not inform a decision (total app downloads since launch, page views without conversion). Ratio of sums or mean of ratios? ¶ Many KPIs are ratios: conversion rate, profit margin, on-time rate. When you combine several units (stores, days, campaigns), there are two different ways to compute "the" rate, and they usually give different answers. Predict, then run. Six stores report visits and orders. Is the company's conversion rate above or below the average of the six stores' conversion rates? stores = pd . DataFrame ({ "store" : [ "Airport" , "Mall" , "Station" , "Harbour" , "Campus" , "Village" ], "visits" : [ 12_000 , 9_500 , 7_000 , 1_200 , 800 , 300 ], "orders" : [ 360 , 380 , 245 , 66 , 52 , 27 ]}) stores [ "conversion" ] = stores [ "orders" ] / stores [ "visits" ] print ( stores . assign ( conversion = stores [ "conversion" ] . map ( " {:.1%} " . format )) . to_string ( index = False )) mean_of_ratios = stores [ "conversion" ] . mean () ratio_of_sums = stores [ "orders" ] . sum () / stores [ "visits" ] . sum () print ( f " \n Mean of the six store rates (each store counts once): { mean_of_ratios : .2% } " ) print ( f "Total orders / total visits (each visit counts once): { ratio_of_sums : .2% } " ) store visits orders conversion Airport 12000 360 3.0% Mall 9500 380 4.0% Station 7000 245 3.5% Harbour 1200 66 5.5% Campus 800 52 6.5% Village 300 27 9.0% Mean of the six store rates (each store counts once): 5.25% Total orders / total visits (each visit counts once): 3.67% The small stores convert better but have few visits. The mean of ratios gives each store equal weight, so the small stores pull it up; the ratio of sums gives each visit equal weight, so it reflects what the company actually achieved. You want Use Example The rate the whole business achieved Ratio of sums : Σ orders ÷ Σ visits Company conversion rate; total profit ÷ total sales for the profit margin How a typical unit performs Mean (or median) of the unit ratios "The typical store converts …" in a store league table In Tableau this is the difference between SUM([Orders]) / SUM([Visits]) (ratio of sums) and AVG([Orders] / [Visits]) (mean of row-level ratios). The Tableau lecture this afternoon returns to it. Always state which one a KPI uses. Anatomy of a KPI tile ¶ A good KPI tile answers "how are we doing?" in two seconds: name and period ("On-time delivery, October"), the value with its unit (92.4%), a comparison (target 95%, −2.6 points; last month 93.1%), a small trend (a sparkline of the last 12 periods), and a status that does not rely on colour alone (an arrow or a "below target" label). Dashboard layout ¶ A dashboard is a set of linked views on one screen that a specific audience uses to monitor or explore something repeatedly. Three kinds serve different readers: Kind Reader Typical content Strategic Executives A few KPIs against targets, monthly or quarterly trends Operational Front-line managers Today's or this week's numbers, alerts, drill-down to the item Analytical Analysts Filters, many dimensions, exploration Layout principles: Purpose first. One sentence: "This dashboard helps regional managers see whether their state is on track and which products cause losses." Reading order. Readers of left-to-right languages start top-left, so put the most important KPIs there, overview first, detail lower down. Overview first, zoom and filter, then details on demand (Shneiderman, 1996): the dashboard shows the whole; clicking filters it; tooltips give detail. Few views. Three to five views fit a screen; more and each becomes too small to read. Consistency. Same colour means the same thing everywhere; same number format; aligned edges on a grid. Make interactivity visible. Say "Click a store to filter" in a subtitle; readers do not discover hidden features. It should answer the audience's recurring questions; everything else is a click or a report away. "The more KPIs, the better informed." Beyond a handful, nobody knows which ones matter. Part 7: Marketing analytics ¶ Gordon's Chapter 6 shows analytics supporting most marketing decisions: which markets to enter, understanding customers , setting prices , choosing channels (distribution), planning promotion , developing products , and segmenting customers. It also warns that analytics only scales when definitions are consistent across teams ( data governance ), and that careless use of customer data breaks trust and privacy rules. This part concentrates on the metrics a digital marketing team reports every week. The funnel ¶ Customers move through stages, and at each stage some drop out. For an online campaign: impressions (ad shown) → clicks → visits → add to cart → orders Metric Formula Question it answers Click-through rate ( CTR ) clicks ÷ impressions Does the ad attract attention? Cost per click ( CPC ) spend ÷ clicks What does attention cost? Conversion rate ( CVR ) orders ÷ clicks (or ÷ visits; say which) Does the landing page and offer persuade? Cost per acquisition ( CPA ) spend ÷ orders (or ÷ new customers) What does one sale or customer cost? Return on ad spend ( ROAS ) revenue ÷ spend How much revenue per dollar of advertising? Average order value ( AOV ) revenue ÷ orders How big is each sale? Predict, then run. Four channels ran in one month. Which channel do you expect to have the best CTR, and will the same channel have the best ROAS? camp = pd . DataFrame ({ "channel" : [ "Search" , "Social" , "Email" , "Display" ], "impressions" : [ 400_000 , 1_500_000 , 60_000 , 2_500_000 ], "clicks" : [ 12_000 , 60_000 , 1_500 , 7_500 ], "orders" : [ 540 , 300 , 120 , 90 ], "spend" : [ 18_000 , 15_000 , 1_200 , 6_000 ], # US dollars "revenue" : [ 43_200 , 19_500 , 7_800 , 6_300 ], # US dollars }) . set_index ( "channel" ) kpi = pd . Social wins attention (the best CTR and the cheapest clicks) but few of those clicks buy; Email is tiny but highly efficient; Search brings the most orders. Three cautions: ROAS uses revenue, not profit. If the product margin is 40%, each dollar of revenue earns 40 cents before advertising, so the break-even ROAS is 1 ÷ 0.40 = 2.5. A ROAS of 2 looks positive and loses money; in this table even Search, at 2.4, is just below break-even on that margin. Efficient is not the same as scalable. Email's numbers come from people who already know the brand, and the list is small; doubling email spend will not double its orders. Ratios hide volume. Always show the counts (orders, spend) next to the rates. The funnel chart below shows where Search loses people between stages. funnel = pd . Series ({ "Impressions" : 400_000 , "Clicks" : 12_000 , "Visits" : 10_800 , "Add to cart" : 3_240 , "Orders" : 540 }) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 9 , 3.6 )) f = funnel . iloc [:: - 1 ] ax . barh ( f . index , np . log10 ( f . values ), color = OI [ "sky" ]) for y , ( stage , v ) in enumerate ( f . items ()): prev = funnel . shift ( 1 ) . get ( stage ) step = "" if pd . isna ( prev ) else f " ( { v / prev : .1% } of previous stage)" ax . text ( np . log10 ( v ) + 0.05 , y , f " { v : , }{ step } " , va = "center" , fontsize = 9 ) ax . set_xlim ( 0 , 7.5 ); ax . set_xticks ([]) ax . set_title ( "After the click, Search loses the most people between cart and order" ) plt . show () The bars use a log scale because the stages differ by a factor of almost a thousand; the labels carry the exact counts and the stage-to-stage rates, which are what a manager acts on. Of those rates, impressions to clicks is always small; among the later steps, cart to order is the weakest, which points to checkout (shipping costs, payment options) rather than to the ad. Customer lifetime value ¶ Customer lifetime value (CLV) estimates the profit a customer brings over the whole relationship, so that you know how much it is worth spending to acquire one. A simple and widely used version assumes each customer brings margin m per year, stays each year with probability r (the retention rate), and future money is discounted at rate d : CLV = m × r ÷ (1 + d − r) This version counts margin from the end of the first year onwards (as Gupta and Lehmann, 2003, set it up); variants add the first year's margin. Compare CLV with the customer acquisition cost (CAC) ; a common rule of thumb in subscription businesses is a CLV of at least three times CAC. def clv ( margin , retention , discount = 0.10 ): return margin * retention / ( 1 + discount - retention ) for r in [ 0.60 , 0.70 , 0.80 , 0.90 ]: print ( f "margin $40/year, retention { r : .0% } : CLV = $ { clv ( 40 , r ) : ,.0f } " ) margin $40/year, retention 60%: CLV = $48 margin $40/year, retention 70%: CLV = $70 margin $40/year, retention 80%: CLV = $107 margin $40/year, retention 90%: CLV = $180 Predict, then run (above). Raising retention from 80% to 90% adds more value than raising it from 60% to 70%. The formula is very sensitive to retention near the top, which is why subscription businesses spend so much on keeping customers. It is also sensitive to error: an estimate of 90% that is really 85% overstates CLV a lot. Report CLV with the assumptions next to it. Segmentation: RFM ¶ Segmentation groups customers who behave similarly so that each group can be treated differently. A simple behavioural method is RFM : score each customer on Recency (days since last purchase; lower is better), Frequency (number of purchases) and Monetary value (total spend). Gordon's chapter also mentions cluster analysis , which finds groups from many variables at once; RFM is the transparent version a manager can check by hand. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 42 ) n = 2000 cust = pd . DataFrame ({ "recency_days" : rng . gamma ( 2.0 , 45 , n ) . round () + 1 , "frequency" : rng . geometric ( 0.3 , n ), }) cust [ "monetary" ] = ( cust [ "frequency" ] * rng . gamma ( 2 , 25 , n )) . round ( 2 ) # US dollars # Score 1-5 by quintile; recency is reversed (recent customers score 5) cust [ "R" ] = pd . qcut ( cust [ "recency_days" ] . rank ( method = "first" ), 5 , labels = [ 5 , 4 , 3 , 2 , 1 ]) . astype ( int ) cust [ "F" ] = pd . qcut ( cust [ "frequency" ] . rank ( method = "first" ), 5 , labels = [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ]) . astype ( int ) cust [ "M" ] = pd . qcut ( cust [ "monetary" ] . rank ( method = "first" ), 5 , labels = [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ]) . astype ( int ) def segment ( row ): if row . FuncFormatter ( lambda v , _ : f " { v : .0% } " )) ax . set_title ( "A minority of customers brings a disproportionate share of revenue (synthetic)" ) plt . show () Each segment suggests a different action: thank and retain the Champions, win back those At risk before they lapse, nurture the Recent ones towards a second purchase. The segment rules are choices ; write them down so others can reproduce them. Attribution and its limits ¶ A customer may see a social ad, later click a search ad, then buy from an email. Which channel "gets" the sale? Attribution models divide the credit by rule: journeys = [ # (channels touched, in order), number of orders that followed that journey (( "Social" , "Search" , "Email" ), 120 ), (( "Search" ,), 200 ), (( "Social" , "Email" ), 80 ), (( "Display" , "Search" ), 60 ), (( "Email" ,), 90 ), (( "Display" , "Social" , "Search" ), 50 ), ] credit = { m : pd . Series ( 0.0 , index = [ "Search" , "Social" , "Email" , "Display" ]) for m in [ "Last click" , "First click" , "Linear" ]} for path , orders in journeys : credit [ "Last click" ][ path [ - 1 ]] += orders credit [ "First click" ][ path [ 0 ]] += orders for ch in path : credit [ "Linear" ][ ch ] += orders / len ( path ) print ( pd . DataFrame ( credit ) . round ( 0 ) . astype ( int ) . to_string ()) Last click First click Linear Search 310 200 287 Social 0 200 97 Email 290 90 170 Display 0 110 47 The same 600 orders give very different channel "results" depending on the rule. Last click favours channels near the purchase (search, email); first click favours channels that introduce the brand (social, display). None of them is "true", because all of them answer a different question from the one the budget holder asks. The deeper limit: attribution divides credit among channels a buyer touched ; it does not tell you whether the sale would have happened without the ad ( incrementality ). Many people who click a search ad for the brand's own name were going to buy anyway. Tracking is also incomplete: privacy rules and browser and phone changes (such as Apple's App Tracking Transparency prompt, introduced in 2021) mean many journeys are only partly observed. The reliable way to measure incrementality is an experiment : show the ad to a random group and hold it back from a similar random control group. A quick A/B test ¶ A shop shows the old checkout page to 5,000 random visitors (A) and a new one to another 5,000 (B). nA , xA = 5_000 , 200 # visitors and orders, old page nB , xB = 5_000 , 232 # visitors and orders, new page pA , pB = xA / nA , xB / nB se = np . sqrt ( pA * ( 1 - pA ) / nA + pB * ( 1 - pB ) / nB ) diff = pB - pA lo , hi = diff - 1.96 * se , diff + 1.96 * se print ( f "Conversion A = { pA : .2% } , B = { pB : .2% } , difference = { diff * 100 : +.2f } percentage points" ) print ( f "Approximate 95% confidence interval for the difference: { lo * 100 : +.2f } to { hi * 100 : +.2f } points" ) Conversion A = 4.00%, B = 4.64%, difference = +0.64 percentage points Approximate 95% confidence interval for the difference: -0.16 to +1.44 points Predict, then run (above). B looks 16% better (4.64% against 4.00%). But the interval for the difference includes zero, so a test of this size cannot rule out that the new page makes no difference. Options: run the test longer, or decide in advance what difference is worth acting on and how many visitors are needed to detect it. The lesson for reports: say how uncertain a difference is before recommending on it. Misconception Better view "The channel with the best ROAS should get all the budget." Returns usually fall as spend rises, and ROAS ignores margin and incrementality. Test increases in steps. "Last-click attribution shows what works." It shows who was last in line. Use experiments to measure what an ad adds. "A higher conversion rate in a test proves the new version is better." Only if the difference is larger than the noise; check the interval and the sample size. "More customer data is always better." Data you collect without a purpose, or without consent, creates privacy risk and erodes trust (Gordon, Ch. 6). Part 8: Two real cases ¶ Case 1: John Snow and the Broad Street pump (London, 1854) ¶ In late August 1854 cholera killed hundreds of people within a few streets of Soho in London. The accepted theory was that cholera spread through bad air ("miasma"). The physician John Snow suspected contaminated water. He collected the addresses of the dead, interviewed families, and found that most deaths clustered around the public water pump on Broad Street, while groups who drank from other sources (workers at a brewery with its own well, residents of a workhouse with its own pump) were largely spared. He persuaded the local board to remove the pump's handle on 8 September. His famous dot map of deaths around the pump was published the following year, in the second edition of his book on cholera. Discussion questions: What made Snow's evidence persuasive? Separate the map (position of each death) from the comparisons (brewery workers, the workhouse, people who walked to Broad Street from further away). Which were stronger evidence, and why? Historians note the outbreak was already declining when the handle was removed. What does that mean for the claim "removing the handle ended the outbreak"? Write a message title for Snow's map that claims exactly what the evidence supports. Snow's map shows counts of deaths , not a rate. When would a map of counts mislead (Part 4, example 5)? Why was it reasonable here? The board acted before the map existed. What, then, was the map for ? Who was its audience? Case 2: predicting customers' life events (Target, United States) ¶ In 2012 a widely read New York Times Magazine article by Charles Duhigg described how the US retailer Target built a model that used changes in shopping baskets (for example, unscented lotion and certain supplements) to estimate which customers were likely to be pregnant, so it could send baby-product offers before competitors did. The article reported that customers found such targeted offers unsettling, and that the company began mixing baby offers in with unrelated products so the targeting was less obvious. Some details of the most-quoted anecdote in the article have been questioned since, but the case is widely used to discuss marketing analytics and privacy. Discussion questions: Which marketing decisions from Gordon's Chapter 6 does this model support (segmentation, promotion, timing)? What metric would the marketing team use to judge it? The model could be accurate and still harm the business. How? Which stakeholders are affected, and what would you measure besides sales? Disguising targeted offers among unrelated ones hides the targeting rather than removing it. Is that an acceptable response? What would a more transparent approach look like? Write the big idea, in one sentence, for a memo against launching such a model at a company you know. Sources for the cases. Snow, J. (1855). On the mode of communication of cholera (2nd ed.).
