docs.text: Explain why time-ordered data needs different tools, and name the components of a series (trend, seasonality, cycle, noise). Decompose a series and read each part. Build baseline forecasts (naive, seasonal naive, mean) and explain why every model must beat them. Forecast with moving averages and exponential smoothing (simple, Holt, Holt-Winters). Explain stationarity , run and read the ADF test , and use differencing . Read ARIMA and SARIMA orders and say what each number means. Split time series data in time order , and measure error with MAE, RMSE and MAPE . Produce and explain forecast intervals , and communicate uncertainty for a decision. This lecture has one period (P4), so it has a core path and extensions . Teach the core in P4; the extensions are for a later study block (Day 6 P3 covers Excel's Forecast Sheet, which uses exponential smoothing), faster students, or self-study. Part Topic Path 1 Time series and their components Core 2 Decomposition Core (one chart) and extension 3 Train and test in time order Core 4 Baselines and error measures Core 5 Moving averages Core (short) 6 Exponential smoothing: simple, Holt, Holt-Winters Extension 7 Stationarity, the ADF test and differencing Core 8 ARIMA and SARIMA Core (orders) and extension (ACF) 9 Forecast intervals Core 10 Choosing a model: rolling-origin evaluation Extension 11 Communicating uncertainty for a decision Core (summary) and extension 12 Business case Extension 13 Lab 4 briefing Core 14 Practice, quiz and summary Self-study Reading Read Chapter 4 of the course reading packet for order-dependence and autocorrelation, the null hypothesis of the ADF test, differencing, the moving-average and exponential-smoothing calculations, and why an error measure must be read against the scale of the series. Gordon's Chapter 9 (summarised there) adds when history stops being a guide. This lecture adds decomposition, baselines, Holt-Winters, SARIMA orders, MAPE, intervals and communicating uncertainty. import warnings import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import statsmodels.api as sm from statsmodels.tsa.holtwinters import ExponentialSmoothing , SimpleExpSmoothing from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller warnings . filterwarnings ( "ignore" ) # hide statsmodels' convergence and frequency notices plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.dpi" : 100 , "figure.figsize" : ( 10 , 3.8 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlesize" : 11 }) # Okabe and Ito colour-blind-safe colours BLUE , ORANGE , GREEN , PURPLE , SKY , GREY = "#0072B2" , "#D55E00" , "#009E73" , "#CC79A7" , "#56B4E9" , "#9A9A9A" # Synthetic monthly sales of a fictional cafe group, thousand US dollars, Jan 2015 to Dec 2024 rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) months = pd . date_range ( "2015-01-01" , periods = 120 , freq = "MS" ) # "MS" = month start growth = 80 * 1.006 ** np . arange ( 120 ) # about 7% a year season = np . array ([ 0.86 , 0.84 , 0.93 , 0.97 , 1.02 , 1.08 , 1.16 , 1.15 , 1.01 , 0.98 , 0.95 , 1.05 ]) noise = rng . normal ( 0 , 0.03 , 120 ) sales = pd . Series ( growth * season [ months . month - 1 ] * ( 1 + noise ), index = months , name = "sales" ) . round ( 1 ) print ( sales . head ( 3 )) print ( "..." ) print ( sales . tail ( 3 )) 2015-01-01 67.2 2015-02-01 68.1 2015-03-01 71.0 Freq: MS, Name: sales, dtype: float64 ... 2024-10-01 161.5 2024-11-01 158.3 2024-12-01 173.5 Freq: MS, Name: sales, dtype: float64
docs.title: What you will be able to do

docs.text: A time series is a sequence of observations at evenly spaced times: monthly sales, daily web visits, hourly electricity demand, weekly CO₂ readings. Two properties set it apart from the tables of Days 1 and 2: Order matters. Shuffle the rows of the diamonds table and every average stays the same. Shuffle a time series and the pattern a forecast depends on is destroyed. Neighbours are related (autocorrelation). This month's sales are close to last month's. That makes forecasting possible, and it breaks the "independent rows" assumption behind ordinary regression and random train/test splits. Most business series are a mix of four components : Component What it is Café example Trend Long-run rise or fall New branches, rising prices Seasonality A pattern that repeats with a fixed period (12 months, 7 days) Summer iced drinks, December gifts Cycle Rises and falls without a fixed period, often years long Economic booms and recessions Noise (irregular) What is left: random, unpredictable Weather, a broken machine Predict, then run. Before plotting: in which month do you expect the café's sales to peak? Will the summer peak in 2024 be the same size in thousand dollars as in 2015, or larger? fig , ( ax1 , ax2 ) = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 13 , 3.8 ), gridspec_kw = { "width_ratios" : [ 2 , 1 ]}) ax1 . plot ( sales . index , sales , color = BLUE ) ax1 . set_title ( "Monthly sales, 2015-2024" ) ax1 . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) for year , colour in [( 2015 , GREY ), ( 2024 , BLUE )]: one = sales [ str ( year )] ax2 . plot ( one . index . month , one . values , marker = "o" , color = colour , label = str ( year )) ax2 . set_xticks ( range ( 1 , 13 ), list ( "JFMAMJJASOND" )) ax2 . set_title ( "Two years side by side" ) ax2 . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () The left chart shows an upward trend and a yearly season . The right chart shows the peak in July and August, a December bump, and a low in February. The swing is larger in 2024 than in 2015: the seasonal effect grows with the level of sales. That is multiplicative seasonality (summer is "about 15% above normal"), as opposed to additive seasonality (summer is "about 15 thousand dollars above normal"). The difference matters when we choose a model.
docs.title: Part 1: Time series and their components (core)

docs.text: Decomposition separates a series into trend, seasonal and remainder parts: Additive: sales = trend + seasonal + remainder. Multiplicative: sales = trend × seasonal × remainder. The classical method estimates the trend with a centred 12-month moving average , averages the detrended values for each calendar month to get the seasonal pattern, and calls whatever is left the remainder. parts = seasonal_decompose ( sales , model = "multiplicative" , period = 12 ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 4 , 1 , figsize = ( 10 , 7.5 ), sharex = True ) for ax , series , title , colour in zip ( axes , [ parts . observed , parts . trend , parts . seasonal , parts . resid ], [ "Observed" , "Trend (centred 12-month moving average)" , "Seasonal factor" , "Remainder" ], [ BLUE , ORANGE , GREEN , GREY ]): ax . plot ( series . index , series , color = colour ) ax . set_title ( title , loc = "left" ) axes [ 2 ] . axhline ( 1 , color = "black" , lw = 0.6 ) axes [ 3 ] . axhline ( 1 , color = "black" , lw = 0.6 ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () factors = parts . seasonal [ "2016" ] . values print ( "Seasonal factor by month (1.00 = an average month):" ) print ( pd . Series ( factors , index = list ( "JFMAMJJASOND" )) . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) Seasonal factor by month (1.00 = an average month): J 0.87 F 0.85 M 0.93 A 0.96 M 1.00 J 1.08 J 1.16 A 1.15 S 1.01 O 0.98 N 0.96 D 1.06 Read the seasonal factors as "July sales are typically about 16% above the trend; February about 15% below". Because we built this series ourselves, we can check: the factors are close to the season values used in the setup cell. On real data you never know the truth, which is why we test forecasts on held-out months. Three cautions (extension): The trend line is missing for the first and last six months: a centred average needs six months on each side. The most recent months, the ones a manager cares about most, are where decomposition is weakest. Classical decomposition assumes the seasonal pattern is the same every year . Methods such as STL ( statsmodels.tsa.seasonal.STL ) let it change slowly. Decomposition describes the past; it is not a forecast. But it tells you what a forecasting model must handle: here, a trend and a multiplicative season. Misconception: "Seasonality means anything that goes up and down." Seasonality has a fixed, known period (a year, a week, a day). Rises and falls of varying length, such as business cycles, are cycles , and they are far harder to forecast.
docs.title: Part 2: Decomposition (core: one chart; extension: the rest)

docs.text: A forecast is only worth something if it works on data the model has not seen . So we hide the most recent months (the test set, or holdout), fit on the rest (the training set), forecast the hidden months and compare. Here we hold out the last 24 months (two full seasonal cycles), so every calendar month is tested twice. HORIZON = 24 train , test = sales . iloc [: - HORIZON ], sales . iloc [ - HORIZON :] print ( f "Training: { train . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { train . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } ( { len ( train ) } months)" ) print ( f "Test: { test . index [ 0 ] : %b %Y } to { test . index [ - 1 ] : %b %Y } ( { len ( test ) } months)" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train . index , train , color = BLUE , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = ORANGE , label = "Test data (hidden from the model)" ) ax . axvline ( test . index [ 0 ], color = "black" , lw = 0.8 , ls = "--" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Hold out the most recent 24 months" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Training: Jan 2015 to Dec 2022 (96 months) Test: Jan 2023 to Dec 2024 (24 months)
docs.title: Part 3: Train and test in time order (core)

docs.text: On Day 4 you will split rows at random into training and test sets. For a time series, that is a mistake. Predict, then run. Suppose we pick 20% of the months at random as the "test" set and "forecast" each one as the average of the month before and the month after it. Will the error be smaller or larger than an honest forecast of the last 24 months? Is that a fair test? rng_split = np . random . default_rng ( 7 ) test_positions = np . sort ( rng_split . choice ( np . arange ( 1 , len ( sales ) - 1 ), size = 24 , replace = False )) neighbour_guess = ( sales . values [ test_positions - 1 ] + sales . values [ test_positions + 1 ]) / 2 leaky_mae = np . mean ( np . abs ( sales . values [ test_positions ] - neighbour_guess )) honest_naive = np . full ( HORIZON , train . iloc [ - 1 ]) # last known value, repeated honest_mae = np . mean ( np . abs ( test . values - honest_naive )) print ( f "Random split, 'forecast' from the months on either side: MAE = { leaky_mae : 5.1f } " ) print ( f "Time-ordered split, simplest honest forecast: MAE = { honest_mae : 5.1f } " ) Random split, 'forecast' from the months on either side: MAE = 5.8 Time-ordered split, simplest honest forecast: MAE = 15.7 The random split looks far better, but it cheated : it used the month after each test month, which a real forecaster never has. A random split lets information from the future leak into training. The time-ordered split mimics real life: stand at a date, use only the past, forecast the future. Rules for the split: Never shuffle. Training data comes first, test data after. Make the test period at least as long as the horizon you will forecast , and cover full seasonal cycles if the series is seasonal. Use the test set once , at the end. If you try twenty models and keep the one with the best test score, the test set has become part of training (Part 10 shows a better way to compare). After choosing the model, refit it on all the data before forecasting the real future.
docs.title: Why not a random split?

docs.text: For each test month, the error is actual − forecast. Three ways to summarise many errors: Measure Formula Units Notes MAE (mean absolute error) mean of |actual − forecast| Same as the data "On average we are off by 7 thousand dollars." Easy to explain RMSE (root mean squared error) √(mean of (actual − forecast)²) Same as the data Squares first, so large misses count more . Always ≥ MAE MAPE (mean absolute percentage error) mean of |actual − forecast| ÷ |actual| × 100 Percent Lets you compare series of different sizes. Undefined when an actual is 0, and huge when actuals are near 0 Predict, then run. Two forecasts for four months. Forecast A misses by 5 every month. Forecast B is perfect for three months and misses by 20 once. Which has the lower MAE? The lower RMSE? def errors ( actual , forecast ): """MAE, RMSE and MAPE of a forecast.""" e = np . asarray ( actual ) - np . asarray ( forecast ) return { "MAE" : np . mean ( np . abs ( e )), "RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean ( e ** 2 )), "MAPE %" : np . mean ( np . abs ( e ) / np . abs ( np . asarray ( actual ))) * 100 } actual_4 = [ 100 , 120 , 110 , 130 ] forecast_a = [ 105 , 115 , 115 , 125 ] # off by 5 every month forecast_b = [ 100 , 120 , 110 , 110 ] # perfect, then one miss of 20 pd . DataFrame ({ "Forecast A" : errors ( actual_4 , forecast_a ), "Forecast B" : errors ( actual_4 , forecast_b )}) . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } Forecast A Forecast B MAE 5.00 5.00 RMSE 5.00 10.00 MAPE % 4.39 3.85 Same MAE, different RMSE: RMSE punishes the single big miss. Choose the measure that matches the cost of errors. If one large miss is a disaster (a stock-out at Christmas), watch RMSE. If cost grows in proportion to the size of the miss, MAE is the natural choice. Read every error against the scale of the series. An MAE of 5 is tiny for sales of 5,000 and enormous for sales of 10. Report the MAE next to the average level, or report MAPE as well.
docs.title: Error measures

docs.text: A baseline is a forecast so simple that any serious model must beat it. If it does not, the model is not worth its complexity. Baseline Forecast for every future month Good when Mean The average of all training data The series has no trend or season (rare) Naive The last observed value The series wanders (stock prices, exchange rates) Seasonal naive The value in the same month last year A strong, stable season Predict, then run. Which baseline will do best on the café test period? Which worst? forecasts = { "Mean" : pd . Series ( train . mean (), index = test . index ), "Naive" : pd . Series ( train . iloc [ - 1 ], index = test . index ), "Seasonal naive" : pd . Series ( np . tile ( train . iloc [ - 12 :] . values , HORIZON // 12 ), index = test . index ), } scores = pd . DataFrame ({ name : errors ( test , f ) for name , f in forecasts . items ()}) . T print ( "Average test-period sales:" , round ( test . mean (), 1 ), "thousand US dollars \n " ) print ( scores . round ( 1 )) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "2020" :] . index , train [ "2020" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , lw = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) for ( name , f ), colour in zip ( forecasts . items (), [ PURPLE , SKY , ORANGE ]): ax . plot ( f . index , f , color = colour , ls = "--" , label = name ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Three baselines on the 24 test months" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , ncol = 2 ) plt . show () Average test-period sales: 152.4 thousand US dollars MAE RMSE MAPE % Mean 44.4 48.2 28.0 Naive 15.7 19.3 10.8 Seasonal naive 17.0 19.3 10.9 The mean is far too low: it averages ten years of a growing series. The naive forecast is flat, so it misses the season. The seasonal naive copies last year's shape but not the growth since then, so it is too low, more so in the second test year. Each baseline misses one component. That is the job of the models that follow: capture level, trend and season together. Keep these numbers; every model below must beat them.
docs.title: Baselines

docs.text: A moving average (MA) of order k averages the last k values. It has two uses that are easily confused: A centred MA smooths the past to show the trend (Part 2 used a centred 12-month MA). It needs future values, so it cannot forecast. A trailing MA averages the most recent k values and uses that as the forecast for the next period. A trailing MA weights the k recent values equally and ignores the rest, so it lags behind any change. The clearest way to see the lag is a sudden step in demand: weeks = pd . RangeIndex ( 1 , 41 , name = "week" ) step_rng = np . random . default_rng ( 3 ) demand = pd . Series ( np . where ( weeks < 20 , 100 , 130 ) + step_rng . normal ( 0 , 4 , 40 ), index = weeks ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( weeks , demand , color = "black" , marker = "." , label = "Weekly demand (steps up in week 20)" ) for k , colour in [( 3 , ORANGE ), ( 10 , BLUE )]: forecast_ma = demand . rolling ( k ) . mean () . shift ( 1 ) # shift: use only weeks before the forecast week ax . plot ( weeks , forecast_ma , color = colour , label = f "Trailing { k } -week MA forecast" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Week" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Units" ) ax . set_title ( "A longer moving average is smoother but slower to react" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () The 3-week MA catches up within three weeks but wobbles with the noise; the 10-week MA is smooth but takes ten weeks to catch up. Every smoother trades responsiveness for stability. Note the .shift(1) : without it, each week's "forecast" would include that week's own value, a small version of the leak in Part 3. On the café series a trailing 12-month MA forecasts a flat line at last year's average: no trend, no season. It is a smoother, not a full forecasting model.
docs.title: Part 5: Moving averages (core, short)

docs.text: Simple exponential smoothing (SES) forecasts with a weighted average of all past values, with weights that shrink geometrically into the past: next forecast = α × latest actual + (1 − α) × latest forecast , with α between 0 and 1. Unrolled, the weight on the value j periods ago is α × (1 − α) j : weights = pd . DataFrame ({ f "alpha = { a } " : [ a * ( 1 - a ) ** j for j in range ( 6 )] for a in [ 0.2 , 0.5 , 0.8 ]}, index = [ f " { j } periods ago" for j in range ( 6 )]) weights . round ( 3 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } alpha = 0.2 alpha = 0.5 alpha = 0.8 0 periods ago 0.200 0.500 0.800 1 periods ago 0.160 0.250 0.160 2 periods ago 0.128 0.125 0.032 3 periods ago 0.102 0.062 0.006 4 periods ago 0.082 0.031 0.001 5 periods ago 0.066 0.016 0.000 A large α trusts the latest value (fast, but jumpy); a small α remembers a long history (smooth, but slow). statsmodels chooses α by minimising the one-step-ahead errors on the training data. SES has only a level , so its forecast is flat. Two extensions add the missing components: Method Components Parameters Forecast shape Simple (SES) Level α Flat Holt (linear trend) Level + trend α, β Straight line Holt-Winters Level + trend + season (additive or multiplicative) α, β, γ Line with the seasonal pattern Predict, then run. Which of the three will beat the seasonal naive baseline on the café test period? smoothers = { "SES" : SimpleExpSmoothing ( train , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit (), "Holt" : ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit (), "Holt-Winters (additive season)" : ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , seasonal = "add" , seasonal_periods = 12 , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit (), "Holt-Winters (multiplicative season)" : ExponentialSmoothing ( train , trend = "add" , seasonal = "mul" , seasonal_periods = 12 , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit (), } for name , fit in smoothers . items (): forecasts [ name ] = fit . forecast ( HORIZON ) scores = pd . DataFrame ({ name : errors ( test , f ) for name , f in forecasts . items ()}) . T print ( scores . round ( 1 )) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "2020" :] . index , train [ "2020" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , lw = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) for name , colour in [( "SES" , SKY ), ( "Holt" , PURPLE ), ( "Holt-Winters (multiplicative season)" , GREEN )]: ax . plot ( test . index , forecasts [ name ], color = colour , ls = "--" , label = name ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Exponential smoothing: each added component fixes one kind of miss" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () MAE RMSE MAPE % Mean 44.4 48.2 28.0 Naive 15.7 19.3 10.8 Seasonal naive 17.0 19.3 10.9 SES 15.6 19.1 10.8 Holt 19.1 22.0 13.5 Holt-Winters (additive season) 7.9 10.0 4.8 Holt-Winters (multiplicative season) 6.9 8.4 4.4 SES is flat like the naive forecast. Holt adds the trend but no season, and here it does worse than the naive forecast: a straight line drawn through the seasonal ups and downs misses badly at the peaks and troughs. Adding one component without the other can hurt. Holt-Winters captures both, and the multiplicative version, which matches the growing swings we saw in Part 1, does best of the smoothers. The lesson is not "Holt-Winters always wins"; it is " match the model's components to the components in the data ", which is why we plot and decompose first. Excel's Forecast Sheet (Day 6) uses an additive Holt-Winters method (ETS AAA).
docs.title: Part 6: Exponential smoothing (extension)

docs.text: A series is stationary if its statistical behaviour does not change over time: constant mean, constant variance, and the same relationship between neighbours. ARIMA models assume stationarity (after any differencing), because they learn "how this month relates to last month" and use that rule forever. Predict, then run. Three simulated series follow. Which are stationary: white noise (independent random values), a random walk (each value = previous value + random step), or a trend plus noise? sim_rng = np . random . default_rng ( 11 ) n = 200 white_noise = pd . Series ( sim_rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n )) random_walk = pd . Series ( sim_rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n )) . cumsum () trend_noise = pd . Series ( 0.05 * np . arange ( n ) + sim_rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n )) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 13 , 3.2 )) for ax , s , title in zip ( axes , [ white_noise , random_walk , trend_noise ], [ "White noise" , "Random walk" , "Trend + noise" ]): ax . plot ( s , color = BLUE , lw = 1 ) ax . set_title ( title ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Only white noise is stationary: it keeps returning to the same mean with the same spread. The trend has a mean that changes. The random walk is the subtle case: it has no trend built in, yet it wanders without ever returning, and its spread grows with time. Many business and financial series behave like random walks.
docs.title: Part 7: Stationarity, the ADF test and differencing (core)

docs.text: Null hypothesis The series has a unit root : it is not stationary (it behaves like a random walk) Small p-value (≤ 0.05) Reject the null: evidence the series is stationary Large p-value (> 0.05) Cannot reject: treat the series as not stationary, and difference it This is the reverse of many tests you know: here the small p-value is the "good" result. adfuller(series) returns the test statistic first and the p-value second. def adf_report ( series , label ): stat , p = adfuller ( series . dropna ())[: 2 ] verdict = "stationary" if p <= 0.05 else "not stationary" print ( f " { label : <16 } ADF statistic = { stat : 7.2f } p-value = { p : .3f } -> { verdict } " ) adf_report ( white_noise , "White noise" ) adf_report ( random_walk , "Random walk" ) adf_report ( trend_noise , "Trend + noise" ) White noise ADF statistic = -14.09 p-value = 0.000 -> stationary Random walk ADF statistic = -1.12 p-value = 0.706 -> not stationary Trend + noise ADF statistic = -0.45 p-value = 0.901 -> not stationary A caution on the trend series: adfuller by default allows for a constant but not a trend, so a steady trend reads as non-stationary. (With regression="ct" it tests "stationary around a trend" instead.) Know which question your test asks.
docs.title: The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test

docs.text: First differencing replaces each value with its change from the previous one: this month minus last month. It removes a trend and turns a random walk into white noise. Seasonal differencing subtracts the value one season ago: this month minus the same month last year, for monthly data. It removes a stable seasonal pattern. Predict, then run. The café training data has a trend and a season. Which of these will the ADF test call stationary: the level, the first difference, the seasonal difference? log_train = np . log ( train ) # logs turn multiplicative growth and seasonality into additive versions = { "Level (log)" : log_train , "First diff" : log_train . diff (), "Seasonal diff" : log_train . diff ( 12 ), "Both" : log_train . diff () . diff ( 12 ), } fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 4 , 1 , figsize = ( 10 , 7.5 ), sharex = True ) for ax , ( label , s ) in zip ( axes , versions . items ()): ax . plot ( s . index , s , color = BLUE , lw = 1 ) ax . set_title ( label , loc = "left" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () for label , s in versions . items (): adf_report ( s , label ) Level (log) ADF statistic = -0.58 p-value = 0.875 -> not stationary First diff ADF statistic = -15.62 p-value = 0.000 -> stationary Seasonal diff ADF statistic = -5.07 p-value = 0.000 -> stationary Both ADF statistic = -2.77 p-value = 0.063 -> not stationary Read the charts and the p-values together: The level trends upward: not stationary. The first difference has no trend, and the ADF test calls it stationary, yet the chart still shows a strong repeating pattern . The ADF test checks for a unit root, not for seasonality. Never read a test without the chart. The seasonal difference removes the season (it is the growth rate compared with the same month last year). Both differences together: no trend, no season, a series that fluctuates around zero. Its ADF p-value may land near 0.05; with short series, tests have limited power, which is one more reason to look at the chart. We took logs first: with multiplicative seasonality, logs turn "15% above normal" into a constant additive shift, and differences of logs are approximately percentage changes . Misconception: "Difference until the p-value is tiny." Each difference throws information away and adds noise. Use the fewest differences that remove the trend and the season: usually d = 1, plus D = 1 for a strong season.
docs.title: Differencing

docs.text: ARIMA(p, d, q) combines three ideas, applied to the differenced series: Letter Name Meaning Intuition p AutoRegressive order Uses the last p values "This month is like last month" d Integrated (differencing) order Differences taken Removes the trend q Moving-Average order Uses the last q forecast errors "Correct for last month's surprise" (not the same as Part 5's moving average) SARIMA(p, d, q)(P, D, Q)ₛ adds the same three ideas at the seasonal lag s (12 for monthly data): P seasonal AR terms (this July is like last July), D seasonal differences, Q seasonal MA terms. Examples: Model Reads as ARIMA(0, 1, 0) The random walk: the naive forecast ARIMA(0, 1, 1) Equivalent to simple exponential smoothing SARIMA(0, 1, 1)(0, 1, 1)₁₂ One ordinary and one seasonal difference, one MA term at each level: the classic "airline model" for monthly series with trend and season SARIMA(1, 1, 0)(1, 1, 0)₁₂ Same differences, AR terms instead of MA terms How are p , q , P , Q chosen? Two common ways: read the autocorrelation plots (extension below), or try a few small orders and keep the one with the lowest AIC (an in-sample score that penalises extra parameters). Keep orders small (0, 1 or 2); large orders overfit. Here we fit the airline model to the log of the training data and transform the forecast back. sarima = sm . tsa . statespace . SARIMAX ( np . log ( train ), order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 ), seasonal_order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 , 12 )) . fit ( disp = False ) sarima_fc = sarima . get_forecast ( steps = HORIZON ) forecasts [ "SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 on logs" ] = np . exp ( sarima_fc . predicted_mean ) scores = pd . DataFrame ({ name : errors ( test , f ) for name , f in forecasts . items ()}) . T . sort_values ( "RMSE" ) print ( f "Average test-period sales: { test . mean () : .1f } thousand US dollars \n " ) print ( scores . round ( 1 )) Average test-period sales: 152.4 thousand US dollars MAE RMSE MAPE % SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 on logs 3.8 4.8 2.5 Holt-Winters (multiplicative season) 6.9 8.4 4.4 Holt-Winters (additive season) 7.9 10.0 4.8 SES 15.6 19.1 10.8 Seasonal naive 17.0 19.3 10.9 Naive 15.7 19.3 10.8 Holt 19.1 22.0 13.5 Mean 44.4 48.2 28.0 Read the table from the top: the models that capture level, trend and multiplicative season beat every baseline, and the best are a few percent off on average (see MAPE). Because our series was built with a trend and a multiplicative season, it is no surprise that the matching models win. On real data the ranking is less predictable, and the gap between models is often smaller than the gap between a model and a naive baseline. Check your understanding. (1) A colleague fits ARIMA(2, 0, 1) to monthly sales that grow every year. What is wrong with d = 0? (2) Which SARIMA order is the same as "the seasonal naive forecast"? (Hint: one seasonal difference and nothing else.)
docs.title: Part 8: ARIMA and SARIMA (core: orders; extension: ACF)

docs.text: The ACF (autocorrelation function) shows the correlation of a series with itself 1, 2, 3, … periods earlier. The PACF shows the same after removing the effect of the shorter lags. On the differenced series, rough rules: a sharp cut-off in the PACF after lag p suggests AR( p ); a sharp cut-off in the ACF after lag q suggests MA( q ); spikes at lag 12 point to seasonal terms. from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf , plot_pacf stationary = np . log ( train ) . diff () . diff ( 12 ) . dropna () fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.4 )) plot_acf ( stationary , lags = 26 , ax = axes [ 0 ], color = BLUE , vlines_kwargs = { "colors" : BLUE }) plot_pacf ( stationary , lags = 26 , ax = axes [ 1 ], method = "ywm" , color = BLUE , vlines_kwargs = { "colors" : BLUE }) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "ACF of the log series after both differences" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "PACF of the same series" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () The large negative spike at lag 1 in the ACF, and another near lag 12, are the signature of the airline model: one MA term and one seasonal MA term. Differencing a series that has noise tends to create exactly this negative lag-1 correlation. The shaded band is roughly the 95% range for "no correlation"; bars inside it are noise.
docs.title: Extension: reading autocorrelation plots

docs.text: A point forecast says "sales next July will be 200". It will almost certainly be wrong by something. A forecast interval says how wrong it could plausibly be: "an 80% interval of 190 to 210" means that, if the model's assumptions hold, about 8 out of 10 such intervals contain the actual value. Predict, then run. Will the interval be the same width for every month of the 24-month test period? ci95 = np . exp ( sarima_fc . conf_int ( alpha = 0.05 )) ci80 = np . exp ( sarima_fc . conf_int ( alpha = 0.20 )) point = forecasts [ "SARIMA(0,1,1)(0,1,1)12 on logs" ] fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( train [ "2020" :] . index , train [ "2020" :], color = GREY , label = "Training data" ) ax . fill_between ( test . index , ci95 . iloc [:, 0 ], ci95 . iloc [:, 1 ], color = SKY , alpha = 0.25 , label = "95 % i nterval" ) ax . fill_between ( test . index , ci80 . iloc [:, 0 ], ci80 . iloc [:, 1 ], color = SKY , alpha = 0.5 , label = "80 % i nterval" ) ax . plot ( test . index , point , color = BLUE , ls = "--" , label = "Point forecast" ) ax . plot ( test . index , test , color = "black" , lw = 2 , label = "Actual (test)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "The further ahead, the wider the interval" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , ncol = 2 ) plt . show () width = ci95 . iloc [:, 1 ] - ci95 . iloc [:, 0 ] print ( f "95% interval width, first test month: { width . iloc [ 0 ] : .1f } ; last test month: { width . iloc [ - 1 ] : .1f } " ) for name , ci in [( "80%" , ci80 ), ( "95%" , ci95 )]: inside = (( test >= ci . iloc [:, 0 ]) & ( test <= ci . iloc [:, 1 ])) . mean () print ( f "Share of test months inside the { name } interval: { inside : .0% } " ) 95% interval width, first test month: 16.7; last test month: 26.5 Share of test months inside the 80% interval: 88% Share of test months inside the 95% interval: 100% Two lessons: Intervals widen with the horizon. Each month ahead adds a new unknown shock on top of the earlier ones. A forecast for next month is much more certain than one for two years out. (On the log scale the interval is symmetric; back on the dollar scale it is wider above than below.) Check the coverage. If the 80% interval contains the actual value in about 80% of test months, the intervals are honest. Ours contain it at least as often as promised; with only 24 months to check, that is as close as we can judge. On real data intervals are often too narrow : they assume the model is right and the future behaves like the past, and they ignore surprises such as a pandemic, a new competitor or a price change. Misconception: "A 95% interval means there is a 95% chance the model is right." It describes the noise the model knows about . It does not cover the model being the wrong model, or the world changing.
docs.title: Part 9: Forecast intervals (core)

docs.text: One test period is one draw of luck. A sturdier comparison repeats the test from several origins : stand at the end of 2020, forecast 2021; stand at the end of 2021, forecast 2022; and so on, always training only on data before the origin. This is rolling-origin (or time-series cross-validation) evaluation. def fit_and_forecast ( name , history , h = 12 ): if name == "Seasonal naive" : return np . tile ( history . iloc [ - 12 :] . values , h // 12 ) if name == "Holt-Winters (mult.)" : return ExponentialSmoothing ( history , trend = "add" , seasonal = "mul" , seasonal_periods = 12 , initialization_method = "estimated" ) . fit () . forecast ( h ) . values fit = sm . tsa . statespace . SARIMAX ( np . log ( history ), order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 ), seasonal_order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 , 12 )) . fit ( disp = False ) return np . exp ( fit . forecast ( h )) . values rows = [] for origin_year in [ 2019 , 2020 , 2021 , 2022 , 2023 ]: history = sales [: str ( origin_year )] actual = sales [ str ( origin_year + 1 )] for name in [ "Seasonal naive" , "Holt-Winters (mult.)" , "SARIMA airline (logs)" ]: rows . append ({ "forecast year" : origin_year + 1 , "model" : name , "MAPE %" : errors ( actual , fit_and_forecast ( name , history ))[ "MAPE %" ]}) backtest = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . pivot ( index = "forecast year" , columns = "model" , values = "MAPE %" ) print ( backtest . round ( 1 )) print ( " \n Average over the five years:" ) print ( backtest . mean () . round ( 1 ) . sort_values () . to_string ()) model Holt-Winters (mult.) SARIMA airline (logs) Seasonal naive forecast year 2020 3.2 4.7 4.7 2021 3.8 3.6 9.7 2022 2.9 3.5 5.2 2023 3.2 2.1 7.5 2024 3.1 2.7 7.4 Average over the five years: model Holt-Winters (mult.) 3.2 SARIMA airline (logs) 3.3 Seasonal naive 6.9 The ranking is more trustworthy because it rests on five years, not one, and you can see how much each model's error varies from year to year. Choose the model with a good and stable error, prefer the simpler one when the difference is small, and then refit it on all the data to forecast the real future.
docs.title: Part 10: Choosing a model: rolling-origin evaluation (extension)

docs.text: A forecast is an input to a decision: how many staff to roster, how much coffee to order, what budget to set. Five rules for presenting one: Give a range, not just a number. "July sales: about 197 thousand dollars, likely between 189 and 206 (80% interval)." Say how good the method has been , in the reader's units: "Over the last five years, this method's monthly forecasts were off by about 3% on average." State the assumptions : "Assumes no new branches, no price change, and a normal summer." Show it as a fan chart (as in Part 9), with the history for context, actual and forecast clearly distinguished, and the horizon labelled. Connect the range to the cost of being wrong. If running out costs more than over-ordering, plan to a high point of the range, not the middle. Here is rule 5 in action. We refit the airline model on all ten years and forecast 2025. For a summer stock order where a shortfall is three times as costly as a surplus, the right quantity is not the point forecast but a higher quantile : the level that demand stays below 75% of the time (because 3 ÷ (3 + 1) = 0.75; this is the "newsvendor" rule). from scipy.stats import norm final = sm . tsa . statespace . SARIMAX ( np . log ( sales ), order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 ), seasonal_order = ( 0 , 1 , 1 , 12 )) . fit ( disp = False ) future = final . get_forecast ( steps = 12 ) mean_log = future . predicted_mean sd_log = future . se_mean plan = pd . DataFrame ({ "point forecast" : np . exp ( mean_log ), "80 % lo w" : np . exp ( mean_log + norm . ppf ( 0.10 ) * sd_log ), "80 % hi gh" : np . exp ( mean_log + norm . ppf ( 0.90 ) * sd_log ), "plan to (75th percentile)" : np . exp ( mean_log + norm . ppf ( 0.75 ) * sd_log ), }) . round ( 1 ) plan . index = plan . index . strftime ( "%b %Y" ) plan . loc [[ "Jun 2025" , "Jul 2025" , "Aug 2025" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } point forecast 80% low 80% high plan to (75th percentile) Jun 2025 183.2 175.4 191.3 187.4 Jul 2025 197.0 188.6 205.7 201.5 Aug 2025 197.2 188.8 206.0 201.8 fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( sales [ "2022" :] . index , sales [ "2022" :], color = "black" , label = "Actual sales" ) for level , alpha in [( 0.95 , 0.2 ), ( 0.80 , 0.4 ), ( 0.50 , 0.6 )]: ci = np . exp ( future . conf_int ( alpha = 1 - level )) ax . fill_between ( ci . index , ci . iloc [:, 0 ], ci . iloc [:, 1 ], color = BLUE , alpha = alpha , lw = 0 , label = f " { level : .0% } interval" ) ax . plot ( mean_log . index , np . exp ( mean_log ), color = BLUE , ls = "--" , label = "Point forecast" ) ax . axvline ( sales . index [ - 1 ], color = GREY , lw = 0.8 ) ax . text ( sales . index [ - 1 ], ax . get_ylim ()[ 1 ] * 0.97 , " forecast starts" , color = GREY , va = "top" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "2025 sales forecast: a fan chart shows the most likely path and how sure we are" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" , ncol = 2 ) plt . show () Words matter as much as the chart. Compare: Weak Better "July sales will be 197." "July sales will most likely be about 197 thousand dollars; 8 times in 10 they should fall between 189 and 206." "The model is 97% accurate." "In tests on each of the last five years, monthly forecasts were off by about 3% on average, and by under 5% in the worst year." "Sales will grow 7%." "If the past trend continues and nothing structural changes, sales will grow about 7%." Gordon's Chapter 9, as summarised in the reading packet, adds a caution: forecasts are weakest when a disruption breaks the pattern, and analysts may need to set aside or adjust unusual periods rather than extend them mechanically. A model fitted to 2015–2019 knew nothing of 2020. Misconception: "A more complex model gives a more certain forecast." Complexity can fit the past better without making the future more knowable. The interval width comes from how noisy the series is and how far ahead you look.

docs.text: A city hospital forecasts daily emergency-department arrivals to set nurse rosters four weeks ahead. Its current method is "same day last year". docs.text: Day 3 lecture: Text mining ¶ Period 3 of Day 3, after the midterm, and the bridge to Lab 3. How a business turns free text into numbers it can act on: structured and unstructured data, the text-mining pipeline, tokenising and normalising, stop words and why "not" must sometimes stay, word frequency and n-grams, word clouds and their limits, TF-IDF, how the VADER sentiment scorer works and where it fails, checking scores against human labels, and turning scores into a decision without harming the people who wrote the text. Run each code cell with Shift + Enter , in order. The examples use forty synthetic hotel reviews written for this lecture (a fictional two-site hotel, the "Lakeside Inn"), each with the guest's star rating. Lab 3 uses a different set of product reviews; this lecture deliberately does not use them, so that you practise each step here and apply it yourself in the lab. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder; NLTK reads its word lists from data/nltk_data , so nothing is downloaded. Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook, run %pip install nltk wordcloud scikit-learn in a first cell, and replace the setup cell with the NLTK download cell from GAP's Lab 3 (see the Lab 3 guide , Route A). What you will be able to do ¶ Explain the difference between structured and unstructured data, and describe the steps of a text-mining pipeline . Tokenise and normalise text, remove stop words , and say when removing a word such as "not" changes the meaning. Count word frequencies and n-grams , and explain what a word cloud can and cannot show. Explain the idea behind stemming , lemmatisation and TF-IDF . Explain how the VADER lexicon scores a sentence (negation, intensifiers, "but", capitals and punctuation), and predict where it will fail. Validate sentiment scores against human labels before trusting them. Turn text-mining results into a decision , and name the ethical risks of mining customer text. This lecture has one period (P3), so it has a core path and extensions . Teach the core in P3; the extensions are for a later study block, faster students, or self-study. Part 1: Structured and unstructured data (core) ¶ Structured data fits a fixed table: every row has the same columns, and each column has one type (a number, a date, a category). The stars column above is structured: you can average it, group it and chart it at once. Unstructured data has no fixed fields. A review, an email, a support chat or a call transcript carries its meaning in the choice and order of words, and its length varies from three words to three pages. Structured Unstructured Example Star rating, price, check-in date Review text, complaint email, social-media post Shape Fixed columns and types Free-length strings Summarise with describe() , groupby() , a pivot table Nothing, until it is converted Share of what organisations collect Smaller Larger (often quoted as about 80%) What it tells you How much (3 stars) Why (the shower was cold) Between the two sits semi-structured data, such as a JSON order record with a free-text "notes" field. Text mining is the conversion from the right-hand column to the left: it creates new structured columns (counts, flags, scores) from text, after which every tool from Days 1 and 2 applies again. Predict, then run. describe() works on stars . What do you expect it to say about the text column? print ( reviews [ "stars" ] . describe () . round ( 2 )) print () print ( reviews [ "text" ] . describe ()) count 40.00 mean 2.98 std 1.44 min 1.00 25% 2.00 50% 3.00 75% 4.00 max 5.00 Name: stars, dtype: float64 count 40 unique 40 top Lovely stay! The staff were friendly and the breakfast was excellent. freq 1 Name: text, dtype: object For text, describe() can only count: 40 values, 40 unique, the "top" is just one of them. To learn anything we must engineer features . Even very simple features are already useful: reviews [ "n_words" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . str . split () . str . len () reviews [ "mentions_breakfast" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower () . str . contains ( "breakfast" ) reviews . groupby ( "mentions_breakfast" )[[ "stars" , "n_words" ]] . agg ([ "mean" , "count" ]) . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead tr th { text-align: left; } .dataframe thead tr:last-of-type th { text-align: right; } stars n_words mean count mean count mentions_breakfast False 2.6 30 13.2 30 True 4.1 10 11.8 10 Two new structured columns, made from text in two lines. The rest of the lecture does the same thing more carefully. Part 2: The pipeline: tokenising and normalising (core) ¶ Every text-mining project follows roughly the same pipeline. The order matters: each step works on the output of the one before. Step What it does Example 1. Collect Gather the text and its context (date, site, rating) Export reviews with their star ratings 2. Clean Remove markup, fix encodings, mask personal data Strip HTML; replace e-mail addresses with [EMAIL] 3. Tokenise Split text into units (tokens) "wasn't clean" → was , n't , clean 4. Normalise Make variants of a word match Breakfast , BREAKFAST → breakfast 5. Filter Drop tokens that carry no topic Remove the , and , punctuation 6. Reduce (optional) Stem or lemmatise rooms → room 7. Represent Turn tokens into numbers Counts, n-grams, TF-IDF, a sentiment score 8. Analyse Find the pattern Top words, sentiment by site, topics 9. Validate Check against human judgement Compare scores with star ratings 10. Decide Interpret the pattern for an action Fix the showers at Riverside first Steps 1 to 8 are text mining ; step 10 is text analytics , the interpretation for a decision. Step 9 is the one most often skipped. Tokenising ¶ Predict, then run. Splitting on spaces is the simplest tokeniser. What will go wrong with the review below? example = reviews . loc [ 3 , "text" ] # review 4 print ( example ) print () print ( "split(): " , example . split ()) print ( "word_tokenize:" , word_tokenize ( example )) Check-in took forty minutes. The receptionist was polite, but nobody could find our booking. split(): ['Check-in', 'took', 'forty', 'minutes.', 'The', 'receptionist', 'was', 'polite,', 'but', 'nobody', 'could', 'find', 'our', 'booking.'] word_tokenize: ['Check-in', 'took', 'forty', 'minutes', '.', 'The', 'receptionist', 'was', 'polite', ',', 'but', 'nobody', 'could', 'find', 'our', 'booking', '.'] split() leaves punctuation stuck to words ( minutes. and minutes would be counted as different words) and keeps Check-in and booking. whole. NLTK's word_tokenize separates punctuation and handles contractions in a consistent way: it splits "wasn't" into was and n't . Remember that last point; it matters in Part 3. Normalising ¶ Normalising makes the variants of one word count as one. The usual steps are: lower-case, remove punctuation and numbers ( isalpha() keeps tokens made only of letters), and sometimes stem or lemmatise (Part 10). Each step is a choice with a cost: Choice Gain Cost Lower-case Breakfast = breakfast Loses GREAT (shouting, which VADER uses) and names such as Bath vs bath Drop punctuation Cleaner counts Loses !!! and ? (emphasis, questions) and emoticons such as :( Drop numbers Fewer junk tokens Loses 8am , 45 minutes , room 212 Keep only letters ( isalpha() ) Drops , and . Also drops n't and check-in raw_tokens = [ t for text in reviews [ "text" ] for t in word_tokenize ( text )] lower_tokens = [ t . lower () for t in raw_tokens ] alpha_tokens = [ t for t in lower_tokens if t . isalpha ()] print ( "Distinct tokens, raw: " , len ( set ( raw_tokens ))) print ( "Distinct tokens, lower-cased: " , len ( set ( lower_tokens ))) print ( "Distinct tokens, letters only: " , len ( set ( alpha_tokens ))) print ( "Variants of 'breakfast' in raw: " , sorted ({ t for t in raw_tokens if t . lower () == "breakfast" })) print ( "Tokens dropped by isalpha(): " , sorted ({ t for t in lower_tokens if not t . isalpha ()})) Distinct tokens, raw: 241 Distinct tokens, lower-cased: 224 Distinct tokens, letters only: 216 Variants of 'breakfast' in raw: ['Breakfast', 'breakfast'] Tokens dropped by isalpha(): ['!', "'s", "'ve", ',', '.', '8am', 'check-in', 'check-out'] Lower-casing merges variants such as Breakfast and breakfast . isalpha() drops the punctuation, but look at what else it drops: check-in , check-out , 8am , and the contraction fragments 's and 've . In reviews that say "didn't" or "wasn't", it would drop n't too. A pipeline is a series of decisions, and every decision removes some information. Part 3: Stop words, and when to keep "not" (core) ¶ Stop words are very frequent words that carry grammar rather than topic: the, is, and, a, of, to . In almost any English text they are the most common words, so a frequency count that keeps them tells you only that the text is in English. Removing them lets the topic words rise to the top. english_stop = set ( stopwords . words ( "english" )) print ( "Words in NLTK's English stop-word list:" , len ( english_stop )) print ( "Some of them:" , sorted ( english_stop )[: 25 ]) print () for w in [ "not" , "no" , "nor" , "never" , "very" , "too" , "but" , "against" , "isn't" , "n't" ]: print ( f " { w !r: 10 } in the list? { w in english_stop } " ) Words in NLTK's English stop-word list: 198 Some of them: ['a', 'about', 'above', 'after', 'again', 'against', 'ain', 'all', 'am', 'an', 'and', 'any', 'are', 'aren', "aren't", 'as', 'at', 'be', 'because', 'been', 'before', 'being', 'below', 'between', 'both'] 'not' in the list? True 'no' in the list? True 'nor' in the list? True 'never' in the list? False 'very' in the list? True 'too' in the list? True 'but' in the list? True 'against' in the list? True "isn't" in the list? True "n't" in the list? False The standard list contains "not", "no", "nor", "very", "too", "but" and full contractions such as "isn't". For counting topics , that is fine. For anything to do with opinion , it is dangerous. Predict, then run. Review 13 says "Not clean. Hair in the sink and dust under the bed." After lower-casing, isalpha() and the standard stop-word list, which words remain? Would a reader of the remaining words know the room was dirty? def clean_tokens ( text , stop ): """Lower-case, tokenise, keep letters only, and drop the given stop words.""" return [ t for t in word_tokenize ( text . lower ()) if t . isalpha () and t not in stop ] text_13 = reviews . loc [ 12 , "text" ] print ( "Original: " , text_13 ) print ( "Standard stop words: " , clean_tokens ( text_13 , english_stop )) NEGATIONS = { "not" , "no" , "nor" , "never" , "n't" , "without" } opinion_stop = english_stop - NEGATIONS def clean_keep_negation ( text ): """As clean_tokens, but keep negations, and turn n't into not so isalpha() keeps it.""" toks = [( "not" if t == "n't" else t ) for t in word_tokenize ( text . lower ())] return [ t for t in toks if t . isalpha () and t not in opinion_stop ] print ( "Negations kept: " , clean_keep_negation ( text_13 )) print () other = reviews . loc [ 36 , "text" ] # review 37 print ( "Original: " , other ) print ( "Standard stop words: " , clean_tokens ( other , english_stop )) print ( "Negations kept: " , clean_keep_negation ( other )) Original: Not clean. Hair in the sink and dust under the bed. Standard stop words: ['clean', 'hair', 'sink', 'dust', 'bed'] Negations kept: ['not', 'clean', 'hair', 'sink', 'dust', 'bed'] Original: The heating did not work and the extra blanket never arrived. Standard stop words: ['heating', 'work', 'extra', 'blanket', 'never', 'arrived'] Negations kept: ['heating', 'not', 'work', 'extra', 'blanket', 'never', 'arrived'] With the standard list, "Not clean" becomes clean : the word count now counts a complaint as praise . Three practical rules: Choose the stop-word list for the task. For topics (what do people talk about?), the standard list is fine. For opinion (what do they think?), keep the negations, or join them to the next word ( not_clean ). Add domain stop words. In hotel reviews, hotel , room and stay may appear everywhere and so tell you little; in a product's reviews, the product's own name does the same. Add them deliberately, and write down which you added. Remember contractions. word_tokenize turns "didn't" into did + n't , and isalpha() silently drops n't . A pipeline can lose a negation even when "not" is not in the stop list. Misconception: "Stop-word removal is a standard step, so it is always safe." It is safe for counting topics. It changes meaning for opinion, and it must happen after tokenising, because the list contains words, not strings of text. Part 4: Frequency and n-grams (core) ¶ Once the text is clean tokens, the simplest analysis is to count . NLTK's FreqDist is a counter with useful methods. Here we use the topic pipeline (standard stop words) plus three domain stop words that appear in almost every hotel review. Predict, then run. Before you run the next cell, write down the three words you expect at the top. Will they be about what guests discuss, or how they feel? An n-gram is a run of n consecutive tokens: bigrams ( n = 2) and trigrams ( n = 3). "Thin" alone is ambiguous; "paper thin" and "walls thin" are not. Bigrams are often where the actionable phrases live: a product name, a part of the service, a complaint. Predict, then run. Joining all reviews into one long string first, as quick scripts often do, creates false bigrams across the boundary (the last word of one review followed by the first word of the next). With ten reviews the effect is tiny; with the n-grams of a large corpus it adds noise. Part 6: How VADER scores text (core) ¶ Sentiment analysis gives each text a score for how positive or negative it is. There are two families: Lexicon-based methods look words up in a dictionary of pre-rated words and combine the ratings with rules. No training data is needed. Machine-learning methods learn which words and phrases predict a label from many labelled examples (Part 12). VADER ( Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner ; Hutto and Gilbert, 2014) is a lexicon method designed for short, informal text such as reviews and social posts. Its dictionary holds about 7,500 words, slang terms and emoticons, each rated by human judges from −4 (most negative) to +4 (most positive). vader = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () print ( "Words in VADER's lexicon:" , len ( vader . lexicon )) for w in [ "excellent" , "friendly" , "good" , "okay" , "fine" , "slow" , "rude" , "dirty" , "worst" , "lukewarm" , "tiny" , "mould" ]: print ( f " { w : <10 } { vader . lexicon . get ( w , 'not in lexicon' ) } " ) Words in VADER's lexicon: 7502 excellent 2.7 friendly 2.2 good 1.9 okay 0.9 fine 0.8 slow not in lexicon rude -2.0 dirty -1.9 worst -3.1 lukewarm not in lexicon tiny not in lexicon mould not in lexicon polarity_scores() returns four numbers. neg , neu and pos are the shares of the text that are negative, neutral and positive (they add up to 1). compound is the summary score: VADER adds up the adjusted ratings of the words it found and squashes the sum into −1 to +1 with compound = s ÷ √(s² + 15) , where s is the sum. One positive word moves the score a lot; each further positive word moves it less, so the score approaches 1 but never reaches it. VADER then adjusts the word ratings with rules : Rule Example Effect Negation "not good" A negation in the three words before a rated word flips and shrinks its rating Intensifiers (booster words) "very good", "kind of good" "very" increases, "kind of" decreases the rating Capitals "GOOD" in otherwise lower-case text Increases the rating Exclamation marks "good!!!" Increase the score (up to four count) "But" "good, but terrible" Words after "but" weigh more, words before it less Emoticons and slang ":)", "lol" Rated in the lexicon like words Predict, then run. Part 8: Validating scores against labels (core) ¶ Before anyone acts on sentiment scores, compare them with a human judgement on a sample. Here each review has a star rating , which we can turn into a reference label: 4–5 stars positive, 3 neutral, 1–2 negative. (Stars are not perfect either: some people write a glowing review and give 3 stars, but they are the customer's own judgement.) Predict, then run. Two more useful numbers come from the matrix. Of the reviews that are negative (by stars), what share did VADER catch? That is recall for the negative class. Of the reviews VADER called negative, what share really were? That is precision . is_neg = reviews [ "star_label" ] == "Negative" called_neg = reviews [ "vader_label" ] == "Negative" recall = ( is_neg & called_neg ) . sum () / is_neg . sum () precision = ( is_neg & called_neg ) . sum () / called_neg . sum () print ( f "Negative reviews by stars: { is_neg . sum () } , called negative by VADER: { called_neg . sum () } " ) print ( f "Recall for negative (share of unhappy guests caught): { recall : .0% } " ) print ( f "Precision for negative (share of flags that were right): { precision : .0% } " ) print ( " \n How the label counts change with the threshold:" ) for cut in [ 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.20 , 0.50 ]: counts = reviews [ "compound" ] . apply ( sentiment_label , cut = cut ) . value_counts () . reindex ( order , fill_value = 0 ) print ( f " cut = { cut : <5 } " + " " . join ( f " { k } : { v : >2 } " for k , v in counts . items ())) Negative reviews by stars: 17, called negative by VADER: 7 Recall for negative (share of unhappy guests caught): 29% Precision for negative (share of flags that were right): 71% How the label counts change with the threshold: cut = 0.01 Negative: 7 Neutral: 9 Positive: 24 cut = 0.05 Negative: 7 Neutral: 10 Positive: 23 cut = 0.2 Negative: 5 Neutral: 13 Positive: 22 cut = 0.5 Negative: 2 Neutral: 24 Positive: 14 The share of "negative" reviews in a report can change a lot with the threshold, and the threshold was never chosen for this business. A validation step therefore answers three questions: How often does the scorer agree with people? Where does it disagree? Which threshold suits the decision? Misconception: "The tool is published and widely used, so its scores are accurate." It is accurate on the kind of text it was built and tested on . Your domain may differ. Validate on a few hundred hand-labelled examples from your own data before you report percentages. The same logic applies to anything a model scores: a fraud score, a churn risk, a CV-screening score. A score you have not checked against reality is an opinion with decimals. Part 9: From scores to decisions (core) ¶ A sentiment distribution ("55% positive") is a finding . A manager needs a decision : what to fix, where, and how to tell whether it worked. Three tools help. 1. Combine topic and sentiment (aspects) ¶ Group words into the aspects a manager can act on, then ask, for each aspect: how many reviews mention it, and how unhappy are those reviewers? If the manager ranked the problems by VADER alone, aspects whose complaints use domain words or plain facts (booking and billing, facilities) would look much less serious than the guests' own ratings say. The method shapes the priority list. Small counts matter too: an aspect mentioned in four reviews is a lead to investigate, not a conclusion. 2. Decide what a score triggers, and count the cost of errors ¶ Suppose the hotel wants to reply personally to every unhappy guest within a day. A rule such as "flag every review VADER calls negative" has two kinds of error: Error Example Cost Missed complaint (false negative) A 1-star review about mould scored neutral An unhappy guest gets no reply; a public complaint stays unanswered False alarm (false positive) A 3-star review flagged as negative A few minutes of staff time Here a missed complaint costs much more than a false alarm, so the rule should catch more, even at the price of more false alarms: use the star rating where it exists, add keyword rules for known domain complaints, and send everything with a score below a generous threshold to a person. The threshold is a business decision about the cost of each error, not a technical default. 3. Write the recommendation ¶ A text-mining recommendation has four parts: Finding , with the count and the method: "Of 40 reviews, n mention [aspect]; x % of those gave 1–2 stars." Evidence a manager can read: two or three short quotes (anonymised). Action with an owner: "Facilities manager to check [item] at [site] by [date]." How we will know : the measure to watch afterwards (share of reviews mentioning the aspect, mean stars) and its limit ("the scorer misses complaints worded as facts, so we read a sample by hand each month"). Part 10: Stemming and lemmatisation (extension) ¶ "room" and "rooms", "help", "helped", "helpful" and "helping": should they count as one word? Two ways to reduce words to a common form: Stemming Lemmatisation How Chops endings with fixed rules Looks the word up in a dictionary, often using its part of speech Output A stem , which may not be a real word ( comfort , friendli ) A lemma , a real dictionary word ( be for "was", good for "better") Speed and needs Fast; no data needed Slower; needs a dictionary such as WordNet Risk Over-stemming ( university , universe → univers ) and under-stemming Needs the right part of speech ("meeting" the noun vs "meeting" the verb) The Porter stemmer needs no data, so we can try it offline: stemmer = PorterStemmer () words = [ "room" , "rooms" , "help" , "helped" , "helpful" , "helping" , "comfortable" , "comfort" , "friendly" , "friendliness" , "was" , "better" , "university" , "universe" , "news" , "new" ] pd . DataFrame ({ "word" : words , "Porter stem" : [ stemmer . stem ( w ) for w in words ]}) . set_index ( "word" ) . T .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } word room rooms help helped helpful helping comfortable comfort friendly friendliness was better university universe news new Porter stem room room help help help help comfort comfort friendli friendli wa better univers univers news new Stemming merges help , helped and helping (good) and turns friendly into friendli (ugly but harmless for counting). It cannot know that was is a form of be (it even cuts it to wa ) or that better is a form of good ; a lemmatiser can, because it uses a dictionary (NLTK's WordNetLemmatizer needs the WordNet data, which this course's bundle does not include, so we do not run it here). It merges university and universe and news and new (bad: different meanings). When to use them: for counting topics in large collections, stemming or lemmatising reduces the vocabulary and merges obvious variants. For sentiment with VADER , do not : VADER's lexicon expects real words, and comfort or friendli may not be in it. Also note that helpful and helping carry different opinions; merging them can blur the signal. Part 11: TF-IDF (extension) ¶ Raw counts favour words that are common everywhere ("room" appears in many reviews, so it tells you little about any one of them). TF-IDF (term frequency × inverse document frequency) scores a word highly in a document when it is frequent in that document but rare across the collection : TF-IDF of word w in document d = tf( w , d ) × log( N ÷ df( w )) , where tf is the count of word w in document d , N is the number of documents, and df is the number of documents that contain w . A word found in every document gets log( N ÷ N ) = log 1 = 0. (Libraries add small adjustments, such as +1 terms, but the idea is the same.) By hand, with three tiny documents ¶ Predict, then run. In the three documents below, which word gets a TF-IDF of exactly 0 in every document? DataFrame ({ name : { w : d . split () . count ( w ) * np . log ( N / df_w [ w ]) for w in vocab } for name , d in docs . items ()}) . round ( 2 ) table [ "documents containing" ] = pd . "cockroach" is in one document and appears twice there, so it dominates document C. TF-IDF picks out what is distinctive about each document. On the reviews ¶ scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer does the counting, weighting and normalising in one step. A useful question for a manager: which words are most distinctive of the unhappy reviews ? We average each word's TF-IDF over the 1–2 star reviews and over the 4–5 star reviews and compare. from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer tfidf = TfidfVectorizer ( stop_words = sorted ( opinion_stop ), token_pattern = r "[a-z]+(?:-[a-z]+)?" ) X = tfidf . fit_transform ( reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower ()) weights = pd . DataFrame ( X . toarray (), columns = tfidf . get_feature_names_out ()) low = weights [ reviews [ "stars" ] <= 2 ] . mean () high = weights [ reviews [ "stars" ] >= 4 ] . mean () distinct = pd . DataFrame ({ "mean TF-IDF, 1-2 stars" : low , "mean TF-IDF, 4-5 stars" : high }) distinct [ "difference" ] = distinct . iloc [:, 0 ] - distinct . iloc [:, 1 ] print ( "Most distinctive of the unhappy reviews:" ) print ( distinct . sort_values ( "difference" , ascending = False ) . head ( 8 ) . round ( 3 )) print ( " \n Most distinctive of the happy reviews:" ) print ( distinct . sort_values ( "difference" ) . head ( 8 ) . round ( 3 )) Most distinctive of the unhappy reviews: mean TF-IDF, 1-2 stars mean TF-IDF, 4-5 stars difference not 0.084 0.0 0.084 night 0.055 0.0 0.055 every 0.054 0.0 0.054 never 0.044 0.0 0.044 smelled 0.044 0.0 0.044 bathroom 0.042 0.0 0.042 work 0.042 0.0 0.042 nobody 0.042 0.0 0.042 Most distinctive of the happy reviews: mean TF-IDF, 1-2 stars mean TF-IDF, 4-5 stars difference staff 0.000 0.121 -0.121 breakfast 0.015 0.131 -0.115 friendly 0.000 0.090 -0.090 comfortable 0.000 0.081 -0.081 quiet 0.000 0.076 -0.076 slow 0.000 0.074 -0.074 clean 0.019 0.083 -0.064 lovely 0.000 0.056 -0.056 The unhappy reviews are distinguished by negations ( not , never , nobody ) and descriptions of what happened ( smelled , bathroom , night , work ), the happy ones by evaluative words ( friendly , comfortable , lovely ) and the things guests liked ( staff , breakfast ). Note slow on the happy side: mild complaints sit inside 4-star reviews too. That is one more reason a pure sentiment lexicon misses complaints: unhappy guests often describe rather than evaluate . TF-IDF is also the usual way to turn text into numeric features for a model, the topic of Day 4. Part 12: Lexicon or machine learning? (extension) ¶ Lexicon (VADER) Machine learning (for example, logistic regression on TF-IDF) Needs labelled data No Yes, usually hundreds to thousands of examples Transparent Yes: you can see which words scored Partly: you can inspect word weights Domain vocabulary Only if you add it Learns it from the labels Speed to start Minutes Days to weeks (labelling) Typical accuracy in a specific domain Moderate Higher, if the labels are good and plentiful Main risk Misses domain words and sarcasm Learns the biases and errors in its labels; drifts as language changes Modern large language models are a third option. They handle context and sarcasm better, but are harder to audit, cost more per document, and still need to be validated on your labels in exactly the same way. A tiny demonstration: train a classifier to spot 1–2 star reviews from their words, and test it fairly with leave-one-out validation (train on 39 reviews, predict the 40th, repeat 40 times). from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut , cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline y = ( reviews [ "stars" ] <= 2 ) . astype ( int ) # 1 = unhappy guest model = make_pipeline ( TfidfVectorizer ( token_pattern = r "[a-z]+(?:-[a-z]+)?" ), LogisticRegression ( C = 10 )) pred = cross_val_predict ( model , reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower (), y , cv = LeaveOneOut ()) vader_pred = ( reviews [ "vader_label" ] == "Negative" ) . astype ( int ) for name , p in [( "VADER (negative label)" , vader_pred ), ( "Logistic regression, leave-one-out" , pred )]: caught = (( p == 1 ) & ( y == 1 )) . sum () print ( f " { name : <36 } accuracy { np . mean ( p == y ) : .0% } unhappy guests caught { caught } of { y . sum () } " ) VADER (negative label) accuracy 65% unhappy guests caught 5 of 17 Logistic regression, leave-one-out accuracy 60% unhappy guests caught 5 of 17 With only 40 examples, neither method is trustworthy, and the comparison could easily flip with another 40 reviews. The point is the workflow: a model is only as good as the amount and quality of labelled data behind it, and both methods are judged the same way , on data the model has not seen. You will meet train/test thinking again in the forecasting lecture and on Day 4. A middle path is to extend the lexicon with domain words. In NLTK, vader.lexicon is a dictionary, so vader.lexicon.update({"lukewarm": -1.5}) changes later scores. That is powerful and risky: whoever picks the ratings decides the results, so record every change, justify it, and re-validate. Part 13: Ethics of mining customer text (core summary, extension detail) ¶ Customer text is written by people, often about other people, and rarely with analysis in mind. Five questions to ask before mining it: Consent and purpose. Did people agree to this use? A review posted to help other travellers is not obviously consent to build a profile of the reviewer. Use the text for the purpose it was collected for, or get consent. Personal data. Reviews and support chats contain names, e-mail addresses, phone and room numbers, and sometimes health or family details. Mask them before analysis and keep only what you need (data minimisation). In China, the Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) applies; in Europe, the GDPR. People named in the text. Complaints often name staff ("the receptionist, Li, was rude"). Using sentiment scores to judge or discipline individual employees, without context or a chance to respond, is unfair and often unlawful. Bias. Lexicons and models work best on the language they were built on. Non-native speakers, dialects, other languages and older or younger customers can be scored systematically differently, so their complaints count for less. Check accuracy by group , not only overall. Manipulation and honesty. Do not use mining to suppress or bury negative reviews, to target vulnerable customers, or to publish "95% positive" when the scorer misses complaints. Fake reviews also exist; mining them as genuine distorts the decision. A simple example of masking personal data with regular expressions: raw = [ "Room 212 was freezing. Call me on 138-0013-8000 or write to guest.wang@example.com." , "Thanks to Ms Chen at reception! My booking ref is LK-55821." , ] def mask ( text ): text = re . sub ( r "[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+" , "[EMAIL]" , text ) text = re . sub ( r "\b\d {3} [- ]?\d {4} [- ]?\d {4} \b" , "[PHONE]" , text ) text = re . sub ( r "\b[A-Z] {2} -\d{4,}\b" , "[BOOKING]" , text ) text = re . sub ( r "\b(Mr|Ms|Mrs|Dr)\.? [A-Z][a-z]+" , "[NAME]" , text ) return text for t in raw : print ( mask ( t )) Room 212 was freezing. Call me on [PHONE] or write to [EMAIL] Thanks to [NAME] at reception! My booking ref is [BOOKING]. Pattern-based masking catches formats (e-mails, phone numbers), but misses free-form names ("ask for Li") and room numbers written as words. In practice it is combined with named-entity recognition and a human check of a sample. Masking is a minimum, not a guarantee of anonymity: a review that mentions a date, a site and an unusual event can still identify a guest. Part 14: Business case (extension) ¶ A food-delivery platform collects about 200,000 written restaurant reviews a month. Product managers propose three uses of automatic sentiment scores: A. Show each restaurant a monthly "sentiment score" next to its star rating. B. Automatically hide restaurants whose sentiment falls below a threshold from the app's front page. C. Route every review with a negative score to a support agent, who contacts the customer within 24 hours. Discuss in groups: For each use, which error matters more: a missed negative or a false alarm? Who bears the cost of each? Which use would you approve first, and what validation would you require before launch (sample size, who labels, which groups to check)? Reviews arrive in Mandarin, Cantonese, English and a mix of all three, with many emoji. What does that do to a lexicon such as VADER, and to the fairness of use B? Restaurant owners discover the scoring rules and start asking customers to "please use the word excellent ". What happens to the measure? (Recall Goodhart's law from Day 2.) Write the one-sentence limitation you would put under any sentiment chart shown to senior managers. Part 15: Lab 3 briefing (core) ¶ In Lab 3 (periods 5 and 6) you run the same pipeline on a small set of product reviews: tokenise, remove stop words (including a few product words), draw a word cloud, list the most frequent keywords, score each review with VADER, label it with the ±0.05 thresholds, chart the label counts, and answer questions about what you see. When a score surprises you, look up the words in vader.lexicon before you explain it. The Lab 3 guide has both routes, checks and known pitfalls. Part 16: Practice, quiz and summary ¶ Practice ¶ Core ¶ Core 1. Write three short hotel reviews of your own: one VADER should score clearly positive, one clearly negative, and one that a person reads as negative but VADER scores as neutral or positive. Score them and explain each result with the rules in Part 6. Core 2. Rebuild the frequency bar chart of Part 4 for the Old Town site only, then for Riverside only. Which words differ? How many reviews does each chart rest on? Core 3. Using the confusion matrix in Part 8, write two sentences for the hotel manager about how far the VADER labels can be trusted, with numbers. Stretch ¶ Stretch 1. Change the threshold in sentiment_label to 0.3. Recompute the confusion matrix and the recall for negative reviews. Is the rule better or worse for the "reply to every unhappy guest" decision? Stretch 2. Score each sentence of a review separately (split with nltk.sent_tokenize ) and report the most negative sentence of each review. Which reviews does this help with? Stretch 3. Find the three bigrams that appear only in 1–2 star reviews and at least twice. If there are none, explain why with this little data. Challenge ¶ Challenge 1. Make a copy of the analyser and add up to eight hotel words to its lexicon with ratings you justify (for example, lukewarm , tiny , mould ). Re-run Part 8. How much does agreement improve? Then argue the other side: why is this "tuning on the test data", and how should it be done properly? Challenge 2. Write a function pipeline_report(texts, stars) that prints the top 10 words, the top 5 bigrams, the VADER label counts and the confusion matrix against the star labels, for any list of reviews. Challenge 3. Extend the mask function to catch room numbers ("room 212") and Chinese mobile numbers written without dashes. Test it on five sentences you write, including two that should not be masked. Quiz ¶ Give two examples each of structured and unstructured business data, and say what each can tell a manager that the other cannot. Put these steps in order: stop-word removal, tokenising, validating, lower-casing, scoring, deciding. Why can removing stop words harm a sentiment analysis? Give an example. What does isalpha() do to the token n't , and why does that matter? Why are bigrams often more useful to a manager than single words? Name two limits of a word cloud and the chart you would use instead. What does TF-IDF give a weight of zero to, and why? Name four of VADER's rules and give an example sentence for each. A review scores compound = 0.0 with neu = 1.0. What does that most likely mean? Define recall for the negative class in words a manager understands. Give one reason to prefer a lexicon method and one to prefer a machine-learning method. Name three ethical risks in mining customer reviews and one safeguard for each. Summary ¶ Idea Remember Unstructured data Text says why ; it needs converting into columns before analysis Pipeline Collect, clean, tokenise, normalise, filter, (reduce), represent, analyse, validate , decide Stop words Fine for topics; keep negations for opinion; add domain stop words deliberately Frequency Counts mentions, not reviewers; report the number of reviews too N-grams Keep phrases and negations together; build them within each document Word clouds First look only; use a sorted bar chart for claims TF-IDF Frequent here, rare elsewhere = distinctive VADER Lexicon plus rules (negation, boosters, capitals, "!", "but"); compound in −1 to +1; ±0.05 labels are a convention Failures Domain words, facts, sarcasm, slang, mixed reviews, other languages Validation Confusion matrix against human labels; recall for the class that matters Decisions Topic × sentiment; error costs set the rule; finding, evidence, action, measure Ethics Consent, mask personal data, do not judge named staff, check bias by group, be honest about limits References: Hutto, C.
