docs.title: Setup

docs.text: Structured data fits a fixed table: every row has the same columns, and each column has one type (a number, a date, a category). The stars column above is structured: you can average it, group it and chart it at once. Unstructured data has no fixed fields. A review, an email, a support chat or a call transcript carries its meaning in the choice and order of words, and its length varies from three words to three pages. Structured Unstructured Example Star rating, price, check-in date Review text, complaint email, social-media post Shape Fixed columns and types Free-length strings Summarise with describe() , groupby() , a pivot table Nothing, until it is converted Share of what organisations collect Smaller Larger (often quoted as about 80%) What it tells you How much (3 stars) Why (the shower was cold) Between the two sits semi-structured data, such as a JSON order record with a free-text "notes" field. Text mining is the conversion from the right-hand column to the left: it creates new structured columns (counts, flags, scores) from text, after which every tool from Days 1 and 2 applies again. Predict, then run. describe() works on stars . What do you expect it to say about the text column? print ( reviews [ "stars" ] . describe () . round ( 2 )) print () print ( reviews [ "text" ] . describe ()) count 40.00 mean 2.98 std 1.44 min 1.00 25% 2.00 50% 3.00 75% 4.00 max 5.00 Name: stars, dtype: float64 count 40 unique 40 top Lovely stay! The staff were friendly and the breakfast was excellent. freq 1 Name: text, dtype: object For text, describe() can only count: 40 values, 40 unique, the "top" is just one of them. To learn anything we must engineer features . Even very simple features are already useful: reviews [ "n_words" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . str . split () . str . len () reviews [ "mentions_breakfast" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower () . str . contains ( "breakfast" ) reviews . groupby ( "mentions_breakfast" )[[ "stars" , "n_words" ]] . agg ([ "mean" , "count" ]) . round ( 2 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead tr th { text-align: left; } .dataframe thead tr:last-of-type th { text-align: right; } stars n_words mean count mean count mentions_breakfast False 2.6 30 13.2 30 True 4.1 10 11.8 10 Two new structured columns, made from text in two lines. The rest of the lecture does the same thing more carefully.

docs.text: Every text-mining project follows roughly the same pipeline. The order matters: each step works on the output of the one before. Step What it does Example 1. Collect Gather the text and its context (date, site, rating) Export reviews with their star ratings 2. Clean Remove markup, fix encodings, mask personal data Strip HTML; replace e-mail addresses with [EMAIL] 3. Tokenise Split text into units (tokens) "wasn't clean" → was , n't , clean 4. Normalise Make variants of a word match Breakfast , BREAKFAST → breakfast 5. Filter Drop tokens that carry no topic Remove the , and , punctuation 6. Reduce (optional) Stem or lemmatise rooms → room 7. Represent Turn tokens into numbers Counts, n-grams, TF-IDF, a sentiment score 8. Analyse Find the pattern Top words, sentiment by site, topics 9. Validate Check against human judgement Compare scores with star ratings 10. Decide Interpret the pattern for an action Fix the showers at Riverside first Steps 1 to 8 are text mining ; step 10 is text analytics , the interpretation for a decision. Step 9 is the one most often skipped.
docs.title: Part 2: The pipeline: tokenising and normalising (core)

docs.text: Predict, then run. Splitting on spaces is the simplest tokeniser. What will go wrong with the review below? example = reviews . loc [ 3 , "text" ] # review 4 print ( example ) print () print ( "split(): " , example . split ()) print ( "word_tokenize:" , word_tokenize ( example )) Check-in took forty minutes. The receptionist was polite, but nobody could find our booking. split(): ['Check-in', 'took', 'forty', 'minutes.', 'The', 'receptionist', 'was', 'polite,', 'but', 'nobody', 'could', 'find', 'our', 'booking.'] word_tokenize: ['Check-in', 'took', 'forty', 'minutes', '.', 'The', 'receptionist', 'was', 'polite', ',', 'but', 'nobody', 'could', 'find', 'our', 'booking', '.'] split() leaves punctuation stuck to words ( minutes. and minutes would be counted as different words) and keeps Check-in and booking. whole. NLTK's word_tokenize separates punctuation and handles contractions in a consistent way: it splits "wasn't" into was and n't . Remember that last point; it matters in Part 3.
docs.title: Tokenising

docs.text: Normalising makes the variants of one word count as one. The usual steps are: lower-case, remove punctuation and numbers ( isalpha() keeps tokens made only of letters), and sometimes stem or lemmatise (Part 10). Each step is a choice with a cost: Choice Gain Cost Lower-case Breakfast = breakfast Loses GREAT (shouting, which VADER uses) and names such as Bath vs bath Drop punctuation Cleaner counts Loses !!! and ? (emphasis, questions) and emoticons such as :( Drop numbers Fewer junk tokens Loses 8am , 45 minutes , room 212 Keep only letters ( isalpha() ) Drops , and . Also drops n't and check-in raw_tokens = [ t for text in reviews [ "text" ] for t in word_tokenize ( text )] lower_tokens = [ t . lower () for t in raw_tokens ] alpha_tokens = [ t for t in lower_tokens if t . isalpha ()] print ( "Distinct tokens, raw: " , len ( set ( raw_tokens ))) print ( "Distinct tokens, lower-cased: " , len ( set ( lower_tokens ))) print ( "Distinct tokens, letters only: " , len ( set ( alpha_tokens ))) print ( "Variants of 'breakfast' in raw: " , sorted ({ t for t in raw_tokens if t . lower () == "breakfast" })) print ( "Tokens dropped by isalpha(): " , sorted ({ t for t in lower_tokens if not t . isalpha ()})) Distinct tokens, raw: 241 Distinct tokens, lower-cased: 224 Distinct tokens, letters only: 216 Variants of 'breakfast' in raw: ['Breakfast', 'breakfast'] Tokens dropped by isalpha(): ['!', "'s", "'ve", ',', '.', '8am', 'check-in', 'check-out'] Lower-casing merges variants such as Breakfast and breakfast . isalpha() drops the punctuation, but look at what else it drops: check-in , check-out , 8am , and the contraction fragments 's and 've . In reviews that say "didn't" or "wasn't", it would drop n't too. A pipeline is a series of decisions, and every decision removes some information.
docs.title: Normalising

docs.text: Stop words are very frequent words that carry grammar rather than topic: the, is, and, a, of, to . In almost any English text they are the most common words, so a frequency count that keeps them tells you only that the text is in English. Removing them lets the topic words rise to the top. english_stop = set ( stopwords . words ( "english" )) print ( "Words in NLTK's English stop-word list:" , len ( english_stop )) print ( "Some of them:" , sorted ( english_stop )[: 25 ]) print () for w in [ "not" , "no" , "nor" , "never" , "very" , "too" , "but" , "against" , "isn't" , "n't" ]: print ( f " { w !r: 10 } in the list? { w in english_stop } " ) Words in NLTK's English stop-word list: 198 Some of them: ['a', 'about', 'above', 'after', 'again', 'against', 'ain', 'all', 'am', 'an', 'and', 'any', 'are', 'aren', "aren't", 'as', 'at', 'be', 'because', 'been', 'before', 'being', 'below', 'between', 'both'] 'not' in the list? True 'no' in the list? True 'nor' in the list? True 'never' in the list? False 'very' in the list? True 'too' in the list? True 'but' in the list? True 'against' in the list? True "isn't" in the list? True "n't" in the list? False The standard list contains "not", "no", "nor", "very", "too", "but" and full contractions such as "isn't". For counting topics , that is fine. For anything to do with opinion , it is dangerous. Predict, then run. Review 13 says "Not clean. Hair in the sink and dust under the bed." After lower-casing, isalpha() and the standard stop-word list, which words remain? Would a reader of the remaining words know the room was dirty? def clean_tokens ( text , stop ): """Lower-case, tokenise, keep letters only, and drop the given stop words.""" return [ t for t in word_tokenize ( text . lower ()) if t . isalpha () and t not in stop ] text_13 = reviews . loc [ 12 , "text" ] print ( "Original: " , text_13 ) print ( "Standard stop words: " , clean_tokens ( text_13 , english_stop )) NEGATIONS = { "not" , "no" , "nor" , "never" , "n't" , "without" } opinion_stop = english_stop - NEGATIONS def clean_keep_negation ( text ): """As clean_tokens, but keep negations, and turn n't into not so isalpha() keeps it.""" toks = [( "not" if t == "n't" else t ) for t in word_tokenize ( text . lower ())] return [ t for t in toks if t . isalpha () and t not in opinion_stop ] print ( "Negations kept: " , clean_keep_negation ( text_13 )) print () other = reviews . loc [ 36 , "text" ] # review 37 print ( "Original: " , other ) print ( "Standard stop words: " , clean_tokens ( other , english_stop )) print ( "Negations kept: " , clean_keep_negation ( other )) Original: Not clean. Hair in the sink and dust under the bed. Standard stop words: ['clean', 'hair', 'sink', 'dust', 'bed'] Negations kept: ['not', 'clean', 'hair', 'sink', 'dust', 'bed'] Original: The heating did not work and the extra blanket never arrived. Standard stop words: ['heating', 'work', 'extra', 'blanket', 'never', 'arrived'] Negations kept: ['heating', 'not', 'work', 'extra', 'blanket', 'never', 'arrived'] With the standard list, "Not clean" becomes clean : the word count now counts a complaint as praise . Three practical rules: Choose the stop-word list for the task. For topics (what do people talk about?), the standard list is fine. For opinion (what do they think?), keep the negations, or join them to the next word ( not_clean ). Add domain stop words. In hotel reviews, hotel , room and stay may appear everywhere and so tell you little; in a product's reviews, the product's own name does the same. Add them deliberately, and write down which you added. Remember contractions. word_tokenize turns "didn't" into did + n't , and isalpha() silently drops n't . A pipeline can lose a negation even when "not" is not in the stop list. Misconception: "Stop-word removal is a standard step, so it is always safe." It is safe for counting topics. It changes meaning for opinion, and it must happen after tokenising, because the list contains words, not strings of text.
docs.title: Part 3: Stop words, and when to keep "not" (core)

docs.text: Once the text is clean tokens, the simplest analysis is to count . NLTK's FreqDist is a counter with useful methods. Here we use the topic pipeline (standard stop words) plus three domain stop words that appear in almost every hotel review. Predict, then run. Before you run the next cell, write down the three words you expect at the top. Will they be about what guests discuss, or how they feel? DOMAIN_STOP = { "hotel" , "stay" , "would" } topic_stop = english_stop | DOMAIN_STOP reviews [ "tokens" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . apply ( lambda t : clean_tokens ( t , topic_stop )) all_words = [ w for toks in reviews [ "tokens" ] for w in toks ] freq = nltk . FreqDist ( all_words ) top = pd . Series ( dict ( freq . most_common ( 12 ))) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.8 )) ax . barh ( top . index [:: - 1 ], top . values [:: - 1 ], color = BLUE ) for y , v in enumerate ( top . values [:: - 1 ]): ax . text ( v + 0.2 , y , str ( v ), va = "center" , fontsize = 9 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Number of times the word appears" ) ax . set_title ( "The twelve most frequent words in 40 hotel reviews" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () print ( "Total words after cleaning:" , len ( all_words ), " distinct:" , len ( freq )) Total words after cleaning: 276 distinct: 169 Frequency answers "what do people talk about?" , not "what do they think about it?" . A word near the top may be praised in some reviews and criticised in others. Frequency also counts mentions, not reviewers : one long review that repeats a word five times counts five times. A safer count for a manager is often the number of reviews that mention the word (document frequency): doc_freq = Counter ( w for toks in reviews [ "tokens" ] for w in set ( toks )) compare = pd . DataFrame ({ "times mentioned" : pd . Series ( dict ( freq . most_common ( 8 ))), "reviews mentioning" : pd . Series ( doc_freq )}) . dropna () . astype ( int ) compare [ "share of reviews" ] = ( compare [ "reviews mentioning" ] / len ( reviews )) . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) compare .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } times mentioned reviews mentioning share of reviews bed 7 7 18% breakfast 10 10 25% clean 6 6 15% comfortable 5 5 12% friendly 5 5 12% great 5 3 8% room 17 17 42% staff 9 9 22%
docs.title: Part 4: Frequency and n-grams (core)

docs.text: Single words lose context. An n-gram is a run of n consecutive tokens: bigrams ( n = 2) and trigrams ( n = 3). "Thin" alone is ambiguous; "paper thin" and "walls thin" are not. Bigrams are often where the actionable phrases live: a product name, a part of the service, a complaint. Predict, then run. Will the bigram list be more or less useful than the word list for a hotel manager? Which pipeline should feed it: the one that drops "not", or the one that keeps it? reviews [ "opinion_tokens" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . apply ( clean_keep_negation ) bigrams = Counter () for toks in reviews [ "opinion_tokens" ]: bigrams . update ( nltk . bigrams ( toks )) # bigrams within one review, never across two print ( "Most common bigrams (negations kept):" ) for ( w1 , w2 ), n in bigrams . most_common ( 12 ): print ( f " { w1 + ' ' + w2 : <22 } { n } " ) print ( " \n Bigrams that start with 'not':" ) print ( sorted ( " " . join ( b ) for b in bigrams if b [ 0 ] == "not" )) Most common bigrams (negations kept): comfortable bed 3 room small 3 staff friendly 2 friendly staff 2 bed comfortable 2 comfortable room 2 staff helpful 2 not work 2 would not 2 room clean 2 lovely stay 1 stay staff 1 Bigrams that start with 'not': ['not advertised', 'not clean', 'not close', 'not stay', 'not work'] The not … bigrams exist only because we kept the negations. With small data, most bigrams appear once; with thousands of reviews, the frequent bigrams become a quick list of the issues customers name in their own words. Note: build n-grams within each document. Joining all reviews into one long string first, as quick scripts often do, creates false bigrams across the boundary (the last word of one review followed by the first word of the next). With ten reviews the effect is tiny; with the n-grams of a large corpus it adds noise.
docs.title: N-grams

docs.text: A word cloud draws each word with a size proportional to its frequency. It is popular because it is quick and attractive. cloud = WordCloud ( width = 800 , height = 360 , background_color = "white" , colormap = "cividis" , random_state = 0 ) . generate_from_frequencies ( freq ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 10 , 4.5 )) ax . imshow ( cloud , interpolation = "bilinear" ) ax . axis ( "off" ) ax . set_title ( "Word cloud of the 40 hotel reviews (size = frequency)" ) plt . show () Now compare it with the bar chart in Part 4, using what you learned on Day 2 about how accurately people read encodings. Question Word cloud Sorted bar chart Which word is most frequent? Usually visible Obvious Is word 3 more frequent than word 4? Hard: size is area , a weak encoding, and long words look bigger Easy: length on a common scale Exact counts? No Yes, with labels Positive or negative? No (colour is usually decorative) No, unless you split the bars by sentiment Context ("not clean")? No No (use bigrams) Same picture each run? Only with a fixed random_state Yes A word cloud is fine as a first look or a slide decoration. For a claim in a report ("breakfast is mentioned in a quarter of reviews"), use a sorted bar chart or a table, and quote the count. When you use a cloud, say what it shows ("size = frequency after removing stop words") and check its claims against the counts.
docs.title: Part 5: Word clouds and their limits (core)

docs.text: Sentiment analysis gives each text a score for how positive or negative it is. There are two families: Lexicon-based methods look words up in a dictionary of pre-rated words and combine the ratings with rules. No training data is needed. Machine-learning methods learn which words and phrases predict a label from many labelled examples (Part 12). VADER ( Valence Aware Dictionary and sEntiment Reasoner ; Hutto and Gilbert, 2014) is a lexicon method designed for short, informal text such as reviews and social posts. Its dictionary holds about 7,500 words, slang terms and emoticons, each rated by human judges from −4 (most negative) to +4 (most positive). vader = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () print ( "Words in VADER's lexicon:" , len ( vader . lexicon )) for w in [ "excellent" , "friendly" , "good" , "okay" , "fine" , "slow" , "rude" , "dirty" , "worst" , "lukewarm" , "tiny" , "mould" ]: print ( f " { w : <10 } { vader . lexicon . get ( w , 'not in lexicon' ) } " ) Words in VADER's lexicon: 7502 excellent 2.7 friendly 2.2 good 1.9 okay 0.9 fine 0.8 slow not in lexicon rude -2.0 dirty -1.9 worst -3.1 lukewarm not in lexicon tiny not in lexicon mould not in lexicon polarity_scores() returns four numbers. neg , neu and pos are the shares of the text that are negative, neutral and positive (they add up to 1). compound is the summary score: VADER adds up the adjusted ratings of the words it found and squashes the sum into −1 to +1 with compound = s ÷ √(s² + 15) , where s is the sum. One positive word moves the score a lot; each further positive word moves it less, so the score approaches 1 but never reaches it. VADER then adjusts the word ratings with rules : Rule Example Effect Negation "not good" A negation in the three words before a rated word flips and shrinks its rating Intensifiers (booster words) "very good", "kind of good" "very" increases, "kind of" decreases the rating Capitals "GOOD" in otherwise lower-case text Increases the rating Exclamation marks "good!!!" Increase the score (up to four count) "But" "good, but terrible" Words after "but" weigh more, words before it less Emoticons and slang ":)", "lol" Rated in the lexicon like words Predict, then run. For each sentence below, predict the sign of compound (+, 0 or −) and whether it will be larger or smaller than for "The coffee is good." Pay special attention to the two "but" sentences and to "isn't bad". sentences = [ "The coffee is good." , "The coffee is very good." , "The coffee is kind of good." , "The coffee is GOOD." , "The coffee is good!!!" , "The coffee is not good." , "The coffee isn't bad." , "The coffee is good, but the service is terrible." , "The coffee is terrible, but the service is good." , "Not bad at all :)" , ] rules = pd . DataFrame ([{ "sentence" : s , ** vader . polarity_scores ( s )} for s in sentences ]) rules . set_index ( "sentence" )[[ "neg" , "neu" , "pos" , "compound" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } neg neu pos compound sentence The coffee is good. 0.000 0.508 0.492 0.4404 The coffee is very good. 0.000 0.556 0.444 0.4927 The coffee is kind of good. 0.000 0.657 0.343 0.3832 The coffee is GOOD. 0.000 0.452 0.548 0.5622 The coffee is good!!! 0.000 0.443 0.557 0.5826 The coffee is not good. 0.376 0.624 0.000 -0.3412 The coffee isn't bad. 0.000 0.513 0.487 0.4310 The coffee is good, but the service is terrible. 0.317 0.534 0.149 -0.4939 The coffee is terrible, but the service is good. 0.159 0.543 0.298 0.4215 Not bad at all :) 0.000 0.339 0.661 0.7050 Check your predictions: Intensifiers, capitals and "!!!" all push the score away from zero; "kind of" pulls it towards zero. "not good" flips the sign. "isn't bad" becomes mildly positive: VADER handles simple double negatives. The two "but" sentences contain the same words, yet get opposite signs: what comes after "but" dominates, as it does for a human reader.
docs.title: Part 6: How VADER scores text (core)

docs.text: To report counts, the compound score is usually cut into three labels with the thresholds recommended by VADER's authors: Compound score Label ≥ 0.05 Positive between −0.05 and 0.05 Neutral ≤ −0.05 Negative The thresholds are a convention , not a law. A score of 0.04 and a score of 0.06 are almost the same, yet get different labels. Part 8 shows how much the counts depend on them. def sentiment_label ( score , cut = 0.05 ): if score >= cut : return "Positive" if score <= - cut : return "Negative" return "Neutral" reviews [ "compound" ] = reviews [ "text" ] . apply ( lambda t : vader . polarity_scores ( t )[ "compound" ]) reviews [ "vader_label" ] = reviews [ "compound" ] . apply ( sentiment_label ) reviews [[ "review_id" , "stars" , "text" , "compound" , "vader_label" ]] . head ( 8 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } review_id stars text compound vader_label 0 1 5 Lovely stay! The staff were friendly and the breakfast was excellent. 0.8999 Positive 1 2 4 Clean room and a comfortable bed. Breakfast was good but the coffee was weak. 0.0258 Neutral 2 3 1 The room was tiny and the walls were paper thin. We heard every word next door. 0.0000 Neutral 3 4 2 Check-in took forty minutes. The receptionist was polite, but nobody could find our booking. 0.0000 Neutral 4 5 5 Best hotel we have stayed in this year. Amazing view of the lake and a really comfortable bed. 0.9117 Positive 5 6 1 Great, the lift broke again. Loved carrying our bags up five flights of stairs. 0.7351 Positive 6 7 3 The room was fine. No frills at all, but the location is convenient for the station. -0.0516 Negative 7 8 2 The shower was lukewarm every morning and the air conditioning rattled all night. 0.0000 Neutral
docs.title: From score to label

docs.text: A lexicon only knows the words in it and the rules it was given. Predict what happens to each sentence below, then run. hard_cases = { "Domain words not in the lexicon" : "The shower was lukewarm and the room was tiny." , "Complaint as a fact, no opinion word" : "I waited 45 minutes for a table." , "Sarcasm" : "Great, another cold shower. Just what I wanted." , "Slang with a positive meaning" : "That concert was sick!" , "Double negative with an unknown word" : "The staff were not unhelpful." , "Mixed review, praise first" : "Lovely staff and a great view, but the bathroom had mould." , } pd . DataFrame ([{ "failure type" : k , "sentence" : s , "compound" : vader . polarity_scores ( s )[ "compound" ]} for k , s in hard_cases . items ()]) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } failure type sentence compound 0 Domain words not in the lexicon The shower was lukewarm and the room was tiny. 0.0000 1 Complaint as a fact, no opinion word I waited 45 minutes for a table. 0.0000 2 Sarcasm Great, another cold shower. Just what I wanted. 0.6249 3 Slang with a positive meaning That concert was sick! -0.5562 4 Double negative with an unknown word The staff were not unhelpful. 0.0000 5 Mixed review, praise first Lovely staff and a great view, but the bathroom had mould. 0.6059 The patterns behind these failures: Failure Why What helps Domain vocabulary ("lukewarm", "tiny", "mould", "overbooked") Not in a general-purpose lexicon, so rated 0 Add domain words to the lexicon with care, or train a model on labelled domain text Facts that imply a complaint ("waited 45 minutes", "charged twice") No opinion words at all Topic or keyword rules; machine learning with labels Sarcasm and irony Positive words with a negative meaning Very hard for any method; human review of a sample Slang and new meanings ("sick", "killer") The lexicon rates the dictionary meaning Update the lexicon; models trained on recent text Mixed reviews One number cannot hold "great staff, mouldy bathroom" Score each sentence or each aspect separately Other languages, code-switching, emoji Lexicon is English A tool for that language; translate with care The reading packet makes the key point: a neutral score for a clearly negative complaint is a limitation of the method , not a bug in your code. The only way to find out how often it happens in your data is to check. Misconception: "A compound score of 0 means the customer was neutral." It often means VADER found no words it knows . Look at neu : a score of 0 with neu = 1.0 is "no opinion words found", which is not the same as "a balanced opinion".
docs.title: Part 7: Where VADER fails (core)

docs.text: Before anyone acts on sentiment scores, compare them with a human judgement on a sample. Here each review has a star rating , which we can turn into a reference label: 4–5 stars positive, 3 neutral, 1–2 negative. (Stars are not perfect either: some people write a glowing review and give 3 stars, but they are the customer's own judgement.) Predict, then run. Out of 40 reviews, how many do you expect VADER's label to agree with the star label? 35? 30? 25? def star_label ( stars ): return "Positive" if stars >= 4 else ( "Negative" if stars <= 2 else "Neutral" ) reviews [ "star_label" ] = reviews [ "stars" ] . apply ( star_label ) order = [ "Negative" , "Neutral" , "Positive" ] confusion = pd . crosstab ( reviews [ "star_label" ], reviews [ "vader_label" ], rownames = [ "Stars say" ], colnames = [ "VADER says" ]) . reindex ( index = order , columns = order , fill_value = 0 ) print ( confusion ) agree = ( reviews [ "star_label" ] == reviews [ "vader_label" ]) . mean () print ( f " \n Agreement: { agree : .0% } of reviews" ) VADER says Negative Neutral Positive Stars say Negative 5 9 3 Neutral 2 0 5 Positive 0 1 15 Agreement: 50% of reviews This table is a confusion matrix : rows are the reference labels, columns are the scorer's labels, and the diagonal holds the agreements. Read it row by row. The positive reviews are mostly recognised. The negative reviews are where VADER struggles: many of the 1–2 star reviews land in Neutral or even Positive. That is the dangerous direction for a business, because those are the customers it most needs to hear. Look at the disagreements themselves; the reason is usually visible in one reading. missed = reviews [( reviews [ "star_label" ] == "Negative" ) & ( reviews [ "vader_label" ] != "Negative" )] missed [[ "review_id" , "stars" , "compound" , "vader_label" , "text" ]] .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } review_id stars compound vader_label text 2 3 1 0.0000 Neutral The room was tiny and the walls were paper thin. We heard every word next door. 3 4 2 0.0000 Neutral Check-in took forty minutes. The receptionist was polite, but nobody could find our booking. 5 6 1 0.7351 Positive Great, the lift broke again. Loved carrying our bags up five flights of stairs. 7 8 2 0.0000 Neutral The shower was lukewarm every morning and the air conditioning rattled all night. 9 10 1 0.0000 Neutral Never again. The bathroom had mould and the sheets smelled of smoke. 17 18 2 0.0000 Neutral The wifi dropped every ten minutes, so I could not work from the room. 19 20 1 0.0000 Neutral Overbooked. They moved us to another hotel across town at midnight. 21 22 2 0.2235 Positive The room was not as advertised. No balcony and the view was a car park. 29 30 1 0.0000 Neutral Cockroach in the bathroom on the first night. Reception just shrugged. 31 32 2 0.0000 Neutral Breakfast ran out of eggs by 8am and nobody refilled the coffee. 36 37 2 0.0000 Neutral The heating did not work and the extra blanket never arrived. 39 40 2 0.2382 Positive Good location, but the room smelled damp and the window would not close. Most of these use words from Part 7's failure list: domain words ("tiny", "lukewarm", "mould", "overbooked"), facts that imply a complaint ("charged", "waited", "moved us"), and sarcasm. Two more useful numbers come from the matrix. Of the reviews that are negative (by stars), what share did VADER catch? That is recall for the negative class. Of the reviews VADER called negative, what share really were? That is precision . is_neg = reviews [ "star_label" ] == "Negative" called_neg = reviews [ "vader_label" ] == "Negative" recall = ( is_neg & called_neg ) . sum () / is_neg . sum () precision = ( is_neg & called_neg ) . sum () / called_neg . sum () print ( f "Negative reviews by stars: { is_neg . sum () } , called negative by VADER: { called_neg . sum () } " ) print ( f "Recall for negative (share of unhappy guests caught): { recall : .0% } " ) print ( f "Precision for negative (share of flags that were right): { precision : .0% } " ) print ( " \n How the label counts change with the threshold:" ) for cut in [ 0.01 , 0.05 , 0.20 , 0.50 ]: counts = reviews [ "compound" ] . apply ( sentiment_label , cut = cut ) . value_counts () . reindex ( order , fill_value = 0 ) print ( f " cut = { cut : <5 } " + " " . join ( f " { k } : { v : >2 } " for k , v in counts . items ())) Negative reviews by stars: 17, called negative by VADER: 7 Recall for negative (share of unhappy guests caught): 29% Precision for negative (share of flags that were right): 71% How the label counts change with the threshold: cut = 0.01 Negative: 7 Neutral: 9 Positive: 24 cut = 0.05 Negative: 7 Neutral: 10 Positive: 23 cut = 0.2 Negative: 5 Neutral: 13 Positive: 22 cut = 0.5 Negative: 2 Neutral: 24 Positive: 14 The share of "negative" reviews in a report can change a lot with the threshold, and the threshold was never chosen for this business. A validation step therefore answers three questions: How often does the scorer agree with people? Where does it disagree? Which threshold suits the decision? Misconception: "The tool is published and widely used, so its scores are accurate." It is accurate on the kind of text it was built and tested on . Your domain may differ. Validate on a few hundred hand-labelled examples from your own data before you report percentages. The same logic applies to anything a model scores: a fraud score, a churn risk, a CV-screening score. A score you have not checked against reality is an opinion with decimals.
docs.title: Part 8: Validating scores against labels (core)

docs.text: A sentiment distribution ("55% positive") is a finding . A manager needs a decision : what to fix, where, and how to tell whether it worked. Three tools help.
docs.title: Part 9: From scores to decisions (core)

docs.text: Group words into the aspects a manager can act on, then ask, for each aspect: how many reviews mention it, and how unhappy are those reviewers? ASPECTS = { "staff" : { "staff" , "receptionist" , "manager" , "reception" , "concierge" , "service" }, "cleanliness" : { "clean" , "dirty" , "mould" , "dust" , "hair" , "cockroach" , "spotless" , "damp" , "smelled" }, "breakfast" : { "breakfast" , "coffee" , "eggs" , "food" , "buffet" }, "noise" : { "noisy" , "quiet" , "heard" , "thin" , "rattled" }, "bed" : { "bed" , "pillows" , "sleep" , "blanket" }, "booking and billing" : { "booking" , "overbooked" , "charged" , "refund" , "waited" , "check-in" }, "facilities" : { "wifi" , "lift" , "shower" , "heating" , "parking" , "window" , "air" }, } lower_tok = reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower () . apply ( word_tokenize ) rows = [] for aspect , words in ASPECTS . items (): hit = lower_tok . apply ( lambda toks : bool ( words & set ( toks ))) sub = reviews [ hit ] rows . append ({ "aspect" : aspect , "reviews" : len ( sub ), "share 1-2 stars" : ( sub [ "stars" ] <= 2 ) . mean (), "share VADER negative" : ( sub [ "vader_label" ] == "Negative" ) . mean (), "mean stars" : sub [ "stars" ] . mean ()}) aspects = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . set_index ( "aspect" ) . sort_values ( "share 1-2 stars" , ascending = False ) shown = aspects . copy () for col in [ "share 1-2 stars" , "share VADER negative" ]: shown [ col ] = shown [ col ] . map ( " {:.0%} " . format ) shown . round ( 1 ) .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } reviews share 1-2 stars share VADER negative mean stars aspect booking and billing 6 67% 33% 2.3 facilities 8 62% 0% 2.5 cleanliness 11 45% 18% 2.8 bed 9 44% 33% 3.0 noise 7 43% 14% 2.9 staff 14 21% 14% 3.6 breakfast 11 9% 0% 4.2 fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.6 )) y = np . arange ( len ( aspects )) ax . barh ( y + 0.2 , aspects [ "share 1-2 stars" ], height = 0.4 , color = ORANGE , label = "Share with 1-2 stars" ) ax . barh ( y - 0.2 , aspects [ "share VADER negative" ], height = 0.4 , color = GREY , label = "Share VADER calls negative" ) ax . set_yticks ( y , [ f " { a } ( { n } )" for a , n in zip ( aspects . index , aspects [ "reviews" ])]) ax . invert_yaxis () ax . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( plt . FuncFormatter ( lambda v , _ : f " { v : .0% } " )) ax . set_xlabel ( "Share of the reviews that mention the aspect (number of reviews in brackets)" ) ax . set_title ( "Which aspects come with unhappy guests? Stars and VADER disagree" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "lower right" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Compare the two bars for each aspect. If the manager ranked the problems by VADER alone, aspects whose complaints use domain words or plain facts (booking and billing, facilities) would look much less serious than the guests' own ratings say. The method shapes the priority list. Small counts matter too: an aspect mentioned in four reviews is a lead to investigate, not a conclusion.
docs.title: 1. Combine topic and sentiment (aspects)

docs.text: Suppose the hotel wants to reply personally to every unhappy guest within a day. A rule such as "flag every review VADER calls negative" has two kinds of error: Error Example Cost Missed complaint (false negative) A 1-star review about mould scored neutral An unhappy guest gets no reply; a public complaint stays unanswered False alarm (false positive) A 3-star review flagged as negative A few minutes of staff time Here a missed complaint costs much more than a false alarm, so the rule should catch more, even at the price of more false alarms: use the star rating where it exists, add keyword rules for known domain complaints, and send everything with a score below a generous threshold to a person. The threshold is a business decision about the cost of each error, not a technical default.
docs.title: 2. Decide what a score triggers, and count the cost of errors

docs.text: A text-mining recommendation has four parts: Finding , with the count and the method: "Of 40 reviews, n mention [aspect]; x % of those gave 1–2 stars." Evidence a manager can read: two or three short quotes (anonymised). Action with an owner: "Facilities manager to check [item] at [site] by [date]." How we will know : the measure to watch afterwards (share of reviews mentioning the aspect, mean stars) and its limit ("the scorer misses complaints worded as facts, so we read a sample by hand each month").
docs.title: 3. Write the recommendation

docs.text: "room" and "rooms", "help", "helped", "helpful" and "helping": should they count as one word? Two ways to reduce words to a common form: Stemming Lemmatisation How Chops endings with fixed rules Looks the word up in a dictionary, often using its part of speech Output A stem , which may not be a real word ( comfort , friendli ) A lemma , a real dictionary word ( be for "was", good for "better") Speed and needs Fast; no data needed Slower; needs a dictionary such as WordNet Risk Over-stemming ( university , universe → univers ) and under-stemming Needs the right part of speech ("meeting" the noun vs "meeting" the verb) The Porter stemmer needs no data, so we can try it offline: stemmer = PorterStemmer () words = [ "room" , "rooms" , "help" , "helped" , "helpful" , "helping" , "comfortable" , "comfort" , "friendly" , "friendliness" , "was" , "better" , "university" , "universe" , "news" , "new" ] pd . DataFrame ({ "word" : words , "Porter stem" : [ stemmer . stem ( w ) for w in words ]}) . set_index ( "word" ) . T .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } word room rooms help helped helpful helping comfortable comfort friendly friendliness was better university universe news new Porter stem room room help help help help comfort comfort friendli friendli wa better univers univers news new Stemming merges help , helped and helping (good) and turns friendly into friendli (ugly but harmless for counting). It cannot know that was is a form of be (it even cuts it to wa ) or that better is a form of good ; a lemmatiser can, because it uses a dictionary (NLTK's WordNetLemmatizer needs the WordNet data, which this course's bundle does not include, so we do not run it here). It merges university and universe and news and new (bad: different meanings). When to use them: for counting topics in large collections, stemming or lemmatising reduces the vocabulary and merges obvious variants. For sentiment with VADER , do not : VADER's lexicon expects real words, and comfort or friendli may not be in it. Also note that helpful and helping carry different opinions; merging them can blur the signal.
docs.title: Part 10: Stemming and lemmatisation (extension)

docs.text: Raw counts favour words that are common everywhere ("room" appears in many reviews, so it tells you little about any one of them). TF-IDF (term frequency × inverse document frequency) scores a word highly in a document when it is frequent in that document but rare across the collection : TF-IDF of word w in document d = tf( w , d ) × log( N ÷ df( w )) , where tf is the count of word w in document d , N is the number of documents, and df is the number of documents that contain w . A word found in every document gets log( N ÷ N ) = log 1 = 0. (Libraries add small adjustments, such as +1 terms, but the idea is the same.)
docs.title: Part 11: TF-IDF (extension)

docs.text: Predict, then run. In the three documents below, which word gets a TF-IDF of exactly 0 in every document? Which word gets the highest score in document C? docs = { "A" : "room clean room quiet" , "B" : "room noisy staff rude" , "C" : "room cockroach cockroach staff" } N = len ( docs ) vocab = sorted ({ w for d in docs . values () for w in d . split ()}) df_w = { w : sum ( w in d . split () for d in docs . values ()) for w in vocab } table = pd . DataFrame ({ name : { w : d . split () . count ( w ) * np . log ( N / df_w [ w ]) for w in vocab } for name , d in docs . items ()}) . round ( 2 ) table [ "documents containing" ] = pd . Series ( df_w ) table .dataframe tbody tr th:only-of-type { vertical-align: middle; } .dataframe tbody tr th { vertical-align: top; } .dataframe thead th { text-align: right; } A B C documents containing clean 1.1 0.00 0.00 1 cockroach 0.0 0.00 2.20 1 noisy 0.0 1.10 0.00 1 quiet 1.1 0.00 0.00 1 room 0.0 0.00 0.00 3 rude 0.0 1.10 0.00 1 staff 0.0 0.41 0.41 2 "room" is in all three documents, so its weight is 0 everywhere, however often it appears. "cockroach" is in one document and appears twice there, so it dominates document C. TF-IDF picks out what is distinctive about each document.
docs.title: By hand, with three tiny documents

docs.text: scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer does the counting, weighting and normalising in one step. A useful question for a manager: which words are most distinctive of the unhappy reviews ? We average each word's TF-IDF over the 1–2 star reviews and over the 4–5 star reviews and compare. from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer tfidf = TfidfVectorizer ( stop_words = sorted ( opinion_stop ), token_pattern = r "[a-z]+(?:-[a-z]+)?" ) X = tfidf . fit_transform ( reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower ()) weights = pd . DataFrame ( X . toarray (), columns = tfidf . get_feature_names_out ()) low = weights [ reviews [ "stars" ] <= 2 ] . mean () high = weights [ reviews [ "stars" ] >= 4 ] . mean () distinct = pd . DataFrame ({ "mean TF-IDF, 1-2 stars" : low , "mean TF-IDF, 4-5 stars" : high }) distinct [ "difference" ] = distinct . iloc [:, 0 ] - distinct . iloc [:, 1 ] print ( "Most distinctive of the unhappy reviews:" ) print ( distinct . sort_values ( "difference" , ascending = False ) . head ( 8 ) . round ( 3 )) print ( " \n Most distinctive of the happy reviews:" ) print ( distinct . sort_values ( "difference" ) . head ( 8 ) . round ( 3 )) Most distinctive of the unhappy reviews: mean TF-IDF, 1-2 stars mean TF-IDF, 4-5 stars difference not 0.084 0.0 0.084 night 0.055 0.0 0.055 every 0.054 0.0 0.054 never 0.044 0.0 0.044 smelled 0.044 0.0 0.044 bathroom 0.042 0.0 0.042 work 0.042 0.0 0.042 nobody 0.042 0.0 0.042 Most distinctive of the happy reviews: mean TF-IDF, 1-2 stars mean TF-IDF, 4-5 stars difference staff 0.000 0.121 -0.121 breakfast 0.015 0.131 -0.115 friendly 0.000 0.090 -0.090 comfortable 0.000 0.081 -0.081 quiet 0.000 0.076 -0.076 slow 0.000 0.074 -0.074 clean 0.019 0.083 -0.064 lovely 0.000 0.056 -0.056 The unhappy reviews are distinguished by negations ( not , never , nobody ) and descriptions of what happened ( smelled , bathroom , night , work ), the happy ones by evaluative words ( friendly , comfortable , lovely ) and the things guests liked ( staff , breakfast ). Note slow on the happy side: mild complaints sit inside 4-star reviews too. That is one more reason a pure sentiment lexicon misses complaints: unhappy guests often describe rather than evaluate . TF-IDF is also the usual way to turn text into numeric features for a model, the topic of Day 4.
docs.title: On the reviews

docs.text: Lexicon (VADER) Machine learning (for example, logistic regression on TF-IDF) Needs labelled data No Yes, usually hundreds to thousands of examples Transparent Yes: you can see which words scored Partly: you can inspect word weights Domain vocabulary Only if you add it Learns it from the labels Speed to start Minutes Days to weeks (labelling) Typical accuracy in a specific domain Moderate Higher, if the labels are good and plentiful Main risk Misses domain words and sarcasm Learns the biases and errors in its labels; drifts as language changes Modern large language models are a third option. They handle context and sarcasm better, but are harder to audit, cost more per document, and still need to be validated on your labels in exactly the same way. A tiny demonstration: train a classifier to spot 1–2 star reviews from their words, and test it fairly with leave-one-out validation (train on 39 reviews, predict the 40th, repeat 40 times). from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut , cross_val_predict from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline y = ( reviews [ "stars" ] <= 2 ) . astype ( int ) # 1 = unhappy guest model = make_pipeline ( TfidfVectorizer ( token_pattern = r "[a-z]+(?:-[a-z]+)?" ), LogisticRegression ( C = 10 )) pred = cross_val_predict ( model , reviews [ "text" ] . str . lower (), y , cv = LeaveOneOut ()) vader_pred = ( reviews [ "vader_label" ] == "Negative" ) . astype ( int ) for name , p in [( "VADER (negative label)" , vader_pred ), ( "Logistic regression, leave-one-out" , pred )]: caught = (( p == 1 ) & ( y == 1 )) . sum () print ( f " { name : <36 } accuracy { np . mean ( p == y ) : .0% } unhappy guests caught { caught } of { y . sum () } " ) VADER (negative label) accuracy 65% unhappy guests caught 5 of 17 Logistic regression, leave-one-out accuracy 60% unhappy guests caught 5 of 17 With only 40 examples, neither method is trustworthy, and the comparison could easily flip with another 40 reviews. The point is the workflow: a model is only as good as the amount and quality of labelled data behind it, and both methods are judged the same way , on data the model has not seen. You will meet train/test thinking again in the forecasting lecture and on Day 4. A middle path is to extend the lexicon with domain words. In NLTK, vader.lexicon is a dictionary, so vader.lexicon.update({"lukewarm": -1.5}) changes later scores. That is powerful and risky: whoever picks the ratings decides the results, so record every change, justify it, and re-validate.
docs.title: Part 12: Lexicon or machine learning? (extension)

docs.text: Customer text is written by people, often about other people, and rarely with analysis in mind. Five questions to ask before mining it: Consent and purpose. Did people agree to this use? A review posted to help other travellers is not obviously consent to build a profile of the reviewer. Use the text for the purpose it was collected for, or get consent. Personal data. Reviews and support chats contain names, e-mail addresses, phone and room numbers, and sometimes health or family details. Mask them before analysis and keep only what you need (data minimisation). In China, the Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) applies; in Europe, the GDPR. People named in the text. Complaints often name staff ("the receptionist, Li, was rude"). Using sentiment scores to judge or discipline individual employees, without context or a chance to respond, is unfair and often unlawful. Bias. Lexicons and models work best on the language they were built on. Non-native speakers, dialects, other languages and older or younger customers can be scored systematically differently, so their complaints count for less. Check accuracy by group , not only overall. Manipulation and honesty. Do not use mining to suppress or bury negative reviews, to target vulnerable customers, or to publish "95% positive" when the scorer misses complaints. Fake reviews also exist; mining them as genuine distorts the decision. A simple example of masking personal data with regular expressions: raw = [ "Room 212 was freezing. Call me on 138-0013-8000 or write to guest.wang@example.com." , "Thanks to Ms Chen at reception! My booking ref is LK-55821." , ] def mask ( text ): text = re . sub ( r "[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+" , "[EMAIL]" , text ) text = re . sub ( r "\b\d {3} [- ]?\d {4} [- ]?\d {4} \b" , "[PHONE]" , text ) text = re . sub ( r "\b[A-Z] {2} -\d{4,}\b" , "[BOOKING]" , text ) text = re . sub ( r "\b(Mr|Ms|Mrs|Dr)\.? [A-Z][a-z]+" , "[NAME]" , text ) return text for t in raw : print ( mask ( t )) Room 212 was freezing. Call me on [PHONE] or write to [EMAIL] Thanks to [NAME] at reception! My booking ref is [BOOKING]. Pattern-based masking catches formats (e-mails, phone numbers), but misses free-form names ("ask for Li") and room numbers written as words. In practice it is combined with named-entity recognition and a human check of a sample. Masking is a minimum, not a guarantee of anonymity: a review that mentions a date, a site and an unusual event can still identify a guest.
docs.title: Part 13: Ethics of mining customer text (core summary, extension detail)

docs.text: A food-delivery platform collects about 200,000 written restaurant reviews a month. Product managers propose three uses of automatic sentiment scores: A. Show each restaurant a monthly "sentiment score" next to its star rating. B. Automatically hide restaurants whose sentiment falls below a threshold from the app's front page. C. Route every review with a negative score to a support agent, who contacts the customer within 24 hours. Discuss in groups: For each use, which error matters more: a missed negative or a false alarm? Who bears the cost of each? Which use would you approve first, and what validation would you require before launch (sample size, who labels, which groups to check)? Reviews arrive in Mandarin, Cantonese, English and a mix of all three, with many emoji. What does that do to a lexicon such as VADER, and to the fairness of use B? Restaurant owners discover the scoring rules and start asking customers to "please use the word excellent ". What happens to the measure? (Recall Goodhart's law from Day 2.) Write the one-sentence limitation you would put under any sentiment chart shown to senior managers.

Day 4 lecture: Predictive regression ¶ Periods 1 to 3 of Day 4, the first day of Module 2. How a regression becomes a prediction tool a manager can trust: prediction versus explanation, simple and multiple regression, reading a coefficient in dollars with its "holding the others constant" clause, dummy variables and the reference category, training and test sets, R², adjusted R², RMSE and MAE, residual plots, log transformations, multicollinearity and the variance inflation factor, overfitting, extrapolation, confounded coefficients, and why a yes/no outcome needs logistic regression instead. Run each code cell with Shift + Enter , in order. Assignment 2 (house prices) and Lab 5 (car fuel economy, tomorrow) use other data; this lecture deliberately uses neither, so that you practise each idea here and apply it yourself there. The other columns are predictors (features, explanatory or independent variables, x ). Part 1: Prediction or explanation? (core) ¶ A regression is one tool with two very different jobs. Decide which job you are doing before you fit anything, because the two jobs need different checks. Prediction Explanation Question "What will this store sell?" "How much does one more checkout add to sales?" What matters How close the predictions are on new cases Whether each coefficient means what it seems to mean Judged by Test-set error (RMSE, MAE), R² on test data Sensible signs and sizes, stable coefficients, no confounding, ideally an experiment Correlated predictors Usually fine A serious problem (Part 9) A missing cause Fine if its effect is picked up by other predictors Biases the coefficients (Part 12) Typical use Sales forecasts for new sites, pricing a house, fraud scores Deciding whether to invest in a lever: a promotion, more staff, a car park The reading packet describes this as the move from describing the data in hand to predicting what has not happened yet. A predictive model is held to a stricter standard: it must work on cases it has never seen. Predict, then run. Which single column do you expect to have the strongest correlation with sales ? Which the weakest? Write down your guesses. numeric = stores . drop ( columns = "region" ) print ( numeric . corr ()[ "sales" ] . drop ( "sales" ) . sort_values ( ascending = False ) . round ( 2 )) floor_area 0.68 staff 0.65 footfall 0.63 checkouts 0.61 promo 0.44 competitor_miles -0.18 parking -0.28 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Floor area, staff, checkouts, footfall and the promotion all go with higher sales; distance to a rival and parking, which are typical of rural stores, are weakly negative . Misconception: "The variable with the biggest correlation is the most important cause." Correlation measures how closely two columns move together. It says nothing about why : several of these columns are bigger in big stores, and the promotion was given to busy stores on purpose. Part 2: Simple regression (core) ¶ A simple linear regression uses one predictor: sales = b₀ + b₁ × floor_area + error b₁, the slope: how much predicted sales change, on average, when floor area is one unit larger. b₀, the intercept: predicted sales when floor area is zero. Often it has no business meaning; it just positions the line. error (residual): actual − predicted, for each store. Least squares picks the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. Squaring keeps positive and negative misses from cancelling, and punishes big misses more. Predict, then run. Roughly how many thousand dollars of extra annual sales would you expect for each extra 100 square feet of floor? Guess a number between 0 and 100. simple = smf . ols ( "sales ~ floor_area" , data = stores ) . fit () b0 , b1 = simple . params [ "Intercept" ], simple . params [ "floor_area" ] print ( f "sales = { b0 : ,.1f } + { b1 : .3f } x floor_area (thousand US dollars)" ) print ( f "Each extra 100 sq ft: about $ { b1 * 100 * 1000 : ,.0f } more annual sales, on average" ) print ( f "R-squared: { simple . rsquared : .2f } " ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . scatter ( stores [ "floor_area" ], stores [ "sales" ], s = 14 , alpha = 0.5 , color = BLUE ) xs = np . linspace ( stores [ "floor_area" ] . min (), stores [ "floor_area" ] . max (), 50 ) ax . plot ( xs , b0 + b1 * xs , color = ORANGE , lw = 2 , label = "Least-squares line" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Floor area (square feet)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Annual sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Bigger stores sell more, with a lot of scatter" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () sales = 428.3 + 0.440 x floor_area (thousand US dollars) Each extra 100 sq ft: about $43,967 more annual sales, on average R-squared: 0.46 Reading the coefficients in business units ¶ Always translate a coefficient into a sentence with units and a sensible step size . "0.44" is meaningless to a manager; "about $44,000 more sales a year for every extra 100 square feet" is not. A template: "Among stores like these, a store with [one step more of x] has, on average , about [b₁ × step, with units] [more / less] [target] ." Three things the sentence deliberately says: "On average" : individual stores scatter widely around the line. "Among stores like these" : the line was fitted to stores from 1,500 to 6,500 square feet (Part 11). "Has" , not "would gain if we enlarged it": the data compares different stores; it did not watch a store being enlarged (Part 12). The intercept here would be the predicted sales of a store with zero floor area. No such store exists, so the intercept is just where the line crosses the axis. Do not interpret it. Misconception: "R² tells us how much of sales floor area causes ." R² is the share of the variation in sales that the line accounts for in this data. About half of the variation is explained by floor area alone; the rest comes from footfall, competition, region and noise. Check your understanding. A colleague writes: "Increasing floor area by 1 square foot increases sales by 0.44." Name the two things wrong with this sentence. Part 3: Multiple regression and "holding constant" (core) ¶ A multiple regression uses several predictors at once: sales = b₀ + b₁ × floor_area + b₂ × footfall + b₃ × competitor_miles + b₄ × parking + error Each coefficient now answers a sharper question: how much do predicted sales differ for one unit more of this predictor, when the other predictors in the model are held at the same values? That clause, "holding the others constant" (in Latin, ceteris paribus ), is what makes multiple regression useful, and what makes its coefficients easy to misread. Predict, then run. Downtown stores have far more footfall than rural ones. When we add footfall to the model, will the floor-area coefficient change a lot or a little? Part 4: Categories: dummy variables and the reference (core) ¶ region is text, not a number. A regression handles a category with dummy variables (also called indicator or one-hot variables): one 0/1 column per category, except one . The category left out is the reference (baseline). Each dummy's coefficient is the difference from the reference, holding the other predictors constant. Why leave one out? With an intercept in the model, the three dummies would always add up to 1, so one is perfectly predictable from the other two. The model cannot separate them: this is the dummy-variable trap . Part 5: Training and test sets (core) ¶ A model fitted to all 300 stores will always fit those 300 stores reasonably well: least squares made it so. That in-sample fit says little about the question a predictive model must answer: how well will it do on a store it has never seen? So we hide some data: Split the rows at random into a training set (commonly 70–80%) and a test set (the rest). Fit the model on the training set only. Predict the test set and measure the errors. The test set plays the role of "new stores". The test score is the honest one. It is almost always a little worse than the training score; a big gap is a warning sign of overfitting (Part 10). Random splitting suits cross-sectional data like these stores, one row per case. On Day 3 you saw that a time series must be split in time order instead, because a random split lets the future leak into training. Predict, then run. Will the model's R² on the test stores be higher or lower than on the training stores? By a lot or a little? features = [ "floor_area" , "footfall" , "competitor_miles" , "parking" ] train , test = train_test_split ( stores , test_size = 0.2 , random_state = 1 ) print ( f "Training stores: { len ( train ) } , test stores: { len ( test ) } " ) lin = LinearRegression () . fit ( train [ features ], train [ "sales" ]) pred_train = lin . predict ( train [ features ]) pred_test = lin . predict ( test [ features ]) print ( f "R-squared on training data: { r2_score ( train [ 'sales' ], pred_train ) : .3f } " ) print ( f "R-squared on test data: { r2_score ( test [ 'sales' ], pred_test ) : .3f } " ) print ( "

Series ( lin . coef_ , index = features ) . round ( 3 )) Training stores: 240, test stores: 60 R-squared on training data: 0.843 R-squared on test data: 0.798 Coefficients (fitted on training data only): floor_area 0.425 footfall 63.079 competitor_miles 15.189 parking 53.081 dtype: float64 Here the gap is small: four sensible predictors and 240 training stores leave little room for memorising noise. On a different random split the numbers move a little; that is normal, and it is one reason Part 10 introduces cross-validation . Rules for using a test set well: Split first , before exploring or choosing features, so that nothing about the test rows shapes the model. Fix random_state so that you and your reader get the same split. Use the test set once , at the end. If you try twenty models and keep the one with the best test score, the test set has quietly become part of training. After choosing the model, it is fine to refit on all the data for the final predictions. Misconception: "The test score is the model's accuracy, so it will be exactly this good in future." It is an estimate from one sample of stores. New stores may differ from old ones (new regions, a new competitor), and then the error will be larger. Part 6: R², adjusted R², RMSE and MAE (core) ¶ For each store, residual = actual − predicted . Four summaries of the residuals: Measure Formula Units How to say it R² 1 − (sum of squared residuals) ÷ (sum of squared deviations from the mean) None (≤ 1) "The model accounts for about 84% of the variation in sales between stores" Adjusted R² 1 − (1 − R²) × (n − 1) ÷ (n − k − 1), with k predictors None Like R², but with a penalty for each predictor: it rises only if a new predictor improves the fit by more than chance would RMSE √(mean of squared residuals) Same as the target "Predictions are typically off by about $X thousand; big misses weigh more" MAE mean of |residuals| Same as the target "On average, predictions miss by about $X thousand" Points that trip people up: R² is not "accuracy" or "percent correct". An R² of 0.84 does not mean 84% of predictions are right. It compares the model's squared errors with those of the simplest possible prediction: the mean. R² on test data can be negative : that happens when the model does worse than just predicting the training mean. RMSE ≥ MAE always. The bigger the gap, the more the errors include a few large misses. Judge RMSE and MAE against the scale : a $150 thousand error is small for a $4 million store and huge for a $1 million one. Predict, then run. Adjusted R² barely moved: its penalty roughly cancels the gain that pure noise gives, so it does not reward the junk (with useless predictors it is as likely to fall as to rise slightly). Part 7: Residual plots (core) ¶ R² and RMSE are averages; they can hide where a model goes wrong. A residual plot (residuals on the vertical axis, predicted values on the horizontal) shows it. What you want is a shapeless band centred on zero , the same width all the way across. Two patterns to recognise: Pattern Name What it means Typical fix A curve (a smile or a frown) Non-linearity A straight line is the wrong shape for the relationship Transform a variable (Part 8), add a squared term, or use a different model A funnel (spread grows or shrinks) Heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance) Errors are bigger for some cases than others; the RMSE overstates accuracy for some and understates it for others Log the target (Part 8); report errors in percent; use robust standard errors The reading packet stresses that two models can share the same R² while one has evenly spread errors and the other has errors that grow for the largest cases. Only the residual plot shows the difference. Predict, then run. Three simulated data sets follow. Before you look at the bottom row, sketch what each residual plot will look like. sim = np . random . default_rng ( 11 ) x = np . sort ( sim . uniform ( 1 , 10 , 200 )) cases = { "Good: straight line, constant noise" : 3 + 2 * x + sim . normal ( 0 , 2 , 200 ), "Curve: true relationship bends" : 1 + 0.4 * x ** 2 + sim . normal ( 0 , 2 , 200 ), "Funnel: noise grows with size" : 3 + 2 * x + sim . normal ( 0 , 0.4 * x , 200 ), } fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 3 , figsize = ( 12 , 6 )) for col , ( title , y ) in enumerate ( cases . items ()): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( x , y , 1 ) fitted = intercept + slope * x axes [ 0 , col ] . scatter ( x , y , s = 8 , color = BLUE , alpha = 0.6 ) axes [ 0 , col ] . plot ( x , fitted , color = ORANGE ) axes [ 0 , col ] . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) axes [ 1 , col ] . scatter ( fitted , y - fitted , s = 8 , color = GREY ) axes [ 1 , col ] . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.8 ) axes [ 1 , col ] . set_xlabel ( "Predicted value" ) axes [ 0 , 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "y" ) axes [ 1 , 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Residual" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Now the store model. We draw the residual plot for the training stores (more points make the pattern easier to see), with a smooth trend line through the residuals to help the eye. def residual_plot ( fitted , residuals , title , ax = None , ylabel = "Residual (thousand US dollars)" ): """Residuals against predicted values, with a binned average to show any curve.""" ax = ax or plt . gca () ax . scatter ( fitted , residuals , s = 12 , alpha = 0.5 , color = BLUE ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.8 ) bins = pd . qcut ( fitted , 10 ) trend = pd . DataFrame ({ "f" : fitted , "r" : residuals }) . groupby ( bins , observed = True ) . mean () ax . plot ( trend [ "f" ], trend [ "r" ], color = ORANGE , lw = 2 , marker = "o" , label = "Average residual (10 bins)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Predicted value" ) ax . set_ylabel ( ylabel ) ax . set_title ( title ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) level_model = smf . ols ( "sales ~ floor_area + footfall + competitor_miles + parking" , data = train ) . fit () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) residual_plot ( level_model . fittedvalues . values , level_model . resid . values , "Store model in dollars: residuals fan out and bend" , ax = ax ) plt . show () Two problems are visible: A funnel. The residuals spread out as predicted sales grow: the model misses big stores by far more dollars than small ones. That is heteroscedasticity, and it makes a single RMSE misleading: it is too pessimistic for small stores and too optimistic for big ones. A slight curve. The average residual is positive at both ends and negative in the middle: the effects multiply rather than add, so a straight line in dollars is the wrong shape. Neither problem stops the model from predicting reasonably on average, but both say we can do better, and that any statement like "accurate to within $X" needs care. Two more checks are worth knowing (extension): Residuals against each predictor : a curve against one predictor says that predictor needs transforming. Influential points : one extreme store can tilt a line. Look at the largest residuals and ask whether they are errors in the data, or real but unusual cases. Misconception: "The residuals should be normally distributed, so the data must be normal." The assumptions are about the errors , not the raw columns. Skewed predictors are fine. And for prediction, a funnel or a curve matters more than exact normality. Part 8: Log transformations (core idea, extension detail) ¶ Money, sizes and counts often behave multiplicatively : a 10% bigger store sells roughly 7% more, whether it is a small store or a big one. In dollars that is a curve with errors that grow with size, exactly the two patterns in Part 7. Taking the natural log turns multiplying into adding, which a linear regression can model. For a column that can be zero, use np.log1p (log of 1 + x) or reconsider. Predict, then run.
