Part 9: Multicollinearity and VIF (core) ¶ Multicollinearity means two or more predictors are strongly correlated with each other . It is normal in business data: bigger stores have more floor area, more checkouts and more staff, for structural reasons. The problem is for explanation . If floor area, checkouts and staff always rise together, the data has almost no stores where one is high and the others are low, so the model cannot tell which one deserves the credit. The coefficients become unstable : small changes in the data swing them, sometimes flipping their signs, while the predictions barely change. The variance inflation factor for predictor j is VIF_j = 1 ÷ (1 − R²_j) , where R²_j comes from regressing predictor j on all the other predictors . A VIF of 1 means no overlap. A VIF of 5 means 80% of that predictor's variation is already explained by the others, and its coefficient's variance is five times what it would be without the overlap. The usual flag is VIF > 5 (some use 10). Predict, then run. We add checkouts and staff to the dollar model. Which predictors will have a VIF above 5? size_cols = [ "floor_area" , "checkouts" , "staff" , "footfall" , "competitor_miles" , "parking" ] print ( "Correlations among the size measures:" ) print ( train [[ "floor_area" , "checkouts" , "staff" ]] . corr () . round ( 2 )) def vif_table ( data , cols ): """VIF by the definition: regress each predictor on all the others.""" out = {} for c in cols : others = [ o for o in cols if o != c ] r2_j = smf . ols ( f " { c } ~ " + " + " . join ( others ), data = data ) . fit () . rsquared out [ c ] = 1 / ( 1 - r2_j ) return pd . Series ( out , name = "VIF" ) . round ( 1 ) print ( " 
 VIF with all six predictors:" ) print ( vif_table ( train , size_cols )) Correlations among the size measures: floor_area checkouts staff floor_area 1.00 0.94 0.97 checkouts 0.94 1.00 0.91 staff 0.97 0.91 1.00 VIF with all six predictors: floor_area 23.9 checkouts 8.4 staff 16.3 footfall 1.6 competitor_miles 1.4 parking 1.3 Name: VIF, dtype: float64 Floor area, checkouts and staff all have VIFs well above 5: each is largely predictable from the other two. Footfall, distance and parking are near 1. statsmodels has a ready-made function, variance_inflation_factor in statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence . It needs a constant column in the design matrix and gives the same numbers as the definition above; computing VIF by hand once makes clear what it measures. What multicollinearity does, and does not, do ¶ Predict, then run. We refit the six-predictor model on five bootstrap samples (training stores drawn at random with replacement). Will the floor-area, checkouts and staff coefficients stay similar? Will the test RMSE? boot = np . random . default_rng ( 3 ) rows = [] for b in range ( 5 ): sample = train . iloc [ boot . integers ( 0 , len ( train ), len ( train ))] m = smf . ols ( "sales ~ " + " + " . join ( size_cols ), data = sample ) . fit () rows . append ({ "sample" : b + 1 , "floor_area (per 100 sq ft)" : m . params [ "floor_area" ] * 100 , "checkouts (per counter)" : m . params [ "checkouts" ], "staff (per FTE)" : m . params [ "staff" ], "test RMSE" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test [ "sales" ], m . predict ( test )))}) print ( pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . round ( 1 ) . to_string ( index = False )) sample floor_area (per 100 sq ft) checkouts (per counter) staff (per FTE) test RMSE 1 34.1 -9.1 23.2 257.7 2 49.4 -33.7 -6.0 260.9 3 49.9 -8.9 -21.6 257.2 4 52.4 -39.8 -5.8 268.6 5 49.9 -50.5 4.5 262.9 The three size coefficients jump around from sample to sample, and some change sign, while the test RMSE hardly moves. That is the reading packet's point in action: For prediction , multicollinearity is usually tolerable: the model still combines the size measures into a good overall prediction, as long as new stores have the same pattern (bigger stores with more staff). If a new store breaks the pattern (huge floor, two checkouts), predictions become unreliable. For explanation , a high VIF disqualifies that coefficient. "Each extra checkout adds $X thousand" cannot be read from this model. What to do about it, depending on the purpose: Option When Leave it The purpose is prediction and new cases follow the old pattern Drop one of the overlapping predictors You need interpretable coefficients and one measure carries the idea (floor area) Combine them into one index (e.g. "store size") The measures are different views of one underlying property Collect data that breaks the pattern, or run an experiment You genuinely need the separate effect (e.g. of adding a checkout) Regularisation (ridge regression) Many correlated predictors; mentioned again in the text-features lecture Misconception: "A high VIF means the model is wrong and must be fixed." It means individual coefficients are unreliable. Whether that matters depends on what the model is for, which is why Part 1 asked the question first. Part 10: Overfitting (core demo, extension cross-validation) ¶ A model overfits when it learns the noise in the training data as if it were pattern. It fits the training data very well and new data badly. Flexible models (many predictors, high-degree curves) on small samples overfit most. Predict, then run. Using only 25 training stores , we fit polynomials of floor area of degree 1 (a line) up to 9 (a very wiggly curve), and test each on 100 other stores. Which degree will have the lowest training error? The lowest test error? small = stores . sample ( 125 , random_state = 4 ) small_train , small_test = small . iloc [: 25 ], small . iloc [ 25 :] centre , scale = small_train [ "floor_area" ] . mean (), small_train [ "floor_area" ] . std () z_train = ( small_train [ "floor_area" ] - centre ) / scale # standardise so high powers stay manageable z_test = ( small_test [ "floor_area" ] - centre ) / scale rows = [] for degree in range ( 1 , 10 ): coefs = np . polyfit ( z_train , small_train [ "sales" ], degree ) rows . append ({ "degree" : degree , "train RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean (( small_train [ "sales" ] - np . polyval ( coefs , z_train )) ** 2 )), "test RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean (( small_test [ "sales" ] - np . polyval ( coefs , z_test )) ** 2 ))}) curve = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4.2 )) axes [ 0 ] . plot ( curve [ "degree" ], curve [ "train RMSE" ], marker = "o" , color = BLUE , label = "Training (25 stores)" ) axes [ 0 ] . plot ( curve [ "degree" ], curve [ "test RMSE" ], marker = "o" , color = ORANGE , label = "Test (100 stores)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "Polynomial degree (model flexibility)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "RMSE (thousand US dollars, log scale)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Training error keeps falling; test error does not" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_yscale ( "log" ) axes [ 0 ] . legend ( frameon = False ) grid = np . linspace ( z_train . min (), z_train . max (), 200 ) axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( small_train [ "floor_area" ], small_train [ "sales" ], color = BLUE , s = 20 , label = "Training stores" ) for degree , colour in [( 1 , GREEN ), ( 9 , ORANGE )]: coefs = np . polyfit ( z_train , small_train [ "sales" ], degree ) axes [ 1 ] . plot ( grid * scale + centre , np . polyval ( coefs , grid ), color = colour , label = f "Degree { degree } " ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylim ( stores [ "sales" ] . min () * 0.5 , stores [ "sales" ] . max () * 1.1 ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Floor area (square feet)" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "A degree-9 curve chases individual stores" ) axes [ 1 ] . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () print ( curve . round ( 1 ) . to_string ( index = False )) degree train RMSE test RMSE 1 493.0 518.9 2 436.3 710.0 3 408.0 754.4 4 407.9 673.5 5 369.4 12479.7 6 366.1 1624.5 7 366.0 5694.2 8 343.6 365411.0 9 342.7 19663.0 Training error falls with every extra degree: more flexibility always fits the sample better. Test error is lowest for the straight line and then rises, explosively for the wiggliest curves (the left chart needs a log scale to show them at all). The degree-9 curve passes close to the training stores and swings wildly between and beyond them. Defences against overfitting: Judge on test data , never on training fit alone. Prefer simpler models unless a more complex one clearly wins on test data. More data : the same degree-9 curve overfits far less with 2,000 stores than with 25. Regularisation (ridge, lasso) shrinks coefficients towards zero; the reading packet's logistic regression reading mentions it as a defence. Cross-validation (below) when choosing between models. Cross-validation (extension) ¶ One random split gives one noisy estimate. k-fold cross-validation splits the training data into k parts, fits on k − 1 of them and tests on the remaining part, k times, then averages. Use it to choose a model; keep the real test set for the final check. folds = KFold ( n_splits = 5 , shuffle = True , random_state = 0 ) X_log = pd . DataFrame ({ "log_area" : np . log ( train [ "floor_area" ]), "footfall" : train [ "footfall" ], "log_comp" : np . log ( train [ "competitor_miles" ]), "parking" : train [ "parking" ]}) for label , X in [( "Floor area only" , X_log [[ "log_area" ]]), ( "Four predictors" , X_log )]: scores = cross_val_score ( LinearRegression (), X , np . log ( train [ "sales" ]), cv = folds , scoring = "r2" ) print ( f " { label : 16s } R2 in each fold: { np . round ( scores , 2 ) } mean { scores . mean () : .2f } " ) Floor area only R2 in each fold: [0.54 0.43 0.41 0.6 0.45] mean 0.48 Four predictors R2 in each fold: [0.92 0.86 0.86 0.88 0.82] mean 0.87 Part 11: Extrapolation (core) ¶ A regression learns the relationship within the range of the data . Using it far outside that range, extrapolation , assumes the relationship carries on unchanged, which the data cannot confirm. Corner & Co. is considering a 15,000 square foot "superstore". The largest store in the data is 6,500 square feet. Predict, then run. Will the dollar model and the log model give similar predictions for the superstore? (They agreed closely on the test stores.) superstore = pd . DataFrame ({ "floor_area" : [ 15000 ], "footfall" : [ 14.0 ], "competitor_miles" : [ 1.0 ], "parking" : [ 1 ], "region" : [ "Suburb" ]}) dollar_pred = level_model . predict ( superstore ) . iloc [ 0 ] log_point = np . exp ( log_model . predict ( superstore ) . iloc [ 0 ]) print ( f "Training range of floor area: { train [ 'floor_area' ] . min () : ,.0f } to { train [ 'floor_area' ] . max () : ,.0f } sq ft" ) print ( f "Dollar model prediction: { dollar_pred : ,.0f } thousand US dollars" ) print ( f "Log model prediction: { log_point : ,.0f } thousand US dollars" ) xs = np . linspace ( 1500 , 15000 , 100 ) grid = pd . DataFrame ({ "floor_area" : xs , "footfall" : 14.0 , "competitor_miles" : 1.0 , "parking" : 1 , "region" : "Suburb" }) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . axvspan ( train [ "floor_area" ] . min (), train [ "floor_area" ] . max (), color = SKY , alpha = 0.2 , label = "Range of the data" ) ax . plot ( xs , level_model . predict ( grid ), color = BLUE , label = "Dollar model" ) ax . plot ( xs , np . exp ( log_model . predict ( grid )), color = ORANGE , label = "Log model" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Floor area (square feet)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Predicted sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Two models that agree inside the data disagree outside it" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () Training range of floor area: 1,500 to 6,500 sq ft Dollar model prediction: 6,811 thousand US dollars Log model prediction: 5,897 thousand US dollars Inside the shaded range the two models agree closely; at 15,000 square feet they differ by about $900 thousand a year, and the data cannot say which is right . Neither may be: a superstore draws customers from further away, needs more parking and competes with supermarkets, none of which appears in data on small stores. Rules: Check the range of every predictor before predicting. Report it with the prediction. Combinations count too. A store inside the range of each predictor separately can still be unusual: a huge floor area with two checkouts (Part 9). Prediction intervals widen away from the centre of the data; the business case below shows them. Time is a predictor too. A model fitted on last year's prices extrapolates when used after a market shift. Misconception: "The model gave a number, so it can predict anything." The model will always give a number. Whether the number means anything depends on whether the new case resembles the data. Part 12: Correlation, causation and confounded coefficients (core) ¶ Head office wants to know whether to roll out the loyalty-app promotion to every store. Last year it ran in about half of them. Predict, then run. Stores with the promotion sold more. Will the promotion's coefficient shrink, grow or stay the same when we add footfall and the other predictors? naive = smf . ols ( "sales ~ promo" , data = stores ) . fit () adjusted = smf . ols ( "np.log(sales) ~ promo + np.log(floor_area) + footfall + np.log(competitor_miles)" " + parking + C(region, Treatment('Suburb'))" , data = stores ) . fit () print ( "Promotion stores vs others (raw difference in average sales):" ) print ( f " { naive . params [ 'promo' ] : ,.0f } thousand US dollars a year" ) print ( " 
 After holding size, footfall, competition, parking and region constant:" ) lo , hi = adjusted . conf_int () . loc [ "promo" ] print ( f " about { 100 * adjusted . params [ 'promo' ] : .1f } % (95% CI { 100 * lo : .1f } % to { 100 * hi : .1f } %)" ) print ( " 
 Average footfall (thousand a week):" ) print ( stores . groupby ( "promo" )[ "footfall" ] . mean () . round ( 1 ) . rename ({ 0 : "no promotion" , 1 : "promotion" })) Promotion stores vs others (raw difference in average sales): 582 thousand US dollars a year After holding size, footfall, competition, parking and region constant: about 2.1% (95% CI -1.2% to 5.5%) Average footfall (thousand a week): promo no promotion 10.7 promotion 19.2 Name: footfall, dtype: float64 The raw difference is large, but almost all of it is footfall : head office gave the promotion to busy stores, and busy stores sell more anyway. Once footfall and the rest are held constant, the promotion's estimated effect is a few percent with a wide interval. (The synthetic truth is 2%.) Footfall here is a confounder : it affects both who got the promotion and sales. Leaving it out does not just add noise; it pushes the promotion's coefficient in one direction. This is omitted-variable bias , and it is the biggest single reason a regression coefficient is not a causal effect. Why even the adjusted coefficient is not proof: There may be confounders we did not measure (a keener manager, a better location within the street). Adding the wrong variables can also bias a coefficient, for example a variable that is itself caused by the promotion (such as app downloads). The data are observational : head office chose, the stores did not get the promotion at random. The reliable way to measure the promotion's effect is an experiment : pick stores at random to get it, then compare. Random assignment breaks every link between the promotion and footfall, measured or not. When an experiment is impossible, be explicit: "Stores with X sell more, after allowing for A, B and C; we cannot rule out other differences." Weak Better "The promotion increases sales by $580 thousand." "Promotion stores sold about $580 thousand more, but they were the busiest stores. Comparing stores of similar footfall and size, the difference is a few percent and uncertain. A randomised trial in 40 stores would settle it." Check your understanding. A regression of hospital deaths on "number of doctors on duty" has a positive coefficient. Give a confounder that explains this, and say what a manager should not conclude. Part 13: Yes/no outcomes: logistic regression as a concept (extension) ¶ Some predictions are about a category , not a number: will a customer churn, will a machine fail this month, is a transaction fraudulent, will a new store reach its sales target? Gordon's Chapter 8 examples (predictive maintenance, fraud detection) are of this kind. You could code the outcome as 1 (yes) and 0 (no) and fit a straight line. That is called a linear probability model , and it has two problems: It can predict below 0 or above 1 , which is not a probability. It assumes each unit of x changes the probability by the same amount everywhere, whereas in reality a store already certain to hit its target cannot become "more certain". Logistic regression fixes this. It computes the same kind of linear combination, z = b₀ + b₁x₁ + …, and passes it through the sigmoid function p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z)) , which squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. A large positive z gives a probability near 1, a large negative z near 0, and z = 0 gives 0.5. A threshold (often 0.5, but it should depend on the costs of each kind of error) turns the probability into a yes/no decision. It is fitted not by least squares but by minimising log loss (cross-entropy), which punishes confident wrong predictions very heavily. This course does not require you to fit logistic models; the demo below is to make the idea concrete. Predict, then run. Target: "sales of at least $2 million". Using footfall alone, will a straight line predict probabilities below 0 for the quietest stores? stores [ "hit_target" ] = ( stores [ "sales" ] >= 2000 ) . astype ( int ) print ( f "Share of stores at or above $2 million: { stores [ 'hit_target' ] . mean () : .0% } " ) X_f = stores [[ "footfall" ]] lpm = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_f , stores [ "hit_target" ]) logit = LogisticRegression () . fit ( X_f , stores [ "hit_target" ]) grid = pd . DataFrame ({ "footfall" : np . linspace ( 0 , 40 , 200 )}) fig , ax = plt . subplots () jitter = np . random . default_rng ( 8 ) . uniform ( - 0.03 , 0.03 , len ( stores )) ax . scatter ( stores [ "footfall" ], stores [ "hit_target" ] + jitter , s = 10 , alpha = 0.4 , color = GREY , label = "Stores (0 = no, 1 = yes)" ) ax . plot ( grid [ "footfall" ], lpm . predict ( grid ), color = BLUE , label = "Straight line (linear probability model)" ) ax . plot ( grid [ "footfall" ], logit . predict_proba ( grid )[:, 1 ], color = ORANGE , lw = 2 , label = "Logistic regression (sigmoid)" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.6 ) ax . axhline ( 1 , color = "black" , lw = 0.6 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Footfall (thousand passers-by a week)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Probability of reaching $2 million" ) ax . set_title ( "A straight line leaves the 0 to 1 range; the sigmoid cannot" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , fontsize = 9 , loc = "lower right" ) plt . show () print ( f "Straight line at footfall 2: { lpm . predict ( pd . DataFrame ({ 'footfall' : [ 2 ]}))[ 0 ] : .2f } " ) print ( f "Straight line at footfall 38: { lpm . predict ( pd . DataFrame ({ 'footfall' : [ 38 ]}))[ 0 ] : .2f } " ) Share of stores at or above $2 million: 44% Straight line at footfall 2: -0.08 Straight line at footfall 38: 1.37 The straight line gives impossible "probabilities" at both ends; the S-shaped sigmoid stays between 0 and 1 and is steepest in the middle, where a store's fate is most uncertain. Log loss for one store is −log(p) if the store did hit the target, and −log(1 − p) if it did not: Model's probability for a store that did hit the target Log loss Squared error (1 − p)² 0.9 (confident, right) 0.11 0.01 0.5 (unsure) 0.69 0.25 0.1 (confident, wrong) 2.30 0.81 0.01 (very confident, wrong) 4.61 0.98 Squared error can never exceed 1, but log loss grows without limit as a wrong prediction becomes more confident. That is why logistic regression produces cautious probabilities. Choosing a threshold is a business decision. For predictive maintenance, missing a failure (a false negative) may cost a production line; an unneeded inspection (a false positive) costs an hour of an engineer's time. A low threshold, flagging any machine above, say, 0.2, can be right. For fraud, blocking an honest customer's card has a cost too. Gordon's point is that the costs of false alarms and missed events should shape the model and its validation. Check your understanding. Why is a logistic coefficient not "the change in probability per unit of x"? (Hint: look at how steep the orange curve is at footfall 5 and at footfall 20.) Part 14: Business case: choosing new store sites (core discussion, extension detail) ¶ Corner & Co. has four candidate sites and budget for two. The property team has measured each one. You are asked for a prediction of annual sales, with honest uncertainty, and a recommendation. We refit the log model on all 300 stores (the model was chosen on training data and checked once on test data, Part 5's rule 4) and ask statsmodels for a 95% prediction interval : a range that should contain the actual sales of about 95 in 100 stores like this one. It is much wider than the confidence interval of the average, because it includes each store's own noise. final = smf . ols ( log_formula , data = stores ) . fit () sites = pd . DataFrame ({ "site" : [ "A: High Street" , "B: Ring Road" , "C: Village" , "D: Station Mall" ], "region" : [ "Downtown" , "Suburb" , "Rural" , "Downtown" ], "floor_area" : [ 2800 , 4800 , 2200 , 9000 ], "footfall" : [ 26.0 , 15.0 , 6.0 , 30.0 ], "competitor_miles" : [ 0.2 , 1.5 , 4.0 , 0.1 ], "parking" : [ 0 , 1 , 1 , 0 ], }) pi = final . get_prediction ( sites ) . summary_frame ( alpha = 0.05 ) sites [ "predicted" ] = np . exp ( pi [ "mean" ]) . round ( 0 ) sites [ "95% PI low" ] = np . exp ( pi [ "obs_ci_lower" ]) . round ( 0 ) sites [ "95% PI high" ] = np . exp ( pi [ "obs_ci_upper" ]) . round ( 0 ) ranges = { c : ( stores [ c ] . min (), stores [ c ] . max ()) for c in [ "floor_area" , "footfall" , "competitor_miles" ]} sites [ "outside data range" ] = sites . apply ( lambda r : ", " . join ( c for c , ( lo , hi ) in ranges . items () if not lo <= r [ c ] <= hi ) or "-" , axis = 1 ) print ( "Predicted annual sales, thousand US dollars" ) print ( sites . drop ( columns = [ "region" , "parking" ]) . to_string ( index = False )) Predicted annual sales, thousand US dollars site floor_area footfall competitor_miles predicted 95% PI low 95% PI high outside data range A: High Street 2800 26.0 0.2 2168.0 1725.0 2725.0 - B: Ring Road 4800 15.0 1.5 2587.0 2059.0 3251.0 - C: Village 2200 6.0 4.0 1057.0 841.0 1330.0 - D: Station Mall 9000 30.0 0.1 5570.0 4407.0 7039.0 floor_area Discussion questions (groups of three, 10 minutes): Which two sites would you recommend on the predictions alone? Now look at the intervals and the range check: does your choice change? Site D's prediction is the highest. What does the "outside data range" column say about it, and what would you ask the property team before trusting it? The model predicts sales , but the decision is about profit . What else would you need (rent, staff, fit-out cost)? Which of those could a second regression predict? Which coefficient would head office be tempted to read causally ("let's add a car park to site A"), and why is that not what this model supports? Write the recommendation in four parts, as on Day 3: finding, evidence, action with an owner, and how you would know it worked (for example, compare actual first-year sales with the interval). A good answer separates the prediction (what the model says, with its interval and its range) from the judgement (what the business should do, including what the model cannot see). Part 15: Practice, quiz and summary ¶ Practice ¶ Core ¶ Core 1. Fit sales ~ footfall on the training stores. Write the slope as a business sentence with units, a sensible step size and the words "on average". Core 2. Add C(region, Treatment('Rural')) to the dollar model. Write one sentence for each region coefficient, naming the reference category. Core 3. For the model in Core 2, compute test R², RMSE and MAE, and compare them with the baseline "predict the training mean". Write two sentences a manager could understand. Core 4. Draw the residual plot of sales ~ floor_area (one predictor, in dollars). Describe the pattern you see in one sentence, using the words "funnel" or "curve". Stretch ¶ Stretch 1. Using the vif_table function, compute VIFs for a model with floor_area and staff only. Then replace them with a single column, staff_per_1000_sqft = staff / floor_area * 1000 . What happens to the VIFs, and what does the new coefficient mean? Stretch 2. Re-run Part 5 with random_state = 2, 3, 4 and 5. How much do the test R² and RMSE move? What does that tell you about quoting a test score to three decimals? Stretch 3. Fit the log model with and without promo . Does adding the promotion improve the test RMSE? Is "it does not improve prediction" the same as "it has no effect"? Challenge ¶ Challenge 1. Use the diamonds data in data/diamonds.csv . Predict price from carat in dollars and in logs (log price on log carat), with an 80/20 split. Draw both residual plots, compare test errors in dollars, and write the log model's slope as an elasticity. (Lab 1 explored diamonds descriptively; this is a different, predictive question.) Challenge 2. Write a function report(model_formula, train, test) that fits a statsmodels formula on train and prints test R², RMSE, MAE (back-transforming if the formula starts with np.log( ), the coefficients with 95% intervals, and the VIFs. Challenge 3. In Part 13, add np.log(floor_area) to the logistic model. Choose a threshold so that at most 10% of stores flagged "will reach $2 million" actually fall short, and explain why a property team might want such a rule. Quiz ¶ Give one business question that calls for a predictive regression and one that calls for an explanatory one. What would you check differently? Write the slope 0.031 in log(sales) ~ … + footfall as a business sentence. A model of salary includes gender with "Female" as the reference. The Male coefficient is 2,500. What exactly does that number compare? Why can't we include a dummy for every region and an intercept? Why is test-set R² a fairer measure of a predictive model than training R²? A model's RMSE is $120 thousand and its MAE is $60 thousand. What does the gap suggest? What does adjusted R² do that R² does not? Sketch a residual plot showing heteroscedasticity. What does it mean for a manager reading "accurate to within $X"? Two predictors have VIFs of 12. Is the model useless? Answer for prediction and for explanation. Training RMSE falls and test RMSE rises as you add predictors. What is happening, and what do you do? Name one danger of extrapolation, with an example from your own field. Why does a straight-line model fail for a yes/no outcome, and what does the sigmoid do about it? Summary ¶ Idea Remember Purpose Decide first: predict (judge test error) or explain (judge coefficients, confounding) Coefficient "On average, among cases like these, one [step] more of x goes with [b × step, units] more y, holding the others constant " Dummies One 0/1 column per category except the reference ; coefficients are differences from it Train/test Split first, fit on training, test once ; random split for cross-sectional data, time order for time series R² / adj R² Share of variation accounted for; adjusted R² penalises useless predictors; neither is "accuracy" RMSE / MAE Typical error in the target's units; RMSE ≥ MAE; compare with a baseline and the scale Residual plots Want a flat, even band; curve = wrong shape, funnel = unequal error sizes Logs Turn multiplicative effects into additive ones; read coefficients as percentages or elasticities VIF 1 ÷ (1 − R²_j); > 5 flags overlap; ruins coefficients, rarely predictions Overfitting Training error always falls with flexibility; test error tells the truth Extrapolation Report the data range; models that agree inside it can disagree wildly outside Causation A coefficient is a comparison, not an intervention; confounders bias it; experiments settle it Logistic Probability via the sigmoid; fitted by log loss; threshold set by error costs References: Gordon, M. E. (2023). Business analytics: Combining data, analysis and judgement to inform decisions (Chapter 8). SAGE. Google (n.d.). Machine learning crash course: Logistic regression . James, G., Witten, D., Hastie, T., & Tibshirani, R. (2021). An introduction to statistical learning (2nd ed., Chapters 3 and 4). Springer. Wooldridge, J. M. (2020). Introductory econometrics: A modern approach (7th ed., Chapters 3 and 6). Cengage. Next: Text as a feature in period 4, with the Assignment 2 briefing, and the Assignment 2 guide . Tomorrow, Lab 5 applies Parts 5–9 to a different data set. For the facilitator ¶ This notebook covers periods P1–P3 of Day 4 (Monday, theory only). The text-features lecture and the Assignment 2 briefing follow in P4. No Assignment 2 or Lab 5 answers are given: the lecture uses synthetic store data, never the house-price generator or the fuel-economy data, and the Challenge using diamonds asks a predictive question that Lab 1 did not. Period Minutes Content Notes P1 5 Setup; the data table; Part 1 prediction vs explanation Ask students for one prediction and one explanation question from their own jobs P1 15 Part 2: simple regression, the coefficient sentence Take guesses for the "per 100 sq ft" prediction; have pairs fix the colleague's sentence P1 15 Part 3: multiple regression, holding constant, the coefficient table Insist on units and the clause in every sentence P1 10 Part 4: dummies, reference category, the Downtown surprise Show of hands on the Downtown prediction before running P2 12 Part 5: train/test Link back to Day 3's time-ordered split P2 15 Part 6: the four measures, baseline, noise columns Students compute one measure by hand on paper for three residuals P2 18 Part 7: three simulated patterns, then the store model Students sketch the bottom row before running P3 8 Part 8: log model (core idea); skip the comparison cell if short of time Read the elasticity sentence aloud P3 12 Part 9: VIF and the bootstrap table Ask: "Would you let head office read the checkouts coefficient?" P3 8 Part 10: overfitting chart (cross-validation is an extension) Collect the degree predictions first P3 5 Part 11: the superstore One-sentence takeaway: report the range P3 7 Part 12: the promotion; Part 14 discussion questions 1–2 if time If short of time, set Part 14 as homework Later 20 Part 13: logistic regression (extension) Fits the Day 7 review, the online week, or faster students Self-study — Part 15: practice and quiz Core items first; Challenge 1 is good preparation for Lab 5 If P1 overruns, shorten Part 4 to the "changing the reference does not change predictions" cell. If students struggle with logs, teach only the percentage reading in Part 8 and leave the table for self-study. If the group finishes Part 12 early, start the text-features lecture's Part 1 in the last minutes of P3.

docs.text: Periods 1 to 3 of Day 4, the first day of Module 2. How a regression becomes a prediction tool a manager can trust: prediction versus explanation, simple and multiple regression, reading a coefficient in dollars with its "holding the others constant" clause, dummy variables and the reference category, training and test sets, R², adjusted R², RMSE and MAE, residual plots, log transformations, multicollinearity and the variance inflation factor, overfitting, extrapolation, confounded coefficients, and why a yes/no outcome needs logistic regression instead. Run each code cell with Shift + Enter , in order. The examples use 300 synthetic convenience stores of a fictional chain, "Corner & Co.", generated in the first cells, with each store's annual sales in thousand US dollars . docs.text: Say whether a regression is being used to predict or to explain , and why the difference changes what you check. Fit simple and multiple linear regressions and read each coefficient in business units, with its holding-constant clause. Use dummy variables for a category and say what the reference category is. Split data into training and test sets and explain why the test score is the honest one. Compute and explain R² , adjusted R² , RMSE and MAE , on training and on test data. Read a residual plot for a curve (non-linearity) and a funnel (heteroscedasticity), and fix them with a log transformation. Detect multicollinearity with the variance inflation factor (VIF) and decide whether it matters for the model's purpose. Recognise overfitting and extrapolation , and say why a regression coefficient is not a causal effect. Explain why a yes/no outcome calls for logistic regression : probabilities, the sigmoid curve and a threshold. This lecture fills three periods (P1 to P3). Each part is marked core (teach in class) or extension (faster students, a later study block, or self-study). Part Topic Path Period 1 Prediction or explanation? Core P1 2 Simple regression Core P1 3 Multiple regression and "holding constant" Core P1 4 Categories: dummy variables and the reference Core P1–P2 5 Training and test sets Core P2 6 R², adjusted R², RMSE and MAE Core P2 7 Residual plots Core P2 8 Log transformations Core (idea), extension (detail) P2–P3 9 Multicollinearity and VIF Core P3 10 Overfitting Core (demo), extension (cross-validation) P3 11 Extrapolation Core P3 12 Correlation, causation and confounded coefficients Core P3 13 Yes/no outcomes: logistic regression as a concept Extension Later 14 Business case: choosing new store sites Core (discussion), extension (detail) P3 15 Practice, quiz and summary Self-study — Reading Read Chapter 5 of the course reading packet for in-sample fit versus out-of-sample accuracy, the residual plot as a check of constant error size, the variance inflation factor and its threshold of 5, why multicollinearity matters for explaining but much less for predicting, and logistic regression as a contrast (the sigmoid and log loss). Read Gordon, Chapter 8 ("Operational Analytics") for the predictive-maintenance and fraud examples, and Google's Machine Learning Crash Course page on logistic regression as a preview. This lecture adds worked examples of every idea, dummy variables, adjusted R², log transformations, overfitting, extrapolation and confounding.
