docs.title: Setup

docs.text: A regression is one tool with two very different jobs. Decide which job you are doing before you fit anything, because the two jobs need different checks. Prediction Explanation Question "What will this store sell?" "How much does one more checkout add to sales?" What matters How close the predictions are on new cases Whether each coefficient means what it seems to mean Judged by Test-set error (RMSE, MAE), R² on test data Sensible signs and sizes, stable coefficients, no confounding, ideally an experiment Correlated predictors Usually fine A serious problem (Part 9) A missing cause Fine if its effect is picked up by other predictors Biases the coefficients (Part 12) Typical use Sales forecasts for new sites, pricing a house, fraud scores Deciding whether to invest in a lever: a promotion, more staff, a car park The reading packet describes this as the move from describing the data in hand to predicting what has not happened yet. A predictive model is held to a stricter standard: it must work on cases it has never seen. Predict, then run. Which single column do you expect to have the strongest correlation with sales ? Which the weakest? Write down your guesses. numeric = stores . drop ( columns = "region" ) print ( numeric . corr ()[ "sales" ] . drop ( "sales" ) . sort_values ( ascending = False ) . round ( 2 )) floor_area 0.68 staff 0.65 footfall 0.63 checkouts 0.61 promo 0.44 competitor_miles -0.18 parking -0.28 Name: sales, dtype: float64 Floor area, staff, checkouts, footfall and the promotion all go with higher sales; distance to a rival and parking, which are typical of rural stores, are weakly negative . Notice that promo clearly correlates with sales. Does that mean the promotion works? Keep the question in mind until Part 12. Misconception: "The variable with the biggest correlation is the most important cause." Correlation measures how closely two columns move together. It says nothing about why : several of these columns are bigger in big stores, and the promotion was given to busy stores on purpose.
docs.title: Part 1: Prediction or explanation? (core)

docs.text: A simple linear regression uses one predictor: sales = b₀ + b₁ × floor_area + error b₁, the slope: how much predicted sales change, on average, when floor area is one unit larger. b₀, the intercept: predicted sales when floor area is zero. Often it has no business meaning; it just positions the line. error (residual): actual − predicted, for each store. Least squares picks the line that makes the sum of squared residuals as small as possible. Squaring keeps positive and negative misses from cancelling, and punishes big misses more. Predict, then run. Roughly how many thousand dollars of extra annual sales would you expect for each extra 100 square feet of floor? Guess a number between 0 and 100. simple = smf . ols ( "sales ~ floor_area" , data = stores ) . fit () b0 , b1 = simple . params [ "Intercept" ], simple . params [ "floor_area" ] print ( f "sales = { b0 : ,.1f } + { b1 : .3f } x floor_area (thousand US dollars)" ) print ( f "Each extra 100 sq ft: about $ { b1 * 100 * 1000 : ,.0f } more annual sales, on average" ) print ( f "R-squared: { simple . rsquared : .2f } " ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . scatter ( stores [ "floor_area" ], stores [ "sales" ], s = 14 , alpha = 0.5 , color = BLUE ) xs = np . linspace ( stores [ "floor_area" ] . min (), stores [ "floor_area" ] . max (), 50 ) ax . plot ( xs , b0 + b1 * xs , color = ORANGE , lw = 2 , label = "Least-squares line" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Floor area (square feet)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Annual sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Bigger stores sell more, with a lot of scatter" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () sales = 428.3 + 0.440 x floor_area (thousand US dollars) Each extra 100 sq ft: about $43,967 more annual sales, on average R-squared: 0.46
docs.title: Part 2: Simple regression (core)

docs.text: Always translate a coefficient into a sentence with units and a sensible step size . "0.44" is meaningless to a manager; "about $44,000 more sales a year for every extra 100 square feet" is not. A template: "Among stores like these, a store with [one step more of x] has, on average , about [b₁ × step, with units] [more / less] [target] ." Three things the sentence deliberately says: "On average" : individual stores scatter widely around the line. "Among stores like these" : the line was fitted to stores from 1,500 to 6,500 square feet (Part 11). "Has" , not "would gain if we enlarged it": the data compares different stores; it did not watch a store being enlarged (Part 12). The intercept here would be the predicted sales of a store with zero floor area. No such store exists, so the intercept is just where the line crosses the axis. Do not interpret it. Misconception: "R² tells us how much of sales floor area causes ." R² is the share of the variation in sales that the line accounts for in this data. About half of the variation is explained by floor area alone; the rest comes from footfall, competition, region and noise. Check your understanding. A colleague writes: "Increasing floor area by 1 square foot increases sales by 0.44." Name the two things wrong with this sentence.
docs.title: Reading the coefficients in business units

docs.text: A multiple regression uses several predictors at once: sales = b₀ + b₁ × floor_area + b₂ × footfall + b₃ × competitor_miles + b₄ × parking + error Each coefficient now answers a sharper question: how much do predicted sales differ for one unit more of this predictor, when the other predictors in the model are held at the same values? That clause, "holding the others constant" (in Latin, ceteris paribus ), is what makes multiple regression useful, and what makes its coefficients easy to misread. Predict, then run. Downtown stores have far more footfall than rural ones. When we add footfall to the model, will the floor-area coefficient change a lot or a little? Why? multi = smf . ols ( "sales ~ floor_area + footfall + competitor_miles + parking" , data = stores ) . fit () table = pd . DataFrame ({ "coefficient" : multi . params , "95% CI low" : multi . conf_int ()[ 0 ], "95% CI high" : multi . conf_int ()[ 1 ], "p-value" : multi . pvalues }) print ( table . round ( 3 )) print ( f " \n R-squared: simple model { simple . rsquared : .2f } , multiple model { multi . rsquared : .2f } " ) coefficient 95% CI low 95% CI high p-value Intercept -492.094 -647.880 -336.307 0.000 floor_area 0.419 0.389 0.449 0.000 footfall 63.380 57.720 69.039 0.000 competitor_miles 21.499 5.468 37.530 0.009 parking 26.671 -44.678 98.021 0.463 R-squared: simple model 0.46, multiple model 0.84 Read each coefficient as a sentence with units and the holding-constant clause: Predictor Sentence (on average, among stores like these) floor_area 100 more square feet goes with about $42,000 more annual sales, at the same footfall, distance to a rival and parking footfall 1,000 more passers-by a week goes with about $63,000 more sales, for stores of the same size, competition and parking competitor_miles Each extra mile to the nearest rival goes with somewhat higher sales, holding the rest constant parking A car park goes with slightly higher sales, but the confidence interval is wide and includes zero The floor-area coefficient barely moved because, in this chain, store size is not related to footfall: big and small stores are found in busy and quiet streets alike. When a new predictor is unrelated to the old ones, the old coefficients stay put. When it is related, they shift; Parts 9 and 12 show both. The confidence interval is a range of plausible values for the coefficient given this sample. A p-value below 0.05 is the usual sign that a coefficient is distinguishable from zero. For prediction these matter less than test-set error; for explanation they are a minimum check, not proof. Misconception: "Holding constant means the model held them constant." Nobody held anything. The model compares stores that differ in one predictor but are similar in the others, using the data you gave it. If an important predictor is missing, it is not being held constant at all.
docs.title: Part 3: Multiple regression and "holding constant" (core)

docs.text:
region is text, not a number. A regression handles a category with dummy variables (also called indicator or one-hot variables): one 0/1 column per category, except one . The category left out is the reference (baseline). Each dummy's coefficient is the difference from the reference, holding the other predictors constant. Why leave one out? With an intercept in the model, the three dummies would always add up to 1, so one is perfectly predictable from the other two. The model cannot separate them: this is the dummy-variable trap . Predict, then run. Downtown stores have the highest average sales. Will the Downtown coefficient be positive in a model that also includes footfall and floor area? print ( "Average sales by region (thousand US dollars):" ) print ( stores . groupby ( "region" )[ "sales" ] . agg ([ "count" , "mean" ]) . round ( 0 )) print ( " 
 The dummies pandas builds (first rows), with 'Downtown' dropped as the reference:" ) print ( pd . get_dummies ( stores [ "region" ], drop_first = True , dtype = int ) . head ( 4 )) Average sales by region (thousand US dollars): count mean region Downtown 81 2467.0 Rural 70 1584.0 Suburb 149 1906.0 The dummies pandas builds (first rows), with 'Downtown' dropped as the reference: Rural Suburb 0 0 0 1 0 1 2 0 1 3 0 1 with_default = smf . ols ( "sales ~ floor_area + footfall + competitor_miles + parking + C(region)" , data = stores ) . fit () with_suburb = smf . ols ( "sales ~ floor_area + footfall + competitor_miles + parking" " + C(region, Treatment('Suburb'))" , data = stores ) . fit () print ( "Reference = Downtown (alphabetical default):" ) print ( with_default . params . filter ( like = "region" ) . round ( 1 )) print ( " 
 Reference = Suburb (the largest group):" ) print ( with_suburb . params . filter ( like = "region" ) . round ( 1 )) same = np . allclose ( with_default . fittedvalues , with_suburb . fittedvalues ) print ( " 
 Are the predictions identical?" , same ) Reference = Downtown (alphabetical default): C(region)[T.Rural] 24.1 C(region)[T.Suburb] 49.3 dtype: float64 Reference = Suburb (the largest group): C(region, Treatment('Suburb'))[T.Downtown] -49.3 C(region, Treatment('Suburb'))[T.Rural] -25.2 dtype: float64 Are the predictions identical? True Three lessons: Changing the reference changes the coefficients but not the predictions. The model is the same; only the comparison point changes. Always say what the reference is: "Rural stores sell about $X thousand less than suburban stores of the same size and footfall." Choose a reference that makes sense to the reader , usually the largest or the "normal" group. Statsmodels and pandas pick the first in alphabetical order unless you say otherwise. A raw average and a coefficient answer different questions. Downtown stores sell the most on average because they have far more footfall. At the same footfall and size , the dollar model even puts Downtown slightly below a suburb. The log model in Part 8, which fits these data better, gives Downtown a small premium; the data's true recipe (setup cell) gives it 5%. Either way, most of Downtown's raw lead is footfall, not the region itself. Check your understanding. A model has day as a category with seven values. How many dummy columns does it need? If "Monday" is the reference, what does the "Saturday" coefficient mean?
docs.title: Part 4: Categories: dummy variables and the reference (core)

docs.text: A model fitted to all 300 stores will always fit those 300 stores reasonably well: least squares made it so. That in-sample fit says little about the question a predictive model must answer: how well will it do on a store it has never seen? So we hide some data: Split the rows at random into a training set (commonly 70–80%) and a test set (the rest). Fit the model on the training set only. Predict the test set and measure the errors. The test set plays the role of "new stores". The test score is the honest one. It is almost always a little worse than the training score; a big gap is a warning sign of overfitting (Part 10). Random splitting suits cross-sectional data like these stores, one row per case. On Day 3 you saw that a time series must be split in time order instead, because a random split lets the future leak into training. Predict, then run. Will the model's R² on the test stores be higher or lower than on the training stores? By a lot or a little? features = [ "floor_area" , "footfall" , "competitor_miles" , "parking" ] train , test = train_test_split ( stores , test_size = 0.2 , random_state = 1 ) print ( f "Training stores: { len ( train ) } , test stores: { len ( test ) } " ) lin = LinearRegression () . fit ( train [ features ], train [ "sales" ]) pred_train = lin . predict ( train [ features ]) pred_test = lin . predict ( test [ features ]) print ( f "R-squared on training data: { r2_score ( train [ 'sales' ], pred_train ) : .3f } " ) print ( f "R-squared on test data: { r2_score ( test [ 'sales' ], pred_test ) : .3f } " ) print ( " \n Coefficients (fitted on training data only):" ) print ( pd . Series ( lin . coef_ , index = features ) . round ( 3 )) Training stores: 240, test stores: 60 R-squared on training data: 0.843 R-squared on test data: 0.798 Coefficients (fitted on training data only): floor_area 0.425 footfall 63.079 competitor_miles 15.189 parking 53.081 dtype: float64 Here the gap is small: four sensible predictors and 240 training stores leave little room for memorising noise. On a different random split the numbers move a little; that is normal, and it is one reason Part 10 introduces cross-validation . Rules for using a test set well: Split first , before exploring or choosing features, so that nothing about the test rows shapes the model. Fix random_state so that you and your reader get the same split. Use the test set once , at the end. If you try twenty models and keep the one with the best test score, the test set has quietly become part of training. After choosing the model, it is fine to refit on all the data for the final predictions. Misconception: "The test score is the model's accuracy, so it will be exactly this good in future." It is an estimate from one sample of stores. New stores may differ from old ones (new regions, a new competitor), and then the error will be larger.
docs.title: Part 5: Training and test sets (core)

docs.text: For each store, residual = actual − predicted . Four summaries of the residuals: Measure Formula Units How to say it R² 1 − (sum of squared residuals) ÷ (sum of squared deviations from the mean) None (≤ 1) "The model accounts for about 84% of the variation in sales between stores" Adjusted R² 1 − (1 − R²) × (n − 1) ÷ (n − k − 1), with k predictors None Like R², but with a penalty for each predictor: it rises only if a new predictor improves the fit by more than chance would RMSE √(mean of squared residuals) Same as the target "Predictions are typically off by about $X thousand; big misses weigh more" MAE mean of |residuals| Same as the target "On average, predictions miss by about $X thousand" Points that trip people up: R² is not "accuracy" or "percent correct". An R² of 0.84 does not mean 84% of predictions are right. It compares the model's squared errors with those of the simplest possible prediction: the mean. R² on test data can be negative : that happens when the model does worse than just predicting the training mean. RMSE ≥ MAE always. The bigger the gap, the more the errors include a few large misses. Judge RMSE and MAE against the scale : a $150 thousand error is small for a $4 million store and huge for a $1 million one. Predict, then run. Compute each measure by hand from the residuals, then check it against scikit-learn. Before running, guess: is the test RMSE closer to $50 thousand, $250 thousand or $500 thousand? resid = test [ "sales" ] . values - pred_test sse = np . sum ( resid ** 2 ) sst = np . sum (( test [ "sales" ] . values - test [ "sales" ] . mean ()) ** 2 ) r2_hand = 1 - sse / sst rmse_hand = np . sqrt ( np . mean ( resid ** 2 )) mae_hand = np . mean ( np . abs ( resid )) n_test , k = len ( test ), len ( features ) adj_r2 = 1 - ( 1 - r2_hand ) * ( n_test - 1 ) / ( n_test - k - 1 ) print ( f "R-squared by hand { r2_hand : .3f } sklearn { r2_score ( test [ 'sales' ], pred_test ) : .3f } " ) print ( f "Adjusted R-squared { adj_r2 : .3f } " ) print ( f "RMSE by hand { rmse_hand : 6.1f } sklearn { np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test [ 'sales' ], pred_test )) : 6.1f } thousand US dollars" ) print ( f "MAE by hand { mae_hand : 6.1f } sklearn { mean_absolute_error ( test [ 'sales' ], pred_test ) : 6.1f } thousand US dollars" ) baseline = np . full ( n_test , train [ "sales" ] . mean ()) # predict the training average for every store print ( f " \n Baseline (always predict the training mean): RMSE { np . sqrt ( np . mean (( test [ 'sales' ] - baseline ) ** 2 )) : 6.1f } " ) print ( f "Typical test store sells about { test [ 'sales' ] . median () : ,.0f } thousand US dollars a year" ) R-squared by hand 0.798 sklearn 0.798 Adjusted R-squared 0.783 RMSE by hand 262.4 sklearn 262.4 thousand US dollars MAE by hand 203.0 sklearn 203.0 thousand US dollars Baseline (always predict the training mean): RMSE 593.0 Typical test store sells about 1,962 thousand US dollars a year The baseline matters: an RMSE means little until you compare it with what you would do without a model . Here the model cuts the typical error by well over half compared with "every store sells the average".
docs.title: Part 6: R², adjusted R², RMSE and MAE (core)

docs.text: Plain R² on the training data never falls when you add a predictor, even one made of pure noise: least squares can always use it a little. Adjusted R² charges a penalty for each extra predictor. Predict, then run. We add 30 columns of random numbers, which have nothing to do with sales, to the training data. What happens to training R², adjusted R², and test RMSE? noise_rng = np . random . default_rng ( 5 ) noise_cols = [ f "noise_ { j } " for j in range ( 30 )] train_noisy = train . copy () test_noisy = test . copy () for col in noise_cols : train_noisy [ col ] = noise_rng . normal ( size = len ( train )) test_noisy [ col ] = noise_rng . normal ( size = len ( test )) rows = [] for label , cols in [( "4 real predictors" , features ), ( "4 real + 30 noise" , features + noise_cols )]: m = smf . ols ( "sales ~ " + " + " . join ( cols ), data = train_noisy ) . fit () p = m . predict ( test_noisy ) rows . append ({ "model" : label , "train R2" : m . rsquared , "train adj R2" : m . rsquared_adj , "test RMSE" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test_noisy [ "sales" ], p ))}) print ( pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . round ( 3 ) . to_string ( index = False )) model train R2 train adj R2 test RMSE 4 real predictors 0.843 0.841 262.377 4 real + 30 noise 0.867 0.845 293.676 Training R² went up noticeably, as it always does. Adjusted R² barely moved: its penalty roughly cancels the gain that pure noise gives, so it does not reward the junk (with useless predictors it is as likely to fall as to rise slightly). The test RMSE got worse : the noise columns fitted quirks of the training stores that do not repeat. This is overfitting in miniature (Part 10). Check your understanding. Model A has training R² 0.90 and test R² 0.60. Model B has training R² 0.82 and test R² 0.80. Which would you deploy for predicting new stores, and why?
docs.title: Why adjusted R² exists

docs.text: R² and RMSE are averages; they can hide where a model goes wrong. A residual plot (residuals on the vertical axis, predicted values on the horizontal) shows it. What you want is a shapeless band centred on zero , the same width all the way across. Two patterns to recognise: Pattern Name What it means Typical fix A curve (a smile or a frown) Non-linearity A straight line is the wrong shape for the relationship Transform a variable (Part 8), add a squared term, or use a different model A funnel (spread grows or shrinks) Heteroscedasticity (non-constant variance) Errors are bigger for some cases than others; the RMSE overstates accuracy for some and understates it for others Log the target (Part 8); report errors in percent; use robust standard errors The reading packet stresses that two models can share the same R² while one has evenly spread errors and the other has errors that grow for the largest cases. Only the residual plot shows the difference. Predict, then run. Three simulated data sets follow. Before you look at the bottom row, sketch what each residual plot will look like. sim = np . random . default_rng ( 11 ) x = np . sort ( sim . uniform ( 1 , 10 , 200 )) cases = { "Good: straight line, constant noise" : 3 + 2 * x + sim . normal ( 0 , 2 , 200 ), "Curve: true relationship bends" : 1 + 0.4 * x ** 2 + sim . normal ( 0 , 2 , 200 ), "Funnel: noise grows with size" : 3 + 2 * x + sim . normal ( 0 , 0.4 * x , 200 ), } fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 2 , 3 , figsize = ( 12 , 6 )) for col , ( title , y ) in enumerate ( cases . items ()): slope , intercept = np . polyfit ( x , y , 1 ) fitted = intercept + slope * x axes [ 0 , col ] . scatter ( x , y , s = 8 , color = BLUE , alpha = 0.6 ) axes [ 0 , col ] . plot ( x , fitted , color = ORANGE ) axes [ 0 , col ] . set_title ( title , fontsize = 10 ) axes [ 1 , col ] . scatter ( fitted , y - fitted , s = 8 , color = GREY ) axes [ 1 , col ] . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.8 ) axes [ 1 , col ] . set_xlabel ( "Predicted value" ) axes [ 0 , 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "y" ) axes [ 1 , 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Residual" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () Now the store model. We draw the residual plot for the training stores (more points make the pattern easier to see), with a smooth trend line through the residuals to help the eye. def residual_plot ( fitted , residuals , title , ax = None , ylabel = "Residual (thousand US dollars)" ): """Residuals against predicted values, with a binned average to show any curve.""" ax = ax or plt . gca () ax . scatter ( fitted , residuals , s = 12 , alpha = 0.5 , color = BLUE ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.8 ) bins = pd . qcut ( fitted , 10 ) trend = pd . DataFrame ({ "f" : fitted , "r" : residuals }) . groupby ( bins , observed = True ) . mean () ax . plot ( trend [ "f" ], trend [ "r" ], color = ORANGE , lw = 2 , marker = "o" , label = "Average residual (10 bins)" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Predicted value" ) ax . set_ylabel ( ylabel ) ax . set_title ( title ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) level_model = smf . ols ( "sales ~ floor_area + footfall + competitor_miles + parking" , data = train ) . fit () fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) residual_plot ( level_model . fittedvalues . values , level_model . resid . values , "Store model in dollars: residuals fan out and bend" , ax = ax ) plt . show () Two problems are visible: A funnel. The residuals spread out as predicted sales grow: the model misses big stores by far more dollars than small ones. That is heteroscedasticity, and it makes a single RMSE misleading: it is too pessimistic for small stores and too optimistic for big ones. A slight curve. The average residual is positive at both ends and negative in the middle: the effects multiply rather than add, so a straight line in dollars is the wrong shape. Neither problem stops the model from predicting reasonably on average, but both say we can do better, and that any statement like "accurate to within $X" needs care. Two more checks are worth knowing (extension): Residuals against each predictor : a curve against one predictor says that predictor needs transforming. Influential points : one extreme store can tilt a line. Look at the largest residuals and ask whether they are errors in the data, or real but unusual cases. Misconception: "The residuals should be normally distributed, so the data must be normal." The assumptions are about the errors , not the raw columns. Skewed predictors are fine. And for prediction, a funnel or a curve matters more than exact normality.
docs.title: Part 7: Residual plots (core)

docs.text: Money, sizes and counts often behave multiplicatively : a 10% bigger store sells roughly 7% more, whether it is a small store or a big one. In dollars that is a curve with errors that grow with size, exactly the two patterns in Part 7. Taking the natural log turns multiplying into adding, which a linear regression can model. How to read the coefficients after logging: Model Coefficient b on x means… log(y) = … + b × x One more unit of x goes with about 100 × b % more y (exact: (e^b − 1) × 100%) log(y) = … + b × log(x) 1% more x goes with about b % more y (an elasticity ) y = … + b × log(x) 1% more x goes with about b ÷ 100 more units of y Logs need positive values. For a column that can be zero, use np.log1p (log of 1 + x) or reconsider. Predict, then run. After logging sales and floor area, will the residual plot still fan out? log_formula = ( "np.log(sales) ~ np.log(floor_area) + footfall + np.log(competitor_miles) + parking" " + C(region, Treatment('Suburb'))" ) log_model = smf . ols ( log_formula , data = train ) . fit () print ( log_model . params . round ( 3 )) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4.5 )) residual_plot ( log_model . fittedvalues . values , log_model . resid . values , "Log model: an even band around zero" , ax = ax , ylabel = "Residual (log sales)" ) plt . show () Intercept 0.870 C(region, Treatment('Suburb'))[T.Downtown] 0.032 C(region, Treatment('Suburb'))[T.Rural] -0.113 np.log(floor_area) 0.762 footfall 0.032 np.log(competitor_miles) 0.071 parking 0.037 dtype: float64 The band is now even and flat. Reading two coefficients: np.log(floor_area) ≈ 0.76: a store with 1% more floor area sells about 0.76% more , holding the rest constant. A 10% bigger store sells roughly 7.5% more, not 10% more. footfall ≈ 0.03: each extra thousand passers-by a week goes with about 3% more sales. These are close to the true values in the setup cell (0.75 and 0.030), which we only know because the data is synthetic.
docs.title: Part 8: Log transformations (core idea, extension detail)

docs.text: To compare with the dollar model, convert predictions back to dollars with np.exp and compute the errors in dollars on the same test stores . (Strictly, exp of a predicted log gives something closer to the median than the mean; with small residuals like these the difference is about 1%, so we ignore it.) level_pred = level_model . predict ( test ) log_pred = np . exp ( log_model . predict ( test )) for label , p in [( "Dollar model (4 predictors)" , level_pred ), ( "Log model (with region)" , log_pred )]: print ( f " { label : 28s } test RMSE { np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test [ 'sales' ], p )) : 6.1f } " f "MAE { mean_absolute_error ( test [ 'sales' ], p ) : 6.1f } R2 { r2_score ( test [ 'sales' ], p ) : .3f } " ) pct_err = np . abs ( test [ "sales" ] - log_pred ) / test [ "sales" ] * 100 print ( f " \n Log model: median absolute error is { pct_err . median () : .1f } % of a store's sales" ) Dollar model (4 predictors) test RMSE 262.4 MAE 203.0 R2 0.798 Log model (with region) test RMSE 235.0 MAE 189.5 R2 0.838 Log model: median absolute error is 8.5% of a store's sales The log model predicts the test stores better, and it gives a more honest way to describe accuracy: in percent . "Half of the predictions are within about 8 or 9% of actual sales" is true for small and large stores alike, whereas a single dollar RMSE is not. Misconception: "Transforming the data is cheating." Choosing the right shape for a relationship is part of modelling. What would be cheating is choosing it by repeatedly checking the test set; choose it from the training residuals, as here, then test once.
docs.title: Comparing the two models fairly (extension)

docs.text: Multicollinearity means two or more predictors are strongly correlated with each other . It is normal in business data: bigger stores have more floor area, more checkouts and more staff, for structural reasons. The problem is for explanation . If floor area, checkouts and staff always rise together, the data has almost no stores where one is high and the others are low, so the model cannot tell which one deserves the credit. The coefficients become unstable : small changes in the data swing them, sometimes flipping their signs, while the predictions barely change. The variance inflation factor for predictor j is VIF_j = 1 ÷ (1 − R²_j) , where R²_j comes from regressing predictor j on all the other predictors . A VIF of 1 means no overlap. A VIF of 5 means 80% of that predictor's variation is already explained by the others, and its coefficient's variance is five times what it would be without the overlap. The usual flag is VIF > 5 (some use 10). Predict, then run. We add checkouts and staff to the dollar model. Which predictors will have a VIF above 5? size_cols = [ "floor_area" , "checkouts" , "staff" , "footfall" , "competitor_miles" , "parking" ] print ( "Correlations among the size measures:" ) print ( train [[ "floor_area" , "checkouts" , "staff" ]] . corr () . round ( 2 )) def vif_table ( data , cols ): """VIF by the definition: regress each predictor on all the others.""" out = {} for c in cols : others = [ o for o in cols if o != c ] r2_j = smf . ols ( f " { c } ~ " + " + " . join ( others ), data = data ) . fit () . rsquared out [ c ] = 1 / ( 1 - r2_j ) return pd . Series ( out , name = "VIF" ) . round ( 1 ) print ( " \n VIF with all six predictors:" ) print ( vif_table ( train , size_cols )) Correlations among the size measures: floor_area checkouts staff floor_area 1.00 0.94 0.97 checkouts 0.94 1.00 0.91 staff 0.97 0.91 1.00 VIF with all six predictors: floor_area 23.9 checkouts 8.4 staff 16.3 footfall 1.6 competitor_miles 1.4 parking 1.3 Name: VIF, dtype: float64 Floor area, checkouts and staff all have VIFs well above 5: each is largely predictable from the other two. Footfall, distance and parking are near 1. statsmodels has a ready-made function, variance_inflation_factor in statsmodels.stats.outliers_influence . It needs a constant column in the design matrix and gives the same numbers as the definition above; computing VIF by hand once makes clear what it measures.
docs.title: Part 9: Multicollinearity and VIF (core)

docs.text: Predict, then run. We refit the six-predictor model on five bootstrap samples (training stores drawn at random with replacement). Will the floor-area, checkouts and staff coefficients stay similar? Will the test RMSE? boot = np . random . default_rng ( 3 ) rows = [] for b in range ( 5 ): sample = train . iloc [ boot . integers ( 0 , len ( train ), len ( train ))] m = smf . ols ( "sales ~ " + " + " . join ( size_cols ), data = sample ) . fit () rows . append ({ "sample" : b + 1 , "floor_area (per 100 sq ft)" : m . params [ "floor_area" ] * 100 , "checkouts (per counter)" : m . params [ "checkouts" ], "staff (per FTE)" : m . params [ "staff" ], "test RMSE" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test [ "sales" ], m . predict ( test )))}) print ( pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . round ( 1 ) . to_string ( index = False )) sample floor_area (per 100 sq ft) checkouts (per counter) staff (per FTE) test RMSE 1 34.1 -9.1 23.2 257.7 2 49.4 -33.7 -6.0 260.9 3 49.9 -8.9 -21.6 257.2 4 52.4 -39.8 -5.8 268.6 5 49.9 -50.5 4.5 262.9 The three size coefficients jump around from sample to sample, and some change sign, while the test RMSE hardly moves. That is the reading packet's point in action: For prediction , multicollinearity is usually tolerable: the model still combines the size measures into a good overall prediction, as long as new stores have the same pattern (bigger stores with more staff). If a new store breaks the pattern (huge floor, two checkouts), predictions become unreliable. For explanation , a high VIF disqualifies that coefficient. "Each extra checkout adds $X thousand" cannot be read from this model. What to do about it, depending on the purpose: Option When Leave it The purpose is prediction and new cases follow the old pattern Drop one of the overlapping predictors You need interpretable coefficients and one measure carries the idea (floor area) Combine them into one index (e.g. "store size") The measures are different views of one underlying property Collect data that breaks the pattern, or run an experiment You genuinely need the separate effect (e.g. of adding a checkout) Regularisation (ridge regression) Many correlated predictors; mentioned again in the text-features lecture Misconception: "A high VIF means the model is wrong and must be fixed." It means individual coefficients are unreliable. Whether that matters depends on what the model is for, which is why Part 1 asked the question first.
docs.title: What multicollinearity does, and does not, do

docs.text: A model overfits when it learns the noise in the training data as if it were pattern. It fits the training data very well and new data badly. Flexible models (many predictors, high-degree curves) on small samples overfit most. Predict, then run. Using only 25 training stores , we fit polynomials of floor area of degree 1 (a line) up to 9 (a very wiggly curve), and test each on 100 other stores. Which degree will have the lowest training error? The lowest test error? small = stores . sample ( 125 , random_state = 4 ) small_train , small_test = small . iloc [: 25 ], small . iloc [ 25 :] centre , scale = small_train [ "floor_area" ] . mean (), small_train [ "floor_area" ] . std () z_train = ( small_train [ "floor_area" ] - centre ) / scale # standardise so high powers stay manageable z_test = ( small_test [ "floor_area" ] - centre ) / scale rows = [] for degree in range ( 1 , 10 ): coefs = np . polyfit ( z_train , small_train [ "sales" ], degree ) rows . append ({ "degree" : degree , "train RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean (( small_train [ "sales" ] - np . polyval ( coefs , z_train )) ** 2 )), "test RMSE" : np . sqrt ( np . mean (( small_test [ "sales" ] - np . polyval ( coefs , z_test )) ** 2 ))}) curve = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 12 , 4.2 )) axes [ 0 ] . plot ( curve [ "degree" ], curve [ "train RMSE" ], marker = "o" , color = BLUE , label = "Training (25 stores)" ) axes [ 0 ] . plot ( curve [ "degree" ], curve [ "test RMSE" ], marker = "o" , color = ORANGE , label = "Test (100 stores)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "Polynomial degree (model flexibility)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "RMSE (thousand US dollars, log scale)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Training error keeps falling; test error does not" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_yscale ( "log" ) axes [ 0 ] . legend ( frameon = False ) grid = np . linspace ( z_train . min (), z_train . max (), 200 ) axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( small_train [ "floor_area" ], small_train [ "sales" ], color = BLUE , s = 20 , label = "Training stores" ) for degree , colour in [( 1 , GREEN ), ( 9 , ORANGE )]: coefs = np . polyfit ( z_train , small_train [ "sales" ], degree ) axes [ 1 ] . plot ( grid * scale + centre , np . polyval ( coefs , grid ), color = colour , label = f "Degree { degree } " ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylim ( stores [ "sales" ] . min () * 0.5 , stores [ "sales" ] . max () * 1.1 ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Floor area (square feet)" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylabel ( "Sales (thousand US dollars)" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "A degree-9 curve chases individual stores" ) axes [ 1 ] . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () print ( curve . round ( 1 ) . to_string ( index = False )) degree train RMSE test RMSE 1 493.0 518.9 2 436.3 710.0 3 408.0 754.4 4 407.9 673.5 5 369.4 12479.7 6 366.1 1624.5 7 366.0 5694.2 8 343.6 365411.0 9 342.7 19663.0 Training error falls with every extra degree: more flexibility always fits the sample better. Test error is lowest for the straight line and then rises, explosively for the wiggliest curves (the left chart needs a log scale to show them at all). The degree-9 curve passes close to the training stores and swings wildly between and beyond them. Defences against overfitting: Judge on test data , never on training fit alone. Prefer simpler models unless a more complex one clearly wins on test data. More data : the same degree-9 curve overfits far less with 2,000 stores than with 25. Regularisation (ridge, lasso) shrinks coefficients towards zero; the reading packet's logistic regression reading mentions it as a defence. Cross-validation (below) when choosing between models.
docs.title: Part 10: Overfitting (core demo, extension cross-validation)

docs.text: One random split gives one noisy estimate. k-fold cross-validation splits the training data into k parts, fits on k − 1 of them and tests on the remaining part, k times, then averages. Use it to choose a model; keep the real test set for the final check. folds = KFold ( n_splits = 5 , shuffle = True , random_state = 0 ) X_log = pd . DataFrame ({ "log_area" : np . log ( train [ "floor_area" ]), "footfall" : train [ "footfall" ], "log_comp" : np . log ( train [ "competitor_miles" ]), "parking" : train [ "parking" ]}) for label , X in [( "Floor area only" , X_log [[ "log_area" ]]), ( "Four predictors" , X_log )]: scores = cross_val_score ( LinearRegression (), X , np . log ( train [ "sales" ]), cv = folds , scoring = "r2" ) print ( f " { label : 16s } R2 in each fold: { np . round ( scores , 2 ) } mean { scores . mean () : .2f } " ) Floor area only R2 in each fold: [0.54 0.43 0.41 0.6 0.45] mean 0.48 Four predictors R2 in each fold: [0.92 0.86 0.86 0.88 0.82] mean 0.87
docs.title: Cross-validation (extension)

docs.text: A regression learns the relationship within the range of the data . Using it far outside that range, extrapolation , assumes the relationship carries on unchanged, which the data cannot confirm. Corner & Co. is considering a 15,000 square foot "superstore". The largest store in the data is 6,500 square feet. Predict, then run. Will the dollar model and the log model give similar predictions for the superstore? (They agreed closely on the test stores.) superstore = pd . DataFrame ({ "floor_area" : [ 15000 ], "footfall" : [ 14.0 ], "competitor_miles" : [ 1.0 ], "parking" : [ 1 ], "region" : [ "Suburb" ]}) dollar_pred = level_model . predict ( superstore ) . iloc [ 0 ] log_point = np . exp ( log_model . predict ( superstore ) . iloc [ 0 ]) print ( f "Training range of floor area: { train [ 'floor_area' ] . min () : ,.0f } to { train [ 'floor_area' ] . max () : ,.0f } sq ft" ) print ( f "Dollar model prediction: { dollar_pred : ,.0f } thousand US dollars" ) print ( f "Log model prediction: { log_point : ,.0f } thousand US dollars" ) xs = np . linspace ( 1500 , 15000 , 100 ) grid = pd . DataFrame ({ "floor_area" : xs , "footfall" : 14.0 , "competitor_miles" : 1.0 , "parking" : 1 , "region" : "Suburb" }) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . axvspan ( train [ "floor_area" ] . min (), train [ "floor_area" ] . max (), color = SKY , alpha = 0.2 , label = "Range of the data" ) ax . plot ( xs , level_model . predict ( grid ), color = BLUE , label = "Dollar model" ) ax . plot ( xs , np . exp ( log_model . predict ( grid )), color = ORANGE , label = "Log model" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Floor area (square feet)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Predicted sales (thousand US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Two models that agree inside the data disagree outside it" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () Training range of floor area: 1,500 to 6,500 sq ft Dollar model prediction: 6,811 thousand US dollars Log model prediction: 5,897 thousand US dollars Inside the shaded range the two models agree closely; at 15,000 square feet they differ by about $900 thousand a year, and the data cannot say which is right . Neither may be: a superstore draws customers from further away, needs more parking and competes with supermarkets, none of which appears in data on small stores. Rules: Check the range of every predictor before predicting. Report it with the prediction. Combinations count too. A store inside the range of each predictor separately can still be unusual: a huge floor area with two checkouts (Part 9). Prediction intervals widen away from the centre of the data; the business case below shows them. Time is a predictor too. A model fitted on last year's prices extrapolates when used after a market shift. Misconception: "The model gave a number, so it can predict anything." The model will always give a number. Whether the number means anything depends on whether the new case resembles the data.
docs.title: Part 11: Extrapolation (core)

docs.text: Head office wants to know whether to roll out the loyalty-app promotion to every store. Last year it ran in about half of them. Predict, then run. Stores with the promotion sold more. Will the promotion's coefficient shrink, grow or stay the same when we add footfall and the other predictors? naive = smf . ols ( "sales ~ promo" , data = stores ) . fit () adjusted = smf . ols ( "np.log(sales) ~ promo + np.log(floor_area) + footfall + np.log(competitor_miles)" " + parking + C(region, Treatment('Suburb'))" , data = stores ) . fit () print ( "Promotion stores vs others (raw difference in average sales):" ) print ( f " { naive . params [ 'promo' ] : ,.0f } thousand US dollars a year" ) print ( " \n After holding size, footfall, competition, parking and region constant:" ) lo , hi = adjusted . conf_int () . loc [ "promo" ] print ( f " about { 100 * adjusted . params [ 'promo' ] : .1f } % (95% CI { 100 * lo : .1f } % to { 100 * hi : .1f } %)" ) print ( " \n Average footfall (thousand a week):" ) print ( stores . groupby ( "promo" )[ "footfall" ] . mean () . round ( 1 ) . rename ({ 0 : "no promotion" , 1 : "promotion" })) Promotion stores vs others (raw difference in average sales): 582 thousand US dollars a year After holding size, footfall, competition, parking and region constant: about 2.1% (95% CI -1.2% to 5.5%) Average footfall (thousand a week): promo no promotion 10.7 promotion 19.2 Name: footfall, dtype: float64 The raw difference is large, but almost all of it is footfall : head office gave the promotion to busy stores, and busy stores sell more anyway. Once footfall and the rest are held constant, the promotion's estimated effect is a few percent with a wide interval. (The synthetic truth is 2%.) Footfall here is a confounder : it affects both who got the promotion and sales. Leaving it out does not just add noise; it pushes the promotion's coefficient in one direction. This is omitted-variable bias , and it is the biggest single reason a regression coefficient is not a causal effect. Why even the adjusted coefficient is not proof: There may be confounders we did not measure (a keener manager, a better location within the street). Adding the wrong variables can also bias a coefficient, for example a variable that is itself caused by the promotion (such as app downloads). The data are observational : head office chose, the stores did not get the promotion at random. The reliable way to measure the promotion's effect is an experiment : pick stores at random to get it, then compare. Random assignment breaks every link between the promotion and footfall, measured or not. When an experiment is impossible, be explicit: "Stores with X sell more, after allowing for A, B and C; we cannot rule out other differences." Weak Better "The promotion increases sales by $580 thousand." "Promotion stores sold about $580 thousand more, but they were the busiest stores. Comparing stores of similar footfall and size, the difference is a few percent and uncertain. A randomised trial in 40 stores would settle it." Check your understanding. A regression of hospital deaths on "number of doctors on duty" has a positive coefficient. Give a confounder that explains this, and say what a manager should not conclude.
docs.title: Part 12: Correlation, causation and confounded coefficients (core)

docs.text: Some predictions are about a category , not a number: will a customer churn, will a machine fail this month, is a transaction fraudulent, will a new store reach its sales target? Gordon's Chapter 8 examples (predictive maintenance, fraud detection) are of this kind. You could code the outcome as 1 (yes) and 0 (no) and fit a straight line. That is called a linear probability model , and it has two problems: It can predict below 0 or above 1 , which is not a probability. It assumes each unit of x changes the probability by the same amount everywhere, whereas in reality a store already certain to hit its target cannot become "more certain". Logistic regression fixes this. It computes the same kind of linear combination, z = b₀ + b₁x₁ + …, and passes it through the sigmoid function p = 1 ÷ (1 + e^(−z)) , which squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. A large positive z gives a probability near 1, a large negative z near 0, and z = 0 gives 0.5. A threshold (often 0.5, but it should depend on the costs of each kind of error) turns the probability into a yes/no decision. It is fitted not by least squares but by minimising log loss (cross-entropy), which punishes confident wrong predictions very heavily. This course does not require you to fit logistic models; the demo below is to make the idea concrete. Predict, then run. Target: "sales of at least $2 million". Using footfall alone, will a straight line predict probabilities below 0 for the quietest stores? stores [ "hit_target" ] = ( stores [ "sales" ] >= 2000 ) . astype ( int ) print ( f "Share of stores at or above $2 million: { stores [ 'hit_target' ] . mean () : .0% } " ) X_f = stores [[ "footfall" ]] lpm = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_f , stores [ "hit_target" ]) logit = LogisticRegression () . fit ( X_f , stores [ "hit_target" ]) grid = pd . DataFrame ({ "footfall" : np . linspace ( 0 , 40 , 200 )}) fig , ax = plt . subplots () jitter = np . random . default_rng ( 8 ) . uniform ( - 0.03 , 0.03 , len ( stores )) ax . scatter ( stores [ "footfall" ], stores [ "hit_target" ] + jitter , s = 10 , alpha = 0.4 , color = GREY , label = "Stores (0 = no, 1 = yes)" ) ax . plot ( grid [ "footfall" ], lpm . predict ( grid ), color = BLUE , label = "Straight line (linear probability model)" ) ax . plot ( grid [ "footfall" ], logit . predict_proba ( grid )[:, 1 ], color = ORANGE , lw = 2 , label = "Logistic regression (sigmoid)" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.6 ) ax . axhline ( 1 , color = "black" , lw = 0.6 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Footfall (thousand passers-by a week)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Probability of reaching $2 million" ) ax . set_title ( "A straight line leaves the 0 to 1 range; the sigmoid cannot" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , fontsize = 9 , loc = "lower right" ) plt . show () print ( f "Straight line at footfall 2: { lpm . predict ( pd . DataFrame ({ 'footfall' : [ 2 ]}))[ 0 ] : .2f } " ) print ( f "Straight line at footfall 38: { lpm . predict ( pd . DataFrame ({ 'footfall' : [ 38 ]}))[ 0 ] : .2f } " ) Share of stores at or above $2 million: 44% Straight line at footfall 2: -0.08 Straight line at footfall 38: 1.37 The straight line gives impossible "probabilities" at both ends; the S-shaped sigmoid stays between 0 and 1 and is steepest in the middle, where a store's fate is most uncertain. Log loss for one store is −log(p) if the store did hit the target, and −log(1 − p) if it did not: Model's probability for a store that did hit the target Log loss Squared error (1 − p)² 0.9 (confident, right) 0.11 0.01 0.5 (unsure) 0.69 0.25 0.1 (confident, wrong) 2.30 0.81 0.01 (very confident, wrong) 4.61 0.98 Squared error can never exceed 1, but log loss grows without limit as a wrong prediction becomes more confident. That is why logistic regression produces cautious probabilities. Choosing a threshold is a business decision. For predictive maintenance, missing a failure (a false negative) may cost a production line; an unneeded inspection (a false positive) costs an hour of an engineer's time. A low threshold, flagging any machine above, say, 0.2, can be right. For fraud, blocking an honest customer's card has a cost too. Gordon's point is that the costs of false alarms and missed events should shape the model and its validation. Check your understanding. Why is a logistic coefficient not "the change in probability per unit of x"? (Hint: look at how steep the orange curve is at footfall 5 and at footfall 20.)
docs.title: Part 13: Yes/no outcomes: logistic regression as a concept (extension)

docs.text: Corner & Co. has four candidate sites and budget for two. The property team has measured each one. You are asked for a prediction of annual sales, with honest uncertainty, and a recommendation. We refit the log model on all 300 stores (the model was chosen on training data and checked once on test data, Part 5's rule 4) and ask statsmodels for a 95% prediction interval : a range that should contain the actual sales of about 95 in 100 stores like this one. It is much wider than the confidence interval of the average, because it includes each store's own noise. final = smf . ols ( log_formula , data = stores ) . fit () sites = pd . Day 4 lecture: Text as a feature ¶ Period 4 of Day 4, with the Assignment 2 briefing. How free text becomes columns that a regression can use: sentiment scores, keyword flags, length, bag of words and TF-IDF; how to test whether a text feature really improves predictions; and the three traps of feature engineering with text: leakage, features that quietly stand in for something else, and a lexicon that does not speak the domain's language. Run each code cell with Shift + Enter , in order. The examples use 600 synthetic listings from a fictional second-hand bicycle marketplace, "CycleSwap", generated in the first cells: each listing has a guide price, whether a shop or a private person is selling, the seller's description, and the price the bike sold for, in US dollars . Assignment 2 uses different data (house prices); this lecture deliberately does not use its data or generator. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder; NLTK reads the VADER lexicon from data/nltk_data , so nothing is downloaded. Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook, run %pip install nltk scikit-learn in a first cell, and replace the setup cell with the NLTK download approach in the Lab 3 guide , Route A. What you will be able to do ¶ Name five ways to turn text into numeric features and say what each one captures. Test whether a text feature improves a regression on test data , against a baseline without it. Explain why a general-purpose sentiment lexicon can miss what matters in a specialised domain. Recognise leakage : a feature that would not exist at the moment of prediction. Recognise a proxy : a text feature whose coefficient really measures something else. Plan Assignment 2: what each part of the analysis is for, and what the report must explain. This lecture has one period (P4), shared with the Assignment 2 briefing, so it has a core path and extensions . Part Topic Path 1 Five ways to turn text into features Core 2 A baseline without text Core 3 A sentiment score as a feature, and lexicon mismatch Core 4 Keyword flags Core 5 Length, and features that stand in for something else Core 6 Bag of words and TF-IDF Extension 7 Leakage Core 8 A checklist for text features Core (summary) 9 Business case: screening job applications Extension 10 Assignment 2 briefing Core 11 Practice, quiz and summary Self-study Reading Read Chapter 5 of the course reading packet for training and test data, error measures, multicollinearity and the question of how a dataset's own construction can make a model look more accurate than it is (its last review question). Chapter 3's account of lexicon-based scoring explains why a domain complaint can come out neutral. This lecture applies both to text used as a predictor. Setup ¶ The first cell points NLTK at the course's offline word lists. Run it once at the start of every session. The second loads the other libraries, and the third builds the listings. import zipfile from pathlib import Path import nltk NLTK_DIR = Path ( "data/nltk_data" ) . resolve () if not ( NLTK_DIR / "tokenizers" / "punkt_tab" ) . exists (): with zipfile .
