Brand new tyres. Aluminium frame. 320.0 1 440.0 0 Good condition for its age. Minor scratches. Brand new tyres. Disc brakes. Collection only. 505.0 2 320.0 1 Some wear and tear. Minor scratches. Recently serviced. Collection only. Disc brakes. Comes with lights an... 285.0 3 840.0 0 Sold as seen. Gears slip sometimes. Aluminium frame. Comes with lights and a lock. 690.0 4 320.0 0 Rides well, normal wear. Collection only. Comes with lights and a lock. Amazing bike!!! 355.0 5 900.0 1 Sold as seen. Some rust on the chain. Minor scratches. Needs new brakes. Recently serviced. Aluminium fram... 810.0 Column Meaning Units book_value Guide price for the bike's model and age, from a price guide US dollars shop 1 if a bike shop is selling, 0 if a private seller 0/1 description The seller's text, written when the bike was listed Text archived_text The listing as stored after it closed, with the marketplace's status line Text price What the bike sold for (the target ) US dollars The real condition of each bike is hidden in true_condition . A buyer, and our model, only sees what the seller wrote. Can the text tell us what the guide price cannot? Part 1: Five ways to turn text into features (core) ¶ A regression needs numbers. Each way of turning text into numbers keeps some information and throws the rest away. Feature What it is Keeps Loses Typical use Sentiment score One number, e.g. VADER's compound in −1 to +1 Overall tone What is good or bad; any domain word the lexicon does not know Reviews, social media Keyword flags 0/1 columns: does the text mention "rust"? Specific, chosen facts Everything you did not think to look for Known important terms Length Number of words or characters Effort, detail Content Rarely useful alone; often a proxy (Part 5) Bag of words One column per word (or word pair): how often it appears Which words are used Word order, meaning Many-feature models with regularisation TF-IDF Bag of words weighted up for words that are rare across documents Distinctive words Order, meaning Search, classification, the same models More advanced methods (word embeddings, large language models) turn text into hundreds of numbers that capture meaning; they are beyond this course, but the traps in this lecture apply to them just as much. The question for every text feature is the same as for any predictor in the regression lecture: does it improve predictions on data the model has not seen? Predict, then run. The seller's description is mostly about condition. Which do you expect to help the price prediction more: the overall sentiment of the description, or a handful of keyword flags such as "rust" and "serviced"? Part 2: A baseline without text (core) ¶ Before adding any text feature, fit the model without it, on the same training and test split, so that every later model is compared with the same yardstick. train , test = train_test_split ( listings , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 3 ) results = [] def evaluate ( cols , label , data_train = None , data_test = None ): """Fit a linear regression on the training listings and report test errors in US dollars.""" data_train = train if data_train is None else data_train data_test = test if data_test is None else data_test model = LinearRegression () . fit ( data_train [ cols ], data_train [ "price" ]) pred = model . predict ( data_test [ cols ]) row = { "model" : label , "test R2" : r2_score ( data_test [ "price" ], pred ), "test RMSE ($)" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( data_test [ "price" ], pred )), "test MAE ($)" : mean_absolute_error ( data_test [ "price" ], pred )} results . append ( row ) return model , row def show ( row ): print ( f " { row [ 'model' ] } : test R2 { row [ 'test R2' ] : .3f } , RMSE $ { row [ 'test RMSE ($)' ] : .1f } , MAE $ { row [ 'test MAE ($)' ] : .1f } " ) base_cols = [ "book_value" , "shop" ] base_model , row = evaluate ( base_cols , "Baseline: guide price + shop" ) print ( pd . Series ( base_model . coef_ , index = base_cols ) . round ( 2 )) show ( row ) book_value 0.98 shop 72.44 dtype: float64 Baseline: guide price + shop: test R2 0.874, RMSE $93.2, MAE $77.3 The guide price does most of the work (each guide-price dollar goes with about a dollar of sale price), and shop listings sell for more, holding the guide price constant. The test RMSE is the number to beat: the typical miss, in dollars, of a model that ignores the text. Part 3: A sentiment score as a feature, and lexicon mismatch (core) ¶ The simplest text feature is VADER's compound score from Day 3: one number per description. Predict, then run. Which of these phrases will VADER score as negative: "Needs new brakes.", "Some rust on the chain.", "Project bike.", "Amazing bike!!!"? for phrase in [ "Needs new brakes." , "Some rust on the chain." , "Gears slip sometimes." , "Project bike." , "Scratched paintwork." , "Amazing bike!!!" , "Great deal, don't miss it!" , "Excellent condition, hardly ridden." ]: print ( f " { vader . polarity_scores ( phrase )[ 'compound' ] : +.3f } { phrase } " ) print ( " 
 Words in VADER's lexicon (None = unknown, so it scores 0):" ) for word in [ "rust" , "rusty" , "scratched" , "needs" , "slip" , "project" , "serviced" , "immaculate" , "amazing" , "excellent" ]: print ( f " { word : 11s } { vader . lexicon . get ( word ) } " ) +0.000 Needs new brakes. +0.000 Some rust on the chain. +0.000 Gears slip sometimes. +0.000 Project bike. +0.000 Scratched paintwork. +0.688 Amazing bike!!! +0.704 Great deal, don't miss it! +0.572 Excellent condition, hardly ridden. Words in VADER's lexicon (None = unknown, so it scores 0): rust None rusty None scratched None needs None slip None project None serviced None immaculate None amazing 2.8 excellent 2.7 None of the condition problems registers. VADER was built for social-media opinion, and words like "rust", "scratched", "slip" and "needs" are facts , not opinions, so they are not in its lexicon. Meanwhile sales talk ("Amazing bike!!!") scores high whatever the bike is like. This is lexicon mismatch : the scorer's vocabulary does not match the domain. Day 3 met the same problem with hotel complaints. How well does the score track the bike's real condition? Because the data is synthetic, we can check. listings [ "sentiment" ] = listings [ "description" ] . map ( lambda t : vader . polarity_scores ( t )[ "compound" ]) train , test = train_test_split ( listings , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 3 ) # same split, new column check = ( pd . DataFrame ({ "true condition" : true_condition , "sentiment" : listings [ "sentiment" ], "shop" : listings [ "shop" ]}) . groupby ( "true condition" )[[ "sentiment" ]] . mean () . reindex ([ "excellent" , "good" , "fair" , "poor" ]) . round ( 2 )) print ( check ) print ( f " 
 Average sentiment: shop listings { listings . loc [ listings . shop == 1 , 'sentiment' ] . mean () : .2f } , " f "private listings { listings . loc [ listings . shop == 0 , 'sentiment' ] . mean () : .2f } " ) print ( f "Distinct sentiment values among { len ( listings ) } listings: { listings [ 'sentiment' ] . nunique () } " ) _ , row = evaluate ( base_cols + [ "sentiment" ], "+ sentiment score" ) show ( row ) sentiment true condition excellent 0.52 good 0.54 fair 0.30 poor 0.30 Average sentiment: shop listings 0.67, private listings 0.34 Distinct sentiment values among 600 listings: 30 + sentiment score: test R2 0.886, RMSE $88.7, MAE $71.9 Three lessons: The score barely separates good bikes from bad ones. "Good" listings score about as high as "excellent", and "poor" about the same as "fair". It mostly measures sales talk , which shops use far more. So part of what the sentiment coefficient picks up is "a shop wrote this" (Part 5 returns to this). It still helps a little on test data, because tone and condition are loosely linked. A small improvement is not proof that the feature measures what its name says. Misconception: "A positive sentiment score means a better product." It means the text contains more words the lexicon rates as positive. Whether that tracks quality is an empirical question you must check, ideally against an independent measure. Part 4: Keyword flags (core) ¶ A keyword flag is a 0/1 column: does the text contain a word or phrase you chose? It is crude, but every flag is easy to explain, and you can pick the words that matter in the domain. Regular expressions ( re ) let one flag catch several spellings. Predict, then run. Which flag will have the largest coefficient in dollars, positive or negative? flags = { "kw_like_new" : r "like new|immaculate|excellent|hardly ridden|barely used" , "kw_rust" : r "rust" , "kw_scratch" : r "scratch" , "kw_repair" : r "needs new|need adjusting|gears slip" , "kw_serviced" : r "servic" , "kw_tyres" : r "new tyres" , } text_lower = listings [ "description" ] . str . lower () for name , pattern in flags . items (): listings [ name ] = text_lower . str . contains ( pattern , regex = True ) . astype ( int ) train , test = train_test_split ( listings , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 3 ) print ( "Share of listings with each flag:" ) print ( listings [ list ( flags )] . mean () . round ( 2 )) flag_model , row = evaluate ( base_cols + list ( flags ), "+ keyword flags" ) print ( " 
 Coefficients (US dollars, holding the other columns constant):" ) print ( pd . Series ( flag_model . coef_ , index = base_cols + list ( flags )) . round ( 1 )) show ( row ) Share of listings with each flag: kw_like_new 0.19 kw_rust 0.21 kw_scratch 0.32 kw_repair 0.16 kw_serviced 0.44 kw_tyres 0.25 dtype: float64 Coefficients (US dollars, holding the other columns constant): book_value 1.0 shop 61.9 kw_like_new 105.2 kw_rust -63.7 kw_scratch -23.0 kw_repair -63.8 kw_serviced 32.1 kw_tyres 15.9 dtype: float64 + keyword flags: test R2 0.948, RMSE $59.7, MAE $47.5 Six flags cut the test error far more than the sentiment score did, and each coefficient reads as a business sentence: "listings that mention rust sell for about $60 less than similar listings that do not, at the same guide price and seller type". The flags work because they measure facts about condition , which is what moves the price. Two cautions: The flags were chosen by reading the data . On real data, choose them from domain knowledge or from the training listings only, then test once; otherwise the test score flatters you. A flag counts a mention, not a meaning: "no rust at all" would trip kw_rust . Check a sample of flagged texts by eye. Part 5: Length, and features that stand in for something else (core) ¶ Does a longer description sell a bike for more? Predict, then run. Fit price on guide price and the number of words in the description, first without the shop column, then with it. Will the coefficient on words keep its sign? listings [ "words" ] = listings [ "description" ] . str . split () . str . len () train , test = train_test_split ( listings , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 3 ) print ( f "Average words: shop listings { listings . loc [ listings . shop == 1 , 'words' ] . mean () : .1f } , " f "private { listings . loc [ listings . shop == 0 , 'words' ] . mean () : .1f } " ) for cols in ([ "book_value" , "words" ], [ "book_value" , "words" , "shop" ], [ "book_value" , "sentiment" ], [ "book_value" , "sentiment" , "shop" ]): m = LinearRegression () . fit ( train [ cols ], train [ "price" ]) coefs = ", " . join ( f " { c } { v : +.1f } " for c , v in zip ( cols , m . coef_ ) if c != "book_value" ) print ( f "price ~ { ' + ' . join ( cols ) : 30s } -> { coefs } " ) Average words: shop listings 26.0, private 11.6 price ~ book_value + words -> words +1.4 price ~ book_value + words + shop -> words -4.4, shop +135.3 price ~ book_value + sentiment -> sentiment +117.3 price ~ book_value + sentiment + shop -> sentiment +93.5, shop +39.1 Without shop , each extra word goes with a slightly higher price; with shop , the sign flips . Length was standing in for who wrote the text : shops write longer listings and charge more. The sentiment coefficient also shrinks once shop is in the model, for the same reason. A text feature is a proxy when its coefficient really measures something else that it happens to correlate with: the seller, the product category, the price tier, the writer's age or language. This is the regression lecture's confounding problem (Part 12) in a new form, and it has a practical consequence: "Write longer descriptions and you will sell for more" does not follow. Neither does "write more positive descriptions". The model compares listings; it did not watch anyone rewrite one. For prediction , a proxy can still be useful, as long as the link it relies on stays the same. For explanation or advice , you must ask what the feature really measures. Check your understanding. In a model of restaurant revenue from online reviews, the number of reviews has a large positive coefficient. Name two things it could be a proxy for. Part 6: Bag of words and TF-IDF (extension) ¶ Instead of choosing keywords, let the data choose. A bag of words makes one column per word (or pair of words, a bigram) and counts how often each appears in each text. With a few hundred listings and a few hundred columns, an ordinary regression would overfit badly, so we use ridge regression , which shrinks coefficients towards zero (the regularisation mentioned in the regression lecture, Part 10). Two rules that prevent leakage between training and test: Fit the vectoriser on the training texts only ( fit_transform on train, transform on test). Otherwise the vocabulary and the IDF weights are learned partly from the test set. Choose the amount of shrinkage ( alpha ) without looking at the test set: by cross-validation on the training data, or fixed in advance as here. def text_model ( vectoriser , text_col = "description" , alpha = 1.0 ): """Ridge regression on scaled structured columns plus the vectorised text.""" X_text_train = vectoriser . fit_transform ( train [ text_col ]) # learn the vocabulary on training texts only X_text_test = vectoriser . transform ( test [ text_col ]) scale = np . array ([ 1000.0 , 1.0 ]) # put book_value on a similar scale to the 0/1 columns X_train = sp . hstack ([ sp . csr_matrix ( train [ base_cols ] . values / scale ), X_text_train ]) . tocsr () X_test = sp . hstack ([ sp . csr_matrix ( test [ base_cols ] . values / scale ), X_text_test ]) . tocsr () model = Ridge ( alpha = alpha ) . fit ( X_train , train [ "price" ]) pred_train , pred_test = model . predict ( X_train ), model . predict ( X_test ) return model , vectoriser , { "columns" : X_train . shape [ 1 ], "train RMSE ($)" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( train [ "price" ], pred_train )), "test RMSE ($)" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test [ "price" ], pred_test )), "test R2" : r2_score ( test [ "price" ], pred_test ), "test MAE ($)" : mean_absolute_error ( test [ "price" ], pred_test )} bow_model , bow_vec , bow_row = text_model ( CountVectorizer ( min_df = 3 )) # single words _ , _ , pairs_row = text_model ( CountVectorizer ( ngram_range = ( 1 , 2 ), min_df = 3 )) # words and word pairs _ , _ , tfidf_row = text_model ( TfidfVectorizer ( min_df = 3 )) print ( pd . DataFrame ([ bow_row , pairs_row , tfidf_row ], index = [ "Bag of words: words" , "Bag of words: words + pairs" , "TF-IDF: words" ]) . round ( 3 )) results . append ({ "model" : "Bag of words (ridge)" , ** { k : bow_row [ k ] for k in [ "test R2" , "test RMSE ($)" , "test MAE ($)" ]}}) words_coef = pd . Series ( bow_model . coef_ [ len ( base_cols ):], index = bow_vec . get_feature_names_out ()) print ( " 
 Words that push the price down most (US dollars per mention):" ) print ( words_coef . sort_values () . head ( 8 ) . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) print ( " 
 ... and up most:" ) print ( words_coef . sort_values () . tail ( 8 ) . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) columns train RMSE ($) test RMSE ($) test R2 test MAE ($) Bag of words: words 106 38.221 40.575 0.976 33.139 Bag of words: words + pairs 404 29.298 48.543 0.966 37.604 TF-IDF: words 106 44.022 45.749 0.970 37.490 Words that push the price down most (US dollars per mention): project -85.1 while -40.7 not -40.7 sold -32.3 as -32.3 seen -29.2 needs -24.4 works -22.6 ... and up most: like 41.7 indoors 41.7 kept 41.7 hardly 45.1 excellent 45.1 condition 53.8 immaculate 57.8 barely 57.8 The single-word bag of words beats the hand-picked flags on test data: it found signals we did not choose, such as the opening phrases that hint at condition ("project", "sold as seen", "not ridden for a while", "immaculate", "kept indoors"). Its strongest words are ones a bike mechanic would recognise, which is reassuring. But: Adding word pairs quadrupled the columns and made the test error worse , with a bigger gap between training and test error: more columns, more chances to fit noise. Many pairs also join the end of one sentence to the start of the next (Day 3's warning about bigrams across boundaries). Even with single words it has about a hundred columns; without shrinkage it would overfit. Its coefficients are harder to explain to a manager than six flags, and correlated words share credit unpredictably (multicollinearity again). With few texts, or texts written from a few templates (as here), it can latch on to the template wording rather than the meaning, and it would break if sellers started writing differently. TF-IDF gives similar results here. It matters more for long, varied documents, where common words would otherwise dominate. Misconception: "More features from the text always help." Every column is another chance to fit noise. Compare on test data, prefer the simplest feature set that does nearly as well, and remember that a manager must be able to trust it. Part 7: Leakage (core) ¶ Leakage happens when a feature contains information that would not be available at the moment the prediction is made , often because it was recorded after the outcome. The model looks excellent in testing and fails in use. CycleSwap's data team pulled the texts from the archive , which stores each listing as it looked when it closed , with the marketplace's status line added at the end. Predict, then run. We fit the same bag-of-words model on archived_text instead of description . Will the test RMSE go up or down? Would that model work for a bike listed today? for text in listings [ "archived_text" ] . iloc [: 3 ]: print ( text ) _ , archive_vec , leak_row = text_model ( CountVectorizer ( min_df = 3 ), text_col = "archived_text" ) results . append ({ "model" : "Bag of words on archived text (LEAKS)" , ** { k : leak_row [ k ] for k in [ "test R2" , "test RMSE ($)" , "test MAE ($)" ]}}) summary = pd . DataFrame ( results ) . drop_duplicates ( "model" ) . set_index ( "model" ) . round ( 3 ) print () print ( summary ) Well looked after. Brand new tyres. Aluminium frame. SOLD. Good condition for its age. Minor scratches. Brand new tyres. Disc brakes. Collection only. SOLD. Some wear and tear. Minor scratches. Recently serviced. Collection only. Disc brakes. Comes with lights and a lock. Aluminium frame. Great deal, don't miss it! Shop warranty included. SOLD after a price drop. test R2 test RMSE ($) test MAE ($) model Baseline: guide price + shop 0.874 93.189 77.262 + sentiment score 0.886 88.737 71.892 + keyword flags 0.948 59.697 47.462 Bag of words (ridge) 0.976 40.575 33.139 Bag of words on archived text (LEAKS) 0.994 19.617 15.759 fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.6 )) colours = [ ORANGE if "LEAKS" in m else BLUE for m in summary . index ] ax . barh ( summary . index [:: - 1 ], summary [ "test RMSE ($)" ][:: - 1 ], color = colours [:: - 1 ]) for y , v in enumerate ( summary [ "test RMSE ($)" ][:: - 1 ]): ax . text ( v + 1 , y , f "$ { v : .0f } " , va = "center" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Test RMSE (US dollars; lower is better)" ) ax . set_title ( "Text features cut the error; the leaky one 'wins' unfairly" ) plt . show () The archived-text model is the "best" by a clear margin, and it is useless. The status lines "SOLD after a price drop" and "SOLD within a day, several offers" were written after the sale and tell the model whether this bike went for more or less than expected. On a bike listed today, that line does not exist. Common forms of leakage: Form Example Text recorded after the outcome Status lines, final notes, a support ticket's resolution text A feature computed from the target "Price per square foot" when predicting price Test data used in preparation Vocabulary, scaling or keyword choice learned on all rows (Part 6) Duplicates across the split The same listing posted twice, once in training and once in test Generated data When a feature and the target were created by the same step of a simulation, the model can recover the simulation rule almost exactly, and its accuracy says more about the generator than about the world The defence is a question asked of every feature: "At the moment we will use this model, would we know this value?" A test score that looks too good to be true usually is. Part 8: A checklist for text features (core summary) ¶ Before you trust, report or act on a text feature, check: Check Question to ask In this lecture Improvement Does it lower the test error compared with the baseline without it? Parts 2–4, 6 Validity Does it measure what its name says? Compare it with an independent measure, or read a sample by eye Part 3 Lexicon fit Does the scorer know the domain's words? Look words up in vader.lexicon Part 3 Variety How many distinct values does it take? A score from a few templates is really a category Part 3 ( nunique ) Proxy Does its coefficient change a lot when you add who wrote it, the product or the region? Part 5 Leakage Would we know it at the moment of prediction? Part 7 Units Is the coefficient stated per one unit of the feature, and is one unit a sensible step? (A sentiment score runs from −1 to +1, so one unit is half its whole range) Parts 3–4 Advice Does the business advice follow from a comparison, or does it assume that changing the text changes the outcome? Part 5 Part 9: Business case: screening job applications (extension) ¶ A company receives 5,000 applications a year for graduate roles and wants a model that predicts each applicant's first-year performance rating from the application text (keyword flags and a bag of words), so that recruiters read the top 20% first. Discussion questions (groups of three, 10 minutes): Target. First-year rating is only known for people who were hired . What does that do to the training data, and to predictions for the kinds of people the company did not hire in the past? Proxies. Which words in an application could stand in for gender, age, nationality or social class (names of clubs, schools, sports, gaps in dates)? A widely reported 2018 case involved a large technology company that dropped an experimental CV-screening model after it learned to penalise words associated with women. How would you test for this before use? Leakage. The HR system stores applications with recruiters' notes added during interviews . Why must those notes be removed before training? Lexicon and style. Applicants who are not native speakers may use fewer of the "confident" words a sentiment lexicon rates highly. What would a sentiment feature do to them? Decision. Recommend whether to use the model, and under what safeguards (human review, regular bias audits by group, explaining to applicants, legal review under the laws that apply, such as China's Personal Information Protection Law or the EU's GDPR), using the four parts from Day 3: finding, evidence, action with an owner, and how you would know it worked. Part 10: Assignment 2 briefing (core) ¶ In Assignment 2 you play the lead data miner at a real-estate analytics firm. GAP gives you the code: it generates 500 synthetic house sales (floor area, bedrooms, age, an agent's description and the sale price), draws two exploratory charts, turns each description into a Text Appeal Score with VADER, fits a multiple linear regression on an 80/20 split, and prints test R², RMSE and the coefficients. You then write a five-section report for the firm's board. Weight 6%; due Sunday 22 November, 23:59 China Standard Time . Before you start, read the Assignment 2 guide . It has a corrected copy of GAP's code for the offline route, the known problems in GAP's code (one line will not run as printed), and checks you can make without seeing anyone's answers. How today's lectures map to the report: Report section (GAP's headings) What it asks you to do Revisit Executive Summary Purpose, structured and unstructured data, the goal of the model Regression lecture Part 1; this lecture Part 1 Exploratory Data Analysis Read a scatter plot and a box plot by bedrooms: relationship, medians, spread Day 1 and Day 2 lectures; regression lecture Part 2 Text Mining Methodology & Value How text became a number, and why that matters for a pricing model Day 3 text mining, Part 6; this lecture Parts 1, 3 and 8 Predictive Analytics Results Test R² and RMSE in plain words; each coefficient in dollars with its holding-constant clause; what one unit of the text score is worth Regression lecture Parts 3, 5 and 6; this lecture Part 8 ("Units") Strategic Recommendations Two actionable recommendations to agents Regression lecture Part 12; this lecture Part 5 ("Advice") Questions to ask your own output while you write (they have no single right answer here, and this lecture does not answer them): Which sentiment scorer actually ran in your notebook: the real VADER lexicon, or the simple fallback built into GAP's code? Your scores depend on it (the guide shows how to check). How many distinct values does your Text Appeal Score take? What does that tell you about how the descriptions were produced? Do the scores agree with how a human would read each description? If one does not, why might that be? (Day 3, Parts 6 and 7; this lecture, Part 3.) Is your test R² high because house prices are easy to predict, or because of how the data was generated ? (This lecture, Part 7, last row of the table.) When you state a coefficient in dollars, what are you holding constant, and over what range of the data does it hold? Does your recommendation about writing descriptions follow from what the model compares, or does it assume that rewriting a description changes the house? (This lecture, Part 5.) Write every number from your own output , with its unit, and name the table or chart it comes from. Part 11: Practice, quiz and summary ¶ Practice ¶ Core ¶ Core 1. Add a flag kw_warranty for "warranty" to the keyword model. Does it improve the test RMSE? What is it a proxy for? Core 2. Score each of your own five bike descriptions with VADER: two that describe a bike in poor condition politely, and three of your choice. Which scores would mislead a pricing model? Core 3. For the keyword model in Part 4, write the kw_repair coefficient as a business sentence with units and the holding-constant clause. Stretch ¶ Stretch 1. Make a copy of the analyser and add "rust", "rusty", "scratched" and "slip" to its lexicon with negative ratings you can justify. Recompute the sentiment feature and the model. How much closer does it get to the keyword model? Why is tuning a lexicon on the same data you test on risky? Stretch 2. Refit the bag-of-words model with alpha = 0.1, 1, 10 and 100. Plot training and test RMSE against alpha (log scale). Where is the best balance? Why should you choose alpha by cross-validation on the training data rather than from this plot? Stretch 3. Score each sentence of a description separately and use the minimum sentence score as a feature. Does it beat the whole-text compound score? Why might it? Challenge ¶ Challenge 1. Build the keyword list automatically from the training listings only : keep the 20 words whose presence is most correlated with the residuals of the baseline model, turn them into flags, and test once. Compare with the hand-picked flags. Challenge 2. Write a function leak_check(df, text_col, target) that fits a bag-of-words model and prints the ten words with the largest coefficients, so that a human can spot suspicious ones (status words, dates, prices). Run it on archived_text . Challenge 3. Simulate your own small "generated data" trap: make 200 rows where a text label and a price premium are created in the same if statement, plus noise. Fit a regression with and without the text feature, and explain to a manager why the impressive R² does not mean text predicts prices in real life. Quiz ¶ Name five ways to turn text into numbers and one weakness of each. Why should every text feature be compared with a baseline model on the same test set? Give two reasons a domain complaint can get a sentiment score of 0. What is a keyword flag, and why is it easy to explain to a manager? A text feature's coefficient changes sign when you add the seller type. What does that tell you? Why must a vectoriser be fitted on the training texts only? Define leakage and give one example involving text. "Listings with more positive descriptions sell for more, so sellers should write more positively." What is wrong with this advice? A sentiment score runs from −1 to +1. What does a coefficient of 50 on it mean, and what is a more realistic step to quote? Why can a model trained on generated data show an R² that would never be reached on real data? Summary ¶ Idea Remember Text features Sentiment, keyword flags, length, bag of words, TF-IDF: each keeps something and loses something Baseline Always compare with the same model without the text feature, on the same test set Lexicon mismatch A general lexicon misses domain facts ("rust", "needs") and rewards sales talk Keyword flags Simple, explainable, often strong; choose them from domain knowledge or training data Proxies A text feature can stand in for who wrote it; check whether its coefficient survives adding that Bag of words Many columns: needs regularisation; fit the vectoriser on training data only Leakage Would we know this value at prediction time? Too good to be true usually is Advice A coefficient compares cases; it does not show that changing the text changes the outcome References: Hutto, C. J., & Gilbert, E. (2014). docs.text: Period 4 of Day 4, with the Assignment 2 briefing. How free text becomes columns that a regression can use: sentiment scores, keyword flags, length, bag of words and TF-IDF; how to test whether a text feature really improves predictions; and the three traps of feature engineering with text: leakage, features that quietly stand in for something else, and a lexicon that does not speak the domain's language. Run each code cell with Shift + Enter , in order. The examples use 600 synthetic listings from a fictional second-hand bicycle marketplace, "CycleSwap", generated in the first cells: each listing has a guide price, whether a shop or a private person is selling, the seller's description, and the price the bike sold for, in US dollars . Assignment 2 uses different data (house prices); this lecture deliberately does not use its data or generator. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder; NLTK reads the VADER lexicon from data/nltk_data , so nothing is downloaded. Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook, run %pip install nltk scikit-learn in a first cell, and replace the setup cell with the NLTK download approach in the Lab 3 guide , Route A.

Recognise a proxy : a text feature whose coefficient really measures something else. Plan Assignment 2: what each part of the analysis is for, and what the report must explain. This lecture has one period (P4), shared with the Assignment 2 briefing, so it has a core path and extensions . Chapter 3's account of lexicon-based scoring explains why a domain complaint can come out neutral. This lecture applies both to text used as a predictor.

docs.title: Setup

docs.text: A regression needs numbers. Each way of turning text into numbers keeps some information and throws the rest away. Feature What it is Keeps Loses Typical use Sentiment score One number, e.g. VADER's compound in −1 to +1 Overall tone What is good or bad; any domain word the lexicon does not know Reviews, social media Keyword flags 0/1 columns: does the text mention "rust"? Specific, chosen facts Everything you did not think to look for Known important terms Length Number of words or characters Effort, detail Content Rarely useful alone; often a proxy (Part 5) Bag of words One column per word (or word pair): how often it appears Which words are used Word order, meaning Many-feature models with regularisation TF-IDF Bag of words weighted up for words that are rare across documents Distinctive words Order, meaning Search, classification, the same models More advanced methods (word embeddings, large language models) turn text into hundreds of numbers that capture meaning; they are beyond this course, but the traps in this lecture apply to them just as much. The question for every text feature is the same as for any predictor in the regression lecture: does it improve predictions on data the model has not seen? Predict, then run. The seller's description is mostly about condition. Which do you expect to help the price prediction more: the overall sentiment of the description, or a handful of keyword flags such as "rust" and "serviced"?
docs.title: Part 1: Five ways to turn text into features (core)

docs.text: Before adding any text feature, fit the model without it, on the same training and test split, so that every later model is compared with the same yardstick. train , test = train_test_split ( listings , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 3 ) results = [] def evaluate ( cols , label , data_train = None , data_test = None ): """Fit a linear regression on the training listings and report test errors in US dollars.""" data_train = train if data_train is None else data_train data_test = test if data_test is None else data_test model = LinearRegression () . fit ( data_train [ cols ], data_train [ "price" ]) pred = model . predict ( data_test [ cols ]) row = { "model" : label , "test R2" : r2_score ( data_test [ "price" ], pred ), "test RMSE ($)" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( data_test [ "price" ], pred )), "test MAE ($)" : mean_absolute_error ( data_test [ "price" ], pred )} results . append ( row ) return model , row def show ( row ): print ( f " { row [ 'model' ] } : test R2 { row [ 'test R2' ] : .3f } , RMSE $ { row [ 'test RMSE ($)' ] : .1f } , MAE $ { row [ 'test MAE ($)' ] : .1f } " ) base_cols = [ "book_value" , "shop" ] base_model , row = evaluate ( base_cols , "Baseline: guide price + shop" ) print ( pd . Series ( base_model . coef_ , index = base_cols ) . round ( 2 )) show ( row ) book_value 0.98 shop 72.44 dtype: float64 Baseline: guide price + shop: test R2 0.874, RMSE $93.2, MAE $77.3 The guide price does most of the work (each guide-price dollar goes with about a dollar of sale price), and shop listings sell for more, holding the guide price constant. The test RMSE is the number to beat: the typical miss, in dollars, of a model that ignores the text.
docs.title: Part 2: A baseline without text (core)

docs.text: The simplest text feature is VADER's compound score from Day 3: one number per description. Predict, then run. Which of these phrases will VADER score as negative: "Needs new brakes.", "Some rust on the chain.", "Project bike.", "Amazing bike!!!"? for phrase in [ "Needs new brakes." , "Some rust on the chain." , "Gears slip sometimes." , "Project bike." , "Scratched paintwork." , "Amazing bike!!!" , "Great deal, don't miss it!" , "Excellent condition, hardly ridden." ]: print ( f " { vader . polarity_scores ( phrase )[ 'compound' ] : +.3f } { phrase } " ) print ( " \n Words in VADER's lexicon (None = unknown, so it scores 0):" ) for word in [ "rust" , "rusty" , "scratched" , "needs" , "slip" , "project" , "serviced" , "immaculate" , "amazing" , "excellent" ]: print ( f " { word : 11s } { vader . lexicon . get ( word ) } " ) +0.000 Needs new brakes. +0.000 Some rust on the chain. +0.000 Gears slip sometimes. +0.000 Project bike. +0.000 Scratched paintwork. +0.688 Amazing bike!!! +0.704 Great deal, don't miss it! +0.572 Excellent condition, hardly ridden. Words in VADER's lexicon (None = unknown, so it scores 0): rust None rusty None scratched None needs None slip None project None serviced None immaculate None amazing 2.8 excellent 2.7 None of the condition problems registers. VADER was built for social-media opinion, and words like "rust", "scratched", "slip" and "needs" are facts , not opinions, so they are not in its lexicon. Meanwhile sales talk ("Amazing bike!!!") scores high whatever the bike is like. This is lexicon mismatch : the scorer's vocabulary does not match the domain. Day 3 met the same problem with hotel complaints. How well does the score track the bike's real condition? Because the data is synthetic, we can check. listings [ "sentiment" ] = listings [ "description" ] . map ( lambda t : vader . polarity_scores ( t )[ "compound" ]) train , test = train_test_split ( listings , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 3 ) # same split, new column check = ( pd . DataFrame ({ "true condition" : true_condition , "sentiment" : listings [ "sentiment" ], "shop" : listings [ "shop" ]}) . groupby ( "true condition" )[[ "sentiment" ]] . mean () . reindex ([ "excellent" , "good" , "fair" , "poor" ]) . round ( 2 )) print ( check ) print ( f " \n Average sentiment: shop listings { listings . loc [ listings . shop == 1 , 'sentiment' ] . mean () : .2f } , " f "private listings { listings . loc [ listings . shop == 0 , 'sentiment' ] . mean () : .2f } " ) print ( f "Distinct sentiment values among { len ( listings ) } listings: { listings [ 'sentiment' ] . nunique () } " ) _ , row = evaluate ( base_cols + [ "sentiment" ], "+ sentiment score" ) show ( row ) sentiment true condition excellent 0.52 good 0.54 fair 0.30 poor 0.30 Average sentiment: shop listings 0.67, private listings 0.34 Distinct sentiment values among 600 listings: 30 + sentiment score: test R2 0.886, RMSE $88.7, MAE $71.9 Three lessons: The score barely separates good bikes from bad ones. "Good" listings score about as high as "excellent", and "poor" about the same as "fair". It mostly measures sales talk , which shops use far more. So part of what the sentiment coefficient picks up is "a shop wrote this" (Part 5 returns to this). It still helps a little on test data, because tone and condition are loosely linked. A small improvement is not proof that the feature measures what its name says. Misconception: "A positive sentiment score means a better product." It means the text contains more words the lexicon rates as positive. Whether that tracks quality is an empirical question you must check, ideally against an independent measure.
docs.title: Part 3: A sentiment score as a feature, and lexicon mismatch (core)

docs.text: A keyword flag is a 0/1 column: does the text contain a word or phrase you chose? It is crude, but every flag is easy to explain, and you can pick the words that matter in the domain. Regular expressions ( re ) let one flag catch several spellings. Predict, then run. Which flag will have the largest coefficient in dollars, positive or negative? flags = { "kw_like_new" : r "like new|immaculate|excellent|hardly ridden|barely used" , "kw_rust" : r "rust" , "kw_scratch" : r "scratch" , "kw_repair" : r "needs new|need adjusting|gears slip" , "kw_serviced" : r "servic" , "kw_tyres" : r "new tyres" , } text_lower = listings [ "description" ] . str . lower () for name , pattern in flags . items (): listings [ name ] = text_lower . str . contains ( pattern , regex = True ) . astype ( int ) train , test = train_test_split ( listings , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 3 ) print ( "Share of listings with each flag:" ) print ( listings [ list ( flags )] . mean () . round ( 2 )) flag_model , row = evaluate ( base_cols + list ( flags ), "+ keyword flags" ) print ( " \n Coefficients (US dollars, holding the other columns constant):" ) print ( pd . Series ( flag_model . coef_ , index = base_cols + list ( flags )) . round ( 1 )) show ( row ) Share of listings with each flag: kw_like_new 0.19 kw_rust 0.21 kw_scratch 0.32 kw_repair 0.16 kw_serviced 0.44 kw_tyres 0.25 dtype: float64 Coefficients (US dollars, holding the other columns constant): book_value 1.0 shop 61.9 kw_like_new 105.2 kw_rust -63.7 kw_scratch -23.0 kw_repair -63.8 kw_serviced 32.1 kw_tyres 15.9 dtype: float64 + keyword flags: test R2 0.948, RMSE $59.7, MAE $47.5 Six flags cut the test error far more than the sentiment score did, and each coefficient reads as a business sentence: "listings that mention rust sell for about $60 less than similar listings that do not, at the same guide price and seller type". The flags work because they measure facts about condition , which is what moves the price. Two cautions: The flags were chosen by reading the data . On real data, choose them from domain knowledge or from the training listings only, then test once; otherwise the test score flatters you. A flag counts a mention, not a meaning: "no rust at all" would trip kw_rust . Check a sample of flagged texts by eye.
docs.title: Part 4: Keyword flags (core)

docs.text: Does a longer description sell a bike for more? Predict, then run. Fit price on guide price and the number of words in the description, first without the shop column, then with it. Will the coefficient on words keep its sign? listings [ "words" ] = listings [ "description" ] . str . split () . str . len () train , test = train_test_split ( listings , test_size = 0.25 , random_state = 3 ) print ( f "Average words: shop listings { listings . loc [ listings . shop == 1 , 'words' ] . mean () : .1f } , " f "private { listings . loc [ listings . shop == 0 , 'words' ] . mean () : .1f } " ) for cols in ([ "book_value" , "words" ], [ "book_value" , "words" , "shop" ], [ "book_value" , "sentiment" ], [ "book_value" , "sentiment" , "shop" ]): m = LinearRegression () . fit ( train [ cols ], train [ "price" ]) coefs = ", " . join ( f " { c } { v : +.1f } " for c , v in zip ( cols , m . coef_ ) if c != "book_value" ) print ( f "price ~ { ' + ' . join ( cols ) : 30s } -> { coefs } " ) Average words: shop listings 26.0, private 11.6 price ~ book_value + words -> words +1.4 price ~ book_value + words + shop -> words -4.4, shop +135.3 price ~ book_value + sentiment -> sentiment +117.3 price ~ book_value + sentiment + shop -> sentiment +93.5, shop +39.1 Without shop , each extra word goes with a slightly higher price; with shop , the sign flips . Length was standing in for who wrote the text : shops write longer listings and charge more. The sentiment coefficient also shrinks once shop is in the model, for the same reason. A text feature is a proxy when its coefficient really measures something else that it happens to correlate with: the seller, the product category, the price tier, the writer's age or language. This is the regression lecture's confounding problem (Part 12) in a new form, and it has a practical consequence: "Write longer descriptions and you will sell for more" does not follow. Neither does "write more positive descriptions". The model compares listings; it did not watch anyone rewrite one. For prediction , a proxy can still be useful, as long as the link it relies on stays the same. For explanation or advice , you must ask what the feature really measures. Check your understanding. In a model of restaurant revenue from online reviews, the number of reviews has a large positive coefficient. Name two things it could be a proxy for.
docs.title: Part 5: Length, and features that stand in for something else (core)

docs.text: Instead of choosing keywords, let the data choose. A bag of words makes one column per word (or pair of words, a bigram) and counts how often each appears in each text. With a few hundred listings and a few hundred columns, an ordinary regression would overfit badly, so we use ridge regression , which shrinks coefficients towards zero (the regularisation mentioned in the regression lecture, Part 10). Two rules that prevent leakage between training and test: Fit the vectoriser on the training texts only ( fit_transform on train, transform on test). Otherwise the vocabulary and the IDF weights are learned partly from the test set. Choose the amount of shrinkage ( alpha ) without looking at the test set: by cross-validation on the training data, or fixed in advance as here. def text_model ( vectoriser , text_col = "description" , alpha = 1.0 ): """Ridge regression on scaled structured columns plus the vectorised text.""" X_text_train = vectoriser . fit_transform ( train [ text_col ]) # learn the vocabulary on training texts only X_text_test = vectoriser . transform ( test [ text_col ]) scale = np . array ([ 1000.0 , 1.0 ]) # put book_value on a similar scale to the 0/1 columns X_train = sp . hstack ([ sp . csr_matrix ( train [ base_cols ] . values / scale ), X_text_train ]) . tocsr () X_test = sp . hstack ([ sp . csr_matrix ( test [ base_cols ] . values / scale ), X_text_test ]) . tocsr () model = Ridge ( alpha = alpha ) . fit ( X_train , train [ "price" ]) pred_train , pred_test = model . predict ( X_train ), model . predict ( X_test ) return model , vectoriser , { "columns" : X_train . shape [ 1 ], "train RMSE ($)" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( train [ "price" ], pred_train )), "test RMSE ($)" : np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( test [ "price" ], pred_test )), "test R2" : r2_score ( test [ "price" ], pred_test ), "test MAE ($)" : mean_absolute_error ( test [ "price" ], pred_test )} bow_model , bow_vec , bow_row = text_model ( CountVectorizer ( min_df = 3 )) # single words _ , _ , pairs_row = text_model ( CountVectorizer ( ngram_range = ( 1 , 2 ), min_df = 3 )) # words and word pairs _ , _ , tfidf_row = text_model ( TfidfVectorizer ( min_df = 3 )) print ( pd . DataFrame ([ bow_row , pairs_row , tfidf_row ], index = [ "Bag of words: words" , "Bag of words: words + pairs" , "TF-IDF: words" ]) . round ( 3 )) results . append ({ "model" : "Bag of words (ridge)" , ** { k : bow_row [ k ] for k in [ "test R2" , "test RMSE ($)" , "test MAE ($)" ]}}) words_coef = pd . Series ( bow_model . coef_ [ len ( base_cols ):], index = bow_vec . get_feature_names_out ()) print ( " \n Words that push the price down most (US dollars per mention):" ) print ( words_coef . sort_values () . head ( 8 ) . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) print ( " \n ... and up most:" ) print ( words_coef . sort_values () . tail ( 8 ) . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) columns train RMSE ($) test RMSE ($) test R2 test MAE ($) Bag of words: words 106 38.221 40.575 0.976 33.139 Bag of words: words + pairs 404 29.298 48.543 0.966 37.604 TF-IDF: words 106 44.022 45.749 0.970 37.490 Words that push the price down most (US dollars per mention): project -85.1 while -40.7 not -40.7 sold -32.3 as -32.3 seen -29.2 needs -24.4 works -22.6 ... and up most: like 41.7 indoors 41.7 kept 41.7 hardly 45.1 excellent 45.1 condition 53.8 immaculate 57.8 barely 57.8 The single-word bag of words beats the hand-picked flags on test data: it found signals we did not choose, such as the opening phrases that hint at condition ("project", "sold as seen", "not ridden for a while", "immaculate", "kept indoors"). Its strongest words are ones a bike mechanic would recognise, which is reassuring. But: Adding word pairs quadrupled the columns and made the test error worse , with a bigger gap between training and test error: more columns, more chances to fit noise. Many pairs also join the end of one sentence to the start of the next (Day 3's warning about bigrams across boundaries). Even with single words it has about a hundred columns; without shrinkage it would overfit. Its coefficients are harder to explain to a manager than six flags, and correlated words share credit unpredictably (multicollinearity again). With few texts, or texts written from a few templates (as here), it can latch on to the template wording rather than the meaning, and it would break if sellers started writing differently. TF-IDF gives similar results here. It matters more for long, varied documents, where common words would otherwise dominate. Misconception: "More features from the text always help." Every column is another chance to fit noise. Compare on test data, prefer the simplest feature set that does nearly as well, and remember that a manager must be able to trust it.
docs.title: Part 6: Bag of words and TF-IDF (extension)

docs.text: Leakage happens when a feature contains information that would not be available at the moment the prediction is made , often because it was recorded after the outcome. The model looks excellent in testing and fails in use. CycleSwap's data team pulled the texts from the archive , which stores each listing as it looked when it closed , with the marketplace's status line added at the end. Predict, then run. We fit the same bag-of-words model on archived_text instead of description . Will the test RMSE go up or down? Would that model work for a bike listed today? for text in listings [ "archived_text" ] . iloc [: 3 ]: print ( text ) _ , archive_vec , leak_row = text_model ( CountVectorizer ( min_df = 3 ), text_col = "archived_text" ) results . append ({ "model" : "Bag of words on archived text (LEAKS)" , ** { k : leak_row [ k ] for k in [ "test R2" , "test RMSE ($)" , "test MAE ($)" ]}}) summary = pd . DataFrame ( results ) . drop_duplicates ( "model" ) . set_index ( "model" ) . round ( 3 ) print () print ( summary ) Well looked after. Brand new tyres. Aluminium frame. SOLD. Good condition for its age. Minor scratches. Brand new tyres. Disc brakes. Collection only. SOLD. Some wear and tear. Minor scratches. Recently serviced. Collection only. Disc brakes. Comes with lights and a lock. Aluminium frame. Great deal, don't miss it! Shop warranty included. SOLD after a price drop. test R2 test RMSE ($) test MAE ($) model Baseline: guide price + shop 0.874 93.189 77.262 + sentiment score 0.886 88.737 71.892 + keyword flags 0.948 59.697 47.462 Bag of words (ridge) 0.976 40.575 33.139 Bag of words on archived text (LEAKS) 0.994 19.617 15.759 fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.6 )) colours = [ ORANGE if "LEAKS" in m else BLUE for m in summary . index ] ax . barh ( summary . index [:: - 1 ], summary [ "test RMSE ($)" ][:: - 1 ], color = colours [:: - 1 ]) for y , v in enumerate ( summary [ "test RMSE ($)" ][:: - 1 ]): ax . text ( v + 1 , y , f "$ { v : .0f } " , va = "center" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Test RMSE (US dollars; lower is better)" ) ax . set_title ( "Text features cut the error; the leaky one 'wins' unfairly" ) plt . show () The archived-text model is the "best" by a clear margin, and it is useless. The status lines "SOLD after a price drop" and "SOLD within a day, several offers" were written after the sale and tell the model whether this bike went for more or less than expected. On a bike listed today, that line does not exist. Common forms of leakage: Form Example Text recorded after the outcome Status lines, final notes, a support ticket's resolution text A feature computed from the target "Price per square foot" when predicting price Test data used in preparation Vocabulary, scaling or keyword choice learned on all rows (Part 6) Duplicates across the split The same listing posted twice, once in training and once in test Generated data When a feature and the target were created by the same step of a simulation, the model can recover the simulation rule almost exactly, and its accuracy says more about the generator than about the world The defence is a question asked of every feature: "At the moment we will use this model, would we know this value?" A test score that looks too good to be true usually is.
docs.title: Part 7: Leakage (core)

docs.text: Before you trust, report or act on a text feature, check: Check Question to ask In this lecture Improvement Does it lower the test error compared with the baseline without it? Parts 2–4, 6 Validity Does it measure what its name says? Compare it with an independent measure, or read a sample by eye Part 3 Lexicon fit Does the scorer know the domain's words? Look words up in vader.lexicon Part 3 Variety How many distinct values does it take? A score from a few templates is really a category Part 3 ( nunique ) Proxy Does its coefficient change a lot when you add who wrote it, the product or the region? Part 5 Leakage Would we know it at the moment of prediction? Part 7 Units Is the coefficient stated per one unit of the feature, and is one unit a sensible step? (A sentiment score runs from −1 to +1, so one unit is half its whole range) Parts 3–4 Advice Does the business advice follow from a comparison, or does it assume that changing the text changes the outcome? Part 5
docs.title: Part 8: A checklist for text features (core summary)

docs.text: A company receives 5,000 applications a year for graduate roles and wants a model that predicts each applicant's first-year performance rating from the application text (keyword flags and a bag of words), so that recruiters read the top 20% first. Discussion questions (groups of three, 10 minutes): Target. First-year rating is only known for people who were hired . What does that do to the training data, and to predictions for the kinds of people the company did not hire in the past? Proxies. Which words in an application could stand in for gender, age, nationality or social class (names of clubs, schools, sports, gaps in dates)? A widely reported 2018 case involved a large technology company that dropped an experimental CV-screening model after it learned to penalise words associated with women. How would you test for this before use? Leakage. The HR system stores applications with recruiters' notes added during interviews . Why must those notes be removed before training? Lexicon and style. Applicants who are not native speakers may use fewer of the "confident" words a sentiment lexicon rates highly. What would a sentiment feature do to them? Decision. Recommend whether to use the model, and under what safeguards (human review, regular bias audits by group, explaining to applicants, legal review under the laws that apply, such as China's Personal Information Protection Law or the EU's GDPR), using the four parts from Day 3: finding, evidence, action with an owner, and how you would know it worked.
docs.title: Part 9: Business case: screening job applications (extension)

docs.text: In Assignment 2 you play the lead data miner at a real-estate analytics firm. GAP gives you the code: it generates 500 synthetic house sales (floor area, bedrooms, age, an agent's description and the sale price), draws two exploratory charts, turns each description into a Text Appeal Score with VADER, fits a multiple linear regression on an 80/20 split, and prints test R², RMSE and the coefficients. You then write a five-section report for the firm's board. Weight 6%; due Sunday 22 November, 23:59 China Standard Time . Before you start, read the Assignment 2 guide . It has a corrected copy of GAP's code for the offline route, the known problems in GAP's code (one line will not run as printed), and checks you can make without seeing anyone's answers. How today's lectures map to the report: Report section (GAP's headings) What it asks you to do Revisit Executive Summary Purpose, structured and unstructured data, the goal of the model Regression lecture Part 1; this lecture Part 1 Exploratory Data Analysis Read a scatter plot and a box plot by bedrooms: relationship, medians, spread Day 1 and Day 2 lectures; regression lecture Part 2 Text Mining Methodology & Value How text became a number, and why that matters for a pricing model Day 3 text mining, Part 6; this lecture Parts 1, 3 and 8 Predictive Analytics Results Test R² and RMSE in plain words; each coefficient in dollars with its holding-constant clause; what one unit of the text score is worth Regression lecture Parts 3, 5 and 6; this lecture Part 8 ("Units") Strategic Recommendations Two actionable recommendations to agents Regression lecture Part 12; this lecture Part 5 ("Advice") Questions to ask your own output while you write (they have no single right answer here, and this lecture does not answer them): Which sentiment scorer actually ran in your notebook: the real VADER lexicon, or the simple fallback built into GAP's code? Your scores depend on it (the guide shows how to check). How many distinct values does your Text Appeal Score take? What does that tell you about how the descriptions were produced? Do the scores agree with how a human would read each description? If one does not, why might that be? (Day 3, Parts 6 and 7; this lecture, Part 3.) docs.text: Name five ways to turn text into numbers and one weakness of each. Why should every text feature be compared with a baseline model on the same test set? Give two reasons a domain complaint can get a sentiment score of 0. What is a keyword flag, and why is it easy to explain to a manager? A text feature's coefficient changes sign when you add the seller type. What does that tell you? Why must a vectoriser be fitted on the training texts only? docs.text: Idea Remember Text features Sentiment, keyword flags, length, bag of words, TF-IDF: each keeps something and loses something Baseline Always compare with the same model without the text feature, on the same test set Lexicon mismatch A general lexicon misses domain facts ("rust", "needs") and rewards sales talk Keyword flags Simple, explainable, often strong; choose them from domain knowledge or training data Proxies A text feature can stand in for who wrote it; check whether its coefficient survives adding that Bag of words Many columns: needs regularisation; fit the vectoriser on training data only Leakage Would we know this value at prediction time? Too good to be true usually is Advice A coefficient compares cases; it does not show that changing the text changes the outcome References: Hutto, C. J., & Gilbert, E. (2014). Gentzkow, M., Kelly, B., & Taddy, M. (2019). Text as data. Journal of Economic Literature , 57(3), 535–574. Next: the Assignment 2 guide . docs.text: Day 5 lecture: Simulation under uncertainty ¶ Periods 1 to 6 of Day 5. How to turn a prediction into a decision when the future is uncertain: reading a regression as a manager and turning its error into a model input, building a spreadsheet model with separate inputs, calculations and outputs, contribution margin and break-even, sensitivity analysis and the tornado chart, one- and two-way What-If Data Tables, Scenario Manager and Goal Seek, the flaw of averages, Monte Carlo simulation with uniform, normal and triangular inputs, how many trials you need, risk measures such as the probability of a loss and the 5th percentile, correlated inputs, freezing a simulation, decision rules, and how to explain risk to executives. Period 6 ends with a bridge to Lab 5. Every spreadsheet step is given twice: as a numbered Excel click path with the formulas , and as a numpy mirror with a fixed random seed, so that you can check one against the other. The case is a fictional drinks start-up, Brightleaf , launching a bottled cold-brew tea for one summer of festivals. All money is in US dollars . Lab 6, Lab 7 and Assignment 3 (tomorrow) use other businesses and other numbers; this lecture deliberately uses none of them, so that you practise each idea here and apply it yourself there. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder. It needs only numpy, pandas, matplotlib, scipy and statsmodels, and it downloads nothing. Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook and run %pip install statsmodels scipy in a first cell. Excel: any desktop Excel from 2016 on (Windows or Mac). Every function used here ( RAND , RANDBETWEEN , NORM.INV , PERCENTILE.INC , FORECAST.LINEAR , STEYX ) is built in. Data Tables, Scenario Manager and Goal Seek are under Data → What-If Analysis (on a Mac: Data → What-If Analysis as well, in the Forecast group on recent versions). What you will be able to do ¶ Read a regression as a manager would, and turn its prediction and its error into an uncertain input for a spreadsheet model. Build a model with separate inputs, calculations and outputs ; compute contribution margin , break-even and margin of safety . Part 2: Anatomy of a spreadsheet model; the deterministic base case (core) ¶ A financial model turns assumptions into a result. A good one has three visibly separate layers: Layer What it holds Convention Inputs (assumptions) Numbers nobody can calculate from anything else: price, unit cost, demand, fees Typed in once, coloured blue Calculations Formulas that combine inputs Black ; never type a number into a formula Outputs The few numbers a decision-maker reads: profit, break-even Clearly labelled, often boxed Why it matters: when the price changes, you change one blue cell and every result updates. A number typed inside a formula ( =40000*4-60000 ) is invisible, cannot be varied by a Data Table, and is the most common cause of wrong spreadsheets. Brightleaf's base case ¶ The deterministic base case uses one value for every input, usually the planners' best guess. "Deterministic" means no randomness: the same inputs always give the same output. Input Value Notes Price per bottle $4.00 Brightleaf's decision Variable cost per bottle $1.70 Tea, bottle, label, cold storage; the most likely value Festival days 30 Booked Stall fee per day $1,200 Charged by the festivals Equipment and marketing $24,000 For the season Demand 40,000 bottles From Part 1 Three ideas carry most of the analysis: Contribution margin per bottle = price − variable cost = $4.00 − $1.70 = $2.30 . Each bottle sold "contributes" $2.30 towards the fixed costs, and then to profit. Fixed costs = 30 × $1,200 + $24,000 = $60,000 . They are paid whether Brightleaf sells one bottle or 60,000. Break-even demand = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin = $60,000 ÷ $2.30 ≈ 26,087 bottles : the sales at which profit is exactly zero. Margin of safety = (expected demand − break-even) ÷ expected demand: how far demand can fall short of the plan before the season loses money. Predict, then run. At 40,000 bottles, will the season's profit be nearer $10,000, $30,000 or $90,000? And how far can demand fall below 40,000 before Brightleaf loses money: about 10%, 35% or 60%? inputs = { "price" : 4.00 , "unit_cost" : 1.70 , "days" : 30 , "stall_fee" : 1200 , "equipment_marketing" : 24000 , "demand" : 40000 } def model ( price , unit_cost , days , stall_fee , equipment_marketing , demand ): """Brightleaf's season, brewing exactly what is sold (the simple model).""" margin = price - unit_cost # contribution margin per bottle fixed = days * stall_fee + equipment_marketing # fixed costs revenue = price * demand variable = unit_cost * demand profit = revenue - variable - fixed break_even = fixed / margin return { "contribution_margin" : margin , "fixed_costs" : fixed , "revenue" : revenue , "variable_costs" : variable , "profit" : profit , "break_even_demand" : break_even , "margin_of_safety" : ( demand - break_even ) / demand } base = model ( ** inputs ) for k , v in base . items (): print ( f " { k : >20 } : { v : >12,.2f } " if k in ( "contribution_margin" , "margin_of_safety" ) else f " { k : >20 } : { v : >12,.0f } " ) contribution_margin: 2.30 fixed_costs: 60,000 revenue: 160,000 variable_costs: 68,000 profit: 32,000 break_even_demand: 26,087 margin_of_safety: 0.35 The base case says $32,000 profit , with a break-even at about 26,100 bottles and a margin of safety of about 35% : demand can fall roughly a third below plan before the season makes a loss. Part 3: Sensitivity analysis and the tornado chart (core) ¶ A sensitivity analysis asks: if one input is wrong, how much does the output move? The simplest version is one at a time : set each input to a plausible low and high value while holding all others at the base case, and record the profit each time. Brightleaf's planners agreed these ranges. For demand they used the 10th and 90th percentiles of the Part 1 distribution, 40,000 ± 1.28 × 9,000. A two-way table varies two inputs and shows one output for every combination. Predict, then run. In the two-way table below, at a price of $3.50 , at roughly what demand does profit cross zero? Is the price needed for $40,000 at 35,000 bottles above or below $4.50? def goal_seek ( f , target , lo , hi , tol = 1e-6 ): """Find x in [lo, hi] with f(x) = target by bisection (Goal Seek does a similar search).""" for _ in range ( 200 ): mid = ( lo + hi ) / 2 if ( f ( lo ) - target ) * ( f ( mid ) - target ) <= 0 : hi = mid else : lo = mid if hi - lo < tol : break return ( lo + hi ) / 2 be = goal_seek ( lambda d : model ( ** { ** inputs , "demand" : d })[ "profit" ], 0 , 1 , 100000 ) p_needed = goal_seek ( lambda p : model ( ** { ** inputs , "demand" : 35000 , "price" : p })[ "profit" ], 40000 , 1 , 10 ) print ( f "Goal Seek, profit = 0 by changing demand: { be : ,.2f } bottles" ) print ( f "Formula check, fixed / margin: { base [ 'break_even_demand' ] : ,.2f } bottles" ) print ( f "Goal Seek, profit = $40,000 at 35,000 by changing price: $ { p_needed : .3f } " ) Goal Seek, profit = 0 by changing demand: 26,086.96 bottles Formula check, fixed / margin: 26,086.96 bottles Goal Seek, profit = $40,000 at 35,000 by changing price: $4.557 Excel steps: Goal Seek ¶ Data → What-If Analysis → Goal Seek… Set cell E8 (profit; it must contain a formula) · To value 0 · By changing cell B9 (demand; it must be a typed input) → OK . How would you report it to the board, and why not to two decimal places? Part 6: The flaw of averages (core) ¶ So far, profit has been a straight-line function of each input. Real businesses have kinks. Brightleaf has one: cold brew must be brewed and bottled before the season , because the festivals have no kitchen. Brightleaf plans to brew 45,000 bottles , a little above expected demand. Then: bottles sold = the smaller of demand and bottles brewed: MIN(demand, 45000) ; the variable cost is paid on every bottle brewed , sold or not; unsold bottles are sold to a discount retailer at a salvage price , about $0.50. There is also a second subtlety. The planners' cost of $1.70 is the most likely value, but they think costs could rise to $2.20 more easily than fall to $1.50. The average of such a skewed range is higher than its most likely value (for a triangular range, (1.50 + 1.70 + 2.20) ÷ 3 = $1.80 ). The flaw of averages (Sam Savage's name for it) is the belief that plugging average inputs into a model gives the average output. It is true only for straight-line models. With a kink like MIN , it is false. A pencil example. Suppose demand is equally likely to be 31,000, 40,000 or 49,000 (average 40,000), the cost is $1.80, and Brightleaf brews 45,000. Demand Sold Revenue + salvage Cost of 45,000 brewed Fixed Profit 31,000 31,000 $124,000 + $7,000 $81,000 $60,000 −$10,000 40,000 40,000 $160,000 + $2,500 $81,000 $60,000 $21,500 49,000 45,000 $180,000 + $0 $81,000 $60,000 $39,000 Average $16,833 The profit at average demand is $21,500, but the average profit is $16,833. In good seasons the extra demand is lost (Brightleaf runs out), while in bad seasons every unsold bottle still cost money. The downside counts in full; the upside is capped. Predict, then run. The code computes Brightleaf's profit three ways: at the most likely inputs, at the average inputs, and as the average of 10,000 simulated seasons. Put the three in order from largest to smallest. PRICE , Q , FIXED = 4.00 , 45000 , 60000 def brew_profit ( demand , unit_cost , salvage , brewed = Q , price = PRICE , fixed = FIXED ): """Season profit when `brewed` bottles are made in advance (works on arrays too).""" sold = np . minimum ( demand , brewed ) return price * sold + salvage * ( brewed - sold ) - unit_cost * brewed - fixed at_most_likely = brew_profit ( 40000 , 1.70 , 0.50 ) at_average = brew_profit ( 40000 , ( 1.50 + 1.70 + 2.20 ) / 3 , 0.50 ) rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) n = 10_000 sim_demand = np . maximum ( 0 , np . round ( rng . normal ( 40000 , 9000 , n ))) sim_cost = rng . triangular ( 1.50 , 1.70 , 2.20 , n ) sim_salvage = rng . uniform ( 0.30 , 0.70 , n ) sim_profit = brew_profit ( sim_demand , sim_cost , sim_salvage ) print ( f "Profit at the most likely inputs (base case): { usd ( at_most_likely ) } " ) print ( f "Profit at the average inputs: { usd ( at_average ) } " ) print ( f "Average profit over { n : , } simulated seasons: { usd ( sim_profit . mean ()) } " ) Profit at the most likely inputs (base case): $26,000 Profit at the average inputs: $21,500 Average profit over 10,000 simulated seasons: $15,771 All three numbers describe "the same" plan, and they differ by about $10,000: Base case to average inputs (about $26,000 to $21,500): the most likely cost is not the average cost when the range is skewed. Average inputs to average outcome (about $21,500 to about $16,000): the MIN kink. Running out in good seasons costs more than average demand reveals. A plan built on the base case overstates the expected profit by more than half. Neither error is visible in a single-number spreadsheet, however carefully built. Kinks like this are everywhere: capacity limits, stock-outs, minimum orders, contract caps, tax thresholds, overtime. Misconception: "If I use the right averages, I get the right answer." Only if the model is a straight line in every uncertain input. The simple model of Part 2 is (and there the average of simulated profits does equal profit at average inputs). The brew-in-advance model is not. Excel steps: add the brew-in-advance model ¶ On the Model sheet, below the simple model: A10 Bottles brewed in advance , B10 45000 . A11 Salvage price per unsold bottle , B11 0.5 . (Blue: these are inputs.) D12 Bottles sold , E12 =MIN(B9,B10) . D13 Unsold bottles , E13 =B10-E12 . D14 Profit, brewing in advance , E14 =B4*E12 + B11*E13 - B5*B10 - E5 . Check: E14 shows $26,000 at the base inputs. Now change B5 to 1.8 and check $21,500 ; put B5 back to 1.7 . Part 7: Monte Carlo simulation: random inputs in Excel and numpy (core) ¶ A Monte Carlo simulation replaces each uncertain input with a random draw from a distribution, computes the output, and repeats this thousands of times. Each row is one possible season. The collection of results is a distribution of outcomes , from which we read averages, ranges and the chance of a loss. Choosing a distribution for each input ¶ Distribution Shape Use it when Excel numpy Uniform (continuous) Flat between a low and a high You know only a range, nothing about where in it =low+(high-low)*RAND() rng.uniform(low, high) Uniform (whole numbers) Flat, integers only Counts with a known range =RANDBETWEEN(low, high) (both ends included) rng.integers(low, high + 1) Normal Bell curve: mean μ, standard deviation σ Symmetric uncertainty, e.g. a regression prediction (Part 1) =NORM.INV(RAND(), μ, σ) rng.normal(μ, σ) Triangular Rises from a minimum to a most likely value, falls to a maximum Expert judgement: "at least, most likely, at most" formula below rng.triangular(min, mode, max) Why NORM.INV(RAND(), μ, σ) works. RAND() gives a number between 0 and 1, every value equally likely. NORM.INV(p, μ, σ) returns the value that a normal variable stays below with probability p . Feeding it a uniform random p turns flat randomness into bell-shaped randomness. This inverse-transform trick works for any distribution whose inverse you can write down. Triangular in Excel. Excel has no triangular function, so use the inverse-transform formula. With a minimum a , mode m , maximum b , and one uniform number U in its own cell : =IF(U < (m-a)/(b-a), a + SQRT(U*(b-a)*(m-a)), b - SQRT((1-U)*(b-a)*(b-m))) U must be one RAND() stored in a cell. Writing RAND() twice inside the formula draws two different numbers and produces a wrong shape. Part 8: Freezing a simulation: Paste Special → Values (core) ¶ RAND() , RANDBETWEEN() and anything built on them are volatile : Excel recalculates them whenever anything in the workbook changes, when you open the file, and when you press F9. That is how the simulation works, but it means the numbers in your report will not match the workbook your manager opens tomorrow. Excel steps: freeze the results ¶ Decide which results to keep. Usually you keep the full trial table and a copy of the summary. Select the simulated block, for example Sim!A1:G1001 , and copy it ( Ctrl+C / Cmd+C ). Best practice: paste onto a new sheet named Sim frozen so that the live model survives: click A1 there → Home → Paste ▾ → Paste Values (the clipboard icon with 123 ). Or right-click → Paste Special… → Values → OK . If you paste the values over the original cells instead, the formulas are gone ; you would have to rebuild them to run again. Keep a saved copy first. Write a note beside the frozen table: date, number of trials, and "frozen with Paste Special → Values". Two alternatives, each with a cost: Formulas → Calculation Options → Manual. Nothing recalculates until you press F9. But this setting travels with Excel, not just the file, and a colleague may see stale numbers everywhere without knowing why. Data → Data Analysis → Random Number Generation (Analysis ToolPak) can generate random numbers from several distributions with a Random Seed box. Its output is plain numbers, not formulas, so it is reproducible, but it does not refresh. In Python the seed does the freezing: the same seed gives the same numbers on every run, on every computer with the same numpy version. def run ( seed , n = 1_000 ): """One simulated batch of Brightleaf seasons; returns the profits.""" r = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) d = np . maximum ( 0 , np . round ( r . normal ( 40000 , 9000 , n ))) c = r . triangular ( 1.50 , 1.70 , 2.20 , n ) s = r . uniform ( 0.30 , 0.70 , n ) return brew_profit ( d , c , s ) print ( "Seed 1, run twice: " , usd ( run ( 1 ) . mean ()), usd ( run ( 1 ) . mean ())) print ( "Seeds 2, 3 and 4: " , usd ( run ( 2 ) . mean ()), usd ( run ( 3 ) . mean ()), usd ( run ( 4 ) . mean ())) Seed 1, run twice: $14,841 $14,841 Seeds 2, 3 and 4: $15,158 $16,708 $15,515 Same seed, same answer; different seeds, slightly different answers. Neither is "the right one". The spread between them is the subject of the next part. Misconception: "Freezing the numbers makes the result more accurate." It makes it repeatable . If 1,000 trials gave a noisy estimate, the frozen copy is the same noisy estimate, now fixed in place. Part 9: How many trials? (core) ¶ Each simulated batch is a sample of possible seasons, so every statistic from it (the average profit, the probability of a loss) has sampling error , exactly like a survey. More trials, less error, but with diminishing returns: the error shrinks with the square root of the number of trials. Standard error of the average: SD of the trial results ÷ √n. Standard error of a probability p : √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n). Quadrupling the trials halves the error. Going from 1,000 to 100,000 trials makes the error ten times smaller. Predict, then run. The true probability of a loss in this model is about 25%. With only 50 trials, how far from 25% could one batch's estimate easily be: 1 point, 5 points or 15 points? rows = [] for n in ( 50 , 500 , 5_000 , 50_000 ): estimates = [ np . mean ( run ( seed , n ) < 0 ) for seed in range ( 100 , 105 )] p = np . mean ( estimates ) rows . append ({ "trials" : n , "five batches (probability of loss)" : " " . join ( f " { e : .1% } " for e in estimates ), "± 2 standard errors" : f "± { 2 * np . sqrt ( p * ( 1 - p ) / n ) : .1% } " }) print ( pd . The running lines wander early and settle as trials accumulate. How to choose the number of trials: Decide how precise each number must be for the decision . If the board will act differently at a 20% and a 30% chance of loss, the estimate must be good to well under ±5 points. Use the standard-error formulas to find the n that gives that precision. For ±2 points at p ≈ 25%: n ≈ 4 × 0.25 × 0.75 ÷ 0.02² ≈ 1,900 trials. Run the batch twice with different seeds (in Excel: press F9 and compare). If the answer that matters moves, add trials. Tails need more trials than averages. A 5th percentile is estimated from the worst few percent of trials only, so it is noisier than the mean. Report the estimate with its precision: "about 25% (± 2 points)". In Excel, 1,000 to 10,000 rows are practical. For more, a classic trick is a one-way Data Table with an empty input cell : list 1 to 1,000 in a column, put a summary cell (such as the average profit of the Sim sheet) in the formula row, choose any empty cell on the same sheet as the Column input cell , and Excel recalculates the whole sheet once per row, collecting 1,000 batch results (an extension; it is slow on large sheets). Misconception: "My simulation gives a 24.1% chance of loss." The decimal is noise unless you ran tens of thousands of trials. Round to what the trials support. Part 10: Risk measures and reading the histogram (core) ¶ An average alone is a poor summary of risk. These measures describe the whole distribution of outcomes: Measure Question it answers Excel (results in Sim!G2:G1001 ) numpy Mean What do we earn on average? =AVERAGE(G2:G1001) profit.mean() Standard deviation How spread out are the outcomes? =STDEV.S(G2:G1001) profit.std(ddof=1) Probability of loss How often do we lose money? =COUNTIF(G2:G1001,"<0")/COUNT(G2:G1001) np.mean(profit < 0) 5th percentile (P5) How bad is a 1-in-20 bad season? =PERCENTILE.INC(G2:G1001, 0.05) np.percentile(profit, 5) Median (P50) What is the middle outcome? =MEDIAN(G2:G1001) np.median(profit) 95th percentile (P95) How good is a 1-in-20 good season? =PERCENTILE.INC(G2:G1001, 0.95) np.percentile(profit, 95) Minimum and maximum What did the worst and best trials show? =MIN(...) , =MAX(...) profit.min() , profit.max() Chance of meeting the plan How often do we reach the base-case profit? =COUNTIF(G2:G1001,">="&26000)/COUNT(G2:G1001) np.mean(profit >= 26000) Expected shortfall (extension) When a bad season happens, how bad is it on average? =AVERAGEIF(G2:G1001,"<="&P5cell) profit[profit <= p5].mean() Two notes on matching Excel and numpy. STDEV.S divides by n − 1, so use ddof=1 ; numpy's default ( ddof=0 ) gives a slightly smaller number. numpy's default percentile method gives the same result as PERCENTILE.INC . P5 as value at risk. Banks summarise risk with value at risk (VaR) : the loss that is exceeded only with a small probability, such as 5%. The 5th percentile of profit plays the same role here. If P5 is −$30,000, then "in one season out of twenty, we lose $30,000 or more". It is not the worst case; one season in twenty is worse. Minimum and maximum are weak measures. They come from a single trial each, so they change a lot from batch to batch, and they grow more extreme as you add trials. Report percentiles instead. Predict, then run.
