docs.text: The first cell loads the libraries and sets colour-blind-safe colours. Every random number in this notebook comes from a numpy generator with a fixed seed , such as np.random.default_rng(2026) . A seed makes the "random" numbers repeat exactly each time the cell runs, which is what lets us talk about specific results. Excel's RAND() has no seed: your spreadsheet's numbers will differ from these, and from your neighbour's. They should be close , not identical (Part 9 explains how close). import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt import statsmodels.formula.api as smf from scipy.stats import norm pd . set_option ( "display.width" , 120 ) pd . set_option ( "display.max_columns" , 20 ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.dpi" : 100 , "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4.2 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlesize" : 11 }) # Okabe and Ito colour-blind-safe colours BLUE , ORANGE , GREEN , PURPLE , SKY , GREY , YELLOW = "#0072B2" , "#D55E00" , "#009E73" , "#CC79A7" , "#56B4E9" , "#9A9A9A" , "#E69F00" def usd ( x ): """Format a dollar amount for printing, with a minus sign for losses.""" return f "-$ { - x : ,.0f } " if x < 0 else f "$ { x : ,.0f } "
docs.title: Setup

docs.text: Yesterday you built regressions. Today a regression's output becomes the input to a decision model, so it pays to read it the way a manager must: what it predicts, how wrong it is likely to be, and where it stops applying. The case. Brightleaf will sell a bottled cold-brew tea at summer festivals for one season, at $4.00 a bottle . It has booked 30 festival days . How many bottles will it sell? The parent company has records of 24 earlier first-season launches by its sister brands: how many festival days each booked, and how many bottles each sold in its first season. Predict, then run. Each extra festival day booked goes with how many extra bottles sold, roughly: 100, 1,000 or 10,000? # 24 earlier first-season launches by sister brands (synthetic) rng = np . random . default_rng ( 185 ) days = rng . integers ( 10 , 46 , 24 ) launches = pd . DataFrame ({ "festival_days" : days , "bottles_sold" : np . round ( - 1500 + 1380 * days + rng . normal ( 0 , 8500 , 24 ), - 1 ), }) print ( launches . describe () . round ( 0 ) . loc [[ "count" , "mean" , "min" , "max" ]]) fit = smf . ols ( "bottles_sold ~ festival_days" , data = launches ) . fit () b0 , b1 = fit . params [ "Intercept" ], fit . params [ "festival_days" ] rmse_in = np . sqrt ( fit . scale ) # standard error of the estimate (Excel: STEYX) print ( f " \n bottles_sold = { b0 : ,.0f } + { b1 : ,.0f } x festival_days" ) print ( f "R-squared: { fit . rsquared : .2f } Standard error of the estimate: { rmse_in : ,.0f } bottles" ) lo , hi = fit . conf_int () . loc [ "festival_days" ] print ( f "95% confidence interval for the slope: { lo : ,.0f } to { hi : ,.0f } bottles per day" ) festival_days bottles_sold count 24.0 24.0 mean 25.0 32500.0 min 10.0 5180.0 max 45.0 61830.0 bottles_sold = -1,753 + 1,396 x festival_days R-squared: 0.77 Standard error of the estimate: 8,668 bottles 95% confidence interval for the slope: 1,055 to 1,736 bottles per day How a manager reads this output: Output Sentence for a manager Slope "Among past launches, each extra festival day booked went with about 1,400 more bottles sold in the first season, on average ." Not "booking a day adds 1,400 bottles": brands that expected to do well may have booked more days (Day 4, Part 12) Intercept The prediction for zero festival days. Nobody launches with zero days, so it has no business meaning; it only positions the line R² Festival days account for about three-quarters of the variation in first-season sales among these 24 launches. A quarter is something else: weather, flavour, location, luck Standard error of the estimate A typical miss for a single launch is about 9,000 bottles . This is the number a planner most needs, and it is often not on the slide Range The 24 launches booked between 10 and 45 days. Thirty days is inside that range, so we are interpolating , not extrapolating (Day 4, Part 11) Sample size 24 launches is a small sample: the slope's 95% interval is wide, and a different 24 launches would give a somewhat different line Now the step that links regression to today's topic. Brightleaf's planners need the prediction for 30 days and, just as importantly, how far off it could be . new = pd . DataFrame ({ "festival_days" : [ 30 ]}) pred = fit . get_prediction ( new ) . summary_frame ( alpha = 0.05 ) point = pred [ "mean" ] . iloc [ 0 ] se_pred = np . sqrt ( pred [ "mean_se" ] . iloc [ 0 ] ** 2 + fit . scale ) # error of a single new launch print ( f "Predicted first-season sales at 30 days: { point : ,.0f } bottles" ) print ( f "Standard error for one new launch: { se_pred : ,.0f } bottles" ) print ( f "95% prediction interval: { pred [ 'obs_ci_lower' ] . iloc [ 0 ] : ,.0f } " f "to { pred [ 'obs_ci_upper' ] . iloc [ 0 ] : ,.0f } bottles" ) xs = np . linspace ( 8 , 47 , 100 ) band = fit . get_prediction ( pd . DataFrame ({ "festival_days" : xs })) . summary_frame ( alpha = 0.05 ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . fill_between ( xs , band [ "obs_ci_lower" ], band [ "obs_ci_upper" ], color = SKY , alpha = 0.3 , label = "95% prediction interval" ) ax . scatter ( launches [ "festival_days" ], launches [ "bottles_sold" ], color = BLUE , s = 22 , label = "Past launches" ) ax . plot ( xs , band [ "mean" ], color = ORANGE , lw = 2 , label = "Fitted line" ) ax . axvline ( 30 , color = GREY , ls = ":" , lw = 1 ) ax . errorbar ( 30 , point , yerr = [[ point - pred [ "obs_ci_lower" ] . iloc [ 0 ]], [ pred [ "obs_ci_upper" ] . iloc [ 0 ] - point ]], fmt = "o" , color = "black" , capsize = 5 , label = "Brightleaf, 30 days" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Festival days booked" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "First-season bottles sold" ) ax . set_title ( "One prediction, a wide range of plausible outcomes" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Predicted first-season sales at 30 days: 40,119 bottles Standard error for one new launch: 8,892 bottles 95% prediction interval: 21,678 to 58,559 bottles The prediction is about 40,000 bottles , but a single new launch could plausibly land anywhere from about 22,000 to 59,000 . A regression's prediction is not a number; it is the centre of a distribution . For the rest of the day, Brightleaf's planners treat demand as uncertain with: mean demand = 40,000 bottles and standard deviation = 9,000 bottles (both rounded from the output above). That pair of numbers is exactly what NORM.INV(RAND(), 40000, 9000) needs in Part 7. This is the bridge from predictive analytics (Day 4) to prescriptive analytics (today): the prediction says what is likely; the simulation says what to do about it.
docs.title: Part 1: Reading a regression for a manager (core)

docs.text: Put the 24 launches in a sheet named Launches , festival days in A2:A25 and bottles sold in B2:B25 . Slope: in D2 type =SLOPE(B2:B25, A2:A25) . Intercept: in D3 type =INTERCEPT(B2:B25, A2:A25) . R²: in D4 type =RSQ(B2:B25, A2:A25) . Prediction at 30 days: in D5 type =FORECAST.LINEAR(30, B2:B25, A2:A25) . (Older Excel: =FORECAST(...) , same arguments.) Standard error of the estimate: in D6 type =STEYX(B2:B25, A2:A25) . Standard error for one new launch (slightly larger than STEYX , because the line itself is uncertain): in D7 type =D6*SQRT(1 + 1/COUNT(A2:A25) + (30-AVERAGE(A2:A25))^2/DEVSQ(A2:A25)) . 95% prediction interval: in D8 type =D5 - T.INV.2T(0.05, COUNT(A2:A25)-2)*D7 and in D9 type =D5 + T.INV.2T(0.05, COUNT(A2:A25)-2)*D7 . Full regression table (optional): File → Options → Add-ins → Manage: Excel Add-ins → Go… → tick Analysis ToolPak → OK (Mac: Tools → Excel Add-ins… → Analysis ToolPak ). Then Data → Data Analysis → Regression → OK ; Input Y Range B1:B25 , Input X Range A1:A25 , tick Labels → OK . The Standard Error in the Regression Statistics block is the same number as STEYX . The numpy mirror below recomputes steps 1–5 from the formulas, so you can see there is nothing hidden in Excel's functions. x , y = launches [ "festival_days" ] . to_numpy (), launches [ "bottles_sold" ] . to_numpy () n = len ( x ) slope = np . sum (( x - x . mean ()) * ( y - y . mean ())) / np . sum (( x - x . mean ()) ** 2 ) # SLOPE intercept = y . mean () - slope * x . mean () # INTERCEPT steyx = np . sqrt ( np . sum (( y - ( intercept + slope * x )) ** 2 ) / ( n - 2 )) # STEYX forecast = intercept + slope * 30 # FORECAST.LINEAR se_new = steyx * np . sqrt ( 1 + 1 / n + ( 30 - x . mean ()) ** 2 / np . sum (( x - x . mean ()) ** 2 )) print ( f "SLOPE { slope : ,.1f } INTERCEPT { intercept : ,.0f } STEYX { steyx : ,.0f } " ) print ( f "FORECAST.LINEAR(30) { forecast : ,.0f } SE for a new launch { se_new : ,.0f } " ) print ( "Matches statsmodels:" , np . isclose ( forecast , point ) and np . isclose ( se_new , se_pred )) SLOPE 1,395.7 INTERCEPT -1,753 STEYX 8,668 FORECAST.LINEAR(30) 40,119 SE for a new launch 8,892 Matches statsmodels: True Misconception: "R² is 0.77, so the prediction is 77% accurate." R² compares the line with simply predicting the average launch. It says nothing directly about how far off one prediction may be. For planning, the standard error (in bottles) is the number that matters. Check your understanding. A colleague plans the season around "40,000 bottles" and nothing else. Using the prediction interval, give one way the plan could go badly wrong in each direction.
docs.title: Excel steps: the same regression in a spreadsheet

docs.text: What is it for? Predicting a number (judge the error on new cases) or explaining a lever (judge the coefficients and confounding)? How big is a typical miss, in the units I care about? Ask for RMSE or the standard error, not only R². Was it tested on data it had not seen? (Part 15; Day 4, Part 5.) Is my case inside the range of the data? Would acting on the lever really change the outcome? A coefficient is a comparison, not a promise.
docs.title: Five questions a manager should ask of any regression

docs.text: A financial model turns assumptions into a result. A good one has three visibly separate layers: Layer What it holds Convention Inputs (assumptions) Numbers nobody can calculate from anything else: price, unit cost, demand, fees Typed in once, coloured blue Calculations Formulas that combine inputs Black ; never type a number into a formula Outputs The few numbers a decision-maker reads: profit, break-even Clearly labelled, often boxed Why it matters: when the price changes, you change one blue cell and every result updates. A number typed inside a formula ( =40000*4-60000 ) is invisible, cannot be varied by a Data Table, and is the most common cause of wrong spreadsheets.
docs.title: Part 2: Anatomy of a spreadsheet model; the deterministic base case (core)

docs.text: The deterministic base case uses one value for every input, usually the planners' best guess. "Deterministic" means no randomness: the same inputs always give the same output. Input Value Notes Price per bottle $4.00 Brightleaf's decision Variable cost per bottle $1.70 Tea, bottle, label, cold storage; the most likely value Festival days 30 Booked Stall fee per day $1,200 Charged by the festivals Equipment and marketing $24,000 For the season Demand 40,000 bottles From Part 1 Three ideas carry most of the analysis: Contribution margin per bottle = price − variable cost = $4.00 − $1.70 = $2.30 . Each bottle sold "contributes" $2.30 towards the fixed costs, and then to profit. Fixed costs = 30 × $1,200 + $24,000 = $60,000 . They are paid whether Brightleaf sells one bottle or 60,000. Break-even demand = fixed costs ÷ contribution margin = $60,000 ÷ $2.30 ≈ 26,087 bottles : the sales at which profit is exactly zero. Margin of safety = (expected demand − break-even) ÷ expected demand: how far demand can fall short of the plan before the season loses money. Predict, then run. At 40,000 bottles, will the season's profit be nearer $10,000, $30,000 or $90,000? And how far can demand fall below 40,000 before Brightleaf loses money: about 10%, 35% or 60%? inputs = { "price" : 4.00 , "unit_cost" : 1.70 , "days" : 30 , "stall_fee" : 1200 , "equipment_marketing" : 24000 , "demand" : 40000 } def model ( price , unit_cost , days , stall_fee , equipment_marketing , demand ): """Brightleaf's season, brewing exactly what is sold (the simple model).""" margin = price - unit_cost # contribution margin per bottle fixed = days * stall_fee + equipment_marketing # fixed costs revenue = price * demand variable = unit_cost * demand profit = revenue - variable - fixed break_even = fixed / margin return { "contribution_margin" : margin , "fixed_costs" : fixed , "revenue" : revenue , "variable_costs" : variable , "profit" : profit , "break_even_demand" : break_even , "margin_of_safety" : ( demand - break_even ) / demand } base = model ( ** inputs ) for k , v in base . items (): print ( f " { k : >20 } : { v : >12,.2f } " if k in ( "contribution_margin" , "margin_of_safety" ) else f " { k : >20 } : { v : >12,.0f } " ) contribution_margin: 2.30 fixed_costs: 60,000 revenue: 160,000 variable_costs: 68,000 profit: 32,000 break_even_demand: 26,087 margin_of_safety: 0.35 The base case says $32,000 profit , with a break-even at about 26,100 bottles and a margin of safety of about 35% : demand can fall roughly a third below plan before the season makes a loss. Part 1 showed that demand could easily land below 26,000, which is the first hint that the base case alone is not enough.
docs.title: Brightleaf's base case

docs.text: Name the sheet Model . Type the labels in column A, the inputs in column B and the calculations in column E, exactly as below. Colour the inputs in B4:B9 blue ( Home → Font Color ). A3 Inputs . A4 Price per bottle , B4 4 . A5 Variable cost per bottle , B5 1.7 . A6 Festival days , B6 30 . A7 Stall fee per day , B7 1200 . A8 Equipment and marketing , B8 24000 . A9 Demand (bottles) , B9 40000 . D3 Calculations and outputs . D4 Contribution margin , E4 =B4-B5 . D5 Fixed costs , E5 =B6*B7+B8 . D6 Revenue , E6 =B4*B9 . D7 Variable costs , E7 =B5*B9 . D8 Profit , E8 =E6-E7-E5 . Put a border round E8 ( Home → Borders → Thick Outside Borders ): it is the output. D9 Break-even demand , E9 =E5/E4 . D10 Margin of safety , E10 =(B9-E9)/B9 , formatted as a percentage ( Home → % ). Format money cells as currency ( Home → Number Format → Currency ). Check: E8 shows $32,000 and E9 about 26,087. Then change B4 to 4.5 and watch E8 , E9 and E10 update; change it back. Misconception: "The base case is the most likely outcome." It is the outcome at the most likely value of each input . With several uncertain inputs, the chance that every one lands on its single most likely value at once is small. Part 6 shows that the base case can even be a poor guide to the average outcome. Check your understanding. The festival organisers offer a package: no stall fee, but they keep $0.40 of every bottle sold. Which cells change, and does the break-even demand rise or fall?
docs.title: Excel steps: build the model sheet

docs.text: A sensitivity analysis asks: if one input is wrong, how much does the output move? The simplest version is one at a time : set each input to a plausible low and high value while holding all others at the base case, and record the profit each time. Brightleaf's planners agreed these ranges. For demand they used the 10th and 90th percentiles of the Part 1 distribution, 40,000 ± 1.28 × 9,000. Input Low Base High Demand (bottles) 28,466 40,000 51,534 Price $3.50 $4.00 $4.50 Variable cost $1.50 $1.70 $2.20 Stall fee per day $1,000 $1,200 $1,500 Equipment and marketing $20,000 $24,000 $30,000 Predict, then run. Rank the five inputs from the one that moves profit most to the one that moves it least. ranges = { "demand" : ( 40000 - 1.2816 * 9000 , 40000 + 1.2816 * 9000 ), "price" : ( 3.50 , 4.50 ), "unit_cost" : ( 1.50 , 2.20 ), "stall_fee" : ( 1000 , 1500 ), "equipment_marketing" : ( 20000 , 30000 ), } rows = [] for name , ( low , high ) in ranges . items (): p_low = model ( ** { ** inputs , name : low })[ "profit" ] p_high = model ( ** { ** inputs , name : high })[ "profit" ] rows . append ({ "input" : name , "profit_at_low" : p_low , "profit_at_high" : p_high , "swing" : abs ( p_high - p_low )}) tornado = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . sort_values ( "swing" , ascending = False ) . reset_index ( drop = True ) print ( tornado . round ( 0 ) . to_string ( index = False )) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.6 )) base_profit = base [ "profit" ] order = tornado . iloc [:: - 1 ] for i , r in enumerate ( order . itertuples ()): left , right = sorted ([ r . profit_at_low , r . profit_at_high ]) ax . barh ( i , base_profit - left , left = left , color = ORANGE , height = 0.6 ) ax . barh ( i , right - base_profit , left = base_profit , color = BLUE , height = 0.6 ) ax . axvline ( base_profit , color = "black" , lw = 1 ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = GREY , ls = ":" , lw = 1 ) ax . set_yticks ( range ( len ( order )), order [ "input" ] . str . replace ( "_" , " " )) ax . set_xlabel ( "Season profit (US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Tornado chart: demand and price matter most" ) ax . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( lambda v , _ : usd ( v )) plt . show () input profit_at_low profit_at_high swing demand 5471.0 58529.0 53058.0 price 12000.0 52000.0 40000.0 unit_cost 40000.0 12000.0 28000.0 stall_fee 38000.0 23000.0 15000.0 equipment_marketing 36000.0 26000.0 10000.0 Read a tornado chart from the top: the widest bar is the input whose uncertainty matters most. Here demand swings profit by about $53,000, more than any other input, and price is second. Two lessons for the business: Spend effort where the bar is wide. Better demand information (a pilot, pre-orders) is worth more than haggling over the equipment budget. Asymmetric bars carry information. The variable-cost bar is longer on the bad side, because the planners think a cost rise to $2.20 is more plausible than a fall to $1.50. Part 6 shows why that skew matters. Price is different from the others: it is Brightleaf's decision , not an uncertainty. A tornado chart can include decisions, but label them, because the response is different (choose it, rather than plan around it).
docs.title: Part 3: Sensitivity analysis and the tornado chart (core)

docs.text: On the Model sheet, set up a small table in G3:J8 : headers G3 Input , H3 Profit at low , I3 Profit at high , J3 Swing ; input names in G4:G8 . Fill H4:I8 by changing each input in column B to its low value, copying the profit from E8 , then its high value, then putting the base value back. (Faster: use one-way Data Tables from Part 4, or paste the values with Paste Special → Values .) Never leave an input at a test value. In J4 type =ABS(I4-H4) and fill down to J8 . Select G3:J8 → Data → Sort → Sort by Swing , Order Largest to Smallest → OK. Add two helper columns: K4 =MIN(H4,I4)-$E$8 (the bar to the left) and L4 =MAX(H4,I4)-$E$8 (the bar to the right); fill down. Select G3:G8 , then hold Ctrl (Mac: Cmd ) and select K3:L8 → Insert → Charts → Bar → Clustered Bar . Right-click a bar → Format Data Series → Series Overlap 100% , Gap Width 50% . Right-click the vertical axis → Format Axis → tick Categories in reverse order , and set Label Position to Low so the labels sit at the left edge. The widest bar is now at the top. The horizontal axis shows the change from the base profit. Misconception: "One-at-a-time sensitivity shows the worst case." It moves one input at a time. In a bad season, demand may be low and the cost high together; that combination is not on the chart. Data Tables (two inputs at once) and simulation (all inputs at once) fill that gap.
docs.title: Excel steps: a tornado chart

docs.text: A Data Table recalculates one formula for a whole list of input values, and lays the results out in a grid. It answers "what if demand is 20,000? 25,000? … 60,000?" in one step, without touching the model. A one-way table varies one input and can show several outputs. A two-way table varies two inputs and shows one output for every combination. Predict, then run. In the two-way table below, at a price of $3.50 , at roughly what demand does profit cross zero? (Hint: contribution margin and fixed costs.) # One-way: profit and revenue for demand from 20,000 to 60,000 bottles demand_values = np . arange ( 20000 , 60001 , 5000 ) one_way = pd . DataFrame ({ "demand" : demand_values , "revenue" : [ model ( ** { ** inputs , "demand" : d })[ "revenue" ] for d in demand_values ], "profit" : [ model ( ** { ** inputs , "demand" : d })[ "profit" ] for d in demand_values ], }) print ( "One-way Data Table (demand)" ) print ( one_way . to_string ( index = False , formatters = { "revenue" : usd , "profit" : usd })) # Two-way: profit for each price (columns) and demand (rows), using numpy broadcasting prices = np . array ([ 3.00 , 3.50 , 4.00 , 4.50 , 5.00 ]) D , P = np . meshgrid ( demand_values , prices , indexing = "ij" ) fixed = inputs [ "days" ] * inputs [ "stall_fee" ] + inputs [ "equipment_marketing" ] profit_grid = ( P - inputs [ "unit_cost" ]) * D - fixed two_way = pd . DataFrame ( profit_grid , index = demand_values , columns = [ f "$ { p : .2f } " for p in prices ]) two_way . index . name = "demand" print ( " \n Two-way Data Table: profit by demand (rows) and price (columns)" ) print ( two_way . map ( lambda v : f " { v : >10,.0f } " ) . to_string ()) One-way Data Table (demand) demand revenue profit 20000 $80,000 -$14,000 25000 $100,000 -$2,500 30000 $120,000 $9,000 35000 $140,000 $20,500 40000 $160,000 $32,000 45000 $180,000 $43,500 50000 $200,000 $55,000 55000 $220,000 $66,500 60000 $240,000 $78,000 Two-way Data Table: profit by demand (rows) and price (columns) $3.00 $3.50 $4.00 $4.50 $5.00 demand 20000 -34,000 -24,000 -14,000 -4,000 6,000 25000 -27,500 -15,000 -2,500 10,000 22,500 30000 -21,000 -6,000 9,000 24,000 39,000 35000 -14,500 3,000 20,500 38,000 55,500 40000 -8,000 12,000 32,000 52,000 72,000 45000 -1,500 21,000 43,500 66,000 88,500 50000 5,000 30,000 55,000 80,000 105,000 55000 11,500 39,000 66,500 94,000 121,500 60000 18,000 48,000 78,000 108,000 138,000 fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 7 , 4 )) im = ax . imshow ( profit_grid / 1000 , cmap = "RdBu" , vmin =- 80 , vmax = 80 , aspect = "auto" , origin = "lower" ) ax . set_xticks ( range ( len ( prices )), [ f "$ { p : .2f } " for p in prices ]) ax . set_yticks ( range ( len ( demand_values )), [ f " { d : , } " for d in demand_values ]) for i in range ( len ( demand_values )): for j in range ( len ( prices )): ax . text ( j , i , f " { profit_grid [ i , j ] / 1000 : ,.0f } " , ha = "center" , va = "center" , fontsize = 8 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Price per bottle" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Demand (bottles)" ) ax . set_title ( "Profit in thousand US dollars: red cells lose money" ) fig . colorbar ( im , ax = ax , label = "Profit (thousand US dollars)" ) plt . show () The table shows the boundary between profit and loss, which no single cell can. At $3.50, the contribution margin is $1.80 and the break-even is $60,000 ÷ $1.80 ≈ 33,300 bottles, so the zero line falls between the 30,000 and 35,000 rows. At $5.00, Brightleaf breaks even below 20,000. A Data Table has a blind spot: it treats price and demand as independent . In reality a higher price usually means fewer bottles sold. The $5.00 column is not wrong arithmetic, but it answers "what if we charged $5.00 and still sold 40,000?", which may be fantasy. Part 11 returns to inputs that move together.
docs.title: Part 4: What-If Data Tables: one-way and two-way (core)

docs.text: The input cell must be on the same sheet as the Data Table. If you build the table on another sheet and click an input cell on Model , Excel refuses with "Input cell reference is not valid." So build the tables on the Model sheet (or move the inputs to the table's sheet). On Model , type the demand values down a column: G13 20000 , G14 25000 , … G21 60000 . (Type the first two, select both, and drag the fill handle down.) In the row above the first value and one column to the right , link the outputs: H12 =E6 (revenue) and I12 =E8 (profit). Leave G12 empty. Select the whole block G12:I21 , including the empty corner, the formula row and the values. Data → What-If Analysis → Data Table… Leave Row input cell empty. In Column input cell , click B9 (demand), because the demand values run down a column . → OK . Excel fills H13:I21 with {=TABLE(,B9)} . You cannot edit one cell of it; to change it, select the whole result range H13:I21 and press Delete , then rebuild. Format the results as currency. Hide the link row if you like (custom number format ;;; on H12:I12 ).
docs.title: Excel steps: one-way Data Table (demand)

docs.text: In K13:K21 type the demand values again (20000 … 60000). In L12:P12 type the prices 3 , 3.5 , 4 , 4.5 , 5 . In the corner cell K12 type =E8 . A two-way table has exactly one output, and it lives in the corner. Select K12:P21 . Data → What-If Analysis → Data Table… → Row input cell B4 (price, because prices run along the row ) → Column input cell B9 (demand) → OK . Colour the result: select L13:P21 → Home → Conditional Formatting → Color Scales → Red-White-Blue (or Highlight Cells Rules → Less Than… 0 in red). Check: the cell for demand 40,000 at price $4.00 shows $32,000 , the base case. Data Table trouble Cause Fix Input cell reference is not valid The input cell is on a different sheet from the table Build the table on the inputs' sheet Every result cell shows the same number Row and column input cells swapped, or the wrong cell chosen Delete the results and rebuild; prices along the top → row input The table does not update when inputs change Formulas → Calculation Options is set to Automatic Except for Data Tables Press F9 , or choose Automatic Cannot change part of a data table You tried to edit one result cell Select the whole result range and delete it Results ignore the corner formula The corner cell holds a number, not a formula linked to the output Type =E8 in the corner Misconception: "The Data Table is a simulation." It is a systematic sweep : every listed value counts once, however unlikely. A value at the edge of the grid looks as important as the centre. A simulation (Part 7) weights values by how likely they are.
docs.title: Excel steps: two-way Data Table (price × demand)
Part 5: Scenario Manager and Goal Seek (core)

docs.text: A scenario changes several inputs together to tell a consistent story. Brightleaf's planners wrote four: Scenario Demand Variable cost Stall fee Story Base 40,000 $1.70 $1,200 The plan Wet summer 28,000 $1.70 $1,200 Rain keeps crowds small Hot summer 52,000 $1.90 $1,200 Big crowds; extra ice and cold storage Supplier squeeze 40,000 $2.10 $1,300 Tea prices rise; festivals raise fees Predict, then run. Which scenario is worst for profit? Is the "Hot summer" better or worse than the base case, given that its cost is higher? scenarios = { "Base" : {}, "Wet summer" : { "demand" : 28000 }, "Hot summer" : { "demand" : 52000 , "unit_cost" : 1.90 }, "Supplier squeeze" : { "unit_cost" : 2.10 , "stall_fee" : 1300 }, } summary = pd . DataFrame ({ name : model ( ** { ** inputs , ** change }) for name , change in scenarios . items ()}) . T summary = summary [[ "revenue" , "variable_costs" , "fixed_costs" , "profit" , "break_even_demand" ]] print ( summary . map ( lambda v : f " { v : >10,.0f } " ) . to_string ()) revenue variable_costs fixed_costs profit break_even_demand Base 160,000 68,000 60,000 32,000 26,087 Wet summer 112,000 47,600 60,000 4,400 26,087 Hot summer 208,000 98,800 60,000 49,200 28,571 Supplier squeeze 160,000 84,000 63,000 13,000 33,158 Scenarios are good for communication ("in a wet summer, profit falls to about $4,000; under a supplier squeeze, to about $13,000") and for checking that the model behaves sensibly in each story. They are not probabilities : four scenarios do not mean each has a 25% chance, and "Base" is not "the" outcome. They also leave out every combination nobody wrote down.
docs.title: Scenarios: coherent stories, not single inputs

docs.text: First give the input cells names, so the report is readable: click B5 → type UnitCost in the Name Box (left of the formula bar) → Enter . Do the same for B7 ( StallFee ), B9 ( Demand ) and E8 ( Profit ). Data → What-If Analysis → Scenario Manager… → Add… Scenario name Base ; Changing cells B5,B7,B9 (type them with commas, or Ctrl-click / Cmd-click) → OK → keep the current values → OK . Add… again: Wet summer , same changing cells → OK → enter 1.7 , 1200 , 28000 → OK . Repeat for Hot summer ( 1.9 , 1200 , 52000 ) and Supplier squeeze ( 2.1 , 1300 , 40000 ). To view one scenario on the model, select it and click Show . To put the base back, show Base . Summary… → Report type Scenario summary , Result cells E8,E9 → OK . Excel adds a new sheet, Scenario Summary , with one column per scenario. It is a static snapshot: re-run the summary if the model changes.
docs.title: Excel steps: Scenario Manager

docs.text: Goal Seek answers "what input value gives the output I want?" by trial and error on one input cell. Break-even demand: set profit to 0 by changing demand. (We know the answer from the formula, so this is a good test of the tool.) Price for a target: at a cautious demand of 35,000 bottles, what price gives a profit of $40,000? Predict, then run. Is the price needed for $40,000 at 35,000 bottles above or below $4.50? def goal_seek ( f , target , lo , hi , tol = 1e-6 ): """Find x in [lo, hi] with f(x) = target by bisection (Goal Seek does a similar search).""" for _ in range ( 200 ): mid = ( lo + hi ) / 2 if ( f ( lo ) - target ) * ( f ( mid ) - target ) <= 0 : hi = mid else : lo = mid if hi - lo < tol : break return ( lo + hi ) / 2 be = goal_seek ( lambda d : model ( ** { ** inputs , "demand" : d })[ "profit" ], 0 , 1 , 100000 ) p_needed = goal_seek ( lambda p : model ( ** { ** inputs , "demand" : 35000 , "price" : p })[ "profit" ], 40000 , 1 , 10 ) print ( f "Goal Seek, profit = 0 by changing demand: { be : ,.2f } bottles" ) print ( f "Formula check, fixed / margin: { base [ 'break_even_demand' ] : ,.2f } bottles" ) print ( f "Goal Seek, profit = $40,000 at 35,000 by changing price: $ { p_needed : .3f } " ) Goal Seek, profit = 0 by changing demand: 26,086.96 bottles Formula check, fixed / margin: 26,086.96 bottles Goal Seek, profit = $40,000 at 35,000 by changing price: $4.557
docs.title: Goal Seek: solving backwards

docs.text: Data → What-If Analysis → Goal Seek… Set cell E8 (profit; it must contain a formula) · To value 0 · By changing cell B9 (demand; it must be a typed input) → OK . Excel reports Goal Seeking with Cell E8 found a solution and shows about 26,087 in B9 . Click Cancel to put the original 40,000 back, or OK to keep the new value. Goal Seek overwrites your input , so choose Cancel unless you mean to keep it. For the price question: set B9 to 35000 , then Set cell E8 , To value 40000 , By changing cell B4 → OK → read the price → Cancel . Put B9 back to 40000 . Goal Seek changes only one input and finds only one answer. For several inputs, or a target such as "the largest profit", Excel's Solver add-in does the job (it is an extension beyond this course). Never point Goal Seek at a cell that contains RAND() : the target moves every time Excel recalculates. Check your understanding. The Goal Seek answer for break-even is 26,086.96 bottles. How would you report it to the board, and why not to two decimal places?
docs.title: Excel steps: Goal Seek

docs.text: So far, profit has been a straight-line function of each input. Real businesses have kinks. Brightleaf has one: cold brew must be brewed and bottled before the season , because the festivals have no kitchen. Brightleaf plans to brew 45,000 bottles , a little above expected demand. Then: bottles sold = the smaller of demand and bottles brewed: MIN(demand, 45000) ; the variable cost is paid on every bottle brewed , sold or not; unsold bottles are sold to a discount retailer at a salvage price , about $0.50. There is also a second subtlety. The planners' cost of $1.70 is the most likely value, but they think costs could rise to $2.20 more easily than fall to $1.50. The average of such a skewed range is higher than its most likely value (for a triangular range, (1.50 + 1.70 + 2.20) ÷ 3 = $1.80 ). The flaw of averages (Sam Savage's name for it) is the belief that plugging average inputs into a model gives the average output. It is true only for straight-line models. With a kink like MIN , it is false. A pencil example. Suppose demand is equally likely to be 31,000, 40,000 or 49,000 (average 40,000), the cost is $1.80, and Brightleaf brews 45,000. Demand Sold Revenue + salvage Cost of 45,000 brewed Fixed Profit 31,000 31,000 $124,000 + $7,000 $81,000 $60,000 −$10,000 40,000 40,000 $160,000 + $2,500 $81,000 $60,000 $21,500 49,000 45,000 $180,000 + $0 $81,000 $60,000 $39,000 Average $16,833 The profit at average demand is $21,500, but the average profit is $16,833. In good seasons the extra demand is lost (Brightleaf runs out), while in bad seasons every unsold bottle still cost money. The downside counts in full; the upside is capped. Predict, then run. The code computes Brightleaf's profit three ways: at the most likely inputs, at the average inputs, and as the average of 10,000 simulated seasons. Put the three in order from largest to smallest. PRICE , Q , FIXED = 4.00 , 45000 , 60000 def brew_profit ( demand , unit_cost , salvage , brewed = Q , price = PRICE , fixed = FIXED ): """Season profit when `brewed` bottles are made in advance (works on arrays too).""" sold = np . minimum ( demand , brewed ) return price * sold + salvage * ( brewed - sold ) - unit_cost * brewed - fixed at_most_likely = brew_profit ( 40000 , 1.70 , 0.50 ) at_average = brew_profit ( 40000 , ( 1.50 + 1.70 + 2.20 ) / 3 , 0.50 ) rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) n = 10_000 sim_demand = np . maximum ( 0 , np . round ( rng . normal ( 40000 , 9000 , n ))) sim_cost = rng . triangular ( 1.50 , 1.70 , 2.20 , n ) sim_salvage = rng . uniform ( 0.30 , 0.70 , n ) sim_profit = brew_profit ( sim_demand , sim_cost , sim_salvage ) print ( f "Profit at the most likely inputs (base case): { usd ( at_most_likely ) } " ) print ( f "Profit at the average inputs: { usd ( at_average ) } " ) print ( f "Average profit over { n : , } simulated seasons: { usd ( sim_profit . mean ()) } " ) Profit at the most likely inputs (base case): $26,000 Profit at the average inputs: $21,500 Average profit over 10,000 simulated seasons: $15,771 All three numbers describe "the same" plan, and they differ by about $10,000: Base case to average inputs (about $26,000 to $21,500): the most likely cost is not the average cost when the range is skewed. Average inputs to average outcome (about $21,500 to about $16,000): the MIN kink. Running out in good seasons costs more than average demand reveals. A plan built on the base case overstates the expected profit by more than half. Neither error is visible in a single-number spreadsheet, however carefully built. Kinks like this are everywhere: capacity limits, stock-outs, minimum orders, contract caps, tax thresholds, overtime. Misconception: "If I use the right averages, I get the right answer." Only if the model is a straight line in every uncertain input. The simple model of Part 2 is (and there the average of simulated profits does equal profit at average inputs). The brew-in-advance model is not.
docs.title: Part 6: The flaw of averages (core)

docs.text: On the Model sheet, below the simple model: A10 Bottles brewed in advance , B10 45000 . A11 Salvage price per unsold bottle , B11 0.5 . (Blue: these are inputs.) D12 Bottles sold , E12 =MIN(B9,B10) . D13 Unsold bottles , E13 =B10-E12 . D14 Profit, brewing in advance , E14 =B4*E12 + B11*E13 - B5*B10 - E5 . Check: E14 shows $26,000 at the base inputs. Now change B5 to 1.8 and check $21,500 ; put B5 back to 1.7 .
docs.title: Excel steps: add the brew-in-advance model

docs.text: A Monte Carlo simulation replaces each uncertain input with a random draw from a distribution, computes the output, and repeats this thousands of times. Each row is one possible season. The collection of results is a distribution of outcomes , from which we read averages, ranges and the chance of a loss.
docs.title: Part 7: Monte Carlo simulation: random inputs in Excel and numpy (core)

docs.text: Distribution Shape Use it when Excel numpy Uniform (continuous) Flat between a low and a high You know only a range, nothing about where in it =low+(high-low)*RAND() rng.uniform(low, high) Uniform (whole numbers) Flat, integers only Counts with a known range =RANDBETWEEN(low, high) (both ends included) rng.integers(low, high + 1) Normal Bell curve: mean μ, standard deviation σ Symmetric uncertainty, e.g. a regression prediction (Part 1) =NORM.INV(RAND(), μ, σ) rng.normal(μ, σ) Triangular Rises from a minimum to a most likely value, falls to a maximum Expert judgement: "at least, most likely, at most" formula below rng.triangular(min, mode, max) Why NORM.INV(RAND(), μ, σ) works. RAND() gives a number between 0 and 1, every value equally likely. NORM.INV(p, μ, σ) returns the value that a normal variable stays below with probability p . Feeding it a uniform random p turns flat randomness into bell-shaped randomness. This inverse-transform trick works for any distribution whose inverse you can write down. Triangular in Excel. Excel has no triangular function, so use the inverse-transform formula. With a minimum a , mode m , maximum b , and one uniform number U in its own cell : =IF(U < (m-a)/(b-a), a + SQRT(U*(b-a)*(m-a)), b - SQRT((1-U)*(b-a)*(b-m))) U must be one RAND() stored in a cell. Writing RAND() twice inside the formula draws two different numbers and produces a wrong shape. Brightleaf's uncertain inputs: Input Distribution Why Demand Normal, mean 40,000, SD 9,000, never below 0 The regression's prediction and its error (Part 1) Variable cost Triangular: $1.50, $1.70, $2.20 The planners' judgement, skewed upwards Salvage price Uniform, $0.30 to $0.70 The discount retailer gave a range, nothing more Price, bottles brewed and fixed costs stay fixed: they are decisions or contracts. Predict, then run. The chart below compares normal demand with RANDBETWEEN(25000, 55000) , which has the same mean (40,000). Which one produces more seasons with demand below 26,000 (the break-even)? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 7 ) n = 10_000 d_normal = rng . normal ( 40000 , 9000 , n ) d_between = rng . integers ( 25000 , 55001 , n ) # RANDBETWEEN(25000, 55000) c_tri = rng . triangular ( 1.50 , 1.70 , 2.20 , n ) s_uni = rng . uniform ( 0.30 , 0.70 , n ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.2 )) axes [ 0 ] . hist ( d_normal , bins = 50 , color = BLUE , alpha = 0.7 , label = "NORM.INV(RAND(), 40000, 9000)" ) axes [ 0 ] . hist ( d_between , bins = 50 , color = ORANGE , alpha = 0.5 , label = "RANDBETWEEN(25000, 55000)" ) axes [ 0 ] . axvline ( 26087 , color = "black" , ls = ":" , lw = 1 ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Demand (bottles)" ) axes [ 0 ] . legend ( frameon = False , fontsize = 7 , loc = "upper left" ) axes [ 1 ] . hist ( c_tri , bins = 50 , color = GREEN ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Variable cost: triangular" ) axes [ 2 ] . hist ( s_uni , bins = 50 , color = PURPLE ) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "Salvage price: uniform" ) for ax in axes : ax . set_yticks ([]) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () print ( f "Share below 26,000 bottles, normal: { np . mean ( d_normal < 26000 ) : .1% } " ) print ( f "Share below 26,000 bottles, RANDBETWEEN: { np . mean ( d_between < 26000 ) : .1% } " ) print ( f "Mean cost, triangular: $ { c_tri . mean () : .3f } (most likely $1.70; formula (a+m+b)/3 = $1.800)" ) Share below 26,000 bottles, normal: 6.1% Share below 26,000 bottles, RANDBETWEEN: 3.1% Mean cost, triangular: $1.801 (most likely $1.70; formula (a+m+b)/3 = $1.800) The two demand distributions have the same average, but the normal one has tails : it puts about twice as many seasons below break-even, including some far below 25,000, which RANDBETWEEN(25000, 55000) rules out completely. The choice of distribution is an assumption , and it changes the answer to "how likely is a loss?". Write it down and justify it, as in the table above.
docs.title: Choosing a distribution for each input

docs.text: Add a sheet named Sim . Formulas on this sheet may refer to Model (only Data Table input cells must share the table's sheet). First add the distribution settings to Model as blue inputs: On Model : A16 Demand mean , B16 40000 ; A17 Demand SD , B17 9000 ; A18 Cost minimum , B18 1.5 ; A19 Cost most likely , B19 1.7 ; A20 Cost maximum , B20 2.2 ; A21 Salvage low , B21 0.3 ; A22 Salvage high , B22 0.7 . On Sim , row 1 headers: A1 Trial , B1 U for cost , C1 Demand , D1 Unit cost , E1 Salvage price , F1 Bottles sold , G1 Profit . A2 1 ; A3 =A2+1 . B2 =RAND() C2 =MAX(0, ROUND(NORM.INV(RAND(), Model!$B$16, Model!$B$17), 0)) D2 =IF(B2<(Model!$B$19-Model!$B$18)/(Model!$B$20-Model!$B$18), Model!$B$18+SQRT(B2*(Model!$B$20-Model!$B$18)*(Model!$B$19-Model!$B$18)), Model!$B$20-SQRT((1-B2)*(Model!$B$20-Model!$B$18)*(Model!$B$20-Model!$B$19))) E2 =Model!$B$21+(Model!$B$22-Model!$B$21)*RAND() F2 =MIN(C2, Model!$B$10) G2 =Model!$B$4*F2 + E2*(Model!$B$10-F2) - D2*Model!$B$10 - Model!$E$5 Copy A3 down to A1001 . Select B2:G2 , copy, select B3:G1001 , paste. You now have 1,000 trials . (Tip: type B2:G1001 in the Name Box and press Ctrl+D to fill down in one step.) The $ signs matter: Model!$B$16 stays fixed when copied down, while B2 moves to B3 , B4 , … Leave them out and row 3 reads the wrong inputs. Press F9 a few times. Every number changes: each press is a fresh set of 1,000 seasons. The numpy mirror draws the same inputs for 1,000 trials and builds the same table. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) n_trials = 1_000 u = rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , n_trials ) # column B: RAND() demand = np . maximum ( 0 , np . round ( norm . ppf ( rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , n_trials ), 40000 , 9000 ))) # NORM.INV(RAND(), ...) a , m , b = 1.50 , 1.70 , 2.20 unit_cost = np . where ( u < ( m - a ) / ( b - a ), # the triangular formula, as in Excel a + np . sqrt ( u * ( b - a ) * ( m - a )), b - np . sqrt (( 1 - u ) * ( b - a ) * ( b - m ))) salvage = 0.30 + ( 0.70 - 0.30 ) * rng . uniform ( 0 , 1 , n_trials ) # low + (high - low) * RAND() sold = np . minimum ( demand , Q ) profit = PRICE * sold + salvage * ( Q - sold ) - unit_cost * Q - FIXED sim = pd . DataFrame ({ "trial" : np . arange ( 1 , n_trials + 1 ), "u_cost" : u , "demand" : demand , "unit_cost" : unit_cost , "salvage" : salvage , "sold" : sold , "profit" : profit }) print ( sim . head () . round ( 3 ) . to_string ( index = False )) print ( f " \n Average profit over { n_trials : , } trials: { usd ( profit . mean ()) } " ) print ( f "Share of trials with a loss: { np . mean ( profit < 0 ) : .1% } " ) trial u_cost demand unit_cost salvage sold profit 1 0.179 47688.0 1.658 0.559 45000.0 45377.639 2 0.640 28283.0 1.845 0.693 28283.0 -18309.121 3 0.467 44778.0 1.768 0.378 44778.0 39627.061 4 0.371 41739.0 1.731 0.686 41739.0 31315.474 5 0.355 44962.0 1.725 0.680 44962.0 42256.127 Average profit over 1,000 trials: $14,833 Share of trials with a loss: 27.1% Misconception: "A random input means the model is guessing." The randomness is structured : each input is drawn from a distribution chosen from data (the regression) or from documented judgement (the triangular cost). What is random is which season we get, not the rules of the business. Check your understanding. A colleague models a count of rainy festival days with =RANDBETWEEN(0, 5) in Excel and mirrors it in numpy as rng.integers(0, 5) . Why will the two never agree, and what is the fix?
docs.title: Excel steps: the simulation sheet

docs.text: RAND() , RANDBETWEEN() and anything built on them are volatile : Excel recalculates them whenever anything in the workbook changes, when you open the file, and when you press F9. That is how the simulation works, but it means the numbers in your report will not match the workbook your manager opens tomorrow.
docs.title: Part 8: Freezing a simulation: Paste Special → Values (core)

docs.text: Decide which results to keep. Usually you keep the full trial table and a copy of the summary. Select the simulated block, for example Sim!A1:G1001 , and copy it ( Ctrl+C / Cmd+C ). Best practice: paste onto a new sheet named Sim frozen so that the live model survives: click A1 there → Home → Paste ▾ → Paste Values (the clipboard icon with 123 ). Or right-click → Paste Special… → Values → OK . If you paste the values over the original cells instead, the formulas are gone ; you would have to rebuild them to run again. Keep a saved copy first. Write a note beside the frozen table: date, number of trials, and "frozen with Paste Special → Values". Two alternatives, each with a cost: Formulas → Calculation Options → Manual. Nothing recalculates until you press F9. But this setting travels with Excel, not just the file, and a colleague may see stale numbers everywhere without knowing why. Data → Data Analysis → Random Number Generation (Analysis ToolPak) can generate random numbers from several distributions with a Random Seed box. Its output is plain numbers, not formulas, so it is reproducible, but it does not refresh. In Python the seed does the freezing: the same seed gives the same numbers on every run, on every computer with the same numpy version. def run ( seed , n = 1_000 ): """One simulated batch of Brightleaf seasons; returns the profits.""" r = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) d = np . maximum ( 0 , np . round ( r . normal ( 40000 , 9000 , n ))) c = r . triangular ( 1.50 , 1.70 , 2.20 , n ) s = r . uniform ( 0.30 , 0.70 , n ) return brew_profit ( d , c , s ) print ( "Seed 1, run twice: " , usd ( run ( 1 ) . mean ()), usd ( run ( 1 ) . mean ())) print ( "Seeds 2, 3 and 4: " , usd ( run ( 2 ) . mean ()), usd ( run ( 3 ) . mean ()), usd ( run ( 4 ) . mean ())) Seed 1, run twice: $14,841 $14,841 Seeds 2, 3 and 4: $15,158 $16,708 $15,515 Same seed, same answer; different seeds, slightly different answers. Neither is "the right one". The spread between them is the subject of the next part. Misconception: "Freezing the numbers makes the result more accurate." It makes it repeatable . If 1,000 trials gave a noisy estimate, the frozen copy is the same noisy estimate, now fixed in place.
docs.title: Excel steps: freeze the results

docs.text: Each simulated batch is a sample of possible seasons, so every statistic from it (the average profit, the probability of a loss) has sampling error , exactly like a survey. More trials, less error, but with diminishing returns: the error shrinks with the square root of the number of trials. Standard error of the average: SD of the trial results ÷ √n. Standard error of a probability p : √(p × (1 − p) ÷ n). Quadrupling the trials halves the error. Going from 1,000 to 100,000 trials makes the error ten times smaller. Predict, then run. The true probability of a loss in this model is about 25%. With only 50 trials, how far from 25% could one batch's estimate easily be: 1 point, 5 points or 15 points? rows = [] for n in ( 50 , 500 , 5_000 , 50_000 ): estimates = [ np . mean ( run ( seed , n ) < 0 ) for seed in range ( 100 , 105 )] p = np . mean ( estimates ) rows . append ({ "trials" : n , "five batches (probability of loss)" : " " . join ( f " { e : .1% } " for e in estimates ), "± 2 standard errors" : f "± { 2 * np . sqrt ( p * ( 1 - p ) / n ) : .1% } " }) print ( pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . to_string ( index = False )) long = run ( 99 , 20_000 ) k = np . arange ( 1 , len ( long ) + 1 ) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 2 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.6 )) axes [ 0 ] . plot ( k , np . cumsum ( long ) / k , color = BLUE ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xscale ( "log" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Running average profit" ) axes [ 0 ] . yaxis . set_major_formatter ( lambda v , _ : usd ( v )) axes [ 1 ] . plot ( k , np . cumsum ( long < 0 ) / k , color = ORANGE ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xscale ( "log" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Running probability of a loss" ) axes [ 1 ] . yaxis . set_major_formatter ( lambda v , _ : f " { v : .0% } " ) for ax in axes : ax . set_xlabel ( "Number of trials (log scale)" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () trials five batches (probability of loss) ± 2 standard errors 50 24.0% 32.0% 26.0% 24.0% 18.0% ± 12.2% 500 26.6% 27.6% 27.0% 26.4% 25.2% ± 4.0% 5000 24.7% 26.4% 25.6% 24.7% 25.7% ± 1.2% 50000 24.9% 25.4% 25.0% 25.2% 25.6% ± 0.4% With 50 trials, one batch can report a probability of loss several points away from another, enough to change how risky the launch sounds. The running lines wander early and settle as trials accumulate. How to choose the number of trials: Decide how precise each number must be for the decision . If the board will act differently at a 20% and a 30% chance of loss, the estimate must be good to well under ±5 points. Use the standard-error formulas to find the n that gives that precision. For ±2 points at p ≈ 25%: n ≈ 4 × 0.25 × 0.75 ÷ 0.02² ≈ 1,900 trials. Run the batch twice with different seeds (in Excel: press F9 and compare). If the answer that matters moves, add trials. Tails need more trials than averages. A 5th percentile is estimated from the worst few percent of trials only, so it is noisier than the mean. Report the estimate with its precision: "about 25% (± 2 points)". In Excel, 1,000 to 10,000 rows are practical. For more, a classic trick is a one-way Data Table with an empty input cell : list 1 to 1,000 in a column, put a summary cell (such as the average profit of the Sim sheet) in the formula row, choose any empty cell on the same sheet as the Column input cell , and Excel recalculates the whole sheet once per row, collecting 1,000 batch results (an extension; it is slow on large sheets). Misconception: "My simulation gives a 24.1% chance of loss." The decimal is noise unless you ran tens of thousands of trials. Round to what the trials support.
docs.title: Part 9: How many trials? (core)

docs.text: An average alone is a poor summary of risk. These measures describe the whole distribution of outcomes: Measure Question it answers Excel (results in Sim!G2:G1001 ) numpy Mean What do we earn on average? =AVERAGE(G2:G1001) profit.mean() Standard deviation How spread out are the outcomes? =STDEV.S(G2:G1001) profit.std(ddof=1) Probability of loss How often do we lose money? =COUNTIF(G2:G1001,"<0")/COUNT(G2:G1001) np.mean(profit < 0) 5th percentile (P5) How bad is a 1-in-20 bad season? =PERCENTILE.INC(G2:G1001, 0.05) np.percentile(profit, 5) Median (P50) What is the middle outcome? =MEDIAN(G2:G1001) np.median(profit) 95th percentile (P95) How good is a 1-in-20 good season? =PERCENTILE.INC(G2:G1001, 0.95) np.percentile(profit, 95) Minimum and maximum What did the worst and best trials show? =MIN(...) , =MAX(...) profit.min() , profit.max() Chance of meeting the plan How often do we reach the base-case profit? =COUNTIF(G2:G1001,">="&26000)/COUNT(G2:G1001) np.mean(profit >= 26000) Expected shortfall (extension) When a bad season happens, how bad is it on average? =AVERAGEIF(G2:G1001,"<="&P5cell) profit[profit <= p5].mean() Two notes on matching Excel and numpy. STDEV.S divides by n − 1, so use ddof=1 ; numpy's default ( ddof=0 ) gives a slightly smaller number. numpy's default percentile method gives the same result as PERCENTILE.INC . P5 as value at risk. Banks summarise risk with value at risk (VaR) : the loss that is exceeded only with a small probability, such as 5%. The 5th percentile of profit plays the same role here. If P5 is −$30,000, then "in one season out of twenty, we lose $30,000 or more". It is not the worst case; one season in twenty is worse. Minimum and maximum are weak measures. They come from a single trial each, so they change a lot from batch to batch, and they grow more extreme as you add trials. Report percentiles instead. Predict, then run. Look back at Part 6: profit is capped when demand exceeds the 45,000 bottles brewed. What will that cap do to the right-hand side of the histogram? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) n = 10_000 demand = np . maximum ( 0 , np . round ( rng . normal ( 40000 , 9000 , n ))) unit_cost = rng . triangular ( 1.50 , 1.70 , 2.20 , n ) salvage = rng . uniform ( 0.30 , 0.70 , n ) profit = brew_profit ( demand , unit_cost , salvage ) p5 = np . percentile ( profit , 5 ) measures = pd . Series ({ "Mean" : usd ( profit . mean ()), "Standard deviation" : usd ( profit . std ( ddof = 1 )), "Probability of loss" : f " { np . mean ( profit < 0 ) : .1% } " , "5th percentile (P5)" : usd ( p5 ), "Median" : usd ( np . median ( profit )), "95th percentile (P95)" : usd ( np . percentile ( profit , 95 )), "Minimum" : usd ( profit . min ()), "Maximum" : usd ( profit . max ()), "Chance of reaching the base-case $26,000" : f " { np . mean ( profit >= 26000 ) : .1% } " , "Expected shortfall (average of the worst 5%)" : usd ( profit [ profit <= p5 ] . mean ()), }) print ( measures . to_string ()) fig , ax = plt . subplots () edges = np . arange ( - 110000 , 60001 , 2500 ) # bin edges that include 0 counts , _ = np . histogram ( profit , bins = edges ) ax . bar ( edges [: - 1 ], counts , width = 2500 , align = "edge" , edgecolor = "white" , color = [ ORANGE if e < 0 else SKY for e in edges [: - 1 ]]) ax . bar ([ 0 ], [ 0 ], color = ORANGE , label = "Loss" ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 1 ) ax . axvline ( profit . mean (), color = BLUE , lw = 2 , label = f "Mean { usd ( profit . mean ()) } " ) ax . axvline ( 26000 , color = GREEN , ls = "--" , lw = 2 , label = "Base case $26,000" ) ax . axvline ( p5 , color = PURPLE , ls = ":" , lw = 2 , label = f "P5 { usd ( p5 ) } " ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Season profit (US dollars)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Number of simulated seasons" ) ax . set_title ( "10,000 simulated seasons, brewing 45,000 bottles" ) ax . xaxis . set_major_formatter ( lambda v , _ : usd ( v )) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Mean $15,771 Standard deviation $25,119 Probability of loss 25.5% 5th percentile (P5) -$31,277 Median $21,837 95th percentile (P95) $45,845 Minimum -$107,088 Maximum $52,110 Chance of reaching the base-case $26,000 44.0% Expected shortfall (average of the worst 5%) -$45,573
docs.title: Part 10: Risk measures and reading the histogram (core)

docs.text: Find zero. Everything to its left is a loss. Here roughly a quarter of seasons lose money: a fact the base case of $26,000 completely hides. Compare the mean with the base case. The mean sits well left of the base case (Part 6). Look at the shape. This one has a long left tail (bad seasons can be very bad) and a pile-up on the right : once demand exceeds 45,000, every bottle is sold and profit can rise no further, so many seasons bunch just below the ceiling. Their remaining spread comes only from the variable cost. A sharp edge or a pile-up in a histogram usually means a limit in the model. Read the tails with percentiles, not with the minimum and maximum. Ask what is missing. The histogram shows only the uncertainties we built in (Part 14).
docs.title: How to read a histogram of outcomes

docs.text: On Sim , build the summary in I1:J10 : labels in column I, formulas from the table above in column J, for example J1 =AVERAGE(G2:G1001) , J3 =COUNTIF(G2:G1001,"<0")/COUNT(G2:G1001) , J4 =PERCENTILE.INC(G2:G1001,0.05) . Select G1:G1001 → Insert → Charts → Insert Statistic Chart → Histogram (Excel 2016 or later; on a Mac the same icon in Insert → Charts ). Right-click the horizontal axis → Format Axis → Bins → Bin width 5000 . Tick Underflow bin and set it to 0 to collect all losses into one bar, if you want the loss share to stand out. Add a title in words, such as "One season in four loses money", not "Histogram of G". Remember the histogram is live : it changes with every F9. Build it from the frozen sheet (Part 8) for a report. Older Excel without the Histogram chart: make a column of bin edges (−100000, −95000, … 60000) in L2:L34 , select M2:M35 , type =FREQUENCY(G2:G1001, L2:L34) and press Ctrl+Shift+Enter (or just Enter in Excel 365), then Insert → Column Chart of the counts. Check your understanding. Two plans have the same mean profit. Plan A has P5 = −$5,000; Plan B has P5 = −$40,000. Which would a small start-up with $30,000 in the bank prefer, and why?
docs.title: Excel steps: a histogram and the summary box

docs.text: So far each input was drawn independently . Real inputs often move together: A heatwave raises demand and the cost of ice and cold storage: positive correlation between demand and cost. Bad news on one side is partly offset on the other (a natural hedge). An economic downturn lowers festival crowds and pushes the tea supplier to raise prices to cover its own losses: negative correlation between demand and cost. Bad news arrives together. Ignoring a correlation does not change the average much, but it can badly misstate the risk , because risk lives in the combinations. Predict, then run. With a correlation of −0.6 between demand and cost, will the probability of a loss be higher or lower than with independent inputs? What about the mean? def run_correlated ( rho , seed = 11 , n = 20_000 ): """Demand and unit cost linked through correlated standard normal draws (a Gaussian copula).""" r = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) z1 = r . standard_normal ( n ) z2 = rho * z1 + np . sqrt ( 1 - rho ** 2 ) * r . standard_normal ( n ) d = np . maximum ( 0 , np . round ( 40000 + 9000 * z1 )) uu = norm . cdf ( z2 ) # a uniform number linked to demand c = np . where ( uu < ( m - a ) / ( b - a ), a + np . sqrt ( uu * ( b - a ) * ( m - a )), b - np . sqrt (( 1 - uu ) * ( b - a ) * ( b - m ))) s = r . uniform ( 0.30 , 0.70 , n ) return d , c , brew_profit ( d , c , s ) rows , samples = [], {} for rho in ( - 0.6 , 0.0 , 0.6 ): d , c , p = run_correlated ( rho ) samples [ rho ] = ( d , c ) rows . append ({ "correlation" : rho , "mean profit" : usd ( p . mean ()), "SD" : usd ( p . std ( ddof = 1 )), "probability of loss" : f " { np . mean ( p < 0 ) : .1% } " , "P5" : usd ( np . percentile ( p , 5 ))}) print ( pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . to_string ( index = False )) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 11 , 3.2 ), sharey = True ) for ax , rho in zip ( axes , ( - 0.6 , 0.0 , 0.6 )): d , c = samples [ rho ] ax . scatter ( d [: 800 ], c [: 800 ], s = 5 , alpha = 0.4 , color = BLUE ) ax . set_title ( f "Correlation { rho : +.1f } " ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Demand (bottles)" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Variable cost ($)" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () correlation mean profit SD probability of loss P5 -0.6 $15,911 $28,139 27.2% -$37,900 0.0 $15,893 $24,727 24.9% -$31,216 0.6 $15,879 $21,001 21.9% -$24,627 The mean barely moves, but the probability of loss and the 5th percentile do. With negative correlation, low demand tends to come with high cost, so the bad tail gets worse; with positive correlation the two partly cancel. A model that draws every input independently can therefore look safer than the business really is. In Excel (extension). Draw two standard normal numbers, then mix them: H2 =NORM.S.INV(RAND()) and I2 =NORM.S.INV(RAND()) . J2 =rho*H2 + SQRT(1-rho^2)*I2 , with rho in a named input cell on Model . Demand: =MAX(0, ROUND(Model!$B$16 + Model!$B$17*H2, 0)) . The uniform number for the triangular cost: =NORM.S.DIST(J2, TRUE) , used in place of column B. Where does the correlation come from? From history (the correlation between past demand and past costs), or from judgement, stated and tested with a sensitivity check, exactly as in the table above. Misconception: "If I don't model a correlation, I am assuming nothing." Drawing inputs independently is an assumption: that the correlation is zero.
docs.title: Part 11: Correlated inputs (core concept, extension build)

docs.text: A simulation describes risk. A decision rule turns that description into a choice. Brightleaf controls one big lever: how many bottles to brew . Brew too few and it runs out in good seasons; brew too many and it pays for bottles it sells off cheaply. To compare options fairly, every option must face the same simulated seasons . This is called common random numbers : draw demand, cost and salvage once, then compute each option's profit on those same draws. Otherwise the differences between options are partly just luck. Predict, then run. Which brew quantity has the highest average profit: 35,000, 40,000, 45,000 or 50,000? Will the quantity with the lowest chance of a loss be the same one? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 31 ) n = 20_000 d = np . maximum ( 0 , np . round ( rng . normal ( 40000 , 9000 , n ))) c = rng . triangular ( 1.50 , 1.70 , 2.20 , n ) s = rng . uniform ( 0.30 , 0.70 , n ) rows = [] for brewed in range ( 30000 , 60001 , 5000 ): p = brew_profit ( d , c , s , brewed = brewed ) # the same seasons for every option rows . append ({ "brewed" : brewed , "mean" : p . mean (), "probability of loss" : np . mean ( p < 0 ), "P5" : np . percentile ( p , 5 ), "P95" : np . percentile ( p , 95 ), "chance of running out" : np . mean ( d > brewed )}) options = pd . DataFrame ( rows ) print ( options . to_string ( index = False , formatters = { "brewed" : " {:,} " . format , "mean" : usd , "P5" : usd , "P95" : usd , "probability of loss" : " {:.1%} " . format , "chance of running out" : " {:.0%} " . format })) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( options [ "brewed" ], options [ "mean" ], "o-" , color = BLUE , label = "Mean profit" ) ax . plot ( options [ "brewed" ], options [ "P5" ], "s--" , color = ORANGE , label = "P5 (1-in-20 bad season)" ) ax . plot ( options [ "brewed" ], options [ "P95" ], "^:" , color = GREEN , label = "P95 (1-in-20 good season)" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = GREY , lw = 1 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Bottles brewed in advance" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Season profit (US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "More brewing raises the upside and deepens the downside" ) ax . yaxis . set_major_formatter ( lambda v , _ : usd ( v )) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () brewed mean probability of loss P5 P95 chance of running out 30,000 $3,850 19.3% -$11,548 $12,265 87% 35,000 $11,227 13.9% -$18,027 $23,964 71% 40,000 $15,303 19.2% -$24,744 $35,215 50% 45,000 $15,632 25.6% -$31,502 $45,630 29% 50,000 $12,716 32.4% -$38,356 $54,374 13% 55,000 $7,717 40.0% -$45,382 $58,383 5% 60,000 $1,691 47.6% -$52,224 $55,706 1% Different rules pick different answers: Rule What it says Brightleaf's choice (from the table) Suits Maximise the mean (expected value) Pick the option with the highest average Around 40,000–45,000; the two are close A firm that can absorb bad seasons, with many similar bets Cap the probability of loss Highest mean among options with, say, at most a 15% chance of loss Around 35,000 A firm that must not have a losing year (a loan covenant, investors) Protect the bad case (maximise P5) Pick the option with the least bad 1-in-20 season The smallest brew A cash-poor start-up that cannot survive a big loss Maximin (best worst case) Judge each option by its worst outcome only The smallest brew Very risk-averse; ignores probabilities, so it is rarely used alone Satisficing First option that meets a target, e.g. 60% chance of profit above $10,000 Depends on the target Clear, explainable rules agreed in advance No rule is "correct". The rule should be chosen before looking at the results, from the firm's situation and its risk appetite , and stated in the recommendation. Changing the rule after seeing the table, to justify a favourite option, is the simulation equivalent of moving the goalposts. Notice also how flat the mean is near the top: the mean differs by only a few hundred dollars between 40,000 and 45,000, while P5 differs by several thousand. When options are close on the mean, risk measures should decide. Extension: the newsvendor rule. For this kind of problem there is a classic formula. Brew until the chance of selling the last bottle equals the critical ratio : (price − cost) ÷ (price − salvage) = (4.00 − 1.80) ÷ (4.00 − 0.50) ≈ 0.63. So brew the 63rd percentile of demand, about 40,000 + 0.33 × 9,000 ≈ 43,000 bottles, which sits where the mean curve peaks. Under-stocking costs $2.20 of lost margin per bottle; over-stocking costs $1.30 per bottle; the ratio balances the two.
docs.title: Part 12: Decision rules: how much to brew (core)

docs.text: Executives do not want a histogram tutorial. They want to know: what do you recommend, how sure are you, what could go wrong, and what would change your mind? Predict, then run. Before running the cell, write a two-sentence summary of the 45,000-bottle plan for Brightleaf's board in your own words. Then compare it with the generated one. p45 = options . set_index ( "brewed" ) . loc [ 45000 ] p35 = options . set_index ( "brewed" ) . loc [ 35000 ] ratio = round ( 1 / p45 [ "probability of loss" ]) print ( f "Brewing 45,000 bottles, we expect a season profit of about { usd ( round ( p45 [ 'mean' ], - 3 )) } , " f "not the { usd ( 26000 ) } of the single-number plan." ) print ( f "About 1 season in { ratio } loses money; in a bad season (1 in 20) we lose " f " { usd ( - round ( p45 [ 'P5' ], - 3 )) } or more." ) print ( f "Brewing 35,000 instead lowers the average to about { usd ( round ( p35 [ 'mean' ], - 3 )) } , but cuts the chance " f "of a loss to about 1 in { round ( 1 / p35 [ 'probability of loss' ]) } and the 1-in-20 loss to about " f " { usd ( - round ( p35 [ 'P5' ], - 3 )) } ." ) print ( "Demand is the main driver (Part 3); a pre-order campaign would narrow the range most." ) Brewing 45,000 bottles, we expect a season profit of about $16,000, not the $26,000 of the single-number plan. About 1 season in 4 loses money; in a bad season (1 in 20) we lose $32,000 or more. Brewing 35,000 instead lowers the average to about $11,000, but cuts the chance of a loss to about 1 in 7 and the 1-in-20 loss to about $18,000. Demand is the main driver (Part 3); a pre-order campaign would narrow the range most. Say Avoid "About 1 season in 4 loses money" "P(profit < 0) = 0.256" "We expect about $16,000; in 9 seasons out of 10 the result lies between a loss of about $30,000 and a profit of about $45,000" "Profit will be $15,632" "In a bad season, 1 in 20, we lose $30,000 or more" "VaR(95) = 31,502" without explaining it "The main driver is demand" A list of every input "This assumes no correlation between demand and cost; if a downturn hits both, the risk is higher" Silence on assumptions "We recommend 35,000 bottles because the board said a loss above $20,000 is unacceptable" A recommendation with no rule Frequencies beat percentages. "1 in 4" and "5 out of 20 seasons" are understood far better than "25%" and "P5", especially by people under time pressure (Gigerenzer's work on natural frequencies). One chart, with words on it. Show the histogram (or the options chart), shade the losses, mark zero and the plan, and give it a headline that states the finding. A one-slide structure: Recommendation in one sentence. Expected outcome and range in words (mean, a P5–P95 range, the chance of loss as a frequency). Main driver (from the tornado chart) and what would reduce the uncertainty. Key assumptions (distributions, independence) and what the model leaves out (Part 14). Decision rule used, and how the choice would change under another rule. Misconception: "More decimals look more rigorous." They signal false precision. A simulation with uncertain inputs supports two significant figures at most.
docs.title: Part 13: Communicating risk to executives (core)

docs.text: The board meets next week. The founders want to brew 45,000 bottles: "the regression says 40,000, plus a safety margin". The finance lead wants 35,000. An investor asks whether to launch at all this year, or to run a ten-festival pilot first. What the simulation shows and does not show: Captured in the model Not captured Demand uncertainty from the regression Customer disappointment when Brightleaf runs out at a festival, and the effect on next year's brand Cost uncertainty (triangular judgement) Waste: unsold bottles that the discount retailer cannot take end up discarded, with an environmental cost and possible reputational cost Salvage price range A food-safety recall, which no input in the model represents The brewing cap The option to brew a second batch mid-season at a higher cost, which would soften the cap Whether past sister-brand launches are a fair guide to a new product (Part 1, question 5) A precise number on a screen can crowd out risks that were never typed into a cell. The model's silence on a risk is not evidence that the risk is small. Discussion questions (pairs, 10 minutes): Which decision rule from Part 12 fits a start-up with $30,000 in the bank? Which fits a large drinks company launching its tenth product? The founders' "safety margin" brews more . Explain, using the histogram, why brewing more is not safer in this model. In what business would a safety margin of extra stock really be safer? Suppose a mid-season second batch is possible at $2.10 a bottle, ordered after the first ten festivals. Without coding it, how would it change the shape of the histogram and the best first-batch size? The pilot costs $8,000 and would shrink the demand standard deviation from 9,000 to 4,000 bottles. Which numbers from this lecture would you use to judge whether that information is worth $8,000? (This is the idea of the value of information .) Write the recommendation in four parts: finding, evidence, action with an owner, and what would change it .
docs.title: Part 14: Business case: Brightleaf's launch decision (core discussion)

docs.text: Lab 5, in periods 7 and 8, returns to predictive regression in Python: you fit a multiple regression on car data, test it on cars it has not seen and check its residuals. This part is a 30-minute recap of the Day 4 ideas the lab uses, on a different data set: weekly cold-brew orders from 250 cafés that stock Brightleaf (synthetic). The lab asks you to interpret your own output; nothing here tells you what that output will show. Lab 5 step What it does Day 4 recap Drop missing values; choose features X and target y A regression cannot use a row with a gap Parts 2–3 Split 80% / 20% with a fixed random_state The test set plays "cars the model has never seen" Part 5 Fit, read the coefficients Each coefficient in units of the target, per sensible step, holding the others constant Parts 2–3 RMSE, MAE, R² on the test set Typical error in the target's units; share of variation explained Part 6 Actual vs predicted plot with a y = x line Points on the line are perfect predictions below Residuals vs predicted A flat, even band is healthy; a curve or funnel is a warning Part 7 Predict, then run. The cafés' true orders rise with temperature, but faster on hot weeks than on mild ones. We fit a straight-line model. What shape will the residual plot show? from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression from sklearn.metrics import mean_absolute_error , mean_squared_error , r2_score from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split rng = np . random . default_rng ( 15 ) n = 250 cafes = pd . DataFrame ({ "temperature" : rng . uniform ( 12 , 34 , n ) . round ( 1 ), # average weekly temperature, deg C "seats" : rng . integers ( 10 , 80 , n ), "promo_display" : rng . integers ( 0 , 2 , n ), }) cafes [ "bottles" ] = ( 20 + 0.25 * ( cafes [ "temperature" ] - 10 ) ** 2 + 0.9 * cafes [ "seats" ] + 15 * cafes [ "promo_display" ] + rng . normal ( 0 , 6 , n )) . round () features = [ "temperature" , "seats" , "promo_display" ] X , y = cafes [ features ], cafes [ "bottles" ] X_train , X_test , y_train , y_test = train_test_split ( X , y , test_size = 0.20 , random_state = 42 ) lin = LinearRegression () . fit ( X_train , y_train ) pred_test = lin . predict ( X_test ) print ( f "Training cafés: { len ( X_train ) } , test cafés: { len ( X_test ) } " ) print ( pd . Series ( lin . coef_ , index = features ) . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) print ( f "Test RMSE { np . sqrt ( mean_squared_error ( y_test , pred_test )) : .1f } bottles, " f "MAE { mean_absolute_error ( y_test , pred_test ) : .1f } bottles, R² { r2_score ( y_test , pred_test ) : .2f } " ) Training cafés: 200, test cafés: 50 temperature 6.89 seats 0.93 promo_display 16.16 Test RMSE 9.7 bottles, MAE 7.9 bottles, R² 0.94 resid = y_test - pred_test lo_ = min ( y_test . min (), pred_test . min ()) # the y = x line should span both axes' data hi_ = max ( y_test . max (), pred_test . max ()) fig , axes = plt . subplots ( 1 , 3 , figsize = ( 12 , 3.6 )) axes [ 0 ] . scatter ( y_test , pred_test , color = BLUE , s = 16 , alpha = 0.7 ) axes [ 0 ] . plot ([ lo_ , hi_ ], [ lo_ , hi_ ], color = ORANGE , ls = "--" , lw = 2 ) axes [ 0 ] . set_xlabel ( "Actual bottles" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_ylabel ( "Predicted bottles" ) axes [ 0 ] . set_title ( "Actual vs predicted (test)" ) axes [ 1 ] . scatter ( pred_test , resid , color = PURPLE , s = 16 , alpha = 0.7 ) axes [ 1 ] . axhline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , ls = "--" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_xlabel ( "Predicted bottles" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_ylabel ( "Residual (actual − predicted)" ) axes [ 1 ] . set_title ( "Residuals vs predicted" ) axes [ 2 ] . scatter ( X_test [ "temperature" ], resid , color = GREEN , s = 16 , alpha = 0.7 ) axes [ 2 ] . axhline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , ls = "--" ) axes [ 2 ] . set_xlabel ( "Temperature (°C)" ) axes [ 2 ] . set_title ( "Residuals vs one feature" ) plt . tight_layout () plt . show () How to read the three plots, step by step (use the same steps on your own Lab 5 output): Actual vs predicted. Are the points close to the dashed line everywhere, or further from it at one end? Points above the line are over-predictions; points below are under-predictions. Residuals vs predicted. Imagine a smooth line through the points. Flat at zero? Or does it bend (a curve : the model has the wrong shape) or fan out (a funnel : errors grow with the prediction)? Residuals vs one feature. If the residual plot shows a pattern, plot the residuals against each feature to find which one causes it. Here the U-shape against temperature points to the curved temperature effect we built in. Write it as a finding , with units: "the model under-predicts on the coldest and the hottest weeks, by up to about … bottles", then say what you would try next (a squared term, a log, another feature). Three habits that prevent most Lab 5 slips: Draw the y = x line across the data actually plotted. A line from the smallest to the largest value of the target works only if the predictions stay inside that range and y still holds the target (see the Lab 5 guide's pitfalls). Test-set numbers are the honest ones. Quote RMSE, MAE and R² from the test set and say so. Name the step size and units in every coefficient sentence: per degree, per 10 seats, per 1,000 of something; choose a step that makes sense for the feature's range. The Lab 5 guide has the offline route, checks you can make without seeing answers, and the known pitfalls.
