Day 6 lecture: Business intelligence strategy, forecasting and ethics ¶ Periods 1 to 6 of Day 6. What business intelligence (BI) is and how value flows from data to a decision; how to build a BI strategy with goals, KPIs, governance, data quality and a maturity model; the parts of a BI architecture, from source systems through ETL or ELT, warehouses, lakes and a semantic layer to dashboards; the tool landscape; real BI successes and failures; Excel's Forecast Sheet with ETS, seasonality and confidence intervals, and why some plans should be built on the upper bound; the ethics of analytics (privacy under PIPL and GDPR, consent, bias and fairness, transparency, Goodhart's law, supply-chain ethics and ESG, responsible-AI frameworks); and how to write a managerial recommendation that weighs financial and ethical evidence. Periods 5 and 6 brief Labs 6 and 7 and Assignment 3. Every Excel step comes with a numbered click path and the formulas , and every calculation has a Python mirror , so you can check one against the other. The running case is a fictional regional coffee roaster, Harbourline Coffee , which roasts green coffee beans for its own cafés and for wholesale customers. All money is in US dollars and every number is invented for this lecture. Labs 6 and 7 and Assignment 3 use other businesses and other numbers; this lecture deliberately uses none of them, so you practise each idea here and apply it yourself there. Route B (Anaconda, offline): open this notebook from the DATA300_GAP folder. It needs numpy, pandas, matplotlib, statsmodels and scikit-learn, and it downloads nothing. Route A (Try JupyterLab): upload this notebook and run %pip install statsmodels scikit-learn in a first cell. Excel: desktop Excel 2016 or later on Windows, or a recent Excel for Mac. Forecast Sheet and the FORECAST.ETS functions are not in Excel 2013 or earlier, and the Forecast Sheet button is not in Excel for the web. What you will be able to do ¶ Define business intelligence , trace the BI value chain from data to an outcome, and say where value usually leaks. Set out a BI strategy : sponsorship, goals and KPIs , data governance , data quality , a maturity assessment, and the choice between self-service and centralised BI. Describe a BI architecture : source systems, ETL and ELT , warehouse, lake and lakehouse , the star schema , the semantic layer and dashboards; place common tools in it. Draw lessons from real BI case studies , including well-known failures. Build a forecast with Excel's Forecast Sheet , explain ETS , seasonality detection and the confidence interval , and mirror it in Python. Explain when and why to plan against an upper bound instead of the point forecast, and choose the right bound for an asymmetric risk. Apply privacy principles under China's PIPL and the EU's GDPR , including consent and re-identification risk. Measure bias with the disparate-impact ratio and other fairness measures, and explain why removing the sensitive column does not remove bias. Explain a model's decision ( transparency ), recognise Goodhart's law , and weigh supply-chain ethics and ESG trade-offs. Use a responsible-AI framework as a checklist, and write a managerial recommendation that balances financial and ethical evidence. This lecture fills six periods (P1 to P6). Each part is marked core (teach in class) or extension (faster students, a study block, or self-study). Part Topic Path Period 1 What BI is, and the BI value chain Core P1 2 BI strategy: goals, KPIs, governance, data quality, maturity Core P1 3 BI architecture and the tool landscape Core P1–P2 4 BI case studies: successes and failures Core P2 5 Integrating a BI case: Harbourline's sourcing decision Core P2 6 Forecasting with Excel Forecast Sheet: ETS, seasonality and intervals Core P3 7 Planning against an upper bound Core P3 8 Privacy, PIPL, GDPR and consent Core P4 9 Bias and fairness: a disparate-impact demonstration Core P4 10 Transparency and explainability Core P4 11 Goodhart's law and metric gaming Core P5 12 Supply-chain ethics and ESG trade-offs Core P5 13 Responsible-AI frameworks Core (summary), extension (detail) P5 14 Writing a managerial recommendation Core P5 15 Lab 6 and Lab 7 briefing Core P5 16 Assignment 3 briefing Core P6 17 Business case: Harbourline's board meeting Core (discussion) P6 18 Practice, quiz and summary Self-study — Reading Read Chapter 7 of the course reading packet for what separates a BI strategy from a single dashboard, the steps both of its assigned readings (Tableau and ThoughtSpot) give for building one, traditional versus self-service BI, why a decision exposed to a cost overrun should be planned against a forecast's worst-case bound, and why a volatile spreadsheet must be frozen before it feeds a visualisation. Re-read the sections of Chapter 6 on Data Tables, Monte Carlo summaries and Paste Special before Lab 6 and Assignment 3. This lecture adds data quality and governance in practice, maturity models, architecture and tools, real case studies, ETS mechanics and the choice of bound, and the whole ethics block. Setup ¶ The first cell loads the libraries and sets colour-blind-safe colours. All data in this notebook is synthetic and made inside the notebook from a numpy generator with a fixed seed , so every run prints the same numbers. Nothing is read from the internet. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt from statsmodels.tsa.exponential_smoothing.ets import ETSModel from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression pd . set_option ( "display.width" , 120 ) pd . set_option ( "display.max_columns" , 20 ) plt . rcParams . update ({ "figure.dpi" : 100 , "figure.figsize" : ( 8 , 4.2 ), "axes.spines.top" : False , "axes.spines.right" : False , "axes.titleweight" : "bold" , "axes.titlesize" : 11 }) # Okabe and Ito colour-blind-safe colours BLUE , ORANGE , GREEN , PURPLE , SKY , GREY , YELLOW = "#0072B2" , "#D55E00" , "#009E73" , "#CC79A7" , "#56B4E9" , "#9A9A9A" , "#E69F00" def usd ( x ): """Format a dollar amount for printing, with a minus sign for losses.""" return f "-$ { - x : ,.0f } " if x < 0 else f "$ { x : ,.0f } " Part 1: What BI is, and the BI value chain (core) ¶ Days 1 to 5 gave you techniques: summaries, charts, text mining, forecasts, regressions and simulations. Business intelligence is what an organisation builds so that techniques like these reach the people who decide, reliably and repeatedly. A working definition: Business intelligence is the combination of data, technology, processes and people that turns an organisation's data into information that its managers trust and use to make decisions. Each of the four words matters. Data without technology stays in files nobody can query. Technology without processes (who defines a KPI, who fixes bad data, who may see what) produces numbers that disagree with each other. And all three fail without people who read the numbers and act on them. BI, analytics and data science ¶ Term Main question Typical output Who uses it Reporting What happened? Fixed monthly reports Everyone, on a schedule Business intelligence What is happening, and is it on target? Dashboards, KPI scorecards, self-service queries, alerts Managers at every level Business analytics Why did it happen, and what will happen? Diagnostic analyses, forecasts, simulations Analysts and the managers they support Data science What can we predict or automate? Models built into products and processes Data scientists and engineers The boundaries blur. In this course the descriptive and diagnostic work of Days 1 and 2 is classic BI; the forecasts and simulations of Days 3 to 5 are analytics; and a BI strategy decides how both reach the decision. The BI value chain ¶ Value from data is created in a chain of stages, and it reaches the business only if every stage works: data captured → integrated and cleaned → turned into a trusted measure → seen by the right person in time → changes a decision → the decision is carried out → the outcome is measured and fed back The last arrow closes the loop: measuring the outcome produces new data, which is how an organisation learns whether its decisions worked. Predict, then run. Suppose five stages each work most of the time: 95%, 85%, 70%, 50% and 80%. What share of the potential value of an insight actually reaches the business: about 80%, 50% or 25%? And which stage would you improve first? chain = pd . DataFrame ({ "stage" : [ "Data captured correctly" , "Integrated into a trusted measure" , "Seen by the decision-maker in time" , "Changes the decision" , "Decision carried out" ], "works" : [ 0.95 , 0.85 , 0.70 , 0.50 , 0.80 ], }) chain [ "value_still_alive" ] = chain [ "works" ] . cumprod () print ( chain . to_string ( index = False , formatters = { "works" : " {:.0%} " . format , "value_still_alive" : " {:.0%} " . format })) base = chain [ "works" ] . prod () print ( f " 
 Share of potential value delivered: { base : .0% } " ) # Improve one stage at a time by 10 percentage points (capped at 100%) and see what each buys gain = { s : ( np . prod ( np . where ( chain [ "stage" ] == s , np . minimum ( chain [ "works" ] + 0.10 , 1 ), chain [ "works" ])) - base ) for s in chain [ "stage" ]} print ( " 
 Extra share of value from improving one stage by 10 points:" ) for s , g in sorted ( gain . items (), key = lambda kv : - kv [ 1 ]): print ( f " { s : <36 } + { g : .1% } " ) stage works value_still_alive Data captured correctly 95% 95% Integrated into a trusted measure 85% 81% Seen by the decision-maker in time 70% 57% Changes the decision 50% 28% Decision carried out 80% 23% Share of potential value delivered: 23% Extra share of value from improving one stage by 10 points: Changes the decision +4.5% Seen by the decision-maker in time +3.2% Decision carried out +2.8% Integrated into a trusted measure +2.7% Data captured correctly +1.2% Only about a quarter of the potential value survives, although no single stage looks terrible. Two lessons follow. Value multiplies, so it leaks. A chain is as strong as the product of its links. A 95% data pipeline feeding a dashboard that changes one decision in two delivers less than half of what it could. Improve the weakest link. Raising the weakest stage (whether the insight changes the decision) buys far more than polishing the strongest (data capture). Many BI programmes spend most of their budget on technology at the left of the chain, when the binding constraint is at the right: adoption, trust and the habit of acting on evidence. Misconception: "More dashboards means more BI value." A dashboard adds value only through the decisions it changes. Organisations often have hundreds of reports that nobody opens; each one still costs money to maintain and adds a chance of conflicting numbers. Count decisions improved, not dashboards built. Check your understanding. Name one thing an organisation could do to raise each of the last two stages (changes the decision; decision carried out). None of them should involve buying software. Part 2: BI strategy: goals, KPIs, governance, data quality, maturity (core) ¶ A BI strategy is an organisation's plan for how it will use data to make decisions: what it wants to achieve, which measures matter, who owns them, which data and tools it needs, and in what order it will build. Chapter 7's two readings agree on the main steps, which we can put in our own words as: Step What it means in practice What goes wrong without it 1. Executive sponsor A senior owner (often a chief data officer) with budget and authority to settle disputes between departments Each department builds its own reports; no one can resolve conflicting numbers 2. Stakeholder interviews Ask the people who will use the output which decisions they make and what they need to know Dashboards answer questions nobody asked 3. Goals and KPIs Pick a small set of measures tied to company goals, each with a written definition and an owner "Revenue" means three different things in three meetings 4. Cross-functional team IT, the business units and a data-governance or compliance role work together A lone analyst's side project that dies when they leave 5. Trusted data infrastructure Governed, documented, access-controlled data pipelines Reports nobody trusts, so nobody uses them 6. Tool selection Choose tools on data access, governance, fit with existing systems and users' skills, not on feature lists Expensive licences, little use 7. Phased roadmap Start with one or two high-value use cases, show results, then extend A two-year "big bang" project that is out of date when it lands A single dashboard, however good, is one output of a strategy, not the strategy itself. Goals to KPIs ¶ A key performance indicator is a measure that tells you whether a goal is being met. Good KPIs share four properties: Tied to a goal. "Grow profitable revenue" leads to revenue and margin; "keep customers" leads to retention. Defined once, in writing. The formula, the data source, the time window, what is included and excluded, and who owns it. Actionable. Someone can change it. "Global coffee price" matters, but it is a driver to monitor , not a KPI anyone is accountable for. Balanced. Every KPI that can be pushed up by cutting corners needs a counter-metric (Part 11). Speed of service goes with accuracy; sales with returns. Distinguish lagging indicators, which report results after the fact (quarterly profit), from leading indicators, which move earlier and can still be acted on (weekly repeat-visit rate, order pipeline). A KPI tree (or driver tree) breaks an outcome into the drivers that multiply or add up to it. Harbourline's café revenue is revenue = cafés × trading days × customers per café-day × average ticket so a change in revenue can be split into the part due to each driver. Because the drivers multiply, the clean way to split the change is on the log scale , where products become sums. Predict, then run. Harbourline opened eight new cafés in 2025, but each café served fewer customers a day. Did revenue grow or shrink, and which driver contributed most? kpi = pd . DataFrame ({ "2024" : [ 52 , 360 , 210 , 6.10 ], "2025" : [ 60 , 360 , 201 , 6.45 ]}, index = [ "cafés" , "trading days" , "customers per café-day" , "average ticket ($)" ]) rev = kpi . prod () change = rev [ "2025" ] - rev [ "2024" ] log_share = np . log ( kpi [ "2025" ] / kpi [ "2024" ]) / np . log ( rev [ "2025" ] / rev [ "2024" ]) tree = pd . DataFrame ({ "2024" : kpi [ "2024" ], "2025" : kpi [ "2025" ], "change" : ( kpi [ "2025" ] / kpi [ "2024" ] - 1 ) . map ( " {:+.1%} " . format ), "contribution ($)" : ( log_share * change ) . map ( usd )}) print ( tree . to_string ()) print ( f " 
 Revenue 2024: { usd ( rev [ '2024' ]) } 2025: { usd ( rev [ '2025' ]) } change: { usd ( change ) } ( { rev [ '2025' ] / rev [ '2024' ] - 1 : +.1% } )" ) 2024 2025 change contribution ($) cafés 52.0 60.00 +15.4% $3,712,014 trading days 360.0 360.00 +0.0% $0 customers per café-day 210.0 201.00 -4.3% -$1,136,233 average ticket ($) 6.1 6.45 +5.7% $1,447,219 Revenue 2024: $23,980,320 2025: $28,003,320 change: $4,023,000 (+16.8%) Revenue grew by about 17%, and the KPI tree shows why : new cafés and a higher average ticket more than made up for fewer customers per café-day. A dashboard that showed only total revenue would hide the one warning sign, the fall in customers per café, which is a leading indicator: it may reflect new cafés still building a following, or existing cafés losing customers to the price rise. The next question for the analyst is diagnostic (Day 1): split customers per café-day into old and new cafés. Excel. Put the four drivers for each year in B2:C5 . Revenue is =PRODUCT(B2:B5) . The contribution of driver i is =LN(C2/B2)/LN(C$6/B$6)*(C$6-B$6) with the revenues in row 6; the four contributions add up exactly to the change. Data governance ¶ Data governance is the set of decisions about who may do what with which data, and who is responsible for its quality. It is a process, not a tool. The common roles: Role Responsible for Example at Harbourline Data owner A business leader accountable for a data domain: its definitions, access and quality targets The head of retail owns café sales data Data steward Day-to-day quality: rules, fixing errors, answering "what does this field mean?" A finance analyst who maintains the store master list Data custodian The technical side: storage, security, backups, access controls The IT team running the warehouse Data consumer Using the data within agreed rules A café manager reading the weekly dashboard The main tools of governance are a business glossary (agreed definitions), a data catalogue (what data exists, where, who owns it), lineage (where each number comes from), access policies (who may see what, especially personal data; Part 8) and master data management (one agreed list of stores, products and customers). Data quality ¶ Data quality has several dimensions , each with its own test: Dimension Question A test Completeness Is the value there? Share of non-missing values in a required field Validity Is it allowed? Amounts above zero, dates inside the period, codes in the agreed list Uniqueness Is each real thing recorded once? No repeated transaction IDs Consistency Is it recorded the same way everywhere? Store codes in one format, matching the master list Timeliness Is it available when needed? Share loaded within 24 hours of the sale Accuracy Does it match reality? Spot checks against receipts or a second source (cannot be tested from the data alone) A data-quality scorecard turns these into numbers with targets, so that quality is managed like any other KPI. Below, a month of synthetic till transactions from Harbourline's cafés with a few typical faults planted in them. Predict, then run. Which dimension do you expect to fail its target? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 71 ) n = 1200 stores = [ f "S { i : 02d } " for i in range ( 1 , 13 )] tx = pd . DataFrame ({ "txn_id" : np . arange ( 500001 , 500001 + n ), "store" : rng . choice ( stores , n ), "date" : pd . Timestamp ( "2025-10-01" ) + pd . to_timedelta ( rng . integers ( 0 , 31 , n ), unit = "D" ), "amount" : np . round ( rng . gamma ( 4 , 1.6 , n ), 2 ), "hours_to_load" : np . round ( rng . exponential ( 5 , n ), 1 ), }) # Plant typical faults tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 22 , replace = False ), "store" ] = np . nan # missing store tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 9 , replace = False ), "amount" ] *= - 1 # refunds keyed as sales tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 4 , replace = False ), "date" ] = pd . Timestamp ( "2026-10-03" ) # wrong year tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 14 , replace = False ), "store" ] = rng . choice ([ "s05" , "Store 5" , "S5" ], 14 ) # inconsistent codes tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 70 , replace = False ), "hours_to_load" ] += 30 # late loads tx = pd . concat ([ tx , tx . sample ( 18 , random_state = 3 )], ignore_index = True ) # duplicated rows checks = { "Completeness: store present" : tx [ "store" ] . notna () . mean (), "Validity: amount > 0 and date in October 2025" : (( tx [ "amount" ] > 0 ) & tx [ "date" ] . between ( "2025-10-01" , "2025-10-31" )) . mean (), "Uniqueness: transaction ID not repeated" : ( ~ tx [ "txn_id" ] . duplicated ( keep = "first" )) . mean (), "Consistency: store code in master list" : tx [ "store" ] . dropna () . isin ( stores ) . mean (), "Timeliness: loaded within 24 hours" : ( tx [ "hours_to_load" ] <= 24 ) . mean (), } targets = [ 0.99 , 0.99 , 1.00 , 0.99 , 0.95 ] card = pd . DataFrame ({ "score" : list ( checks . values ()), "target" : targets }, index = list ( checks . keys ())) card [ "status" ] = np . where ( card [ "score" ] >= card [ "target" ], "pass" , "FAIL" ) print ( f "Rows checked: { len ( tx ) : , } 
 " ) print ( card . to_string ( formatters = { "score" : " {:.1%} " . format , "target" : " {:.0%} " . format })) Rows checked: 1,218 score target status Completeness: store present 98.4% 99% FAIL Validity: amount > 0 and date in October 2025 98.9% 99% FAIL Uniqueness: transaction ID not repeated 98.5% 100% FAIL Consistency: store code in master list 98.8% 99% FAIL Timeliness: loaded within 24 hours 93.8% 95% FAIL Every dimension fails its target, although each fault touches only a few per cent of the rows. That is normal for raw operational data, and it is why trusted data infrastructure is a step in every BI strategy: if the café dashboards were built on this table, totals would be inflated by the duplicates, twelve stores would appear as fifteen, and late loads would make yesterday's sales look low every morning. The scorecard also tells the data steward where to start. Duplicates and inconsistent codes are fixed once, upstream, in the pipeline (Part 3); late loads are a process problem for IT; refunds keyed as sales are a training problem at the till. Excel. Dashboards aggregate, and aggregation hides faults: a duplicate adds to a total silently, and a wrong store code simply becomes a new bar. Quality is checked on the rows , before aggregation. Maturity: where is the organisation now? ¶ A maturity model describes stages an organisation passes through as it learns to use data. Published models (from TDWI, Gartner and others) differ in detail; most share a ladder like this one: Level Name What it looks like Typical next step 1 Ad hoc Spreadsheets e-mailed around; each team has its own numbers Agree definitions for five core KPIs 2 Repeatable reporting Regular reports from one system; still mostly manual Build a governed data store and automate the main pipeline 3 Integrated BI A warehouse joins several systems; shared dashboards; a glossary exists Self-service for trained users; data-quality scorecards 4 Analytics-driven Forecasts and simulations feed planning; decisions cite evidence Embed models in processes; measure decision outcomes 5 Optimising Data and models are part of everyday operations; experiments are routine; ethics reviews are standard Keep governance ahead of new uses (AI, new data) Maturity is uneven: a company can be at level 4 in finance and level 1 in HR. The use of a model is to make the next step explicit, not to award a score. Skipping levels (buying an AI platform at level 1) is the most common and expensive mistake. Check your understanding. Harbourline's finance team builds its monthly report by copying figures from the till system into Excel; the cafés' managers each keep their own spreadsheet of staff hours. Which level is each team at, and what is the next step for each? Self-service or centralised? ¶ Centralised (traditional) Self-service (modern) Hub and spoke (common compromise) Who builds reports A central BI team Business users, with drag-and-drop tools The hub builds certified data sets and core KPIs; spokes build their own views on top Strengths Consistent definitions, strong control Speed, relevance, less waiting Consistency where it matters, speed elsewhere Risks Backlog, slow answers, reports that miss the need Conflicting numbers, "spreadmarts", exposure of personal data Needs clear rules on what is certified Needs A capable central team Training, governed data sets, a semantic layer (Part 3) Both, plus a BI competency centre that sets standards Self-service needs more governance, not less: more people touch the data, so definitions, access rules and a semantic layer must already exist. Part 3: BI architecture and the tool landscape (core) ¶ A BI architecture moves data from where it is created to where it is used, in layers: Layer What happens Examples Sources Data is created by operational systems Till (point-of-sale) system, ERP for purchasing and finance, CRM and loyalty app, website logs, spreadsheets, external data (weather, commodity prices) Integration: ETL or ELT Data is extracted, cleaned, joined and loaded Scheduled pipelines; data-quality checks (Part 2) run here Storage Data is kept in a form built for analysis Data warehouse, data lake, lakehouse Semantic layer Business names and KPI definitions are defined once "Net revenue", "active customer" as governed formulas Presentation People and programs consume the data Dashboards, scheduled reports, self-service queries, alerts, models ETL or ELT? ¶ ETL: extract, transform, load ELT: extract, load, transform Order Clean and reshape before loading into the warehouse Load raw data first; transform inside the warehouse Suits Older on-premises warehouses with limited computing power; strict control of what enters Cloud warehouses with cheap storage and elastic computing Strength Only clean, conformed data is stored Raw data is kept, so a transformation can be rerun or changed later Risk Rework when requirements change; lost raw detail Raw personal data sits in the warehouse, so access control matters more Warehouse, lake or lakehouse? ¶ A data warehouse stores structured, cleaned data in tables designed for queries, with a fixed structure decided in advance ( schema on write ). Fast and trusted, but less flexible. A data lake stores raw data of any kind (tables, logs, text, images) cheaply, and structure is applied when the data is read ( schema on read ). Flexible, but without governance it becomes a data swamp that nobody can trust. A lakehouse puts warehouse-style tables, transactions and governance on top of lake storage, aiming for both. The semantic layer: one definition per KPI ¶ Now a common problem. Three teams report the number of active customers for 2025: Marketing: customers who bought at least once in the last 90 days of the year. Finance: customers with at least 12 purchases in the year (roughly monthly). Operations: customers who bought in December . Predict, then run. Will the three counts be close, or far apart? window_start = pd . The problem is calling all three by the same name. In a meeting, marketing's number and finance's number would contradict each other, and the meeting would argue about data instead of deciding. A semantic layer fixes this: each KPI is defined once , with a name, a formula, an owner and a description, and every dashboard and query uses that definition. In industry this is done with tools such as Power BI semantic models, Looker's modelling language, dbt's metrics layer or Tableau's published data sources. In Excel, a modest version is a single Definitions sheet with named cells, and every report linking to it rather than retyping formulas. Misconception: "If two reports show different numbers, one of them has a bug." Often both are correct, under different definitions. The fix is governance (one agreed definition and a name for each variant), not debugging. Part 4: BI case studies: successes and failures (core) ¶ Real cases show where in the value chain (Part 1) BI succeeds or breaks. All of these are documented in the business press or in official reports; read the original sources for detail. Case What happened Where in the chain Lesson Tesco Clubcard (UK, from 1995, with dunnhumby) Loyalty-card data on what each household bought was used to target offers and plan ranges; widely credited with helping Tesco become the UK's largest grocer Data → decision → action, closed loop Data creates value when it changes everyday decisions (offers, ranges), and the loop is measured Walmart Retail Link (US, from the early 1990s) Walmart shared store-level sales and stock data with its suppliers, who used it to plan production and replenishment Integration and sharing across firms Sharing governed data with partners can be worth more than hoarding it UPS ORION (US, rolled out 2012–2016) Route-optimisation software for drivers; UPS reported large annual savings in miles and fuel Model → action, after years of change management Adoption by drivers took longer than building the model Google Flu Trends (2008–2015) Estimated flu levels from search queries; in the 2012–13 season it estimated about double the official figure, and it was closed (Lazer et al., 2014) Measure no longer matched reality Patterns found in big data drift; validate against ground truth and keep checking Target Canada (2013–2015) The new supply-chain system was loaded with large amounts of wrong product data (dimensions, case sizes); shelves were empty while warehouses overflowed; Target left Canada in 2015 Data quality at the source No dashboard can rescue bad master data; data quality is a strategy step, not a clean-up job Public Health England (UK, October 2020) About 16,000 positive COVID-19 test results were left out of daily reports because a pipeline saved data in Excel's old .xls format, which holds only 65,536 rows Integration (ETL) Know the limits of every tool in the pipeline; reconcile totals at each step JPMorgan "London Whale" (2012) A risk model built partly in spreadsheets, with manual copying and a formula error, understated risk while trading losses grew to about $6 billion (JPMorgan's 2013 task-force report) Model governance Spreadsheet models that drive large decisions need controls, testing and review (Day 5) Zillow Offers (US, 2018–2021) An algorithm priced homes for Zillow to buy and resell; when prices turned, it overpaid at scale and Zillow closed the unit in 2021 with large write-downs and job cuts Forecast → decision, ignoring the downside When being wrong in one direction is very costly, plan against the bound, not the point forecast (Part 7) Wells Fargo (US, 2016) Aggressive sales targets for accounts per customer led staff to open millions of accounts customers had not asked for; large fines followed KPI design A metric that becomes a target can be gamed (Part 11) Amazon recruiting model (reported 2018) A CV-screening model trained on past hiring learnt to mark down CVs that mentioned women's activities; it was dropped Model built on biased history Historical decisions encode historical bias (Part 9) Discussion (5 minutes in pairs). Pick two of the failures. For each, name the first stage of the value chain that broke, and one control (a check, a role, a process) that would probably have caught it. Which of your controls is technical, and which is about people? Three patterns run through the failures: bad data at the source (Target Canada, Public Health England), models trusted beyond what they had shown (Google Flu Trends, London Whale, Zillow), and metrics that people were rewarded to move (Wells Fargo). None of them was caused by a missing dashboard. A useful habit after any BI failure, or any project, is a blameless post-mortem : what did we expect, what happened, where did the chain break, what will we change? Writing it down is how the organisation, not just the person, learns. Part 5: Integrating a BI case: Harbourline's sourcing decision (core) ¶ A BI case combines the course's tools into one decision. Part 6: Forecasting with Excel Forecast Sheet: ETS, seasonality and intervals (core) ¶ Day 3 introduced exponential smoothing in Python. Excel offers the same family of models in two places: the Forecast Sheet button, which builds a forecast table and chart in one step, and the FORECAST.ETS functions, which do the same cell by cell. What ETS does, in one paragraph ¶ ETS stands for E rror, T rend and S easonality. The model keeps three running estimates, each updated every period as a weighted average of "what the newest data says" and "what we believed before": the level (where the series is now), updated with weight α (alpha); the trend (how much it rises per period), with weight β (beta); the seasonal effect of each quarter (how far that quarter usually sits above or below the level), with weight γ (gamma). A weight near 1 means "follow the latest data"; near 0 means "change slowly". The forecast for h periods ahead is: level + h × trend + that quarter's seasonal effect. Excel uses the additive version of all three parts (Microsoft calls it the AAA version of ETS): errors, trend and seasonal effects are added in dollars, not multiplied in percentages. Seasonality detection ¶ Excel can detect the season length itself. Roughly, it looks for the lag at which the series (after removing the trend) is most strongly correlated with itself: in quarterly data with a yearly pattern, the value four quarters ago. The Python cell below does a similar check by hand, so you can see what "detection" means. Predict, then run. In the detrended bean cost, which lag between 1 and 8 quarters will have the highest autocorrelation? y = bean [ "cost_per_kg" ] . to_numpy () detrended = np . diff ( y ) # first differences remove the trend acf = { lag : np . corrcoef ( detrended [ lag :], detrended [: - lag ])[ 0 , 1 ] for lag in range ( 1 , 9 )} for lag , r in acf . items (): print ( f "lag { lag } : { r : +.2f } { '#' * int ( max ( r , 0 ) * 30 ) } " ) strong = [ lag for lag , r in acf . items () if r > 0.5 ] print ( "

That is what a season length of 4 means. In Excel, the function =FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY(B2:B21, A2:A21) returns the season length Excel detects (0 means it found none). Check it before trusting an automatic forecast: a series that is too short, or noisy, may give 0 or an odd length. Keep the text labels out of the selection. Data → Forecast Sheet (in the Forecast group, next to What-If Analysis). A preview window opens with the history and a forecast. Choose the line chart (left icon) or the column chart. Forecast End: type 28 (period 28 = Q4-2027, eight quarters after period 20). Seasonality : Detect Automatically , or Set Manually and type 4 . Include forecast statistics : tick it to get α, β, γ and error measures (MAE, RMSE, MASE, SMAPE). Excel adds a new sheet with a table and a chart. The new table has five columns: Timeline , Values (the history), Forecast , Lower Confidence Bound and Upper Confidence Bound . For the history rows the last three are empty, except the last actual row , where Excel copies the actual value into all three so that the chart's lines join. The forecast rows (periods 21 to 28) hold formulas such as =FORECAST.ETS(A22, $B$2:$B$21, $A$2:$A$21, 1, 1) for the forecast, and =C22 + FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT(A22, $B$2:$B$21, $A$2:$A$21, 0.95, 1, 1) for the upper bound (the exact columns depend on where Excel places the table). So you can always find the bound for a given future period by reading across that period's row to the Upper Confidence Bound column, and you can check any cell by clicking it and reading its formula. The timeline must be numeric ¶ Forecast Sheet needs a timeline of numbers or dates with a constant step . Text labels such as Q1-2025 are not a timeline: Excel cannot tell how far apart they are, and Forecast Sheet refuses them or does not offer the expected options. Two fixes: Period numbers 1, 2, 3, … (always safe). The forecast end is then a period number: to forecast four quarters past period n , set Forecast End to n + 4. Real dates , one per quarter, three calendar months apart (for example the first or the last day of each quarter). Excel recognises steps measured in months. If Excel still complains, fall back to period numbers. Keep the readable labels in another column for your report. It means that, if the model is right , the actual value should fall inside the band about 95 times in 100. Two cautions. First, the band assumes the future behaves like the past; a shock the history never showed (a frost in Brazil, a shipping crisis) can push the actual value outside it. Second, Excel calls it a confidence interval, but statisticians would call it a prediction interval : it covers a future value , not just the average, which is why it is wide. Misconception: "More history always helps." More relevant history helps. If the market changed structurally three years ago, older data pulls the forecast towards a world that no longer exists. And for seasonality, ETS needs at least two full seasons to estimate the pattern; with fewer, set seasonality to 0. Which number should feed the plan? The point forecast is right when being wrong in either direction costs about the same . Many decisions are asymmetric . Harbourline must fix its 2026 bean budget with its bank now. If actual costs come in below budget, the unused money sits idle: a small cost. If they come in above , Harbourline must borrow at short notice at a penalty rate, delay payments to farmers, or cut production: a large cost. Say each dollar of overrun costs 3 times as much as each dollar of unused budget. Decision theory gives a clean answer. If an overrun costs u per dollar and an unused dollar costs o , the budget that minimises the expected cost is the quantile of the forecast distribution at u ÷ ( u + o ) which is the same critical ratio as the newsvendor rule at the end of Day 5, Part 12. With u = 3 and o = 1 that is the 75th percentile : plan for a cost that will be exceeded only one year in four. Budgeting at the point forecast is not "neutral": it accepts a 50% chance of the expensive mistake. The 95% upper bound is one particular quantile : the 97.5th percentile. It is the right planning number when an overrun is roughly 39 times as costly as unused budget (0.975 = 39 ÷ 40), for example when an overrun would break a loan covenant or a fixed-price contract. Part 8: Privacy, PIPL, GDPR and consent (core) ¶ The rest of the lecture asks a different question: not "is the analysis right?" but "is it right to do , and right to do this way ?" Ethics in analytics is not a separate subject added at the end; each choice in the value chain (what to collect, how to define a KPI, which model to deploy, what to recommend) has consequences for people. Why personal data needs special care ¶ Harbourline's loyalty app records who bought what, where and when. That data improves offers and stock planning. It can also reveal a person's routine, health (decaf every day after a diagnosis?), religion (fasting months) or income. Personal information is any information about an identified or identifiable person, and "identifiable" is broader than most people think. Two laws you will meet ¶ China: Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) EU: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) In force 1 November 2021 25 May 2018 Applies to Processing in China, and processing abroad that targets or analyses people in China Processing in the EU, and processing abroad that targets or monitors people in the EU Legal bases Consent, or one of several others (a contract with the person, HR management, legal duties, public-health emergencies, news reporting, reasonable use of information the person made public) Six lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests Consent Informed, voluntary and explicit; can be withdrawn; separate consent needed for sensitive information, for sharing with another handler, for making it public and for transfer abroad Freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; as easy to withdraw as to give Sensitive data Includes biometrics, religious belief, specific identities, health, financial accounts, location tracking, and all data on children under 14 "Special categories": health, biometrics, religion, ethnicity, sexual orientation, political opinions, trade-union membership, genetics Automated decisions Must be transparent and fair, with no unreasonable differences in prices or terms between people; people can ask for an explanation and refuse decisions made solely by automated means that significantly affect them Right not to be subject to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, with safeguards Impact assessment Required before processing sensitive data, automated decision-making, sharing or transfer abroad Data protection impact assessment (DPIA) for high-risk processing Moving data abroad A security assessment, a standard contract or certification, depending on volume and type Adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses or other safeguards Penalties Up to 50 million yuan or 5% of the previous year's turnover for serious cases Up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover China's Data Security Law (2021) and Cybersecurity Law (2017) sit alongside PIPL, and the 2022 penalty of more than 8 billion yuan imposed on the ride-hailing company Didi for data violations showed that enforcement is real. This table is a summary for analysts, not legal advice; a company's legal or compliance team applies the details. The principles behind both laws are the same and are what an analyst can apply every day: Purpose limitation: collect for a stated purpose and do not quietly reuse the data for another. Data minimisation: collect and keep only what the purpose needs. An analysis of café traffic does not need names. Storage limitation: delete or anonymise when the purpose is served. Security and access control: only those who need personal data can see it (Part 2's governance roles). Transparency and rights: people can find out what is held about them, correct it and, in many cases, delete it. Consent that means something ¶ Consent is valid only if the person understood what they agreed to and could have said no . Warning signs of consent that does not mean much: Bundling: "agree to marketing or you cannot use the app." Pre-ticked boxes and dark patterns : a bright "Accept all" next to a grey "Manage settings" three screens deep. Vague purposes: "to improve our services" covering profiling, resale and model training. No real withdrawal: opting out takes a phone call. PIPL's separate consent requirement means, for example, that Harbourline could not hide "we share your purchase history with partner brands" inside the general terms: it needs its own clear request. "Anonymous" data often is not ¶ Removing names is pseudonymisation , not anonymisation. Combinations of ordinary fields ( quasi-identifiers ) can single people out. In a well-known study, Latanya Sweeney estimated that about 87% of the US population could be uniquely identified by ZIP code, birth date and sex alone; and researchers re-identified people in Netflix's "anonymised" movie-ratings data by matching it to public reviews. A simple measure is k-anonymity : every combination of quasi-identifiers must be shared by at least k people. Below, 3,000 synthetic Harbourline loyalty members with no names at all. That trade-off between privacy and analytical precision is a decision to make deliberately, and it belongs in the data-governance rules. Excel. Stronger techniques exist (adding calibrated noise, known as differential privacy , or generating synthetic data), but the analyst's first defences are the principles above: do not collect what you do not need, and do not publish row-level data that someone could match. Misconception: "It's legal, so it's ethical." Laws set a floor and lag behind technology. Target, the US retailer, was reported in 2012 to have used purchase patterns to predict which customers were pregnant and send them baby-product offers; it was probably lawful, and many customers still found it intrusive. A useful test is the front-page test : would the people in the data be comfortable reading exactly what you did with it? Part 9: Bias and fairness: a disparate-impact demonstration (core) ¶ A model can treat groups of people differently even when nobody intends it. Common sources of bias: Source What happens Example Historical bias The data records past decisions that were themselves unfair A model trained on past loan approvals copies past officers' prejudices Representation bias Some groups are under-represented in the data A face-recognition model trained mostly on one skin tone Measurement bias The label measures the wrong thing, or measures it worse for some groups Using "arrests" as a stand-in for "crime" Proxy variables A feature stands in for a protected one Postcode or district standing in for ethnicity or migrant status Deployment bias A model is used for a purpose or population it was not built for A credit model from one country used in another The demonstration ¶ Harbourline plans to offer instant credit in its app for buying coffee machines. A credit partner has 5,000 past applicants with their monthly income , a credit score , their district , whether a loan officer approved them in the past, and whether they repaid . Applicants belong to two groups, A and B , standing for any protected characteristic (for example gender, ethnicity or migrant status). Group membership is not used by the model. In this synthetic data, as often in reality, group B lives mainly in two districts, earns a little less on average, and past officers approved group B less often than its repayment record justified. The disparate-impact ratio compares approval rates: DI = (approval rate of group B) ÷ (approval rate of group A) A common screening rule, the four-fifths rule from US employment guidelines, treats a ratio below 0.8 as a warning sign that needs investigating. It is a rule of thumb, not a proof of discrimination, and other jurisdictions use other tests. Predict, then run. Being fairer did not cost accuracy in this case; it often costs less than people assume, because the biased decisions were also worse decisions. A gap remains , because group B's incomes are lower on average and income genuinely predicts repayment. Whether that gap is acceptable is a value judgement , not a statistical one: it depends on the law, the purpose (credit, hiring, insurance) and the organisation's values. Which fairness measure? ¶ Measure Equal across groups Question it answers Demographic parity (DI ratio) Approval rates Do groups get the benefit at similar rates? Equal opportunity Approval rates among people who would repay (true-positive rates) Are qualified people treated alike? Predictive parity Repayment rates among the approved Does a "yes" mean the same in each group? Calibration For each score, the actual repayment rate Does a score of 0.7 mean 70% in every group? When groups differ in their underlying rates, these measures cannot all be equal at once (results by Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, and by Chouldechova, prompted by the debate over the COMPAS risk scores used in US courts). So an organisation must choose which fairness it is committing to, write that choice down and justify it. That choice belongs to the business owner and the ethics or compliance function, informed by the analyst, not to the analyst alone. Excel. Misconception: "The algorithm is objective because it is maths." A model is a summary of its training data and of the choices made in building it: which label, which features, which threshold. Each choice can introduce or remove bias. Part 10: Transparency and explainability (core) ¶ People affected by a decision, and the managers responsible for it, need to know why it was made. Both PIPL and GDPR give people rights in relation to automated decisions (Part 8), and lenders in many countries must give reasons when they decline credit. Good practice includes: Model cards (Mitchell and colleagues, 2019): a short document for each model: its purpose, the data it was trained on, its performance overall and by group , its limits, and who is responsible. A simple model can still hide a biased label (Part 9, model 1, was a plain logistic regression). And a complex model can be explained well enough for its purpose. The test is whether the people affected and the people accountable can understand and challenge the decision. Part 11: Goodhart's law and metric gaming (core) ¶ Goodhart's law , as it is usually quoted: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. A KPI is useful because it tracks something we care about. Once people are rewarded for moving the KPI itself, they find ways to move it that do not move the thing we care about, or that harm it. Related is Campbell's law : the more a measure is used for important decisions, the more it is subject to corruption pressures and the more it distorts the process it was meant to monitor. Famous examples: Wells Fargo's accounts-per-customer target (Part 4); Volkswagen's diesel cars, which detected the emissions test and behaved differently during it (2015); hospitals meeting waiting-time targets by delaying the moment a patient is officially "waiting"; software teams rewarded for lines of code. A demonstration. Harbourline's customer-service centre has 40 agents. Management introduces a bonus for keeping the average handle time (AHT) of a call under 6 minutes. But first-contact resolution falls, customers call back more often, and the agent time needed to actually solve a problem goes up . Customers are worse off and so is the cost base. Nobody broke a rule. How to design KPIs that resist gaming: Pair every target with a counter-metric it could be traded against: handle time with resolution rate; sales with returns and complaints; speed with error rate. Measure the outcome, not the activity, where possible: problems solved, not calls closed. Use a balanced set (a balanced scorecard : financial, customer, process, learning) rather than one number. Watch for sudden improvements , and audit a sample: a jump in a KPI with no change in the process is a signal, not just good news. Ask the people being measured how the KPI could be gamed, before launch. They know. Keep some measures for learning only , not tied to pay. Check your understanding. Part 12: Supply-chain ethics and ESG trade-offs (core) ¶ Most of a product's social and environmental impact sits upstream , with suppliers. For Harbourline that means coffee farms: farmer incomes that can fall below a living income when prices drop, child and forced labour risks in some regions, deforestation when farms expand, and climate exposure. In 2013 the collapse of the Rana Plaza factory building in Bangladesh, which made clothes for well-known brands, killed more than 1,100 workers and changed how buyers think about responsibility for suppliers' conditions. ESG (environmental, social and governance) is the umbrella term investors and companies use for these factors. Some useful vocabulary: Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions: a company's own direct emissions; emissions from the energy it buys; and everything else in its value chain, including suppliers. For a roaster, Scope 3 (farming and shipping) is usually most of the total. Due diligence: identifying, preventing and accounting for human-rights and environmental harms in the supply chain. It is increasingly required by law, for example under Germany's Supply Chain Act (in force since 2023) and EU rules on corporate sustainability due diligence and on deforestation-free products (which cover coffee), whose details and timetables have been revised since adoption. Certification and traceability: independent standards (for example Fairtrade or Rainforest Alliance for coffee) and the ability to trace a bag of beans back to a co-operative or a farm. Greenwashing: claiming more sustainability than the evidence supports. Regulators increasingly fine it. Making the trade-off explicit ¶ Ethical sourcing usually costs money now, while its benefits (lower legal and reputational risk, supply security, customer and employee loyalty, access to customers and lenders who require standards) are real but harder to put in a spreadsheet. Two disciplined ways to bring both into one decision: Price what you can, describe what you cannot. The extra cost of option B or C per year, per kg and per cup is easy to compute; reputational risk is not, but it can be described with evidence (customer surveys, buyer requirements, past incidents in the industry). Multi-criteria scoring , with the weights written down. Below, Harbourline's analysts score the three options from 1 (poor) to 5 (strong) on four non-financial criteria. If the board's honest answer is "less than that", the decision is made; if not, the disagreement is now about values, stated openly, rather than hidden in a spreadsheet. Two rules keep multi-criteria scoring honest: Red lines are constraints, not weights. If an option involves forced or child labour, no profit advantage can compensate for it, so it is excluded , not scored low. Putting it in the scoring implies a price at which it would be acceptable. Write down the weights before seeing the scores , and test how sensitive the answer is to them (exactly as you did with decision rules in Day 5, Part 12). Misconception: "Ethics and profit are always in conflict." Sometimes they are, in the short run, and pretending otherwise is greenwashing. But over longer horizons many ethical choices also reduce risk : option C's fixed price protects Harbourline in a bad year (Part 7), and secure relationships with farmers protect supply when markets are tight. A good recommendation states both the cost and the risk reduction. Part 13: Responsible-AI frameworks (core summary, extension detail) ¶ Several frameworks turn the ideas of Parts 8 to 12 into checklists and rules. You do not need to memorise them; you should recognise them and be able to use one as a structure for a review. Framework From Core idea OECD AI Principles (2019, updated 2024) OECD member countries and others Inclusive growth and well-being; human rights and fairness; transparency and explainability; robustness and safety; accountability UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) UNESCO member states Human rights and dignity, fairness, sustainability, human oversight; impact assessments NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (2023) US National Institute of Standards and Technology (voluntary) Four functions: Govern (culture, roles), Map (context and risks), Measure (test and track), Manage (prioritise and act) EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689, in force from August 2024, obligations phased in over several years) European Union (law) Risk tiers: unacceptable (banned, such as social scoring by public authorities), high-risk (such as credit scoring and recruitment: strict requirements), limited (transparency duties, such as telling people they are talking to a chatbot), minimal China's AI rules Cyberspace Administration of China and other regulators (law) Rules on algorithmic recommendation (2022: transparency, an option to turn off personalisation, no unreasonable price discrimination), deep synthesis (2023), generative AI services (2023) and labelling of AI-generated content (2025) ISO/IEC 42001 (2023) International standard A certifiable management system for AI, in the style of ISO quality standards A practical checklist for any analytics project ¶ Before launch, the analyst and the business owner should be able to answer: Purpose: what decision does this support, and is it a legitimate use of the data? Data: do we have the right to use it (consent or another basis)? Is it the minimum needed? Is personal data protected? Fairness: have we checked outcomes by group? Which fairness measure did we choose, and why? Transparency: can we explain a decision to the person affected? Is there a model card? Human oversight: who reviews significant decisions, and can they overrule the model? Gaming and side effects: how could the KPI or the model be gamed? What are the counter-metrics? Monitoring: how will we know if it drifts or causes harm after launch? Who is accountable? This maps closely onto NIST's four functions: questions 1 and 7 are Govern , 2 is Map , 3, 4 and 6 are Measure , 5 and 7 are Manage . Part 14: Writing a managerial recommendation (core) ¶ Every graded report in Module 2 ends in a recommendation. A recommendation that balances financial and ethical evidence has a recognisable shape. The structure ¶ The answer first. One or two sentences: what to do, and the main reason. Executives read the first paragraph; many read nothing else. The financial evidence , with numbers, units and their uncertainty: the point estimate and the range or the bound (Part 7). The ethical and societal evidence : who is affected and how; legal and reputational exposure; what the organisation has publicly committed to. Use evidence (surveys, standards, cases), not adjectives. The trade-off, stated plainly : what the recommended option costs compared with the alternative, in terms people can picture (per year, per unit, per customer), and what it buys. Risks and conditions : what would change the recommendation, and what to monitor (KPIs and counter-metrics). The decision requested : what you need the reader to approve, and by when. This is the pyramid principle (Barbara Minto): conclusion first, then the supporting arguments, then the detail. Separate three kinds of statement ¶ Kind Example How to write it Fact "Bean costs rose about 80 cents per kg from 2021 to 2025." State it with its source Estimate "The 2026 average is forecast at about $6.32, and is unlikely to exceed about $6.49." Give the method and the uncertainty Judgement "Traceability to farm level is worth paying for." Say whose judgement and why; never disguise it as a fact A worked example for Harbourline ¶ The cell below assembles the numbers from Parts 7 and 12 into the opening of a memo. docs.text: Define business intelligence , trace the BI value chain from data to an outcome, and say where value usually leaks. Set out a BI strategy : sponsorship, goals and KPIs , data governance , data quality , a maturity assessment, and the choice between self-service and centralised BI. Describe a BI architecture : source systems, ETL and ELT , warehouse, lake and lakehouse , the star schema , the semantic layer and dashboards; place common tools in it. Draw lessons from real BI case studies , including well-known failures. Build a forecast with Excel's Forecast Sheet , explain ETS , seasonality detection and the confidence interval , and mirror it in Python. Explain when and why to plan against an upper bound instead of the point forecast, and choose the right bound for an asymmetric risk. Apply privacy principles under China's PIPL and the EU's GDPR , including consent and re-identification risk. Measure bias with the disparate-impact ratio and other fairness measures, and explain why removing the sensitive column does not remove bias. Explain a model's decision ( transparency ), recognise Goodhart's law , and weigh supply-chain ethics and ESG trade-offs. Use a responsible-AI framework as a checklist, and write a managerial recommendation that balances financial and ethical evidence. This lecture fills six periods (P1 to P6). Each part is marked core (teach in class) or extension (faster students, a study block, or self-study).
