docs.title: Setup

docs.text: Days 1 to 5 gave you techniques: summaries, charts, text mining, forecasts, regressions and simulations. Business intelligence is what an organisation builds so that techniques like these reach the people who decide, reliably and repeatedly. A working definition: Business intelligence is the combination of data, technology, processes and people that turns an organisation's data into information that its managers trust and use to make decisions. Each of the four words matters. Data without technology stays in files nobody can query. Technology without processes (who defines a KPI, who fixes bad data, who may see what) produces numbers that disagree with each other. And all three fail without people who read the numbers and act on them.
docs.title: Part 1: What BI is, and the BI value chain (core)

docs.text: Term Main question Typical output Who uses it Reporting What happened? Fixed monthly reports Everyone, on a schedule Business intelligence What is happening, and is it on target? Dashboards, KPI scorecards, self-service queries, alerts Managers at every level Business analytics Why did it happen, and what will happen? Diagnostic analyses, forecasts, simulations Analysts and the managers they support Data science What can we predict or automate? Models built into products and processes Data scientists and engineers The boundaries blur. In this course the descriptive and diagnostic work of Days 1 and 2 is classic BI; the forecasts and simulations of Days 3 to 5 are analytics; and a BI strategy decides how both reach the decision.
docs.title: BI, analytics and data science

docs.text: Value from data is created in a chain of stages, and it reaches the business only if every stage works: data captured → integrated and cleaned → turned into a trusted measure → seen by the right person in time → changes a decision → the decision is carried out → the outcome is measured and fed back The last arrow closes the loop: measuring the outcome produces new data, which is how an organisation learns whether its decisions worked. Predict, then run. Suppose five stages each work most of the time: 95%, 85%, 70%, 50% and 80%. What share of the potential value of an insight actually reaches the business: about 80%, 50% or 25%? And which stage would you improve first? chain = pd . DataFrame ({ "stage" : [ "Data captured correctly" , "Integrated into a trusted measure" , "Seen by the decision-maker in time" , "Changes the decision" , "Decision carried out" ], "works" : [ 0.95 , 0.85 , 0.70 , 0.50 , 0.80 ], }) chain [ "value_still_alive" ] = chain [ "works" ] . cumprod () print ( chain . to_string ( index = False , formatters = { "works" : " {:.0%} " . format , "value_still_alive" : " {:.0%} " . format })) base = chain [ "works" ] . prod () print ( f " \n Share of potential value delivered: { base : .0% } " ) # Improve one stage at a time by 10 percentage points (capped at 100%) and see what each buys gain = { s : ( np . prod ( np . where ( chain [ "stage" ] == s , np . minimum ( chain [ "works" ] + 0.10 , 1 ), chain [ "works" ])) - base ) for s in chain [ "stage" ]} print ( " \n Extra share of value from improving one stage by 10 points:" ) for s , g in sorted ( gain . items (), key = lambda kv : - kv [ 1 ]): print ( f " { s : <36 } + { g : .1% } " ) stage works value_still_alive Data captured correctly 95% 95% Integrated into a trusted measure 85% 81% Seen by the decision-maker in time 70% 57% Changes the decision 50% 28% Decision carried out 80% 23% Share of potential value delivered: 23% Extra share of value from improving one stage by 10 points: Changes the decision +4.5% Seen by the decision-maker in time +3.2% Decision carried out +2.8% Integrated into a trusted measure +2.7% Data captured correctly +1.2% Only about a quarter of the potential value survives, although no single stage looks terrible. Two lessons follow. Value multiplies, so it leaks. A chain is as strong as the product of its links. A 95% data pipeline feeding a dashboard that changes one decision in two delivers less than half of what it could. Improve the weakest link. Raising the weakest stage (whether the insight changes the decision) buys far more than polishing the strongest (data capture). Many BI programmes spend most of their budget on technology at the left of the chain, when the binding constraint is at the right: adoption, trust and the habit of acting on evidence. Misconception: "More dashboards means more BI value." A dashboard adds value only through the decisions it changes. Organisations often have hundreds of reports that nobody opens; each one still costs money to maintain and adds a chance of conflicting numbers. Count decisions improved, not dashboards built. Check your understanding. Name one thing an organisation could do to raise each of the last two stages (changes the decision; decision carried out). None of them should involve buying software.
docs.title: The BI value chain

docs.text: A BI strategy is an organisation's plan for how it will use data to make decisions: what it wants to achieve, which measures matter, who owns them, which data and tools it needs, and in what order it will build. Chapter 7's two readings agree on the main steps, which we can put in our own words as: Step What it means in practice What goes wrong without it 1. Executive sponsor A senior owner (often a chief data officer) with budget and authority to settle disputes between departments Each department builds its own reports; no one can resolve conflicting numbers 2. Stakeholder interviews Ask the people who will use the output which decisions they make and what they need to know Dashboards answer questions nobody asked 3. Goals and KPIs Pick a small set of measures tied to company goals, each with a written definition and an owner "Revenue" means three different things in three meetings 4. Cross-functional team IT, the business units and a data-governance or compliance role work together A lone analyst's side project that dies when they leave 5. Trusted data infrastructure Governed, documented, access-controlled data pipelines Reports nobody trusts, so nobody uses them 6. Tool selection Choose tools on data access, governance, fit with existing systems and users' skills, not on feature lists Expensive licences, little use 7. Phased roadmap Start with one or two high-value use cases, show results, then extend A two-year "big bang" project that is out of date when it lands A single dashboard, however good, is one output of a strategy, not the strategy itself.
docs.title: Part 2: BI strategy: goals, KPIs, governance, data quality, maturity (core)

docs.text: A key performance indicator is a measure that tells you whether a goal is being met. Good KPIs share four properties: Tied to a goal. "Grow profitable revenue" leads to revenue and margin; "keep customers" leads to retention. Defined once, in writing. The formula, the data source, the time window, what is included and excluded, and who owns it. Actionable. Someone can change it. "Global coffee price" matters, but it is a driver to monitor , not a KPI anyone is accountable for. Balanced. Every KPI that can be pushed up by cutting corners needs a counter-metric (Part 11). Speed of service goes with accuracy; sales with returns. Distinguish lagging indicators, which report results after the fact (quarterly profit), from leading indicators, which move earlier and can still be acted on (weekly repeat-visit rate, order pipeline). A KPI tree (or driver tree) breaks an outcome into the drivers that multiply or add up to it. Harbourline's café revenue is revenue = cafés × trading days × customers per café-day × average ticket so a change in revenue can be split into the part due to each driver. Because the drivers multiply, the clean way to split the change is on the log scale , where products become sums. Predict, then run. Harbourline opened eight new cafés in 2025, but each café served fewer customers a day. Did revenue grow or shrink, and which driver contributed most? kpi = pd . DataFrame ({ "2024" : [ 52 , 360 , 210 , 6.10 ], "2025" : [ 60 , 360 , 201 , 6.45 ]}, index = [ "cafés" , "trading days" , "customers per café-day" , "average ticket ($)" ]) rev = kpi . prod () change = rev [ "2025" ] - rev [ "2024" ] log_share = np . log ( kpi [ "2025" ] / kpi [ "2024" ]) / np . log ( rev [ "2025" ] / rev [ "2024" ]) tree = pd . DataFrame ({ "2024" : kpi [ "2024" ], "2025" : kpi [ "2025" ], "change" : ( kpi [ "2025" ] / kpi [ "2024" ] - 1 ) . map ( " {:+.1%} " . format ), "contribution ($)" : ( log_share * change ) . map ( usd )}) print ( tree . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Revenue 2024: { usd ( rev [ '2024' ]) } 2025: { usd ( rev [ '2025' ]) } change: { usd ( change ) } ( { rev [ '2025' ] / rev [ '2024' ] - 1 : +.1% } )" ) 2024 2025 change contribution ($) cafés 52.0 60.00 +15.4% $3,712,014 trading days 360.0 360.00 +0.0% $0 customers per café-day 210.0 201.00 -4.3% -$1,136,233 average ticket ($) 6.1 6.45 +5.7% $1,447,219 Revenue 2024: $23,980,320 2025: $28,003,320 change: $4,023,000 (+16.8%) Revenue grew by about 17%, and the KPI tree shows why : new cafés and a higher average ticket more than made up for fewer customers per café-day. A dashboard that showed only total revenue would hide the one warning sign, the fall in customers per café, which is a leading indicator: it may reflect new cafés still building a following, or existing cafés losing customers to the price rise. The next question for the analyst is diagnostic (Day 1): split customers per café-day into old and new cafés. Excel. Put the four drivers for each year in B2:C5 . Revenue is =PRODUCT(B2:B5) . The contribution of driver i is =LN(C2/B2)/LN(C$6/B$6)*(C$6-B$6) with the revenues in row 6; the four contributions add up exactly to the change.
docs.title: Goals to KPIs

docs.text: Data governance is the set of decisions about who may do what with which data, and who is responsible for its quality. It is a process, not a tool. The common roles: Role Responsible for Example at Harbourline Data owner A business leader accountable for a data domain: its definitions, access and quality targets The head of retail owns café sales data Data steward Day-to-day quality: rules, fixing errors, answering "what does this field mean?" A finance analyst who maintains the store master list Data custodian The technical side: storage, security, backups, access controls The IT team running the warehouse Data consumer Using the data within agreed rules A café manager reading the weekly dashboard The main tools of governance are a business glossary (agreed definitions), a data catalogue (what data exists, where, who owns it), lineage (where each number comes from), access policies (who may see what, especially personal data; Part 8) and master data management (one agreed list of stores, products and customers).
docs.title: Data governance

docs.text: Data quality has several dimensions , each with its own test: Dimension Question A test Completeness Is the value there? Share of non-missing values in a required field Validity Is it allowed? Amounts above zero, dates inside the period, codes in the agreed list Uniqueness Is each real thing recorded once? No repeated transaction IDs Consistency Is it recorded the same way everywhere? Store codes in one format, matching the master list Timeliness Is it available when needed? Share loaded within 24 hours of the sale Accuracy Does it match reality? Spot checks against receipts or a second source (cannot be tested from the data alone) A data-quality scorecard turns these into numbers with targets, so that quality is managed like any other KPI. Below, a month of synthetic till transactions from Harbourline's cafés with a few typical faults planted in them. Predict, then run. Which dimension do you expect to fail its target? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 71 ) n = 1200 stores = [ f "S { i : 02d } " for i in range ( 1 , 13 )] tx = pd . DataFrame ({ "txn_id" : np . arange ( 500001 , 500001 + n ), "store" : rng . choice ( stores , n ), "date" : pd . Timestamp ( "2025-10-01" ) + pd . to_timedelta ( rng . integers ( 0 , 31 , n ), unit = "D" ), "amount" : np . round ( rng . gamma ( 4 , 1.6 , n ), 2 ), "hours_to_load" : np . round ( rng . exponential ( 5 , n ), 1 ), }) # Plant typical faults tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 22 , replace = False ), "store" ] = np . nan # missing store tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 9 , replace = False ), "amount" ] *= - 1 # refunds keyed as sales tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 4 , replace = False ), "date" ] = pd . Timestamp ( "2026-10-03" ) # wrong year tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 14 , replace = False ), "store" ] = rng . choice ([ "s05" , "Store 5" , "S5" ], 14 ) # inconsistent codes tx . loc [ rng . choice ( n , 70 , replace = False ), "hours_to_load" ] += 30 # late loads tx = pd . concat ([ tx , tx . sample ( 18 , random_state = 3 )], ignore_index = True ) # duplicated rows checks = { "Completeness: store present" : tx [ "store" ] . notna () . mean (), "Validity: amount > 0 and date in October 2025" : (( tx [ "amount" ] > 0 ) & tx [ "date" ] . between ( "2025-10-01" , "2025-10-31" )) . mean (), "Uniqueness: transaction ID not repeated" : ( ~ tx [ "txn_id" ] . duplicated ( keep = "first" )) . mean (), "Consistency: store code in master list" : tx [ "store" ] . dropna () . isin ( stores ) . mean (), "Timeliness: loaded within 24 hours" : ( tx [ "hours_to_load" ] <= 24 ) . mean (), } targets = [ 0.99 , 0.99 , 1.00 , 0.99 , 0.95 ] card = pd . DataFrame ({ "score" : list ( checks . values ()), "target" : targets }, index = list ( checks . keys ())) card [ "status" ] = np . where ( card [ "score" ] >= card [ "target" ], "pass" , "FAIL" ) print ( f "Rows checked: { len ( tx ) : , } \n " ) print ( card . to_string ( formatters = { "score" : " {:.1%} " . format , "target" : " {:.0%} " . format })) Rows checked: 1,218 score target status Completeness: store present 98.4% 99% FAIL Validity: amount > 0 and date in October 2025 98.9% 99% FAIL Uniqueness: transaction ID not repeated 98.5% 100% FAIL Consistency: store code in master list 98.8% 99% FAIL Timeliness: loaded within 24 hours 93.8% 95% FAIL Every dimension fails its target, although each fault touches only a few per cent of the rows. That is normal for raw operational data, and it is why trusted data infrastructure is a step in every BI strategy: if the café dashboards were built on this table, totals would be inflated by the duplicates, twelve stores would appear as fifteen, and late loads would make yesterday's sales look low every morning. The scorecard also tells the data steward where to start. Duplicates and inconsistent codes are fixed once, upstream, in the pipeline (Part 3); late loads are a process problem for IT; refunds keyed as sales are a training problem at the till. Excel. With the table in A1:E1219 : completeness =1-COUNTBLANK(B2:B1219)/ROWS(B2:B1219) ; validity =COUNTIFS(D2:D1219,">0",C2:C1219,">="&DATE(2025,10,1),C2:C1219,"<="&DATE(2025,10,31))/ROWS(D2:D1219) ; a duplicate flag in a helper column =COUNTIF(A$2:A2,A2)>1 ; timeliness =COUNTIF(E2:E1219,"<=24")/ROWS(E2:E1219) . In Excel 365, =ROWS(UNIQUE(A2:A1219)) counts distinct IDs. Misconception: "Our data is clean because the dashboard has no blanks." Dashboards aggregate, and aggregation hides faults: a duplicate adds to a total silently, and a wrong store code simply becomes a new bar. Quality is checked on the rows , before aggregation.
docs.title: Data quality

docs.text: A maturity model describes stages an organisation passes through as it learns to use data. Published models (from TDWI, Gartner and others) differ in detail; most share a ladder like this one: Level Name What it looks like Typical next step 1 Ad hoc Spreadsheets e-mailed around; each team has its own numbers Agree definitions for five core KPIs 2 Repeatable reporting Regular reports from one system; still mostly manual Build a governed data store and automate the main pipeline 3 Integrated BI A warehouse joins several systems; shared dashboards; a glossary exists Self-service for trained users; data-quality scorecards 4 Analytics-driven Forecasts and simulations feed planning; decisions cite evidence Embed models in processes; measure decision outcomes 5 Optimising Data and models are part of everyday operations; experiments are routine; ethics reviews are standard Keep governance ahead of new uses (AI, new data) Maturity is uneven: a company can be at level 4 in finance and level 1 in HR. The use of a model is to make the next step explicit, not to award a score. Skipping levels (buying an AI platform at level 1) is the most common and expensive mistake. Check your understanding. Harbourline's finance team builds its monthly report by copying figures from the till system into Excel; the cafés' managers each keep their own spreadsheet of staff hours. Which level is each team at, and what is the next step for each?
docs.title: Maturity: where is the organisation now?

docs.text: Centralised (traditional) Self-service (modern) Hub and spoke (common compromise) Who builds reports A central BI team Business users, with drag-and-drop tools The hub builds certified data sets and core KPIs; spokes build their own views on top Strengths Consistent definitions, strong control Speed, relevance, less waiting Consistency where it matters, speed elsewhere Risks Backlog, slow answers, reports that miss the need Conflicting numbers, "spreadmarts", exposure of personal data Needs clear rules on what is certified Needs A capable central team Training, governed data sets, a semantic layer (Part 3) Both, plus a BI competency centre that sets standards Self-service needs more governance, not less: more people touch the data, so definitions, access rules and a semantic layer must already exist.
docs.title: Self-service or centralised?

docs.text: A BI architecture moves data from where it is created to where it is used, in layers: Layer What happens Examples Sources Data is created by operational systems Till (point-of-sale) system, ERP for purchasing and finance, CRM and loyalty app, website logs, spreadsheets, external data (weather, commodity prices) Integration: ETL or ELT Data is extracted, cleaned, joined and loaded Scheduled pipelines; data-quality checks (Part 2) run here Storage Data is kept in a form built for analysis Data warehouse, data lake, lakehouse Semantic layer Business names and KPI definitions are defined once "Net revenue", "active customer" as governed formulas Presentation People and programs consume the data Dashboards, scheduled reports, self-service queries, alerts, models
docs.title: Part 3: BI architecture and the tool landscape (core)

docs.text: ETL: extract, transform, load ELT: extract, load, transform Order Clean and reshape before loading into the warehouse Load raw data first; transform inside the warehouse Suits Older on-premises warehouses with limited computing power; strict control of what enters Cloud warehouses with cheap storage and elastic computing Strength Only clean, conformed data is stored Raw data is kept, so a transformation can be rerun or changed later Risk Rework when requirements change; lost raw detail Raw personal data sits in the warehouse, so access control matters more
docs.title: ETL or ELT?

docs.text: A data warehouse stores structured, cleaned data in tables designed for queries, with a fixed structure decided in advance ( schema on write ). Fast and trusted, but less flexible. A data lake stores raw data of any kind (tables, logs, text, images) cheaply, and structure is applied when the data is read ( schema on read ). Flexible, but without governance it becomes a data swamp that nobody can trust. A lakehouse puts warehouse-style tables, transactions and governance on top of lake storage, aiming for both.
docs.title: Warehouse, lake or lakehouse?

docs.text: Warehouses for BI are usually organised as a star schema : one fact table of events (sales, with numeric measures such as amount and quantity) in the middle, joined by keys to dimension tables that describe the events (store, product, customer, date). Dashboards then slice the facts by any dimension. Below, a small Harbourline star schema. rng = np . random . default_rng ( 12 ) dim_store = pd . DataFrame ({ "store_key" : range ( 1 , 7 ), "store" : [ "Pier" , "Old Town" , "Station" , "Campus" , "Riverside" , "Market" ], "region" : [ "Harbour" , "Harbour" , "Central" , "Central" , "East" , "East" ]}) dim_customer = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer_key" : range ( 1 , 401 ), "channel" : rng . choice ([ "app" , "card only" ], 400 , p = [ 0.55 , 0.45 ])}) n_sales = 6000 fact_sales = pd . DataFrame ({ "customer_key" : rng . integers ( 1 , 401 , n_sales ), "store_key" : rng . choice ( range ( 1 , 7 ), n_sales , p = [ 0.22 , 0.18 , 0.2 , 0.12 , 0.16 , 0.12 ]), "date" : pd . Timestamp ( "2025-01-01" ) + pd . to_timedelta ( rng . integers ( 0 , 365 , n_sales ), unit = "D" ), "amount" : np . round ( rng . gamma ( 3 , 2.2 , n_sales ), 2 ), }) # A star-schema query: join the fact table to its dimensions, then slice sales = fact_sales . merge ( dim_store , on = "store_key" ) . merge ( dim_customer , on = "customer_key" ) sales [ "quarter" ] = sales [ "date" ] . dt . quarter print ( "Fact rows:" , len ( fact_sales ), " Dimension rows:" , len ( dim_store ), "stores," , len ( dim_customer ), "customers \n " ) print ( sales . pivot_table ( index = "region" , columns = "quarter" , values = "amount" , aggfunc = "sum" ) . round ( 0 )) Fact rows: 6000 Dimension rows: 6 stores, 400 customers quarter 1 2 3 4 region Central 3284.0 3381.0 3004.0 3158.0 East 2656.0 2810.0 3035.0 2984.0 Harbour 4171.0 4008.0 3755.0 3709.0 That pivot is exactly what a dashboard does behind the scenes: join, filter, group, aggregate . In Tableau, the joins live in the data source and the pivot is the view; in Excel, the same table is a PivotTable on a joined sheet (Day 1).
docs.title: The star schema

docs.text: Now a common problem. Three teams report the number of active customers for 2025: Marketing: customers who bought at least once in the last 90 days of the year. Finance: customers with at least 12 purchases in the year (roughly monthly). Operations: customers who bought in December . Predict, then run. Will the three counts be close, or far apart? window_start = pd . Timestamp ( "2025-10-03" ) # the last 90 days of 2025: 3 October to 31 December per_customer = fact_sales . groupby ( "customer_key" ) . agg ( last = ( "date" , "max" ), purchases = ( "date" , "size" ), bought_dec = ( "date" , lambda d : ( d . dt . month == 12 ) . any ())) definitions = { "Marketing: bought in the last 90 days" : ( per_customer [ "last" ] >= window_start ) . sum (), "Finance: 12 or more purchases in the year" : ( per_customer [ "purchases" ] >= 12 ) . sum (), "Operations: bought in December" : per_customer [ "bought_dec" ] . sum (), } for name , count in definitions . items (): print ( f " { name : <45 } { count : >4 } active customers" ) # A tiny semantic layer: each KPI is defined once, with its owner, and every report calls it SEMANTIC_LAYER = { "active_customers" : { "definition" : "Distinct customers with at least one purchase in the 90 days up to the period end" , "owner" : "Head of marketing" , "formula" : lambda f , start : f . loc [ f [ "date" ] >= start , "customer_key" ] . nunique (), }, } kpi_def = SEMANTIC_LAYER [ "active_customers" ] print ( f " \n Governed KPI: { kpi_def [ 'definition' ] } (owner: { kpi_def [ 'owner' ] } )" ) print ( "Value for 2025:" , kpi_def [ "formula" ]( fact_sales , window_start )) Marketing: bought in the last 90 days 394 active customers Finance: 12 or more purchases in the year 323 active customers Operations: bought in December 288 active customers Governed KPI: Distinct customers with at least one purchase in the 90 days up to the period end (owner: Head of marketing) Value for 2025: 394 The three "active customer" counts differ by more than a hundred, and none of them is wrong: each answers a different question. The problem is calling all three by the same name. In a meeting, marketing's number and finance's number would contradict each other, and the meeting would argue about data instead of deciding. A semantic layer fixes this: each KPI is defined once , with a name, a formula, an owner and a description, and every dashboard and query uses that definition. In industry this is done with tools such as Power BI semantic models, Looker's modelling language, dbt's metrics layer or Tableau's published data sources. In Excel, a modest version is a single Definitions sheet with named cells, and every report linking to it rather than retyping formulas. Misconception: "If two reports show different numbers, one of them has a bug." Often both are correct, under different definitions. The fix is governance (one agreed definition and a name for each variant), not debugging.
docs.title: The semantic layer: one definition per KPI

docs.text: Layer Widely used tools Notes Spreadsheets Microsoft Excel, Google Sheets, WPS Office Still the most used BI tool in the world; strong for models (Day 5), weak for governance BI and dashboards Microsoft Power BI, Tableau (Salesforce), Qlik Sense, Looker (Google), Oracle Analytics; in China also FineBI and FineReport (Fanruan), Alibaba Cloud Quick BI, Tencent Cloud BI Choose on data connections, governance, cost per user and users' skills Warehouse and lakehouse Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift, Azure Synapse and Microsoft Fabric, Databricks; Alibaba Cloud MaxCompute and Hologres Cloud warehouses made ELT the default Integration and transformation Fivetran, Airbyte, Informatica, Azure Data Factory; dbt for SQL transformations; Apache Airflow for scheduling Data-quality tests usually run here Governance Data catalogues such as Collibra, Alation, Microsoft Purview, DataHub Glossary, lineage, ownership Analytics and data science Python (Jupyter), R, SQL The tools of Days 1–5 Tool markets change quickly, and names in this table will date. The selection criteria do not: data access and connectors, governed sharing and security, fit with existing systems, total cost (licences, training, maintenance), the skills of the people who will use it, and whether it supports the organisation's language and regulations (for example, where data must be stored; Part 8). Check your understanding. A 40-person company keeps its sales in a till system and its costs in Excel. A vendor proposes a lakehouse and an AI assistant. Using the maturity table and the architecture layers, what would you build first instead?
docs.title: The tool landscape

docs.text: Real cases show where in the value chain (Part 1) BI succeeds or breaks. All of these are documented in the business press or in official reports; read the original sources for detail. Case What happened Where in the chain Lesson Tesco Clubcard (UK, from 1995, with dunnhumby) Loyalty-card data on what each household bought was used to target offers and plan ranges; widely credited with helping Tesco become the UK's largest grocer Data → decision → action, closed loop Data creates value when it changes everyday decisions (offers, ranges), and the loop is measured Walmart Retail Link (US, from the early 1990s) Walmart shared store-level sales and stock data with its suppliers, who used it to plan production and replenishment Integration and sharing across firms Sharing governed data with partners can be worth more than hoarding it UPS ORION (US, rolled out 2012–2016) Route-optimisation software for drivers; UPS reported large annual savings in miles and fuel Model → action, after years of change management Adoption by drivers took longer than building the model Google Flu Trends (2008–2015) Estimated flu levels from search queries; in the 2012–13 season it estimated about double the official figure, and it was closed (Lazer et al., 2014) Measure no longer matched reality Patterns found in big data drift; validate against ground truth and keep checking Target Canada (2013–2015) The new supply-chain system was loaded with large amounts of wrong product data (dimensions, case sizes); shelves were empty while warehouses overflowed; Target left Canada in 2015 Data quality at the source No dashboard can rescue bad master data; data quality is a strategy step, not a clean-up job Public Health England (UK, October 2020) About 16,000 positive COVID-19 test results were left out of daily reports because a pipeline saved data in Excel's old .xls format, which holds only 65,536 rows Integration (ETL) Know the limits of every tool in the pipeline; reconcile totals at each step JPMorgan "London Whale" (2012) A risk model built partly in spreadsheets, with manual copying and a formula error, understated risk while trading losses grew to about $6 billion (JPMorgan's 2013 task-force report) Model governance Spreadsheet models that drive large decisions need controls, testing and review (Day 5) Zillow Offers (US, 2018–2021) An algorithm priced homes for Zillow to buy and resell; when prices turned, it overpaid at scale and Zillow closed the unit in 2021 with large write-downs and job cuts Forecast → decision, ignoring the downside When being wrong in one direction is very costly, plan against the bound, not the point forecast (Part 7) Wells Fargo (US, 2016) Aggressive sales targets for accounts per customer led staff to open millions of accounts customers had not asked for; large fines followed KPI design A metric that becomes a target can be gamed (Part 11) Amazon recruiting model (reported 2018) A CV-screening model trained on past hiring learnt to mark down CVs that mentioned women's activities; it was dropped Model built on biased history Historical decisions encode historical bias (Part 9) Discussion (5 minutes in pairs). Pick two of the failures. For each, name the first stage of the value chain that broke, and one control (a check, a role, a process) that would probably have caught it. Which of your controls is technical, and which is about people? Three patterns run through the failures: bad data at the source (Target Canada, Public Health England), models trusted beyond what they had shown (Google Flu Trends, London Whale, Zillow), and metrics that people were rewarded to move (Wells Fargo). None of them was caused by a missing dashboard. A useful habit after any BI failure, or any project, is a blameless post-mortem : what did we expect, what happened, where did the chain break, what will we change? Writing it down is how the organisation, not just the person, learns.
docs.title: Part 4: BI case studies: successes and failures (core)

docs.text:
A BI case combines the course's tools into one decision. A reliable sequence: Frame the decision. Who decides what, by when, and what would change their mind? Agree the KPIs and constraints. Which measures decide it (profit, risk, ethical standards), and which options are ruled out from the start? Describe the history (Days 1–2): what has happened, with honest charts. Forecast the uncertain drivers (Day 3, and Part 6 today), with intervals. Model the options (Day 5): a spreadsheet model, Data Tables, a simulation. Weigh the evidence , financial and ethical, and recommend (Parts 12 and 14). The case. Harbourline Coffee roasts 300,000 kg of green coffee a year (75,000 kg a quarter), for its own cafés and for wholesale customers. Its board must choose how to buy beans for 2026 : Option How it buys Cost per kg of green coffee A. Spot, conventional Buys on the open market each quarter, no certification The market price that quarter B. Spot, certified Buys certified beans each quarter (an independent standard for farm income, labour and environment) Market price + a $0.60 premium C. Direct-trade contract A one-year contract with two farmer co-operatives: fixed price, a guaranteed minimum for farmers, full traceability $7.00 fixed for all of 2026 The other figures for 2026 are fixed: revenue $22.00 per kg (sold as roasted coffee), other variable costs (roasting, packing, freight) $9.50 per kg, and fixed costs $1.40 million . So profit is profit = 300,000 × (22.00 − 9.50 − bean cost per kg) − 1,400,000 Below is the history of the market price Harbourline paid, by quarter, from 2021 to 2025 (synthetic). rng = np . random . default_rng ( 33 ) n_q = 20 season_shape = np . tile ([ 0.16 , - 0.04 , - 0.20 , 0.08 ], n_q // 4 ) level = 5.20 + np . cumsum ( 0.05 + rng . normal ( 0 , 0.09 , n_q )) bean = pd . DataFrame ({ "period" : np . arange ( 1 , n_q + 1 ), "cost_per_kg" : np . round ( level + season_shape + rng . normal ( 0 , 0.04 , n_q ), 2 ), "quarter" : [ f "Q { q } - { y } " for y in range ( 2021 , 2026 ) for q in range ( 1 , 5 )], }) print ( bean . to_string ( index = False )) wide = bean . assign ( year = bean [ "quarter" ] . str [ - 4 :], q = bean [ "quarter" ] . str [: 2 ]) . pivot ( index = "year" , columns = "q" , values = "cost_per_kg" ) print ( " 
 Average cost by year: 
 " , wide . mean ( axis = 1 ) . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) print ( " 
 Average difference from the year's mean, by quarter: 
 " , wide . sub ( wide . mean ( axis = 1 ), axis = 0 ) . mean () . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( bean [ "period" ], bean [ "cost_per_kg" ], marker = "o" , color = BLUE ) ax . set_xticks ( bean [ "period" ][:: 4 ], bean [ "quarter" ][:: 4 ]) ax . set_ylabel ( "Green coffee cost ($ per kg)" ) ax . set_title ( "Harbourline's bean cost: rising, with a quarterly pattern" ) plt . show () period cost_per_kg quarter 1 5.43 Q1-2021 2 5.27 Q2-2021 3 5.14 Q3-2021 4 5.49 Q4-2021 5 5.55 Q1-2022 6 5.45 Q2-2022 7 5.28 Q3-2022 8 5.72 Q4-2022 9 6.09 Q1-2023 10 5.83 Q2-2023 11 5.71 Q3-2023 12 5.98 Q4-2023 13 6.16 Q1-2024 14 5.91 Q2-2024 15 5.78 Q3-2024 16 6.23 Q4-2024 17 6.26 Q1-2025 18 6.02 Q2-2025 19 5.99 Q3-2025 20 6.26 Q4-2025 Average cost by year: year 2021 5.33 2022 5.50 2023 5.90 2024 6.02 2025 6.13 Average difference from the year's mean, by quarter: q Q1 0.12 Q2 -0.08 Q3 -0.20 Q4 0.16 The descriptive step already says a lot. The cost has risen by about 80 cents a kilogram (about 15%) over five years, and it has a seasonal pattern : the fourth and first quarters are usually the dearest and the third the cheapest, a swing of about 35 cents within a year. A forecast for 2026 must capture both. The columns period and quarter are deliberate: Excel's forecasting tools need a numeric timeline ( period ), while people read the quarter labels (Part 6). To use these numbers in Excel, copy the printed table into a sheet named History with period in A1:A21 , cost_per_kg in B1:B21 and quarter in C1:C21 , or run print(bean.to_csv(index=False)) and paste the result into Excel with Data → Text to Columns (comma). Predict. At today's prices, option A is clearly cheapest. Before forecasting, which option do you expect the board to choose, and what would change your mind?

docs.text: Day 3 introduced exponential smoothing in Python. Excel offers the same family of models in two places: the Forecast Sheet button, which builds a forecast table and chart in one step, and the FORECAST.ETS functions, which do the same cell by cell.
docs.title: Part 6: Forecasting with Excel Forecast Sheet: ETS, seasonality and intervals (core)

docs.text: ETS stands for E rror, T rend and S easonality. The model keeps three running estimates, each updated every period as a weighted average of "what the newest data says" and "what we believed before": the level (where the series is now), updated with weight α (alpha); the trend (how much it rises per period), with weight β (beta); the seasonal effect of each quarter (how far that quarter usually sits above or below the level), with weight γ (gamma). A weight near 1 means "follow the latest data"; near 0 means "change slowly". The forecast for h periods ahead is: level + h × trend + that quarter's seasonal effect. Excel uses the additive version of all three parts (Microsoft calls it the AAA version of ETS): errors, trend and seasonal effects are added in dollars, not multiplied in percentages.
docs.title: What ETS does, in one paragraph

docs.text: Excel can detect the season length itself. Roughly, it looks for the lag at which the series (after removing the trend) is most strongly correlated with itself: in quarterly data with a yearly pattern, the value four quarters ago. The Python cell below does a similar check by hand, so you can see what "detection" means. Predict, then run. In the detrended bean cost, which lag between 1 and 8 quarters will have the highest autocorrelation? y = bean [ "cost_per_kg" ] . to_numpy () detrended = np . diff ( y ) # first differences remove the trend acf = { lag : np . corrcoef ( detrended [ lag :], detrended [: - lag ])[ 0 , 1 ] for lag in range ( 1 , 9 )} for lag , r in acf . items (): print ( f "lag { lag } : { r : +.2f } { '#' * int ( max ( r , 0 ) * 30 ) } " ) strong = [ lag for lag , r in acf . items () if r > 0.5 ] print ( " \n Lags with autocorrelation above 0.5:" , strong , "-> season length" , min ( strong ), "quarters" ) lag 1: -0.05 lag 2: -0.86 lag 3: +0.03 # lag 4: +0.84 ######################### lag 5: -0.08 lag 6: -0.89 lag 7: +0.16 #### lag 8: +0.87 ########################## Lags with autocorrelation above 0.5: [4, 8] -> season length 4 quarters Lags 4 and 8 stand out: this quarter looks like the same quarter one and two years ago. That is what a season length of 4 means. In Excel, the function =FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY(B2:B21, A2:A21) returns the season length Excel detects (0 means it found none). Check it before trusting an automatic forecast: a series that is too short, or noisy, may give 0 or an odd length.
docs.title: Seasonality detection

docs.text: On the History sheet (period in column A, cost in B, quarter labels in C): Select the timeline and the values , side by side with their headers: A1:B21 . Keep the text labels out of the selection. Data → Forecast Sheet (in the Forecast group, next to What-If Analysis). A preview window opens with the history and a forecast. Choose the line chart (left icon) or the column chart. Forecast End: type 28 (period 28 = Q4-2027, eight quarters after period 20). Click Options and check each setting: Forecast Start : the last actual period (20) by default. Leave it. Confidence Interval : 95% by default. You can type another level (Part 7 uses this). Seasonality : Detect Automatically , or Set Manually and type 4 . Include forecast statistics : tick it to get α, β, γ and error measures (MAE, RMSE, MASE, SMAPE). Timeline Range and Values Range : should show $A$2:$A$21 and $B$2:$B$21 . Fill Missing Points Using : Interpolation . Aggregate Duplicates Using : Average . Click Create . Excel adds a new sheet with a table and a chart. The new table has five columns: Timeline , Values (the history), Forecast , Lower Confidence Bound and Upper Confidence Bound . For the history rows the last three are empty, except the last actual row , where Excel copies the actual value into all three so that the chart's lines join. The forecast rows (periods 21 to 28) hold formulas such as =FORECAST.ETS(A22, $B$2:$B$21, $A$2:$A$21, 1, 1) for the forecast, and =C22 + FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT(A22, $B$2:$B$21, $A$2:$A$21, 0.95, 1, 1) for the upper bound (the exact columns depend on where Excel places the table). So you can always find the bound for a given future period by reading across that period's row to the Upper Confidence Bound column, and you can check any cell by clicking it and reading its formula.
docs.title: The Excel click path: Forecast Sheet

docs.text: Forecast Sheet needs a timeline of numbers or dates with a constant step . Text labels such as Q1-2025 are not a timeline: Excel cannot tell how far apart they are, and Forecast Sheet refuses them or does not offer the expected options. Two fixes: Period numbers 1, 2, 3, … (always safe). The forecast end is then a period number: to forecast four quarters past period n , set Forecast End to n + 4. Real dates , one per quarter, three calendar months apart (for example the first or the last day of each quarter). Excel recognises steps measured in months. If Excel still complains, fall back to period numbers. Keep the readable labels in another column for your report.
docs.title: The timeline must be numeric

docs.text: Function Returns FORECAST.ETS(target, values, timeline, [seasonality], [data_completion], [aggregation]) The point forecast for the target period. Seasonality: 1 (or omitted) = detect, 0 = none, a number = that length FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT(target, values, timeline, [confidence_level], …) The half-width of the interval: forecast ± this number. Default level 0.95 FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY(values, timeline, …) The detected season length FORECAST.ETS.STAT(values, timeline, statistic_type, …) One fitted statistic: 1 = α, 2 = β, 3 = γ, 4 = MASE, 5 = SMAPE, 6 = MAE, 7 = RMSE, 8 = step size FORECAST.LINEAR(target, values, timeline) A straight-line trend forecast, for comparison (Day 5)
docs.title: The functions, for a forecast without the button

docs.text: statsmodels has the same model: ETSModel with additive error, trend and seasonality. Excel's fitting procedure is not published in full and differs in details (starting values, how the parameters are optimised), so expect numbers that are close to Excel's but not identical , usually within a few cents here. When you report, quote the tool you used. Predict, then run. Will the 95% interval for Q4-2027 be wider or narrower than for Q1-2026? By roughly how much? y_q = pd . Series ( bean [ "cost_per_kg" ] . to_numpy (), index = pd . date_range ( "2021-01-01" , periods = n_q , freq = "QS" )) fits = {} for name , seasonal in [( "trend only (AAN)" , None ), ( "trend + season (AAA)" , "add" )]: fits [ name ] = ETSModel ( y_q , error = "add" , trend = "add" , seasonal = seasonal , seasonal_periods = 4 if seasonal else None ) . fit ( disp = False ) print ( f " { name : <22 } AIC { fits [ name ] . aic : 7.1f } in-sample RMSE { np . sqrt ( fits [ name ] . mse ) : .3f } " ) ets = fits [ "trend + season (AAA)" ] print ( " \n Smoothing weights:" , { k : round ( v , 3 ) for k , v in zip ( ets . param_names , ets . params ) if k . startswith ( "smoothing" )}) fc = ets . get_prediction ( start = "2026-01-01" , end = "2027-10-01" ) . summary_frame ( alpha = 0.05 ) table = pd . DataFrame ({ "period" : np . arange ( 21 , 29 ), "quarter" : [ f "Q { q } - { y } " for y in ( 2026 , 2027 ) for q in range ( 1 , 5 )], "forecast" : fc [ "mean" ] . to_numpy (), "lower_95" : fc [ "pi_lower" ] . to_numpy (), "upper_95" : fc [ "pi_upper" ] . to_numpy ()}) table [ "width" ] = table [ "upper_95" ] - table [ "lower_95" ] print ( " \n " , table . round ( 2 ) . to_string ( index = False )) trend only (AAN) AIC -2.3 in-sample RMSE 0.178 trend + season (AAA) AIC -25.6 in-sample RMSE 0.077 Smoothing weights: {'smoothing_level': 0.655, 'smoothing_trend': 0.0, 'smoothing_seasonal': 0.0} period quarter forecast lower_95 upper_95 width 21 Q1-2026 6.45 6.29 6.60 0.30 22 Q2-2026 6.24 6.06 6.42 0.36 23 Q3-2026 6.13 5.92 6.33 0.41 24 Q4-2026 6.48 6.25 6.71 0.46 25 Q1-2027 6.65 6.40 6.90 0.50 26 Q2-2027 6.44 6.17 6.71 0.54 27 Q3-2027 6.33 6.04 6.62 0.57 28 Q4-2027 6.68 6.38 6.99 0.61 How to read this output: The seasonal model has a much lower AIC (the lower the better; Day 3) and a smaller in-sample error than the trend-only model, so the quarterly pattern is real enough to keep. Excel's automatic detection should agree. The forecast keeps both the trend and the quarterly shape: Q4 and Q1 high, Q3 low. The interval widens with the horizon, from about 30 cents wide one quarter ahead to about 60 cents two years ahead. Each step ahead adds new uncertainty to the uncertainty already there. An interval that did not widen would be claiming knowledge the model does not have. fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( bean [ "period" ], bean [ "cost_per_kg" ], marker = "o" , color = BLUE , label = "History" ) ax . plot ( table [ "period" ], table [ "forecast" ], marker = "o" , color = ORANGE , label = "ETS (AAA) forecast" ) ax . fill_between ( table [ "period" ], table [ "lower_95" ], table [ "upper_95" ], color = ORANGE , alpha = 0.18 , label = "95 % i nterval" ) ax . set_xticks ( list ( bean [ "period" ][:: 4 ]) + [ 21 , 25 ], list ( bean [ "quarter" ][:: 4 ]) + [ "Q1-2026" , "Q1-2027" ]) ax . set_ylabel ( "Green coffee cost ($ per kg)" ) ax . set_title ( "Forecast with a 95 % i nterval that widens with the horizon" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , loc = "upper left" ) plt . show () Misconception: "A 95% confidence interval means the forecast is 95% accurate." It means that, if the model is right , the actual value should fall inside the band about 95 times in 100. Two cautions. First, the band assumes the future behaves like the past; a shock the history never showed (a frost in Brazil, a shipping crisis) can push the actual value outside it. Second, Excel calls it a confidence interval, but statisticians would call it a prediction interval : it covers a future value , not just the average, which is why it is wide. Misconception: "More history always helps." More relevant history helps. If the market changed structurally three years ago, older data pulls the forecast towards a world that no longer exists. And for seasonality, ETS needs at least two full seasons to estimate the pattern; with fewer, set seasonality to 0.
