docs.text: Symptom Likely cause Fix The Forecast Sheet button is greyed out No cell inside the data is selected, the sheet is protected, or the Excel version is too old Click inside the data; use desktop Excel 2016 or later Excel complains about the timeline Text labels, uneven steps, or a blank in the timeline Use period numbers 1, 2, 3, …, or evenly spaced dates The forecast has no seasonal shape Detection found no season (short or noisy series) Check FORECAST.ETS.SEASONALITY ; set it manually only if you have a business reason and two or more full seasons The forecast goes too few periods ahead Forecast End was left at the default Set Forecast End to the last period you need Your numbers differ slightly from a classmate's Python output Excel and statsmodels fit the same model differently Expected. Quote Excel's numbers if your work is in Excel Your numbers differ from a classmate's Excel Different data, a different confidence level or a manual seasonality setting Compare the Options settings and the data cell by cell
docs.title: Common Forecast Sheet problems

docs.text: A forecast gives a point (the middle) and an interval . Which number should feed the plan? The point forecast is right when being wrong in either direction costs about the same . Many decisions are asymmetric . Harbourline must fix its 2026 bean budget with its bank now. If actual costs come in below budget, the unused money sits idle: a small cost. If they come in above , Harbourline must borrow at short notice at a penalty rate, delay payments to farmers, or cut production: a large cost. Say each dollar of overrun costs 3 times as much as each dollar of unused budget. Decision theory gives a clean answer. If an overrun costs u per dollar and an unused dollar costs o , the budget that minimises the expected cost is the quantile of the forecast distribution at u ÷ ( u + o ) which is the same critical ratio as the newsvendor rule at the end of Day 5, Part 12. With u = 3 and o = 1 that is the 75th percentile : plan for a cost that will be exceeded only one year in four. To find that percentile for the whole year , we simulate many possible 2026s from the fitted ETS model and average the four quarters in each. Predict, then run. Is the 75th percentile of the 2026 average cost closer to the point forecast or to the 95% upper bound? reps = 10_000 errors = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) . normal ( 0 , np . sqrt ( ets . mse ), size = ( 4 , reps )) paths = ets . simulate ( nsimulations = 4 , anchor = "end" , repetitions = reps , random_errors = errors ) annual = paths . mean ( axis = 0 ) . to_numpy () # average cost per kg over the four quarters of 2026 point = table [ "forecast" ] . iloc [: 4 ] . mean () print ( f "Point forecast, 2026 average: $ { point : .3f } per kg" ) for q in ( 0.50 , 0.75 , 0.90 , 0.975 ): print ( f " { q : >6.1% } percentile of the simulated average: $ { np . quantile ( annual , q ) : .3f } per kg" ) print ( f "Average of the four quarterly upper bounds: $ { table [ 'upper_95' ] . iloc [: 4 ] . mean () : .3f } per kg" ) # Expected cost of each budget level, with an overrun costing 3x an unused dollar volume = 300_000 budgets = np . linspace ( 6.10 , 6.60 , 101 ) u , o = 3.0 , 1.0 exp_cost = [ volume * np . mean ( u * np . maximum ( annual - b , 0 ) + o * np . maximum ( b - annual , 0 )) for b in budgets ] best = budgets [ int ( np . argmin ( exp_cost ))] print ( f " \n Budget with the lowest expected cost: $ { best : .3f } per kg " f "(critical ratio { u / ( u + o ) : .0% } ; simulated 75th percentile $ { np . quantile ( annual , 0.75 ) : .3f } )" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( budgets , np . array ( exp_cost ) / 1000 , color = BLUE ) ax . axvline ( point , color = GREY , ls = ":" , label = "Point forecast" ) ax . axvline ( best , color = ORANGE , ls = "--" , label = "Lowest expected cost" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Bean budget for 2026 ($ per kg)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Expected cost of a wrong budget ($ thousand)" ) ax . set_title ( "With an overrun 3x as costly, the best budget sits above the forecast" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () Point forecast, 2026 average: $6.325 per kg 50.0% percentile of the simulated average: $6.325 per kg 75.0% percentile of the simulated average: $6.380 per kg 90.0% percentile of the simulated average: $6.427 per kg 97.5% percentile of the simulated average: $6.487 per kg Average of the four quarterly upper bounds: $6.517 per kg Budget with the lowest expected cost: $6.380 per kg (critical ratio 75%; simulated 75th percentile $6.380) Four things to take from this. The best budget is above the point forecast , at about the 75th percentile, because an overrun hurts three times as much. Budgeting at the point forecast is not "neutral": it accepts a 50% chance of the expensive mistake. The 95% upper bound is one particular quantile : the 97.5th percentile. It is the right planning number when an overrun is roughly 39 times as costly as unused budget (0.975 = 39 ÷ 40), for example when an overrun would break a loan covenant or a fixed-price contract. For milder asymmetries, a lower bound is better. Choose the quantile from the consequences , not by habit. Quarterly bounds do not add up to an annual bound. The average of the four quarterly upper bounds is higher than the 97.5th percentile of the annual average, because four quarters are unlikely to all land at their worst together. For a single quarter (one future period), the bound Excel prints is the right number; for a total over several periods, simulate. Excel can give any quantile for a single period. The upper bound of a two-sided interval at confidence level c is the (1 + c ) ÷ 2 quantile. For the 75th percentile, use c = 0.50: =FORECAST.ETS(22,History!B$2:B$21,History!A$2:A$21,4) + FORECAST.ETS.CONFINT(22,History!B$2:B$21,History!A$2:A$21,0.5,4) gives the 75th percentile for period 22. Misconception: "Planning on the upper bound is pessimism." It is matching the plan to the shape of the risk . The upper bound is not a prediction that costs will be high; it is the cost the plan must survive.
docs.title: Part 7: Planning against an upper bound (core)

docs.text: Now return to Harbourline's three sourcing options (Part 5). Options A and B pay the market price, so their cost moves with the forecast; option C pays a fixed $7.00. Compare profit at the point forecast and at the 97.5th percentile of the simulated 2026 average. Predict, then run. At the point forecast, B is cheaper than C. Is it still cheaper at the upper bound? revenue_per_kg , other_var , fixed = 22.00 , 9.50 , 1_400_000 def profit ( bean_cost_per_kg ): return volume * ( revenue_per_kg - other_var - bean_cost_per_kg ) - fixed def option_cost ( option , market ): return { "A. Spot, conventional" : market , "B. Spot, certified" : market + 0.60 , "C. Direct-trade contract" : np . full_like ( market , 7.00 )}[ option ] upper = np . quantile ( annual , 0.975 ) rows = [] for opt in [ "A. Spot, conventional" , "B. Spot, certified" , "C. Direct-trade contract" ]: sim_profit = profit ( option_cost ( opt , annual )) rows . append ({ "option" : opt , "profit at point forecast" : usd ( profit ( option_cost ( opt , np . array ( point )))), "profit at 97.5th percentile" : usd ( profit ( option_cost ( opt , np . array ( upper )))), "spread of profit (P2.5 to P97.5)" : usd ( np . quantile ( sim_profit , 0.975 ) - np . quantile ( sim_profit , 0.025 ))}) print ( pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . to_string ( index = False )) option profit at point forecast profit at 97.5th percentile spread of profit (P2.5 to P97.5) A. Spot, conventional $452,597 $403,821 $97,463 B. Spot, certified $272,597 $223,821 $97,463 C. Direct-trade contract $250,000 $250,000 $0 At the point forecast, the certified spot option B beats the contract C by about $20,000. At the upper bound the order reverses : the contract's fixed price protects it, while B carries the full market risk plus the premium. Option C also has no spread at all in bean cost: its profit is known in advance, which has value for a company with a bank budget to meet. That reversal is the reason to look at the bound. When options carry different exposure to the uncertain driver, the ranking can change between the middle and the tail of the forecast. When every option shifts by the same amount (a fixed premium on the same market price), the ranking cannot change, but the bound still tells you whether the chosen option stays profitable. Option A is the cheapest at both points. Whether that settles the decision is the subject of Parts 8 to 14: the board also cares about the people and the land that grow the coffee, and about what its customers and lenders expect. Check your understanding. A café chain signs a two-year fixed-price lease and wants to budget its electricity. Overspending its budget forces it to close for a month; underspending costs nothing. Which percentile would you plan on, and would Excel's default 95% interval be enough?
docs.title: Which option at which bound?

docs.text: The rest of the lecture asks a different question: not "is the analysis right?" but "is it right to do , and right to do this way ?" Ethics in analytics is not a separate subject added at the end; each choice in the value chain (what to collect, how to define a KPI, which model to deploy, what to recommend) has consequences for people.
docs.title: Part 8: Privacy, PIPL, GDPR and consent (core)

docs.text: Harbourline's loyalty app records who bought what, where and when. That data improves offers and stock planning. It can also reveal a person's routine, health (decaf every day after a diagnosis?), religion (fasting months) or income. Personal information is any information about an identified or identifiable person, and "identifiable" is broader than most people think.
docs.title: Why personal data needs special care

docs.text: China: Personal Information Protection Law (PIPL) EU: General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) In force 1 November 2021 25 May 2018 Applies to Processing in China, and processing abroad that targets or analyses people in China Processing in the EU, and processing abroad that targets or monitors people in the EU Legal bases Consent, or one of several others (a contract with the person, HR management, legal duties, public-health emergencies, news reporting, reasonable use of information the person made public) Six lawful bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, legitimate interests Consent Informed, voluntary and explicit; can be withdrawn; separate consent needed for sensitive information, for sharing with another handler, for making it public and for transfer abroad Freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous; as easy to withdraw as to give Sensitive data Includes biometrics, religious belief, specific identities, health, financial accounts, location tracking, and all data on children under 14 "Special categories": health, biometrics, religion, ethnicity, sexual orientation, political opinions, trade-union membership, genetics Automated decisions Must be transparent and fair, with no unreasonable differences in prices or terms between people; people can ask for an explanation and refuse decisions made solely by automated means that significantly affect them Right not to be subject to a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects, with safeguards Impact assessment Required before processing sensitive data, automated decision-making, sharing or transfer abroad Data protection impact assessment (DPIA) for high-risk processing Moving data abroad A security assessment, a standard contract or certification, depending on volume and type Adequacy decision, standard contractual clauses or other safeguards Penalties Up to 50 million yuan or 5% of the previous year's turnover for serious cases Up to €20 million or 4% of worldwide annual turnover China's Data Security Law (2021) and Cybersecurity Law (2017) sit alongside PIPL, and the 2022 penalty of more than 8 billion yuan imposed on the ride-hailing company Didi for data violations showed that enforcement is real. This table is a summary for analysts, not legal advice; a company's legal or compliance team applies the details. The principles behind both laws are the same and are what an analyst can apply every day: Purpose limitation: collect for a stated purpose and do not quietly reuse the data for another. Data minimisation: collect and keep only what the purpose needs. An analysis of café traffic does not need names. Storage limitation: delete or anonymise when the purpose is served. Security and access control: only those who need personal data can see it (Part 2's governance roles). Transparency and rights: people can find out what is held about them, correct it and, in many cases, delete it.
docs.title: Two laws you will meet

docs.text: Consent is valid only if the person understood what they agreed to and could have said no . Warning signs of consent that does not mean much: Bundling: "agree to marketing or you cannot use the app." Pre-ticked boxes and dark patterns : a bright "Accept all" next to a grey "Manage settings" three screens deep. Vague purposes: "to improve our services" covering profiling, resale and model training. No real withdrawal: opting out takes a phone call. PIPL's separate consent requirement means, for example, that Harbourline could not hide "we share your purchase history with partner brands" inside the general terms: it needs its own clear request.
docs.title: Consent that means something

docs.text: Removing names is pseudonymisation , not anonymisation. Combinations of ordinary fields ( quasi-identifiers ) can single people out. In a well-known study, Latanya Sweeney estimated that about 87% of the US population could be uniquely identified by ZIP code, birth date and sex alone; and researchers re-identified people in Netflix's "anonymised" movie-ratings data by matching it to public reviews. A simple measure is k-anonymity : every combination of quasi-identifiers must be shared by at least k people. Below, 3,000 synthetic Harbourline loyalty members with no names at all. Predict, then run. The app stores each member's district (8 districts), birth month and year (for birthday offers, years 1960 to 2005) and gender. What share of members is unique on those fields: about 5%, 25% or 75%? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 88 ) m = 3000 members = pd . DataFrame ({ "district" : rng . choice ([ f "D { i } " for i in range ( 1 , 9 )], m ), "birth_year" : rng . integers ( 1960 , 2006 , m ), "birth_month" : rng . integers ( 1 , 13 , m ), # collected for birthday offers "gender" : rng . choice ([ "F" , "M" ], m ), "visits_per_week" : rng . poisson ( 2.2 , m ), }) def k_report ( df , cols ): size = df . groupby ( cols )[ cols [ 0 ]] . transform ( "size" ) # how many members share each combination return { "combinations" : df . groupby ( cols ) . ngroups , "unique (k = 1)" : f " { ( size == 1 ) . mean () : .1% } " , "in groups smaller than 5" : f " { ( size < 5 ) . mean () : .1% } " , "smallest group (k)" : int ( size . min ())} general = members . assign ( age_band = (( 2025 - members [ "birth_year" ]) // 10 * 10 ) . astype ( str ) + "s" , zone = np . where ( members [ "district" ] . isin ([ "D1" , "D2" , "D3" , "D4" ]), "North" , "South" )) print ( pd . DataFrame ({ "raw: district, birth month and year, gender" : k_report ( members , [ "district" , "birth_year" , "birth_month" , "gender" ]), "generalised: zone, age band, gender" : k_report ( general , [ "zone" , "age_band" , "gender" ])})) raw: district, birth month and year, gender generalised: zone, age band, gender combinations 2530 20 unique (k = 1) 70.7% 0.0% in groups smaller than 5 99.7% 0.0% smallest group (k) 1 93 With no names at all, most members are unique on these ordinary fields, and almost all sit in groups smaller than five. Anyone who knows a neighbour's district, birthday and gender could find their visit pattern. Generalising (zones instead of districts, ten-year age bands instead of birth years) raises the smallest group to about ninety people, at the cost of detail. That trade-off between privacy and analytical precision is a decision to make deliberately, and it belongs in the data-governance rules. Excel. In a helper column, =COUNTIFS(A:A, A2, B:B, B2, C:C, C2) gives each row's group size k ; =COUNTIF(E:E, 1)/COUNT(E:E) is the share of unique rows. Generalise with =FLOOR(2025-B2, 10) for age bands. Stronger techniques exist (adding calibrated noise, known as differential privacy , or generating synthetic data), but the analyst's first defences are the principles above: do not collect what you do not need, and do not publish row-level data that someone could match. Misconception: "It's legal, so it's ethical." Laws set a floor and lag behind technology. Target, the US retailer, was reported in 2012 to have used purchase patterns to predict which customers were pregnant and send them baby-product offers; it was probably lawful, and many customers still found it intrusive. A useful test is the front-page test : would the people in the data be comfortable reading exactly what you did with it?
docs.title: "Anonymous" data often is not

docs.text: A model can treat groups of people differently even when nobody intends it. Common sources of bias: Source What happens Example Historical bias The data records past decisions that were themselves unfair A model trained on past loan approvals copies past officers' prejudices Representation bias Some groups are under-represented in the data A face-recognition model trained mostly on one skin tone Measurement bias The label measures the wrong thing, or measures it worse for some groups Using "arrests" as a stand-in for "crime" Proxy variables A feature stands in for a protected one Postcode or district standing in for ethnicity or migrant status Deployment bias A model is used for a purpose or population it was not built for A credit model from one country used in another
docs.title: Part 9: Bias and fairness: a disparate-impact demonstration (core)

docs.text: Harbourline plans to offer instant credit in its app for buying coffee machines. A credit partner has 5,000 past applicants with their monthly income , a credit score , their district , whether a loan officer approved them in the past, and whether they repaid . Applicants belong to two groups, A and B , standing for any protected characteristic (for example gender, ethnicity or migrant status). Group membership is not used by the model. In this synthetic data, as often in reality, group B lives mainly in two districts, earns a little less on average, and past officers approved group B less often than its repayment record justified. The disparate-impact ratio compares approval rates: DI = (approval rate of group B) ÷ (approval rate of group A) A common screening rule, the four-fifths rule from US employment guidelines, treats a ratio below 0.8 as a warning sign that needs investigating. It is a rule of thumb, not a proof of discrimination, and other jurisdictions use other tests. Predict, then run. A model trained to copy past officers' approvals, without the group column but with district: will its DI ratio be above or below 0.8? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 300 ) n_app = 5000 in_b = ( rng . random ( n_app ) < 0.4 ) . astype ( int ) apps = pd . DataFrame ({ "group" : np . where ( in_b == 1 , "B" , "A" )}) apps [ "district" ] = np . where ( rng . random ( n_app ) < np . where ( in_b == 1 , 0.7 , 0.15 ), rng . choice ([ "East" , "South" ], n_app ), rng . choice ([ "North" , "West" , "Centre" , "Harbour" ], n_app )) inc = rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n_app ) - 0.25 * in_b # group B earns a little less on average hist = rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n_app ) apps [ "monthly_income" ] = np . round ( 4200 * np . exp ( 0.35 * inc ), - 1 ) apps [ "credit_score" ] = np . round ( 650 + 70 * hist ) . clip ( 400 , 850 ) apps [ "repaid" ] = ( rng . random ( n_app ) < 1 / ( 1 + np . exp ( - ( 1.8 + 0.9 * inc + 1.0 * hist )))) . astype ( int ) # Past officers: same evidence, plus an unjustified penalty on group B apps [ "past_approved" ] = (( 0.9 * inc + 1.0 * hist - 1.0 * in_b + rng . normal ( 0 , 0.7 , n_app )) > - 0.4 ) . astype ( int ) print ( apps . groupby ( "group" )[[ "repaid" , "past_approved" ]] . mean () . round ( 3 ) . rename ( columns = { "repaid" : "repayment rate" , "past_approved" : "past approval rate" })) def features ( df , with_district ): X = pd . DataFrame ({ "log_income" : np . log ( df [ "monthly_income" ]), "credit_score" : df [ "credit_score" ]}) if with_district : X = X . join ( pd . get_dummies ( df [ "district" ], prefix = "district" , drop_first = True ) . astype ( float )) return X def audit ( label , with_district , approve_share = 0.6 ): X = features ( apps , with_district ) model = LogisticRegression ( max_iter = 5000 ) . fit ( X , apps [ label ]) score = model . predict_proba ( X )[:, 1 ] approved = score >= np . quantile ( score , 1 - approve_share ) # approve the top 60% of scores rate = pd . Series ( approved ) . groupby ( apps [ "group" ]) . mean () good = apps [ "repaid" ] == 1 tpr = pd . Series ( approved [ good ]) . groupby ( apps . loc [ good , "group" ] . to_numpy ()) . mean () return model , { "approval A" : rate [ "A" ], "approval B" : rate [ "B" ], "DI ratio" : rate [ "B" ] / rate [ "A" ], "repayers approved A" : tpr [ "A" ], "repayers approved B" : tpr [ "B" ], "default rate among approved" : 1 - apps . loc [ approved , "repaid" ] . mean ()} results = {} for name , label , with_d in [( "1. copy past approvals, with district" , "past_approved" , True ), ( "2. copy past approvals, no district" , "past_approved" , False ), ( "3. predict repayment, no district" , "repaid" , False )]: model_i , results [ name ] = audit ( label , with_d ) fair_model = model_i # model 3, used again in Part 10 print ( " \n " , pd . DataFrame ( results ) . T . round ( 3 ) . to_string ()) repayment rate past approval rate group A 0.802 0.611 B 0.761 0.276 approval A approval B DI ratio repayers approved A repayers approved B default rate among approved 1. copy past approvals, with district 0.663 0.502 0.758 0.756 0.592 0.091 2. copy past approvals, no district 0.632 0.550 0.870 0.724 0.648 0.089 3. predict repayment, no district 0.630 0.553 0.877 0.721 0.651 0.091 res = pd . DataFrame ( results ) . T fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.6 )) ax . barh ( res . index [:: - 1 ], res [ "DI ratio" ][:: - 1 ], color = [ GREEN , SKY , ORANGE ]) ax . axvline ( 0.8 , color = "black" , ls = "--" , lw = 1 ) ax . text ( 0.805 , 2.35 , "four-fifths line" , fontsize = 9 ) ax . set_xlim ( 0.6 , 1.0 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Disparate-impact ratio (approval rate B / approval rate A)" ) ax . set_title ( "Removing the group column is not enough; the label and the proxies matter" ) plt . show () What the audit shows: Model 1 falls below the four-fifths line although it never sees the group column. It learnt the past officers' penalty on group B through district , which stands in for group membership. "We don't use the protected attribute" ( fairness through unawareness ) is not a defence. Dropping the proxy (model 2) raises the ratio, but the model still copies a biased label. Changing the label (model 3) , so the model predicts repayment instead of copying past approvals , gives the fairest result here, with the same default rate among approved applicants. Being fairer did not cost accuracy in this case; it often costs less than people assume, because the biased decisions were also worse decisions. A gap remains , because group B's incomes are lower on average and income genuinely predicts repayment. Whether that gap is acceptable is a value judgement , not a statistical one: it depends on the law, the purpose (credit, hiring, insurance) and the organisation's values.
docs.title: The demonstration

docs.text: Measure Equal across groups Question it answers Demographic parity (DI ratio) Approval rates Do groups get the benefit at similar rates? Equal opportunity Approval rates among people who would repay (true-positive rates) Are qualified people treated alike? Predictive parity Repayment rates among the approved Does a "yes" mean the same in each group? Calibration For each score, the actual repayment rate Does a score of 0.7 mean 70% in every group? When groups differ in their underlying rates, these measures cannot all be equal at once (results by Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, and by Chouldechova, prompted by the debate over the COMPAS risk scores used in US courts). So an organisation must choose which fairness it is committing to, write that choice down and justify it. That choice belongs to the business owner and the ethics or compliance function, informed by the analyst, not to the analyst alone. Excel. With the approvals in column F and groups in column A: =AVERAGEIFS(F:F, A:A, "B")/AVERAGEIFS(F:F, A:A, "A") is the DI ratio; add a condition G:G, 1 (repaid) for the equal-opportunity rates. Misconception: "The algorithm is objective because it is maths." A model is a summary of its training data and of the choices made in building it: which label, which features, which threshold. Each choice can introduce or remove bias.
docs.title: Which fairness measure?

docs.text: People affected by a decision, and the managers responsible for it, need to know why it was made. Both PIPL and GDPR give people rights in relation to automated decisions (Part 8), and lenders in many countries must give reasons when they decline credit. Two kinds of explanation: Global: how the model works overall. Which features matter, in which direction? For a linear or logistic model, the coefficients answer this (Day 4). For complex models, tools such as permutation importance or SHAP values estimate it. Local: why this person got this decision. For a logistic model, each feature's contribution to the score is its coefficient times how far the person's value is from the average. Predict, then run. An applicant with a below-average credit score and an average income is declined by model 3. Which reason will come first? X3 = features ( apps , with_district = False ) coefs = pd . Series ( fair_model . coef_ [ 0 ], index = X3 . columns ) print ( "Global view (coefficients):" , coefs . round ( 4 ) . to_dict ()) score3 = fair_model . predict_proba ( X3 )[:, 1 ] cutoff = np . quantile ( score3 , 0.4 ) declined = np . where ( score3 < cutoff )[ 0 ] person = declined [ np . argmin ( np . abs ( X3 . iloc [ declined ][ "log_income" ] - X3 [ "log_income" ] . mean ()))] contrib = coefs * ( X3 . iloc [ person ] - X3 . mean ()) # push on the log-odds, relative to average print ( f " \n Applicant { person } : income $ { apps . loc [ person , 'monthly_income' ] : ,.0f } , credit score { apps . loc [ person , 'credit_score' ] : .0f } , " f "score { score3 [ person ] : .2f } (cut-off { cutoff : .2f } )" ) print ( "Reasons, largest push towards decline first:" ) for feat , c in contrib . sort_values () . items (): print ( f " { feat : <13 } { c : +.2f } on the log-odds" ) Global view (coefficients): {'log_income': 2.4027, 'credit_score': 0.0147} Applicant 387: income $4,090, credit score 553, score 0.57 (cut-off 0.80) Reasons, largest push towards decline first: credit_score -1.41 on the log-odds log_income -0.00 on the log-odds The explanation names the credit score as the main reason, in a form a person can act on ("your credit score is below what we usually approve; your income is not the issue"). That is a reason code , the standard local explanation in credit. Transparency is more than explaining one decision. Good practice includes: Model cards (Mitchell and colleagues, 2019): a short document for each model: its purpose, the data it was trained on, its performance overall and by group , its limits, and who is responsible. Datasheets for data sets (Gebru and colleagues): where the data came from, how it was collected, what it should not be used for. Human review for decisions with significant effects, with the authority to overrule the model. Logging , so a decision can be reconstructed later. Misconception: "Explainable means simple." A simple model can still hide a biased label (Part 9, model 1, was a plain logistic regression). And a complex model can be explained well enough for its purpose. The test is whether the people affected and the people accountable can understand and challenge the decision.
docs.title: Part 10: Transparency and explainability (core)

docs.text: Goodhart's law , as it is usually quoted: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. A KPI is useful because it tracks something we care about. Once people are rewarded for moving the KPI itself, they find ways to move it that do not move the thing we care about, or that harm it. Related is Campbell's law : the more a measure is used for important decisions, the more it is subject to corruption pressures and the more it distorts the process it was meant to monitor. Famous examples: Wells Fargo's accounts-per-customer target (Part 4); Volkswagen's diesel cars, which detected the emissions test and behaved differently during it (2015); hospitals meeting waiting-time targets by delaying the moment a patient is officially "waiting"; software teams rewarded for lines of code. A demonstration. Harbourline's customer-service centre has 40 agents. Management introduces a bonus for keeping the average handle time (AHT) of a call under 6 minutes. Some agents genuinely work faster; others end calls before the problem is solved. Unresolved problems come back as repeat calls. Predict, then run. After the bonus, AHT falls. Does the total agent time needed to solve each customer's problem fall too? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 111 ) agents , problems_each = 40 , 400 def month ( gaming_share , speed_up_honest , speed_up_gaming , fcr_honest , fcr_gaming ): gaming = rng . random ( agents ) < gaming_share base_minutes = rng . normal ( 7.5 , 0.6 , agents ) minutes = base_minutes * np . where ( gaming , speed_up_gaming , speed_up_honest ) fcr = np . where ( gaming , fcr_gaming , fcr_honest ) # first-contact resolution rate calls_per_problem = 1 / fcr # repeat calls until solved return { "average handle time (min)" : np . mean ( minutes ), "first-contact resolution" : np . mean ( fcr ), "calls per problem solved" : np . mean ( calls_per_problem ), "agent minutes per problem solved" : np . mean ( minutes * calls_per_problem ), "agent hours per month" : np . sum ( minutes * calls_per_problem * problems_each ) / 60 } before = month ( 0.0 , 1.0 , 1.0 , 0.82 , 0.82 ) after = month ( 0.40 , 0.95 , 0.62 , 0.81 , 0.40 ) cmp_ = pd . DataFrame ({ "before bonus" : before , "after bonus" : after }) cmp_ [ "change" ] = ( cmp_ [ "after bonus" ] / cmp_ [ "before bonus" ] - 1 ) . map ( " {:+.0%} " . format ) print ( cmp_ . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 3.4 )) pct = ( cmp_ [ "after bonus" ] / cmp_ [ "before bonus" ] - 1 ) * 100 ax . barh ( pct . index [:: - 1 ], pct [:: - 1 ], color = [ ORANGE if v > 0 else GREEN for v in pct [:: - 1 ]]) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = "black" , lw = 0.8 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Change after the bonus (%)" ) ax . set_title ( "The target metric improves; the outcome gets worse" ) plt . show () before bonus after bonus change average handle time (min) 7.48 6.25 -16% first-contact resolution 0.82 0.67 -19% calls per problem solved 1.22 1.68 +38% agent minutes per problem solved 9.12 9.75 +7% agent hours per month 2433.11 2599.31 +7% The dashboard KPI (AHT) improves by about a sixth, and management might celebrate. But first-contact resolution falls, customers call back more often, and the agent time needed to actually solve a problem goes up . Customers are worse off and so is the cost base. Nobody broke a rule. How to design KPIs that resist gaming: Pair every target with a counter-metric it could be traded against: handle time with resolution rate; sales with returns and complaints; speed with error rate. Measure the outcome, not the activity, where possible: problems solved, not calls closed. Use a balanced set (a balanced scorecard : financial, customer, process, learning) rather than one number. Watch for sudden improvements , and audit a sample: a jump in a KPI with no change in the process is a signal, not just good news. Ask the people being measured how the KPI could be gamed, before launch. They know. Keep some measures for learning only , not tied to pay. Check your understanding. Harbourline's purchasing team is rewarded for "average cost per kg below budget". Name two ways that KPI could be gamed in sourcing, and one counter-metric for each.
docs.title: Part 11: Goodhart's law and metric gaming (core)

docs.text: Most of a product's social and environmental impact sits upstream , with suppliers. For Harbourline that means coffee farms: farmer incomes that can fall below a living income when prices drop, child and forced labour risks in some regions, deforestation when farms expand, and climate exposure. In 2013 the collapse of the Rana Plaza factory building in Bangladesh, which made clothes for well-known brands, killed more than 1,100 workers and changed how buyers think about responsibility for suppliers' conditions. ESG (environmental, social and governance) is the umbrella term investors and companies use for these factors. Some useful vocabulary: Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions: a company's own direct emissions; emissions from the energy it buys; and everything else in its value chain, including suppliers. For a roaster, Scope 3 (farming and shipping) is usually most of the total. Due diligence: identifying, preventing and accounting for human-rights and environmental harms in the supply chain. It is increasingly required by law, for example under Germany's Supply Chain Act (in force since 2023) and EU rules on corporate sustainability due diligence and on deforestation-free products (which cover coffee), whose details and timetables have been revised since adoption. Certification and traceability: independent standards (for example Fairtrade or Rainforest Alliance for coffee) and the ability to trace a bag of beans back to a co-operative or a farm. Greenwashing: claiming more sustainability than the evidence supports. Regulators increasingly fine it.
docs.title: Part 12: Supply-chain ethics and ESG trade-offs (core)

docs.text: Ethical sourcing usually costs money now, while its benefits (lower legal and reputational risk, supply security, customer and employee loyalty, access to customers and lenders who require standards) are real but harder to put in a spreadsheet. Two disciplined ways to bring both into one decision: Price what you can, describe what you cannot. The extra cost of option B or C per year, per kg and per cup is easy to compute; reputational risk is not, but it can be described with evidence (customer surveys, buyer requirements, past incidents in the industry). Multi-criteria scoring , with the weights written down. Below, Harbourline's analysts score the three options from 1 (poor) to 5 (strong) on four non-financial criteria. These scores are judgements , made by people and open to challenge; the code only makes the consequences of the weights visible. criteria = pd . DataFrame ({ "farmer income" : [ 1 , 3 , 5 ], "traceability" : [ 1 , 3 , 5 ], "environment (deforestation, climate)" : [ 2 , 4 , 4 ], "price-risk protection" : [ 1 , 1 , 5 ], }, index = [ "A. Spot, conventional" , "B. Spot, certified" , "C. Direct-trade contract" ]) profit_point = pd . Series ({ opt : profit ( option_cost ( opt , np . array ( point ))) for opt in criteria . index }) criteria [ "profit (scaled 1-5)" ] = 1 + 4 * ( profit_point - profit_point . min ()) / ( profit_point . max () - profit_point . min ()) print ( criteria . round ( 1 ) . to_string ()) non_fin = [ "farmer income" , "traceability" , "environment (deforestation, climate)" , "price-risk protection" ] weights_fin = np . linspace ( 0 , 1 , 101 ) scores = { opt : [ w * criteria . loc [ opt , "profit (scaled 1-5)" ] + ( 1 - w ) * criteria . loc [ opt , non_fin ] . mean () for w in weights_fin ] for opt in criteria . index } winner = [ max ( scores , key = lambda o : scores [ o ][ i ]) for i in range ( len ( weights_fin ))] switch = weights_fin [ next ( i for i , w in enumerate ( winner ) if w . startswith ( "A" ))] print ( f " \n Option A wins only when profit carries at least { switch : .0% } of the total weight" ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () for opt , col in zip ( criteria . index , [ ORANGE , SKY , GREEN ]): ax . plot ( weights_fin * 100 , scores [ opt ], color = col , lw = 2 , label = opt ) ax . axvline ( switch * 100 , color = GREY , ls = ":" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "Weight on profit (%); the rest is shared equally by the four other criteria" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Weighted score (1-5)" ) ax . set_title ( "The decision depends on the weights: show where it switches" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () farmer income traceability environment (deforestation, climate) price-risk protection profit (scaled 1-5) A. Spot, conventional 1 1 2 1 5.0 B. Spot, certified 3 3 4 1 1.4 C. Direct-trade contract 5 5 4 5 1.0 Option A wins only when profit carries at least 47% of the total weight The chart is more useful than any single weighted score: it shows the board how much weight on profit it would take for the conventional option to win. If the board's honest answer is "less than that", the decision is made; if not, the disagreement is now about values, stated openly, rather than hidden in a spreadsheet. Two rules keep multi-criteria scoring honest: Red lines are constraints, not weights. If an option involves forced or child labour, no profit advantage can compensate for it, so it is excluded , not scored low. Putting it in the scoring implies a price at which it would be acceptable. Write down the weights before seeing the scores , and test how sensitive the answer is to them (exactly as you did with decision rules in Day 5, Part 12). Misconception: "Ethics and profit are always in conflict." Sometimes they are, in the short run, and pretending otherwise is greenwashing. But over longer horizons many ethical choices also reduce risk : option C's fixed price protects Harbourline in a bad year (Part 7), and secure relationships with farmers protect supply when markets are tight. A good recommendation states both the cost and the risk reduction.
docs.title: Making the trade-off explicit

docs.text: Several frameworks turn the ideas of Parts 8 to 12 into checklists and rules. You do not need to memorise them; you should recognise them and be able to use one as a structure for a review. Framework From Core idea OECD AI Principles (2019, updated 2024) OECD member countries and others Inclusive growth and well-being; human rights and fairness; transparency and explainability; robustness and safety; accountability UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of AI (2021) UNESCO member states Human rights and dignity, fairness, sustainability, human oversight; impact assessments NIST AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 (2023) US National Institute of Standards and Technology (voluntary) Four functions: Govern (culture, roles), Map (context and risks), Measure (test and track), Manage (prioritise and act) EU AI Act (Regulation 2024/1689, in force from August 2024, obligations phased in over several years) European Union (law) Risk tiers: unacceptable (banned, such as social scoring by public authorities), high-risk (such as credit scoring and recruitment: strict requirements), limited (transparency duties, such as telling people they are talking to a chatbot), minimal China's AI rules Cyberspace Administration of China and other regulators (law) Rules on algorithmic recommendation (2022: transparency, an option to turn off personalisation, no unreasonable price discrimination), deep synthesis (2023), generative AI services (2023) and labelling of AI-generated content (2025) ISO/IEC 42001 (2023) International standard A certifiable management system for AI, in the style of ISO quality standards
docs.title: Part 13: Responsible-AI frameworks (core summary, extension detail)

docs.text: Before launch, the analyst and the business owner should be able to answer: Purpose: what decision does this support, and is it a legitimate use of the data? Data: do we have the right to use it (consent or another basis)? Is it the minimum needed? Is personal data protected? Fairness: have we checked outcomes by group? Which fairness measure did we choose, and why? Transparency: can we explain a decision to the person affected? Is there a model card? Human oversight: who reviews significant decisions, and can they overrule the model? Gaming and side effects: how could the KPI or the model be gamed? What are the counter-metrics? Monitoring: how will we know if it drifts or causes harm after launch? Who is accountable? This maps closely onto NIST's four functions: questions 1 and 7 are Govern , 2 is Map , 3, 4 and 6 are Measure , 5 and 7 are Manage .
docs.title: A practical checklist for any analytics project

docs.text: Every graded report in Module 2 ends in a recommendation. A recommendation that balances financial and ethical evidence has a recognisable shape.
docs.title: Part 14: Writing a managerial recommendation (core)

docs.text: The answer first. One or two sentences: what to do, and the main reason. Executives read the first paragraph; many read nothing else. The financial evidence , with numbers, units and their uncertainty: the point estimate and the range or the bound (Part 7). The ethical and societal evidence : who is affected and how; legal and reputational exposure; what the organisation has publicly committed to. Use evidence (surveys, standards, cases), not adjectives. The trade-off, stated plainly : what the recommended option costs compared with the alternative, in terms people can picture (per year, per unit, per customer), and what it buys. Risks and conditions : what would change the recommendation, and what to monitor (KPIs and counter-metrics). The decision requested : what you need the reader to approve, and by when. This is the pyramid principle (Barbara Minto): conclusion first, then the supporting arguments, then the detail.
docs.title: The structure

docs.text: Kind Example How to write it Fact "Bean costs rose about 80 cents per kg from 2021 to 2025." State it with its source Estimate "The 2026 average is forecast at about $6.32, and is unlikely to exceed about $6.49." Give the method and the uncertainty Judgement "Traceability to farm level is worth paying for." Say whose judgement and why; never disguise it as a fact

docs.text: The cell below assembles the numbers from Parts 7 and 12 into the opening of a memo. Assume about 80 cups of coffee per kg of green beans , so 300,000 kg is about 24 million cups a year (an assumption; state it in the memo). cups = 300_000 * 80 p_a , p_c = profit_point [ "A. Spot, conventional" ], profit_point [ "C. Direct-trade contract" ] gap = p_a - p_c p_c_upper = profit ( 7.00 ) p_a_upper = profit ( upper ) memo = f """ RECOMMENDATION. Buy 2026 beans under the direct-trade contract (option C) at a fixed $7.00 per kg. Financial evidence. At the forecast 2026 market price (about $ { point : .2f } per kg), option C earns { usd ( p_c ) } , which is { usd ( gap ) } less than buying conventional beans on the spot market (option A, { usd ( p_a ) } ). That gap is about { gap / cups * 100 : .1f } US cents per cup. In a bad year for prices (the 97.5th percentile, about $ { upper : .2f } per kg) option A falls to { usd ( p_a_upper ) } , while option C still earns { usd ( p_c_upper ) } : the contract fixes our bean cost, so our profit is known in advance. Ethical evidence. Option C guarantees the co-operatives a minimum price and traces every bag to the farm, which the conventional option cannot. [Add evidence: buyer requirements, customer survey, industry incidents.] Trade-off. We would pay about { usd ( gap ) } a year, under one cent a cup, for traceable, fairly paid supply and for certainty about our largest cost. Conditions and risks. Review if market prices fall far below the forecast. Track: cost per kg against budget, farmer price paid, share of beans traced to farm, and customer complaints (as a counter-metric). Decision requested: approval of the contract by the end of the month. """ print ( memo ) RECOMMENDATION. Buy 2026 beans under the direct-trade contract (option C) at a fixed $7.00 per kg. Financial evidence. At the forecast 2026 market price (about $6.32 per kg), option C earns $250,000, which is $202,597 less than buying conventional beans on the spot market (option A, $452,597). That gap is about 0.8 US cents per cup. In a bad year for prices (the 97.5th percentile, about $6.49 per kg) option A falls to $403,821, while option C still earns $250,000: the contract fixes our bean cost, so our profit is known in advance. Ethical evidence. Option C guarantees the co-operatives a minimum price and traces every bag to the farm, which the conventional option cannot. [Add evidence: buyer requirements, customer survey, industry incidents.] Trade-off. We would pay about $202,597 a year, under one cent a cup, for traceable, fairly paid supply and for certainty about our largest cost. Conditions and risks. Review if market prices fall far below the forecast. Track: cost per kg against budget, farmer price paid, share of beans traced to farm, and customer complaints (as a counter-metric). Decision requested: approval of the contract by the end of the month. Notice what the memo does and does not do. It leads with the decision and the main reason. It quantifies the ethical premium in three ways (per year, compared with profit, per cup), so the board can judge whether it is large or small. It uses the bound as well as the point estimate, because the options carry different risk. It leaves a placeholder where evidence is still needed, rather than filling it with adjectives such as "customers love ethical brands". It names counter-metrics and a trigger for review . Say Avoid "Option C costs about $200,000 a year more at the forecast price, under one cent a cup." "Option C is slightly more expensive." "In a bad year, option C earns more than option A." "Option C is safer." (Safer how, by how much?) "We judge that farm-level traceability is worth this cost, because …" "It is the right thing to do." (A judgement with no reason) "Our forecast assumes the market behaves as in 2021–2025." Hiding the assumption "If prices fall below $5.80, we should revisit." A recommendation with no condition under which it would change Misconception: "A recommendation must be neutral." A recommendation takes a position: that is its job. What it must be is transparent : the reader can see which parts are evidence and which are judgement, and could reach a different judgement from the same evidence. Check your understanding. Rewrite the memo's first sentence for a board that has decided profit must carry at least 60% of the weight (Part 12). Does the recommendation change?

docs.text: Work in groups of four. Each person takes a role: chief financial officer , head of sustainability , head of retail (cafés and customers), and the bank's relationship manager . Hedge or bet? The head of retail says the fixed $7.00 contract "is a bet that prices will rise". Is it? Days 1 and 2 mostly describe, with the first diagnostic steps already there (Simpson's paradox on Day 1; funnels and an A/B test on Day 2); Day 3 adds more diagnosis and the first prediction; Day 4 predicts; Days 5 and 6 prescribe. The dependency runs one way : A diagnostic claim needs a description to explain. Simpson's paradox (Day 1) only appears after you have the overall and the group-level summaries. A prediction needs an honest description of the past. The ADF test (Day 3) is only meaningful once you have plotted the series and seen whether it drifts. A prescription needs a prediction with its uncertainty. A Data Table or a Monte Carlo run (Day 5) varies a base case that someone first had to forecast. Three misconceptions ¶ Misconception Why it is wrong "Prescriptive is the most advanced, so it is always the best answer." A prescription built on a careless description is worse than a careful description, because it looks authoritative. Use the lowest level that answers the question. "Descriptive analytics is just the warm-up." Most business questions are descriptive ("which region fell?"), and most failed models fail because the description was skipped. "A predictive model tells you what to do." It tells you what is likely if nothing changes. Choosing what to do needs costs, constraints and values, which belong to the prescriptive level and to the people deciding. Self-check (one sentence each). Part 3: One discipline, six checks (core) ¶ Every modelling day had a check that came before you could trust the result. They look unrelated: a p-value from a unit-root test, a ratio from a regression, a grid of profits, a histogram, an interval. Underneath, each one does the same three things: Name a condition the technique quietly assumes. Test whether this data or this model meets it. Report what happens to the answer when the condition is stressed instead of assumed. A model that skips the check still produces a number. What it cannot tell you is how far to trust that number. The ADF test: a drift is not a trend ¶ Two independent random walks share nothing: each step of one is unrelated to the other. Regress one on the other, in levels and then in differences. Predict, then run. Will the regression in levels find a strong relationship between two series that are unrelated by construction? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 10 ) n = 120 walk_a = 100 + np . cumsum ( rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n )) # random walk: today = yesterday + noise walk_b = 50 + np . cumsum ( rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n )) # an independent random walk for name , series in [( "walk A, levels" , walk_a ), ( "walk A, first difference" , np . diff ( walk_a ))]: with warnings . catch_warnings (): # newer statsmodels warns about a future return type warnings . simplefilter ( "ignore" , FutureWarning ) stat , pvalue = adfuller ( series )[: 2 ] print ( f "ADF on { name : <26 } statistic { stat : 6.2f } p-value { pvalue : .3f } " ) r2_levels = sm . OLS ( walk_b , sm . add_constant ( walk_a )) . fit () . rsquared r2_diffs = sm . OLS ( np . diff ( walk_b ), sm . add_constant ( np . diff ( walk_a ))) . fit () . rsquared print ( f " \n R² of B on A in levels: { r2_levels : .2f } " ) print ( f "R² of B on A in differences: { r2_diffs : .2f } " ) ADF on walk A, levels statistic -1.76 p-value 0.402 ADF on walk A, first difference statistic -8.53 p-value 0.000 R² of B on A in levels: 0.89 R² of B on A in differences: 0.00 The ADF test's null hypothesis is "the series has a unit root" (it is not stationary) . A large p-value for the levels means we cannot reject a wandering mean; after differencing, the p-value is tiny and the series is stationary. In levels, the two unrelated walks show a large R², because both happen to drift over the same stretch. In differences, the relationship disappears, because there was never one. What the ADF test protects against: building a forecast, or a regression, on a drift. B. VIF: entangled predictors give unstable coefficients ¶ A rent model with two predictors that move together almost perfectly: floor area and number of rooms. Fit it on two random halves of the same data. Predict, then run. Both halves come from the same process. Will the two fitted coefficients for floor area be close? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2 ) n = 80 area = rng . uniform ( 40 , 120 , n ) # square metres rooms = area / 25 + rng . normal ( 0 , 0.15 , n ) # rooms track area closely rent = 300 + 9 * area + 60 * rooms + rng . normal ( 0 , 90 , n ) flats = pd . DataFrame ({ "area" : area , "rooms" : rooms , "rent" : rent }) X = sm . add_constant ( flats [[ "area" , "rooms" ]]) vif = { col : variance_inflation_factor ( X . values , i ) for i , col in enumerate ( X . columns ) if col != "const" } print ( "VIF:" , ", " . join ( f " { k } { v : .1f } " for k , v in vif . items ())) half = rng . permutation ( n ) for label , idx in [( "first half " , half [: 40 ]), ( "second half" , half [ 40 :])]: fit = smf . ols ( "rent ~ area + rooms" , data = flats . iloc [ idx ]) . fit () print ( f " { label } : area coefficient { fit . params [ 'area' ] : 6.1f } rooms coefficient { fit . params [ 'rooms' ] : 7.1f } " f " R² { fit . rsquared : .2f } " ) VIF: area 43.4, rooms 43.4 first half : area coefficient 13.6 rooms coefficient -58.0 R² 0.83 second half: area coefficient 6.8 rooms coefficient 138.2 R² 0.89 The VIFs are far above the usual warning level of about 5 to 10, and the two halves disagree about how much each variable is worth (one half even gives rooms a negative effect), even though the R² stays healthy in both. That is the pattern to remember: multicollinearity hurts explanation, not prediction . If the model only has to predict rent for flats like these, it may be fine. If a manager asks "how much is one extra room worth?", the coefficients cannot answer. What VIF protects against: telling someone the wrong lever. C. Monte Carlo: the average plan is not the average outcome ¶ Same model, but now margin and volume are uncertain at the same time: margin around $20 (standard deviation $3), volume around 5,000 units (standard deviation 900). Draw 10,000 trials. Predict, then run. The average inputs give a profit of $20,000. Will the average simulated profit be close to that? What chance of a loss do you expect? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) trials = 10_000 margin = rng . normal ( 20 , 3 , trials ) volume = rng . normal ( 5000 , 900 , trials ) profit = margin * volume - fixed_cost print ( f "Profit at average inputs: { usd ( 20 * 5000 - fixed_cost ) } " ) print ( f "Mean simulated profit: { usd ( profit . mean ()) } " ) print ( f "5th to 95th percentile: { usd ( np . percentile ( profit , 5 )) } to { usd ( np . percentile ( profit , 95 )) } " ) print ( f "Probability of a loss: { ( profit < 0 ) . mean () : .1% } " ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . hist ( profit / 1000 , bins = 60 , color = SKY , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 , label = "break-even" ) ax . axvline ( profit . mean () / 1000 , color = BLUE , linestyle = "--" , label = "mean" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "profit (thousand $)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "number of trials" ) ax . set_title ( "Same mean as the plan, but a real chance of a loss" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () Profit at average inputs: $20,000 Mean simulated profit: $20,023 5th to 95th percentile: -$16,469 to $60,513 Probability of a loss: 20.4% Here the mean is close to the plan because profit is a simple product of independent inputs. With a cap (capacity, stock, a contract limit), the mean of the outputs falls below the output of the mean inputs: that is the flaw of averages (Day 5, Part 6), and you will see it in Part 5. Either way, the mean hides the spread: there is a material chance of a loss that the single-number plan never showed. What Monte Carlo protects against: planning on one number when several inputs are uncertain together. F. Confidence bounds: planning on the point is a coin toss ¶ A forecast says next quarter's demand is 1,000 units, with a forecast standard error of 120 units (assume the errors are roughly normal). How often is each plan exceeded? Predict, then run. If you plan capacity exactly at the point forecast, how often will demand be higher than your plan? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 5 ) demand = rng . normal ( 1000 , 120 , 100_000 ) # many possible quarters consistent with the forecast plans = { "point forecast" : 1000 , "80 % u pper bound (z = 1.28)" : 1000 + 1.28 * 120 , "95 % u pper bound (z = 1.96)" : 1000 + 1.96 * 120 } for name , plan in plans . items (): print ( f "Plan at the { name : <28 } { plan : 7.0f } units demand exceeds plan in { ( demand > plan ) . mean () : 5.1% } of quarters" ) Plan at the point forecast 1000 units demand exceeds plan in 50.1% of quarters Plan at the 80% upper bound (z = 1.28) 1154 units demand exceeds plan in 10.1% of quarters Plan at the 95% upper bound (z = 1.96) 1235 units demand exceeds plan in 2.5% of quarters A plan at the point forecast is exceeded about half the time. The upper limit of a two-sided 95% interval is the 97.5th percentile, so it is exceeded only about 2.5% of the time (Day 6, Part 7). Which bound to use is a business choice, set by how much an overrun costs compared with a surplus. What the bound protects against: treating "most likely" as "safe". Error measures need a scale ¶ The same discipline applies to error metrics. An RMSE of 40 units is excellent for a product that sells 4,000 a month and useless for one that sells 50. Always report an error next to the scale of what it measures : the mean of the outcome, a naive forecast's error, or a percentage. An R² alone is not evidence of a good model either: Part 3B had a healthy R² with untrustworthy coefficients, and Part 3C's flexible curve had an excellent training fit. Part 4: Integrated case, step 1: from text to a model (core) ¶ The case ¶ Kestrel Bikes rents electric bikes by monthly subscription. A year-long pilot in its home city went well enough that the board is ready to launch in a second city. The open question is how big a fleet to lease there: 250 bikes or 400? A bigger fleet can serve more riders, but every leased bike costs money whether anyone rides it or not. Two sources of evidence are on the table: Pilot data (structured and unstructured). 80 pilot riders wrote a short comment after their first month, and Kestrel knows whether each one renewed at the six-month mark. New-city test rides (unstructured only). At a weekend test-ride event in the new city, 40 people tried a bike and left a comment. Nobody there has subscribed yet. The chain we will follow is the one the capstone asks you to follow with different data and a different question: text → model → simulation → chart → recommendation . Not every comment lands well, though. "Smooth ride and the booking is simple" is praise for a bike, but none of its words are in VADER's general-purpose lexicon, so it scores zero. "Too expensive for what you get, and the brakes squeal" is a complaint, but "expensive" and "squeal" carry no score either. Domain words (price, brakes, ride quality) are exactly where a lexicon built for social media goes blind. In a report you would say so , give an example, and treat the score as a noisy measure. Model: from a sentiment score to a renewal rate ¶ Two models, one simple enough for a spreadsheet and one smoother: Band table. The renewal rate within each VADER band. In Excel: =AVERAGEIFS(renewed_range, band_range, "Positive") . Logistic regression of renewal on the compound score (Day 4, Part 13): it gives a renewal probability for any score between −1 and 1. Predict, then run. Part 5: Integrated case, step 2: from a model to a simulation (core) ¶ Apply the model to the new city ¶ Score the 40 test-ride comments, then predict a renewal rate for the new city in two ways: from the logistic model (average the predicted probabilities) and from the band table (weight each band's rate by its share of comments). rng = np . random . default_rng ( 1119 ) city_satisfaction = rng . normal ( 0.5 , 1 , 40 ) # the event attracted keener people (see below) city = pd . DataFrame ({ "comment" : [ write_comment ( s , rng )[ 1 ] for s in city_satisfaction ]}) city [ "compound" ] = city [ "comment" ] . apply ( lambda t : sia . polarity_scores ( t )[ "compound" ]) city [ "band" ] = city [ "compound" ] . apply ( band ) renewal_logit = logit . predict ( city ) . mean () shares = city [ "band" ] . value_counts ( normalize = True ) . reindex ( band_table . index , fill_value = 0 ) renewal_bands = ( shares * band_table [ "renewal_rate" ]) . sum () renewal_pilot = pilot [ "renewed" ] . mean () print ( f "Mean compound score: pilot { pilot [ 'compound' ] . mean () : +.2f } , new-city test rides { city [ 'compound' ] . mean () : +.2f } " ) print ( f "Band shares in the new city: " + ", " . join ( f " { b } { s : .0% } " for b , s in shares . items ())) print ( f " \n Predicted six-month renewal, logistic model: { renewal_logit : .1% } " ) print ( f "Predicted six-month renewal, band table: { renewal_bands : .1% } " ) print ( f "Actual six-month renewal in the pilot city: { renewal_pilot : .1% } " ) Mean compound score: pilot +0.08, new-city test rides +0.21 Band shares in the new city: Positive 68%, Neutral 2%, Negative 30% Predicted six-month renewal, logistic model: 56.8% Predicted six-month renewal, band table: 55.7% Actual six-month renewal in the pilot city: 51.2% The new city's comments are more positive, so both models predict a higher renewal rate than the pilot achieved. Should we believe it? Think about who wrote the comments . Pilot riders were paying customers a month into their subscription. Test-ride visitors chose to come to a weekend event and rode a new bike for twenty minutes; they are keener than the average future subscriber, and a short ride shows none of the battery, repair and docking problems that drive the pilot's complaints. This is selection bias , and it is the second weak seam: the model is fine, but the input is not drawn from the population we want to predict. A defensible analyst does not pick one number. She carries a range forward: the pilot's actual rate as a cautious case, the model's prediction as an optimistic case, and lets the simulation show whether the decision depends on which is true. The simulation ¶ The monthly business model, with every input stated (all invented): Input Value Uncertain? Subscription price $69 per rider per month No Variable cost (insurance, batteries, repairs) $15 per rider per month No Lease cost $20 per bike per month, for every bike leased No Fixed cost (depot, staff) $5,000 per month No Launch cost $25,000 once No New sign-ups per month Poisson, with a monthly average drawn once per trial from Normal(45, 12) Yes Six-month renewal rate Normal around the central estimate, standard deviation 7 points Yes Capacity Active riders can never exceed the fleet Fixed by the decision A six-month renewal rate R is turned into a monthly retention rate R 1/6 , so that six months of retention multiply back to R . Each month, active riders = retained riders + new sign-ups, capped at the fleet size. Profit is summed over 24 months. Predict, then run. Which fleet has the higher average 24-month profit? Which has the higher chance of a loss? Are those the same fleet? PRICE , VAR_COST , LEASE , FIXED , LAUNCH , MONTHS = 69 , 15 , 20 , 5_000 , 25_000 , 24 def simulate ( fleet , renewal_mean , renewal_sd = 0.07 , signups_mean = 45 , signups_sd = 12 , trials = 5_000 , seed = 2026 ): """Return cumulative profit by month (months x trials) for one fleet size.""" g = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) # same seed for both fleets: a fair comparison renewal = np . clip ( g . normal ( renewal_mean , renewal_sd , trials ), 0.2 , 0.97 ) retention = renewal ** ( 1 / 6 ) signup_rate = np . clip ( g . normal ( signups_mean , signups_sd , trials ), 5 , None ) active = np . zeros ( trials ) cumulative = np . full ( trials , - float ( LAUNCH )) path = np . empty (( MONTHS , trials )) for month in range ( MONTHS ): active = np . minimum ( np . round ( active * retention ) + g . poisson ( signup_rate ), fleet ) cumulative = cumulative + ( PRICE - VAR_COST ) * active - LEASE * fleet - FIXED path [ month ] = cumulative return path def summarise ( final ): return { "mean" : final . mean (), "5th pct" : np . percentile ( final , 5 ), "median" : np . median ( final ), "95th pct" : np . percentile ( final , 95 ), "P(loss)" : ( final < 0 ) . mean ()} central = ( renewal_pilot + renewal_logit ) / 2 # midway between the cautious and optimistic cases paths = { fleet : simulate ( fleet , central ) for fleet in ( 250 , 400 )} summary = pd . DataFrame ({ f " { fleet } bikes" : summarise ( p [ - 1 ]) for fleet , p in paths . items ()}) . T print ( f "Central six-month renewal used: { central : .1% } \n " ) print ( summary . assign ( ** { c : summary [ c ] . map ( usd ) for c in [ "mean" , "5th pct" , "median" , "95th pct" ]}, ** { "P(loss)" : summary [ "P(loss)" ] . map ( " {:.0%} " . format )}) . to_string ()) Central six-month renewal used: 54.0% mean 5th pct median 95th pct P(loss) 250 bikes $10,829 -$54,459 $20,660 $37,025 21% 400 bikes $21,656 -$126,459 $43,403 $110,015 33% The larger fleet has the higher average profit and also the higher chance of a loss and the worse bad case. That is the normal shape of a capacity decision: the big fleet earns more when demand is strong, and leaves more bikes idle, still costing lease, when it is weak. Neither number alone settles the question; which matters more depends on how much loss Kestrel can absorb. Notice also the flaw of averages from Part 3E at work: because riders are capped at the fleet size, a good month cannot make up fully for a bad one. Where does the decision switch? renewal_grid = np . round ( np . arange ( 0.35 , 0.751 , 0.05 ), 2 ) sweep = pd . DataFrame ({ f " { fleet } bikes" : [ simulate ( fleet , r , trials = 2_000 )[ - 1 ] . mean () for r in renewal_grid ] for fleet in ( 250 , 400 )}, index = pd . Index ( renewal_grid , name = "six-month renewal" )) print ( "Mean 24-month profit by renewal rate:" ) print ( sweep . map ( usd ) . to_string ()) fine_grid = np . round ( np . arange ( 0.40 , 0.651 , 0.01 ), 2 ) # a finer sweep to locate the switch gap = np . array ([ simulate ( 400 , r , trials = 2_000 )[ - 1 ] . mean () - simulate ( 250 , r , trials = 2_000 )[ - 1 ] . mean () for r in fine_grid ]) switch = fine_grid [ np . argmax ( gap > 0 )] print ( f " \n The larger fleet first wins on average at a renewal rate of about { switch : .0% } " f "(pilot actual { renewal_pilot : .0% } , test-ride prediction { renewal_logit : .0% } )." ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( renewal_grid , sweep [ "250 bikes" ] / 1000 , marker = "o" , color = BLUE , label = "250 bikes" ) ax . plot ( renewal_grid , sweep [ "400 bikes" ] / 1000 , marker = "o" , color = ORANGE , label = "400 bikes" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = GREY , linewidth = 1 ) for value , label in [( renewal_pilot , "pilot actual" ), ( renewal_logit , "model, test rides" )]: ax . axvline ( value , color = GREY , linestyle = ":" ) ax . text ( value , ax . get_ylim ()[ 1 ] * 0.92 , label , rotation = 90 , va = "top" , ha = "right" , fontsize = 8 , color = "dimgray" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "six-month renewal rate" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "mean 24-month profit (thousand $)" ) ax . set_title ( "The fleet decision depends on renewal" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () Mean 24-month profit by renewal rate: 250 bikes 400 bikes six-month renewal 0.35 -$13,438 -$53,844 0.40 -$4,659 -$31,904 0.45 $2,121 -$11,336 0.50 $7,225 $7,118 0.55 $11,047 $23,197 0.60 $13,944 $36,751 0.65 $16,228 $47,934 0.70 $18,026 $57,043 0.75 $19,495 $64,419 The larger fleet first wins on average at a renewal rate of about 51% (pilot actual 51%, test-ride prediction 57%). The sweep turns an argument about adjectives ("renewal will be good") into a question with a number in it: is renewal in the new city above or below the switching value? The pilot's actual rate sits almost on the switching value; only the optimistic test-ride prediction is clearly above it. Below the switch the larger fleet loses money fast, while above it the gain grows more slowly. So the honest answer is that the evidence does not yet settle the fleet size, and the recommendation should be built around that fact rather than hiding it. The chart must show the two options, over time, with their range , not just a central line (Chapter 8's point about carrying the honest range forward). A fan chart does that: the median path and a band from the 5th to the 95th percentile. months = np . arange ( 1 , MONTHS + 1 ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8.5 , 4.5 )) for fleet , colour in [( 250 , BLUE ), ( 400 , ORANGE )]: p = paths [ fleet ] / 1000 ax . fill_between ( months , np . percentile ( p , 5 , axis = 1 ), np . percentile ( p , 95 , axis = 1 ), color = colour , alpha = 0.18 ) ax . plot ( months , np . median ( p , axis = 1 ), color = colour , linewidth = 2.2 ) ax . text ( MONTHS + 0.3 , np . median ( p [ - 1 ]), f " { fleet } bikes" , color = colour , va = "center" , fontweight = "bold" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = GREY , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_xlim ( 1 , MONTHS + 4 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "month after launch" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "cumulative profit (thousand $)" ) ax . set_title ( "400 bikes earns more in a good case and loses more in a bad one \n " "median line, shaded band = 5th to 95th percentile" , fontsize = 10 ) plt . show () Choices worth copying: a message title that states the finding; direct labels instead of a legend; a zero line , because "do we lose money?" is the board's first question; colour-blind-safe colours; the range shaded. The same chart in Tableau (the tool the capstone uses for its chart). Export a table with one row per month and columns for each option's 5th percentile, median and 95th percentile. What each hand-over needed ¶ Hand-over What could break The check that catches it Text → score The lexicon misreads domain words Validate against labelled or hand-read examples (Day 3, Part 8) Score → model Small sample; a loose, noisy relationship Look at counts per band and the slope's standard error; test on held-out riders if there are enough Model → new city The new inputs come from a different population (selection bias) Ask who wrote the text and why; carry a range, not a point Model → simulation One "expected" input hides the spread Monte Carlo with the uncertain inputs; a sweep of the least trusted one Simulation → chart A single line implies certainty Show the band or the percentiles; zero line; message title Chart → recommendation The answer ignores the downside or the ethics Fact, estimate, judgement; conditions; limits; the decision requested Part 7: Business case discussion: Kestrel's board (self-study, discussion) ¶ Work in groups of three: one analyst, one finance director, one head of operations. The finance director is worried about the downside; the head of operations wants enough bikes to avoid turning riders away. The finance director says: "Your model is built on 80 comments and a sentiment score that cannot read the word expensive . Why should I trust any of it?" Answer in three sentences, without claiming more than the evidence shows. The head of operations says: "If we start with 250 bikes and demand is strong, we will turn riders away and they will go to a competitor." Is that a cost the simulation includes? How would you add it? Which of the inputs in the Part 5 table would you most like to measure better before launch, and how would you measure it cheaply? The marketing team proposes to quote the most positive test-ride comments in the launch campaign. What permission and privacy questions does that raise (Day 6, Part 8)? A board member asks for "just one number". Which single number would you give, and what sentence would you always put next to it? Suppose six months later renewal in the new city is exactly at the switching value. What would you recommend then, and why? price what you can; treat red lines as constraints Mixing facts, estimates and judgements Readers cannot tell what is measured Label them, or make it clear in the wording A chart in the report that is not discussed The evidence is not used Every chart gets a sentence that says what it shows Part 9: Exam technique (core) ¶ The final exam is in periods 3 and 4 today. Your facilitator confirms the format, the length and what you may bring (for example, whether a basic calculator is allowed). Whatever the format, the habits below earn marks. Read the command word ¶ Command word What it asks for A weak answer A strong answer Define The meaning, precisely An example only One-sentence definition, then an example Describe What it is or what happens Opinion Features or steps, in order Explain Why or how A restated description A cause or mechanism, with "because" Calculate A number, with working The number alone Formula, substitution, result with units Interpret What a result means in context "It is 0.62" "62% of …, which means … for the manager" Compare Similarities and differences Two separate descriptions Point-by-point, with a conclusion Evaluate A judgement on strengths and limits One side only Both sides, then a reasoned verdict Recommend A decision with justification A list of options One option, the evidence, the trade-off and a condition Budget your time ¶ Before you start, divide the time by the marks: in a 90-minute paper worth 100 marks, a 10-mark question deserves about 9 minutes. Answer the questions you are surest of first, but number them clearly. Leave five minutes at the end to check units, signs and that every part of every question has an answer. Lay out a calculation ¶ Write the formula in words or symbols. Substitute the numbers, with units. Give the result, rounded sensibly, with units. Add one sentence saying what it means. Even if the arithmetic slips, steps 1, 2 and 4 usually earn marks. Interpret a number for a manager ¶ Use the pattern number + unit + context + so what + caveat . For example: "The test RMSE is 40 units, about 3% of average monthly sales, so the forecast is precise enough for stock planning; it was tested on only eight months, so we will re-check it after the next quarter." Read a statistical output ¶ Find what was measured first (the outcome, the units, the sample) before the numbers. For a test, write down the null hypothesis before reading the p-value (the ADF trap in Part 8). For a model, ask on which data the metric was computed: training or test. Rehearse out loud ¶ Chapter 8's advice is to prepare by speaking, not by memorising. For each chapter, say three things in under a minute, without notes: what the technique does , in plain words; what it assumes or where it fails ; and one link to a technique from another chapter . Then ask a friend to interrupt with "why does that matter?" and "what if that assumption fails?". The link is what turns a correct answer into a good one. Part 10: Practice set (self-study) ¶ Twelve questions written for this page, in the style of a closed-book paper. They are not taken from any exam and the exam does not reuse them. No answers are given here: work them alone, then compare with a classmate and with the lecture parts named in brackets. Allow about 60 minutes. Q1. Hierarchy (5 marks). A café chain uses: (a) a dashboard of daily sales by branch; (b) a regression of sales on temperature to set tomorrow's milk order; (c) a breakdown showing that the sales drop came from one branch's closure; (d) a simulation of three opening-hours plans. Place each on the analytics hierarchy and say what each needs from the level below. (Part 2) Q2. Stationarity (6 marks). An ADF test on 60 months of a shop's sales gives a p-value of 0.41. After first differencing, the p-value is 0.002. State the null hypothesis, interpret both results, and say what this means for the d in an ARIMA( p , d , q ) model. (Part 3A; Day 3, Part 7) Q3. Error and scale (6 marks). Two forecasts were tested on the last 12 months. Product A: RMSE 35 units, average monthly sales 1,750 units. Product B: RMSE 35 units, average monthly sales 140 units. Express each error as a percentage of average sales and say which forecast you would trust for ordering stock, and why. (Part 3) Q4. Multicollinearity (6 marks). A delivery-time model uses distance (km) and fuel used (litres) as predictors. Both VIFs are about 14; the test R² is 0.83. A manager asks how many minutes one extra kilometre adds. What do you tell her, and what would you change if that question is the main purpose of the model? (Part 3B; Day 4, Part 9) Q5. Over-fitting (5 marks). A model has a training R² of 0.96 and a test R² of 0.38. Diagnose the problem in one sentence and give two ways to address it. (Part 3C; Day 4, Part 10) Q6. Sentiment (6 marks). VADER gives these compound scores: "The delivery was not bad at all" +0.43; "This charger is sick" −0.51; "Arrived on Tuesday" 0.00. Label each with the usual thresholds (±0.05). Which label would a human disagree with, and why does VADER make that mistake? (Day 3, Parts 6 and 7) Q7. Data Table (6 marks). A two-way Data Table of monthly profit ($) has prices $8, $9 and $10 across the top and volumes 2,000, 2,500 and 3,000 down the side: volume \ price $8 $9 $10 2,000 −6,000 −4,000 −2,000 2,500 −3,500 −1,000 1,500 3,000 −1,000 2,000 5,000 Describe which combinations make a loss, which input the profit is more sensitive to over the ranges shown, and what further information the manager needs before choosing a price. (Part 3D; Day 5, Part 4) Q8. Monte Carlo (6 marks). Option X: 2,000 trials, mean profit $52,000, 5th percentile −$30,000, 360 trials below zero. Option Y: mean profit $44,000, 5th percentile $6,000, probability of a loss 2%. Calculate X's probability of a loss. Which option would you recommend to a small firm with little cash, and which to a large firm running many such projects? Explain the difference. (Part 3E; Day 5, Part 10) Q9. Forecast bounds (5 marks). Next quarter's demand forecast is 3,200 units, with a 95% interval of 2,700 to 3,700. Renting extra warehouse space at short notice costs four times as much as an unused booked space. Which number would you plan on, and why? (Part 3F; Day 6, Part 7) Q10. Chart critique (5 marks). A slide shows monthly revenue for two products as a 3D pie chart for each month, twelve pies in a row, with a legend in the corner. Name two problems and describe a better chart for the question "how has the gap between the two products changed this year?" (Day 2, Parts 1–4) Q11. Fairness (5 marks). A screening model approves 54% of applicants from group P and 36% from group Q. Calculate the disparate-impact ratio, say whether it passes the common four-fifths rule of thumb, and name one further check you would make before concluding the model is unfair. (Day 6, Part 9) Q12. Integration (10 marks). A retailer wants to decide whether to stock a new line. You have 300 online reviews of the line from another market, two years of monthly sales of a similar line, and the supplier's price and minimum order. Describe, step by step, how you would get from these inputs to a recommendation, naming one technique and one check at each step, and the chart you would show the board. (Parts 3–6) Part 11: Capstone briefing (P5) ¶ The capstone (Assignment 4, 25% , CLO 4 and CLO 5) is launched in period 5 and worked on in periods 6 to 8; it is due Sunday 29 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , on GAP.
