Part 13: Extra practice, quiz and summary ¶ Practice on the Kestrel case ¶ Core ¶ Core 1. In Part 4, add three comments of your own to the positive bank that VADER would misread, and check them. What kinds of words does VADER miss? Core 2. In Part 5, change the sign-up average from 45 to 35 a month and rerun the simulation and the sweep. Which fleet does the change hurt more, and why? Core 3. Rebuild the band table of Part 4 in Excel with AVERAGEIFS and COUNTIFS from the pilot data (export it with pilot.to_excel("kestrel_pilot.xlsx", index=False) ). Do your numbers match? Stretch ¶ Stretch 1. Add a cost for turned-away riders to the simulation: each rider who cannot get a bike costs $30 in lost goodwill. Does the recommendation change? Stretch 2. Replace the two fleet options with five (200, 250, 300, 350 and 400 bikes) and plot the mean and the 5th percentile of 24-month profit against fleet size. Which fleet would a cautious board choose? Stretch 3. Hold out 20 pilot riders, refit the logistic model on the other 60, and check how well it predicts the held-out renewals. What does the result say about the model's reliability? Challenge ¶ Challenge 1. Value the staged plan. Simulate a launch with 250 bikes and a rule that adds 150 bikes in month 7 if the simulated renewal rate is above the switching value. Compare its mean and 5th percentile with the two fixed fleets. Challenge 2. Correct for selection bias. Suppose test-ride visitors' compound scores run 0.15 higher on average than future subscribers' would. Subtract 0.15 from each test-ride score (capped at −1), repredict renewal, and say whether the recommendation changes. Challenge 3. Build the fan chart of Part 6 in Tableau from an exported table of percentiles by month, with a reference band and a message title. Quiz ¶ Name the four levels of the analytics hierarchy and give one technique from this course at each. What does a prescriptive analysis need from the predictive level? State the null hypothesis of the ADF test. Why can two unrelated random walks show a high R² when one is regressed on the other? Does high multicollinearity damage prediction, explanation, or both? Explain. Why must a time-series train/test split be in time order? What does a two-way Data Table show that a single base case cannot? Give one reason the mean of a simulation can differ from the result of the mean inputs. How often is a plan set at the upper limit of a two-sided 95% interval exceeded, if the forecast is well calibrated? Name two ways a sentiment score can mislead when it is used as a model input. What is selection bias, and where did it appear in the Kestrel case? What makes a staged decision with a trigger a good answer when the evidence is uncertain? ax . set_xticks ( range ( counts . shape [ 1 ]), [ f "Day { d } " for d in counts . columns ]) ax . set_yticks ( range ( len ( levels )), counts . index ) ax . set_title ( "The course climbs the grain (one row = one thing) 1 Pivot tables and groupby Descriptive Sensible groups and a stated measure 1 Correlation Descriptive Paired numeric data, a look at the scatter 1 Confounding and Simpson's Descriptive Tokenised, normalised text 3 VADER sentiment scores Descriptive Text in the language the lexicon knows 3 Checking scores against human labels Diagnostic A labelled sample 3 Decomposition: trend and season Diagnostic A regular, time-ordered series 3 ADF test and differencing Diagnostic A plot of the series first 3 SARIMA forecast with RMSE and MAE Predictive Stationarity and a time-ordered test set 4 Multiple regression for prediction Predictive Explored data and a train/test split 4 Residual plots Diagnostic A fitted model 4 VIF for multicollinearity Diagnostic The Risk measures: percentiles, P(loss) Prescriptive Many frozen trials 5 Decision rule: how much to stock Prescriptive Costs of too much and too little 6 KPI trees and data-quality scorecards Diagnostic Governed definitions 6 Forecast Sheet (ETS) with a bound Predictive A numeric timeline and enough history 6 Planning against an upper bound Prescriptive A forecast interval and a cost of overrun 6 Disparate-impact audit Diagnostic Outcomes recorded by group 6 Multi-criteria scoring with red lines Prescriptive Agreed weights and constraints 6 Managerial recommendation Prescriptive Evidence from every level below Read the chart from bottom left to top right: the course climbs. Days 1 and 2 mostly describe, with the first diagnostic steps already there (Simpson's paradox on Day 1; funnels and an A/B test on Day 2); Day 3 adds more diagnosis and the first prediction; Day 4 predicts; Days 5 and 6 prescribe. The dependency runs one way : A diagnostic claim needs a description to explain. Simpson's paradox (Day 1) only appears after you have the overall and the group-level summaries. A prediction needs an honest description of the past. The ADF test (Day 3) is only meaningful once you have plotted the series and seen whether it drifts. A prescription needs a prediction with its uncertainty. A Data Table or a Monte Carlo run (Day 5) varies a base case that someone first had to forecast.
docs.title: Part 2: The analytics hierarchy revisited (core)

docs.text: Misconception Why it is wrong "Prescriptive is the most advanced, so it is always the best answer." A prescription built on a careless description is worse than a careful description, because it looks authoritative. Use the lowest level that answers the question. "Descriptive analytics is just the warm-up." Most business questions are descriptive ("which region fell?"), and most failed models fail because the description was skipped. "A predictive model tells you what to do." It tells you what is likely if nothing changes. Choosing what to do needs costs, constraints and values, which belong to the prescriptive level and to the people deciding. Self-check (one sentence each). Place each of these on the hierarchy and say what it needs from below: a residual plot; a Tableau filter; a word cloud; a probability of loss; a forecast confidence interval.
docs.title: Three misconceptions

docs.text: Every modelling day had a check that came before you could trust the result. They look unrelated: a p-value from a unit-root test, a ratio from a regression, a grid of profits, a histogram, an interval. Underneath, each one does the same three things: Name a condition the technique quietly assumes. Test whether this data or this model meets it. Report what happens to the answer when the condition is stressed instead of assumed. A model that skips the check still produces a number. What it cannot tell you is how far to trust that number. Check Technique it protects The assumption it tests What goes wrong if you skip it What to report Where taught ADF test (and differencing) ARIMA and SARIMA forecasts The series has a stable mean and variance (stationarity) after any differencing The model treats a random drift as a pattern; two drifting series look related when they are not (a spurious regression) The test result before and after differencing, and the differencing order used Day 3, Part 7 VIF Multiple regression The predictors are not so entangled that their separate effects cannot be told apart Coefficients swing, change sign or look "insignificant" although the variables matter; a manager is told the wrong lever VIFs, and whether the model is for prediction (tolerable) or explanation (act on it) Day 4, Part 9 Train and test split Any predictive model Accuracy on the data used for fitting says nothing about new data Over-fitting: a model that memorises the past and fails on the future; for time series, a random split leaks the future Error on the test set, set against the scale of the outcome Day 3, Part 3; Day 4, Part 5 Data Table sweep A deterministic spreadsheet model The base case is representative of the plausible inputs A comfortable base case hides a region of losses next door; nobody knows which input matters most The range of outputs, and the input values at which the decision switches Day 5, Parts 3–5 Monte Carlo A model with several uncertain inputs at once Average inputs give the average output (they often do not), and the spread does not matter The flaw of averages; a plan with a large chance of loss looks fine on its mean Percentiles, the probability of a loss, and the number of trials Day 5, Parts 6–10 Confidence bound A forecast used for a plan A point forecast is a safe planning number A plan set at the point is exceeded about half the time; costly when an overrun hurts more than a surplus The interval, which bound the plan uses, and why Day 3, Part 9; Day 6, Parts 6–7 Two more checks belong in the same family: the residual plot (Day 4, Part 7: is the model's error pattern-free?) and validating sentiment against human labels (Day 3, Part 8: does the score measure what we think?). The six short demonstrations below each show the failure that one check catches. All the data is synthetic.
docs.title: Part 3: One discipline, six checks (core)

docs.text: Two independent random walks share nothing: each step of one is unrelated to the other. Regress one on the other, in levels and then in differences. Predict, then run. Will the regression in levels find a strong relationship between two series that are unrelated by construction? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 10 ) n = 120 walk_a = 100 + np . cumsum ( rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n )) # random walk: today = yesterday + noise walk_b = 50 + np . cumsum ( rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , n )) # an independent random walk for name , series in [( "walk A, levels" , walk_a ), ( "walk A, first difference" , np . diff ( walk_a ))]: with warnings . catch_warnings (): # newer statsmodels warns about a future return type warnings . simplefilter ( "ignore" , FutureWarning ) stat , pvalue = adfuller ( series )[: 2 ] print ( f "ADF on { name : <26 } statistic { stat : 6.2f } p-value { pvalue : .3f } " ) r2_levels = sm . OLS ( walk_b , sm . add_constant ( walk_a )) . fit () . rsquared r2_diffs = sm . OLS ( np . diff ( walk_b ), sm . add_constant ( np . diff ( walk_a ))) . fit () . rsquared print ( f " \n R² of B on A in levels: { r2_levels : .2f } " ) print ( f "R² of B on A in differences: { r2_diffs : .2f } " ) ADF on walk A, levels statistic -1.76 p-value 0.402 ADF on walk A, first difference statistic -8.53 p-value 0.000 R² of B on A in levels: 0.89 R² of B on A in differences: 0.00 The ADF test's null hypothesis is "the series has a unit root" (it is not stationary) . A large p-value for the levels means we cannot reject a wandering mean; after differencing, the p-value is tiny and the series is stationary. In levels, the two unrelated walks show a large R², because both happen to drift over the same stretch. In differences, the relationship disappears, because there was never one. What the ADF test protects against: building a forecast, or a regression, on a drift.
docs.title: A. The ADF test: a drift is not a trend

docs.text: A rent model with two predictors that move together almost perfectly: floor area and number of rooms. Fit it on two random halves of the same data. Predict, then run. Both halves come from the same process. Will the two fitted coefficients for floor area be close? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2 ) n = 80 area = rng . uniform ( 40 , 120 , n ) # square metres rooms = area / 25 + rng . normal ( 0 , 0.15 , n ) # rooms track area closely rent = 300 + 9 * area + 60 * rooms + rng . normal ( 0 , 90 , n ) flats = pd . DataFrame ({ "area" : area , "rooms" : rooms , "rent" : rent }) X = sm . add_constant ( flats [[ "area" , "rooms" ]]) vif = { col : variance_inflation_factor ( X . values , i ) for i , col in enumerate ( X . columns ) if col != "const" } print ( "VIF:" , ", " . join ( f " { k } { v : .1f } " for k , v in vif . items ())) half = rng . permutation ( n ) for label , idx in [( "first half " , half [: 40 ]), ( "second half" , half [ 40 :])]: fit = smf . ols ( "rent ~ area + rooms" , data = flats . iloc [ idx ]) . fit () print ( f " { label } : area coefficient { fit . params [ 'area' ] : 6.1f } rooms coefficient { fit . params [ 'rooms' ] : 7.1f } " f " R² { fit . rsquared : .2f } " ) VIF: area 43.4, rooms 43.4 first half : area coefficient 13.6 rooms coefficient -58.0 R² 0.83 second half: area coefficient 6.8 rooms coefficient 138.2 R² 0.89 The VIFs are far above the usual warning level of about 5 to 10, and the two halves disagree about how much each variable is worth (one half even gives rooms a negative effect), even though the R² stays healthy in both. That is the pattern to remember: multicollinearity hurts explanation, not prediction . If the model only has to predict rent for flats like these, it may be fine. If a manager asks "how much is one extra room worth?", the coefficients cannot answer. What VIF protects against: telling someone the wrong lever.
docs.title: B. VIF: entangled predictors give unstable coefficients

docs.text: Twenty-four months of a smooth relationship plus noise. Fit a straight line and a flexible curve (a polynomial of degree 4) to the first 16 points, and test both on the last 8. Predict, then run. Which model will have the smaller error on the training data? Which on the test data? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 7 ) x = np . linspace ( 0 , 1 , 24 ) y = 20 + 15 * x + rng . normal ( 0 , 2 , 24 ) train , test = slice ( 0 , 16 ), slice ( 16 , 24 ) # time order: fit on the past, test on the future def rmse ( a , b ): return float ( np . sqrt ( np . mean (( a - b ) ** 2 ))) rows = [] fits = {} for degree in ( 1 , 4 ): model = np . polynomial . Polynomial . fit ( x [ train ], y [ train ], degree ) fits [ degree ] = model rows . append ({ "degree" : degree , "train RMSE" : rmse ( model ( x [ train ]), y [ train ]), "test RMSE" : rmse ( model ( x [ test ]), y [ test ])}) print ( pd . DataFrame ( rows ) . round ( 2 ) . to_string ( index = False )) grid = np . linspace ( 0 , 1 , 200 ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . scatter ( x [ train ], y [ train ], color = GREY , label = "training months" ) ax . scatter ( x [ test ], y [ test ], color = "black" , marker = "s" , label = "test months" ) ax . plot ( grid , fits [ 1 ]( grid ), color = BLUE , label = "straight line" ) ax . plot ( grid , np . clip ( fits [ 4 ]( grid ), 0 , 60 ), color = ORANGE , label = "degree-4 curve" ) ax . axvline ( x [ 16 ] - 0.02 , color = GREY , linestyle = ":" ) ax . set_ylim ( 0 , 60 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "time (scaled)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "sales" ) ax . set_title ( "The flexible curve wins on the past and loses on the future" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False , fontsize = 9 ) plt . show () degree train RMSE test RMSE 1 1.22 2.83 4 1.10 37.41 On the training months the flexible curve wins; on the test months it loses badly, because it bent itself around the noise and then extrapolated that bend into the future. What the train and test split protects against: reporting the training error as if it were the error on next month. For time series the split must be in time order (Day 3, Part 3); a random split lets the model peek at the future.
docs.title: C. Train and test: a flexible model can memorise noise

docs.text: A product line earns a margin per unit on its sales volume and pays a fixed cost. The base case is a margin of $20 on 5,000 units, against fixed costs of $80,000. Sweep both inputs, as a two-way Data Table would (Day 5, Part 4). Predict, then run. The base case makes a profit. Roughly what share of this plausible grid of inputs makes a loss? fixed_cost = 80_000 margins = np . array ([ 14 , 16 , 18 , 20 , 22 , 24 , 26 ]) # $ per unit volumes = np . array ([ 3500 , 4000 , 4500 , 5000 , 5500 , 6000 , 6500 ]) # units grid = pd . DataFrame ( np . outer ( volumes , margins ) - fixed_cost , index = pd . Index ( volumes , name = "units" ), columns = pd . Index ( margins , name = "margin $" )) print ( "Profit ($) for each margin (columns) and volume (rows):" ) print ( grid . to_string ()) print ( f " \n Base case (margin $20, 5,000 units): { usd ( 20 * 5000 - fixed_cost ) } " ) print ( f "Share of the grid with a loss: { ( grid < 0 ) . to_numpy () . mean () : .0% } " ) print ( f "Break-even volume at a $20 margin: { fixed_cost / 20 : ,.0f } units" ) Profit ($) for each margin (columns) and volume (rows): margin $ 14 16 18 20 22 24 26 units 3500 -31000 -24000 -17000 -10000 -3000 4000 11000 4000 -24000 -16000 -8000 0 8000 16000 24000 4500 -17000 -8000 1000 10000 19000 28000 37000 5000 -10000 0 10000 20000 30000 40000 50000 5500 -3000 8000 19000 30000 41000 52000 63000 6000 4000 16000 28000 40000 52000 64000 76000 6500 11000 24000 37000 50000 63000 76000 89000 Base case (margin $20, 5,000 units): $20,000 Share of the grid with a loss: 24% Break-even volume at a $20 margin: 4,000 units The base case looks comfortable, yet a sizeable part of the grid is red, and the cliff starts close to the base case. The sweep also shows which input matters more (compare a step along a row with a step down a column) and the switching values (the break-even volume for each margin). What the sweep protects against: a single number that hides how close the decision is to changing.
docs.title: D. The Data Table sweep: the base case hides the cliff

docs.text: Same model, but now margin and volume are uncertain at the same time: margin around $20 (standard deviation $3), volume around 5,000 units (standard deviation 900). Draw 10,000 trials. Predict, then run. The average inputs give a profit of $20,000. Will the average simulated profit be close to that? What chance of a loss do you expect? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) trials = 10_000 margin = rng . normal ( 20 , 3 , trials ) volume = rng . normal ( 5000 , 900 , trials ) profit = margin * volume - fixed_cost print ( f "Profit at average inputs: { usd ( 20 * 5000 - fixed_cost ) } " ) print ( f "Mean simulated profit: { usd ( profit . mean ()) } " ) print ( f "5th to 95th percentile: { usd ( np . percentile ( profit , 5 )) } to { usd ( np . percentile ( profit , 95 )) } " ) print ( f "Probability of a loss: { ( profit < 0 ) . mean () : .1% } " ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . hist ( profit / 1000 , bins = 60 , color = SKY , edgecolor = "white" ) ax . axvline ( 0 , color = ORANGE , linewidth = 2 , label = "break-even" ) ax . axvline ( profit . mean () / 1000 , color = BLUE , linestyle = "--" , label = "mean" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "profit (thousand $)" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "number of trials" ) ax . set_title ( "Same mean as the plan, but a real chance of a loss" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () Profit at average inputs: $20,000 Mean simulated profit: $20,023 5th to 95th percentile: -$16,469 to $60,513 Probability of a loss: 20.4% Here the mean is close to the plan because profit is a simple product of independent inputs. With a cap (capacity, stock, a contract limit), the mean of the outputs falls below the output of the mean inputs: that is the flaw of averages (Day 5, Part 6), and you will see it in Part 5. Either way, the mean hides the spread: there is a material chance of a loss that the single-number plan never showed. What Monte Carlo protects against: planning on one number when several inputs are uncertain together.
docs.title: E. Monte Carlo: the average plan is not the average outcome

docs.text: A forecast says next quarter's demand is 1,000 units, with a forecast standard error of 120 units (assume the errors are roughly normal). How often is each plan exceeded? Predict, then run. If you plan capacity exactly at the point forecast, how often will demand be higher than your plan? rng = np . random . default_rng ( 5 ) demand = rng . normal ( 1000 , 120 , 100_000 ) # many possible quarters consistent with the forecast plans = { "point forecast" : 1000 , "80 % u pper bound (z = 1.28)" : 1000 + 1.28 * 120 , "95 % u pper bound (z = 1.96)" : 1000 + 1.96 * 120 } for name , plan in plans . items (): print ( f "Plan at the { name : <28 } { plan : 7.0f } units demand exceeds plan in { ( demand > plan ) . mean () : 5.1% } of quarters" ) Plan at the point forecast 1000 units demand exceeds plan in 50.1% of quarters Plan at the 80% upper bound (z = 1.28) 1154 units demand exceeds plan in 10.1% of quarters Plan at the 95% upper bound (z = 1.96) 1235 units demand exceeds plan in 2.5% of quarters A plan at the point forecast is exceeded about half the time. The upper limit of a two-sided 95% interval is the 97.5th percentile, so it is exceeded only about 2.5% of the time (Day 6, Part 7). Which bound to use is a business choice, set by how much an overrun costs compared with a surplus. What the bound protects against: treating "most likely" as "safe".
docs.title: F. Confidence bounds: planning on the point is a coin toss

docs.text: The same discipline applies to error metrics. An RMSE of 40 units is excellent for a product that sells 4,000 a month and useless for one that sells 50. Always report an error next to the scale of what it measures : the mean of the outcome, a naive forecast's error, or a percentage. An R² alone is not evidence of a good model either: Part 3B had a healthy R² with untrustworthy coefficients, and Part 3C's flexible curve had an excellent training fit.
docs.title: Error measures need a scale
Part 4: Integrated case, step 1: from text to a model (core)

docs.text: Kestrel Bikes rents electric bikes by monthly subscription. A year-long pilot in its home city went well enough that the board is ready to launch in a second city. The open question is how big a fleet to lease there: 250 bikes or 400? A bigger fleet can serve more riders, but every leased bike costs money whether anyone rides it or not. Two sources of evidence are on the table: Pilot data (structured and unstructured). 80 pilot riders wrote a short comment after their first month, and Kestrel knows whether each one renewed at the six-month mark. New-city test rides (unstructured only). At a weekend test-ride event in the new city, 40 people tried a bike and left a comment. Nobody there has subscribed yet. The chain we will follow is the one the capstone asks you to follow with different data and a different question: text → model → simulation → chart → recommendation . At each hand-over we stop and ask what could break. Step Question Tool in this notebook How you would do it in the capstone's tools Text What do riders say, as a number? VADER compound scores Python (JupyterLab) Model How does that number relate to renewal? Renewal rate by sentiment band; logistic regression Excel AVERAGEIFS for the band table Simulation What profit range does each fleet size give? numpy Monte Carlo and a sweep Excel RAND() , NORM.INV , Data Tables Chart What does the board need to see? matplotlib fan chart Tableau: dimension on Columns, Measure Values on Rows Recommendation Which fleet, and on what condition? A short memo Word, as a PDF
docs.title: The case

docs.text: Each comment below was written for this lecture from three banks of phrases (positive, mixed and negative), chosen according to an invisible "satisfaction" for each rider; renewal was then drawn from that same satisfaction. So we know the truth, and we can see whether VADER recovers it. POSITIVE = [ "Love the bike, the commute is so much easier now." , "Great service and the battery easily lasts all week." , "Really happy with it, I cycle to work every day now." , "The app works well and swapping a battery takes a minute." , "Excellent value compared with taxis. Highly recommend." , "Friendly repair team and the bike feels solid." , "Brilliant for hills, I arrive at work without sweating." , "Smooth ride and the booking is simple." ] MIXED = [ "Good bike, but the app crashes when I try to book a repair." , "The ride is fine, but the monthly fee feels high." , "Nice bike, although the battery drains fast in the cold." , "Okay overall. The seat is uncomfortable on long trips." , "Useful, but the docking station is often full." , "Decent bike, but the lock is awkward to use." ] NEGATIVE = [ "The bike broke twice in the first month. Very disappointed." , "Terrible support, I waited a week for a repair." , "Too expensive for what you get, and the brakes squeal." , "The battery died halfway home. Not worth it." , "Frustrating app and nobody answers the phone." , "The bike was stolen from the dock and the process was awful." ] def write_comment ( satisfaction , rng ): """Pick a phrase bank from the rider's satisfaction, then a phrase at random.""" if satisfaction > 0.45 : tier , bank = "positive" , POSITIVE elif satisfaction > - 0.45 : tier , bank = "mixed" , MIXED else : tier , bank = "negative" , NEGATIVE return tier , bank [ rng . integers ( len ( bank ))] rng = np . random . default_rng ( 719 ) satisfaction = rng . normal ( 0 , 1 , 80 ) written = [ write_comment ( s , rng ) for s in satisfaction ] p_renew_true = 1 / ( 1 + np . exp ( - ( 0.3 + 1.5 * satisfaction ))) pilot = pd . DataFrame ({ "rider" : range ( 1 , 81 ), "written_as" : [ w [ 0 ] for w in written ], "comment" : [ w [ 1 ] for w in written ], "renewed" : ( rng . random ( 80 ) < p_renew_true ) . astype ( int )}) def band ( score ): """VADER's usual thresholds.""" return "Positive" if score >= 0.05 else ( "Negative" if score <= - 0.05 else "Neutral" ) pilot [ "compound" ] = pilot [ "comment" ] . apply ( lambda t : sia . polarity_scores ( t )[ "compound" ]) pilot [ "band" ] = pilot [ "compound" ] . apply ( band ) print ( pilot [[ "rider" , "comment" , "compound" , "band" , "renewed" ]] . head ( 8 ) . to_string ( index = False )) print ( f " \n Pilot riders: { len ( pilot ) } renewed: { pilot [ 'renewed' ] . mean () : .0% } " ) rider comment compound band renewed 1 Excellent value compared with taxis. Highly recommend. 0.8357 Positive 1 2 Smooth ride and the booking is simple. 0.0000 Neutral 1 3 Great service and the battery easily lasts all week. 0.7579 Positive 1 4 The ride is fine, but the monthly fee feels high. 0.1027 Positive 0 5 Okay overall. The seat is uncomfortable on long trips. -0.1779 Negative 0 6 The bike broke twice in the first month. Very disappointed. -0.7346 Negative 0 7 Terrible support, I waited a week for a repair. -0.1027 Negative 0 8 Love the bike, the commute is so much easier now. 0.8062 Positive 1 Pilot riders: 80 renewed: 51%
docs.title: Score the pilot comments

docs.text: Chapter 8's warning is that a number made from text deserves the same scrutiny as any other engineered feature. We have the writers' intended tone, so we can check VADER against it (Day 3, Part 8). Predict, then run. Will every comment written as negative get a negative VADER score? check = pd . crosstab ( pilot [ "written_as" ], pilot [ "band" ]) . reindex ( index = [ "positive" , "mixed" , "negative" ], columns = [ "Positive" , "Neutral" , "Negative" ], fill_value = 0 ) print ( "Intended tone (rows) against VADER's band (columns):" ) print ( check . to_string ()) phrases = pd . DataFrame ([( tier , t , sia . polarity_scores ( t )[ "compound" ]) for tier , bank in [( "positive" , POSITIVE ), ( "mixed" , MIXED ), ( "negative" , NEGATIVE )] for t in bank ], columns = [ "written_as" , "phrase" , "compound" ]) misreads = phrases [(( phrases [ "written_as" ] == "positive" ) & ( phrases [ "compound" ] < 0.05 )) | (( phrases [ "written_as" ] == "negative" ) & ( phrases [ "compound" ] > - 0.05 ))] print ( " \n Phrases VADER misreads:" ) print ( misreads . to_string ( index = False )) Intended tone (rows) against VADER's band (columns): band Positive Neutral Negative written_as positive 24 3 0 mixed 17 0 9 negative 0 3 24 Phrases VADER misreads: written_as phrase compound positive Smooth ride and the booking is simple. 0.0 negative Too expensive for what you get, and the brakes squeal. 0.0 Most comments written as clearly positive or clearly negative land in the right band, and the mixed comments split both ways, as you would expect from "good, but" sentences. Not every comment lands well, though. "Smooth ride and the booking is simple" is praise for a bike, but none of its words are in VADER's general-purpose lexicon, so it scores zero. "Too expensive for what you get, and the brakes squeal" is a complaint, but "expensive" and "squeal" carry no score either. Domain words (price, brakes, ride quality) are exactly where a lexicon built for social media goes blind. In a report you would say so , give an example, and treat the score as a noisy measure.
docs.title: Validate the score before you use it

docs.text: Two models, one simple enough for a spreadsheet and one smoother: Band table. The renewal rate within each VADER band. In Excel: =AVERAGEIFS(renewed_range, band_range, "Positive") . Logistic regression of renewal on the compound score (Day 4, Part 13): it gives a renewal probability for any score between −1 and 1. Predict, then run. How much higher do you expect the renewal rate of Positive riders to be than that of Negative riders? band_table = ( pilot . groupby ( "band" )[ "renewed" ] . agg ( riders = "count" , renewal_rate = "mean" ) . reindex ([ "Positive" , "Neutral" , "Negative" ])) print ( band_table . round ( 2 ) . to_string ()) logit = smf . logit ( "renewed ~ compound" , data = pilot ) . fit ( disp = 0 ) print ( f " \n Logistic regression: intercept { logit . params [ 'Intercept' ] : .2f } , " f "slope { logit . params [ 'compound' ] : .2f } (standard error { logit . bse [ 'compound' ] : .2f } )" ) for score in ( - 0.6 , 0.0 , 0.6 ): p = logit . predict ( pd . DataFrame ({ "compound" : [ score ]}))[ 0 ] print ( f " predicted renewal at a compound score of { score : +.1f } : { p : .0% } " ) riders renewal_rate band Positive 41 0.66 Neutral 6 0.50 Negative 33 0.33 Logistic regression: intercept -0.10, slope 1.90 (standard error 0.57) predicted renewal at a compound score of -0.6: 22% predicted renewal at a compound score of +0.0: 48% predicted renewal at a compound score of +0.6: 74% The relationship is real but loose: sentiment moves renewal by tens of percentage points, not from zero to one, and the slope's standard error is large because 80 riders is a small sample. Note also the Neutral row: it is built from very few riders, so its rate is little more than noise. This is the hand-over from text to model, and its weak seam is double: a noisy score (misreads) feeding a small sample .
docs.title: Model: from a sentiment score to a renewal rate
Part 5: Integrated case, step 2: from a model to a simulation (core)

docs.text: Score the 40 test-ride comments, then predict a renewal rate for the new city in two ways: from the logistic model (average the predicted probabilities) and from the band table (weight each band's rate by its share of comments). rng = np . random . default_rng ( 1119 ) city_satisfaction = rng . normal ( 0.5 , 1 , 40 ) # the event attracted keener people (see below) city = pd . DataFrame ({ "comment" : [ write_comment ( s , rng )[ 1 ] for s in city_satisfaction ]}) city [ "compound" ] = city [ "comment" ] . apply ( lambda t : sia . polarity_scores ( t )[ "compound" ]) city [ "band" ] = city [ "compound" ] . apply ( band ) renewal_logit = logit . predict ( city ) . mean () shares = city [ "band" ] . value_counts ( normalize = True ) . reindex ( band_table . index , fill_value = 0 ) renewal_bands = ( shares * band_table [ "renewal_rate" ]) . sum () renewal_pilot = pilot [ "renewed" ] . mean () print ( f "Mean compound score: pilot { pilot [ 'compound' ] . mean () : +.2f } , new-city test rides { city [ 'compound' ] . mean () : +.2f } " ) print ( f "Band shares in the new city: " + ", " . join ( f " { b } { s : .0% } " for b , s in shares . items ())) print ( f " \n Predicted six-month renewal, logistic model: { renewal_logit : .1% } " ) print ( f "Predicted six-month renewal, band table: { renewal_bands : .1% } " ) print ( f "Actual six-month renewal in the pilot city: { renewal_pilot : .1% } " ) Mean compound score: pilot +0.08, new-city test rides +0.21 Band shares in the new city: Positive 68%, Neutral 2%, Negative 30% Predicted six-month renewal, logistic model: 56.8% Predicted six-month renewal, band table: 55.7% Actual six-month renewal in the pilot city: 51.2% The new city's comments are more positive, so both models predict a higher renewal rate than the pilot achieved. Should we believe it? Think about who wrote the comments . Pilot riders were paying customers a month into their subscription. Test-ride visitors chose to come to a weekend event and rode a new bike for twenty minutes; they are keener than the average future subscriber, and a short ride shows none of the battery, repair and docking problems that drive the pilot's complaints. This is selection bias , and it is the second weak seam: the model is fine, but the input is not drawn from the population we want to predict. A defensible analyst does not pick one number. She carries a range forward: the pilot's actual rate as a cautious case, the model's prediction as an optimistic case, and lets the simulation show whether the decision depends on which is true.
docs.title: Apply the model to the new city

docs.text: The monthly business model, with every input stated (all invented): Input Value Uncertain? Subscription price $69 per rider per month No Variable cost (insurance, batteries, repairs) $15 per rider per month No Lease cost $20 per bike per month, for every bike leased No Fixed cost (depot, staff) $5,000 per month No Launch cost $25,000 once No New sign-ups per month Poisson, with a monthly average drawn once per trial from Normal(45, 12) Yes Six-month renewal rate Normal around the central estimate, standard deviation 7 points Yes Capacity Active riders can never exceed the fleet Fixed by the decision A six-month renewal rate R is turned into a monthly retention rate R 1/6 , so that six months of retention multiply back to R . Each month, active riders = retained riders + new sign-ups, capped at the fleet size. Profit is summed over 24 months. Predict, then run. Which fleet has the higher average 24-month profit? Which has the higher chance of a loss? Are those the same fleet? PRICE , VAR_COST , LEASE , FIXED , LAUNCH , MONTHS = 69 , 15 , 20 , 5_000 , 25_000 , 24 def simulate ( fleet , renewal_mean , renewal_sd = 0.07 , signups_mean = 45 , signups_sd = 12 , trials = 5_000 , seed = 2026 ): """Return cumulative profit by month (months x trials) for one fleet size.""" g = np . random . default_rng ( seed ) # same seed for both fleets: a fair comparison renewal = np . clip ( g . normal ( renewal_mean , renewal_sd , trials ), 0.2 , 0.97 ) retention = renewal ** ( 1 / 6 ) signup_rate = np . clip ( g . normal ( signups_mean , signups_sd , trials ), 5 , None ) active = np . zeros ( trials ) cumulative = np . full ( trials , - float ( LAUNCH )) path = np . empty (( MONTHS , trials )) for month in range ( MONTHS ): active = np . minimum ( np . round ( active * retention ) + g . poisson ( signup_rate ), fleet ) cumulative = cumulative + ( PRICE - VAR_COST ) * active - LEASE * fleet - FIXED path [ month ] = cumulative return path def summarise ( final ): return { "mean" : final . mean (), "5th pct" : np . percentile ( final , 5 ), "median" : np . median ( final ), "95th pct" : np . percentile ( final , 95 ), "P(loss)" : ( final < 0 ) . mean ()} central = ( renewal_pilot + renewal_logit ) / 2 # midway between the cautious and optimistic cases paths = { fleet : simulate ( fleet , central ) for fleet in ( 250 , 400 )} summary = pd . DataFrame ({ f " { fleet } bikes" : summarise ( p [ - 1 ]) for fleet , p in paths . items ()}) . T print ( f "Central six-month renewal used: { central : .1% } \n " ) print ( summary . assign ( ** { c : summary [ c ] . map ( usd ) for c in [ "mean" , "5th pct" , "median" , "95th pct" ]}, ** { "P(loss)" : summary [ "P(loss)" ] . map ( " {:.0%} " . format )}) . to_string ()) Central six-month renewal used: 54.0% mean 5th pct median 95th pct P(loss) 250 bikes $10,829 -$54,459 $20,660 $37,025 21% 400 bikes $21,656 -$126,459 $43,403 $110,015 33% The larger fleet has the higher average profit and also the higher chance of a loss and the worse bad case. That is the normal shape of a capacity decision: the big fleet earns more when demand is strong, and leaves more bikes idle, still costing lease, when it is weak. Neither number alone settles the question; which matters more depends on how much loss Kestrel can absorb. Notice also the flaw of averages from Part 3E at work: because riders are capped at the fleet size, a good month cannot make up fully for a bad one.
docs.title: The simulation

docs.text: The renewal rate is the assumption we trust least, so sweep it, as a one-way Data Table would, holding everything else at its central value. Where does the decision switch? renewal_grid = np . round ( np . arange ( 0.35 , 0.751 , 0.05 ), 2 ) sweep = pd . DataFrame ({ f " { fleet } bikes" : [ simulate ( fleet , r , trials = 2_000 )[ - 1 ] . mean () for r in renewal_grid ] for fleet in ( 250 , 400 )}, index = pd . Index ( renewal_grid , name = "six-month renewal" )) print ( "Mean 24-month profit by renewal rate:" ) print ( sweep . map ( usd ) . to_string ()) fine_grid = np . round ( np . arange ( 0.40 , 0.651 , 0.01 ), 2 ) # a finer sweep to locate the switch gap = np . array ([ simulate ( 400 , r , trials = 2_000 )[ - 1 ] . mean () - simulate ( 250 , r , trials = 2_000 )[ - 1 ] . mean () for r in fine_grid ]) switch = fine_grid [ np . argmax ( gap > 0 )] print ( f " \n The larger fleet first wins on average at a renewal rate of about { switch : .0% } " f "(pilot actual { renewal_pilot : .0% } , test-ride prediction { renewal_logit : .0% } )." ) fig , ax = plt . subplots () ax . plot ( renewal_grid , sweep [ "250 bikes" ] / 1000 , marker = "o" , color = BLUE , label = "250 bikes" ) ax . plot ( renewal_grid , sweep [ "400 bikes" ] / 1000 , marker = "o" , color = ORANGE , label = "400 bikes" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = GREY , linewidth = 1 ) for value , label in [( renewal_pilot , "pilot actual" ), ( renewal_logit , "model, test rides" )]: ax . axvline ( value , color = GREY , linestyle = ":" ) ax . text ( value , ax . get_ylim ()[ 1 ] * 0.92 , label , rotation = 90 , va = "top" , ha = "right" , fontsize = 8 , color = "dimgray" ) ax . set_xlabel ( "six-month renewal rate" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "mean 24-month profit (thousand $)" ) ax . set_title ( "The fleet decision depends on renewal" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () Mean 24-month profit by renewal rate: 250 bikes 400 bikes six-month renewal 0.35 -$13,438 -$53,844 0.40 -$4,659 -$31,904 0.45 $2,121 -$11,336 0.50 $7,225 $7,118 0.55 $11,047 $23,197 0.60 $13,944 $36,751 0.65 $16,228 $47,934 0.70 $18,026 $57,043 0.75 $19,495 $64,419 The larger fleet first wins on average at a renewal rate of about 51% (pilot actual 51%, test-ride prediction 57%). The sweep turns an argument about adjectives ("renewal will be good") into a question with a number in it: is renewal in the new city above or below the switching value? The pilot's actual rate sits almost on the switching value; only the optimistic test-ride prediction is clearly above it. Below the switch the larger fleet loses money fast, while above it the gain grows more slowly. So the honest answer is that the evidence does not yet settle the fleet size, and the recommendation should be built around that fact rather than hiding it.
docs.title: Sweep the uncertain assumption
Part 6: Integrated case, step 3: from a simulation to a chart and a recommendation (core)

docs.text: A board member has thirty seconds. The chart must show the two options, over time, with their range , not just a central line (Chapter 8's point about carrying the honest range forward). A fan chart does that: the median path and a band from the 5th to the 95th percentile. months = np . arange ( 1 , MONTHS + 1 ) fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8.5 , 4.5 )) for fleet , colour in [( 250 , BLUE ), ( 400 , ORANGE )]: p = paths [ fleet ] / 1000 ax . fill_between ( months , np . percentile ( p , 5 , axis = 1 ), np . percentile ( p , 95 , axis = 1 ), color = colour , alpha = 0.18 ) ax . plot ( months , np . median ( p , axis = 1 ), color = colour , linewidth = 2.2 ) ax . text ( MONTHS + 0.3 , np . median ( p [ - 1 ]), f " { fleet } bikes" , color = colour , va = "center" , fontweight = "bold" ) ax . axhline ( 0 , color = GREY , linewidth = 1 ) ax . set_xlim ( 1 , MONTHS + 4 ) ax . set_xlabel ( "month after launch" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "cumulative profit (thousand $)" ) ax . set_title ( "400 bikes earns more in a good case and loses more in a bad one \n " "median line, shaded band = 5th to 95th percentile" , fontsize = 10 ) plt . show () Choices worth copying: a message title that states the finding; direct labels instead of a legend; a zero line , because "do we lose money?" is the board's first question; colour-blind-safe colours; the range shaded. The same chart in Tableau (the tool the capstone uses for its chart). Export a table with one row per month and columns for each option's 5th percentile, median and 95th percentile. Then: Put Month on Columns and make sure it is a dimension (or a continuous dimension), not SUM(Month) . Put Measure Values on Rows, and keep only the measures you want on the Measure Values card. Put Measure Names on Color, choose Line marks, and format the axis as currency . For the band, use two median lines and add a reference band between the percentile measures, or show the percentiles as thin lines.
docs.title: The chart for the board

docs.text: Day 6, Part 14 gave the structure: answer first , then the evidence, the trade-off in plain units, the conditions, and the decision requested. Label each statement as a fact (measured), an estimate (modelled) or a judgement (yours). The memo below is generated from the numbers above, so it stays consistent with them. s250 , s400 = summary . loc [ "250 bikes" ], summary . loc [ "400 bikes" ] memo = f """ TO: Kestrel Bikes board FROM: BI team RE: Fleet size for the second city RECOMMENDATION. Launch with 250 bikes, with a pre-agreed option to lease 150 more once the first six-month renewal rate in the new city is known. Add them if renewal is at or above about { switch : .0% } . EVIDENCE. - [Fact] In the pilot, { renewal_pilot : .0% } of riders renewed at six months; riders whose comments scored Positive renewed at { band_table . loc [ 'Positive' , 'renewal_rate' ] : .0% } and those scored Negative at { band_table . loc [ 'Negative' , 'renewal_rate' ] : .0% } . - [Estimate] Test-ride comments predict a renewal rate of { renewal_logit : .0% } , but test riders are keener than paying subscribers, so we treat this as an optimistic case. - [Estimate] Over 24 months, 400 bikes averages { usd ( s400 [ 'mean' ]) } against { usd ( s250 [ 'mean' ]) } for 250 bikes, but its chance of a loss is { s400 [ 'P(loss)' ] : .0% } against { s250 [ 'P(loss)' ] : .0% } , and its bad case (5th percentile) is { usd ( s400 [ '5th pct' ]) } against { usd ( s250 [ '5th pct' ]) } . TRADE-OFF. The larger fleet buys about { usd ( s400 [ 'mean' ] - s250 [ 'mean' ]) } of extra average profit at the cost of a deeper bad case. Which fleet wins depends on renewal, which the evidence cannot yet pin down. CONDITIONS. [Judgement] The staged plan is right if the extra bikes can be leased within about two months and the lease allows it. If the lessor offers only one fleet size, the board must choose between the higher average and the safer downside, and should say which it values. LIMITS. Sentiment scores misread domain words such as price and brakes; the pilot sample is 80 riders; all costs are budget estimates. Comments were analysed in aggregate and no rider is identified. DECISION REQUESTED. Approve a 250-bike launch and negotiate the expansion option now. """ print ( memo ) TO: Kestrel Bikes board FROM: BI team RE: Fleet size for the second city RECOMMENDATION. Launch with 250 bikes, with a pre-agreed option to lease 150 more once the first six-month renewal rate in the new city is known. Add them if renewal is at or above about 51%. EVIDENCE. - [Fact] In the pilot, 51% of riders renewed at six months; riders whose comments scored Positive renewed at 66% and those scored Negative at 33%. - [Estimate] Test-ride comments predict a renewal rate of 57%, but test riders are keener than paying subscribers, so we treat this as an optimistic case. - [Estimate] Over 24 months, 400 bikes averages $21,656 against $10,829 for 250 bikes, but its chance of a loss is 33% against 21%, and its bad case (5th percentile) is -$126,459 against -$54,459. TRADE-OFF. The larger fleet buys about $10,827 of extra average profit at the cost of a deeper bad case. Which fleet wins depends on renewal, which the evidence cannot yet pin down. CONDITIONS. [Judgement] The staged plan is right if the extra bikes can be leased within about two months and the lease allows it. If the lessor offers only one fleet size, the board must choose between the higher average and the safer downside, and should say which it values. LIMITS. Sentiment scores misread domain words such as price and brakes; the pilot sample is 80 riders; all costs are budget estimates. Comments were analysed in aggregate and no rider is identified. DECISION REQUESTED. Approve a 250-bike launch and negotiate the expansion option now. Three things make this memo defensible rather than merely confident: It carries the range. The average, the bad case and the probability of a loss all appear, and the trade-off between them is stated in dollars. It names the seams. The misread domain words and the selection bias are stated as limits, not hidden. It turns uncertainty into an action. Instead of guessing renewal, the recommendation buys the information (six months of real renewals) before committing to the larger fleet. When the evidence cannot settle a decision, a staged decision with a clear trigger is often the best prescriptive answer.
docs.title: The recommendation

docs.text: Hand-over What could break The check that catches it Text → score The lexicon misreads domain words Validate against labelled or hand-read examples (Day 3, Part 8) Score → model Small sample; a loose, noisy relationship Look at counts per band and the slope's standard error; test on held-out riders if there are enough Model → new city The new inputs come from a different population (selection bias) Ask who wrote the text and why; carry a range, not a point Model → simulation One "expected" input hides the spread Monte Carlo with the uncertain inputs; a sweep of the least trusted one Simulation → chart A single line implies certainty Show the band or the percentiles; zero line; message title Chart → recommendation The answer ignores the downside or the ethics Fact, estimate, judgement; conditions; limits; the decision requested
docs.title: What each hand-over needed

docs.text: Work in groups of three: one analyst, one finance director, one head of operations. The finance director is worried about the downside; the head of operations wants enough bikes to avoid turning riders away. The finance director says: "Your model is built on 80 comments and a sentiment score that cannot read the word expensive . Why should I trust any of it?" Answer in three sentences, without claiming more than the evidence shows. The head of operations says: "If we start with 250 bikes and demand is strong, we will turn riders away and they will go to a competitor." Is that a cost the simulation includes? How would you add it? Which of the inputs in the Part 5 table would you most like to measure better before launch, and how would you measure it cheaply? The marketing team proposes to quote the most positive test-ride comments in the launch campaign. What permission and privacy questions does that raise (Day 6, Part 8)? A board member asks for "just one number". Which single number would you give, and what sentence would you always put next to it? Suppose six months later renewal in the new city is exactly at the switching value. What would you recommend then, and why?
docs.title: Part 7: Business case discussion: Kestrel's board (self-study, discussion)

docs.text: These are the mistakes that cost the most marks and the most money. Scan the table in class; read the detail before the capstone.
docs.title: Part 8: Common errors by topic (core scan, self-study detail)

docs.text: Error Why it matters Fix Running cells out of order, so a variable holds an old value Results you cannot reproduce Restart and run all before exporting Reading a mean without checking skew or outliers A few large values move the mean; the "typical" case is misdescribed Report the median too; look at the histogram Treating missing values as zeros Totals and means are biased Count missing values first; decide and state how you handle them Calling a correlation a cause Confounders and reverse causation Say "is associated with"; look for the third variable (Simpson's paradox)
docs.title: Python and data exploration (Days 0 and 1)

docs.text: Error Why it matters Fix Bar chart with a truncated axis Small differences look huge Bars start at zero A date or year field left as a measure Tableau adds the years together into one mark Make it a dimension (or a date) Too many measures on Measure Values Unrelated lines on one axis Keep only the measures you mean to compare A title that names the chart instead of the finding The reader has to work out the message Write a message title Colour as the only way to tell series apart Unreadable for colour-blind readers and in greyscale print Direct labels, colour-blind-safe palette
docs.title: Charts and Tableau (Day 2)

docs.text: Error Why it matters Fix Removing "not" with the stop words "not good" becomes "good" Keep negations for sentiment Trusting VADER on domain language "Expensive", "sick", "unpredictable plot" are read wrongly or not at all Validate on a hand-labelled sample Averaging scores from a handful of texts as if they were a survey Five comments are anecdotes, not a population Report the count; treat the average as a weak signal A silent fallback scorer Code that quietly uses a different scorer when a download fails gives different numbers with no warning Print which scorer ran
docs.title: Text mining (Days 3 and 4)

docs.text: Error Why it matters Fix Random train/test split on a time series The model sees the future; the error looks too good Split in time order Reading a small ADF p-value as "not stationary" The null hypothesis is non -stationarity Small p-value: reject the unit root, the series is stationary Reporting RMSE without a scale Nobody can tell whether it is good Compare with the mean, a naive forecast, or as a percentage Text labels as a timeline in Excel Forecast Sheet Excel needs numbers or dates Use a period number or a real date
docs.title: Forecasting (Days 3 and 6)

docs.text: Error Why it matters Fix Judging the model by training R² Over-fitting goes unnoticed Report test-set error Reading a coefficient "holding others constant" when VIFs are high The separate effects cannot be told apart Say so; drop or combine predictors if you need explanation Predicting far outside the data's range The fitted line has no evidence there State the range; refuse or flag extrapolations Forgetting the reference category of a dummy variable The coefficient is misread Say "relative to …"
docs.title: Regression (Day 4)

docs.text: Error Why it matters Fix Typing numbers inside formulas Changing an assumption means hunting through cells Put every input in its own labelled cell A Data Table whose input cells are on another sheet Excel refuses Keep the input cells on the table's sheet Writing about a simulation that has not been frozen The numbers change when the file reopens Paste Special → Values first Reporting only the mean of a simulation The flaw of averages; the risk is hidden Report percentiles and the probability of a loss Planning on the point forecast when an overrun is costly Exceeded about half the time Choose a bound by the cost of being wrong
docs.title: Spreadsheets and simulation (Days 5 and 6)

docs.text: Error Why it matters Fix Recommending without stating the trade-off The board cannot see what it gives up State the cost of the choice in plain units Treating an ethical issue as "a soft factor" with no evidence It is dismissed Describe it concretely; price what you can; treat red lines as constraints Mixing facts, estimates and judgements Readers cannot tell what is measured Label them, or make it clear in the wording A chart in the report that is not discussed The evidence is not used Every chart gets a sentence that says what it shows
docs.title: BI, ethics and reports (Days 6 and 7)

docs.text: The final exam is in periods 3 and 4 today. Your facilitator confirms the format, the length and what you may bring (for example, whether a basic calculator is allowed). Whatever the format, the habits below earn marks.
docs.title: Part 9: Exam technique (core)

docs.text: Command word What it asks for A weak answer A strong answer Define The meaning, precisely An example only One-sentence definition, then an example Describe What it is or what happens Opinion Features or steps, in order Explain Why or how A restated description A cause or mechanism, with "because" Calculate A number, with working The number alone Formula, substitution, result with units Interpret What a result means in context "It is 0.62" "62% of …, which means … for the manager" Compare Similarities and differences Two separate descriptions Point-by-point, with a conclusion Evaluate A judgement on strengths and limits One side only Both sides, then a reasoned verdict Recommend A decision with justification A list of options One option, the evidence, the trade-off and a condition
docs.title: Read the command word

docs.text: Before you start, divide the time by the marks: in a 90-minute paper worth 100 marks, a 10-mark question deserves about 9 minutes. Answer the questions you are surest of first, but number them clearly. Leave five minutes at the end to check units, signs and that every part of every question has an answer.
docs.title: Budget your time

docs.text: Write the formula in words or symbols. Substitute the numbers, with units. Give the result, rounded sensibly, with units. Add one sentence saying what it means. Even if the arithmetic slips, steps 1, 2 and 4 usually earn marks.
docs.title: Lay out a calculation

docs.text: Use the pattern number + unit + context + so what + caveat . For example: "The test RMSE is 40 units, about 3% of average monthly sales, so the forecast is precise enough for stock planning; it was tested on only eight months, so we will re-check it after the next quarter."
docs.title: Interpret a number for a manager

docs.text: Find what was measured first (the outcome, the units, the sample) before the numbers. For a test, write down the null hypothesis before reading the p-value (the ADF trap in Part 8). For a model, ask on which data the metric was computed: training or test.
docs.title: Read a statistical output

docs.text: Chapter 8's advice is to prepare by speaking, not by memorising. For each chapter, say three things in under a minute, without notes: what the technique does , in plain words; what it assumes or where it fails ; and one link to a technique from another chapter . Then ask a friend to interrupt with "why does that matter?" and "what if that assumption fails?". The link is what turns a correct answer into a good one.
docs.title: Rehearse out loud

docs.text: Twelve questions written for this page, in the style of a closed-book paper. They are not taken from any exam and the exam does not reuse them. No answers are given here: work them alone, then compare with a classmate and with the lecture parts named in brackets. Allow about 60 minutes. Q1. Hierarchy (5 marks). A café chain uses: (a) a dashboard of daily sales by branch; (b) a regression of sales on temperature to set tomorrow's milk order; (c) a breakdown showing that the sales drop came from one branch's closure; (d) a simulation of three opening-hours plans. Place each on the analytics hierarchy and say what each needs from the level below. (Part 2) Q2. Stationarity (6 marks). An ADF test on 60 months of a shop's sales gives a p-value of 0.41. After first differencing, the p-value is 0.002. State the null hypothesis, interpret both results, and say what this means for the d in an ARIMA( p , d , q ) model. (Part 3A; Day 3, Part 7) Q3. Error and scale (6 marks). Two forecasts were tested on the last 12 months. Product A: RMSE 35 units, average monthly sales 1,750 units. Product B: RMSE 35 units, average monthly sales 140 units. Express each error as a percentage of average sales and say which forecast you would trust for ordering stock, and why. (Part 3) Q4. Multicollinearity (6 marks). A delivery-time model uses distance (km) and fuel used (litres) as predictors. Both VIFs are about 14; the test R² is 0.83. A manager asks how many minutes one extra kilometre adds. What do you tell her, and what would you change if that question is the main purpose of the model? (Part 3B; Day 4, Part 9) Q5. Over-fitting (5 marks). A model has a training R² of 0.96 and a test R² of 0.38. Diagnose the problem in one sentence and give two ways to address it. (Part 3C; Day 4, Part 10) Q6. Sentiment (6 marks). VADER gives these compound scores: "The delivery was not bad at all" +0.43; "This charger is sick" −0.51; "Arrived on Tuesday" 0.00. Label each with the usual thresholds (±0.05). Which label would a human disagree with, and why does VADER make that mistake? (Day 3, Parts 6 and 7) Q7. Data Table (6 marks). A two-way Data Table of monthly profit ($) has prices $8, $9 and $10 across the top and volumes 2,000, 2,500 and 3,000 down the side: volume \ price $8 $9 $10 2,000 −6,000 −4,000 −2,000 2,500 −3,500 −1,000 1,500 3,000 −1,000 2,000 5,000 Describe which combinations make a loss, which input the profit is more sensitive to over the ranges shown, and what further information the manager needs before choosing a price. (Part 3D; Day 5, Part 4) Q8. Monte Carlo (6 marks). Option X: 2,000 trials, mean profit $52,000, 5th percentile −$30,000, 360 trials below zero. Option Y: mean profit $44,000, 5th percentile $6,000, probability of a loss 2%. Calculate X's probability of a loss. Which option would you recommend to a small firm with little cash, and which to a large firm running many such projects? Explain the difference. (Part 3E; Day 5, Part 10) Q9. Forecast bounds (5 marks). Next quarter's demand forecast is 3,200 units, with a 95% interval of 2,700 to 3,700. Renting extra warehouse space at short notice costs four times as much as an unused booked space. Which number would you plan on, and why? (Part 3F; Day 6, Part 7) Q10. Chart critique (5 marks). A slide shows monthly revenue for two products as a 3D pie chart for each month, twelve pies in a row, with a legend in the corner. Name two problems and describe a better chart for the question "how has the gap between the two products changed this year?" (Day 2, Parts 1–4) Q11. Fairness (5 marks). A screening model approves 54% of applicants from group P and 36% from group Q. Calculate the disparate-impact ratio, say whether it passes the common four-fifths rule of thumb, and name one further check you would make before concluding the model is unfair. (Day 6, Part 9) Q12. Integration (10 marks). A retailer wants to decide whether to stock a new line. You have 300 online reviews of the line from another market, two years of monthly sales of a similar line, and the supplier's price and minimum order. Describe, step by step, how you would get from these inputs to a recommendation, naming one technique and one check at each step, and the chart you would show the board. (Parts 3–6)

Text mining in JupyterLab Score the focus-group comments and turn the average into a demand multiplier Day 3, Parts 6–9; Part 4 above Which scorer actually ran; what a compound score measures and misses 2. Financial model in Excel Apply the multiplier to a five-year demand plan and compute profit under two suppliers Day 5, Parts 2–3; Day 6, Part 12 Inputs in their own cells; every row checked by hand once 3. Chart in Tableau Plot both profit paths by year Day 2 (Tableau); Day 6, Part 16; Part 6 above Year as a dimension; only the two profits on Measure Values; currency axis 4. Managerial report Recommend a supplier, balancing profit against ethics; explain the value of the three-tool chain Day 6, Parts 12 and 14; Part 6 above Answer first; trade-off in plain units; fact, estimate, judgement; limits Two reminders from this morning that apply directly: A number made from text deserves scrutiny (Part 4). Say what the score can and cannot capture in five short comments. A recommendation weighs a trade-off and states it (Part 6). docs.text: Setup ¶ Get the three course tools working before the first day: JupyterLab for Python, Tableau Desktop and Microsoft Excel. For Python there are two routes. Route A is the browser version GAP describes; Route B runs on your own laptop and works without internet. What you need ¶ Tool Used for How to get it JupyterLab (Python) Activity 1, Labs 1, 3, 4 and 5, Assignments 1 and 2, the capstone Route A: Try JupyterLab in a browser. Route B: Anaconda on your laptop Tableau Desktop Activity 1, Lab 2, Lab 7, the capstone Free student licence Microsoft Excel Labs 6 and 7, Assignment 3, the capstone Your own copy or the lab PCs A PDF tool Every submission Word, macOS Preview or Adobe Acrobat (see below) Each guide page says which tool a task needs. Python, Route A: Try JupyterLab (as on GAP) ¶ GAP's instructions use Try JupyterLab , a version of JupyterLab that runs entirely in your web browser. Open https://jupyter.org/try-jupyter/lab/ in Chrome, Edge or Firefox. In the Launcher, under Notebook , click Python (Pyodide) . Rename the notebook straight away (right-click its tab → Rename Notebook… ) with the name the task asks for. How Try JupyterLab differs from ordinary Python ¶ Try JupyterLab runs Python through Pyodide : Python translated so that a browser can run it, inside the tab itself. That has three consequences. On an ordinary computer In Try JupyterLab Packages are installed once and stay installed Start each session with a %pip install … cell for the packages the task uses. A package installed yesterday, or in another tab, is not there today pd.read_csv("https://…") downloads a file directly The browser has to fetch the file, so GAP's code wraps the address with open_url(...) from pyodide.http Files and results stay on your disk Python's memory ends when the tab closes. The notebook file is kept only in that browser's storage, which is cleared with the browsing data and is not on any other computer Save your work out of the browser, every time Before you close the tab: run every cell, export a PDF ( File → Print → Save as PDF ), and download the notebook (right-click it in the file browser → Download ). Treat anything left only in the browser as lost. If the data will not download ¶ GAP's code fetches datasets from GitHub, which is often slow or blocked in mainland China. If a cell hangs or ends in a network error: Ask your facilitator for the course folder (Route B below) and take the CSV file you need from its data folder. Drag the CSV file into Try JupyterLab's file browser on the left. Load it by name instead of by address, for example pd.read_csv("penguins.csv") . If that also fails in your browser, switch to Route B for the rest of the task. The results are the same. Python, Route B: Anaconda on your laptop (offline) ¶ Route B runs the same Python on your own computer. It does not need the internet once it is installed, and your work is saved as ordinary files. 1. Install Anaconda ¶ Download the Anaconda Distribution installer for Windows or macOS and run it with the default options. (Your facilitator can supply the installer on a USB drive if downloads are slow.) Open Anaconda Navigator and click Launch under JupyterLab , or type jupyter lab in Anaconda Prompt (Windows) or Terminal (macOS). JupyterLab opens in a browser tab, but it runs on your computer . Anaconda already includes pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, statsmodels, scikit-learn and NLTK. You do not need any %pip install lines in Route B; delete them if you copy code from GAP. 2. Copy the course folder ¶ Your facilitator gives you the course folder, DATA300_GAP , as a zip file or on a USB drive. Copy it to your Documents folder and unzip it. Inside are the lecture notebooks and a data folder with every dataset the course uses: penguins.csv , diamonds.csv , tips.csv , mpg.csv , datasaurus_dozen.csv and the NLTK word lists in nltk_data . Keep your own notebooks in the DATA300_GAP folder, next to data . Code then loads files with short paths such as pd.read_csv("data/penguins.csv") . 3. Check that it works ¶ Create a new notebook inside DATA300_GAP and run this cell: import pandas as pd , matplotlib , seaborn , statsmodels , sklearn , nltk penguins = pd . read_csv ( "data/penguins.csv" ) print ( "pandas" , pd . __version__ , "| rows loaded:" , len ( penguins )) If it prints the pandas version and a row count, Route B is ready. A FileNotFoundError means the notebook is not in the same folder as data ; a ModuleNotFoundError means Anaconda did not install fully. Turning GAP code into Route B code ¶ Each guide page gives the Route B code in full. If you adapt GAP's code yourself, make three changes: GAP (Try JupyterLab) Route B (Anaconda) %pip install seaborn Delete the line from pyodide.http import open_url Delete the line pd.read_csv(open_url(url)) pd.read_csv("data/<file>.csv") Tableau Desktop ¶ Go to the Tableau for Students page ( https://www.tableau.com/academic/students ) and request a free licence with your university email address . You may be asked to prove you are a student. The product key arrives by email. Download Tableau Desktop , install it and enter the key. Open Tableau and click Sample – Superstore under Saved Data Sources on the start page. If a blank sheet opens with the Superstore fields listed on the left, Tableau is ready. Do this in the pre-class week: verification can take a day or two, and Activity 1 needs Tableau. Microsoft Excel ¶ Labs 6 and 7, Assignment 3 and the capstone use Excel's What-If Analysis → Data Table , RAND() , NORM.INV() and Data → Forecast Sheet . These are built into Excel for Windows and Excel for Mac (Microsoft 365 or Excel 2016 and later). Excel on the web lacks some of them, so use the desktop program or a lab PC. Open Excel once before Day 5 (Tuesday 17 November) to check it starts. Saving and exporting ¶ Tool Save your working file Export for submission JupyterLab Ctrl + S (Cmd + S on macOS). Route A: also download the .ipynb Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells , check every output, then File → Print → Save as PDF with Background graphics ticked Tableau File → Save As a packaged workbook ( .twbx ) File → Print to PDF (choose Entire workbook when every sheet is needed); or Worksheet → Export → Image and paste the image into Word Excel File → Save As .xlsx File → Save As → PDF , or submit the .xlsx if the task asks for it Always restart and run all before exporting a notebook, so the outputs in the PDF match the code. Combining PDFs without internet ¶ Several tasks ask for one PDF made from two or three parts. Online PDF mergers are often blocked or unreliable, and uploading course work to them is unnecessary. Combine files on your own computer: Word (Windows or macOS): put your written answers in a Word document, then insert the other parts as pictures on new pages ( Insert → Pictures ). Use screenshots or exported images of the notebook and Tableau sheets. Finish with File → Save As → PDF . macOS Preview: open the first PDF, choose View → Thumbnails , drag the next PDF into the sidebar below the last page, repeat, then File → Export as PDF . Adobe Acrobat (the full program, if installed): Tools → Combine Files . Open the final PDF and check that every part is there, in the order the task gives, and that the file has the exact name the task asks for. Submitting on GAP (Moodle) ¶ Open the course on GAP , find the item (for example Activity 1 ) and click Add submission . Upload the file with the required name and click Save changes . If the item has a Submit assignment button, click it; until you do, the work stays a draft. Check that the status reads Submitted for grading and that the file opens. Deadlines are 23:59 China Standard Time . Submit early: GAP can be slow near a deadline. Only use course data Never use private company, customer or personal data in course work.

docs.text: Activity 1: Readiness self-check ¶ A short diagnostic before the course starts: run a ready-made Python analysis of the Palmer Penguins data, build two Tableau charts on the Superstore sample, answer five questions, and submit one combined PDF on GAP. Adapted from the DATA 300 GAP course, Pre-In Class Module, Activity 1. Written in our own words; follow GAP for the official wording. 1. What and why ¶ What you do Run a given Python script in JupyterLab, answer three questions about its output; build two Tableau charts, answer two questions; combine everything into one PDF Why It proves your tools work before the intensive days, when a setup problem would cost a graded lab, and it shows you where your analytics vocabulary needs work CLOs CLO 1 (kinds of analytics), CLO 2 (visual tools), CLO 3 and CLO 4 (the computing groundwork for later labs) Weight 4% Deadline Monday 9 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , on GAP Before you start Read the setup page ; work through the Python and Jupyter refresher You do not write new code for the Python part. The aim is to run code correctly, read its output and describe what you see. 2. Route A: Try JupyterLab and Tableau (as on GAP) ¶ Part 1: Open a notebook ¶ Open Try JupyterLab, start a Python (Pyodide) notebook and rename it with the file name GAP gives (your last name, the course code and "Self_Check"). Part 2: Run the script ¶ Paste GAP's single code block into one cell and run it with Shift + Enter . In outline, the script: installs seaborn into the browser session with %pip ; imports pandas, seaborn and matplotlib, and open_url from pyodide.http ; loads the penguins CSV from the seaborn-data repository on GitHub; shows the first five rows and the summary statistics table ( describe() ); draws a scatter plot of body mass against flipper length, coloured by species; draws a box plot of body mass by island, split by sex. If the data load hangs, see Known pitfalls below. Part 3: Answer the three Python questions ¶ GAP asks about the summary statistics table (a value from the body mass column), the overall pattern in the scatter plot, and which species sits highest in it. Read each answer from your own output , write it in a sentence, and say which table or chart it comes from. Part 4: Export the notebook ¶ Check that both tables and both charts are visible, then File → Print → Save as PDF with Background graphics ticked. Tableau: claim the licence and build two sheets ¶ Claim the student licence, install Tableau Desktop and activate it ( setup ). Open Sample – Superstore from Saved Data Sources . Sheet 1: a horizontal bar chart of total Sales for each Category (Category on Rows, Sales on Columns). Sorting the bars is optional but helps. Sheet 2: a map of Profit by state (double-click the state field, then drag Profit to Color on the Marks card). Blue means profit, orange means a loss. Answer GAP's two Tableau questions: the category with the highest sales, and at least one state making a loss. File → Print to PDF , Entire workbook , so both sheets are included. 3. Route B: offline in Anaconda JupyterLab ¶ Use this route if Try JupyterLab will not load the data, or if you prefer to work on your own laptop. It follows the same steps as GAP's script but loads the bundled copy of the data, so there is nothing to install or download. Create a notebook inside the DATA300_GAP folder (next to data ), paste this into one cell and run it. The questions and the Tableau part are exactly the same as in Route A. # Route B for Activity 1: run offline in Anaconda JupyterLab. # The penguins file comes from the course folder, so nothing is installed or downloaded. import pandas as pd import seaborn as sns import matplotlib.pyplot as plt pd . set_option ( "display.max_columns" , None ) # show every column when printing # Read the bundled penguins table df = pd . read_csv ( "data/penguins.csv" ) print ( "Rows and columns:" , df . shape ) # A first look: five rows, then the numeric summary print ( " \n First five rows:" ) print ( df . head ()) print ( " \n Summary of the numeric columns:" ) print ( df . describe ()) # Chart 1: scatter of flipper length (x) and body mass (y), coloured by species plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) sns . scatterplot ( data = df , x = "flipper_length_mm" , y = "body_mass_g" , hue = "species" , palette = "deep" ) plt . title ( "Flipper length and body mass of each penguin, by species" ) plt . xlabel ( "Flipper length (mm)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Body mass (g)" ) plt . show () # Chart 2: box plot of body mass on each island, one box per sex plt . figure ( figsize = ( 8 , 5 )) sns . boxplot ( data = df , x = "island" , y = "body_mass_g" , hue = "sex" , palette = "pastel" ) plt . title ( "Spread of body mass on each island, female and male" ) plt . xlabel ( "Island" ) plt . ylabel ( "Body mass (g)" ) plt . show () In JupyterLab you may replace the print(df.head()) and print(df.describe()) lines with display(df.head()) and display(df.describe()) for nicer tables; the numbers are the same. Export with Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells , then File → Print → Save as PDF . 4. Checks you can make ¶ These tell you whether your output is right without giving any answers away. The data has 344 rows and 7 columns : species , island , three body measurements, body_mass_g and sex . In the summary table, the count row is lower than 344 for the measurement columns. Some penguins have missing measurements, and describe() quietly leaves them out. That is expected. describe() lists only the four numeric columns. Species, island and sex do not appear, because they are text. The scatter plot has three colours , one per species, and a legend. The box plot has three islands along the bottom and two boxes (male and female) on each where both sexes were measured. Your answers say which table or chart each one comes from, and the body mass answer has its unit (grams). In Tableau, Sheet 1 has three bars (one per category) and Sheet 2 shows a map of the United States with the states coloured on a blue–orange scale. 5. Known pitfalls and fixes ¶ Problem Cause Fix The cell hangs or ends with a network error GitHub is slow or blocked Drag penguins.csv from the course folder into Try JupyterLab's file browser and use pd.read_csv("penguins.csv") in place of the open_url line, or switch to Route B ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'seaborn' in Try JupyterLab The %pip install line did not run in this session Run the whole cell again from the top; every new Try JupyterLab session needs it ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyodide' in Anaconda GAP's browser-only code was pasted into Route B Use the Route B code above, which has no pyodide line FileNotFoundError: data/penguins.csv The notebook is not in the DATA300_GAP folder Save the notebook inside DATA300_GAP , next to data , and run again A UserWarning mentioning palette or missing values seaborn is telling you about rows it skipped Not an error; your charts are still correct Charts print in grey or are missing from the PDF Background graphics was off, or the cells were not run before printing Tick Background graphics ; restart and run all, then print The notebook vanished from Try JupyterLab The browser's storage was cleared, or you used another browser Always export the PDF and download the .ipynb before closing the tab No field called State/Province in Tableau Older Tableau versions call it State Use whichever state field your version shows The map shows only a few dots, or none Tableau did not recognise the field as geographic Right-click the state field → Geographic Role → State/Province ; check the country is the United States Print to PDF is missing from the File menu Some Tableau versions on macOS Use File → Print and choose Save as PDF , or export each sheet as an image and paste it into Word GAP's instructions give two different names for the notebook PDF, and mention both a Markdown cell and a Word document for answers Inconsistent wording The intermediate names do not matter once the files are merged. What counts is one PDF containing all five answers, the notebook output and the Tableau sheets, named as GAP's final instruction says. Ask your facilitator if unsure 6. Beyond the activity ¶ Optional, not graded. Try these in the same notebook if you finish early: Count the missing values in every column with df.isnull().sum() . Which column has the most, and why might sex be harder to record than a measurement? Make a table of how many penguins of each species were measured on each island with pd.crosstab(df["island"], df["species"]) . Does every species live on every island? What does that mean for comparing islands in the box plot? Plot bill length against bill depth, first without colour, then with hue="species" . Describe how the overall pattern changes once species is shown. (This is a preview of confounding, from Day 1.) In Tableau, add Profit to the colour of the Sales by Category bars. Is the category with the most sales also the most profitable? 7. Submission ¶ File Contents Answers Your five answers in full sentences, each naming the table or chart it comes from Notebook PDF The executed notebook with both tables and both charts visible Tableau PDF Both sheets ( Entire workbook ) Final file The three parts combined, answers first, named YourLastName_DATA300_Week1_Readiness.pdf Combine the three PDFs offline with Word, macOS Preview or Acrobat, as described in Combining PDFs without internet . Open the combined file and check that all three parts are present and readable. Upload it to Activity 1 on GAP and submit before Monday 9 November, 23:59 China Standard Time ( how to submit ).
