docs.text: Assignment 1: Descriptive analytics report ¶ Your first written analytics report. You run a given Python script on a restaurant's transaction records (bills, tips, party sizes, days and shifts), which prints two summary tables and draws three figures, and you turn what they show into a four-section business report for the restaurant's owner. You submit the report and the executed notebook as one PDF on GAP. Adapted from the DATA 300 GAP course, In-Class Module 1, Assignment 1: Data Visualization and Descriptive Analytics Report. Written in our own words; follow GAP for the official wording. 1. What and why ¶ What you do Run GAP's script (no coding of your own is required), read Table 1, Table 2 and Figures 1–3, and write a report under four fixed headings with two recommendations Why You play an analyst at a consulting firm, Bistro Analytics . The owner wants to schedule staff for the busiest periods and to understand tipping well enough to train servers in upselling. The skill being graded is turning tables and charts into evidence-based, specific advice CLOs CLO 1 (how descriptive analytics supports decisions), CLO 2 (visualisations that communicate findings), CLO 3 (computational methods to organise and analyse data) Weight 6% Deadline Sunday 15 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , on GAP (briefing and studio in periods 9 and 10 of Day 2; finish over the weekend) Before you start Visualising and communicating data (Parts 1, 5 and 6) and Tableau concepts and dashboards , Part 10, which practises reading a box plot and a regression line The data has one row per restaurant bill (a transaction): total_bill and tip in US dollars , the server's sex , whether the party included a smoker , the day ( Thur , Fri , Sat , Sun ), the time ( Lunch or Dinner ) and the party size (number of diners). 2. Route A: Try JupyterLab (as on GAP) ¶ Part 1: Open and name a notebook ¶ Open Try JupyterLab, start a Python (Pyodide) notebook and rename it YourLastName_DATA300_Assignment1.ipynb . Part 2: Run the script ¶ Paste GAP's whole script into the first cell and press Shift + Enter . In outline, it: installs seaborn, pandas and matplotlib with %pip , and loads tips.csv from GitHub with open_url ; prints Table 1 : the mean bill, mean tip and mean party size for each day; prints Table 2 : the total of all bills for each shift (Lunch and Dinner); draws Figure 1 : a bar chart of total bills by day; draws Figure 2 : a box plot of tips for each shift; draws Figure 3 : a scatter plot of tip against bill, with a fitted (OLS) regression line and a shaded band. Check that both tables and all three figures appear before you start writing. Part 3: Write the report ¶ Write the report in Word (or Markdown) using GAP's four headings exactly ; see How to write the report below. Use paragraphs, except for the two recommendations, which are bullet points. Part 4: Export ¶ Run the notebook from the top, then File → Print → Save as PDF with Background graphics ticked, named YourLastName_Jupyter.pdf . Save the report as YourLastName_Report.pdf . See Submission below. How to write the report ¶ The four headings, exactly as GAP gives them, in this order: 1. Executive Summary , 2. Descriptive Data Overview , 3. Visual Insights & Graphical Trends , 4. Strategic Business Recommendations . What goes under each: Executive Summary : one paragraph. The client's objective, who you are (Bistro Analytics), the data analysed (the tips dataset and its number of transactions; check the count with len(df) ), and the two operational goals: scheduling staff for peak demand, and growing revenue while keeping good servers. Lead with your main finding and what you recommend, in one or two sentences (the finding-first rule from the morning lecture). Descriptive Data Overview : one or two paragraphs. From Table 1 , which day has the highest average bill and which the highest average tip, with the values. From Table 2 , total revenue for Lunch and for Dinner and how far apart they are. Visual Insights & Graphical Trends : two or three paragraphs, one per figure. Figure 1 : compare the weekday days in the data with the weekend days and name the peak days. Figure 2 : compare the medians and interquartile ranges of tips at Lunch and Dinner, discuss what that means for a server's earnings, and comment on the points beyond the upper whiskers. Figure 3 : describe the slope and direction of the regression line and what it suggests for upselling. Strategic Business Recommendations : two detailed bullet points. Recommendation 1 (staffing): which days and shifts should get the strongest servers, and why. Recommendation 2 (upselling and training): a concrete programme justified by the bill-to-tip relationship, explaining how a higher bill benefits both the restaurant and the server. Evidence and numbers. Every claim should point to a table or figure and carry a number with its unit: Weak Strong "[Day] is busy." Assignment 2: Predictive data mining report ¶ Your second written analytics report. You run GAP's Python code, which generates 500 synthetic house sales, draws two exploratory charts, turns each agent's written description into a Text Appeal Score with sentiment analysis, and fits a multiple linear regression that predicts the sale price. You then explain what it found to a real-estate firm's board in a five-section report, and submit the report and the executed notebook as one PDF on GAP. Adapted from the DATA 300 GAP course, In-Class Module 2, Assignment 2: Predictive Data Mining Report. Written in our own words; follow GAP for the official wording. 1. What and why ¶ What you do Run GAP's two code blocks (no coding of your own is required; one line needs a fix, see Known pitfalls ), read the data snapshot, the two charts, the text-mining table, the test R² and RMSE, and the coefficient table, and write a report under GAP's five headings Why You play the lead data miner at UrbanTrend Real Estate Analytics , which wants an automated way to estimate a home's market value. Each row has the floor area ( SqFt , square feet), the number of Bedrooms , the Age of the home in years, the agent's Description , and the sale Price in US dollars . 2. How to write the report ¶ The five headings, exactly as GAP gives them, in this order: Executive Summary , Exploratory Data Analysis , Text Mining Methodology & Value , Predictive Analytics Results , Strategic Recommendations . Write in paragraphs , not bullet lists, except for the two recommendations. What goes under each: Executive Summary : one paragraph. The project's purpose, the two kinds of data (structured facts about each home; unstructured agent descriptions) and what the predictive model is for. Exploratory Data Analysis : one or two paragraphs on the two charts. The relationship between floor area and price (direction, form, strength, scatter). From the box plot: whether more bedrooms always means a higher median price, and how the spread of prices (box heights) changes from 2 to 5 bedrooms. Text Mining Methodology & Value : one or two paragraphs. What the text-mining step did, in words an executive understands: how a sentence became a number, what the score's range means, and why a pricing model needs text turned into a number at all. Describe the scores your table actually shows for each kind of description (see Known pitfalls : GAP's wording assumes the fallback scorer's results). Predictive Analytics Results : two paragraphs. Accuracy : the test R² and what it says about predicting homes the model has not seen; the RMSE in dollars and what "typical error" means. Business drivers : the coefficient for one extra bedroom and for one more year of age, in dollars, each with its holding-constant clause. The value of text : what a one-unit change in the Text Appeal Score is worth in dollars according to your coefficient, remembering that the score runs from −1 to +1. Strategic Recommendations : two bullet points of actionable advice to agents, each backed by a specific number from your output. Evidence and numbers. Every claim should point to a chart or table and carry a number with its unit: Weak Strong "The model is accurate." "On the 100 test homes it had not seen, the model's R² was [value]: it accounts for about [X]% of the variation in their prices. Its RMSE of $[value] means a typical prediction misses by roughly that amount." "Bedrooms add value." "Holding floor area, age and the text score constant, each additional bedroom is associated with about $[value] [more / less] in predicted price (coefficient table)." "Good descriptions are worth a lot." "The Text Appeal Score coefficient is $[value] per unit. Moving from a neutral description (0) to a highly positive one (+1) is associated with about $[value] in predicted price, other features held constant." The brackets are placeholders: fill them from your own output , and only with what it shows. Reading coefficients correctly (Predictive regression lecture, Parts 3 and 12): Each coefficient has its own unit : dollars per square foot, per bedroom, per year of age, per one unit of the text score. GAP's table puts a $ on all of them, but they are not all "per one thing" of the same kind. Each holds the other features constant : say so. A coefficient describes how prices differ between homes in this data, not what would happen if an agent changed something. Think about this before advising agents to rewrite descriptions (Text as a feature, Part 5). R² is not a percentage of correct predictions, and RMSE is a typical error size, not a guaranteed margin (Predictive regression, Part 6). Recommendations that are actionable. Each says who does what , why (citing your evidence) and how you would know it worked . Stay within what the data supports, and say so where it limits the advice (the data is synthetic; it has no location, no market timing, and only a few kinds of description). 3. docs.text: Assignment 3: Simulation decision model ¶ Your graded spreadsheet simulation. For a company launching a new smart thermostat, you simulate twelve months of demand with random market volatility in Excel, compare two marketing strategies month by month, freeze the simulation, chart the two monthly profit lines in Tableau, and write a short executive report on which strategy to choose and why simulation is safer than a single fixed forecast. Adapted from the DATA 300 GAP course, In-Class Module 2, Assignment 3: Spreadsheet Simulation and Decision Model. Written in our own words; follow GAP for the official wording and figures. 1. What and why ¶ What you do Build a 12-month simulation table in Excel with RANDBETWEEN , lock it with Paste Special → Values, build a two-line profit chart in Tableau, and write a report answering two questions with the chart included Why You are an analytics planner at SmartHome Tech . Earlier data mining gave a baseline monthly demand, a range of random monthly swings and a fixed profit margin per unit. The company must choose between a standard and an aggressive marketing strategy, which differ in fixed monthly cost and in how much they lift demand. The assignment practises building a decision model under uncertainty, moving frozen results into a visual tool, and recommending a strategy from the evidence CLOs CLO 3 (computational problem-solving applied to a business scenario), CLO 4 (a predictive simulation model that projects outcomes), CLO 5 (evaluating what the results mean for a strategic decision) Weight 6% Deadline Sunday 22 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , on GAP (briefed in period 6 of Day 6; support in periods 7 and 8 of Day 7) Before you start Simulation under uncertainty , Parts 2, 6, 7, 8, 10 and 13; Tableau concepts and dashboards ; and BI strategy, forecasting and ethics , Parts 14 and 16 Use GAP's figures for the baseline, the volatility range, the margin, the two marketing costs and the demand multiplier. All money is in US dollars , as on GAP. 2. Route A: Excel and Tableau (as on GAP) ¶ Part 1: The simulation in Excel ¶ Open a blank workbook and save it with GAP's file name (your last name, the course code and "Assignment3", as .xlsx ). Headers. Type GAP's seven headers in A1:G1 : month, baseline demand, market volatility, standard demand, aggressive demand, standard profit and aggressive profit, spelt exactly as GAP gives them (with underscores). Month and baseline. Type 1 to 12 in A2:A13 , and GAP's baseline demand in every cell of B2:B13 . Volatility. In C2 type GAP's RANDBETWEEN formula, with GAP's lower and upper limits, and fill it down to C13 . RANDBETWEEN returns a whole number, and both limits can occur (Day 5, Part 7). Demand. In D2 , standard demand is baseline plus volatility. In E2 , aggressive demand is GAP's formula: the same demand times GAP's multiplier, rounded to a whole unit with ROUND(…, 0) . Fill both down to row 13. Profit. In F2 and G2 , type GAP's two profit formulas: demand × the margin per unit, minus that strategy's fixed monthly marketing cost. Fill both down to row 13. Press F9 a few times (Mac: Fn + F9 or Cmd + = ) and watch every month change. Part 2: Lock the simulation ¶ RANDBETWEEN recalculates whenever the workbook changes or opens, so the numbers you write about would no longer be the numbers in the file (Chapter 7, section 7.3; Day 5, Part 8). Select A1:G13 and copy ( Ctrl + C , Mac Cmd + C ). With the selection still in place, right-click A1 → Paste Special → Values (the clipboard icon marked 123 ). On Windows, Ctrl + Alt + V , then V , then Enter does the same. Click any cell in C2:G13: the formula bar should now show a number , not a formula. Press F9: nothing should change. Save and close Excel before you open Tableau. Part 3: The Tableau view ¶ Open Tableau Desktop. Under Connect , choose Microsoft Excel and open your saved workbook. On the data-source page, the Excel sheet ( Sheet1 ) should appear on the canvas. If it does not, drag it there. Then click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom to open a worksheet. Drag Month to the Columns shelf. Tableau treats it as a measure (a green SUM(Month) pill). Right-click the pill and choose Dimension , so each month becomes its own position on the axis. Drag Measure Values (at the bottom of the Data pane) to the Rows shelf. A Measure Values card appears below the Marks card, listing every numeric field. Remove every entry except the standard profit and aggressive profit sums (drag each other pill off the card, or right-click → Remove ). Tableau may show the field names with spaces instead of underscores. On the Marks card, change Automatic to Line . Drag Measure Names onto Color on the Marks card, so each strategy has its own colour and a legend appears. Worksheet → Export → Image… , save it as PNG or JPEG, and insert it into a blank Word document. Part 4: The executive report ¶ In the Word document with your chart, write a short executive report answering GAP's two questions: Strategic decision: from your chart, which strategy gives the higher and more consistent profit over the twelve months; and, in your simulation, whether there were any months in which the aggressive strategy did worse than the standard one because of its higher fixed cost in a weak month. Answer from your own frozen data; check any month you mention against the Excel table. The value of simulation: from a manager's point of view, why putting random volatility into the forecast is safer for planning than assuming exactly the baseline demand every month. Write for a manager: lead with your answer, give numbers with units and the month they come from, and keep the evidence and your judgement separate (Day 6, Part 14). 3. Route B: a Python mirror (offline) ¶ The graded products are an Excel workbook and a Tableau chart, so there is no Python route that replaces them. The block below mirrors Part 1 in numpy, so you can check that your columns follow the right rules, and draws the two profit lines as a preview of the Tableau view. Run it in Anaconda JupyterLab from the DATA300_GAP folder (it reads no files). Your Excel numbers will differ from these: RANDBETWEEN has no seed, while the mirror uses a fixed one so it prints the same months every run. Change the seed to see other possible years. Answer the report questions from your Excel simulation, not from this mirror. # Route B mirror for Assignment 3: GAP's simulation in numpy, plus a preview chart. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import matplotlib.pyplot as plt # GAP's inputs (money in US dollars) baseline = 1000 # units per month swing = 150 # RANDBETWEEN(-150, 150) margin = 100 # profit per unit cost_standard , cost_aggressive = 10_000 , 25_000 # fixed marketing per month multiplier = 1.4 # aggressive demand lift rng = np . random . default_rng ( 2026 ) # Excel has no seed; change this number to see another year sim = pd . DataFrame ({ "Month" : np . arange ( 1 , 13 ), "Baseline_Demand" : baseline }) sim [ "Market_Volatility" ] = rng . integers ( - swing , swing + 1 , size = 12 ) # +1: integers() excludes its top sim [ "Standard_Demand" ] = sim [ "Baseline_Demand" ] + sim [ "Market_Volatility" ] # Excel's ROUND rounds halves away from zero and numpy rounds halves to even; # here 1.4 x a whole number never ends in exactly .5, so the two agree. sim [ "Aggressive_Demand" ] = np . round ( sim [ "Standard_Demand" ] * multiplier ) . astype ( int ) sim [ "Standard_Profit" ] = sim [ "Standard_Demand" ] * margin - cost_standard sim [ "Aggressive_Profit" ] = sim [ "Aggressive_Demand" ] * margin - cost_aggressive print ( sim . to_string ( index = False )) # Rule checks: the same checks as section 4 of the guide assert sim [ "Market_Volatility" ] . between ( - swing , swing ) . all () assert ( sim [ "Aggressive_Demand" ] == np . round ( sim [ "Standard_Demand" ] * multiplier )) . all () print ( " \n All rule checks passed." ) # Preview of the Tableau view: Month as a dimension, two measures, line marks, colour by measure fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) ax . plot ( sim [ "Month" ], sim [ "Standard_Profit" ], marker = "o" , color = "#0072B2" , label = "Standard_Profit" ) ax . plot ( sim [ "Month" ], sim [ "Aggressive_Profit" ], marker = "o" , color = "#D55E00" , label = "Aggressive_Profit" ) ax . set_xticks ( sim [ "Month" ]) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Profit (US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Simulated monthly profit by strategy (one possible year)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () # To open this mirror in Tableau for practice, save it (needs openpyxl, included in Anaconda): # sim.to_excel("Assignment3_python_practice.xlsx", index=False) 4. Checks you can make ¶ These tell you whether your work is right without giving any answers away. Row 1 holds GAP's seven headers, spelt as GAP gives them, and rows 2 to 13 hold months 1 to 12. Every baseline cell holds GAP's baseline, and every volatility value is a whole number within GAP's limits. Standard demand = baseline + volatility in every row. Aggressive demand = standard demand × GAP's multiplier, rounded to a whole number , in every row. Each profit = that row's demand × the margin − that strategy's fixed cost. Check one row by hand. After Paste Special, clicking any cell in C2:G13 shows a number in the formula bar, and F9 changes nothing. The workbook was saved and closed before you connected Tableau, and the values in your chart match the table in Excel for at least two months you checked. Your Tableau chart has 12 points on each line, two lines, and a legend naming the two profit measures, and no other measure appears on the Measure Values card. Every month you mention in the report can be found in your frozen Excel table. Your answer to question 2 is about planning decisions (staffing, stock, cash, budgets), not just a definition of randomness. 5. Known pitfalls and fixes ¶ Problem Cause Fix The numbers in your report do not match the file you submitted The simulation was not frozen, so it recalculated when you saved or reopened Paste Special → Values over A1:G13 before writing (Part 2). If it is already too late, freeze now and rewrite the numbers from the frozen table Paste Special pasted formulas again, or #REF! appeared Paste (or Paste Special → All ) was chosen instead of Values , or the selection moved before pasting Undo, select A1:G13, copy, right-click A1 and choose Values (123) Tableau shows one point or one bar, not twelve Month is still a measure, so Tableau adds all twelve months into one SUM(Month) Right-click the Month pill → Dimension Many lines, or a line for the month or the demand columns The Measure Values card still lists other measures Remove every pill from the Measure Values card except the two profits One line only, in one colour Measure Names is not on Color Drag Measure Names onto Color on the Marks card Bars or shapes instead of lines The mark type is Automatic Choose Line on the Marks card Tableau cannot open the workbook, or shows old values The file was still open in Excel, or Tableau connected before you saved the frozen version Save, close Excel, then in Tableau Data → Refresh (or reconnect) No Measure Values field in the Data pane It appears at the bottom of the Data pane, below the other fields Scroll down the Data pane; or double-click one profit measure and then drag the other onto the same axis The field names show spaces instead of underscores Tableau tidies field names automatically Nothing to fix: Standard Profit in Tableau is your Standard_Profit column Some aggressive demands have decimals ROUND(…, 0) was left out of the aggressive-demand formula Use GAP's formula with ROUND , then freeze again Volatility never reaches the limits Not an error: with only 12 draws the extremes are unlikely Leave it; RANDBETWEEN can return both limits F9 does nothing on a Mac The function keys control brightness or volume Fn + F9 , or Cmd + = The exported image is blank or cut off The view was exported before it finished drawing, or the window was small Enlarge the worksheet, wait for the chart, then Worksheet → Export → Image… again Your report's answer matches a classmate's exactly Each simulation is different Write from your chart and table; a classmate's months are not your evidence 6. Beyond the assignment ¶ Optional, not graded. Do these in a copy of your workbook, after you have frozen the graded one. Many years, not one. Keep the formulas live in a copy and add a summary row: total annual profit for each strategy. Use a one-way Data Table with an empty input cell (Day 5, Part 9) to recalculate it 200 times, and describe the spread of each strategy's annual total. A normal swing. Replace RANDBETWEEN with NORM.INV(RAND(), 0, 75) rounded to whole units. How does the shape of monthly demand change, and does it change your conclusion? A seasonal baseline. Thermostats sell more before winter and summer. Replace the flat baseline with a seasonal one (for example 20% above the average in four months and 20% below in four others, with the same annual total) and describe how the monthly lines change. Uncertain lift. Make the multiplier itself uncertain (for example between 1.1 and 1.6) and compare the risk of the two strategies (Day 5, Part 10). A dashboard. In Tableau, add a second sheet with each strategy's monthly profit as a bar and a reference line at zero, and combine both sheets in a dashboard with a short message title. Write the recommendation. Turn your report into a one-page memo in the structure of Day 6, Part 14, with one condition that would change your recommendation. 7. Submission ¶ File Contents Workbook The frozen simulation (values, not formulas), saved with GAP's file name ( YourLastName_DATA300_Assignment3.xlsx ) Report Your executive report with the Tableau image included, saved as YourLastName_Assignment3_Report.pdf Check that the workbook holds values only (click a few cells in C2:G13) and that your report's numbers match it. Insert the exported Tableau image into the Word document before saving, so the report is one PDF. If you must combine separate files, do it offline ( Combining PDFs without internet ). Save the report from Word with File → Save As → PDF . Upload both files to Assignment 3 on GAP and submit before Sunday 22 November, 23:59 China Standard Time ( how to submit ).

DataFrame ({ "Month" : np . arange ( 1 , 13 ), "Baseline_Demand" : baseline }) sim [ "Market_Volatility" ] = rng . integers ( - swing , swing + 1 , size = 12 ) # +1: integers() excludes its top sim [ "Standard_Demand" ] = sim [ "Baseline_Demand" ] + sim [ "Market_Volatility" ] # Excel's ROUND rounds halves away from zero and numpy rounds halves to even; # here 1.4 x a whole number never ends in exactly .5, so the two agree. sim [ "Aggressive_Demand" ] = np . round ( sim [ "Standard_Demand" ] * multiplier ) . astype ( int ) sim [ "Standard_Profit" ] = sim [ "Standard_Demand" ] * margin - cost_standard sim [ "Aggressive_Profit" ] = sim [ "Aggressive_Demand" ] * margin - cost_aggressive print ( sim . to_string ( index = False )) # Rule checks: the same checks as section 4 of the guide assert sim [ "Market_Volatility" ] . between ( - swing , swing ) . all () assert ( sim [ "Aggressive_Demand" ] == np . round ( sim [ "Standard_Demand" ] * multiplier )) . all () print ( " \n All rule checks passed." ) # Preview of the Tableau view: Month as a dimension, two measures, line marks, colour by measure fig , ax = plt . subplots ( figsize = ( 8 , 4 )) ax . plot ( sim [ "Month" ], sim [ "Standard_Profit" ], marker = "o" , color = "#0072B2" , label = "Standard_Profit" ) ax . plot ( sim [ "Month" ], sim [ "Aggressive_Profit" ], marker = "o" , color = "#D55E00" , label = "Aggressive_Profit" ) ax . set_xticks ( sim [ "Month" ]) ax . set_xlabel ( "Month" ) ax . set_ylabel ( "Profit (US dollars)" ) ax . set_title ( "Simulated monthly profit by strategy (one possible year)" ) ax . legend ( frameon = False ) plt . show () # To open this mirror in Tableau for practice, save it (needs openpyxl, included in Anaconda): # sim.to_excel("Assignment3_python_practice.xlsx", index=False)

docs.text: Assignment 4: Capstone ¶ The course's final project, worth a quarter of your grade. For an electronics company about to sign a five-year manufacturing contract, you turn five focus-group comments into a demand multiplier in Python, build a five-year profit model for two suppliers in Excel, chart the choice in Tableau, and write the board a recommendation that weighs profit against ethics. Adapted from the DATA 300 GAP course, Post-Class Module, Assignment 4: Final Comprehensive Assignment (Capstone). Written in our own words; follow GAP for the official wording, figures and rubric. 1. What and why ¶ What you do Score five focus-group comments with VADER and turn their average into a demand multiplier (JupyterLab); apply it to a five-year demand plan and compute profit under two suppliers (Excel); chart both profit paths by year (Tableau); write an executive summary that answers GAP's two questions (Word, saved as PDF) Why You are the lead BI analyst at EcoVate , which is launching a smart-home energy manager. Before it signs the contract, the executive team wants to know how well the product will sell, judging by what focus groups said, and whether to use a cheaper standard overseas manufacturer with a record of carbon-emission violations or a costlier Fair-Trade Green Certified one. The capstone practises the whole chain of the course: text → number → model → chart → recommendation CLOs CLO 4 (a predictive model that projects outcomes: the sentiment-adjusted demand and the profit model), CLO 5 (evaluating BI tools in a case and writing a managerial report that weighs ethical and societal context) Weight 25% Deadline Sunday 29 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , on GAP (launched in period 5 of Day 7; studio in periods 6–8) Before you start Course review and integration , Parts 4–6 and 11; Text mining , Parts 6–9; Simulation under uncertainty , Parts 2–3; BI strategy, forecasting and ethics , Parts 12 and 14 Use GAP's figures for the five-year base demand, the selling price, the fixed cost and the two suppliers' unit costs. All money is in US dollars , as on GAP. Read GAP's capstone rubric before you start: everyone works from the same inputs, so the quality of your reasoning is what sets your report apart. The studio afternoon (Day 7, periods 5–8) ¶ Use the afternoon to get every tool step done and checked while help is in the room, and leave the writing for the post-class week. Each checkpoint is something you can show your facilitator. Period Goal Checkpoint P5 13:45–14:30 Launch: read sections 1, 4 and 5 of this guide; choose Route A or Route B; run the text-mining step 1. The notebook runs from the top; you have written down the multiplier exactly as printed and which scorer produced it (see section 5); the notebook PDF is exported P6 14:40–15:25 Build the Excel model 2. Six columns and five years; every check in section 4 for the workbook passes; the file is saved as .xlsx and closed P7 15:40–16:25 Build the Tableau chart 3. Two series, one point or bar per year, a currency axis and a legend; the image is exported and pasted into a Word document P8 16:35–17:20 Plan the report (and get help with Assignments 2 and 3 if needed) 4. An outline: a two-sentence introduction; for question 1, your answer, the evidence you will quote (with the cell it comes from), the trade-off and one condition; for question 2, three reasons the three-tool chain beats a static spreadsheet After Day 7, aim for a full draft by the middle of the post-class week, so you have time to cut it down and check every number against your workbook before Sunday 29 November . 2. Route A: Try JupyterLab, Excel and Tableau (as on GAP) ¶ Part 1: Text mining in Try JupyterLab ¶ Open Try JupyterLab, start a Python (Pyodide) notebook and rename it with the file name GAP gives (your last name, the course code and "Capstone", as .ipynb ). Paste GAP's single code block into a cell and run it. In outline, it: installs pandas and NLTK into the browser session with %pip ; tries to download NLTK's VADER lexicon with nltk.download and create the VADER analyser, and if anything goes wrong, quietly switches to a small keyword-based stand-in scorer that gives one of three fixed scores depending on a few words; puts the five focus-group comments in a DataFrame; scores each comment and stores the compound score; averages the five scores and turns the average into a demand multiplier : 1, plus the average score times 0.20, so a fully positive average would add at most 20% to demand; shows the table and prints the average and the multiplier to three decimal places. Add one cell under GAP's cell and run print(type(analyzer).__name__) . It prints the name of the scorer that actually ran: SentimentIntensityAnalyzer is VADER; anything else is the stand-in. Keep this cell in your PDF. Write the multiplier down exactly as printed (three decimals). Export: File → Print → Save as PDF , with GAP's file name for the notebook PDF. Part 2: The financial model in Excel ¶ Open a blank workbook and save it with GAP's file name (your last name, the course code and "Capstone", as .xlsx ). Headers. Type GAP's six headers in A1:F1 : Year , Base_Demand , Colab_Multiplier , Adjusted_Demand , Standard_Profit , Ethical_Profit . (The third header is a leftover from an older version that used Google Colab; see section 5.) Years and base demand. Type 1 to 5 in A2:A6 and GAP's five base-demand figures in B2:B6 . Multiplier. Type your multiplier, as printed, into C2:C6 (the same value in all five cells). Adjusted demand. In D2 , type GAP's formula: base demand times the multiplier, rounded to a whole unit with ROUND(…, 0) . Fill it down to D6 . Profit. In E2 and F2 , type GAP's two profit formulas: adjusted demand times that supplier's margin per unit (the selling price minus that supplier's unit cost), minus the yearly fixed cost. Fill both down to row 6. Optionally format E2:F6 as Currency (Home → Number Format). Save, then close Excel before you open Tableau. Part 3: The chart in Tableau ¶ Open Tableau Desktop. Under Connect , choose Microsoft Excel and open your saved workbook. Drag the sheet onto the canvas if it is not there already, then click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom. Drag Year to Columns . Tableau makes it a green SUM(Year) pill; right-click it and choose Dimension . Drag Measure Values (at the bottom of the Data pane) to Rows . On the Measure Values card below the Marks card, remove every measure except the sums of Standard Profit and Ethical Profit . On the Marks card, choose Line or Bar , and drag Measure Names onto Color . Format the vertical axis as currency (see section 5 for the menu path). Worksheet → Export → Image… , save the image and insert it into a blank Word document. Part 4: The managerial report ¶ In the Word document that holds your chart, write a short executive summary: a brief introduction, then your answers to GAP's two questions. Strategic and ethical recommendation (CLO 5). GAP asks you to assume that the focus groups showed the target customers care a great deal about a company's carbon footprint, and to recommend one supply chain to the board, weighing how large the profit difference is against the ethical context and the long-term value of the brand. The value of an integrated BI chain. GAP asks why moving from text mining to a spreadsheet model to a visual story gives a sounder, more realistic plan than a static spreadsheet alone. Use the structure from Day 6, Part 14 and Day 7, Part 6: answer first, the evidence with its numbers, the trade-off stated in plain units, the conditions and limits. Part 5: Submit ¶ See section 7. 3. Route B: offline in Anaconda JupyterLab ¶ Use this route if %pip or the NLTK download fails in Try JupyterLab, or if you prefer your own laptop. It scores the same five comments with real VADER , reading the lexicon from the course folder ( data/nltk_data ), and it stops with an error instead of switching to a stand-in scorer if the lexicon cannot be found. Create a notebook inside the DATA300_GAP folder (next to data ), named as in Route A. The five comments are bundled in data/ecovate_focus_group.csv . # Route B for the capstone, Part 1: VADER offline, no downloads and no silent fallback. from pathlib import Path import nltk import pandas as pd NLTK_DIR = Path ( "data/nltk_data" ) . resolve () nltk . data . path . insert ( 0 , str ( NLTK_DIR )) from nltk.sentiment.vader import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer analyzer = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () # raises an error if the lexicon is missing: no silent fallback print ( "Scorer used:" , type ( analyzer ) . __name__ , "| NLTK" , nltk . __version__ ) # The five focus-group comments from GAP, bundled with the course df = pd . read_csv ( "data/ecovate_focus_group.csv" ) assert len ( df ) == 5 , "expected five comments" # Score each comment: the compound score runs from -1 (very negative) to +1 (very positive) df [ "Sentiment_Score" ] = df [ "Review_Text" ] . apply ( lambda text : analyzer . polarity_scores ( text )[ "compound" ]) # GAP's rule: baseline demand 1.0, plus up to 0.20 for a fully positive average avg_sentiment = df [ "Sentiment_Score" ] . mean () demand_multiplier = 1.0 + avg_sentiment * 0.20 pd . set_option ( "display.max_colwidth" , 100 ) print ( df [[ "Review_ID" , "Review_Text" , "Sentiment_Score" ]] . to_string ( index = False )) print ( f " \n Average sentiment score: { avg_sentiment : .3f } " ) print ( f "Demand multiplier (type this, as printed, into Excel C2:C6): { demand_multiplier : .3f } " ) In JupyterLab you may replace the print(... .to_string(index=False)) line with display(df) for a nicer table. Build the Excel workbook by hand as in Route A, Part 2: Route B covers only the text-mining step. Export the notebook with Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells , then File → Print → Save as PDF . 4. Checks you can make ¶ These tell you whether your work is right without giving any answers away. Notebook The table has five rows , one per comment, and every score lies between −1 and +1 . Your PDF shows which scorer ran (VADER's SentimentIntensityAnalyzer or a stand-in). The multiplier lies between 0.8 and 1.2 , as GAP's rule allows, and equals 1 + 0.20 × the printed average (check it on a calculator). Every score and the average are visible in the PDF, not cut off. Workbook Row 1 holds six headers; rows 2 to 6 hold years 1 to 5 and GAP's five base-demand figures. C2:C6 all hold the same multiplier, exactly as your notebook printed it. Every adjusted demand is a whole number , and equals base demand × multiplier rounded. Each profit = adjusted demand × that supplier's margin − the fixed cost. Check one row by hand for each supplier. Clicking D2, E2 or F2 shows a formula in the formula bar, not a typed number. Chart Five years on the horizontal axis, two series, and a legend that names the two profit measures; nothing else on the Measure Values card. The vertical axis shows dollar signs. The values in the chart match your workbook for at least two years you checked (hover over a mark). Report The introduction says what was decided and how, in two or three sentences. Your answer to question 1 names one supply chain, quotes numbers from your workbook, states how big the profit difference is in plain terms, and weighs it against the ethical and brand context. Your answer to question 2 explains what each tool added that a static spreadsheet could not, not just what each tool is. You say which scorer produced your multiplier, and you note at least one limit of scoring five short comments. 5. Known pitfalls and fixes ¶ Problem Cause Fix A header called Colab_Multiplier , though the course does not use Colab GAP's header list is a leftover from a version that used Google Colab Any clear header works (for example Demand_Multiplier ), as long as you use the same name in Tableau . Keeping GAP's header is simplest: it matches GAP's instructions and Tableau shows it as Colab Multiplier Your multiplier differs from a classmate's GAP's code silently switches to a stand-in keyword scorer if nltk.download fails, as it may in the browser or behind a blocked network, and the stand-in gives different scores from VADER Add print(type(analyzer).__name__) (Route A, Part 1 step 3) or use Route B. Carry your multiplier consistently through Excel, Tableau and the report, and say in the report which scorer produced it. If you are unsure which to use, ask your facilitator nltk.download hangs or fails offline No internet access, or GitHub is blocked Use Route B: the lexicon is already in data/nltk_data and nothing is downloaded %pip errors in Anaconda %pip install lines are for the browser session Delete them in Route B; Anaconda already has pandas and NLTK NameError: name 'display' is not defined display exists only inside Jupyter Run the code in a notebook, or use print(df.to_string(index=False)) FileNotFoundError for data/ecovate_focus_group.csv The notebook is not in the DATA300_GAP folder Save the notebook next to the data folder, or fix the path Adjusted demand differs by one unit from a classmate's Different numbers of decimals in the multiplier Type the multiplier exactly as printed (three decimals) in all five cells; do not paste a longer unrounded value Adjusted demand has decimals ROUND(…, 0) left out Use GAP's formula with ROUND Only C2 holds the multiplier and later rows show zero demand C3:C6 were left empty Fill the multiplier into every cell of C2:C6 Tableau shows one bar or point instead of five Year is a measure, so Tableau adds the five years together into SUM(Year) Right-click the Year pill → Dimension Extra lines or bars (base demand, the multiplier, adjusted demand) The Measure Values card still lists every measure Remove every pill from the Measure Values card except the two profit sums; or right-click Measure Names → Filter and tick only the two profits Double-clicking the axis does not offer currency Double-click opens Edit Axis (range and title), not the number format Right-click the axis → Format… → in the Format pane, Axis tab → Scale → Numbers → Currency (Standard) or Currency (Custom) with 0 decimals. Or right-click each profit field in the Data pane → Default Properties → Number Format… → Currency Tableau cannot open the workbook, or shows old values The file is still open in Excel, or it was saved after Tableau connected Save and close Excel, then in Tableau Data → Refresh (or reconnect) Field names show spaces instead of underscores Tableau tidies field names automatically Nothing to fix: Standard Profit is your Standard_Profit column The workbook was saved as .csv Save As chose the wrong type Save again as Excel Workbook (.xlsx) ; GAP asks for the .xlsx The Try JupyterLab notebook is gone the next day The browser session ended Export the PDF and download the .ipynb before closing the tab ( why ) The exported image is blank or cut off Exported before the view finished drawing, or the window was small Enlarge the worksheet, wait, then Worksheet → Export → Image… again 6. Beyond the capstone ¶ Optional, not graded. Do these in copies of your notebook and workbook, after the graded files are finished. Read the comments yourself. Score the five comments by hand on a scale from −1 to +1, then compare your scores with VADER's. Which comment would you score differently, and which words explain the difference (Day 3, Part 7)? How much does the 0.20 matter? GAP caps the sentiment effect at 20%. In a copy of the workbook, put the 0.20 in its own input cell and build a one-way Data Table (Day 5, Part 4) with values from 0.10 to 0.30. Describe how the adjusted demand responds. Uncertain demand. Base demand is a forecast, not a fact. Replace it with =ROUND(NORM.INV(RAND(), B2, 0.15*B2), 0) in a copy, simulate 500 trials of each year's two profits with a Data Table (Day 5, Part 9), and describe each supplier's range and chance of a loss. A dashboard. In Tableau, add a second sheet showing adjusted demand by year as bars, and combine both sheets in a dashboard with a message title. A one-page memo. Rewrite your answer to question 1 as a one-page memo in the structure of Day 6, Part 14, labelling each statement as a fact, an estimate or a judgement, and adding one condition that would change your recommendation. 7. Submission ¶ File Contents Report Your executive summary with the Tableau image, saved as YourLastName_Capstone_Report.pdf Notebook The executed notebook as a PDF, with GAP's name for it ( LastName_JupyterLabLab.pdf , or as GAP instructs), attached to the end of the report or submitted as a separate file Workbook YourLastName_DATA300_Capstone.xlsx , with formulas in columns D to F Run the notebook from the top (Route B: Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells ) and export it with File → Print → Save as PDF , Background graphics ticked. Insert the Tableau image into the Word document before writing around it, and save the report from Word with File → Save As → PDF . If you attach the notebook PDF to the end of the report, combine the files offline ( Combining PDFs without internet ), then open the result and check that every page is there. Check that every number in the report matches your workbook and that the workbook is the final version. Upload the files to Assignment 4 on GAP and submit before Sunday 29 November, 23:59 China Standard Time ( how to submit ).

Tableau makes it a green SUM(Year) pill; right-click it and choose Dimension . Drag Measure Values (at the bottom of the Data pane) to Rows . On the Measure Values card below the Marks card, remove every measure except the sums of Standard Profit and Ethical Profit . On the Marks card, choose Line or Bar , and drag Measure Names onto Color . Format the vertical axis as currency (see section 5 for the menu path). Worksheet → Export → Image… , save the image and insert it into a blank Word document.

docs.text: In the Word document that holds your chart, write a short executive summary: a brief introduction, then your answers to GAP's two questions. Strategic and ethical recommendation (CLO 5). GAP asks you to assume that the focus groups showed the target customers care a great deal about a company's carbon footprint, and to recommend one supply chain to the board, weighing how large the profit difference is against the ethical context and the long-term value of the brand. The value of an integrated BI chain. GAP asks why moving from text mining to a spreadsheet model to a visual story gives a sounder, more realistic plan than a static spreadsheet alone. Use the structure from Day 6, Part 14 and Day 7, Part 6: answer first, the evidence with its numbers, the trade-off stated in plain units, the conditions and limits.

docs.text: Use this route if %pip or the NLTK download fails in Try JupyterLab, or if you prefer your own laptop. It scores the same five comments with real VADER , reading the lexicon from the course folder ( data/nltk_data ), and it stops with an error instead of switching to a stand-in scorer if the lexicon cannot be found. Create a notebook inside the DATA300_GAP folder (next to data ), named as in Route A. The five comments are bundled in data/ecovate_focus_group.csv . # Route B for the capstone, Part 1: VADER offline, no downloads and no silent fallback. from pathlib import Path import nltk import pandas as pd NLTK_DIR = Path ( "data/nltk_data" ) . resolve () nltk . data . path . insert ( 0 , str ( NLTK_DIR )) from nltk.sentiment.vader import SentimentIntensityAnalyzer analyzer = SentimentIntensityAnalyzer () # raises an error if the lexicon is missing: no silent fallback print ( "Scorer used:" , type ( analyzer ) . __name__ , "| NLTK" , nltk . __version__ ) # The five focus-group comments from GAP, bundled with the course df = pd . read_csv ( "data/ecovate_focus_group.csv" ) assert len ( df ) == 5 , "expected five comments" # Score each comment: the compound score runs from -1 (very negative) to +1 (very positive) df [ "Sentiment_Score" ] = df [ "Review_Text" ] . apply ( lambda text : analyzer . polarity_scores ( text )[ "compound" ]) # GAP's rule: baseline demand 1.0, plus up to 0.20 for a fully positive average avg_sentiment = df [ "Sentiment_Score" ] . mean () demand_multiplier = 1.0 + avg_sentiment * 0.20 pd . set_option ( "display.max_colwidth" , 100 ) print ( df [[ "Review_ID" , "Review_Text" , "Sentiment_Score" ]] . to_string ( index = False )) print ( f " \n Average sentiment score: { avg_sentiment : .3f } " ) print ( f "Demand multiplier (type this, as printed, into Excel C2:C6): { demand_multiplier : .3f } " ) In JupyterLab you may replace the print(... .to_string(index=False)) line with display(df) for a nicer table. Build the Excel workbook by hand as in Route A, Part 2: Route B covers only the text-mining step. Export the notebook with Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells , then File → Print → Save as PDF .
docs.title: 3. Route B: offline in Anaconda JupyterLab

docs.text: These tell you whether your work is right without giving any answers away. Notebook The table has five rows , one per comment, and every score lies between −1 and +1 . Your PDF shows which scorer ran (VADER's SentimentIntensityAnalyzer or a stand-in). The multiplier lies between 0.8 and 1.2 , as GAP's rule allows, and equals 1 + 0.20 × the printed average (check it on a calculator). Every score and the average are visible in the PDF, not cut off. Workbook Row 1 holds six headers; rows 2 to 6 hold years 1 to 5 and GAP's five base-demand figures. C2:C6 all hold the same multiplier, exactly as your notebook printed it. Every adjusted demand is a whole number , and equals base demand × multiplier rounded. Each profit = adjusted demand × that supplier's margin − the fixed cost. Check one row by hand for each supplier. Clicking D2, E2 or F2 shows a formula in the formula bar, not a typed number. Chart Five years on the horizontal axis, two series, and a legend that names the two profit measures; nothing else on the Measure Values card. The vertical axis shows dollar signs. The values in the chart match your workbook for at least two years you checked (hover over a mark). Report The introduction says what was decided and how, in two or three sentences. Your answer to question 1 names one supply chain, quotes numbers from your workbook, states how big the profit difference is in plain terms, and weighs it against the ethical and brand context. Your answer to question 2 explains what each tool added that a static spreadsheet could not, not just what each tool is. You say which scorer produced your multiplier, and you note at least one limit of scoring five short comments.

docs.text: Optional, not graded. Do these in copies of your notebook and workbook, after the graded files are finished. Read the comments yourself. Score the five comments by hand on a scale from −1 to +1, then compare your scores with VADER's. Which comment would you score differently, and which words explain the difference (Day 3, Part 7)? How much does the 0.20 matter? GAP caps the sentiment effect at 20%. In a copy of the workbook, put the 0.20 in its own input cell and build a one-way Data Table (Day 5, Part 4) with values from 0.10 to 0.30. Describe how the adjusted demand responds. Uncertain demand. Base demand is a forecast, not a fact. Replace it with =ROUND(NORM.INV(RAND(), B2, 0.15*B2), 0) in a copy, simulate 500 trials of each year's two profits with a Data Table (Day 5, Part 9), and describe each supplier's range and chance of a loss. A dashboard. In Tableau, add a second sheet showing adjusted demand by year as bars, and combine both sheets in a dashboard with a message title. A one-page memo. Rewrite your answer to question 1 as a one-page memo in the structure of Day 6, Part 14, labelling each statement as a fact, an estimate or a judgement, and adding one condition that would change your recommendation.

docs.text:
Lab 1: Data exploration ¶ Your first graded Python lab. You explore a table of diamonds for an imaginary jewellery retailer: check its structure and quality, build a pivot table of average price, draw a correlation heatmap, a violin plot and a hexbin plot, answer short questions about what you see, and submit one PDF on GAP. Adapted from the DATA 300 GAP course, In-Class Module 1, Lab 1: Data Exploration. Written in our own words; follow GAP for the official wording. 1. What and why ¶ What you do Run four steps of given Python code on the diamonds data (structure, pivot table, three charts), then answer seven questions in a Markdown cell at the bottom of the notebook Why Every later lab and assignment assumes you can check a dataset before trusting it, summarise it by group, and read a chart without over-reading it. The lab's scenario is a buyer deciding how to price and stock diamonds CLOs CLO 1 (the business question descriptive analytics can answer), CLO 2 (charts that communicate a finding), CLO 3 (computing to find relationships in structured data) Weight 3% Deadline Tuesday 10 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , on GAP (worked on in periods 7 and 8 of Day 1) Before you start The two Day 1 lectures: Foundations of data-driven decisions and Exploring data The data has one row per diamond: its weight ( carat ), three quality grades ( cut , color , clarity ), two proportions ( depth and table , both percentages), its price in US dollars , and its length, width and depth in millimetres ( x , y , z ). 2. Route A: Try JupyterLab (as on GAP) ¶ Part 1: Open and name a notebook ¶ Open Try JupyterLab, start a Python (Pyodide) notebook and rename it with the file name GAP gives (your last name, the course code and "AppliedLab1"). Part 2: Load the data and inspect its structure ¶ Paste GAP's first code block into a cell and run it. In outline, it: installs seaborn into the browser session with %pip ; imports pandas, seaborn, matplotlib and numpy, and open_url from pyodide.http ; loads diamonds.csv from the seaborn-data repository on GitHub; prints info() , the missing-value count per column and the describe() summary. Part 3: Pivot table ¶ Paste and run GAP's second block. It builds a pivot table of the mean price with cut quality down the side and colour grade across the top. On GAP's scales, colour runs from D (colourless, best) to J (faint yellow), and cut from Fair (lowest) to Ideal (best). Part 4: Three charts for a large dataset ¶ Paste and run GAP's third block. It draws: a correlation heatmap of the numeric columns, annotated, on a fixed −1 to +1 scale; a violin plot of price for each cut; a hexbin plot of carat against price, with a colour bar for the number of diamonds per hexagon. Part 5: Answer the questions ¶ Add a Markdown cell at the bottom and answer GAP's seven questions in full sentences. They come in three groups: data quality and structure (two questions), the pivot table (an unexpected comparison and the hidden variable behind it), and the charts (the strongest correlation with price, the shape of the price distribution, and where the hexbin is densest). Read every answer from your own output and name the table or chart it comes from. Part 6: Export and submit ¶ Run everything from the top, then File → Print → Save as PDF with Background graphics ticked. See Submission below. 3. Route B: offline in Anaconda JupyterLab ¶ Use this route if Try JupyterLab will not load the data, or if you prefer your own laptop. It follows the same steps as GAP's code but reads the bundled copy of the data, so nothing is installed or downloaded. Create a notebook inside the DATA300_GAP folder (next to data ). You can paste the whole block into one cell, or split it at the # --- lines into four cells, which matches GAP's parts. The questions are exactly the same as in Route A. # Route B for Lab 1: run offline in Anaconda JupyterLab. # The diamonds file comes from the course folder, so nothing is installed or downloaded. import numpy as np import pandas as pd import seaborn as sns import matplotlib.pyplot as plt pd . set_option ( "display.max_columns" , None ) # show every column when printing # --- Part 2: load the data and inspect its structure diamonds = pd . read_csv ( "data/diamonds.csv" ) print ( "--- Structure ---" ) diamonds . info () print ( " 
 --- Missing values in each column ---" ) print ( diamonds . isnull () . sum ()) print ( " 
 --- Summary of the numeric columns ---" ) print ( diamonds . describe () . round ( 2 )) # --- Part 3: pivot table of mean price (US dollars) by cut and colour price_pivot = pd . pivot_table ( diamonds , values = "price" , index = "cut" , columns = "color" , aggfunc = "mean" ) print ( " 
 --- Mean price (US dollars) by cut (rows) and colour grade (columns) ---" ) print ( price_pivot . round ( 2 )) # --- Part 4: three charts sns . set_theme ( style = "whitegrid" ) # Chart 1: correlation heatmap of the numeric columns corr_matrix = diamonds . select_dtypes ( include = "number" ) . corr () plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 8 )) sns . heatmap ( corr_matrix , annot = True , fmt = ".2f" , cmap = "coolwarm" , linewidths = 0.5 , vmin =- 1 , vmax = 1 ) plt . title ( "Correlations between the numeric diamond attributes" ) plt . show () # Chart 2: violin plot of price for each cut (one colour, works on any seaborn version) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 10 , 6 )) sns . violinplot ( data = diamonds , x = "cut" , y = "price" , color = "#9cc3ef" ) plt . title ( "Distribution of price for each cut quality" ) plt . xlabel ( "Cut quality" ) plt . ylabel ( "Price (US dollars)" ) plt . show () # Chart 3: hexbin of carat (x) against price (y) plt . figure ( figsize = ( 9 , 6 )) plt . hexbin ( diamonds [ "carat" ], diamonds [ "price" ], gridsize = 40 , cmap = "Blues" , mincnt = 1 ) plt . colorbar ( label = "Number of diamonds in the hexagon" ) plt . title ( "Where the diamonds concentrate: carat and price" ) plt . xlabel ( "Carat (weight)" ) plt . ylabel ( "Price (US dollars)" ) plt . show () In JupyterLab you may replace the print(...) around describe() and the pivot table with display(...) for nicer tables; the numbers are the same. Export with Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells , then File → Print → Save as PDF . 4. Checks you can make ¶ These tell you whether your output is right without giving any answers away. The table has 10 columns : three text columns ( cut , color , clarity ) and seven numeric ones. The row count you report comes from info() (the RangeIndex line) or from diamonds.shape ; it is more than 50,000. describe() lists the seven numeric columns only, and its count row agrees with what info() and the missing-value check say. The pivot table has 5 rows (one per cut) and 7 columns (colour grades D to J), and every value is a price in US dollars. The heatmap is a 7 × 7 square with 1.00 down the diagonal; the colour bar runs from −1 to +1. The violin plot has five violins , one per cut, and a y-axis in US dollars. The hexbin plot has carat along the bottom, price up the side and a colour bar counting diamonds. Each answer names the output it comes from, gives numbers with units (US dollars, carats), and, for the "why" question, names a variable and says how you would check it. 5. Known pitfalls and fixes ¶ Problem Cause Fix The first cell hangs or ends with a network error GitHub is slow or blocked Drag diamonds.csv from the course folder into Try JupyterLab's file browser and use pd.read_csv("diamonds.csv") in place of the open_url line, or switch to Route B ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'seaborn' in Try JupyterLab The %pip install line did not run in this session Run the first cell again; every new Try JupyterLab session needs it ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyodide' in Anaconda GAP's browser-only code was pasted into Route B Use the Route B code above FileNotFoundError: data/diamonds.csv The notebook is not in the DATA300_GAP folder Save the notebook inside DATA300_GAP , next to data , and run again NameError: name 'display' is not defined display() exists only inside Jupyter, not in a plain Python script Run the code in JupyterLab, or use print() as Route B does The violin plot shows thin violins shifted away from their labels, plus a legend GAP's code uses hue="cut" with legend=False , which needs seaborn 0.13 or later . Older seaborn (for example in an older Anaconda) ignores legend=False and squeezes the violins side by side Check with print(sns.__version__) . On an older version, delete hue="cut" , palette="muted" and legend=False and use color="#9cc3ef" , as Route B does The cuts in the pivot table are in the order Fair, Good, Ideal, Premium, Very Good pandas sorts text alphabetically, not by quality The values are still correct. To read the table in quality order, add .reindex(["Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal"]) after pivot_table(...) The violins are in a different order from the pivot table seaborn uses the order in which each cut first appears in the data Add order=["Fair", "Good", "Very Good", "Premium", "Ideal"] to violinplot if you want quality order Unsure what currency the prices are in — price is in US dollars , as in the original dataset; write "US dollars" or "$" in your answers x , y and z look like coordinates They are the stone's length, width and depth in millimetres Treat them as size measurements when you read the heatmap You notice repeated rows, or some diamonds with a length, width or depth of 0 The dataset contains 146 fully duplicated rows and a few rows with a zero dimension, which is physically impossible These are worth mentioning as data-quality observations in your answers if you find them. Do not delete them: GAP's questions are about the data as loaded Charts print in grey or are missing from the PDF Background graphics was off, or cells were not run before printing Tick Background graphics ; restart and run all, then print The PDF cuts off the wide pivot table or the describe() table The browser's print width Print in landscape, or reduce the scale in the print dialog until the full table fits 6. Beyond the lab ¶ Optional, not graded. Try these in the same notebook after you have answered GAP's questions: Count the problem rows yourself: diamonds.duplicated().sum() and (diamonds[["x", "y", "z"]] == 0).any(axis=1).sum() . Which data quality dimensions from the morning lecture do they break? Build a second pivot table with aggfunc="count" in place of "mean" . Which cells rest on few diamonds, and how should that change how much you trust their averages? Draw a histogram of price with np.log10(diamonds["price"]) on the x-axis. How does the shape change compared with the violin plot? Take the variable you named as hidden in your answer, split it into a few bands of your choice with pd.cut , and build a pivot table of mean price by band and cut. Does the comparison between cuts look different within each band? Calculate a price per carat ( diamonds["price"] / diamonds["carat"] ) and compare its median across cuts. Write one sentence for the retailer's buyer. 7. Submission ¶ File Contents Final file The executed notebook as one PDF: structure output, pivot table, all three charts and the Markdown cell with your seven answers, named YourLastName_DATA300_AppliedLab1.pdf Run Kernel → Restart Kernel and Run All Cells (Route B) or run every cell from the top (Route A), and check that every table and chart is visible. Export with File → Print → Save as PDF , Background graphics ticked. If you wrote answers in a separate document instead, combine the PDFs offline as described in Combining PDFs without internet . Open the PDF and check every part is present and readable. Upload it to Applied Lab 1 on GAP and submit before Tuesday 10 November, 23:59 China Standard Time ( how to submit ).

docs.text: Lab 2: Dashboard ¶ Your first graded Tableau lab. You build three sheets from Tableau's built-in Sample – Superstore data (a monthly sales trend, a filled map of profit by state and a bar chart of sales by sub-category coloured by profit), combine them into one interactive executive dashboard in which clicking a state filters the other two charts, answer GAP's questions about what the dashboard shows, and submit one PDF on GAP. Adapted from the DATA 300 GAP course, In-Class Module 1, Lab 2: Dashboard Creation. Written in our own words; follow GAP for the official wording. 1. What and why ¶ What you do Build three worksheets in Tableau Desktop, assemble them on a dashboard with the map as a filter, use the dashboard to answer GAP's questions in a separate document, and submit the answers and the dashboard as one PDF Why Regional managers in the scenario cannot see their sales trend or which products lose money in their state. A linked dashboard lets each manager answer both questions with one click. Building one teaches the difference between a set of static charts and an interactive view CLOs CLO 2 (visualisation tools that communicate user-centred analytics), CLO 1 (descriptive analytics to evaluate performance), CLO 3 (organising information with computational tools) Weight 3% Deadline Wednesday 11 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , on GAP (worked on in periods 7 and 8 of Day 2) Before you start The two Day 2 lectures: Visualising and communicating data and Tableau concepts and dashboards . Tableau Desktop installed and activated ( setup ) Your Superstore may differ from your neighbour's Sample – Superstore ships inside Tableau Desktop, and Tableau has changed it between versions: field names (for example State or State/Province , Country or Country/Region ), the range of order years, and therefore the totals. That is expected. Build the dashboard from the Superstore in your Tableau, read every answer from your own dashboard, and if a field name in GAP's steps does not exist, use the equivalent field you have. 2. Route A: Tableau Desktop (as on GAP) ¶ Part 1: Connect to the data ¶ Open Tableau Desktop and click Sample – Superstore under Saved Data Sources on the start page. A blank Sheet 1 opens with the Superstore fields in the Data pane. Part 2: Build the three sheets ¶ Sheet 1, Monthly Sales Trend. Rename the tab. Put Order Date on Columns. Open the pill's menu and choose the second Month entry, the one with a year in its example (such as "May 2015"): it is in the lower list of date values , and the pill turns green (continuous). Put Sales on Rows. You should see one line running across all the years, not twelve points. (Why: Tableau lecture, Part 2 .) Sheet 2, Profitability by State. New worksheet, renamed. Double-click the state field ( State or State/Province ). Tableau draws a dot per state. On the Marks card, change Automatic to Map to make a filled map, then drag Profit onto Color . Profit is shown on a diverging palette: by default blue for profit and orange for loss. Sheet 3, Sales by Sub-Category. New worksheet, renamed. Sub-Category on Rows, Sales on Columns, then the Sort Descending button on the toolbar. Drag Profit onto Color : now bar length shows sales and colour shows profit. Part 3: Assemble the dashboard ¶ Click New Dashboard (next to New Worksheet at the bottom). In the Size menu on the left, choose Automatic , as GAP asks. (Your version may start from Fixed size rather than Range ; choose Automatic either way.) Drag the map to the top half, the trend to the bottom left and the sub-category bars to the bottom right. Click the map once to select it, then click its Use as Filter icon (a small funnel on the map's border, top right). Clicking a state now filters the other two charts. Part 4: Answer the questions ¶ Open a Word document and answer GAP's questions in full sentences. They come in three groups: Baseline (nothing selected): the sub-category with the most sales nationally and whether it is profitable; two states operating at a loss. Interactive (click a state): for one named state, the sub-category with the largest loss and the month and year of an unusual spike in sales; for a second named state, whether its top three sub-categories by sales match the first state's. Critical thinking: why colouring the sales bars by profit is more useful than colouring them by sales, and what it reveals that a plain bar chart hides. Name the sheet each answer comes from, give the values you read (with units: US dollars, months and years) and say how you read them (tooltip, colour, bar order). Part 5: Export ¶ Clear any selection on the map, then File → Print to PDF , Active Sheet (with the dashboard as the active sheet). Save your answers as a PDF too, and combine the two files. See Submission below. 3. Route B: if Tableau Desktop is not working ¶ There is no Python route for this lab , and that is deliberate. The graded product is a working Tableau dashboard; a Python chart would not show that skill, and Superstore is not part of the course folder (it comes with Tableau, in a version that differs between installations). An offline Python copy would give different numbers and could not be graded against your own Tableau. If Tableau does not work on your laptop, in order of preference: Activation problems: Tableau Desktop runs as a free 14-day trial without a product key. Choose the trial, do the lab, and enter the student key when it arrives. Sample – Superstore is included in the trial. No laptop or installation fails: use a lab PC with Tableau Desktop, or pair with a classmate to build it on their machine, then rebuild it on your own before the deadline. Your submission must be your own work. Still stuck: tell your facilitator during period 7, not after the deadline. To practise the same ideas without Superstore, the Tableau lecture builds a linked three-view dashboard in Python on a synthetic bookshop chain (Part 8). Its facilitator note also shows how to save that data as a CSV, which you can open in Tableau with Connect → To a File → Text file for extra practice. Practice data does not replace the lab. 4. Checks you can make ¶ These tell you whether your dashboard is right without giving any answers away. The trend sheet shows one continuous line across several years, with a green month pill, not twelve points or twelve bars. The map is filled (states shaded, not dots), and the colour legend runs from orange through to blue across zero. The sub-category bars are sorted longest first, and their colours vary with profit. On the dashboard, clicking a state makes the trend and the bars change ; clicking the state again (or pressing Esc ) brings back the national view. Dashboard → Actions lists one filter action with the map as its source. Your PDF shows the national view (no state highlighted) and all three charts are readable. Every answer names the chart it comes from and gives values with units. For the loss questions, you checked the value in the tooltip (a negative profit), not only the shade. 5. Known pitfalls and fixes ¶ Problem Cause Fix No field called State , or no State/Province Superstore's field names differ between Tableau versions Use whichever state field your Data pane shows ( State or State/Province ); the steps are the same Double-clicking the state field gives a list, or a map with no states The field does not have a geographic role, or the country is not recognised Right-click the state field → Geographic Role → State/Province . If an "unknown" indicator appears at the bottom right of the map, click it and choose Edit Locations , with the country set to the United States The map shows dots, not shaded states The mark type is still Automatic (a symbol map) On the Marks card, open the mark-type menu and choose Map (the filled map) The trend shows twelve points, or the pill is blue The first Month entry (a discrete date part ) was chosen Open the pill's menu again and choose the second Month entry, in the lower list, showing a year (for example "May 2015") A state looks orange-ish but its tooltip shows a positive profit, or shades change after clicking a state The colour range is recomputed from the data in view, and the palette's midpoint may not sit at zero Color → Edit Colors → Advanced , tick Center and set it to 0 . Always confirm a "loss" with the tooltip value The sort order seems wrong after clicking a state The bars were sorted by hand (dragging) rather than with the sort button Use Sort Descending on the toolbar, or the axis sort icon; this sorts by the measure and updates with the filter No Range option to change, or the size menu shows Fixed size Newer versions start dashboards at a fixed size Choose Automatic as GAP asks. If the PDF then looks cramped, choose a Fixed size such as Letter landscape or A4 landscape before printing Can't find the filter icon on the map The map is not selected, or the icon is small Click once inside the map on the dashboard so a grey border appears; the Use as Filter funnel is on that border at the top right (hover to see its name). When on, it is filled in Clicking a state does nothing to the other charts The filter icon was not switched on, or was switched on for another sheet Check Dashboard → Actions : there should be a filter action with the map as source and the other two sheets as targets. If not, select the map and click Use as Filter again The PDF shows only one state's data A state was still selected when you printed Click an empty area of the map (the sea, or outside the states) or press Esc so nothing is selected, check both charts show national data, then print again Print to PDF is missing from the File menu Some versions and platforms (often macOS) do not have it Use File → Print… and choose Save as PDF in the print dialog; or Dashboard → Export Image… and paste the image into your Word document The PDF has several pages, or only one sheet Print Range was set to Entire Workbook , or the wrong sheet was active Click the dashboard tab first, then choose Active Sheet under Print Range GAP mentions "the 5 questions" but lists more Inconsistent wording Answer every question GAP lists, each under its own number GAP calls the coloured bar chart "dual-axis" In Tableau, dual axis means two measures on two overlaid axes; this chart has one axis plus colour (a dual encoding ) Answer the question GAP means: what the second encoding (colour) adds Online PDF merger is blocked or slow — Combine the PDFs offline : see Combining PDFs without internet 6. Beyond the lab ¶ Optional, not graded. Try these after you have submitted: Add Profit Ratio as a calculated field, SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) , and put it on the map's Color instead of Profit. Which states change colour, and why might a rate be fairer than a total (Day 2 morning lecture, Part 4)? Change the dashboard action from Filter to Highlight ( Dashboard → Actions → Edit ). When would a manager prefer each? Rewrite each sheet's title as a message title that states what the national view shows, with a number where you can ( morning lecture, Part 5 ). Add a KPI text sheet at the top showing total sales, total profit and profit ratio, and let the map filter it too. Run through the dashboard design checklist and fix the two weakest points. 7. Submission ¶ File Contents Answers Your answers to every GAP question, in full sentences, saved as Answers_Lab2.pdf Dashboard The dashboard, national view, from File → Print to PDF ( Active Sheet ), saved as Tableau_Dashboard_Lab2.pdf Final file The two combined into one PDF, named YourLastName_DATA300_AppliedLab2.pdf In Tableau, clear the selection on the map and check that the trend and bars show national data. Export the dashboard and your answers as the two PDFs above. Combine them offline ( Combining PDFs without internet ). In Word you can instead paste an exported image of the dashboard below your answers and save once as PDF. Open the final PDF and check that the answers and the full dashboard are present and readable. Upload it to Applied Lab 2 on GAP and submit before Wednesday 11 November, 23:59 China Standard Time ( how to submit ). Save your workbook as a .twbx too, in case your facilitator asks for it.

docs.text: Lab 3: Text mining ¶ Your third graded Python lab. You turn ten short customer reviews of a tablet into numbers: clean and tokenise the text, find the most frequent keywords, draw a word cloud, score each review's sentiment with VADER, chart how many reviews are positive, neutral and negative, answer questions about what you see, and submit one PDF on GAP. Adapted from the DATA 300 GAP course, In-Class Module 1, Lab 3: Text Mining Application. Written in our own words; follow GAP for the official wording. 1. What and why ¶ What you do Run GAP's setup code, then two blocks of given Python code (key terms, then sentiment) on ten product reviews, and answer five questions in three sections in a Markdown cell at the bottom of the notebook Why Most of what customers tell a business is free text. The lab's scenario is a consultant asked to summarise a batch of tablet reviews for the product's engineering teams without reading thousands of them by hand CLOs CLO 3 (computational methods to find patterns in unstructured data), CLO 1 (the business question descriptive and predictive analytics can answer), CLO 2 (communicating findings with a chart) Weight 3% Deadline Thursday 12 November, 23:59 China Standard Time , on GAP (worked on in periods 5 and 6 of Day 3) Before you start The Text mining lecture, especially Parts 2–8 The data is a small table built inside the notebook: one row per review, with a review number and the review text. There is no rating column; the sentiment comes only from the text. 2. Route A: Try JupyterLab (as on GAP) ¶ Part 1: Open and name a notebook ¶ Open Try JupyterLab, start a Python (Pyodide) notebook and rename it with the file name GAP gives (your last name, the course code and "AppliedLab3"). Part 2: Set up NLTK and load the reviews ¶ Paste GAP's first code block into a cell and run it. In outline, it: installs nltk , wordcloud and seaborn into the browser session with %pip ; imports pandas, matplotlib, seaborn, NLTK's VADER analyser, stop-word list and tokeniser, and WordCloud ; defines a small helper that downloads NLTK data files from GitHub with pyfetch and unzips them, then uses it (with await ) to fetch the VADER lexicon, the Punkt tokeniser tables ( punkt and punkt_tab ) and the stop-word lists; builds a DataFrame of ten reviews and shows the first rows. The downloads take a few seconds each. Wait until the cell finishes (the [*] becomes a number) before going on. Part 3: Preprocessing and key terms ¶ Paste and run GAP's second block. It joins all ten reviews into one lower-case string, tokenises it, keeps only alphabetic tokens that are not stop words (NLTK's English list plus three product words GAP adds), draws a word cloud , and prints the five most frequent keywords with their counts. Part 4: Sentiment with VADER ¶ Paste and run GAP's third block. It downloads the VADER lexicon again (harmless if you already have it), creates the analyser, rebuilds the same ten-review table, adds each review's compound score , labels it Positive (≥ 0.05), Negative (≤ −0.05) or Neutral (in between), shows the table, and draws a bar chart of how many reviews fall in each label . Part 5: Answer the questions ¶ Add a Markdown cell at the bottom and answer GAP's questions in full sentences. They come in three sections: preprocessing and key terms (what a stop word is and why removing it matters for frequency counts; which product feature is discussed most), the sentiment scores (the exact score of one named review and whether it matches a human reading; why another named review is labelled Neutral), and a business recommendation to an engineering team, backed by specific outputs. Read every value from your own output and name the table or chart it comes from. Part 6: Export and submit ¶ Run everything from the top, then File → Print → Save as PDF with Background graphics ticked. See Submission below. 3. Route B: offline in Anaconda JupyterLab ¶ Use this route if the NLTK downloads from GitHub fail or hang, or if you prefer your own laptop. It follows the same steps as GAP's code but reads NLTK's data from the course folder ( data/nltk_data ), so nothing is installed or downloaded. Create a notebook inside the DATA300_GAP folder (next to data ), named as in Route A. Paste the block into one cell, or split it at the # --- lines into cells that match GAP's parts. The ten reviews and the questions are the same as in Route A.
