docs.text: T1 lab: Can we trust the sales table, in Tableau? ¶ Connect Tableau to the Superstore file, set the same scope as the Python sessions, and prove you can count rows, orders and returned orders correctly. Then draw the shape of order value and delivery time. This lab rebuilds parts of the Session 2 lab and the Session 4 lab in Tableau. If you get stuck, look back at how you did the same step in Python. Desktop and web editor The click paths on this page are written for Tableau Desktop Public Edition . If you use the Tableau Public web editor in a browser, the menus differ slightly. Look for the same command in a nearby menu, or ask your facilitator. The business decision ¶ The head of a retail business says: "Before you show me any chart in this new tool, can I trust it? Does Tableau give the same number of orders and returns as your earlier analysis? And what does a typical order and a typical delivery look like?" A new tool is a new chance to count the wrong thing. Today you set up the data carefully and check every number by reconciliation: the parts must add up to the total. About the data Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units . The file does not state a currency, so we never call them dollars or any other currency. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Setup Connect to the file and set the course scope, everyone together Setup Core Count rows, orders and returned orders; build a filtered bar chart; save C1–C4 Stretch Draw distributions of order value and ship days S1–S2 Challenge Check one order by hand; fix a colleague's summary X1–X2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Connect Tableau to an Excel file and relate two of its sheets. Set a data source filter so every sheet uses the course scope. Count order lines and orders and explain why they differ. Count returned orders and reconcile them with the total. Build a bar chart with a filter, and check that its parts add up. Save your work as a packaged workbook ( .twbx ). Evidence you keep: your saved workbook, a rows-versus-orders table, a returned-orders table, a filtered bar chart and your reconciliation notes. Before you start, work through the T1 lecture . Have the downloaded sample_-_superstore.xls file and your evidence log ready (see the Tableau overview ). Set up the Superstore data source ¶ Later labs (T2 and T3) start from this setup, so take care with each step. Use the downloaded file, not the built-in sample Tableau Desktop Public Edition has a built-in data source called Sample - Superstore . It may be a different version of the data. Always connect to the sample_-_superstore.xls file you downloaded, so your numbers match the course and your Python work. Step 1: Connect to the file ¶ Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition . In the Connect pane on the left, under To a File , click Microsoft Excel . Find and open sample_-_superstore.xls . Tableau opens the Data Source page. On the left, under Sheets , you see Orders , People and Returns . Step 2: Add the Orders sheet ¶ Drag Orders onto the large empty area (the canvas) at the top. A preview of the rows appears below. Look at the small icon above each column: Abc for text, # for numbers and a calendar for dates. Check the IDs Order ID should show Abc (text). Row ID shows # , but it is an identifier, not an amount. You will never add it up. Step 3: Relate Returns to Orders on Order ID ¶ Drag Returns onto the canvas, next to Orders . Tableau draws a line between the two boxes. This line is a relationship . Click the line. In the panel that opens below, check that the matching fields are Order ID (Orders) = Order ID (Returns). If they are not, choose Order ID in both lists. Close the panel. What the relationship does The Returns sheet lists each returned order once. The relationship lets Tableau look up whether an order's Order ID is on that list. It does not change the Orders sheet. Step 4: Add the course scope as a data source filter ¶ At the top right of the Data Source page, under Filters , click Add . In the Edit Data Source Filters window, click Add... . Choose Order Date (from the Orders table) and click OK . Choose Range of Dates and click Next . Set the start date to 1 January 2023 and the end date to 31 December 2025 . Both dates are included. Click OK , then OK again. The Filters area now shows 1 filter. Every sheet in this workbook will use only orders placed from 2023 to 2025, the same scope as the Python sessions. Check the date format Tableau shows dates in your computer's format. 01/12/2025 can mean 1 December or 12 January. Read the dates back after you type them. Step 5: Create the Returned Order field ¶ Click the Sheet 1 tab at the bottom of the window. In the Data pane on the left, you now see two tables: Orders and Returns . The Order ID from Returns is shown as Order ID (Returns) . Choose Analysis → Create Calculated Field... . Name the field Returned Order and type this formula: NOT ISNULL([Order ID (Returns)]) Check that the message under the formula says The calculation is valid , then click OK . In plain words: an order is returned when Tableau finds its Order ID on the Returns sheet. Step 6: Save straight away ¶ Choose File → Save As . Choose your course folder and save as a * Tableau Packaged Workbook ( .twbx) named T1_lab_YourName . Save again ( Ctrl + S on Windows, Cmd + S on Mac) after each task. Core tasks ¶ C1 (Core): Rows versus orders ¶ The (Count) field counts rows. In Superstore one row is one order line , so this is not the number of orders. Rename Sheet 1 to Rows vs orders : double-click the tab and type the new name. Create a calculated field named Distinct Orders with this formula: COUNTD([Order ID]) In the Data pane, double-click Orders (Count) . Tableau shows one number: the number of order lines. Double-click Distinct Orders . Tableau now shows both numbers in a small table, labelled by Measure Names . Write both numbers in your evidence log. Write one sentence explaining why the two numbers differ. Another way to count orders You can also drag Order ID into the view, right-click its pill and choose Measure → Count (Distinct) . The Distinct Orders field saves you doing this every time. Compare with Python Check your two numbers against the rows and orders you found in the Session 2 lab . They should be the same. If they are not, check the data source filter in Step 4 first. C2 (Core): Returned orders ¶ Create a new sheet: click the New Worksheet icon next to the sheet tabs. Name it Returned orders . Drag Returned Order to Rows . Drag Distinct Orders to Text on the Marks card. You see True for orders on the Returns sheet. The other orders show as False or as Null , depending on how Tableau matches the two tables. Both mean "not on the Returns sheet". Choose Analysis → Totals → Show Column Grand Totals . Reconcile: Add the two numbers by hand. Do they equal the Grand Total ? Is the Grand Total the same as Distinct Orders in C1? Now swap Distinct Orders for Orders (Count) . The number next to True gets bigger. In one sentence, explain what it is counting now and why it is not the number of returned orders. Returned means on the list The Returns sheet has no return date, quantity or refund amount. An order that is not on the list is not proof that nothing came back. Write "orders on the returns list" when you report this number. C3 (Core): Orders by segment, with a filter ¶ Create a new sheet named Orders by segment . Drag Segment to Rows and Distinct Orders to Columns . You get one bar per segment. Click the Sort descending icon in the toolbar so the longest bar is at the top. Drag Distinct Orders onto Label on the Marks card, so each bar shows its value. Choose Analysis → Totals → Show Column Grand Totals . Double-click the sheet title and write a title that says what the chart shows and for which period, for example Orders by customer segment, orders placed 2023–2025 . Reconcile: add the three segment bars by hand. Do they equal the Grand Total, and the Distinct Orders number from C1? Now add a filter: Drag Region to the Filters shelf. In the window that opens, tick one region only and click OK . Right-click the Region pill on the Filters shelf and choose Show Filter . A filter control appears on the right. Add your region to the title, for example ... (Region: West) . Add up the segment bars again. Do they still equal the new Grand Total? Switch the filter back to (All) before you move on. Write your filters down Every time you filter, record it in your evidence log. A chart without its filters written down is easy to misread later. Think about it. Make a copy of the sheet (right-click the tab → Duplicate ) and replace Segment with Category . Add the category bars by hand. Do they equal the Grand Total this time? Write one sentence on why not. Hint: can one order contain products from more than one category? Can one order belong to more than one segment? C4 (Core): Save and reopen ¶ Save your workbook ( File → Save ). Close Tableau completely. Open Tableau again and open T1_lab_YourName.twbx . Check that all your sheets, the Returned Order and Distinct Orders fields and the data source filter are still there. Stretch tasks ¶ S1 (Stretch): Histogram of order value ¶ To describe orders, you first need the value of each order , not each line. In Session 4 you built an order-level table in Python. In Tableau you create an order total field. Create a new sheet named Order value . Create a calculated field named Order Total : { FIXED [Order ID] : SUM([Sales]) } In plain words: for each Order ID, add up the Sales of all its lines. Every line of an order then carries that order's total. You learn how this kind of formula works in T2. In the Data pane, right-click Order Total and choose Create → Bins... . Choose a round Size of bins , for example 100 , and click OK . A new field Order Total (bin) appears. Drag Order Total (bin) to Columns and Distinct Orders to Rows . Title the chart, for example Order value, orders placed 2023–2025 (file's own monetary units) . Count orders, not rows Every line of an order carries the same Order Total. If you used Orders (Count) on Rows, an order with three lines would be counted three times. Distinct Orders counts each order once. Reconcile: every order falls in exactly one bin, so the bars must add up to Distinct Orders. Drag Distinct Orders onto Label on the Marks card. Right-click that Label pill and choose Quick Table Calculation → Running Total . Each label now adds its bar to all the bars before it. You meet running totals properly in T2. Read the label on the last bar. Does it equal Distinct Orders from C1? Right-click the Label pill and choose Clear Table Calculation . Read it. In one or two sentences, describe the shape. Where are most orders? Is there a long tail to one side? Does it match the histogram you drew in the Session 4 lab ? Create a calculated field named Ship Days : DATEDIFF('day', [Order Date], [Ship Date]) In plain words: the number of days from the order date to the ship date. Drag Ship Mode to Columns and Ship Days to Rows . Tableau shows SUM(Ship Days) . Right-click the pill and choose Measure → Average . Drag Order ID onto Detail on the Marks card. You now have one mark per order . In the Marks card drop-down, choose Circle . Right-click the vertical axis and choose Add Reference Line . At the top of the window, choose Box Plot , then click OK . Title the chart, for example Days from order to shipment by ship mode, orders placed 2023–2025 . Why Average and not Sum? Every line of an order has the same Order Date and Ship Date, so the same Ship Days. The average of identical values is that value. SUM would add it once per line and make orders with more lines look slower. Hover over a box to see its median and quartiles. Read it. Which ship mode is fastest? Which has the widest spread? Write one sentence a customer service lead could use when making a delivery promise. Compare with the ship-days results in the Session 4 lab . Drag Order ID to Rows and Orders (Count) to Text . Click the Sort descending icon in the toolbar, so orders with the most lines are at the top. Which two mistakes are in this sentence? Which field should each number use instead? How would you check your corrected numbers? Name the reconciliation. Write your corrected sentence in your log. Remember the wording from C2: "on the returns list". docs.text: T1 lecture: Tableau fundamentals ¶ Learn how Tableau thinks about a table. Once you know how it sorts fields, adds up numbers and applies filters, every chart you build is easier to read and to check. You already know the Superstore data from the Python sessions. Today you meet the same data in a new tool. The questions stay the same: what is one row, what are we counting, and which records are included? What you will be able to explain ¶ How Tableau reads a table: the data source , sheets and fields . The difference between dimensions and measures . The difference between discrete (blue) and continuous (green) fields. How Tableau aggregates numbers, and what the level of detail of a view is. What each part of the Marks card does. The four main filter types and the order in which Tableau applies them. Why the grain of Superstore (one row per order line) matters in Tableau too. Part 1: How Tableau reads a table ¶ Tableau works in three places. Place What it is Where you see it Data source The connection to your file, plus any tables you link and any filters you set on the whole data The Data Source tab, bottom left Sheet One chart or table. A workbook can hold many sheets The tabs along the bottom: Sheet 1 , Sheet 2 , ... Fields The columns of your data, listed in the Data pane on the left of each sheet The Data pane You build a chart by dragging fields from the Data pane onto the shelves : Columns , Rows , Filters and the Marks card. Tableau never changes your file Everything you do in Tableau (calculations, filters, renamed fields) lives in the workbook. The original Excel file stays as it was. One file, several tables ¶ The Superstore file has three sheets: Orders , People and Returns . In Tableau each sheet can become a table in the data source. You can link two tables with a relationship : a line that says which field they share. In the lab you link Orders to Returns on Order ID , so you can tell which orders were returned. Part 2: Dimensions and measures ¶ When Tableau connects, it sorts every field into one of two groups. Group What it is Examples in Superstore What Tableau does with it Dimension A label you group or split by Segment, Region, Category, Order ID, Order Date Makes one header, bar or mark per value Measure A number you add up or summarise Sales, Profit, Quantity, Discount Aggregates it, by default with SUM In the Data pane, dimensions are listed above the line and measures below it. Tableau's first guess is not always right Tableau guesses from the data type. A number is not always a quantity. Row ID is a number, but adding Row IDs up means nothing. It is an identifier. If an ID shows up as a measure, drag it up into the dimensions, or right-click it and choose Convert to Dimension . This is the same idea as the levels of measurement in the Session 2 lecture : ask what a column means before you decide what to do with it. Part 3: Discrete and continuous ¶ Tableau also marks every field as discrete or continuous . The colour tells you which. Type Colour What it draws Example Discrete Blue Separate headers, one per value Segment on Rows gives one row per segment Continuous Green An axis, a smooth range of values SUM(Sales) on Columns gives a horizontal axis Dimensions are usually blue and measures usually green, but the two ideas are separate: Dimension or measure decides whether Tableau groups by the field or adds it up. Discrete or continuous decides whether Tableau draws headers or an axis. Dates show the difference clearly. Drag Order Date to Columns and you get YEAR(Order Date) in blue: one header per year. Right-click it and choose the second Year in the menu (the green one) and you get a continuous time axis instead. Read the pill colour first When a chart looks strange, look at the colour of each pill on the shelves. A blue pill where you expected green (or the reverse) explains many surprises. Part 4: Aggregation and the level of detail ¶ When you drag a measure into a view, Tableau does not show every row. It aggregates : it adds up (or counts, or averages) the rows that belong to each mark. Drag Sales to Columns on an empty sheet. You get one bar: SUM(Sales) over every row. Now drag Segment to Rows. You get one bar per segment. Each bar adds up only that segment's rows. The dimensions in the view set the level of detail : how many marks there are and which rows go into each one. Add a dimension and the view splits into more, smaller marks. Remove one and the marks merge. Common aggregations ¶ Aggregation What it does Example SUM Adds the values Total Sales AVG Mean of the values Average Sales per line MEDIAN Middle value Median Sales per line COUNT Counts rows with a value Number of order lines COUNTD Counts distinct values Number of different Order IDs, that is, orders MIN / MAX Smallest / largest value First and last order date To change an aggregation, right-click a green pill and choose Measure → ... . Rows are not orders Superstore has one row per order line . An order with three products has three rows. So counting rows counts order lines, not orders. To count orders, use COUNTD([Order ID]) . You did the same in Python with nunique() . The row-count field ¶ Tableau adds a field to each table called Orders (Count) (named after the table). It counts rows . In Superstore that means order lines. Part 5: The Marks card ¶ The Marks card controls how each mark looks. It sits to the left of the view. Control What it does Mark type (drop-down) Bar, line, circle, square, text, and more. Automatic lets Tableau choose Color Colours marks by a field Size Sizes marks by a field Label Writes a value on or next to each mark Detail Adds a dimension to the level of detail without a header or colour Tooltip Sets what appears when you hover over a mark Detail is the one people forget. Put Order ID on Detail and you get one mark per order, even though no Order ID header appears. You use this in the lab for the ship-days box plot. Part 6: Filters and their order ¶ Tableau can filter at several stages. Each stage happens before the next one, so the order changes your results. Order Filter type Where you set it What it affects 1 Extract filter When you create an extract of the data Which rows are copied into the extract 2 Data source filter The Data Source page, top right: Filters → Add Every sheet in the workbook 3 Dimension filter Drag a dimension (for example Region) to the Filters shelf One sheet, unless you apply it to more 4 Measure filter Drag a measure (for example SUM(Sales)) to the Filters shelf One sheet; keeps only marks whose total passes the test Two more stages you will meet later Context filters sit between data source and dimension filters, and table calculation filters come last. You meet them in T2. Why the order matters ¶ A measure filter works on the aggregated marks that are left after the dimension filters. docs.text: Learn how Tableau thinks about a table. Once you know how it sorts fields, adds up numbers and applies filters, every chart you build is easier to read and to check. You already know the Superstore data from the Python sessions. Today you meet the same data in a new tool. The questions stay the same: what is one row, what are we counting, and which records are included?
docs.title: T1 lecture: Tableau fundamentals

docs.text: How Tableau reads a table: the data source , sheets and fields . The difference between dimensions and measures . The difference between discrete (blue) and continuous (green) fields. How Tableau aggregates numbers, and what the level of detail of a view is. What each part of the Marks card does. The four main filter types and the order in which Tableau applies them. Why the grain of Superstore (one row per order line) matters in Tableau too.
docs.title: What you will be able to explain

docs.text: Tableau works in three places. Place What it is Where you see it Data source The connection to your file, plus any tables you link and any filters you set on the whole data The Data Source tab, bottom left Sheet One chart or table. A workbook can hold many sheets The tabs along the bottom: Sheet 1 , Sheet 2 , ... Fields The columns of your data, listed in the Data pane on the left of each sheet The Data pane You build a chart by dragging fields from the Data pane onto the shelves : Columns , Rows , Filters and the Marks card. Tableau never changes your file Everything you do in Tableau (calculations, filters, renamed fields) lives in the workbook. The original Excel file stays as it was.
docs.title: Part 1: How Tableau reads a table

docs.text: The Superstore file has three sheets: Orders , People and Returns . In Tableau each sheet can become a table in the data source. You can link two tables with a relationship : a line that says which field they share. In the lab you link Orders to Returns on Order ID , so you can tell which orders were returned.
docs.title: One file, several tables

docs.text: When Tableau connects, it sorts every field into one of two groups. Group What it is Examples in Superstore What Tableau does with it Dimension A label you group or split by Segment, Region, Category, Order ID, Order Date Makes one header, bar or mark per value Measure A number you add up or summarise Sales, Profit, Quantity, Discount Aggregates it, by default with SUM In the Data pane, dimensions are listed above the line and measures below it. Tableau's first guess is not always right Tableau guesses from the data type. A number is not always a quantity. Row ID is a number, but adding Row IDs up means nothing. It is an identifier. If an ID shows up as a measure, drag it up into the dimensions, or right-click it and choose Convert to Dimension . This is the same idea as the levels of measurement in the Session 2 lecture : ask what a column means before you decide what to do with it.
docs.title: Part 2: Dimensions and measures

docs.text: Tableau also marks every field as discrete or continuous . The colour tells you which. Type Colour What it draws Example Discrete Blue Separate headers, one per value Segment on Rows gives one row per segment Continuous Green An axis, a smooth range of values SUM(Sales) on Columns gives a horizontal axis Dimensions are usually blue and measures usually green, but the two ideas are separate: Dimension or measure decides whether Tableau groups by the field or adds it up. Discrete or continuous decides whether Tableau draws headers or an axis. Dates show the difference clearly. Drag Order Date to Columns and you get YEAR(Order Date) in blue: one header per year. Right-click it and choose the second Year in the menu (the green one) and you get a continuous time axis instead. Read the pill colour first When a chart looks strange, look at the colour of each pill on the shelves. A blue pill where you expected green (or the reverse) explains many surprises.
docs.title: Part 3: Discrete and continuous

docs.text: When you drag a measure into a view, Tableau does not show every row. It aggregates : it adds up (or counts, or averages) the rows that belong to each mark. Drag Sales to Columns on an empty sheet. You get one bar: SUM(Sales) over every row. Now drag Segment to Rows. You get one bar per segment. Each bar adds up only that segment's rows. The dimensions in the view set the level of detail : how many marks there are and which rows go into each one. Add a dimension and the view splits into more, smaller marks. Remove one and the marks merge.
docs.title: Part 4: Aggregation and the level of detail

docs.text: Aggregation What it does Example SUM Adds the values Total Sales AVG Mean of the values Average Sales per line MEDIAN Middle value Median Sales per line COUNT Counts rows with a value Number of order lines COUNTD Counts distinct values Number of different Order IDs, that is, orders MIN / MAX Smallest / largest value First and last order date To change an aggregation, right-click a green pill and choose Measure → ... . Rows are not orders Superstore has one row per order line . An order with three products has three rows. So counting rows counts order lines, not orders. To count orders, use COUNTD([Order ID]) . You did the same in Python with nunique() .
docs.title: Common aggregations

docs.text: Tableau adds a field to each table called Orders (Count) (named after the table). It counts rows . In Superstore that means order lines.
docs.title: The row-count field

docs.text: The Marks card controls how each mark looks. It sits to the left of the view. Control What it does Mark type (drop-down) Bar, line, circle, square, text, and more. Automatic lets Tableau choose Color Colours marks by a field Size Sizes marks by a field Label Writes a value on or next to each mark Detail Adds a dimension to the level of detail without a header or colour Tooltip Sets what appears when you hover over a mark Detail is the one people forget. Put Order ID on Detail and you get one mark per order, even though no Order ID header appears. You use this in the lab for the ship-days box plot.
docs.title: Part 5: The Marks card

docs.text: T2 lab: Which segment deserves a closer look, and how are sales moving? ¶ Build a segment KPI table in Tableau that reconciles with its totals, find out why a colleague's profit ratio is wrong, and add monthly growth figures that keep their comparison month. This lab rebuilds parts of the Session 5 lab (segment KPIs) and the Session 7 lab (monthly trend and growth) in Tableau. If you get stuck, look back at how you did the same step in Python. Desktop and web editor The click paths on this page are written for Tableau Desktop Public Edition . If you use the Tableau Public web editor in a browser, the menus differ slightly. Look for the same command in a nearby menu, or ask your facilitator. The business decision ¶ The head of a retail business has one analyst free next month and asks: "Which customer segment should we look at first? I want to see sales, profit and orders side by side, and the profit we make on each unit of sales. Then show me how sales have moved month by month, without being fooled by the time of year." A big Sales total alone is not enough to decide. A segment can sell a lot and still earn little per unit of sales. And a month can look like a crash or a boom just because of the season. Today you build fair measures and check each one by reconciliation. About the data Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units . The file does not state a currency, so we never call them dollars or any other currency. The file does not explain how Profit is calculated, so we call Profit ÷ Sales the profit ratio , not "gross margin". How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Setup Open your T1 workbook and check its fields, everyone together Setup Core Build a segment KPI table that reconciles; debug a colleague's profit ratio; write a recommendation C1–C3 Stretch Draw the monthly trend with a running total; add MoM and YoY growth S1–S2 Challenge Count the orders that appear in more than one category, with an LOD expression X1 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Create aggregate calculated fields and format them. Build a KPI table with a grand total, and reconcile it. Show why AVG([Profit] / [Sales]) is not the profit ratio. Explain why order counts by category do not add up to the total. Add a running total and MoM and YoY growth with table calculations. Focus on one year without breaking the growth figures. Use a FIXED LOD expression to answer a question about each order. Evidence you keep: your saved workbook, a segment KPI table with reconciliation notes, your explanation of the colleague's mistake, a short recommendation, and any Stretch and Challenge sheets. Before you start, work through the T2 lecture . Have your T1 workbook and your evidence log ready. Setup: open your T1 workbook ¶ Step 1: Save a copy ¶ Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition and open T1_lab_YourName.twbx . Choose File → Save As and save it as a * Tableau Packaged Workbook ( .twbx) named T2_lab_YourName . Now you work in the copy, and your T1 workbook stays as you submitted it. No T1 workbook? Follow Set up the Superstore data source in the T1 lab first, then come back here and save as T2_lab_YourName . Step 2: Check the data source ¶ Click the Data Source tab at the bottom left. Check that Orders and Returns are on the canvas with a relationship line between them. Check that the Filters area at the top right shows 1 filter. Click Edit and confirm it keeps Order Date from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025. The scope must be right before you build KPIs Without the data source filter, every total includes orders outside the course period, and none of your numbers will match your Python work. Step 3: Check your fields ¶ Go to any sheet and look in the Data pane. You need these two calculated fields from T1: Field Formula Distinct Orders COUNTD([Order ID]) Order Total {FIXED [Order ID] : SUM([Sales])} If one is missing (for example, you did not do T1 Stretch S1), create it now with Analysis → Create Calculated Field... . Use exactly these names: T3 uses them too. Core tasks ¶ C1 (Core): The segment KPI table ¶ Part A: Build the table ¶ Create a new sheet and name it Segment KPIs . Create a calculated field named Profit Ratio : SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) In plain words: add up Profit, add up Sales, then divide once. Format it as a percentage. In the Data pane, right-click Profit Ratio and choose Default Properties → Number Format... . Choose Percentage , set Decimal places to 1 and click OK . Drag Segment to Rows . Drag Measure Names to Columns . Drag Measure Values onto Text on the Marks card. A Measure Values card appears below the Marks card, listing every measure in the data. On the Measure Values card, drag off every pill except SUM(Sales) , SUM(Profit) , AGG(Profit Ratio) and AGG(Distinct Orders) . If one of these is missing, drag it from the Data pane onto the card. Choose Analysis → Totals → Show Column Grand Totals . Double-click the sheet title and write a title that says what the table shows and for which period, for example Segment KPIs, orders placed 2023–2025 (file's own monetary units) . Another way to choose the measures Instead of dragging pills off the Measure Values card, you can drag Measure Names to the Filters shelf and tick only the four measures you want. Part B: Reconcile ¶ Write each check in your evidence log, with the numbers you added up. Add the three segment Sales values by hand. Do they equal the Grand Total? Add the three segment Profit values. Do they equal the Grand Total? Add the three segment Distinct Orders values. Do they equal the Grand Total, and the Distinct Orders number from T1 C1? Divide the Grand Total Profit by the Grand Total Sales with a calculator. Does it equal the Grand Total Profit Ratio ? Now take the simple average of the three segment Profit Ratios. Is it the same as the Grand Total Profit Ratio? Which one is the business's profit ratio? Small rounding differences Tableau adds up the full values, then rounds what it shows. If your hand total differs from the Grand Total only in the last decimal place, that is rounding, not an error. Part C: The same table by category ¶ Duplicate the sheet (right-click the tab → Duplicate ) and name the copy Category KPIs . Drag Category onto the Segment pill on Rows to replace it. Reconcile again: do the category Sales add up to the Grand Total? Do the category Distinct Orders ? Subtract the Grand Total Distinct Orders from your hand-added sum of category orders. Write the difference in your log. In one or two sentences, explain why the sum is larger than the total, and why the same did not happen for segments. Hint: Part 3 of the lecture. The Grand Total is right; the hand sum is not Tableau's Grand Total recounts the distinct orders over all rows, so it is the true number of orders. Adding up the category rows counts some orders more than once. C2 (Core): Debug a colleague's profit ratio ¶ A colleague built the same table, but with this field: AVG([Profit] / [Sales]) They say: "I calculated the average profit ratio, so it is the profit ratio for each segment." Go back to the Segment KPIs sheet. Create a calculated field named Avg Line Ratio with the colleague's formula. Format it as a percentage with one decimal place, as in C1 Part A step 3. Drag Avg Line Ratio onto the Measure Values card, so it appears as a new column next to Profit Ratio . Compare the two columns and answer in your log: For each segment, which is larger: Profit Ratio or Avg Line Ratio? For which segment is the gap largest? Look at the Grand Total row. Are the two numbers close or far apart? If they are close, does that make the colleague's field correct? Explain in one sentence. In one sentence each, say what Profit Ratio calculates and what Avg Line Ratio calculates. Use the words "order line" and "weight". Which segment has the most influence on the overall Profit Ratio, and why? Check the weights To see each segment's weight, right-click SUM(Sales) on the Measure Values card and choose Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total . Then right-click it again and choose Edit Table Calculation , and under Compute Using choose Segment (or Table (down) ). Otherwise each row is calculated on its own and shows 100%. Each segment's share of Sales is its weight in the overall Profit Ratio. Right-click again and choose Clear Table Calculation when you are done. Finally, remove Avg Line Ratio from the table (drag it off the Measure Values card), so your submitted table shows only the correct measures. Keep the field in the Data pane so your facilitator can see it. C3 (Core): Write a recommendation and save ¶ Write three sentences to the head of the business: Recommendation: which segment to look at first. Evidence: two measures from your Segment KPIs table that support it. Describe how they compare; you do not need to copy every number. Limitation: one thing this table cannot tell you. For example, it shows which segment looks different, not why . Save your workbook ( File → Save ). Stretch tasks ¶ S1 (Stretch): Monthly trend with a running total ¶ Create a new sheet named Monthly sales . Drag Order Date to Columns . Tableau shows YEAR(Order Date) . Right-click the pill and choose the second Month in the menu (the green one, with an example such as May 2015 ). The pill turns green: a continuous month axis. Drag Sales to Rows . You get a line chart with one point per month. Title the chart, for example Monthly Sales, orders placed 2023–2025 (file's own monetary units) . Check the calendar. Look at the status bar at the bottom left of the window. It shows the number of marks. With the course scope you expect one mark for each month of three full years. If the number is different, a month is missing, and LOOKUP in S2 will compare the wrong months. Read it. Write three observations. Are some months high every year? Are some always low? Add a running total: Drag Sales to Rows again, next to the first SUM(Sales) pill. You get a second chart below the first. Right-click the second pill and choose Quick Table Calculation → Running Total . Right-click it again and choose Compute Using → Order Date (Tableau may label it Month of Order Date ). Reconcile: hover over the last point of the running total. It must equal the Grand Total Sales in your Segment KPIs table. If it does not, check the Compute Using setting and the data source filter. S2 (Stretch): MoM and YoY growth ¶ Duplicate Monthly sales and name the copy Growth . Remove the running total pill (drag it off Rows). Create two calculated fields: MoM Growth SUM([Sales]) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) - 1 YoY Growth SUM([Sales]) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) - 1 Format both as percentages with one decimal place ( Default Properties → Number Format... ). Drag MoM Growth onto the SUM(Sales) pill on Rows to replace it. In the Marks card drop-down, choose Bar . Right-click the MoM Growth pill and choose Compute Using → Order Date (or Month of Order Date ). Drag YoY Growth to Rows , next to MoM Growth. Set its Compute Using the same way. Title the sheet, for example Sales growth by month, MoM and YoY, orders placed 2023–2025 . Reconcile your MoM formula with Tableau's own: Drag Sales to Rows again. Right-click it and choose Quick Table Calculation → Percent Difference , then Compute Using → Order Date . Hover over three months. The Percent Difference must equal your MoM Growth for each. Drag the extra pill off Rows. Check the blanks. Which months have no MoM bar? Which have no YoY bar? Explain each in one sentence. Read it. Find the month with the largest MoM growth. Write it down with the Sales of that month and of the month before (from Monthly sales ). Is this a real boom, or something else? Find January 2025. Compare its MoM and YoY growth. Which one should the head of the business see, and why? The filter trap ¶ Drag Order Date to the Filters shelf. Choose Years , click Next , tick 2025 only, and click OK . Look at January 2025. What happened to its MoM growth? What happened to the YoY bars? Write one sentence explaining why. Hint: Part 5 of the lecture. Remove the filter: drag the YEAR(Order Date) pill off the Filters shelf. Highlight instead of filter ¶ Create a calculated field named Focus Year : IF YEAR(MIN([Order Date])) = 2025 THEN "2025" ELSE "Earlier years" END In plain words: label each month's mark "2025" or "Earlier years". Drag Focus Year onto Color on the Marks card. The 2025 bars now stand out. Reconcile: hover over January 2025. Its MoM and YoY growth must be the same as before you tried the filter. Why this field does not break the growth Focus Year is an aggregate calculation, so it is a measure. A measure on Color does not split the view, so LOOKUP still moves along all the months. A dimension on Color, such as YEAR(Order Date) , would split the view into one part per year, and each January would lose its comparison month. Challenge tasks ¶ X1 (Challenge): Orders in more than one category ¶ In C1 Part C, the category order counts added up to more than the total. Now find out exactly how many orders contain more than one category. Create a new sheet named Categories per order . Create a calculated field named Categories in Order : {FIXED [Order ID] : COUNTD([Category])} In plain words: for each order, count how many different categories its lines belong to. In the Data pane, right-click Categories in Order and choose Convert to Dimension . If its icon is still green, right-click it again and choose Convert to Discrete . Drag Categories in Order to Rows and Distinct Orders to Text . Choose Analysis → Totals → Show Column Grand Totals . Reconcile two ways: Add the rows by hand. Do they equal the Grand Total, and Distinct Orders from C1? Why must they, this time? Multiply each row's Distinct Orders by its number of categories, and add the results. Does this equal your hand-added sum of category orders from C1 Part C? Explain why in one sentence. Explain: how many orders appear in more than one category? How does this number relate to the difference you wrote down in C1 Part C? Hint: an order with three categories is counted twice too many. Try a filter. Drag Category to the Filters shelf and keep only Furniture . Do the labels 1, 2 and 3 still describe the whole order, or only its Furniture lines? Use the warning in Part 6 of the lecture to explain what you see. Remove the filter when you are done. Evidence checklist ¶ Before you submit, check that you have: the Segment KPIs sheet with Sales, Profit, Profit Ratio and Distinct Orders, a grand total and a title your five reconciliation checks from C1 Part B the Category KPIs sheet and your sentence on why category orders do not add up the Avg Line Ratio field and your answers to the four C2 questions your three-sentence recommendation Stretch and Challenge sheets and notes, if you did them Submit on Moodle ¶ Save your workbook as T2_lab_YourName.twbx ( File → Save ). Export your Segment KPIs sheet: choose File → Print to PDF , or Worksheet → Export → Image... . Open the T2 lab assignment on the course Moodle page. Upload the .twbx file, the PDF or image, and your written answers (from your evidence log). Do not publish this lab You do not need to publish anything to Tableau Public for this lab. Anything published there is public. If you use the web editor, saving puts the workbook and its data on your Tableau Public profile. Keep your Superstore work on your own computer: never save or publish Superstore to Tableau Public, because the course has not found a clear permission to republish the file ( T4 lecture, Part 2 ). Ask your facilitator how to work on this lab without saving to Tableau Public, and how to get your workbook for Moodle. Next ¶ Keep this workbook. In T3 you combine the Segment KPIs table and the monthly views into a decision dashboard, using the same fields.

docs.text: T2 lecture: Calculations and KPIs ¶ Learn to build your own measures in Tableau and to know when they can be trusted. A KPI is only useful if it is calculated at the right level, adds up where it should, and keeps its comparison when you filter. In the Python sessions you built a segment KPI table ( Session 5 ) and monthly growth rates ( Session 7 ). Today you learn the Tableau tools that do the same jobs: calculated fields, table calculations and a first level of detail (LOD) expression. The traps are the same as in Python, so watch for them. What you will be able to explain ¶ What a calculated field is, and the difference between row-level and aggregate calculations. Why a ratio must be calculated as a ratio of sums , and why AVG([Profit]/[Sales]) gives a different answer. Why distinct counts do not always add up, and when they do. What a table calculation is: running totals, and growth with LOOKUP . What Compute Using means for a table calculation. Why filtering months breaks growth figures, and what to do instead. What a FIXED level of detail expression is, using the order total as an example. Part 1: Calculated fields ¶ A calculated field is a new field you define with a formula. You create one with Analysis → Create Calculated Field... . It appears in the Data pane next to the fields from your file, and you can drag it into a view like any other field. You already made three in T1: Field Formula Returned Order NOT ISNULL([Order ID (Returns)]) Distinct Orders COUNTD([Order ID]) Ship Days DATEDIFF('day', [Order Date], [Ship Date]) These three are not the same kind of calculation. Row-level and aggregate calculations ¶ Kind What it does Example What you get Row-level Works on one row at a time, like a new column in the table DATEDIFF('day', [Order Date], [Ship Date]) One value per order line. Tableau aggregates it when you drag it into a view, for example as SUM or AVG Aggregate Adds up (or counts) many rows first, then calculates COUNTD([Order ID]) , SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) One value per mark. The rows that go into each mark depend on the dimensions in the view You can tell them apart from the formula. If every field in it sits inside an aggregation such as SUM , AVG or COUNTD , it is an aggregate calculation. If no field is aggregated, it is row-level. Cannot mix aggregate and non-aggregate arguments A formula such as SUM([Profit]) / [Sales] mixes the two kinds: a total divided by one row's value. Tableau refuses it with this error message. Decide first whether you want one value per row or one value per mark, then aggregate every field or none. In the Data pane, an aggregate calculated field shows as AGG(...) when you drag it into a view. You cannot change its aggregation, because the aggregation is already inside the formula. Same idea as in pandas A row-level field is like adding a column to your DataFrame. An aggregate field is like a calculation after groupby(...).agg(...) . You used both in the Session 5 lab . Part 2: Ratio of sums versus mean of ratios ¶ The profit ratio tells you how much profit each unit of sales earned. In the Session 5 lecture you learnt the rule: totals first, then divide . In Tableau, the correct field is an aggregate calculation: Profit Ratio = SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) Tableau adds up Profit and Sales over the rows of each mark, then divides once. In a grand total row, it adds up over all rows and divides again. It does not add or average the segment ratios. There is a tempting wrong version: AVG([Profit] / [Sales]) This works out a profit ratio for every order line (a row-level calculation), then takes the simple average of those ratios. Each line counts the same, whether it sold a pen or a large table. A small example ¶ Line Sales Profit Line ratio A 10,000 1,000 10% B 100 50 50% Ratio of sums: 1,050 ÷ 10,100, about 10.4% . This is what the business really earned per unit of sales. Mean of ratios: (10% + 50%) ÷ 2 = 30% . The tiny line pulls the result as hard as the big one. The ratio of sums is a weighted average of the line ratios, with each line weighted by its Sales. The mean of ratios gives every line the same weight. A close answer is not a correct answer On some data the two versions give similar numbers by chance. That does not make the mean of ratios correct. Split by a dimension, such as Segment, and the gap usually opens up. You test this in the lab. Division by zero If a mark has no Sales, SUM([Sales]) is zero and Tableau shows the ratio as blank ( Null ), not as an error. A blank means "not available". Never read it as 0%. Part 3: Distinct counts do not always add up ¶ Sums are additive. The Sales of the three segments add up to total Sales, because each order line belongs to exactly one segment. Distinct counts may not be. COUNTD([Order ID]) counts each order once within each mark . Whether the marks add up to the total depends on whether an order can sit in more than one mark. Split by Can one order appear in two marks? Do the order counts add up to the total? Segment No. Every line of an order has the same Segment Yes . Segment splits the orders into separate groups Category Yes. One order can contain Furniture and Office Supplies and Technology No . An order with lines in two categories is counted once in each, so the sum is larger than the total You noticed this at the end of C3 in the T1 lab . The grand total in Tableau is correct in both cases: Tableau recounts the distinct orders over all rows, it does not add up the bars. The mistake happens when you , or a colleague with a spreadsheet, add up the category values by hand and call it the number of orders. The test for additivity Ask: can one item belong to more than one group? If yes, distinct counts across those groups do not add up. Medians, percentiles and ratios do not add up either. Always recalculate them for the total. Part 4: Table calculations ¶ A table calculation works on the numbers already in the view , after Tableau has aggregated them. It does not go back to the rows of your file. It looks at the other marks in the table: the one before, the one after, or all of them. You met one in the T1 lab: the running total on the order-value histogram. Table calculation What it does Typical use Running total Adds each mark to all the marks before it Sales so far this year Difference / Percent difference Compares each mark with the one before Month-on-month change Percent of total Each mark as a share of all marks A segment's share of Sales Rank Orders the marks Top 10 products The quickest way to add one is to right-click a green pill in the view and choose Quick Table Calculation . A table calculation pill shows a small triangle ( Δ ) on its right. LOOKUP: the value from another mark ¶ LOOKUP returns the value of an expression from another mark, a set number of steps away. Formula Returns LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) Sales of the previous mark LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) Sales of the mark 12 steps back LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), 0) Sales of this mark With one mark per month, in date order, you can write growth rates: MoM Growth = SUM([Sales]) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) - 1 YoY Growth = SUM([Sales]) / LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) - 1 Month-on-month (MoM) compares each month with the month before. Year-on-year (YoY) compares each month with the same month one year earlier. In the Session 7 lecture you saw why the YoY comparison is fairer for a seasonal business: January after a busy December always looks like a crash. LOOKUP counts marks, not months LOOKUP(..., -12) means "12 marks back", not "12 months back". It gives the same month last year only if every month is in the view, in order, with none missing. Always check the number of marks in the status bar at the bottom left of the window: with the course scope you expect one mark per month, for three full years. The first month in the view has no previous mark, so its MoM growth is blank. The first twelve months have no mark 12 steps back, so their YoY growth is blank. Blank means "no comparison available", never 0%. Compute Using: which direction? ¶ A table calculation needs to know which marks to look along . This is called Compute Using , and you set it by right-clicking the pill and choosing Compute Using . Setting Meaning Table (across) Move left to right along the whole table Table (down) Move top to bottom A named field, for example Order Date Move along that field's values, whatever the layout Naming the field is safer than across or down . If you later swap rows and columns, the calculation still moves through the months. Partitions Any dimension in the view that is not in Compute Using splits the table into separate parts. The table calculation restarts in each part. If you add Segment to Color on a monthly growth chart, each segment gets its own growth line, and each segment's first month is blank. Part 5: Why filtering months breaks growth ¶ In T1 you learnt the order in which Tableau applies filters. Table calculations come after all the ordinary filters: Extract filters Data source filters Context filters Dimension filters Measure filters Table calculations are worked out here Table calculation filters So a dimension filter removes months before LOOKUP runs. Suppose you filter a monthly growth chart to the year 2025 to focus on it: December 2024 is no longer in the view. LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -1) for January 2025 finds no previous mark. January 2025's MoM growth becomes blank , and every YoY growth value becomes blank, even though the data is still in your file. Highlight, do not filter To focus on part of a time series, keep all months in the view and make the months you care about stand out , for example with colour. Then every growth value still has its comparison month. This is the same trap you met in Python in the Session 7 lecture : calculate growth on the full series first, then choose what to show. There is also a more advanced fix. A table calculation filter (a filter on a table calculation field) runs last , after the growth values are calculated. It hides marks without removing them from the calculation. You do not need it today; highlighting is simpler and keeps the context visible. Part 6: A first level of detail expression ¶ Sometimes you need a value at a different level from the view. The most common case in Superstore: you want the value of each order , but the rows are order lines . A level of detail (LOD) expression calculates an aggregate at a level you choose. You used one in T1 S1: Order Total = {FIXED [Order ID] : SUM([Sales])} Read it as: for each Order ID, add up Sales over all its lines . The result is written back onto every line of that order. An order with three lines has the same Order Total on all three. Table calculation FIXED LOD expression Works on The marks already in the view The rows of the data source Level Set by the view and Compute Using Set by the dimensions in the braces Changes when you add a dimension to the view? Yes No Because Order Total is repeated on every line, count orders with Distinct Orders , not with rows, when you use it. In T1 you did this for the order-value histogram. LOD expressions also let you ask questions about each order, for example how many different categories does this order contain? : {FIXED [Order ID] : COUNTD([Category])} You build this in the lab Challenge. FIXED ignores dimension filters A FIXED expression is calculated before dimension filters (step 4 in Part 5). If you filter a sheet to one Category, Order Total still adds up all the order's lines, in every category. The data source filter still applies, so the course scope holds. This is often what you want for an order total, but say so when you report it. Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the T2 lab. Your facilitator will go through the answers. Is DATEDIFF('day', [Order Date], [Ship Date]) a row-level or an aggregate calculation? How can you tell from the formula? A colleague calculates the profit ratio as AVG([Profit] / [Sales]) . In one sentence, what does this calculate, and why is it not the business's profit ratio? In a segment table with a grand total, how does Tableau calculate the grand total of SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) ? You show Distinct Orders by Segment and by Category. In which table do the rows add up to the total number of orders, and why? Your monthly growth chart shows MoM growth for every month in 2025, but after you filter the view to 2025, January becomes blank. Why, and what should you do instead? What does LOOKUP(SUM([Sales]), -12) return, and when does it not give the same month last year? Every line of an order carries the same Order Total . Why should you count orders with Distinct Orders and not with the row count when you chart order values?

Why should you count orders with Distinct Orders and not with the row count when you chart order values?
