docs.text: T3 lab: One page for the leadership team ¶ Rebuild the Session 14 decision dashboard in Tableau: KPI tiles, a monthly trend and a region chart that filters the rest of the page when you click it. Check that every number still reconciles after a click, write a message headline, and make sure the page works without colour. This lab rebuilds the decision dashboard from the Session 14 lab (task I1, retail case) in Tableau. The Stretch task builds a second dashboard on the marketing case from the Session 12 lab . If you get stuck, look back at how you built the same page in Python. Desktop and web editor The click paths on this page are written for Tableau Desktop Public Edition . If you use the Tableau Public web editor in a browser, the menus differ slightly. Look for the same command in a nearby menu, or ask your facilitator. The business decision ¶ The commercial lead from Session 14 is back: "Next week I present our plans to the leadership team. I need one page that shows how 2025 went against 2024, and whether anything should worry us before we expand. They will want to click a region and see its numbers. Make it impossible to misunderstand." The decision is where to focus next year and what to check before expanding . The page must answer it in a minute, and it must stay correct when someone clicks. About the data Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company. Sales and Profit are in the file's own monetary units . The file does not state a currency, so we never call them dollars or any other currency. The returns list says only which orders appear on it: no dates, amounts or reasons. marketing-v1 (Stretch only) is synthetic data generated by the course: seven paid campaigns, every day of 2025, amounts in neutral currency units . Attributed revenue is a synthetic single-campaign allocation; it does not prove a campaign caused a sale. How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Setup Open your T2 workbook, check its fields and add the year fields, everyone together Setup Core Build the tiles, trend and region chart; lay out the dashboard; add a filter action and reconcile; finish, check and export C1–C4 Stretch Build a one-page dashboard for the marketing case, with a filter action and a highlight action S1 Challenge Critique a deliberately poor dashboard, then prove two of its problems in Tableau X1–X2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. What you will be able to do ¶ Build KPI tiles that show a value for one year with a comparison. Lay out a dashboard in reading order with containers and a fixed size. Add a filter action and check that the tiles still reconcile for every selection. Write a message headline and a scope note that stay true when the page is filtered. Check a dashboard for accessibility, including without colour. Add a phone layout and export the dashboard as a PDF. Evidence you keep: your saved workbook, your dashboard PDF, your region reconciliation table, your headline and accessibility check, and any Stretch and Challenge notes. Before you start, work through the T3 lecture . Have your T2 workbook, your evidence log and your Session 14 dashboard image to hand. Setup: open your T2 workbook ¶ Step 1: Save a copy ¶ Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition and open T2_lab_YourName.twbx . Choose File → Save As and save it as a * Tableau Packaged Workbook ( .twbx) named T3_lab_YourName . No T2 workbook? Follow Set up the Superstore data source in the T1 lab first. Then create the fields in Step 3 below, and save as T3_lab_YourName . Step 2: Check the data source ¶ Click the Data Source tab at the bottom left. Check that Orders and Returns are on the canvas with a relationship line between them. Check that the Filters area at the top right shows 1 filter: Order Date from 1 January 2023 to 31 December 2025. Step 3: Check your fields ¶ Go to any sheet and look in the Data pane. You need these fields from T1 and T2, with exactly these names: Field Formula Made in Returned Order NOT ISNULL([Order ID (Returns)]) T1 setup Distinct Orders COUNTD([Order ID]) T1 C1 Profit Ratio SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) T2 C1 Create any field that is missing with Analysis → Create Calculated Field... . Step 4: Add the year fields ¶ The tiles show 2025 with a comparison to 2024 , so they need both years in the same sheet ( T3 lecture, Part 3 ). Create these calculated fields. Check that each says The calculation is valid before you click OK . Field Formula Format Sales 2025 SUM(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 THEN [Sales] END) Number, 0 decimals, thousands separator Sales 2024 SUM(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2024 THEN [Sales] END) Number, 0 decimals, thousands separator Sales Growth [Sales 2025] / [Sales 2024] - 1 Percentage, 1 decimal Orders 2025 COUNTD(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 THEN [Order ID] END) Number, 0 decimals, thousands separator Profit Ratio 2025 SUM(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 THEN [Profit] END) / [Sales 2025] Percentage, 1 decimal Returned Orders 2025 COUNTD(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 AND [Returned Order] THEN [Order ID] END) Number, 0 decimals Returned Share 2025 [Returned Orders 2025] / [Orders 2025] Percentage, 1 decimal To set a format: in the Data pane, right-click the field and choose Default Properties → Number Format... . For a number with no decimals, choose Number (Custom) , set Decimal places to 0 and tick Include thousands separators . In plain words: Sales 2025 keeps the Sales of order lines placed in 2025, then adds them up. Orders 2025 counts each 2025 order once. Lines from other years give a blank, and COUNTD ignores blanks. Returned Share 2025 is a ratio of counts : orders on the returns list divided by all orders, both for 2025. It is not an average of anything. Call it the share on the returns list Returned Share 2025 is the share of orders on the returns list , not a "return rate". The list says nothing about how many items came back or what was refunded. Save your workbook ( File → Save ). Core tasks ¶ C1 (Core): Build the sheets ¶ You need six sheets: four tiles, one trend and one region chart. Build each on its own sheet; the dashboard comes in C2. Part A: The first KPI tile ¶ Create a new sheet and name it Tile Sales . Drag Sales 2025 onto Text on the Marks card. The view shows one number. Drag Sales Growth onto Text as well. Both pills now sit on the Marks card. Click Text on the Marks card, then click the ... button. The Edit Label window opens. Delete what is there and write three lines. Use Insert to add the fields: Sales, 2025 <AGG(Sales 2025)> <AGG(Sales Growth)> vs 2024 Select the middle line and set a large font size, for example 24 , in bold. Set the other two lines to about 10 . Click OK . Right-click the sheet title and choose Hide Title . The first line of the tile is its label. If the pills show SUM instead of AGG Sales 2025 already contains its aggregation, so Tableau shows it as AGG(Sales 2025) . If you see SUM(Sales) instead, you dragged the wrong field. Part B: Three more tiles ¶ Duplicate Tile Sales three times (right-click the tab → Duplicate ). In each copy, drag the old pills off the Marks card, drag the new fields onto Text , and edit the text: Sheet Fields on Text Label text Tile Orders Orders 2025 Orders, 2025 / value / distinct orders Tile Profit Ratio Profit Ratio 2025 Profit ratio, 2025 / value / Profit ÷ Sales Tile Returns Returned Share 2025 , Returned Orders 2025 , Orders 2025 Orders on returns list, 2025 / share / <Returned Orders 2025> of <Orders 2025> orders A comparison on every tile The Sales tile compares with 2024. If you have time at the end, give the Orders and Profit Ratio tiles a 2024 comparison too: create Orders 2024 and Profit Ratio 2024 in the same way as the 2025 fields, and add them to the tile text. Part C: The trend ¶ The Session 14 trend drew 2025 against 2024, month by month, so the reader can see whether growth was steady or came from one lucky month. Create a new sheet named Trend . Drag Order Date to Columns . Right-click the pill and choose the first Month in the menu (the blue one, with an example such as May ). The axis now shows the twelve months of the year. Drag Sales to Rows . Drag Order Date onto Color on the Marks card. Tableau shows YEAR(Order Date) : one line per year. Drag Order Date to the Filters shelf, choose Years , click Next , tick 2024 and 2025 only, and click OK . Set the colours: click Color → Edit Colors... . Give 2024 a grey and 2025 a blue. Click OK . Make the years readable without colour: drag Order Date onto Label (it shows YEAR(Order Date) ). Click Label , tick Show mark labels , and under Marks to Label choose Line Ends . Check the vertical axis starts at zero: right-click it, choose Edit Axis... , and make sure Include zero is ticked. Title the sheet, for now descriptively: Monthly Sales, 2025 against 2024 (file's own monetary units) . You rewrite it as a message title in C4. Is this year filter safe? Yes. This sheet has no table calculation, so removing 2023 changes nothing for 2024 and 2025. Compare the growth chart in T2 S2 , where filtering months broke LOOKUP . Part D: The region chart ¶ Create a new sheet named Returns by region . Drag Region to Rows and Returned Share 2025 to Columns . Click the Sort descending icon in the toolbar, so the longest bar is at the top. Drag Returned Share 2025 onto Label , so each bar shows its value. Drag Returned Orders 2025 and Orders 2025 onto Tooltip . Hover over a bar to check both appear. Drag Region onto Color . Click Color → Edit Colors... . Give every region the same grey, then give the one region your message is about an orange. Click OK . Title the sheet: Share of 2025 orders on the returns list, by region . Look at the chart and decide which region your message is about. Write one sentence in your log saying why. Save your workbook. C2 (Core): Lay out the dashboard ¶ Before you start, sketch the page on paper: headline, a row of four tiles, the trend across the full width, the region chart, and the scope note at the bottom. Choose Dashboard → New Dashboard . Name the tab Decision dashboard . In the Dashboard pane on the left, under Size , choose Fixed size and Generic Desktop (or another fixed size your facilitator gives). Do this first . Under Objects , check that Tiled is selected at the bottom. Drag a Horizontal object from Objects to the top of the page. This container holds the tiles. Drag the four tile sheets, one by one, into the horizontal container. Watch for the grey shaded area: it shows where the sheet will land. Order: Sales, Orders, Profit Ratio, Returns. Click the container's edge to select it. Open its drop-down menu (the small arrow at the top right) and choose Distribute Contents Evenly . Drag Trend below the tiles, across the full width. Drag Returns by region below the trend. Drag a Text object to the bottom of the page and write the scope note: Scope: Superstore orders placed in 2024 and 2025 (fictitious sample published by Tableau). Sales in the file's own monetary units. Profit ratio = Profit ÷ Sales. Returns list = which orders appear on it; no dates, amounts or reasons. Click a region to filter the tiles and trend; click it again to clear. Patterns describe what happened, not why. Choose Dashboard → Show Title . Leave the default title for now; you write the headline in C4. Remove what you do not need Tableau adds legends to the dashboard automatically, for example the YEAR(Order Date) colour legend. The trend already labels its lines, and the region chart labels its bars, so you can remove these legends: select one and click the x at its top right. Sheet moved to the wrong place? Press Ctrl + Z (Windows) or Cmd + Z (Mac) to undo, and drag again. The Layout pane, next to the Dashboard pane, shows the tree of containers and lets you select an object that is hard to click. Save your workbook. C3 (Core): Add a filter action, then reconcile ¶ The leadership team wants to click a region and see its numbers. Part A: Add the action ¶ Choose Dashboard → Actions... and click Add Action → Filter... . Name the action Filter by region . Under Source Sheets , choose Decision dashboard in the drop-down and tick only Returns by region . Under Run action on , choose Select . Under Target Sheets , tick the four tile sheets and Trend . Untick Returns by region , so the reader can still see and click every region. Under Clearing the selection will , choose Show all values . Click OK , then OK again. Click one region's bar on the dashboard. The tiles and the trend now show that region only. Click the same bar again to clear the selection. Part B: Reconcile across regions ¶ A tile that changes when you click must still add up. Click each region in turn and copy the tile values into a table in your log: Region Sales 2025 Orders 2025 Returned Orders 2025 Returned Share 2025 (first region) (second region) (third region) (fourth region) Added up (do not add) No region selected Then check, and write each answer in your log: Do the four regions' Sales 2025 add up to the value with no region selected? Why must they? Do the four regions' Orders 2025 add up to the value with no region selected? If they do, what does that tell you about orders and regions? Compare with categories in T2 C1 Part C . Do the four regions' Returned Orders 2025 add up? Divide the added-up Returned Orders by the added-up Orders with a calculator. Does it equal the Returned Share 2025 tile with no region selected? Now take the simple average of the four regions' shares. Is it the same? Which one is the company's share, and why? Hint: T2 lecture, Part 2 . Part C: Reconcile the tiles with the trend ¶ Right-click the Trend sheet tab and choose Duplicate as Crosstab . Tableau creates a table of Sales by month and year. Choose Analysis → Totals → Show Column Grand Totals (if the totals appear across instead of down, try Show Row Grand Totals ). The 2025 total must equal the Sales 2025 tile with no region selected. Divide the 2025 total by the 2024 total and subtract 1. The result must equal the Sales Growth on the tile. Count the months in which 2025 Sales are higher than in the same month of 2024. Write the count in your log; you use it in your headline. Small rounding differences The tile rounds to whole units. If your totals differ from it only by rounding, that is not an error. Save your workbook. C4 (Core): Headline, accessibility, phone layout and export ¶ Part A: Message titles ¶ Rewrite the Trend title as a message title : what should the reader notice about 2025 against 2024? Use the month count from C3 Part C. The title must be true for the data shown. Rewrite the Returns by region title as a message title that names the region your orange bar is about. Double-click the dashboard title and write your headline : your big idea in one sentence, with a point of view and what is at stake. Look back at your big idea from the Session 14 lab. Test the titles after a click. Click each region in turn. Is the trend title still true for every region? If not, rewrite it so it is true for every selection, or say in the title that it describes all regions. The region chart is not filtered, so its title does not change. Part B: Accessibility check ¶ Go through your dashboard with this list. Write yes , no or fixed next to each line in your log. The headline and the tiles can be read without looking at any chart. No more than five views (the four tiles count as one). Each colour means one thing everywhere: grey = context, blue = 2025, orange = needs attention. Nothing is shown only by colour: the years are written at the line ends, and the orange bar has its value and a title that names it. No red–green pair is the only difference between two things. Text is large enough to read when the page is shown at half size. The trend's axis starts at zero and the bars start at zero. The scope note gives period, units, source, how to use the click, and the main limit. See it without colour. Export the dashboard (Part D) and view the PDF in greyscale (print preview in black and white, or your phone's greyscale setting). Can you still find the region your title is about? How? Part C: Phone layout ¶ At the top of the Dashboard pane, click Device Preview . Under Device type , choose Phone , then click Add Phone Layout . In the phone layout, keep the headline, the tiles and the region chart. Remove or move the other objects so nothing is too small to read. Click Default at the top of the Dashboard pane to go back to the desktop layout. Write one sentence in your log: which view did you leave out of the phone layout, and why? Part D: Export and save ¶ Click any selected bar again so that no region is selected . With the Decision dashboard tab open, choose File → Print to PDF... . Under Range , choose Active Sheet , and click OK . Save as T3_lab_YourName.pdf . Open the PDF and check that the headline, tiles, titles and scope note are all readable. Save your workbook ( File → Save ). Stretch tasks ¶ S1 (Stretch): A dashboard for the marketing case ¶ In the Session 14 lab, the marketing case asked: which channels deserve more budget next year, and which need a review? Build a one-page Tableau dashboard that answers it. Re-read the Session 12 lecture first if you need to. Step 1: Download the file ¶ The marketing-v1 files are on this course's public GitHub page, the same place the Python notebooks download them from. Open the marketing-v1 folder on GitHub . Click README.md and read the field list and rules. Note the unit of the money columns. Go back and click marketing_daily.csv . Click the Download raw file button (a downward arrow, at the top right of the file view). Save it in your course data folder. Keep the name marketing_daily.csv . If the download button is missing Open the raw file instead. Your browser shows the text. Save it with File → Save Page As... (or Ctrl + S / Cmd + S ) and keep the .csv ending. Step 2: Connect and check ¶ In your T3 workbook, choose Data → New Data Source . Under To a File , click Text file and open marketing_daily.csv . Look at the field types in the preview. date must show a calendar icon. If it shows Abc , click the icon and choose Date . Go to a new sheet. In the Data pane, check that the marketing data source is selected at the top. The fields may appear with tidied names, for example Attributed Revenue for attributed_revenue . Use the names you see in the formulas below. Check the grain. README says one row per day and campaign. Drag the count field ( marketing_daily.csv (Count) ) onto Text . It must equal 365 days × 7 campaigns. Then drag campaign_id onto Text , right-click its pill and choose Measure → Count (Distinct) : it must give 7. Do the same with date : it must give 365. Step 3: Create the measures ¶ README says rates are ratios of sums and must never be averaged. Create: Field Formula Format ROAS SUM([attributed_revenue]) / SUM([spend]) Number, 2 decimals CPA SUM([spend]) / SUM([conversions]) Number, 2 decimals Review Case [spend] = 0 AND [conversions] > 0 (a True/False field) In plain words: ROAS is attributed revenue per unit of spend; CPA is spend per conversion. A row with no spend but some conversions is a review case (README): it cannot have a ROAS of its own. Put Review Case on Rows and the count field on Text , and write the number of review rows in your log. Step 4: Build the sheets ¶ Sheet How to build it Four tiles: M Tile Spend , M Tile Revenue , M Tile ROAS , M Tile CPA As in C1 Part A, with SUM(spend) , SUM(attributed_revenue) , ROAS and CPA . Third line: the unit (currency units, revenue per unit of spend, spend per conversion) ROAS by channel channel on Rows, ROAS on Columns, sorted descending, ROAS on Label. Add SUM(spend) to Tooltip , then right-click it and choose Quick Table Calculation → Percent of Total to show each channel's share of spend CPA by channel The same, with CPA M Trend Continuous MONTH(date) on Columns (the second Month , green). Drag spend to Rows, then drag attributed_revenue onto the same axis so Tableau shows Measure Values with Measure Names on Color. Label the line ends Use the same colour rule as the Core dashboard: grey for context and one highlight colour for the channel your message is about, in both channel charts. Step 5: Lay out and add the actions ¶ Create a dashboard named Marketing dashboard , Fixed size , laid out like the Core dashboard: headline, tiles, trend, then the two channel charts side by side in a horizontal container, then a scope note. The scope note gives the period (2025), the unit (currency units), the source (synthetic marketing-v1), what attributed revenue does not show, and the review cases. Add a filter action : source ROAS by channel , run on Select , targets the four tiles and M Trend , clearing shows all values. Add a highlight action : Dashboard → Actions... → Add Action → Highlight... . Source sheets: ROAS by channel and CPA by channel . Target sheets: the same two. Run on Select . Under Target Highlighting , choose Selected Fields and tick channel . Click a channel in the ROAS chart. The tiles and trend filter to that channel, and the same channel lights up in the CPA chart. Step 6: Reconcile and read ¶ Click each channel and write its Spend tile. Do the five add up to the Spend tile with no channel selected? Divide total attributed revenue by total spend with a calculator. Does it equal the ROAS tile with no selection? Take the simple average of the five channel ROAS values. Is it the same as the overall ROAS? Which is right, and why? Find the channel with the highest ROAS. What is its share of spend? Would you move most of the budget there? Use the CPA chart and the scope note in your answer. Write a message headline for the marketing dashboard. It must not claim that a channel caused revenue. Export the dashboard as a PDF too: T3_lab_YourName_marketing.pdf . Synthetic does not mean publishable yet The marketing data is synthetic, but you do not need to publish this dashboard. T4 covers what is safe to publish to Tableau Public. Challenge tasks ¶ X1 (Challenge): Critique a poor dashboard ¶ A colleague built this dashboard for a regional review and asks for your feedback. It has at least eight problems from this course. Read the description carefully. Title: Dashboard # Component What it shows and how 1 Six KPI tiles across the top Sales, Profit, Quantity, SUM(Discount) , Orders , and Avg returns share . Each tile is a red or green box with one number and no label for the period. The Orders tile uses the Orders (Count) field 2 Avg returns share tile Calculated with WINDOW_AVG over the four region shares 3 Sales by region bar chart Four bars, each a different bright colour. The value axis starts well above zero ( Include zero is unticked), so the smallest region's bar is a stub 4 Sales trend line chart Only December 2024 to February 2025, filtered by hand. Orange line. Title: Sales are falling fast 5 Region filter control On the right edge. Apply to Worksheets is set to Only This Worksheet , on the trend sheet 6 Sales by sub-category pie chart One slice for each sub-category, each in its own colour, with a legend 7 Profit by state map Coloured from red (loss) to green (profit) 8 Ship days table Every order with its ship mode and ship days, scrolling 9 A floating colour legend Placed over the top right of the trend chart — Scope note None. No units anywhere on the page — Size Automatic For each problem, write one row in your log: Problem Which rule or check it breaks Your fix Then answer: What would the leadership team wrongly believe from the trend panel and its title? What would a fair comparison be? Hint: the Session 7 and T2 growth labs. Which two tiles are wrong as measures, not only as design? What should each one use instead? A reader picks West in the Region filter. Which views change and which do not? What would they wrongly conclude? Sketch your redesign: one headline, at most five views, and where each sits. Which components did you remove completely? X2 (Challenge): Prove two of the problems in Tableau ¶ Use your own Decision dashboard workbook to show that two of the problems change the numbers, not only the look. Problem A: the average of shares. Duplicate Returns by region and name the copy Average of shares . Create a calculated field named Avg of Region Shares : WINDOW_AVG([Returned Share 2025]) In plain words: the simple average of the share bars in the view, each region counting the same. Drag Avg of Region Shares onto Label . Right-click it and choose Compute Using → Region . Compare the label with the Returned Share 2025 tile with no region selected. Which is larger? Use the Orders 2025 values from C3 Part B to explain why, in two sentences: which regions have the most orders, and what weight does the simple average give them? Problem B: a filter that applies to one sheet. Go to the Trend sheet. Drag Region to the Filters shelf, keep all regions, and click OK . Right-click the pill and choose Show Filter . On the dashboard, click the Trend sheet, open its drop-down menu and choose Filters → Region to add the filter control to the page. Pick one region in the control. Which views change? Write down what the tiles say and what the trend says. Do they describe the same selection? Open the filter control's drop-down menu and choose Apply to Worksheets → Selected Worksheets... . Tick the tiles and Trend . Pick the region again. Now which views change? Remove the filter control and the Region pill from the Filters shelf, so your submitted dashboard uses only the filter action. Optional, Problem C: the truncated axis. On a duplicate of the trend or region chart, right-click the value axis, choose Edit Axis... and untick Include zero . Write one sentence on how the picture changes. Then delete the duplicate. Evidence checklist ¶ Before you submit, check that you have: the four tile sheets, Trend and Returns by region , each with a title the Decision dashboard with a headline, fixed size, scope note and the Filter by region action your region reconciliation table and the five checks from C3 Part B your trend reconciliation and month count from C3 Part C your accessibility check and your sentence on the phone layout the dashboard PDF Stretch and Challenge sheets and notes, if you did them Submit on Moodle ¶ Save your workbook as T3_lab_YourName.twbx ( File → Save ). Export the Decision dashboard as a PDF (C4 Part D): T3_lab_YourName.pdf . If you did the Stretch task, export the Marketing dashboard too. Open the T3 lab assignment on the course Moodle page. Upload the .twbx file, the dashboard PDF (or PDFs), and your written answers (from your evidence log). Do not publish this lab You do not need to publish anything to Tableau Public for this lab. Anything published there is public. If you use the web editor, saving puts the workbook and its data on your Tableau Public profile. Keep your Superstore work on your own computer: never save or publish Superstore to Tableau Public, because the course has not found a clear permission to republish the file ( T4 lecture, Part 2 ). Ask your facilitator how to work on this lab without saving to Tableau Public, and how to get your workbook and a PDF of your dashboard for Moodle. Next ¶ Keep this workbook. In T4 you learn what Tableau Public makes public, what is safe to publish, and how to turn a dashboard into a portfolio piece from your capstone analysis.

Check that each says The calculation is valid before you click OK . Field Formula Format Sales 2025 SUM(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 THEN [Sales] END) Number, 0 decimals, thousands separator Sales 2024 SUM(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2024 THEN [Sales] END) Number, 0 decimals, thousands separator Sales Growth [Sales 2025] / [Sales 2024] - 1 Percentage, 1 decimal Orders 2025 COUNTD(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 THEN [Order ID] END) Number, 0 decimals, thousands separator Profit Ratio 2025 SUM(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 THEN [Profit] END) / [Sales 2025] Percentage, 1 decimal Returned Orders 2025 COUNTD(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 AND [Returned Order] THEN [Order ID] END) Number, 0 decimals Returned Share 2025 [Returned Orders 2025] / [Orders 2025] Percentage, 1 decimal To set a format: in the Data pane, right-click the field and choose Default Properties → Number Format... . For a number with no decimals, choose Number (Custom) , set Decimal places to 0 and tick Include thousands separators . In plain words: Sales 2025 keeps the Sales of order lines placed in 2025, then adds them up. Orders 2025 counts each 2025 order once. Lines from other years give a blank, and COUNTD ignores blanks. Returned Share 2025 is a ratio of counts : orders on the returns list divided by all orders, both for 2025. It is not an average of anything. Call it the share on the returns list Returned Share 2025 is the share of orders on the returns list , not a "return rate". The list says nothing about how many items came back or what was refunded. Save your workbook ( File → Save ).

docs.text: Before you start, sketch the page on paper: headline, a row of four tiles, the trend across the full width, the region chart, and the scope note at the bottom. Choose Dashboard → New Dashboard . Name the tab Decision dashboard . In the Dashboard pane on the left, under Size , choose Fixed size and Generic Desktop (or another fixed size your facilitator gives). Do this first . Under Objects , check that Tiled is selected at the bottom. Drag a Horizontal object from Objects to the top of the page. This container holds the tiles. Drag the four tile sheets, one by one, into the horizontal container. Watch for the grey shaded area: it shows where the sheet will land. Order: Sales, Orders, Profit Ratio, Returns. Click the container's edge to select it. Open its drop-down menu (the small arrow at the top right) and choose Distribute Contents Evenly . Drag Trend below the tiles, across the full width. Drag Returns by region below the trend. Drag a Text object to the bottom of the page and write the scope note: Scope: Superstore orders placed in 2024 and 2025 (fictitious sample published by Tableau). Sales in the file's own monetary units. Profit ratio = Profit ÷ Sales. Returns list = which orders appear on it; no dates, amounts or reasons. Click a region to filter the tiles and trend; click it again to clear. Patterns describe what happened, not why. Choose Dashboard → Show Title . Leave the default title for now; you write the headline in C4. Remove what you do not need Tableau adds legends to the dashboard automatically, for example the YEAR(Order Date) colour legend. The trend already labels its lines, and the region chart labels its bars, so you can remove these legends: select one and click the x at its top right. Sheet moved to the wrong place? Press Ctrl + Z (Windows) or Cmd + Z (Mac) to undo, and drag again. The Layout pane, next to the Dashboard pane, shows the tree of containers and lets you select an object that is hard to click. Save your workbook.

docs.text: A colleague built this dashboard for a regional review and asks for your feedback. It has at least eight problems from this course. Read the description carefully. Title: Dashboard # Component What it shows and how 1 Six KPI tiles across the top Sales, Profit, Quantity, SUM(Discount) , Orders , and Avg returns share . Each tile is a red or green box with one number and no label for the period. The Orders tile uses the Orders (Count) field 2 Avg returns share tile Calculated with WINDOW_AVG over the four region shares 3 Sales by region bar chart Four bars, each a different bright colour. The value axis starts well above zero ( Include zero is unticked), so the smallest region's bar is a stub 4 Sales trend line chart Only December 2024 to February 2025, filtered by hand. Orange line. Title: Sales are falling fast 5 Region filter control On the right edge. Apply to Worksheets is set to Only This Worksheet , on the trend sheet 6 Sales by sub-category pie chart One slice for each sub-category, each in its own colour, with a legend 7 Profit by state map Coloured from red (loss) to green (profit) 8 Ship days table Every order with its ship mode and ship days, scrolling 9 A floating colour legend Placed over the top right of the trend chart — Scope note None. No units anywhere on the page — Size Automatic For each problem, write one row in your log: Problem Which rule or check it breaks Your fix Then answer: What would the leadership team wrongly believe from the trend panel and its title? What would a fair comparison be? Hint: the Session 7 and T2 growth labs. Which two tiles are wrong as measures, not only as design? What should each one use instead? A reader picks West in the Region filter. Which views change and which do not? What would they wrongly conclude? Sketch your redesign: one headline, at most five views, and where each sits. Which components did you remove completely?

docs.text: Use your own Decision dashboard workbook to show that two of the problems change the numbers, not only the look. Problem A: the average of shares. Duplicate Returns by region and name the copy Average of shares . Create a calculated field named Avg of Region Shares : WINDOW_AVG([Returned Share 2025]) In plain words: the simple average of the share bars in the view, each region counting the same. Drag Avg of Region Shares onto Label . Right-click it and choose Compute Using → Region . Compare the label with the Returned Share 2025 tile with no region selected. Which is larger? Use the Orders 2025 values from C3 Part B to explain why, in two sentences: which regions have the most orders, and what weight does the simple average give them? Problem B: a filter that applies to one sheet. Go to the Trend sheet. Drag Region to the Filters shelf, keep all regions, and click OK . Right-click the pill and choose Show Filter . On the dashboard, click the Trend sheet, open its drop-down menu and choose Filters → Region to add the filter control to the page. Pick one region in the control. Which views change? Write down what the tiles say and what the trend says. Do they describe the same selection? Open the filter control's drop-down menu and choose Apply to Worksheets → Selected Worksheets... . Tick the tiles and Trend . Pick the region again. Now which views change? Remove the filter control and the Region pill from the Filters shelf, so your submitted dashboard uses only the filter action. Optional, Problem C: the truncated axis. On a duplicate of the trend or region chart, right-click the value axis, choose Edit Axis... and untick Include zero . Write one sentence on how the picture changes. Then delete the duplicate.

docs.text: T3 lecture: Dashboards ¶ Learn to put several sheets on one page that a busy manager can read in a minute. A good dashboard answers one question, is read in a set order, lets the reader filter without breaking the numbers, and still makes sense without colour. In the Session 14 lecture you built a decision dashboard in Python: KPI tiles, a monthly trend, two ranked comparisons and a scope note. Today you learn how Tableau builds the same kind of page. The design rules do not change; only the tools do. In the T3 lab you rebuild the Session 14 dashboard in Tableau, using the fields you made in T1 and T2. The Stretch task builds a second dashboard on the marketing case from Session 12 . What you will be able to explain ¶ The difference between a sheet and a dashboard , and why a dashboard has one message . How readers scan a page, and how to use that reading order in a layout. What a good KPI tile shows, and how to build one in Tableau. The difference between a filter , a filter action and a highlight action , and which views each one changes. How to use colour with purpose and make a dashboard readable for people with colour-vision deficiency: never colour alone . How to write message titles , annotations and a scope note in Tableau. Why you check a dashboard's size and its phone layout before you share it. Part 1: From sheets to a dashboard ¶ In T1 and T2 every chart lived on its own sheet (worksheet). A dashboard is a separate tab that places several sheets on one page, together with text, images and filter controls. Sheet Dashboard What it holds One chart or table Several sheets, plus text, filters and legends Where you build it Shelves and the Marks card The Dashboard pane: drag sheets onto the page How you create it Worksheet → New Worksheet Dashboard → New Dashboard Where you edit a chart On the sheet On the sheet. The dashboard shows the sheet; it does not copy it Edit the sheet, not the dashboard A dashboard shows live sheets. If you change a sheet (its colour, its title, a filter on it), the dashboard changes too. To change a chart, go back to its sheet tab. One message per dashboard ¶ A dashboard is explanatory , not exploratory ( Session 14, Part 1 ). Before you open a new dashboard, write down three things: Who will read it, and what they already know. What decision they face. Your big idea : one sentence with a point of view and what is at stake ( Storytelling with data ). Every view on the page must help with that one message. If a chart does not, it belongs in your workbook, not on the dashboard. Session 14 gave a rule of thumb: three to five views , with the KPI tiles counting as one. Sketch it on paper first Draw boxes on paper for the tiles, the charts and the scope note before you open Tableau. Moving a box on paper takes a second. Moving a sheet on a dashboard takes much longer. Part 2: Layout and reading order ¶ Readers of a page in English start at the top left , move right, then down. They spend most attention on the top of the page and less on each step down. So a decision dashboard uses this order: Position What goes there Why Top , as the dashboard title The headline : your big idea as a message title Read first. If the reader stops here, they still have the message Top row KPI tiles : three to five headline numbers, each with a comparison Answers "how are we doing?" before any chart Middle, full width The main view , usually the trend The widest space for the view that needs it Bottom row Supporting comparisons, for example by segment or region Detail for the reader who wants it Bottom edge The scope note Period, units, source, filters and the main limit: small, but always on the page This is the layout of the Session 14 decision dashboard. You rebuild it in the lab. Tiled and floating objects ¶ When you drag a sheet onto a dashboard, it is either tiled or floating . You choose at the bottom of the Objects section in the Dashboard pane. Tiled Floating How it sits In a grid. Objects never overlap; Tableau resizes the neighbours On top of the page, at a position and size you set Use it for Almost everything Small items, such as a legend placed over an empty corner of a chart Risk Few Objects can cover each other, especially on a smaller screen Use tiled objects for this course. Containers ¶ A container is a box that holds other objects and arranges them in one line. A Horizontal container places its objects side by side. Use it for a row of KPI tiles, or for two comparison charts. A Vertical container stacks its objects. A whole dashboard can be one vertical container holding the rows of your sketch. You find both under Objects in the Dashboard pane. To share space equally, select the container (click its grey top edge, or choose it in the Layout pane) and choose Distribute Contents Evenly from its drop-down menu. Size ¶ Tableau can draw a dashboard at a fixed size or let it stretch to the screen ( Automatic ). You set this under Size in the Dashboard pane. Size setting What happens When to use Fixed size , for example Generic Desktop The page always has the same width and height When you export a PDF or image, or share with others. What you see is what they see Automatic The page fits whatever window opens it For your own use. Text and charts can be squeezed on a small screen Set the size before you arrange anything If you change the size after laying out the page, Tableau moves and resizes every object. Choose Fixed size first, then build. Part 3: KPI tiles ¶ A KPI tile (also called a big number) is a small sheet that shows one headline number. A good tile has four parts: Part Example Label : what is measured, and for which period Sales, 2025 Value , large the number, rounded for reading Comparison , so the reader knows if it is good +x% vs 2024 , or target y Unit , on the tile or in the scope note file's own monetary units A number without a comparison cannot be judged. Is a profit ratio of 10% good? Only a comparison (last year, another region, a target) tells you. Building a tile in Tableau ¶ A tile is a sheet with one mark and only text: Create a sheet and drag the measure onto Text on the Marks card. The view shows one number. Drag the comparison measure onto Text as well. Both pills now sit on the Marks card. Click Text on the Marks card, then the ... button, to edit the text. Write the label on the first line, the value on the second and the comparison on the third. Make the value larger. Hide the sheet title or turn it into the label. The tile uses the same rules as any KPI from T2: Ratios are ratios of sums , for example SUM([Profit]) / SUM([Sales]) , never the average of ratios. Order counts use Distinct Orders , never the row count. Growth compares whole years , so the season cancels out ( Session 7 lecture ). A value for one year ¶ A tile for 2025 with a comparison to 2024 needs both years in the same sheet. A filter to 2025 would remove 2024. Instead, put the year inside the calculation: Sales 2025 = SUM(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 THEN [Sales] END) Read it as: for each order line, keep Sales if the order was placed in 2025, otherwise leave it blank; then add up . The IF works row by row; the SUM around it makes the whole field an aggregate. You met both kinds in T2, Part 1 . With a matching Sales 2024 field, the growth is: Sales Growth = [Sales 2025] / [Sales 2024] - 1 Tiles must reconcile A tile is still a number you can check. Sales 2025 on the tile must equal the 2025 Sales of your trend chart added up, and the 2025 Sales of the regions added up. You do these checks in the lab. Part 4: Filters and actions ¶ A dashboard is interactive: the reader can narrow it down. Tableau offers several ways, and they differ in which views change and what happens to the other marks . Tool How the reader uses it What it does Where you set it up Filter (a filter control) Picks values in a list or drop-down on the page Removes the other values from the views it applies to On a sheet: right-click a pill on the Filters shelf → Show Filter Filter action Clicks a mark in one view, for example a region bar Removes the other values from the target views Dashboard → Actions... → Add Action → Filter... Highlight action Clicks a mark Keeps every mark, but dims the marks that do not match Dashboard → Actions... → Add Action → Highlight... , or the highlighter on a colour legend Filters: which sheets do they apply to? ¶ A filter you add on one sheet applies only to that sheet at first. On a dashboard, the other views ignore it. So the trend may change while the tiles do not, and the page tells two different stories. To make one filter control change several views, click the filter control's drop-down menu on the dashboard and choose Apply to Worksheets : Option Applies to Only This Worksheet One sheet (the default) Selected Worksheets... The sheets you tick All Using Related Data Sources / All Using This Data Source Every sheet that uses the same data Write the filter on the page A reader who prints the dashboard does not see which region was selected. If a view is filtered, say so in its title or in the scope note. Filter actions: click to filter ¶ A filter action turns a chart into a filter. The reader clicks the West bar, and the KPI tiles and the trend show West only. Click the bar again (or press Esc ) and everything comes back. When you add a filter action, Tableau asks: Setting Meaning Usual choice Source Sheets The view the reader clicks The comparison chart, for example the region bars Run action on Hover , Select (click) or Menu Select Target Sheets The views that change The tiles and the trend. Usually not the source itself, so the reader still sees all regions to click Clearing the selection will What happens when the reader clicks the mark again Show all values There is also a shortcut. On a dashboard, select a sheet and click its Use as Filter icon (a funnel) at the top right of the sheet. Tableau creates a filter action from that sheet to every other sheet on the dashboard. Open Dashboard → Actions... afterwards to see and edit it. A filter action is a dimension filter In the filter order from T1, Part 6 , a filter action works like a dimension filter . So everything you learned in T2 still applies. Table calculations such as LOOKUP see only the marks left after the filter: filtering on Region is safe for a monthly growth chart, but filtering on months breaks it ( T2, Part 5 ). A FIXED expression such as Order Total ignores the action, because FIXED is calculated before dimension filters. Highlight actions: keep the context ¶ A highlight action dims the marks that do not match the reader's click, but keeps them on the page. Use it when the other marks are useful context: On a chart with one bar per channel in two views, clicking a channel in one view highlights the same channel in the other. On a line chart with one line per year, clicking the legend's 2025 dims the other years. Use a filter (or filter action) when... Use a highlight when... The reader wants the numbers for one group only, for example the tiles for one region The reader wants to see one group against the others Totals and tiles must change Totals and tiles must stay the same Part 5: Colour and accessibility ¶ Designing clear visuals and Session 14, Part 5 gave the rules. Here is how they look in Tableau. Colour with a purpose ¶ Grey for context, one colour for attention. Session 14 used grey for comparison values, blue for the current period and orange for the one thing that needs attention. In Tableau, click Color on the Marks card and choose Edit Colors... to set each value's colour by hand. One meaning per colour, across the whole page. If 2025 is blue in the trend, it must be blue on every sheet. If orange means "needs attention", nothing else is orange. Do not colour by a field just because you can. A bar chart of four regions does not need four colours: the bar labels already tell the regions apart. Colour-blind-safe palettes ¶ About one in twelve men has some colour-vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green . Tableau has a palette designed for this: Click Color on the Marks card and choose Edit Colors... . Open the Select Color Palette list and choose Color Blind . Click Assign Palette , then OK . Blue and orange, the pair used in Session 14, stay easy to tell apart for most readers. Red against green, the default "bad against good" pair, does not. Never colour alone ¶ Colour should repeat a message, not carry it alone. Every highlighted mark also needs at least one of these: Instead of only colour Add An orange bar Its value as a label, and a message title that names it A blue line for 2025 and a grey line for 2024 The year written at the end of each line A red or green tile A sign (+ or -) and the words vs 2024 Test it: print the dashboard in black and white, or look at it through your phone's greyscale mode. Can you still find the bar your title is about? Text you can read Keep text at a size you can still read when the page is shown at half size. Grey text on a white background must be dark enough to read: Tableau's lightest greys are for gridlines, not for words. Part 6: Message titles, annotations and the scope note ¶ Message titles ¶ A message title says what the reader should notice; a descriptive title only says what is plotted ( Session 14, Part 2 ). In Tableau: Sheet title: double-click the title on the sheet and type. The Insert menu in the edit window can add a field value, such as the selected region, to the title. Dashboard title: choose Dashboard → Show Title , then double-click the title to edit it. This is where your headline goes. A title must stay true A message title is written for the data you see now. When a reader clicks a region, the trend shows that region only, but a title such as " Sales rose in every month " may no longer be true. Write titles that hold for every selection, or say in the title which selection it describes, and check by clicking every region yourself. Annotations ¶ An annotation is a short note placed on the chart, next to the mark it explains. It is read at the right moment, unlike a paragraph under the chart. On a sheet, right-click a mark and choose Annotate . Choose Mark (a note tied to one mark), Point (a position on the chart) or Area (a region of the chart). Type a short note, for example "Same month last year was the year's low." Keep annotations to one or two per view. The scope note ¶ On the dashboard, drag a Text object from Objects to the bottom of the page. Write: the period (orders placed 2023 to 2025, or the years shown), the units (the file's own monetary units, or the case's currency units), the source (Superstore, a fictitious sample published by Tableau), any filters or actions the reader should know about, the main limit (for example, the returns list shows which orders are listed, not why or for how much). Part 7: Size, phone layout and export ¶ A dashboard is often opened on a phone. Tableau lets you design a separate phone layout of the same dashboard. At the top of the Dashboard pane, click Device Preview . Choose Phone as the device type. Click Add Phone Layout . Tableau creates a layout that stacks the views in one column. In the phone layout, remove or reorder views. On a phone, keep the headline, the tiles and the one most important chart. Click Default (at the top of the Dashboard pane) to return to the desktop layout. The phone layout shows the same sheets, so a change to a sheet changes both layouts. Exporting for others ¶ When you send a dashboard as a file, the reader cannot click it. So the PDF or image must stand on its own: headline, tiles, titles and the scope note must say everything. File → Print to PDF... saves the dashboard as a PDF. Choose Active Sheet when the dashboard is the open tab. Dashboard → Export Image... saves a picture of the page. Clear any selection before you export, unless the export is meant to show one region; then say so in the title. Quiz ¶ Answer these at the start of the T3 lab. Your facilitator will go through the answers. Readers scan a dashboard from the top left. Where do you place the headline, the KPI tiles, the main trend and the scope note, and why? A KPI tile shows only "Sales: 1.2 million" . Name two things it is missing, and explain why each matters. You add a Region filter control on the trend sheet. On the dashboard, the trend changes when you pick a region, but the KPI tiles do not. Why, and how do you fix it? What is the difference between a filter action and a highlight action ? Give one situation where each is the better choice. A dashboard colours tiles red for "below target" and green for "above target", with no other sign. Name two problems and two fixes. Your dashboard title names the region with the highest share of orders on the returns list. A reader clicks a different region's bar, which filters the tiles and the trend. Which parts of the page can still be trusted, and what would you change so the title stays true?

docs.text: A tile for 2025 with a comparison to 2024 needs both years in the same sheet. A filter to 2025 would remove 2024. Instead, put the year inside the calculation: Sales 2025 = SUM(IF YEAR([Order Date]) = 2025 THEN [Sales] END) Read it as: for each order line, keep Sales if the order was placed in 2025, otherwise leave it blank; then add up . The IF works row by row; the SUM around it makes the whole field an aggregate. You met both kinds in T2, Part 1 . With a matching Sales 2024 field, the growth is: Sales Growth = [Sales 2025] / [Sales 2024] - 1 Tiles must reconcile A tile is still a number you can check. Sales 2025 on the tile must equal the 2025 Sales of your trend chart added up, and the 2025 Sales of the regions added up. You do these checks in the lab.
docs.title: A value for one year

docs.text: A dashboard is interactive: the reader can narrow it down. Tableau offers several ways, and they differ in which views change and what happens to the other marks . Tool How the reader uses it What it does Where you set it up Filter (a filter control) Picks values in a list or drop-down on the page Removes the other values from the views it applies to On a sheet: right-click a pill on the Filters shelf → Show Filter Filter action Clicks a mark in one view, for example a region bar Removes the other values from the target views Dashboard → Actions... → Add Action → Filter... Highlight action Clicks a mark Keeps every mark, but dims the marks that do not match Dashboard → Actions... → Add Action → Highlight... , or the highlighter on a colour legend
docs.title: Part 4: Filters and actions

docs.text: A filter you add on one sheet applies only to that sheet at first. On a dashboard, the other views ignore it. So the trend may change while the tiles do not, and the page tells two different stories. To make one filter control change several views, click the filter control's drop-down menu on the dashboard and choose Apply to Worksheets : Option Applies to Only This Worksheet One sheet (the default) Selected Worksheets... The sheets you tick All Using Related Data Sources / All Using This Data Source Every sheet that uses the same data Write the filter on the page A reader who prints the dashboard does not see which region was selected. If a view is filtered, say so in its title or in the scope note.
docs.title: Filters: which sheets do they apply to?

docs.text: A filter action turns a chart into a filter. The reader clicks the West bar, and the KPI tiles and the trend show West only. Click the bar again (or press Esc ) and everything comes back. When you add a filter action, Tableau asks: Setting Meaning Usual choice Source Sheets The view the reader clicks The comparison chart, for example the region bars Run action on Hover , Select (click) or Menu Select Target Sheets The views that change The tiles and the trend. Usually not the source itself, so the reader still sees all regions to click Clearing the selection will What happens when the reader clicks the mark again Show all values There is also a shortcut. On a dashboard, select a sheet and click its Use as Filter icon (a funnel) at the top right of the sheet. Tableau creates a filter action from that sheet to every other sheet on the dashboard. Open Dashboard → Actions... afterwards to see and edit it. A filter action is a dimension filter In the filter order from T1, Part 6 , a filter action works like a dimension filter . So everything you learned in T2 still applies. Table calculations such as LOOKUP see only the marks left after the filter: filtering on Region is safe for a monthly growth chart, but filtering on months breaks it ( T2, Part 5 ). A FIXED expression such as Order Total ignores the action, because FIXED is calculated before dimension filters.
docs.title: Filter actions: click to filter

docs.text: A highlight action dims the marks that do not match the reader's click, but keeps them on the page. Use it when the other marks are useful context: On a chart with one bar per channel in two views, clicking a channel in one view highlights the same channel in the other. On a line chart with one line per year, clicking the legend's 2025 dims the other years. Use a filter (or filter action) when... Use a highlight when... The reader wants the numbers for one group only, for example the tiles for one region The reader wants to see one group against the others Totals and tiles must change Totals and tiles must stay the same
docs.title: Highlight actions: keep the context

docs.text: Designing clear visuals and Session 14, Part 5 gave the rules. Here is how they look in Tableau.
docs.title: Part 5: Colour and accessibility

docs.text: Grey for context, one colour for attention. Session 14 used grey for comparison values, blue for the current period and orange for the one thing that needs attention. In Tableau, click Color on the Marks card and choose Edit Colors... to set each value's colour by hand. One meaning per colour, across the whole page. If 2025 is blue in the trend, it must be blue on every sheet. If orange means "needs attention", nothing else is orange. Do not colour by a field just because you can. A bar chart of four regions does not need four colours: the bar labels already tell the regions apart.
docs.title: Colour with a purpose

docs.text: About one in twelve men has some colour-vision deficiency, most often difficulty telling red from green . Tableau has a palette designed for this: Click Color on the Marks card and choose Edit Colors... . Open the Select Color Palette list and choose Color Blind . Click Assign Palette , then OK . Blue and orange, the pair used in Session 14, stay easy to tell apart for most readers. Red against green, the default "bad against good" pair, does not.
docs.title: Colour-blind-safe palettes

docs.text: Colour should repeat a message, not carry it alone. Every highlighted mark also needs at least one of these: Instead of only colour Add An orange bar Its value as a label, and a message title that names it A blue line for 2025 and a grey line for 2024 The year written at the end of each line A red or green tile A sign (+ or -) and the words vs 2024 Test it: print the dashboard in black and white, or look at it through your phone's greyscale mode. Can you still find the bar your title is about? Text you can read Keep text at a size you can still read when the page is shown at half size. Grey text on a white background must be dark enough to read: Tableau's lightest greys are for gridlines, not for words.
docs.title: Never colour alone
Part 6: Message titles, annotations and the scope note

docs.text: A message title says what the reader should notice; a descriptive title only says what is plotted ( Session 14, Part 2 ). In Tableau: Sheet title: double-click the title on the sheet and type. The Insert menu in the edit window can add a field value, such as the selected region, to the title. Dashboard title: choose Dashboard → Show Title , then double-click the title to edit it. This is where your headline goes. A title must stay true A message title is written for the data you see now. When a reader clicks a region, the trend shows that region only, but a title such as " Sales rose in every month " may no longer be true. Write titles that hold for every selection, or say in the title which selection it describes, and check by clicking every region yourself.
docs.title: Message titles

docs.text: An annotation is a short note placed on the chart, next to the mark it explains. It is read at the right moment, unlike a paragraph under the chart. On a sheet, right-click a mark and choose Annotate . Choose Mark (a note tied to one mark), Point (a position on the chart) or Area (a region of the chart). Type a short note, for example "Same month last year was the year's low." Keep annotations to one or two per view.
docs.title: Annotations

docs.text: On the dashboard, drag a Text object from Objects to the bottom of the page. Write: the period (orders placed 2023 to 2025, or the years shown), the units (the file's own monetary units, or the case's currency units), the source (Superstore, a fictitious sample published by Tableau), any filters or actions the reader should know about, the main limit (for example, the returns list shows which orders are listed, not why or for how much).
docs.title: The scope note

docs.text: A dashboard is often opened on a phone. Tableau lets you design a separate phone layout of the same dashboard. At the top of the Dashboard pane, click Device Preview . Choose Phone as the device type. Click Add Phone Layout . Tableau creates a layout that stacks the views in one column. In the phone layout, remove or reorder views. On a phone, keep the headline, the tiles and the one most important chart. Click Default (at the top of the Dashboard pane) to return to the desktop layout. The phone layout shows the same sheets, so a change to a sheet changes both layouts.
docs.title: Part 7: Size, phone layout and export

docs.text: When you send a dashboard as a file, the reader cannot click it. So the PDF or image must stand on its own: headline, tiles, titles and the scope note must say everything. File → Print to PDF... saves the dashboard as a PDF. Choose Active Sheet when the dashboard is the open tab. Dashboard → Export Image... saves a picture of the page. Clear any selection before you export, unless the export is meant to show one region; then say so in the title.
docs.title: Exporting for others

docs.text: Answer these at the start of the T3 lab. Your facilitator will go through the answers. Readers scan a dashboard from the top left. Where do you place the headline, the KPI tiles, the main trend and the scope note, and why? A KPI tile shows only "Sales: 1.2 million" . Name two things it is missing, and explain why each matters. You add a Region filter control on the trend sheet. On the dashboard, the trend changes when you pick a region, but the KPI tiles do not. Why, and how do you fix it? What is the difference between a filter action and a highlight action ? Give one situation where each is the better choice. A dashboard colours tiles red for "below target" and green for "above target", with no other sign. Name two problems and two fixes. Your dashboard title names the region with the highest share of orders on the returns list. A reader clicks a different region's bar, which filters the tiles and the trend. Which parts of the page can still be trusted, and what would you change so the title stays true?
docs.title: Quiz

docs.text: T4 lab: A portfolio piece from your capstone ¶ Turn the strongest finding of your capstone into a portfolio piece: one Tableau dashboard and a three-point story that a stranger can follow in a minute. Save it on your own computer with a clear version history, check that everyone can read it, and, only if you choose to and only with safe data, publish it to Tableau Public. This lab builds on your capstone from the Session 15 lab and your briefing from the Session 16 lab . You already have the decision, the evidence register, the checks and the recommendation. Today you show one part of that argument in Tableau. If you get stuck on a finding, look back at how you computed it in Python. Desktop and web editor The click paths on this page are written for Tableau Desktop Public Edition . If you use the Tableau Public web editor in a browser, the menus differ slightly. Look for the same command in a nearby menu, or ask your facilitator. In the web editor, saving publishes : read the warning in the Setup section before you save anything there. The business decision ¶ Your capstone was written for the chief operating officer of the teaching frame. A portfolio piece has a different reader: Hiring manager: "Show me one piece of analysis you are proud of. I have a minute. Tell me what question you answered, what the data showed, what it could not show, and what you recommended." The decision is which one finding from your capstone best shows your work, and how to tell it so that a reader who has never seen this course understands it, trusts it, and knows its limits. About the data: five separate contexts Superstore is a sample published by Tableau about a fictitious company, with Sales and Profit in the file's own monetary units . The marketing-v1 , finance-v1 , operations-v1 and hr-v1 files are synthetic data generated separately by the course for fictional organisations, with amounts in neutral currency units . They share no customers, orders, employees or keys. Never join, relate or blend two of them, and never explain one with another ( Session 15, Part 5 ). How this lab works ¶ Part What you do Tasks Setup Choose your finding and its data, start a versioned workbook Setup Core Plan the piece in four sentences; build one dashboard; build a three-point story; save and export C1–C4 Stretch Keep a version log; check the piece for accessibility S1–S2 Challenge Decide what is safe to publish; optionally publish to Tableau Public after the privacy checklist X1–X2 Each task has a level: Core : everyone completes it; it is enough for your portfolio. Stretch : for when you finish the core tasks early. Challenge : optional, harder reasoning. Publishing is never required. What you will be able to do ¶ Choose one capstone finding and write it as question, evidence, limitation, action . Build a one-message dashboard on your capstone data, with each dataset on its own data source. Build a three-point Tableau story with a headline and a caption on each point. Save versions of a .twbx with dated names and a change log. Check a portfolio piece for accessibility. Decide whether a workbook is safe to publish, using the privacy checklist. Evidence you keep: your four-sentence plan, your saved workbook, the PDF of your dashboard and story, and any Stretch and Challenge notes. Before you start, work through the T4 lecture . Have your capstone outline, evidence register and Session 16 brief to hand, and your T3 workbook for reference. Setup: choose your finding and start the workbook ¶ Step 1: Choose one finding ¶ Open your capstone evidence register from the Session 15 lab (G2–G3). Pick the one finding that carries your recommendation. It should come from one dataset. Write in your log: the finding, its dataset, its metric, grain and period, and the check you ran in Python. You use the check again in C2. Which dataset should I choose? Any of the five datasets is fine for the Core tasks, because you keep the work on your own computer. If you think you may do the publishing Challenge (X2), choose a finding from one of the synthetic datasets now: Superstore must not be published in this course. Step 2: Download the data ¶ Download only the file or files your finding needs. Dataset Where to get it File to use Superstore Tableau's sample-data page, as in the Tableau overview sample_-_superstore.xls (you already have it) marketing-v1 marketing-v1 folder marketing_daily.csv finance-v1 finance-v1 folder finance_actuals.csv , finance_budget.csv operations-v1 operations-v1 folder shipments.csv hr-v1 hr-v1 folder employees.csv , department_history.csv , recruitment.csv For a synthetic dataset: Open its folder on GitHub and read README.md first: the grain, the units and the rules for each measure. Click the CSV file, then click the Download raw file button at the top right of the file view, as in the T3 lab, S1 Step 1 . Save it in your course data folder without renaming it. Step 3: Start a versioned workbook ¶ Open Tableau Desktop Public Edition . Connect to your file: Microsoft Excel for Superstore (then follow Set up the Superstore data source ), or Text file for a synthetic CSV. Check the field types in the preview: every date must show a calendar icon. Choose File → Save As , pick **Tableau Packaged Workbook (*.twbx)**, and name the file with today's date and a version number: T4_portfolio_YourName_YYYY-MM-DD_v01.twbx For example T4_portfolio_AnitaShrestha_2026-11-20_v01.twbx . If you use the web editor In the Tableau Public web editor, saving puts your workbook and its data on your public profile. If your finding uses Superstore , ask your facilitator before you start: you may need to work in Tableau Desktop Public Edition, or with a synthetic dataset, so that nothing is saved to Tableau Public. One dataset per data source If your piece uses two datasets, add the second as a separate data source ( Data → New Data Source ). Do not drag it onto the first data source's canvas: that creates a relationship, which is a false join between two fictional organisations. Core tasks ¶ C1 (Core): Plan the piece in four sentences ¶ Before you open a sheet, write four sentences in your log. Use the T4 lecture, Part 5 and your Session 16 brief. Part Your sentence Question What decision, for whom? Evidence What the data shows, with a comparison, period and unit (no number yet: you fill it in from Tableau in C2) Limitation What the data cannot show; that the data is synthetic or a fictitious sample Action What should happen, who owns it, what to monitor Then sketch the dashboard on paper, as in the T3 lab, C2 : headline, tiles, the main view, at most one supporting view, and the scope note. C2 (Core): Build the dashboard ¶ Build the sheets first, then the dashboard. Reuse the methods from T1 to T3. Create the measures your finding needs as calculated fields. Rates are ratios of sums , never averages of rates ( T2 lecture, Part 2 ). Counts of orders, shipments or employees use COUNTD on the right ID. Build two or three KPI tiles with a period label and a comparison ( T3 lab, C1 Part A ). Build the main view that shows your evidence, for example a monthly trend or a ranked bar chart. Use grey for context and one highlight colour for the thing your message is about. Reconcile. Compare each tile with the value in your Python evidence register. They must agree, apart from rounding. If they do not, find out why before you go on, and write the reason in your log. Choose Dashboard → New Dashboard , name it Portfolio dashboard , and set Size → Fixed size first. Lay out the page in reading order: tiles at the top, the main view in the middle, the scope note at the bottom. Write a so-what headline ( Dashboard → Show Title , then double-click the title) and message titles on each view. Each must stay true for every selection a reader can make. Add a Text object at the bottom with the scope note : dataset and version (for example operations-v1, synthetic data for a fictional retailer ), period, units, definitions of your measures, and the main limitation. Fewer views, stronger message A portfolio dashboard has one message. If a view does not help a stranger understand your finding, leave it in the workbook and off the page. Save your workbook ( File → Save ). C3 (Core): Build a three-point story ¶ Choose Story → New Story . Name the tab Portfolio story . Double-click the story title and write your headline : the same big idea as the dashboard. Build three story points, each with a one-sentence caption: Point What it shows Caption 1. Question and evidence Your Portfolio dashboard The question, and the finding with its number in context 2. A closer look The main view, or a second view that tests the finding (for example the same measure by month, or one group against the rest) What the closer look confirms, or where the finding is weaker 3. Limitation and action The view that best supports the recommendation What the data cannot show, then the action, owner and monitoring measure To add a point, click Blank under New story point in the Story pane, then drag a sheet or dashboard onto the story. Use Duplicate to keep the same view with a different selection; click Update to keep a change in the current point. Click through the three points in order. Read only the captions: do they tell the whole argument? Check every point after a click In a story, readers can still click and filter. Click a mark in each point, then check that the caption and titles are still true. Save your workbook. C4 (Core): Save a version and export ¶ Choose File → Save As and save a new version: T4_portfolio_YourName_YYYY-MM-DD_v02.twbx . Keep v01. Open the Portfolio dashboard tab, clear any selection, and choose File → Print to PDF... . Under Range , choose Active Sheet . Save as T4_portfolio_YourName_dashboard.pdf . Open the Portfolio story tab and do the same: T4_portfolio_YourName_story.pdf . Open both PDFs. Check that the headline, titles, captions and scope note are readable, and that all three story points appear. If the story PDF shows only one point, click each point in turn and export it on its own. Stretch tasks ¶ S1 (Stretch): A version log ¶ Keep a change log in your evidence log, as in the T4 lecture, Part 3 : Version Date What changed Why Checked v01 v02 Fill in v01 and v02 from today's work. Ask a classmate to read your PDFs for one minute, then tell you the question, the finding and the action in their own words. Make the change their answer shows you need (often the headline or one caption). Save it as v03 with File → Save As , and add the row to the log. The Checked column must say what you verified after the change. S2 (Stretch): An accessibility check ¶ Go through your dashboard and story with this list. Write yes , no or fixed next to each line in your log. The headline and captions alone tell the argument. Nothing is shown only by colour: the highlighted mark also has a label, a value or a title that names it. No red–green pair is the only difference between two things. Text is large enough to read when the page is shown at half size; grey text is dark enough to read. Axes start at zero for bars. Every number has its unit, period and comparison. Tooltips are written in plain words, not raw field names such as AGG(ROAS) . (Click Tooltip on the Marks card to edit them.) The scope note says the data is synthetic or a fictitious sample, and gives its source. View the dashboard PDF in greyscale. Can you still find the mark your headline is about? Challenge tasks ¶ X1 (Challenge): Safe to publish? ¶ For each case, write publish , do not publish or publish only after a change , and one sentence why. Use the T4 lecture, Part 2 . Your T3 marketing dashboard on marketing-v1, with a scope note that says synthetic data . Your T3 decision dashboard on Superstore. A dashboard of your employer's monthly sales by branch, with branch names replaced by letters. A dashboard on hr-v1 whose scope note calls it "Our company's staff turnover" . A workbook on operations-v1 that also contains, on a hidden sheet, a second data source with Superstore. A public dataset you found on a website with no licence, about house prices in your city. A dashboard of course survey answers from your classmates, with names removed but with age and home town. X2 (Challenge, optional): Publish to Tableau Public ¶ Only do this if you want a public portfolio link. It is not needed to pass the lab, and nothing you submit on Moodle depends on it. Step 1: Complete the privacy checklist ¶ Synthetic course data may be published only once the course confirms its reuse terms, so ask your facilitator first. Write each line in your log with yes or no . If any line is no , stop: do not publish. Every data source in the workbook is synthetic course data (marketing-v1, finance-v1, operations-v1 or hr-v1). Check the Data pane: every data source listed is published, even if no sheet uses it. No data source holds workplace, customer or employee data, or anything copied from them. Superstore is not in the workbook, not even on an unused or hidden sheet. The scope note says the data is synthetic , describes a fictional organisation, and gives units (currency units) and period. Nothing names a real person, a real company or your employer. I have decided whether to allow downloads, and I know the views stay public either way. I know that hiding the viz does not make it private, and that a downloaded copy cannot be recalled. If your finding uses Superstore Build a second, smaller piece on one synthetic dataset and publish that instead, or do not publish. Keep your Superstore work on your own computer. Step 2: Save a local copy first ¶ Save your workbook locally with File → Save As (a new version number). Publishing does not replace your local file, and your Moodle submission is always the local .twbx . Step 3: Publish ¶ Choose File → Save to Tableau Public As… . Sign in with your Tableau Public account. Enter a clear, descriptive title, for example "Peak-season delivery reliability (synthetic data)" , and click Save . Tableau creates an extract of your data and opens the viz on the Tableau Public website. Step 4: Check what a stranger sees ¶ On the viz page, open the viz settings . Decide whether to allow others to download the workbook and its data, and set the option. (Tableau's FAQ describes this option in the viz settings; the exact label may differ.) Click Edit Details and write a short description: the question, that the data is synthetic and generated by a course for a fictional organisation, and the link to the dataset's folder on GitHub. Copy the viz's URL. Open a private browser window (not signed in) and paste it. This is what a stranger sees. Check the download button and every tooltip. Write the URL in your log. Changed your mind? You can delete the viz from your Tableau Public profile. Deleting removes it from the website, but anyone who has already downloaded it or taken a screenshot keeps their copy. Evidence checklist ¶ Before you submit, check that you have: your four-sentence plan (question, evidence, limitation, action) and your paper sketch your reconciliation of the tiles with your Python evidence register the Portfolio dashboard with headline, message titles and scope note the Portfolio story with three points and a caption on each at least two dated versions of your workbook the dashboard and story PDFs Stretch and Challenge notes, if you did them (version log, accessibility check, X1 answers, the privacy checklist and URL if you published) Submit on Moodle ¶ Save your final version locally ( File → Save As ): for example T4_portfolio_YourName_YYYY-MM-DD_v03_submitted.twbx . Do not change this file after you submit. Export the dashboard and the story as PDFs (C4). Open the T4 lab assignment on the course Moodle page. Upload the .twbx file, the PDF (or PDFs) of your portfolio piece, and your written answers (from your evidence log). If you published in X2, add the URL. Moodle, not Tableau Public Your submission is the local .twbx and the PDF. A Tableau Public link alone is not a submission, and you never need to publish to pass. Next ¶ This is the last Tableau session. Keep your portfolio workbook and its version log with your capstone notebook and brief from Session 15 and Session 16 : together they show the whole path from a business question to a checked recommendation.
